summary: The Abhayapaddhati is an extensive commentary by the late Indian Buddhist master Abhayākaragupta (fl. late 11th–early 12th century) on the Buddhakapālamahātantra, an important scripture of the Yoginītantra class. Written at Vikramaśīla monastery in the 25th regnal year of King Rāmapāla, it interprets esoteric ritual practices, internal alchemy, and completion-stage yoga aimed at realizing Mahāmudrā. This digital file comprises chapters 9 through 14, focusing on post-initiatory conduct (caryā), medicinal-alchemical lore (mahauṣadhi), and higher initiatory yogas.

summary: The Abhidharmadīpa is an orthodox Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika verse treatise dating to roughly the 5th–6th century CE. Composed in close structural and metrical imitation of Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośakārikā, it defends orthodox Vaibhāṣika ontology while polemicizing sharply against Vasubandhu's Sautrāntika positions and Mahāyāna doctrine. This e-text provides an incomplete transcription of the verses (kārikās 1–383, covering chapters 1–5) based on P. S. Jaini's 1959 edition of the unique Sanskrit manuscript recovered from Tibet.

summary: The Abhidharmadīpa along with its prose auto-commentary (Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti) is an important post-Vasubandhu Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika treatise composed around the 5th to 6th century CE. Written by an anonymous author conventionally designated as the Dīpakāra, it parallels the structure of Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya across eight chapters while defending orthodox Kāśmīra Vaibhāṣika positions. The work is noted for its rigorous defense of Vaibhāṣika realism and its polemical critiques directed against Sautrāntika doctrines and Vasubandhu (consistently called the 'Kośakāra').

summary: The Abhidharmakośakārikā consists of approximately six hundred verses in eight chapters composed by Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE), synthesizing the doctrinal system of the Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika school of Abhidharma. The text classifies all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena across eight subjects: ultimate constituents (dhātu), sensory and psychological faculties (indriya), cosmological realms (loka), intentional action (karma), underlying afflictions (anuśaya), noble spiritual paths and attainers (mārgapudgala), transcendent cognitions (jñāna), and meditative absorptions (samāpatti). Designed for memorization, it served as the baseline verse manual upon which Vasubandhu constructed his famous auto-commentary (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya) offering critical Sautrāntika critiques of Vaibhāṣika tenets, and it remains the fundamental Abhidharma textbook throughout East Asian and Tibetan Buddhism.

summary: The Abhidharmasamuccaya is Asaṅga's definitive synthesis of Abhidharma doctrine from a Mahāyāna and Yogācāra perspective. The treatise is structured into two main parts: the Lakṣaṇasamuccaya, which categorizes dharmas across the skandhas, dhātus, āyatanas, and fifty-one mental factors (caittas), and the Viniścayasamuccaya, which analyzes the noble truths, doctrinal exposition, attainment of liberation, and rules of philosophical dialectic. Providing the scholastic foundation of Yogācāra dogmatics, it served as the standard textbook for Abhidharma study in Tibetan and East Asian Buddhism.

attribution_note: Authorship is historically disputed. The unique Sanskrit manuscript does not record an author in its colophon, recording only the patron/scribe (paṇḍita-vaidya-śrī-Amaracandra). The Tibetan Tanjur (D 4053) attributes the Bhāṣya to Jinaputra (rgyal ba'i sras). In Chinese tradition, Kuiji states that an early commentary was composed by Buddhasiṃha, while Sthiramati compiled the composite Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā (T 1606). Tatia's editio princeps ascribed the Bhāṣya to Sthiramati following Pralhad Pradhan, but modern scholars (such as Noriaki Hakamaya and Robert Kritzer) distinguish the Bhāṣya from the Vyākhyā and accept Jinaputra as the traditional author.

summary: The Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya is an essential 6th-century Yogācāra prose commentary on Asaṅga's Abhidharmasamuccaya. It provides extensive analytical glosses on Asaṅga's concise definitions of mental factors, aggregates (skandha), sense bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and the path, harmonizing classical Abhidharma categories with foundational Yogācāra doctrines such as the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna). Preserved in a single palm-leaf manuscript discovered by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana in Tibet and in Tibetan translation, it is traditionally ascribed to Jinaputra.

summary: The Abhidharmāmṛta (or Abhidharmāmṛtarasaśāstra) is an early, systematic manual of Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma attributed to Bhadanta Ghoṣaka, one of the four great venerable masters of the Vaibhāṣika lineage associated with the western/Gandhāran tradition. Organized into sixteen chapters (bindus), it provides a clear exposition of Buddhist scholastic categories, including charity and moral discipline, realms of rebirth, the skandhas, dhātus, and āyatanas, causal conditions, latent defilements, the path of meditation, and unconditioned dharmas. No original Sanskrit manuscripts are extant; this digital text represents Shanti Bhikshu Sastri's 1953 retroversion into Sanskrit based on the 3rd-century CE Chinese translation preserved in the Taishō Canon (T 1553).

summary: Haribhadra's Sphuṭārthā (titled Abhisamayālaṅkārakārikāśāstravivṛti in the surviving Sanskrit manuscript tradition, composed c. late 8th century CE) is a concise running commentary (vṛtti) on the root kārikās of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra attributed to Maitreya. Composed during the reign of King Dharmapāla to complement the author's extensive Abhisamayālaṅkārālokā, it systematically explicates the eight realizations (aṣṭāv abhisamayāḥ) and seventy topics that align the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras with the progressive stages of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path. Following its translation and dissemination by rNgog Blo ldan shes rab, it became the standard foundational textbook for Prajñāpāramitā scholastic curricula across all major Tibetan Buddhist traditions.

summary: The Abhisamayālaṅkārāntaḥpātināṃ padārthānāṃ saṃkṣepato vivaraṇam is a modern Sanskrit scholastic manual written by Prof. Ram Shankar Tripathi as an appendix to his 1977 edition of Haribhadra's Abhisamayālaṅkāravṛtti Sphuṭārthā. Adopting the structure of traditional Tibetan monastic textbooks (don bdun cu), it delineates the eight general subjects (aṣṭau padārthāḥ) and seventy specific topics (saptatiḥ padārthāḥ) of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra. Each topic is systematically analyzed by its formal definition (lakṣaṇa), taxonomic divisions (bheda), and spiritual stage boundary (avadhi / sīmā).

summary: The Abhisamayālaṅkārāloka (full title: Abhisamayālaṅkārālokā Prajñāpāramitāvyākhyā) is Haribhadra's extensive commentary composed in the late 8th century CE under the patronage of the Pāla emperor Dharmapāla. From a Yogācāra-Svātantrika-Madhyamaka philosophical standpoint, it coordinates the 273 verses of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra with the corresponding prose passages of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitāsūtra, demonstrating how the sūtra systematically articulates the eight realizations (abhisamaya) and seventy topics of the Mahāyāna path. As one of only two surviving Indian Sanskrit commentaries on the Aṣṭasāhasrikā (alongside Ratnākaraśānti's Sāratamā), it remains a primary foundation for Prajñāpāramitā exegesis across Indian and Tibetan Buddhist scholasticism.

summary: An anonymous Vajrayāna ritual manual prescribing the procedure for conferring initiation (abhiṣeka) upon disciples entering the maṇḍala. It details preliminary rites—including refuge-taking, bodhicittotpāda, vow-taking (saṃvara), tooth-stick casting (dantakāṣṭhapātana), and protection rites—followed by sequential initiations including the flask, garland (mālā), crown (paṭṭa), vajra, bell (ghaṇṭā), mudrā, secret initiation (guhyābhiṣeka), and wisdom-knowledge initiation (prajñājñānābhiṣeka).

summary: The Adhikaraṇavastu is the sixteenth chapter of the seventeen vastus comprising the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu. It systematically governs legal disputes within the monastic community, classifying conflicts into four types (vivādādhikaraṇa, anuvādādhikaraṇa, āpattādhikaraṇa, and kṛtyādhikaraṇa) and laying out the seven formal procedures (adhikaraṇa-śamatha) for resolving them. Preserved in a single 6th-century CE birch-bark manuscript from Gilgit as well as in the Tibetan Kanjur ('Dul ba, Toh 1-16), it is a vital primary document for the study of classical Buddhist jurisprudence.

summary: The Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 150 Lines'), also widely known as the Prajñāpāramitānaya or Rishukyō, is an esoteric scripture bridging late Prajñāpāramitā doctrine and Yoga Tantra ritualism. Expounded by Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas led by Mahāvairocana and Vajrapāṇi, the sūtra teaches seventeen aphorisms on the innate purity of passion, sensory experience, and phenomenal reality (viśuddhi-pada) through the lens of emptiness. The text occupies a central doctrinal and liturgical role in East Asian esoteric Buddhism (especially Japanese Shingon) and is also preserved across Tibetan canonical collections (Toh 17, Toh 489).

summary: The Adhyātmasāraśataka, ascribed to the mahāpaṇḍita Prabhākaragupta, is a Buddhist Vajrayāna work in mandākrāntā and other long metres, given here with a word-by-word (anvaya) ṭīkā. The preserved verses argue that all things up to consciousness are without intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) and survey the doctrines of Buddhists, Sāṃkhyas, Jainas, Vaiṣṇavas, Śaivas and Cārvākas. They then turn to yogic practice with the winds, the central channel and the preservation of the bodily 'nectar' against ageing and death. The e-text stops after verse 17.

summary: The Advayasiddhi is a foundational Sahajayāna/Vajrayāna treatise in 35 verses attributed to the female mahāsiddhā Lakṣmīṅkarā. It advocates non-dual realization (advaya) of innately luminous reality (prakṛti-prabhāsvara), critiquing external rituals, physical asceticism, and material deity worship while emphasizing internal somatic transformation, antinomian samaya practices, and devotion to the guru as the embodiment of Vajrasattva.

summary: The Ajitasenavyākaraṇa (or Ajitasenavyākaraṇanirdeśa) is a transitional Mahāyāna sūtra surviving in Sanskrit in the 6th–7th-century Gilgit cache and in Central Asian manuscript fragments, but absent from both the Tibetan and Chinese Buddhist canons. Structurally sharing traits with mainstream avadāna literature, it depicts the Buddha predicting future buddhahood (vyākaraṇa) for King Ajitasena of Rājagṛha. The text is celebrated in Buddhist studies for documenting an early developmental phase of the Mahāyāna, emphasizing devotion, the merit of hearing and pronouncing the Buddha's name, stūpa worship, and textual transmission prior to the full systematization of emptiness (dharmaśūnyatā) doctrine.

summary: The Amoghapāśakalparāja is an extensive Buddhist Kriyātantra ritual manual focused on Amoghapāśa Avalokiteśvara. This portion (comprising Chapter 21, corresponding to Part VII of the modern diplomatic transcription, folios 91a1–97b4) opens with Vajrapāṇi questioning the Buddha Śākyamuni regarding the exhaustive ritual requirements, maṇḍala designs, and mudrās of the Amoghapāśahṛdaya cycle. summary: The Antarvyāptisamarthana ('Vindication of Internal Pervasion') by the 11th-century master Ratnākaraśānti is a pivotal text in late Buddhist epistemology. It champions the doctrine of 'internal pervasion' (antarvyāpti) in the proof of momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) from existence (sattva), arguing that invariable concomitance is grasped directly within the subject itself (pakṣa / sādhyadharmin) through conceptual entailment and an invalidating cognition (bādhakapramāṇa), thereby discarding external corroborating examples (dṛṣṭānta / bahirvyāpti) as superfluous.

summary: The Anupalabdhirahasya ('The Secret of Non-Apprehension') is a treatise on Buddhist epistemology by Jñānaśrīmitra addressing the problem of negative cognition. Building on Dharmakīrti's framework, Jñānaśrīmitra defines non-perception (anupalabdhi) not as a mere absence of awareness (upalabdhivirahamātra), but as an implicative negation (paryudāsa) consisting in the apprehension of something incompatible or distinct. He defends the status of anupalabdhi as a valid inferential sign (liṅga) for proving absence (abhāva) against rival Buddhist formulations and non-Buddhist theories such as the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā doctrine of an independent means of knowledge (abhāvapramāṇa).

summary: The Aparimitāyurnāmamahāyānasūtra is a popular Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture wherein the Buddha instructs Mañjuśrī on the longevity dhāraṇī and boundless merits of the Buddha Aparimitāyurjñānasuviniścitatejorāja, who dwells in the pure land Aparimitaguṇasaṃcaya. The text explains that copying, reading, reciting, or honoring this sūtra neutralizes the danger of untimely death, extends lifespan to one hundred years, and guarantees favorable rebirth. Due to its association with longevity and merit accumulation, it became one of the most widely transcribed scriptures across Central Asia and Tibet, surviving in thousands of copies among the Dunhuang manuscript collections.

summary: The Apohasiddhi is a concise philosophical treatise on semantics and epistemology by the 11th-century Buddhist logician Ratnakīrti of Vikramaśīla. Systematizing the arguments of his teacher Jñānaśrīmitra's Apohaprakaraṇa, Ratnakīrti rejects both exclusive affirmationism (vidhivāda) and pure negative exclusion (pratiṣedhavāda), arguing that words convey a positive entity intrinsically qualified by the exclusion of dissimilar things (anyāpohaviśiṣṭo vidhiḥ). The work forms an important milestone in late Buddhist nominalism, answering realist objections from the Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā systems.

summary: The Arthaviniścayasūtra ('Discourse on the Ascertainment of Meaning') is an early Buddhist doctrinal compendium that systematically presents twenty-seven core categories of Buddhist doctrine and meditation practice. It opens with a thematic list (uddeśa) followed by analytical definitions (vibhaṅga) of the five aggregates, eighteen elements, twelve sense fields, twelvefold dependent origination, four noble truths, twenty-two faculties, thirty-seven aids to awakening (bodhipakṣadharmāḥ), the absorptions (dhyānas), formless attainments, and the marks of a Buddha. Closely aligned with mainstream Abhidharma and Sautrāntika taxonomies, it served as the base text for Vīryaśrīdatta's 8th-century *Nibandhana*.

summary: The Avalokiteśvarahayagrīvadhāraṇī is an esoteric Mahāyāna dhāraṇī text centering on the wrathful deity Hayagrīva ('Horse-necked'), regarded as a ferocious emanational protector associated with the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Opening with homage to the Triratna and an epithet litany invoking Avalokiteśvara as the dispeller of fear and worldly suffering, the text proclaims the supreme heart incantation of Hayagrīva (hayagrīvabrahmaparamahṛdayam) to eliminate poisons, banish spirits, and destroy malevolent sorcery (kākhorda) and planetary afflictions (graha). Closely related to the Gilgit birchbark Hayagrīvavidyā, this recension represents the Sanskrit version preserved primarily through Tibetan canonical transmission (Toh 733 / 906).

summary: A devotional hymn (stava) of 9 verses composed in Toṭaka meter in praise of Avalokiteśvara, the bodhisattva of compassion. Proceeding in keśādipāda ('hair-to-foot') order, the hymn portrays the physical attributes, iconographic marks, and spiritual perfections of Avalokiteśvara, extolling his ten pāramitās, conquest over Māra, and residence on Mount Potalaka. Preserved in the Nepalese Sanskrit stotra corpus, it represents a rare surviving devotional work ascribed to an Indian Buddhist nun (bhikṣuṇī).

summary: A short Mahāyāna devotional hymn in six verses addressed to Avalokiteśvara, legendary attributed to the Nāga king Vāsuki. Verses 1 to 5 celebrate the Bodhisattva's radiant beauty, compassionate eyes, cosmic multidimensional form (with a thousand arms, four or six arms), and nature born from wisdom and means, concluding with the refrain 'namāmi nāthaṃ maṇipadmasaṃbhavam' ('I revere the protector born from the jewel and lotus'). The final verse offers reverent praise to the lotus-bearing protector who bestows compassion upon all sentient beings.

summary: The Avalokiteśvarastotra (also known as Lokanāthastotra) is a 25-stanza devotional hymn attributed to the Buddhist mahāsiddha Carpaṭipāda (Carpaṭi). Composed in the rhyming Mātrāsamaka metre, it represents one of the earliest prominent examples of systematic end-rhyme in Sanskrit Buddhist poetry. The hymn petitions Avalokiteśvara for protection from the ocean of saṃsāra, confesses bodily, verbal, and mental sins, and concludes with an aspiration for rebirth on Mount Potalaka; it has enjoyed enduring liturgical use in Nepalese Buddhism and was translated three independent times into Tibetan.

summary: The Avalokiteśvarāṣṭakastotra is an anonymous Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of praise addressed to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (Lokeśvara), consisting of eight descriptive stanzas followed by a benefit verse (phalaśruti). The hymn praises the bodhisattva's thirty-two physical marks, compassion toward suffering beings, retinue of deities and semi-divine beings, and role as supreme refuge from saṃsāra. The work forms part of the living liturgical stotra corpus transmitted among Newar Buddhists in the Kathmandu Valley.

summary: The Avayavinirākaraṇa ('Refutation of the Composite Whole') is a short polemical treatise by the late Buddhist logician Aśoka (c. late 10th to early 11th century CE). Defending the Dignāga–Dharmakīrti pramāṇa tradition against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika realists, Aśoka refutes the objective reality of the avayavin (a single composite whole posited as distinct from its parts). Applying the core Buddhist criterion that assigning contradictory properties (such as motion and rest, or visibility and obscuration) to an entity necessitates numerical multiplicity, he demonstrates that gross objects are mental superimpositions upon aggregates of partless atomic particulars.

summary: The Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī is a short Mahāyāna dhāraṇī-sūtra setting forth the doctrinal method for entering the nonconceptual realm (avikalpa-/nirvikalpadhātu). It outlines the sequential abandonment of four categories of conceptual signs—fundamental defiled phenomena (the five aggregates), remedies (the perfections), reality/suchness, and fruition/attainment—effected through non-mental engagement (amanasikāra). Widely regarded as a key scriptural source for the Dharmadharmatāvibhāga, the sūtra was extensively cited and commented upon by Indian Yogācāra and Madhyamaka authors, including Kamalaśīla, Ratnākaraśānti, and Maitrīpa.

summary: The Aṣṭamātṛkāstotra is an 11-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn venerating the Eight Mothers (Aṣṭamātṛkā), preserved in Nepalese Newar Buddhist manuscript and ritual collections. Following an opening salutation to Vighneśvara (Gaṇeśa), each stanza addresses one of the eight protective mother goddesses assigned to a compass direction (Brahmāṇī in the East, Vārāhī in the South, Indrāṇī in the West, Māheśvarī in the North, Kaumārī in the Southeast, Vaiṣṇavī in the Southwest, Cāmuṇḍā in the Northwest, and Caṇḍikā/Mahālakṣmī in the Northeast), identifying her vehicle, complexion, and emblems. The final verses invoke the goddesses collectively in connection with the eight pilgrimage seats (aṣṭapīṭha), sacred trees, and the eight Bhairavas, concluding with reverence to the planetary deities (navagraha) and Yama.

summary: The Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines') is the foundational and earliest extensive scripture in the Prajñāpāramitā corpus. Centered on dialogues between the Buddha and disciples including Subhūti, Śāriputra, and Ānanda at Vulture Peak, it expounds the core Mahāyāna doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā), the non-apprehension (anupalambha) of independent dharmas, and the altruistic path of the bodhisattva aiming at omniscience (sarvākārajñatā). Across 32 chapters, it promotes the veneration, recitation, and copying of Prajñāpāramitā manuscripts, culminating in the pilgrimage and self-sacrifice of Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita under the teacher Dharmodgata.

summary: The Balimālikā ('Garland of Oblations') by Ācārya Sumatisiṃha is a tantric Buddhist ritual manual setting forth verses, mantras, and procedures for presenting bali (food/torma) offerings. Beginning with verses derived from the Subāhuparipṛcchātantra, the manual prescribes 63 distinct offerings addressed to diverse Vajrayāna deities, protectors, and spirits, including Vajrayoginī, Parṇaśavarī, Mahākāla, the Ten Wrathful Deities (daśakrodha), local protectors (kṣetrapāla), and the Pañcarakṣā goddesses. The text was preserved in Nepalese manuscript witnesses and transmitted to Tibet, where it was transliterated and translated by Zha lu Lotsawa and Dharmadīpaṅkara.

summary: A modern Sanskrit essay on Buddhist epistemology (pramāṇamīmāṃsā). It argues that Buddhist discussion of the means of knowledge cannot be shown to be later than the Nyāyasūtra, as Vidyabhusana and Dasgupta held, pointing to the Buddhist positions criticised in the Nyāyasūtra's pūrvapakṣas and to the Vigrahavyāvartanī, and to the canonical emphasis on refuting other doctrines (Udāna, Aṣṭasāhasrikā). It then discusses Dignāga's and Dharmakīrti's doctrine of the twofold form (dvairūpya) of cognition, defended both on the externalist and on the Vijñānavāda view.

summary: A modern comparative scholarly treatise composed in Sanskrit examining the concept and practice of compassion (karuṇā) in Buddhism and the Hindu Purāṇas. The author analyzes the early Buddhist canonical understanding of compassion, the Bodhisattva ideal, and the cultivation of the brahmavihāras, comparing them with depictions of empathy, grace, and forgiveness in Purāṇic narratives (including the Matsya, Viṣṇu, and Kūrma Purāṇas). The work concludes by emphasizing the fundamental ethical affinity between Buddhist and Purāṇic philosophical thought, as exemplified by the Purāṇic assimilation of the Buddha into the daśāvatāra.

summary: The Bhadracaryāpraṇidhāna (or Bhadracarīpraṇidhāna) consists of 62 verses formulating the bodhisattva Samantabhadra's supreme vows and aspiration prayer. It forms the climactic conclusion of the Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra (the final chapter of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra) and circulated widely throughout Mahāyāna Asia as an independent liturgical text and devotional hymn. It articulates the canonical sevenfold worship (saptavidhānapūjā: homage, offerings, confession of sins, rejoicing in merit, entreating buddhas to turn the Dharma wheel, requesting them to remain in the world, and dedication of merit) before concluding with aspirations for rebirth in Sukhāvatī.

summary: The Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharājasūtra is a canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra set in Vaiśālī, in which Śākyamuni Buddha expounds to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī the twelve past aspirations made by the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabha (the Medicine Buddha) during his bodhisattva career. The text describes his eastern pure realm, Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa, and prescribes ritual veneration—such as reciting his name and sūtra, erecting images, and offering banners and lamps—to heal diseases, prevent untimely death, and protect states from turmoil. The work concludes with protective pledges uttered by twelve yakṣa generals.

summary: The Bhaktiśataka ('Century of Devotion', also known as Bauddhaśataka) is a 15th-century Sanskrit stotra composed in 107 verses across diverse classical metres by the Bengali Brahmin poet Rāmacandra Kavibhāratī, who immigrated to Sri Lanka and converted to Buddhism under King Parākramabāhu VI of Kotte (r. 1412–1467 CE). Adopting the emotional register and rhetorical idioms of devotional kāvya, the poem extols Gautama Buddha as the supreme, omniscient refuge free of passion and defilement, explicitly contrasting him with Hindu deities such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. The text became widely celebrated in Sri Lanka, where it was equipped with a Sinhala prose gloss (sanne) by Sumaṅgala Muni and served as an essential reader in monastic Sanskrit instruction.

summary: The Bhavasaṅkrāntisūtra is a short Mahāyāna sūtra set at the Veṇuvana near Rājagṛha, in which King Bimbisāra asks the Buddha how karmic actions that have long since ceased can reappear at the moment of death and produce rebirth if all conditioned entities (saṃskāra) are empty. The Buddha answers with the analogy of a man dreaming of a beautiful woman, demonstrating that although no permanent self or entity transmigrates from one world to another, rebirth occurs uninterruptedly through the causal stream of consciousness (cittasaṃtati). The text concludes with seven verses elucidating the relation between conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) and ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).

summary: The Bhavasaṅkrāntiṭīkā is an exegetical treatise attributed to Maitreyanātha that comments upon Nāgārjuna's Bhavasaṅkrāntiśāstra. It explains how rebirth and transmigration through existences (bhava-saṅkrānti) occur across cyclic existence without an enduring self (ātman) or substantial entity, reconciling karmic continuity with the Mahāyāna doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā) and the two truths (saṃvṛti and paramārtha). summary: The Bhikṣuṇīvinaya of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school is the sole Vinaya text governing Buddhist nuns preserved substantially in Sanskrit. It recounts the origin narrative of the nuns' order with Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the formulation of the eight 'weighty rules' (gurudharma), followed by an extensive vibhaṅga (rule-by-rule casuistry and commentary) on the nuns' Prātimokṣa, miscellaneous disciplinary matters (Bhikṣuṇīprakīrṇaka), and a concluding uddāna summary of the monks' miscellaneous section (Bhikṣuprakīrṇaka). Preserved in an 11th–12th century palm-leaf manuscript found at Zha lu monastery in Tibet by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana, its Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit idioms make it a cornerstone witness for early Buddhist sectarian law and linguistics.

summary: The Bhāvanākrama ('Stages of Meditation') by Kamalaśīla (c. 740–795 CE) is an influential triad of treatises formulating the graduated Mahāyāna path according to the Yogācāra-Madhyamaka synthesis. Composed in Tibet in connection with the Samyé (bSam yas) debate, it defends the classical Indian gradualist method of spiritual development against the sudden, non-conceptualizing quietism attributed to the Chinese Chan master Heshang Moheyan. Across the three works, Kamalaśīla systematizes the cultivation of compassion (karuṇā), the awakening mind (bodhicitta), and the balanced union (yuganaddha) of calm abiding (śamatha) and analytical discernment (vipaśyanā) leading to the non-conceptual realization of emptiness.

summary: The Bodhicaryāvatāra ('Entering the Way of Awakening') is an influential Mahāyāna verse manual and classic of Buddhist devotional-philosophical literature composed in ten chapters by Śāntideva. It outlines the spiritual cultivation of the bodhisattva, tracing the generation and stabilization of the awakening mind (bodhicitta), ritual confession, vigilance (apramāda), guard over awareness (saṃprajanya), and the perfections of patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), meditative absorption (dhyāna), and dedication of merit (pariṇāmanā). The ninth chapter develops a Madhyamaka dialectical critique of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), refuting rival Buddhist and non-Buddhist philosophical systems.

summary: Śāntideva's Bodhicaryāvatāra (c. 8th century CE) is a foundational Mahāyāna Buddhist poetic treatise detailing the development and practice of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) through the perfections (pāramitā). Prajñākaramati's Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā (c. late 10th to early 11th century CE) is the principal surviving Sanskrit commentary, offering running grammatical glosses, extensive canonical citations, and detailed Madhyamaka exegesis across chapters 1 through 9. Its extensive commentary on chapter 9 (Prajñāpariccheda) forms a crucial monument of late Indian Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka philosophy, critiquing both non-Mahāyāna Buddhist and non-Buddhist systems.

summary: The Bodhisattvabhūmi constitutes the fifteenth and most influential section of the encyclopedic Yogācārabhūmi, composed in approximately the 4th century CE. It serves as an exhaustive manual of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path, systematically treating spiritual lineage (gotra), the generation of the aspiration for awakening (bodhicitta), the perfections (pāramitās), ethics (śīla), and the stages of spiritual maturation (vihāras and bhūmis). Its fourth chapter, the Tattvārthapaṭala, forms a cornerstone of early Yogācāra philosophy, presenting a foundational analysis of the inexpressible nature of reality (nirabhilāpyasvabhāva) underlying linguistic and conceptual designations (prajñapti).

summary: This is a short liturgical manual for conferring the threefold bodhisattva discipline: saṃvaraśīla, kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhakaśīla and sattvārthakriyāśīla. It covers the request to a qualified bodhisattva preceptor, confession, taking refuge, the threefold formal question and acceptance of the vows, and the sign that appears to the buddhas and bodhisattvas once the rite is complete. It ends with instructions for taking the vows by oneself before an image of the Tathāgata when no qualified preceptor is available. Much of the wording follows the vow ritual of the Śīlapaṭala of the Bodhisattvabhūmi.

summary: The Bodhisattvādikarmikamārgāvatāradeśanā is a practical liturgical and behavioral handbook by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (11th century) outlining the progressive spiritual discipline required of a beginner bodhisattva (ādikarmika). It provides step-by-step guidance on relying on a qualified spiritual teacher (kalyāṇamitra), taking refuge, generating bodhicitta, and performing the sevenfold supreme worship (saptavidhānuttarapūjā). It instructs the practitioner on cultivating calm abiding (śamatha) and special insight (vipaśyanā) according to the nine limbs set forth in Bodhibhadra's Samādhisambhāraparivarta, maintaining mindfulness of all phenomena as illusion-like (māyopama) in post-meditation, and promptly purifying ethical infractions.

The commentary explicates the scriptural status and setting of the practice, the method of purifying bodhisattva downfalls using the four opponent powers (caturbāla), the names, qualities, and iconography of the Thirty-Five Confession Buddhas, and the concluding dedication of merits. Although traditionally ascribed to the Madhyamaka founder Nāgārjuna, the work presupposes Dharmakīrti's epistemological terminology and dates to approximately the 7th–8th century CE; this e-text provides the 2001 CIHTS Sanskrit restoration based on the Tibetan Tanjur version.

summary: The Buddhabhaṭṭārakastotra is a Buddhist devotional hymn in anuṣṭubh meter eulogizing the Buddha under the honorific designation Bhaṭṭāraka. Preserved in Nepalese manuscripts with a traditional colophonic attribution to Brahmā, the hymn also circulated widely in Sri Lanka under the title Nāmāṣṭaśataka, where it served as a foundational Sanskrit school text in monastic pirivenas.

summary: The Buddhacarita ('Acts of the Buddha') is an early Sanskrit court poem (mahākāvya) composed by the Buddhist author Aśvaghoṣa in the 1st–2nd century CE. Although the complete narrative comprised twenty-eight cantos narrating the life of Siddhārtha Gautama from his birth to his parinirvāṇa and the distribution of relics (fully preserved in Tibetan and Chinese translations), only the first fourteen cantos (concluding with the enlightenment) survive in the authentic Sanskrit manuscript tradition. Masterfully synthesizing sophisticated kāvya aesthetics with Buddhist philosophy, it is the earliest surviving complete court epic in Sanskrit literature.

summary: An 11-verse Sanskrit devotional hymn praising Śākyamuni Buddha, drawn from the concluding chapter (Nigamanaparivarta) of the Mahāyāna scripture Suvarṇaprabhāsottamasūtra. Spoken in the sūtra narrative by the tutelary goddess Bodhisattvasamuccayā, it celebrates the Buddha's rare appearance in the world like the udumbara blossom, his entrance into peaceful nirvāṇa, and the empty (śūnya) nature of all conditioned dharmas and beings. summary: The Bāhyārthasiddhikārikā ('Verses Establishing External Objects') is a major philosophical treatise in 188 kārikās by the 8th-century Buddhist realist thinker Śubhagupta. Defending an atomistic external realism against Yogācāra (Vijñānavāda) idealism, Śubhagupta mounts a systematic critique of idealist arguments advanced by Vasubandhu, Diṅnāga, and Dharmakīrti (particularly targeting the sahopalambhaniyama thesis and the denial of external causes for cognitions). While the continuous Sanskrit text is lost in India and survives as a whole only in classical Tibetan translation, this e-text presents N. Aiyaswami Sastri's modern Sanskrit retroversion.

summary: An 18-verse Vajrayāna stotra celebrating the tutelary deity Cakrasaṃvara (Heruka) and his maṇḍala retinue. Following salutations to Heruka and Vajravārāhī, the hymn maps the twenty-four ḍākinīs to their traditional sacred pilgrimage sites (pīṭhas such as Pullīramalaya, Jālandhara, and Oḍḍiyāna) and the internal channels of the human body across the body, speech, and mind wheels (kāyavākcittacakra). The stotra concludes with praises to the four animal-faced peripheral goddesses (Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, etc.) and four gatekeeping deities, ending with a dedication of merit wishing that all beings attain the status of Vajraḍāka.

summary: The Cakrasaṃvaratantra (also called Laghusaṃvara or Śrīherukābhidhāna) is a seminal scripture of the Buddhist Yoginītantra/Anuttarayoga class, focused on the wrathful deity Heruka/Cakrasaṃvara embraced by Vajravārāhī. Composed around the late 8th to early 9th century CE, it details the maṇḍala, mantras, sacred pīṭhas, classifications of yoginīs and ḍākinīs, secret hand gestures (chommā), and antinomian yogic rites. This digital text presents the first 25 chapters of the root scripture accompanied by the extensive commentary (Vivṛti) of Bhavabhaṭṭa, an influential exegete from Vikramaśīla.

summary: The Cakrasaṃvaratantra (also known as the Laghusaṃvara or Śrīherukābhidhāna) is one of the principal esoteric Buddhist scriptures belonging to the Yoginītantra (Anuttarayogatantra) class, centered on Heruka and Vajravārāhī. This e-text contains chapters 26 through 51 of the root tantra together with the Sanskrit Vivṛti (Pañjikā) commentary composed by the Indian master Bhavabhaṭṭa (fl. c. late 9th–early 10th century CE). The chapters discuss the examination of disciples, consecrations, internal and external sacred geography (pīṭhas), yoginī retinues, mantra rites, and non-dual realization.

summary: The Caryāsaṃgraha is an anthology of 165 tantric Buddhist caryā songs (caryāgīti, preserved in the living Newar tradition as cacā or chachā), based on a manuscript collected in Nepal by Jagannath Upadhyaya. The songs, accompanied by melodic rāga and rhythmic tāla performance instructions, were composed in late Middle Indo-Aryan and tantric Sanskrit by Indian and Nepalese mahāsiddhas and Vajrācāryas such as Līlāvajra and Suratavajra. Performed as part of esoteric ritual dances (caryānṛtya), the songs convey non-dual yogic realization (sahaja) and praise deities of the Anuttarayogatantras, including Cakrasaṃvara, Vajravārāhī, Hevajra, and Nairātmyā, through intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā).

summary: The Catuḥśatikā ('Four Hundred Verses') is the principal treatise of Āryadeva (c. 3rd century CE), the foremost disciple of Nāgārjuna, laying out the Madhyamaka philosophy across sixteen chapters. The first eight chapters focus on the bodhisattva's cultivation of merit by removing four fundamental delusions (regarding permanence, pleasure, purity, and selfhood), while chapters 9–16 refute non-Buddhist systems (such as Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika) and realists to establish universal emptiness (śūnyatā). This electronic text contains only 21 verses from chapters 1–5 preserved in secondary Sanskrit citations, as printed in the short appendix (pp. 159–160) of Bhagchandra Jain's 1971 edition.

summary: The Catuḥṣaṣṭisaṃvarastotra is an anonymous Buddhist tantric hymn of the Cakrasaṃvara/Heruka cycle preserved in Nepalese manuscript collections. In 75 anuṣṭubh stanzas, it invokes Śrī Heruka Cakrasaṃvara and an elaborate retinue of sixty-four theriomorphic aspects or emanations (such as Meṣasaṃvara, Aśvasaṃvara, Vyāghrasaṃvara, and Kūrmasaṃvara) conjoined with their consorts. The final portion consists of an extensive phalaśruti detailing worldly protection, pacification of epidemics and famines, and the attainment of classical tantric accomplishments (siddhis).

summary: The Catuṣpariṣatsūtra ('Discourse on the Four Assemblies') is a canonical text belonging to the Dīrghāgama of the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda school, chronicling the emergence of the Buddhist monastic community from the awakening under the Bodhi tree to the conversion of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. This e-text preserves solely the reconstructed preliminary episode, 'Vorgang E' (§§ 1–25), published by Ernst Waldschmidt (1960) from Turfan manuscript fragments. It describes the Bodhisattva's meditation at Uruvilvā, the attainment of the supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) during the watches of the night, the direct realization of the Four Noble Truths, and the destruction of the taints (āsrava).

summary: The Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra (also known as the Ekalavīratantra) is an Anuttarayoga / Yoginī tantra centered on the fierce deity Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa (a form of Acala) and his consort Dveṣavajrī. summary: A short rhythmic Sanskrit hymn of 9 verses in praise of the wrathful goddess Caṇḍikā (invoked as Siddhicaṇḍī and Ugracaṇḍī). The first eight stanzas feature repetitive, alliterative bījamantras and vivid descriptions of her terrifying aspects, weapons, and retinue, ending in a concluding devotional anuṣṭubh stanza. Preserved in Nepalese Buddhist manuscript collections, it exemplifies the shared esoteric Śākta-Vajrayāna pantheon in the religious culture of the Kathmandu Valley.

summary: The Chandoratnākara ('Ocean of Metres') along with its autocommentary (Chandoratnākaravṛtti) by the 11th-century Vikramaśīla master Ratnākaraśānti is a foundational Buddhist manual of Indian metrics (chandaḥśāstra). Spanning six chapters, it systematically expounds syllabic metres (varṇavṛtta), moraic metres (mātravṛtta/jāti), and combinatorial algorithms (pratyaya) for calculating and generating metrical variations. A hallmark pedagogical feature of the treatise is that each definition is composed in the exact metre that it defines; the text played an influential role in the study of metrics in medieval Nepal and in Tibetan monastic universities.

summary: The Citralakṣaṇa is an ancient Indian śilpaśāstra treatise on painting and image proportions (iconometry), traditionally ascribed to King Nagnajit and cited by Varāhamihira (6th century CE) in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā [3915, 5657]. The first chapter relates the mythical genesis of painting: King Bhayajit, having vanquished naked pretas (hence named Nagnajit), disputes with Yama to retrieve a brāhmaṇa's dead son; Brahmā intervenes, instructing the king to paint the boy's likeness and breathing life into it [3970, Granoff]. The subsequent chapters detail iconometric standards (parimāṇa/tālamāna) for universal monarchs (cakravartins), gods, and other figures [8758]. Preserved solely in Tibetan in the Tanjur (Toh 4317 / Peking Q5806), this Sanskrit e-text represents Asoke Chatterjee Sastri's 1987 metrical reconstruction from the Tibetan.

summary: The Cittatattvasaṅgraha (also titled Vijñaptimātratāsiddhipañcāśikā in its colophon) is a modern Sanskrit verse composition in 50 kārikās by the Sri Lankan Theravāda monk and scholar Pandit Dickwela Piyananda (Bhikṣu Priyānanda). The work harmonizes early Buddhist psychology from the Pāli Nikāyas—specifically referencing the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya), skandha analysis, and cognitive processing (vīthicitta)—with Yogācāra concepts of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā) and storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).

summary: The Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa ('Treatise on the Purification of the Mind') is a Vajrayāna verse treatise in 134 kārikās expounding the principle that spiritual liberation depends entirely on internal mental purity rather than external ritual ablutions or rigid asceticism. It argues that emotional afflictions and transgressive practices, when transformed through discernment of emptiness and skilful means (upāya), serve as the very antidote to bondage, just as poison can cure poison or water remove water from the ear. Doctrinally aligned with the Guhyasamāja exegesis of the tantric Āryadeva (Āryadeva II), the text supports its tantric hermeneutic by citing classical Vinaya rules and Mahāyāna precedents to demonstrate that moral value resides strictly in intentionality (āśaya).

summary: The Cittotpādasaṃvaravidhikrama is an 11th-century liturgical manual composed by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna setting forth the rite and sequence for arousing bodhicitta and formally receiving the bodhisattva discipline. Synthesizing the ritual traditions of Asaṅga's Bodhisattvabhūmi and Śāntideva's Śikṣāsamuccaya, it provides liturgies for taking refuge, petitioning a spiritual preceptor, taking the bodhisattva vows in the presence of an ācārya or directly before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas if no guru is present, and instructions on abandoning the four corrupting factors while cultivating the four counteracting wholesome factors. Although lost in its original Indic manuscript form, the work was preserved in the Tibetan Tengyur (Toh 3969) and reconstructed into Sanskrit in modern scholarship.

summary: The Daśabhūmikasūtra ('Sūtra on the Ten Stages'), also preserved as a major chapter of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra, is one of the most influential texts in Mahāyāna Buddhist literature. Set in the realm of the Paranirmitavaśavartin deities, the text records an exposition by the bodhisattva Vajragarbha detailing the progressive ten stages (bhūmis) of spiritual ascent from Pramuditā to Dharmameghā. Each stage systematically outlines moral, meditative, and cognitive requirements, correlated directly with the perfections (pāramitās) and the realization of emptiness. Extensively cited by Indian master exegetes and commented on by Vasubandhu in his Daśabhūmikavyākhyāna, it became the foundational source of the Chinese Dilun (Daśabhūmika) school.

summary: A 54-verse Buddhist devotional and liturgical work with concluding prose summarizing the bodhisattva path across the ten spiritual stages (daśabhūmi) and their corresponding perfections (pāramitā). It is extracted from the concluding summary verses (upasaṃhāragāthāḥ) of the tenth chapter of the canonical Daśabhūmikasūtra. In Newar Buddhism, it circulated independently within ritual Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha compendia as an auspicious protective text and hymn.

summary: The Daśākuśalakarmapathadeśanā is a concise ethical treatise setting forth the ten unwholesome paths of action (daśākuśalakarmapatha): three bodily, four verbal, and three mental. Each transgression is analyzed according to its constituent criteria and conditions (such as the five factors of killing, the five of stealing, and the four illicit circumstances of sexual misconduct), citing the Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānasūtra. Attributed to Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (982–1054) and preserved in the Tibetan Tengyur (D 3958), the Sanskrit text presented here is a modern retroversion by Ramesh Chandra Negi.

summary: A short prose tale about the poor brahmin Daṇḍin, who, after losing a borrowed ox, is taken to the king's court and on the way causes a series of mishaps: he lames a runaway mare with a stone, falls from a wall and kills a weaver, and makes a carpenter drop the axe held in his mouth into a river. The king answers each plaintiff with a reciprocal penalty that makes the complaint absurd, so all withdraw and Daṇḍin is acquitted. The story is known from the Tibetan mDzangs blun and the Chinese Xianyu jing (T 202); this Sanskrit text appears to be a modern rendering, published by Biswanath Bhattacharya in 1970 according to DSBC.

summary: A hymn of 21 stanzas in several metres arguing for the Buddha's superiority over the Brahmanical gods (Viṣṇu, Śiva, Skanda, Brahmā, Indra, Pārvatī, Vināyaka): the gods' weapons, passions and violent deeds are contrasted with the Buddha's peacefulness, compassion and freedom from faults. The poet addresses the reader rather than the Buddha, so the text is as much an apology for conversion to Buddhism as a hymn. It was translated into Tibetan together with Prajñāvarman's commentary, which became a source for Tibetan knowledge of Indian epic narratives.

summary: The Deśanāstava ('Hymn in the form of a confession') is a 52-verse Mahāyāna hymn in rathoddhatā metre ascribed in its colophon to Candragomin, which combines praise of the Buddha with confession: the speaker describes how each remedy he tries (the four brahmavihāras, generosity, patience, insight into emptiness) is undone by a further defilement. Hahn and later scholars regard it as a genuine work of Candragomin, the author of the Lokānandanāṭaka and Śiṣyalekha. It was long known only from the Tibetan Tengyur translation with Buddhaśānti's commentary; the Sanskrit text was published from a manuscript from Tibet by Liu and Schneider (2022).

summary: A verse treatise (147 stanzas) attributed to Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (Atiśa) on the vision of the dharmadhātu, preserved only in Tibetan and here given in a modern Sanskrit restoration. It explains the dharmadhātu with tathāgatagarbha-type similes (butter in milk, lamp in a pot, gem in rock, grain in husk) as obscured by defilements, presents the Madhyamaka two truths, and reviews Buddhist and non-Buddhist doctrinal positions (Sāṃkhya etc.), ending with a defence of the Mahāyāna.

summary: A brief seven-verse Buddhist tantric liturgical hymn preserved in the Newar manuscript tradition of Nepal. In each verse, an invocation and obeisance (namo 'stu te) are offered to one of the Five Tathāgatas (Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi), the Dharmadhātu, and Siddhivajra, associating each with an esoteric seed-syllable (bīja: vaṃ, a, ra, etc.) and elemental or cosmological attributes. It is entirely distinct from the renowned ~100-verse philosophical hymn Dharmadhātustava ascribed to Nāgārjuna.

The stotra pays systematic homage to the central deity, the Tathāgatas and their families, consorts, gatekeepers, the ten bhūmis, the pāramitās, the vaśitās, dhāraṇī goddesses, pratisaṃvids, offering goddesses, bodhisattvas, wrathful deities, directional guardians, and astral bodies (nakṣatras). Preserved in the Newar Buddhist liturgical tradition of Nepal, it serves as a verse devotional accompaniment to the complex 219-deity maṇḍala described in the Niṣpannayogāvalī.

summary: The Dharmasamuccaya ('Compendium of Dharmas') is a Sanskrit Buddhist verse anthology compiled by Bhikṣu Avalokitasiṃha, consisting of approximately 2,700 stanzas organized into 36 chapters (vargas) under four thematic udānas. The verses are systematically extracted from the expansive canonical Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānasūtra to serve as a concise, memorizable manual of Buddhist ethics, karma and the realms of rebirth, sense restraint, monastic conduct, and the cultivation of mindfulness. In the eleventh century, the anthology was translated into Chinese by Richeng (Sūryayaśas) and others under the title Zhufajiyaojing (諸法集要經, Taishō 728).

summary: The Dharmasaṃgraha is a concise Sanskrit Buddhist glossary consisting of 140 numbered entries categorizing doctrinal concepts and numerical dharmas (mātṛkā). It enumerates foundational Buddhist frameworks common to early Buddhism and Mahāyāna, including the three jewels, three vehicles, five Buddhas, four immeasurables (brahmavihāra), perfections (pāramitā), aggregates (skandha), sense fields (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and conditioned mental factors (caitasika). The text served as an essential pedagogical and reference manual for monastic education, especially within the Nepalese Buddhist manuscript tradition.

Widely preserved and copied in Nepalese Buddhist manuscript culture, the compendium includes well-known scriptures such as the Pañcarakṣā texts, the Amoghapāśahṛdaya, the Vasudhārādhāraṇī, the Uṣṇīṣavijayādhāraṇī, and short Prajñāpāramitā texts. These texts were primarily copied and recited for ritual protection, longevity, healing, and the warding off of obstacles.

summary: The Ekādaśamukha (also known as Ekādaśamukhahṛdaya) is an early esoteric Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra in which the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara reveals his eleven-faced heart-spell (hṛdaya) before the Buddha in the Jetavana monastery at Śrāvastī. The text details ten mundane benefits (including freedom from illness, weapons, poison, fire, and untimely death) and four transcendental fruits (including beholding the Tathāgatas at death and rebirth in Sukhāvatī) promised to practitioners who recite the spell, followed by prescriptive ritual instructions for bali offerings, lustrations, and homa rites. Surviving in Sanskrit in a 5th- to 6th-century birch-bark manuscript unearthed at Gilgit, the scripture formed a foundational text for the cult of the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara throughout Central and East Asia.

summary: The Garbhasaṃgraha ('Compendium of the Essence', Tib. Snying po bsdus pa) is a concise 14-verse doctrinal treatise composed by Atīśa Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna (c. 982–1054). It presents a summary of the Mahāyāna path, tracing the roots of cyclic suffering to dualistic grasping (dvaidhagrahaṇa) and prescribing meditation on space-like emptiness together with the cultivation of bodhicitta and universal compassion. It details traversal of the five paths (pañcamārga) and perfections to overcome the two obscurations and realize the three Buddha bodies (trikāya). The original Sanskrit text is lost; this e-text is a 20th-century retroversion from the Tibetan translation preserved in the Tengyur (Toh 3949).

summary: The Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra is a major Mahāyāna scripture that circulated both independently and as the climactic final section of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra. It recounts the spiritual pilgrimage of the youth Sudhana, who is instructed by Mañjuśrī to seek out fifty-three spiritual mentors (kalyāṇamitra)—representing varied genders, occupations, and stations—to learn the practice of a bodhisattva. The narrative culminates in visions of Maitreya's kūṭāgāra and Samantabhadra, depicting the cosmos (dharmadhātu) as an interconnected web of mutual interpenetration and closing with the famous Samantabhadracaryāpraṇidhāna aspiration.

summary: A Buddhist devotional hymn (stotra) of 34 stanzas composed in elaborate classical kāvya style, primarily in the twenty-one-syllable sragdharā metre. It celebrates the sounding of the monastic wooden gong (gaṇḍī), framing its percussive rhythm as an acoustic manifestation of the Dharma that awakens living beings, summons the saṅgha, and dispels the hosts of Māra. Stanza 5 is noted for its acoustic mimicry of the gong strikes using onomatopoeic syllables ('ṛmpaṃ ṛmpaṃ... ṭama ṭama ṭaṭamaṃ...'). While canonical East Asian and Tibetan witnesses credit the work to Aśvaghoṣa, the surviving Nepalese Sanskrit recension attributes it to Āryadeva.

summary: The Guhyavajravilāsinīsādhana (also entitled Yoginīsarvasva) is an extensive tantric evocation and ritual manual (sādhana) in 151 verses dedicated to Guhyavajravilāsinī ('Secret Vajra Playful One'), a form within the Vajrayoginī/Vajravārāhī tantric cycle. Attributed to the mahāsiddha Śabarapāda, it details the visualization of the deity, preparatory rites, mantras, offerings, and esoteric internal yogic practices (karmamudrā) undertaken in secluded mountain hermitage retreats. Preserved as text no. 10 (GSS 10) in the Nepalese codex of the Guhyasamayasādhanamālā, it is distinctive among works in that collection in that the practitioner visualizes himself as the male deity Padmanarteśvara while evoking the goddess.

summary: The Guhyeśvarīstotra is a seven-verse Newar Buddhist devotional hymn in Mālinī metre dedicated to the goddess Guhyeśvarī, venerated at her sacred shrine in the Kathmandu Valley as the root (mūla) of the lotus supporting the Svayambhū caitya and identified with Prajñāpāramitā or Nairātmyā. Extracted from the Svayambhūpurāṇa, the hymn is attributed in the narrative to the Bodhisattva Mañjunātha (Mañjuśrī), who praises the cosmic form (viśvarūpa) and transcendent nature of the goddess. The first six verses close with the uniform refrain praising her lotus feet ('caraṇakamalayugmaṃ naumi devi tvadīyam'), followed by a seventh verse detailing the spiritual accomplishments (siddhi) granted by devout recitation.

summary: The Guhyāvalī is an esoteric Buddhist tantric treatise of 25 Sanskrit stanzas attributed to the siddhācārya Dauḍīpāda. Opening with an invocation to Vajrayoginī, it expounds Anuttarayoga tantric praxis, focusing on consort meditation (vajrābjayoga), immutable bliss (akṣarasukha), the four blisses, and the non-dual realization imparted directly through the spiritual guru's empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna). The text survives in Nepalese palm-leaf manuscripts (e.g. Cambridge University Library MS Add. 1699.2), where it is preserved with a Sanskrit commentary (Guhyāvalīvivṛti) by Paṇḍitasthavira Śrīghanadeva.

summary: The Gurukriyākrama (also called Saṃkṣiptagurukriyākrama) is a brief manual detailing the liturgical and instructional sequence (krama) to be followed by a spiritual master (ācārya / guru) when guiding a disciple in the generation of bodhicitta and the Mahāyāna path. It covers inspiring faith and enthusiasm in the disciple, making offerings and performing the preliminary sevenfold worship (saptāṅgapūjā), arousing relative and ultimate bodhicitta, and conferring instruction on the perfections (pāramitā), means of gathering disciples (saṃgrahavastu), immeasurables (apramāṇa), and the threefold training. Because the ancient Indic text does not survive, this Sanskrit e-text represents a modern reconstruction (pratyuddhāra) produced by Ramesh Chandra Negi from the Tibetan canonical translation.

summary: The Gurupañcāśikā ('Fifty Verses on the Guru') is a classic Vajrayāna manual prescribing the obligations, ritual protocols, and devotional posture of a disciple toward the spiritual master (vajrācārya). Drawing on doctrines found in major Anuttarayoga tantras such as the Guhyasamāja, it details the criteria for examining a guru and disciple, behavioral etiquette, samaya vows, and the karmic consequences of guru disparagement. Although traditionally attributed to the 1st–2nd-century CE poet Aśvaghoṣa, the work is a medieval tantric compilation (ca. 9th–10th century CE) that became an indispensable prerequisite curriculum text in Tibetan Buddhism.

summary: The Gururatnatrayastotra is a seven-verse Newar Buddhist liturgical stotra praising the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha) and venerating the Guru. The text contains three distinct two-verse subsections praising the Buddha as the conqueror of mental afflictions, the Dharma (incorporating the opening mangala stanza of Haribhadra's Abhisamayālaṅkārāloka in praise of Prajñāpāramitā), and the Saṅgha (honoring both the eight classes of noble disciples and the great Bodhisattvas). It concludes with a popular devotional verse equating the Guru directly with the Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, and Vajradhara.

summary: The Guṇakāraṇḍavyūhasūtra is an all-verse Mahāyāna sūtra composed in Nepal around the early 15th century as an extensive poetical reworking and expansion of the earlier prose Kāraṇḍavyūhasūtra. Framed as a dialogue between Jinaśrīrāja and Jayaśrī recounting the spiritual instructions given to King Aśoka by Upagupta, it glorifies the cosmic deeds and salvific emanations of Avalokiteśvara (Karuṇāmaya), promotes the six-syllable mantra (oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ), and details the merits of the poṣadha (aṣṭamīvrata) fasting ritual. Alongside the Svayaṃbhūpurāṇa, the work served as a foundational liturgical and doctrinal scripture for medieval and modern Newar Buddhism.

summary: The Hastavālaprakaraṇa ('Treatise of the Handful' or 'Hand-Grasp') with its autocommentary (vṛtti) consists of six anuṣṭubh verses and prose commentary demonstrating the lack of inherent existence (svabhāva) in both composite macro-objects and partless indivisible atoms (paramāṇu). Employing the classic analogy of the rope mistaken for a snake and mereological part-whole analysis, the treatise shows that external entities are conventional conceptual designations (vyavahāramātra) without ultimate reality. The Indic original having been lost, the text survives in Tibetan and Chinese recensions and is known in Sanskrit through modern reconstructions.

summary: The Hetubindu ('Drop of Reason') is an epistemological and logical treatise by the Buddhist master Dharmakīrti (c. 6th–7th century CE), counted among his seven fundamental pramāṇa works. The text focuses specifically on the theory of the logical reason or probans (hetu), elucidating its threefold character (trairūpya) and classifying valid reasons into identity (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi). It systematically investigates fallacies of reason (hetvābhāsa) and marks a pivotal development in Dharmakīrti's thought wherein explicit statement of the thesis (pakṣa) is treated as dispensable because it is already established by implication.

summary: The Hetubinduṭīkā by Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa (c. 8th century CE) is an extensive commentary on Dharmakīrti's Hetubindu, an independent treatise examining the theory of logical reasons and inference. Arcaṭa discusses essential epistemological topics of Buddhist pramāṇavāda, including the preliminary statement of purpose (prayojana), the three conditions of a valid mark (trairūpya), the threefold classification of valid probantia, and the proof of momentariness (kṣaṇikatvānumāna). Preserved in Sanskrit and Tibetan, it served as a crucial intermediate authority between Dharmakīrti and later commentators such as Dharmottara and Durveka Miśra.

summary: The Hetutattvopadeśa ('Instruction on the True Nature of the Logical Reason') is an introductory compendium of Buddhist logic (hetuvidyā/pramāṇa) composed by Jitāri in the late 10th century. Following Dignāga's Nyāyapraveśa and Dharmakīrtian pramāṇa terminology, it systematically expounds proof (sādhana), refutation (dūṣaṇa), the threefold mark of the reason (trairūpya), and the various fallacies of the thesis (pakṣābhāsa), reason (hetvābhāsa), and example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa). This e-text preserves Durgacharan Chattopadhyaya's 1939 Sanskrit retro-translation made from the Tibetan translation prior to Tucci's recovery of the original palm-leaf manuscript.

summary: A Hevajra sādhana by the mahāmaṇḍalācārya Rāhulagupta. Written for practitioners of lesser ability, it combines Jālandharipāda's Vajrapradīpā on Saroruha's Hevajrasādhana with Bhadrapāda's Dveṣavajrasādhana into one manual. The manual is organised in 32 'sūtras', from the preliminary worship and brahmavihāras through the generation of the maṇḍala, consecration, the six-limbed yoga and clear light, to mantra recitation, bali, subtle yoga, daily conduct and re-emergence. The only known Sanskrit manuscript (1272 CE) is noted for its post-colophon dated in years from the Buddha's parinirvāṇa.

summary: The Hāratīstotra is a short nine-verse Buddhist devotional stotra addressed to Hārītī (spelled Hāratī in the Nepalese manuscript tradition), the yakṣiṇī subdued by the Buddha who became revered as a protectress of children and a healer of eruptive diseases such as smallpox (visphoṭaka). The text describes her seated in lalitāsana upon an eight-petaled lotus on a jeweled throne, adorned with diadems and jewelry, embracing her child with her left arm while granting fearlessness with her right hand. The concluding verse promises health, wealth, and safety for children to anyone who recites the hymn in their household at daybreak.

summary: The Jambhalastotra is a concise nine-verse Sanskrit hymn in Āryā metre attributed to Candragomin, praising Jambhala, the Buddhist deity of wealth and abundance. The poet approaches the compassionate deity as an afflicted, weeping devotee, contrasting inanimate wish-granting objects with Jambhala's living mercy and lamenting that poverty continues to afflict him. The hymn concludes with a dedication wishing that by the merit of this prayer, living beings may become like Jambhala in bestowing all desired gifts.

summary: The Jñānasiddhi is a foundational late 8th- to early 9th-century Vajrayāna treatise attributed to King Indrabhūti of Oḍḍiyāna, regarded in Tibetan tradition as one of the seven primary siddhi treatises (Grub pa sde bdun). In twenty chapters, the work elucidates the nature of non-dual awakening (advayajñāna), antinomian yogic discipline, and the soteriological transformation of worldly defilements through the unity of prajñā and upāya. It quotes and expounds upon key early tantras including the Guhyasamājatantra, Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, and Advayasamatāvijaya.

summary: The Jātakamālā ('Garland of Birth-Stories'), also entitled Bodhisattvāvadānamālā, is an ornate Buddhist campū composition (mixed verse and prose) by Āryaśūra, datable to approximately the 4th century CE. It retells thirty-four stories exemplifying the Bodhisattva's practice of the perfections (pāramitās), such as giving (dāna), moral discipline (śīla), and patience (kṣānti), in previous births as human, divine, or animal figures. Widely celebrated as a masterpiece of classical Sanskrit kāvya, strophes from this work are inscribed on the 5th-century murals at Ajanta.

summary: The Jātinirākṛti ('Refutation of the Universal') is a short polemical treatise by the 10th-century Buddhist logician-philosopher Jitāri of Vikramaśīlā. Formulated as an opening tract among topics of debate (vādasthānāni), it refutes the realist doctrine of real and eternal universals (jāti / sāmānya) held by Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā thinkers. Grounded in Dharmakīrtian epistemological logic, Jitāri establishes that universals cannot be said to be either identical with or distinct from particular individuals, undermines the relation of inherence (samavāya), and refutes Kumārila Bhaṭṭa's reliance on recognition (pratyabhijñā).

It invokes Svayambhū and the Five Buddhas with their Prajñās, the protective goddesses (Pañcarakṣā etc.), the past Buddhas, the great bodhisattvas, and the sacred sites (vītarāgas, Gokarṇeśvara, Mañjuśrī's caitya) of the Kathmandu Valley, following the legends of the Svayambhūpurāṇa, from which the colophon says it is extracted.

summary: The Kalyāṇatriṃśatikāstotra is an anonymous Buddhist tantric hymn of thirty verses in anuṣṭubh meter addressed to Vajradevī (identified in the colophon as Trikāyanivāsinī Vajradevī and in verse 17 as Vajrayoginī). Adopting the syntactic structure and famous refrain of the Hindu Devīmāhātmya (namas tasyai namas tasyai namas tasyai namo namaḥ), the stotra reframes the goddess within a Vajrayāna esoteric matrix, invoking the seed syllable evaṃ (v. 1), the vowels and consonants (ālikāli, v. 21), and the tantric sacred geography of internal and external pilgrimage centers (pīṭha, kṣetra, upapīlava, vv. 22–23). Preserved in the Newar Buddhist tradition of the Kathmandu Valley, it culminates in a phalaśruti promising the swift attainment of awakening (buddhatva).

summary: The Kamalākarasarvatathāgatastotra ('Praise of All Tathāgatas [from the Chapter on the] Lotus Pool') is a 33-verse Buddhist devotional hymn extracted from the Mahāyāna Suvarṇabhāsottamasūtra (Chapter 4, Kamalākaraparivarta). In the sūtra narrative, King Suvarṇabhujendra pronounces this hymn in praise of past, present, and future Buddhas across all ten directions, concluding with an extensive bodhisattva resolution (praṇidhāna) to eradicate karmic obscurations and attain supreme awakening. In Newar and general Nepalese Buddhist ritual practice, the chapter circulated independently as an excerpted stotra included in liturgical Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha and Stotrasaṃgraha anthologies.

summary: The Karmavibhaṅgopadeśa is an anonymous Buddhist exegetical treatise (upadeśa) preserved in a single 15th-century Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript (dated Nepāla Saṃvat 531 / 1410 CE). Serving as an exposition and commentary to the Mahākarmavibhaṅga, it examines the mechanics of karma and karmic fruition (vipāka). The text defends and elucidates key doctrinal positions—such as why making offerings to a stūpa after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa remains profoundly meritorious despite the absence of an embodied recipient—by citing canonical Āgama/Nikāya, Abhidharma, and avadāna parallels.

summary: The Karuṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra ('The White Lotus of Compassion') is a prominent Mahāyāna scripture composed around the 3rd to 4th century CE. It contrasts the aspirations and vows of various buddhas and bodhisattvas: whereas buddhas such as Amitābha and Akṣobhya chose to preside over purified buddha-fields free of spiritual decline, Śākyamuni made vows in a past life as the priest Samudrareṇu to attain awakening and guide sentient beings in an impure world (the Sahā world) during the era of the five degenerations (pañcakaṣāya). The text celebrates Śākyamuni's supreme compassion, likening him to an exceptionally fragrant white lotus (puṇḍarīka) blooming amidst lesser flowers.

summary: A concise Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā sūtra spoken by the Buddha to Śakra (Kauśika) on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha. The text expounds the nondual nature of the perfection of wisdom through negative dialectical statements, eighteen modes of emptiness (aṣṭādaśaśūnyatā), and verses found in the Vajracchedikā and the opening maṅgalācaraṇa of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. It concludes with a series of protective mantras and dhāraṇīs honoring Prajñāpāramitā, bridging exoteric Prajñāpāramitā philosophy with esoteric protective practice.

summary: The Kaṭhināvadāna is an edifying Buddhist ritual and narrative text preserved in Nepalese manuscripts that extols the spiritual merit of offering the kaṭhina cloth to the monastic Saṃgha at the conclusion of the rains-retreat (varṣā). Opening with Mahākāśyapa questioning the Buddha on the proper time and ceremonial procedures for spreading the kaṭhina, the work outlines detailed Vinaya prescriptions for measuring, stitching, marking, and dedicating the robe before presenting past-life narratives that illustrate karmic retribution and the fruits of generosity. Several of its embedded story motifs have direct parallels in the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya Bhaiṣajyavastu.

summary: The Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā by Kuladatta (fl. c. late 11th–12th century CE) is an extensive Sanskrit manual of Vajrayāna Buddhist ritual, famous for preserving liturgy closely related to the Śaiva Pratiṣṭhātantra tradition and central to Newar Buddhism. It details the examination of building sites, the construction and consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of monasteries, caityas, and images, as well as initiation (abhiṣeka) and fire sacrifice (homa). This digital text contains an excerpt (sections 1.4–3.5.8) from Ryūgen Tanemura's 2004 critical edition, dealing with site inspection (bhūmiparīkṣā), site testing, omens (nimittokti), and the ritual marking of foundation cords and lines (sūtrapātana).

summary: The Kriyāsaṃgrahakārikā is a concise ten-verse mnemonic summary (uddāna) attributed to the tantric Nāgārjuna, outlining the essential sequence of Vajrayāna temple construction, consecration, and monastic ritual procedures. It enumerates the preliminary examination of guru and disciple, site selection and purification, propitiation of the earth deity and site serpent (vāstunāgaparīkṣā), brick-laying and architectural measurements, maṇḍala layout and thread-casting, fire rites (homa), image installation and consecration (pratiṣṭhā), monastic ordination (pravrajyā), and the repair of dilapidated shrines (jīrṇoddhāra). The thematic sequence mirrors the major chapters of Kuladatta's comprehensive manual, the Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā.

summary: The Kālacakragaṇitopadeśa is an astronomical handbook (karaṇa) affiliated with the Buddhist Kālacakratantra tradition. Beginning with calculations based on the epoch date Śakābda 1091 (1169 CE), it provides practical computational procedures for the sexagenary cycle (ṣaṣṭisaṁvatsara), intercalary months (adhikamāsa), lunar days, and planetary equations (manda- and śīghra-karma for Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, and Ketu).

summary: The Kālacakrāvatāra is a short technical manual (karaṇa) of Kālacakra calendrical astronomy by Abhayākaragupta. It gives procedures for computing the year, month and day constants, weekdays, lunar mansions, solar and lunar positions, eclipses and the variation of daylight in different regions, drawing on the Laghukālacakratantra and the Vimalaprabhā. Its epoch figure of 463 years is central to Newman's reconstruction of the Kālacakra epoch, and it survives in a unique palm-leaf manuscript copied in 1125 CE.

summary: A pivotal Mahāyāna sūtra dedicated to glorifying the salvific activities and cosmic compassion of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara across various realms of saṃsāra, including Avīci hell and the preta realm. The text is historically famous as the earliest known source to teach the six-syllable mantra Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ (the ṣaḍakṣarī mahāvidyā) and to detail its benefits and mandala ritual. Composed in northern India circa the 4th to 5th century CE, it demonstrates direct thematic engagements with contemporary Śaiva cosmologies—such as presenting Hindu deities like Maheśvara, Brahmā, and Nārāyaṇa as emanations from Avalokiteśvara's body—and provided the foundation for Avalokiteśvara worship and the Maṇi Kabum in Tibet.

summary: The Kāśyapaparivartasūtra is an early Mahāyāna scripture cast as a dialogue between the Buddha and Mahākāśyapa on Vulture Peak at Rājagṛha. It expounds the bodhisattva path, emphasizing moral purity and warning against spiritual hypocrisy, attachment to monastic privileges, and intellectual pride. The text famously articulates the Middle Way between the extremes of eternalism and annihilationism and contains the influential simile comparing the dogmatic reification of emptiness to a medicine that itself becomes a deadly disease.

summary: A collection of 32 rhymed couplets (dohās) in Apabhraṃśa composed by the Buddhist mahāsiddha Kāṇha (Kṛṣṇācārya, c. 8th–10th century CE), embedded within an anonymous continuous Sanskrit commentary entitled Dohākoṣamekhalāṭīkā. The verses articulate Sahajayāna tantric teachings, critiquing exoteric Vedic and scholastic scriptural ritualism while teaching internal yogic realization through the subtle-body channels (lalanā, rasanā, avadhūtī), cakras, and the manipulation of bodhicitta to attain innate bliss (sahajasukha). The Sanskrit commentary provides word-by-word glosses and interprets the Apabhraṃśa couplets within the framework of Anuttarayogatantra systems, frequently citing authorities such as the Hevajratantra and the Caturdevīparipṛcchā.

summary: The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhir anvayātmikā is a philosophical treatise by the eleventh-century Buddhist epistemologist Ratnakīrti (fl. c. 1000–1050 CE) of Vikramaśīla. It establishes the Buddhist doctrine of universal momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga) via positive pervasion (anvayavyāpti): whatever exists is causally efficient (arthakriyākārin), and causal efficiency can only occur instantaneously, not successively or simultaneously over time (kramākramābhyām). Defending the inference against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā realists, Ratnakīrti deploys reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) and contraposition (prasaṅgaviparyaya) to show that permanent entities cannot possess causal efficacy.

summary: The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi vyatirekātmikā is an epistemological treatise by the 11th-century Buddhist master Ratnakīrti demonstrating the universal momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) of all existents by way of negative pervasion (vyatirekavyāpti) or contraposition. Developing the earlier insights of his teacher Jñānaśrīmitra, Ratnakīrti argues that whatever lacks causal efficiency through succession or simultaneity (kramākrama) cannot exist, thereby proving that eternal entities are impossible and that only momentary particulars are real. The treatise is particularly famous for its thorough refutation of the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika objection of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi) when formulating inferences concerning uninstantiated or fictitious entities.

summary: The Laghusiddhāntakaumudī is a 17th-century pedagogical abridgement of Pāṇinian Sanskrit grammar composed by Varadarāja, a disciple of Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita. Reordering Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī topically after the pattern of Bhaṭṭoji's Siddhāntakaumudī, it selects approximately 1,272 essential sūtras along with concise vṛtti glosses and illustrative derivations across all core grammatical categories. Designed as an accessible entry point (bālapraveśa) into the Pāṇinian system, it has served as the paramount introductory Sanskrit grammar textbook across India for centuries.

summary: The Laghutantraṭīkā (also known as Lakṣābhidhānāduddhṛtalaghutantrapiṇḍārthavivaraṇa) is an important commentary by Vajrapāṇi on the introductory portion (verses 1–10 1/2) of the Cakrasaṃvaratantra (Laghusaṃvara). Together with Vajragarbha's Hevajrapiṇḍārthaṭīkā and Puṇḍarīka's Vimalaprabhā, it constitutes one of the three core commentaries of the 'Bodhisattva trilogy' (sems 'grel skor gsum) foundational to the Kālacakra exegetical corpus. The work interprets the Heruka/Cakrasaṃvara system through an emergent Kālacakra framework, emphasizing internal subtle-body physiology, the retention of bodhicitta, and the integration of Yoginītantra practice within monastic discipline.

summary: The Lalitavistara ('The Extensive Account of the [Buddha's] Play') is an elaborate Mahāyāna sūtra in 27 chapters composed in mixed Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit prose and verse. It narrates the sacred biography of Śākyamuni Buddha from his decision to descend from Tuṣita heaven, his miraculous conception and birth in Lumbinī, his luxurious princely youth, four encounters, and great renunciation, to his austerities, defeat of Māra, awakening beneath the Bodhi tree, and first turning of the wheel of Dharma in Ṛṣipatana. Blending early biographical accounts (primarily Sarvāstivādin) with a docetic Mahāyāna perspective, the sūtra depicts the Buddha's earthly career as the deliberate, compassionate sport (lalita) of an already fully enlightened being, and served as a major inspiration for classical Buddhist art and literature across Asia.

The hymn concludes with a modesty stanza asking forgiveness for any linguistic or metrical flaws, dedicating the verses as an offering of pure devotion.

summary: A Newar Buddhist ritual manual belonging to the distinctive Nepalese 'Pārājikā' corpus. Cast as a revelation from Bodhisattva Lokeśvara (Avalokiteśvara) to Tārā on ominous portents (utpāta) and pacification procedures (śāntividhi), the text catalogues various domestic and environmental prodigies—such as eclipses, meteors, unnatural animal behavior, domestic intrusions by predators or serpents, and poisoned wells—and prescribes apotropaic rites (śānti) including homa fire offerings, recitation of the Pañcarakṣā, kalaśapūjā, and donations to the saṅgha. Despite adopting the classical Vinaya designation 'pārājikā', the work does not address monastic expulsion but rather lay and household expiatory and pacification rituals.

summary: An anonymous Nepalese Buddhist devotional hymn in eleven verses praising the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara under the names Lokeśvara and Lokanātha. Verses 1–10 describe his iconography, compassionate intervention, and adoration by celestial and earthly beings, each concluding with the refrain 'śrīlokanāthavibudhaṃ śubhadaṃ bhajāmi'. Verse 6 alludes to his entry into an excellent chariot (rathavara), reflecting the living Newar chariot procession (rathayātrā) traditions of Patan/Kathmandu. The final stanza (verse 11) serves as a phalaśruti promising the fulfillment of the reciter's desires.

summary: The Lokeśvaraśataka ('Centum in Praise of the Lord of the World') is an ornate Mahāyāna stotra of 100 Sragdharā stanzas composed in the 9th century CE by the Pāla court poet and chancellor Vajradatta. Composed in an elaborate Gauḍīya kāvya style marked by complex compounds, Yamaka, and anuprāsa, the hymn systematically describes Avalokiteśvara in the traditional nakha-śikha manner (from toenails to head), extolling his physical attributes, compassionate vows, and soteriological power. It is one of the most prominent datable works of later Buddhist Sanskrit court poetry and was translated into Tibetan several times in the Tanjur.

summary: The Madhyamakahṛdaya ('Heart of the Middle Way') is an independent verse treatise in eleven chapters by the sixth-century master Bhāvaviveka (c. 500–570 CE). It systematizes the bodhisattva path and Madhyamaka philosophy, pioneering the use of autonomous logical inference (svatantra-anumāna) to demonstrate emptiness. The text serves as one of the most comprehensive early doxographical compendia in classical Indian philosophy, examining and refuting rival Śrāvaka, Yogācāra, Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Vedānta, and Mīmāṃsā doctrines.

summary: The Madhyamakaśālistambasūtra is a unique Sanskrit adaptation of the Śālistambasūtra, preserved in a single paper manuscript discovered by V. V. Gokhale at the Kundeling Monastery in Lhasa. The work opens with the eight negations from the dedicatory verse of Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and dispenses with the standard introductory narrative frame between Maitreya and Śāriputra, recasting the classical Buddhist exposition of internal and external dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) in explicit Madhyamaka terminology. The latter part of the text incorporates śāstric dialectic concerning the conditioned nature of entities (paratantrāś ca bhāvā vivādapadam) and cites the Candrapradīpasūtra (Samādhirājasūtra).

summary: The Mūlamadhyamakakārikā ('Root Verses on the Middle Way') is the foundational treatise of the Madhyamaka philosophical school, composed by Nāgārjuna (ca. 2nd–3rd century CE). Across 27 chapters, it rigorously examines and deconstructs core metaphysical categories and conceptual frameworks—including causation, motion, sense faculties, the skandhas, the self, time, suffering, defilements, the four noble truths, and nirvāṇa. Nāgārjuna demonstrates that all phenomena are empty (śūnya) of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) precisely because they are dependently originated (pratītyasamutpanna), establishing emptiness as the middle way between the ontological extremes of substantialism and nihilism.

summary: The Madhyamakaśāstrastuti is a 14-verse hymnic eulogy composed by Candrakīrti (c. 7th century CE) in veneration of Nāgārjuna and his Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. Although transmitted independently in Nepalese and Tibetan collections as a stotra, these verses originally formed the concluding stanzas (nigamana) of Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā. The text is of singular historiographical and doctrinal importance because stanza 10 enumerates eight core treatises authored by Nāgārjuna (including the Sūtrasamuccaya, Ratnāvalī, Yuktiṣaṣṭikā, Śūnyatāsaptati, and Vigrahavyāvartanī), and traces the lineage of Madhyamaka commentary through Rāhulabhadra and Buddhapālita down to Candrakīrti.
