summary: The Madhyamakāloka ('Illumination of the Middle Way') is Kamalaśīla's (c. 740–795 CE) comprehensive independent treatise of Madhyamaka philosophy, traditionally counted among the 'Three Works of the Eastern Svātantrikas' (dbu ma shar ba gsum). Synthesizing Nāgārjunian emptiness with Dharmakīrtian epistemological logic (pramāṇa), the work systematically defends the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena (sarvadharmaniḥsvabhāvatā), expounds the doctrine of the two truths and the single vehicle (ekayāna), and refutes non-Buddhist as well as rival Buddhist positions. Although the original Sanskrit manuscript transmission is lost, the complete work survived in the Tibetan Tanjur (D 3887) and is represented here through Penpa Dorjee's 2001 Sanskrit reconstruction.

summary: The Madhyamakāvatāra ('Introduction to the Middle Way') along with its autocommentary (Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya) is Candrakīrti's celebrated 7th-century exposition of the Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka school. summary: Candrakīrti's Madhyamakāvatāra ('Introduction to the Middle Way'), composed in the 7th century CE, is a foundational Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka treatise designed to introduce Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā along the structure of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path. Structured around the ten bodhisattva stages (bhūmi), this sixth chapter corresponds to the abhimukhī-bhūmi ('Facing Ground') and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Chapter 6 comprises the philosophical core and roughly two-thirds of the entire work, expounding the refutation of intrinsic production (the catuṣkoṭi), an extensive critique of Yogācāra positions (such as the reality of consciousness, reflexive awareness, and the ālayavijñāna), the two truths, and the sixteen forms of emptiness.

summary: The Madhyamārthasaṃgraha is a concise Madhyamaka treatise in eleven stanzas setting forth the schema of the two truths (satyadvaya). It articulates a distinct hierarchical division of ultimate truth (paramārtha) into expressible/discursive (paryāyaparamārtha) and inexpressible/non-discursive (aparyāyaparamārtha), alongside conventional truth (saṃvṛti) classified into valid conventional reality (tathyasaṃvṛti) and false convention (mithyāsaṃvṛti). It is an influential pedagogical summary of Svātantrika epistemological taxonomy.

summary: The Madhyāntavibhāgakārikā ('Verses Distinguishing the Middle from the Extremes') is a foundational doctrinal treatise of the Yogācāra school, traditionally counted as one of the 'Five Treatises of Maitreya'. In 111 verses across five chapters—on characteristics (lakṣaṇa), obscurations (āvaraṇa), reality (tattva), spiritual cultivation and results (pratipakṣabhāvanā-avasthā-phala), and the supreme vehicle (yānānuttarya)—it formulates the middle way (madhyamā pratipad) as avoiding both the extreme of reification and that of nihilistic denial. The treatise provides classical expositions of unreal mental construct (abhūtaparikalpa), the three natures (trisvabhāva), and emptiness (śūnyatā) understood as the absence of subject-object duality within that construct.

summary: The Mahogratārāstuti is a short devotional hymn addressed to Mahogratārā ('Great Fierce Tārā'), a wrathful tantric manifestation of Tārā prominent in Newar Buddhist ritual. Following an opening Sragdharā stanza celebrating her terrifying iconography—with protruding fangs, a garland of human heads, and a skull-cup—ten anuṣṭubh verses petition her for refuge using the refrain 'trāhi māṃ śaraṇāgatam'. The hymn identifies Tārā syncretically as the supreme śakti encompassing Gaurī, Lakṣmī, Mahāmāyā, Umā, and Sarasvatī, concluding with a five-verse phalaśruti that promises liberation, worldly boons, and victory in battle to reciters on auspicious lunar days.

summary: The Mahogratārāṣṭakastotra (widely transmitted in Śākta tantric literature as Tārāṣṭaka or Nīlasarasvatīstotra) is an anonymous tantric hymn of praise to the wrathful goddess Mahogratārā / Nīlasarasvatī. Composed of eight verses in ornate Sragdharā metre followed by a three-verse phalaśruti, it eulogizes her fierce iconography—standing in pratyālīḍha posture on a corpse (śava) and bearing a sword, kartrī (chopper), skull-cup (kapāla), and blue lotus—imploring her for literary brilliance, protection, and liberation. The hymn provides a clear example of shared ritual poetry spanning Newar Vajrayāna Buddhism and Śākta Tantra.

summary: The Mahābodhibhaṭṭārakastotra is an eight-verse Sanskrit devotional hymn (aṣṭaka) celebrating Gautama Buddha under the epithet Mahābodhibhaṭṭāraka ('the Venerable Lord of the Great Awakening'). Every stanza concludes with the refraining hemistich 'śrīśākyasiṃhaṃ praṇamāmi nityam' ('I perpetually bow to the glorious Lion of the Śākyas'). The hymn extols the somatic perfection and auspicious major and minor marks (lakṣaṇa and anuvyañjana) of the Buddha—including his crown, ūrṇā, lotus-like eyes, golden hue, knee-reaching arms, and wheel-marked hands—while praising him as the supreme teacher who delivers beings from threefold suffering.

summary: The Mahābodhivandanāṣṭaka is an anonymous eight-verse Buddhist Sanskrit hymn of salutation (aṣṭaka) addressed to the Mahābodhi (the Great Enlightenment embodied in the Buddha and associated with the sacred site of Bodhgayā). The hymn extols the Buddha's physical marks, his golden complexion, the triumph over Māra, and his identity with the Three Jewels (Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha), concluding each verse with the refrain 'śrīmanmahābodhim ahaṃ namāmi' ('I bow to the glorious Mahābodhi').

summary: The Mahācakravartināmāṣṭottaraśatastotra is a 20-verse Buddhist tantric litany and formal supplication (adhyeṣaṇā) addressed to Sarvatathāgatamahācakravartin, an esoteric manifestation of Vajrasattva associated with Trailokyavijaya. Verses 1–16 enumerate 108 devotional epithets and honorific invocations ending with 'namo 'stu te', followed by praise of the deity as the firm essence (vajradṛḍhaṃ cittam) and progenitor of all Tathāgatas (vv. 17–18), a benefit verse (phalaśruti, v. 19), and a formal prayer (adhyeṣaṇā, v. 20) entreating the lord to manifest his tantric family for the welfare of beings. Originally situated in Chapter 6 (Trilokavijayamahāmaṇḍalavidhivistara) of the Yoga Tantra scripture Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, it also circulated as an independent liturgical hymn in the Newar Buddhist tradition.

summary: The Mahākālastotra is a short Buddhist devotional hymn in 13 anuṣṭubh stanzas addressed to the two-armed (dvibhuja) wrathful protector Mahākāla. It invokes the deity as the granter of all prosperity (sarvasampattidāyaka) and protector of practitioners (siddhasādhakarakṣaka), describing his fierce iconographic attributes including the crown of skulls, necklace of severed heads, adornment of eight serpents, tiger-skin garment, chopper (kartikā), and skull-cup (kapāla). The hymn concludes with a phalaśruti promising deliverance from fear and the realization of all spiritual accomplishments (sarvasiddhi).

summary: The Mahāmeghasūtra (also known as the Meghasūtra) is an apotropaic Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture dedicated to rainmaking and drought alleviation. Set in the aquatic palace of the serpent kings Nanda and Upananda, the text relates the Buddha's instruction on loving-kindness (maitrī) as the supreme antidote to suffering, followed by protective dhāraṇīs and ritual manual procedures for bringing rain. While closely related to chapters 64–65 of the larger doctrinal Mahāmeghasūtra (T387 / Toh 232), this sūtra circulated independently throughout Asia as a specialized rain-ritual text (Tibetan Toh 235/657; Chinese T989, T991, T992, T993).

summary: A concise Vajrayāna liturgical manual (sādhana) for evoking the deity Mahāmāyā (Heruka) and his retinue, belonging to the Mahāmāyā Tantra cycle and attributed to the mahāsiddha Kukkuripa. It details preliminary purification, generation of bodhicitta, and reflection on emptiness (śūnyatā). The yogin then visualizes the central four-faced, four-armed Heruka (Karuṇācalavajra) embraced by Buddhaḍākinī amidst the eight cremation grounds, initiated through an Apabhraṃśa tantric song (vajragīti) sung by four directional ḍākinīs, and concludes with syllable distribution (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) and mantra recitation.

summary: The Mahāmāyātantra is an Anuttarayoga / Yoginī class Buddhist tantra in three chapters (nirdeśas) centered on the four-faced, four-armed deity Mahāmāyā and her retinue of ḍākinīs, renowned especially for teachings on dream yoga (svapnadarśana), subtle drop yoga (binduyoga), and transgressive yogic practices. The Guṇavatī commentary by the Vikramaśīla scholar-monk Ratnākaraśānti (late 10th to early 11th century) provides an exegesis grounded in a Yogācāra-Mādhyamika framework. The e-text concludes with two ancillary ritual practice texts: Ratnākaraśānti's Mahāmāyāsādhana and the mahāsiddha Kukkuripāda's Mahāmāyāsādhanopāyikā.

summary: The Mahāsannipātaratnaketudhāraṇīsūtra (also known as the Ratnaketuparivarta) is an influential Mahāyāna scripture that circulated both independently and as a major component of the expansive Mahāsannipāta corpus. Set in Rājagṛha, the narrative depicts the conversion of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, the Buddha's subjugation of Māra and his host, discourses on karmic results and bodhisattva training, and potent protective dhāraṇī incantations. This digital text reproduces the incomplete Sanskrit text recovered from the Gilgit manuscript and edited by Nalinaksha Dutt, containing chapters 1–6 and 10–11 of the thirteen chapters preserved in classical Tibetan and Chinese translations.

summary: A Buddhist metrical avadāna in 1,077 verses forming chapter 49 of the late medieval Nepalese anthology Mahajjātakamālā. Framed as a dialogue between King Aśoka and the arhat Upagupta, the narrative recounts the past life of the Buddha as King Maṇicūḍa of Sāketa, who was born with a miraculous wish-granting jewel in his crest. To perfect the virtue of generosity (dāna-pāramitā), Maṇicūḍa gives away his magical elephant, his kingdom, and the merit of his sacrifice, undergoes voluntary exile in the forest, provides his own flesh and blood to satiate a demon, and ultimately allows his skull to be cleaved to extract and bestow his crest-jewel.

summary: The Mahāsāṃghikaprātimokṣasūtra is the liturgical rule code of monastic discipline for monks (bhikṣus) belonging to the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin lineage, recited fortnightly at the poṣadha (confession) assembly. It sets forth 218 training rules systematically classified in descending order of severity: pārājika, saṃghātiśeṣa, aniyata, niḥsargika-pācattika, pācattika, pratideśanīya, śaikṣa, and adhikaraṇaśamatha. Composed in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit with substantial Middle Indo-Aryan morphological elements, this text represents the sole substantially preserved Indic Prātimokṣasūtra of the Mahāsāṃghika branch, preserved in a single palm-leaf manuscript discovered in Tibet by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana.

Volume 1 recounts the past karmic preparations of Śākyamuni Buddha under earlier Buddhas such as Dīpaṅkara, presents the four bodhisattva practices (caryās) and an early version of the ten stages (daśabhūmi), depicts cosmological realms including the naraka hells, and relates numerous jātakas up to the Bodhisattva's residence in Tuṣita heaven prior to descent.

summary: The Mahāvyutpatti ('Great Detailed Exposition' or 'Essential Etymology'; Tib. Bye-brag-tu rtogs-par byed-pa chen-po) is an early ninth-century bilingual Sanskrit–Tibetan glossary compiled in Tibet under imperial decree (c. 814 CE during the reign of King Sadnalegs). Arranged systematically across 284 topical categories containing 9,565 lexical entries, it provided standardized equivalents for Buddhist philosophical terminology, canonical scripture titles, monastic rules, proper names, and linguistic forms. Designed to guide and regulate the translation of Buddhist texts from Sanskrit into Tibetan, it became the foundation for the Tibetan canonical translation language (chos skad) and was later expanded into polyglot versions including Chinese, Mongolian, and Manchu.

summary: The Mahāyānapathasādhanasaṅgraha (colophon title: Atisaṃkṣiptamahāyānapathasādhana) is a short 10-verse instructional manual outlining the bodhisattva path attributed to Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (982–1054 CE). It condenses core Mahāyāna practice: taking refuge, abandoning non-virtue, adhering to pure ethical discipline (adhiśīla) as the vehicle of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), mindfulness of death, adopting the bodhisattva vows and the six perfections, and the non-abiding nirvāṇa attained through the union of wisdom and means (prajñopāya). Because the original Sanskrit text was lost to history, this Sanskrit e-text represents a modern Sanskrit reconstruction (punaruddhāra) executed from the Tibetan Tanjur canonical translation (Toh 3955) by Ramesh Chandra Negi (1992).

summary: The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra ('Ornament of the Mahāyāna Sūtras') is a foundational Yogācāra treatise of ca. 800 verses in 21 chapters, here transmitted together with its prose bhāṣya. It defends the authenticity of the Mahāyāna as Buddha's word and systematically treats refuge, spiritual lineage (gotra), the arising of bodhicitta, practice, reality (tattva), the perfections, the factors of awakening and the bodhisattva's qualities and stages, culminating in buddhahood. The bhāṣya explains each verse and supplies the structure of the argument; the work was translated into Chinese (T 1604) and Tibetan (D 4020, 4026) and commented upon by Asvabhāva and Sthiramati.

summary: The Mahāyānaviṃśikā ('Twenty Verses on the Great Vehicle') is a brief Buddhist treatise traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna that synthesizes Madhyamaka and Yogācāra doctrines. It argues that external objects lack independent reality and that the world of saṃsāra is an illusory projection arising from conceptual fabrication (kalpanā) upon mind alone (cittamātra). The text concludes by urging practitioners to rely upon the Mahāyāna vehicle as the only means to cross the ocean of delusion.

summary: The Mantroddhāra (or Bhavotpattikramasādhanamantroddhāra) is a short Sanskrit liturgical text of the Guhyasamāja Ārya school attributed to Candrakīrti. Functioning as a mantra manual complementing the author's Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra, it provides the mantras and seed syllables for the generation-stage (utpattikrama) practice across four phases: mantra retention/extraction (mantrāvadhāraṇa), deity placement (nyāsa), deity arrangement (vyavastholi), and realization of reality (tattvadarśana), concluding with verses of praise to the thirty-two mandala deities.

summary: The Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi of Śūnyasamādhipāda is an Anuttarayogatantra treatise and sādhana centered on the cult of Vajravārāhī and Caṇḍālī yoga, expounding the realization of non-dual gnosis (tattvajñāna) through internal yogic control of prāṇa, bindu, and innate bliss (sahajānanda). The Marmakalikāpañjikā by the Vikramaśīla scholar-monk Vīryaśrīmitra provides an extensive commentary on the root verses, elucidating the esoteric vital points (marman) of practice and quoting extensively from early Siddha songs, Caryāpadas, and the lineage of Śabarapāda.

summary: The Mañjuvajramukhyākhyāna (or Mañjuvajramukhākhyāna) is an anonymous medieval Nepalese ritual manual belonging to the mukhākhyāna genre, focusing on the generation and worship of the nineteen-deity maṇḍala of Mañjuvajra. Although affiliated with the Jñānapāda school (Jñānapādasaṃpradāya) of the Guhyasamājatantra, it integrates practices from the Ārya school and quotes verses 10–18 of Buddhajñānapāda's Samantabhadrasādhana. The digital text also includes Tanaka's diplomatic edition of a related liturgical fragment from Cambridge University Library MS Add. 1708 (III).

summary: A devotional Buddhist hymn (stotra) of nine verses in the classical mālinī meter praising Mañjuśrī under the names Mañjuvajra and Mañjughoṣa. It depicts the youthful bodhisattva bearing his characteristic attributes—the sword of wisdom and the manuscript—accompanied by protective and attendant deities. The hymn evokes the founding legend of the Kathmandu Valley from the Svayambhūpurāṇa, in which Mañjuśrī cleaves the hills to drain the waters and reveal the primordial lotus light of the Svayambhū caitya, concluding with a verse on the spiritual and rhetorical fruits (phalaśruti) of reciting this prayer.

summary: A short Mahāyāna devotional litany consisting of 19 anuṣṭubh verses enumerating 108 names and epithets of Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva of transcendent wisdom. Following an opening verse of obeisance, the hymn celebrates Mañjuśrī as embodiment of emptiness (śūnyatā), supreme guide, healer, Ādibuddha, and the cosmic source of deities across both Buddhist and classical Indic pantheons. Preserved in Newar Sanskrit stotra manuscripts from Nepal, it appears as hymn 4 in Pāṇḍeya's Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha.

summary: A short nine-verse Sanskrit devotional hymn (stotra) dedicated to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (also addressed as Mañjunātha and Mañjughoṣa). The text extols his youthful appearance (sukumārarūpa, bālākṛti), ornaments, and iconographic emblems—specifically the sword cutting through ignorance, the sacred book, and the alms bowl. He is praised as the embodiment of discriminative insight (prajñānidhāna) who removes all affliction across the three worlds.

summary: The Mañjuśrīpārājikā (also known by its colophon title Pāpaparimocana) is a late Nepalese Buddhist scripture composed in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit, framed as an exposition given by the Buddha to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī. Purporting to be extracted from a 12,000-verse Vinaya work (Sarvatathāgatadvādaśasāhasrapārājikāvinaya), it adapts traditional Indic life-cycle sacraments (saṃskāras / daśakarma from birth through tonsure and monastic ordination) into a Newar Vajrayāna framework, providing ritual and doctrinal legitimation for the hereditary Vajrācārya priesthood. The text also covers grave transgressions (pārājikā), funeral and post-mortuary rites, and expiatory purification procedures including the use of pañcagavya.

summary: The Maṅgalaṣoḍaśastuti ('Sixteen-Verse Auspicious Hymn of Praise') is a sixteen-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn dedicated to the Buddha Śākyamuni (Śākyasiṃha), extracted from the Bhadrakalpāvadāna, an avadānamālā collection preserved in Nepalese manuscripts. Each verse recalls a distinct narrative episode or previous life (jātaka/avadāna) of the Buddha—including Maitrakanyaka, Supriya, Sudhana, Kuśa, and Saudāsa, and concluding with his journey from Kapilavastu to venerate the Svayambhū caitya in the Kathmandu Valley—invoking his protective power with the refrain 'sa no rakṣatu'. The hymn exemplifies the ritual and liturgical repurposing of narrative avadāna literature within Newar Buddhism.

summary: An eight-verse Sanskrit benedictory hymn (maṅgalāṣṭaka) composed in the classical Sragdharā metre, preserved within the Nepalese Buddhist liturgical tradition. Every verse concludes with a refrain entreating the buddhas and bodhisattvas to grant success, auspiciousness, and realization ('tuṣṭāḥ sarvārthasiddhiṃ dadatu samarasā maṅgalaṃ bodhisattvāḥ'). The stanzas invoke the Three Jewels, wrathful protector figures, female wisdom deities and prajñās, sacred pilgrimage sites (such as Lumbinī, Śrāvastī, and Gṛdhrakūṭa), and auspicious emblems (aṣṭamaṅgala).

summary: The Meghasūtra is a Mahāyāna rain-making text set in the palace of the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda. A nāga king asks how nāgas may be freed from suffering and send rain; the Buddha teaches friendliness (maitrī), a dhāraṇī and the names of cloud-related Tathāgatas, and then prescribes a ritual with a 'great cloud circle' (mahāmeghamaṇḍala) for use in drought. The colophons present it as chapters 64–65 of the Mahāmeghasūtra; the Chinese versions contain only chapter 64.

summary: The Munimatālaṅkāra ('Ornament of the Sage's Doctrine') by Abhayākaragupta (composed c. 1113 CE at Vikramaśīla) is an encyclopedic synthesis of non-tantric Mahāyāna philosophy and praxis, integrating Madhyamaka, Yogācāra, and the Prajñāpāramitā-Abhisamayālaṅkāra traditions. This excerpt from Chapter 1 (manuscript folios 59v4–61r5) investigates the nature of conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) under six alternative philosophical definitions, critically establishing the relationship between conceptual overlay, linguistic convention, and ultimate reality. The section is especially significant for recovering substantial Sanskrit citations from Kamalaśīla's Madhyamakāloka, the Sanskrit original of which is otherwise largely lost.

summary: The Mūlamadhyamakakārikā ('Root Verses on the Middle Way') is the foundational treatise of the Madhyamaka philosophical school, composed by Nāgārjuna (ca. 2nd–3rd century CE). Across 27 chapters, it rigorously examines and deconstructs core metaphysical categories and conceptual frameworks—including causation, motion, sense faculties, the skandhas, the self, time, suffering, defilements, the four noble truths, and nirvāṇa. Nāgārjuna demonstrates that all phenomena are empty (śūnya) of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) precisely because they are dependently originated (pratītyasamutpanna), establishing emptiness as the middle way between the ontological extremes of substantialism and nihilism.

summary: The Nairātmyaparipṛcchā ('Questions on Selflessness') is a short Mahāyāna scripture consisting of a prose opening dialogue and 26 verses. Departing from standard sūtra narrative conventions, it depicts non-Buddhist wanderers (tīrthikas) approaching Mahāyāna practitioners to question how bodily actions and affective states (laughter, crying, anger, jealousy) can arise if the body is devoid of a supreme self (paramātman). The Buddhist respondents elucidate the non-duality of existence and non-existence, the distinction between conventional reality (saṃvṛti) and ultimate reality (paramārtha), and the nature of all phenomena as illusory, dream-like appearances empty of intrinsic self-nature.

summary: The Nairātmyāśīḥstuti is a seven-verse Buddhist tantric benedictory hymn celebrating the goddess Nairātmyā, the principal consort in the Hevajratantra cycle. The verses praise her terrifying dancing form adorned with bone ornaments, carrying the kartrī and kapāla, and invoke her blessing to eliminate mental afflictions and worldly evils. The concluding verse identifies her with the internal yogic subtle body, specifically the synthesis of the three channels lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtikā.

summary: The Nairātmāṣṭakastotra is a short eight-verse hymn (aṣṭaka) in anuṣṭubh meter addressed to the tantric Buddhist goddess Nairātmyā (Nairātmā), consort of Hevajra and personification of selflessness (nairātmya). The hymn praises her absolute nature as free of conceptual construct (nirvikalpa) and without support (nirālamba), while describing her wrathful iconographic attributes (one-faced, three-eyed, dancing on a corpse, carrying a chopper and skull-cup) and her retinue of the eight maṇḍala yoginīs (Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī). Preserved in the Sanskrit manuscript collections of the Kathmandu Valley, it forms part of traditional Newar Vajrayāna devotional and liturgical practice.

summary: The Narakoddhārastotra ('Hymn on Rescue from Hell') is a 15-verse Sanskrit Buddhist devotional prayer seeking salvation from the sufferings of saṃsāra and the tortures of the hell realms. The speaker confesses grievous misdeeds—including the five heinous crimes (pañcānantarya), harming sentient beings, and desecrating stūpas—and repeatedly entreats the Buddha with the refrain 'trāhi māṃ hi tathāgata' ('rescue me, O Tathāgata!'). The concluding verse hails the Lord (Lokanātha) as the supreme king of physicians (vaidyarāja) capable of curing all diseases and delivering sentient beings across the three worlds.

summary: The Niraupamyastava ('Hymn to the Incomparable One') is a devotional philosophical poem of 25 stanzas in anuṣṭubh metre composed by Nāgārjuna, forming part of his famous Catuḥstava ('Four Hymns'). Composed as an encomium praising the Buddha, the work formulates foundational Madhyamaka themes in a devotional idiom: praising the Tathāgata as having neither originated nor extinguished any dharma, having spoken not a single syllable while yet teaching all disciples, and being empty of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) and conceptual proliferation (vikalpa). The hymn also contains prominent discussions of the two bodies of the Buddha (dharmakāya and janmakāya/rūpakāya) and affirms the ultimate unity of the vehicles (ekayāna) grounded in the non-differentiation of the dharmadhātu.

summary: The Nityakarmapūjāvidhi is a Sanskrit liturgical manual from the Newar Buddhist Vajrayāna tradition that details the sequence of rites for daily obligatory worship (nityakarma). It specifies preliminary purifications (ācamana, kāyaviśodhana), the consecration of offerings, worship of the guru and Vajrasattva, the construction and offering of the cosmic Meru maṇḍala, standard sensory offerings (pañcopacāra), and concluding prayers for forgiveness (kṣamāpaṇa) and dismissal of the invoked deities (visarjana).

summary: The Nyāyabindu ('Drop of Logic') is Dharmakīrti's concise foundational primer on Buddhist epistemology and logic, articulating the core doctrines of the Dignāga–Dharmakīrti school. Written in terse prose aphorisms (sūtras), the work is structured into three chapters: direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna). It defines perception as non-conceptual (kalpanāpoḍha) and non-erroneous (abhrānta), formulates the threefold requirement of the logical reason (trairūpya), classifies valid reasons into essential nature (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi), and provides a taxonomy of logical fallacies. Due to its clarity and pedagogical conciseness, it became the primary introductory manual of Buddhist logic in India and Tibet.

summary: An anonymous ṭippaṇī (set of glosses) on Dharmottara's Nyāyabinduṭīkā, the main commentary on Dharmakīrti's Nyāyabindu. The extant part explains the maṅgala and introduction and the first chapter on perception, glossing words and grammar of the ṭīkā and discussing the definition of right cognition (samyagjñāna), freedom from conceptual construction (kalpanāpoḍha), non-erroneousness (abhrānta), the kinds of perception and the relation of perception to the determining judgement (niścaya); it repeatedly criticises Vinītadeva's interpretations. It survives in one incomplete manuscript edited by Stcherbatsky in 1909.

summary: The Nyāyapraveśakasūtra (commonly known as the Nyāyapraveśa), authored by Dignāga's pupil Śaṅkarasvāmin (c. 6th century CE), is an influential introductory manual of Buddhist logic and epistemology (hetuvidyā). It systematically defines the members of formal proof (sādhana) and refutation (dūṣaṇa), the three characteristics of a valid logical reason (trairūpya), the varieties of logical fallacies (pakṣābhāsa, hetvābhāsa, dṛṣṭāntābhāsa), and valid cognition through perception and inference. Translated into Chinese by Xuanzang in 647 CE, it became the standard foundational treatise for the East Asian Buddhist logical tradition (yinming / inmyō), and was widely preserved and commented upon in medieval India, notably by Jaina scholars.

summary: The Nyāyapraveśapravṛtti (also titled Śiṣyahitā or Nyāyapraveśakavṛtti) is an 8th-century commentary by the Śvetāmbara Jain master Haribhadrasūri on the Nyāyapraveśa, an introductory manual of Buddhist pramāṇa logic authored by Śaṅkarasvāmin (c. 6th century CE). Haribhadrasūri provides a concise, student-oriented word-by-word explanation of the treatise's definitions of valid proof (sādhana), refutation (dūṣaṇa), their corresponding fallacies (ābhāsa), direct perception (pratyakṣa), and inference (anumāna). The commentary is a major historical milestone illustrating the cross-sectarian study and integration of Dignāgean Buddhist epistemology into early medieval Jain intellectual culture.

summary: The Nāgānanda ('Joy of the Serpents') is a five-act Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) attributed to King Harṣa of Kanauj (7th century CE), dramatizing the Buddhist legend of the Vidyādhara prince Jīmūtavāhana. The opening acts combine standard courtly kāvya romance with Jīmūtavāhana's courtship and marriage to Princess Malayavatī, while the fourth and fifth acts center on his Bodhisattva-like self-sacrifice: offering his own flesh on the slaughter stone to Garuḍa to rescue the young Nāga Śaṅkhacūḍa. Moved by Jīmūtavāhana's radical compassion and non-violence, Garuḍa renounces the slaughter of serpents and revives those previously consumed. Famous for invoking both the Buddha (munīndra / jina) and the Hindu goddess Gaurī, the work is an exceptional surviving exemplar of classical Buddhist dramatic literature.

summary: Nālandādahana ('The Burning of Nālandā') is a modern Sanskrit dance-drama of the ḍima type by V. Subramaniam. It is composed as Carnatic-style songs (pallavi, anupallavi, caraṇam) in various rāgas, mostly in ādi tāla. Students sing the praise of Nālandā, the abbot and senior monks discuss how to resist the coming Turkish army, and the destruction of the monastery follows. It ends with the librarian nun proclaiming that the fame and the truths of the Buddha's teaching taught at Nālandā cannot be destroyed.

summary: A short anonymous Sanskrit anthology of yogic instructions (upadeśa) ascribed to fourteen siddhas, among them Saraha, Kṛṣṇācārya, Virūpa, Vīṇāpāda, Diṅnāga and Matsyendra. The instructions deal with caṇḍālī, the 'swing' (dolā) of the breath, the drop (bindu) and seed-syllables in the cakras, and the kākatuṇḍī breathing technique, and are followed by an explanatory summary (uddeśasamuccaya). It is preserved only in a Nepalese manuscript and has no Tibetan translation.

summary: A Buddhist apotropaic dhāraṇī scripture focused on state protection and military victory. Set on Mount Svarṇaśṛṅga at the abode of Vaiśravaṇa, the Brahmanical deity Nārāyaṇa approaches the Buddha after suffering defeat at the hands of the asuras and requests a protective formula to ensure victory in combat. In response, the Buddha reveals the Mahāmāyāvijayavāhinī ('Victory-Bearing Great Illusion') dhāraṇī, recounts having received it in a previous age from Tathāgata Sarveśvara, and outlines the ritual application of the spell for monarchs facing battlefield conflict.

summary: Nṛtyaprasūti ('The Birth of Dance') is a modern Sanskrit dance-drama of the ḍima type by V. Subramaniam, written as songs set to Carnatic rāgas (Gauḷa, Haṃsadhvani, Darbār, Nāṭakuriñji, Pantuvarāḷi, Nītimati, etc.) with pallavi/anupallavi/caraṇam divisions. The nāndī praises the Buddha as conqueror of Māra, tamer of the elephant and turner of the dharmacakra under the tree. The two scenes then show the gods oppressed by the Tripura demons and appealing to Śiva, the destruction of Tripura (narrated by Nārada at Pārvatī's request), and the gods celebrating Śiva's tāṇḍava and Pārvatī's lāsya at Kailāsa as the origin of dance.

summary: The Paramārthastava ('Hymn to Ultimate Reality') is a short hymn of eleven verses attributed to Nāgārjuna and canonical as the fourth praise in the Catuḥstava quartet. It articulates Madhyamaka apophasis within devotional verse: because the Buddha is unarisen (anutpanna), unlocated (asthita), and beyond language (vākpathātīta), he cannot be praised in an ultimate sense (paramārtha). Consequently, praise can only take place conditionally via conventional designation (lokaprajñapti), culminating in the realization that in emptiness there is neither praised nor praiser.

It arranges the maxims by the adhyāya and pāda of the Aṣṭādhyāyī in which they become relevant, and explains their justification (jñāpaka, yukti) and application with frequent discussion of the Nyāsa and other earlier commentators. This e-text contains paribhāṣās 1–102, up to the end of the eighth adhyāya.

summary: The Pañcakrama ('Five Stages') is the foundational manual of the completion stage (niṣpannakrama) according to the Ārya tradition of the Guhyasamāja Tantra. It outlines five sequential yogic stages of subtle-body meditation leading to awakening: speech isolation (vajrajāpa), mind purification (sarvaśuddhiviśuddhi / cittaviśuddhi), self-consecration / illusory body (svādhiṣṭhāna / māyādeha), clear light (abhisaṃbodhi / prabhāsvara), and nondual union (yuganaddha). Composed c. 8th–9th century CE, chapters 1 and 3–5 are attributed to the tantric Nāgārjuna, while chapter 2 is attributed to Śākyamitra.

summary: Pañcarakṣādevīstotrāṇi is a cycle of five five-verse hymns (25 verses total) celebrating the five protective goddesses of the Pañcarakṣā pentad: Mahāpratisarā, Mahāmantrānusāriṇī, Mahāmāyūrī, Mahāśītavatī, and Mahāsāhasrapramardinī. Each hymn extols the apotropaic efficacy of the deity and her dhāraṇī in dispelling snakebites, illnesses, hostile planetary influences (graha), and calamities. The cycle forms a core component of traditional Newar Buddhist devotional and liturgical practice.

summary: The Pañcaskandhaprakaraṇa (or Pañcaskandhaka) is an introductory Abhidharma manual composed by Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE) that presents a systematic categorization of mental and physical phenomena according to the Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda framework. It defines the components of existence categorized under the five aggregates (skandhas), twelve sense fields (āyatanas), and eighteen elements (dhātus), famously incorporating the specifically Yogācāra doctrines of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and afflicted mentality (kliṣṭamanas) alongside the standard catalogue of fifty-one mental factors (caittas). This specific electronic text represents the 1955/1956 Sanskrit retro-translation from Tibetan executed by Shanti Bhikshu Shastri, which historically served as the primary Sanskrit surrogate for the work prior to the rediscovery and 2008 publication of the original Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscript from the Potala Palace.

summary: A short five-verse Sanskrit Buddhist devotional hymn (stotra) dedicated to the Five Tathāgatas presiding over the five Buddha families (kulas): Buddha/Vairocana, Vajra/Akṣobhya, Ratna/Ratnasambhava, Padma/Amitābha, and Viśva/Amoghasiddhi. Each stanza employs elaborate alliteration (yamaka) built upon the family name (buddha, vajra, ratna, padma, viśva) to celebrate the respective Tathāgata's enlightened qualities and salvific activity. Preserved in Newar devotional anthologies, it reflects traditional Mahāyāna-Vajrayāna liturgical worship.

summary: The Pañcaśatikāprajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 500 Lines') is a late Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā sūtra set on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, in which the Buddha instructs the Elder Subhūti on the nature of dharmas. The text is celebrated for integrating core Prajñāpāramitā emptiness ontology with Yogācāra terminology and concepts akin to the three natures (trisvabhāva), repeatedly analyzing dharmas in terms of non-existence (abhāva), actual/true existence (sadbhāva), and suchness (tathābhāva). Due to this synthesis, Tibetan Jonang master Dölpopa Sherab Gyaltsen and later gzhan stong thinkers considered it a sūtra of definitive meaning (nītārtha). Thought to be lost in the original Sanskrit, the sūtra was rediscovered in a unique palm-leaf manuscript preserved at the Norbulingka in Lhasa and first critically edited by Li Xuezhu and Fujita Yoshimichi in 2016.

summary: A short modern Sanskrit poem of 15 anuṣṭubh stanzas by the Sri Lankan monk Davuldena Jñāneśvara, written at the age of 87 and addressed to Dharmaratna (Tampalawela Dhammaratana). The poet laments the infirmities of old age: trembling, failing sight that spectacles (upacakṣus) no longer help, loss of memory, and his books lying unread in the library to be gnawed by worms and mice. Recalling the Buddhist teaching that everything in saṃsāra ends in decay, except the imperishable liberation taught by the Muni, he voices regret (paścāttāpa) for his lost youth and his inability to compose further poetry.

summary: The Piṇḍīkrama (also known as Piṇḍīkramasādhana or Piṇḍīkṛtasādhana) is the principal generation-stage (utpattikrama) liturgical manual of the Ārya exegesis of the Guhyasamāja Tantra, traditionally attributed to the tantric master Nāgārjuna (c. 8th–9th century CE). Consisting of 226 verses and interspersed ritual mantras, it details the purification of conceptual thought (vikalpa), the erection of the protective circle, the generation of the 32-deity Akṣobhyaguhyasamāja maṇḍala, and subsequent internal and external offerings. Although often transmitted alongside the completion-stage treatise Pañcakrama, it is an independent foundational manual for the Ārya school's practice.

summary: The Potalakāṣṭaka is an anonymous eight-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn (aṣṭaka) eulogizing Avalokiteśvara in association with his mythical mountain residence, Mount Potalaka. The verses praise his physical markers, his crown bearing Amitābha, and his salvific compassion in freeing sentient beings from disease and the cycles of samsara. Preserved in the Newar Buddhist liturgical tradition of Nepal, it was edited by Janardan Shastri Pandey in the Bauddha Stotra Saṃgraha (1994).

summary: The Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi ('Attainment of the Certainty of Wisdom and Skilful Means') by the 8th-century tantric master Anaṅgavajra is one of the foundational texts in the Tibetan canonical cycle of the Seven Siddhi Texts (Saptasiddhi / Grub pa sde bdun). Originally composed in five chapters (represented in this e-text by chapters 1–4), it articulates the nondual synthesis of prajñā and upāya as mahāsukha, treating the worship of the vajrācārya, the esoteric consecration of bodhicitta (bodhicittābhiṣeka), and the meditation on reality (tattvabhāvanā). Verses from chapter 4 were famously cited and absorbed into later Yoginītantra literature, notably the Sampuṭodbhavatantra.

summary: A short commentary on the Heart Sūtra (Prajñāpāramitāhṛdaya) attributed to Atīśa Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna, composed in Tibet at the request of a monk Sādhuprajña (per the closing verses). It frames the sūtra with Dignāga's account of the sūtra introduction (citing Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārtha 3–4) and Vimalamitra's eightfold exegesis, and reads the sūtra as teaching the five paths, the eight profound points and, for those of sharp faculties, the mantra. The Sanskrit text here is a modern restoration from the Tibetan translation.

summary: The Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra ('Heart Sūtra') is one of the most widely recited and influential texts of Mahāyāna Buddhism, condensing the vast Prajñāpāramitā literature into an essential doctrinal summary. This e-text presents the short recension (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā), which omits the traditional introductory frame (nidāna) and concludes directly with the mantra. Avalokiteśvara explains to Śāriputra that the five aggregates and all constituent phenomena of Buddhist abhidharma are empty of inherent existence ('form is emptiness, emptiness is form'), culminating in the celebrated mantra 'gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā'.

summary: The Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra ('Heart of the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra') is one of the most widely recited and commented-upon texts in Mahāyāna Buddhism. This e-text preserves the complete longer recension (vistaramātṛkā), which includes the full narrative setting (nidāna) on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha and concludes with the Buddha rising from samādhi to praise Avalokiteśvara's exposition. The bodhisattva expounds to Śāriputra the emptiness of intrinsic existence (svabhāvaśūnyatā) of all five aggregates, sense spheres, and Noble Truths, concluding with the famous mantra: gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.

summary: The Prajñāpāramitāstuti is a short five-verse devotional hymn (stotra) composed in anuṣṭubh metre extolling the Perfection of Wisdom. Prajñāpāramitā is addressed as the supreme goddess, free from conceptual construction and change, the mother of the Buddhas, the grandmother of the Bodhisattvas, and the embodiment of wisdom, mindfulness, and the ten perfections. The hymn forms part of the Newar Sanskrit Buddhist liturgical and stotra repertoire.

summary: The Pramāṇavārttika ('Commentary on Valid Cognition') is the foundational masterwork of Dharmakīrti (ca. 6th–7th century CE) and the definitive text of Buddhist epistemology, logic, and philosophy of language. Composed in verse as an extensive critical development of Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya, it establishes perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna) as the only two means of valid cognition, formulates the Buddhist theory of conceptual exclusion (apoha), and provides rational defenses of the Buddha's authority, rebirth, and the Four Noble Truths. This e-text contains the complete set of metrical root verses (kārikās) across four chapters arranged according to the commentarial tradition of Manorathanandin.

summary: Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā ('Clear Words'), also titled Madhyamakaśāstravṛtti, is a 7th-century CE Sanskrit prose commentary on the 27 chapters of Nāgārjuna's fundamental Madhyamakaśāstra (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā). It is the only fully surviving Indian commentary on Nāgārjuna's root verses preserved in Sanskrit. Candrakīrti defines the Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka approach by defending Buddhapālita's method of reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) against Bhāvaviveka's use of autonomous inference (svatantra), making the work an essential foundation for the study of Indian and Tibetan Madhyamaka philosophy.

summary: The Pratimālakṣaṇavivaraṇa is a Buddhist Sanskrit commentary explaining the canonical iconometric treatise Pratimālakṣaṇa (or Samyaksambuddhabhāṣitapratimālakṣaṇa). summary: The Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā ('Verses on the Heart of Dependent Origination') is a concise seven-stanza Madhyamaka treatise that condenses the twelve links (nidāna) of dependent arising into three interrelated categories: defilements (kleśa), karma, and suffering (duḥkha). It demonstrates that empirical entities arise entirely through conditioned causal processes without any transmigrating soul or independent entity (sattva). Employing eight classical analogies (such as a lamp, an echo, a reflection in a mirror, and an imprint of a seal), the text establishes that cyclic rebirth takes place without substantial transmigration (asaṅkrama), culminating in the celebrated assertion that in ultimate reality nothing is to be subtracted and nothing added.

summary: The Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayakārikā with Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayavyākhyāna is an epitome of the doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna. It reduces the twelve links of existence into three fundamental categories: afflictions (kleśa), karma, and suffering (duḥkha), explaining how they perpetuate cyclic existence like an endlessly turning wheel without any permanent agent or substantial soul transmigrating between lives. Emphasizing that purely empty factors arise from empty conditions, the text concludes with well-known verses declaring that in ultimate reality nothing is to be removed and nothing added.

summary: The Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśasūtra is a canonical Buddhist discourse delivered by the Buddha at Jetavana in Śrāvastī. It is divided into two parts: the 'fundamental exposition' (ādi), which articulates the standard twelvefold formula of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) from ignorance (avidyā) to aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), and the 'detailed analysis' (vibhaṅga), which provides concise definitions of each link. The text represents an early stage of doctrinal systematization parallel to the Pāḷi Vibhaṅgasutta (SN 12.2), Sūtra 16 (Ādisūtra) of the Sanskrit Nidānasaṃyukta, Taishō 124 (translated by Xuanzang) in the Chinese Canon, and Toh 211 in the Tibetan Kangyur.

summary: The Pāramitāsamāsa ("Compendium of the Perfections") is a kāvya-style verse treatise in six chapters on the six perfections of the bodhisattva: generosity, morality, patience, vigour, meditation and wisdom. Each is presented as grounded in compassion and the bodhisattva's resolve, with the final chapter on prajñā. It is ascribed to (Ārya)Śūra and was translated into Tibetan by Vairocanarakṣita (D 3944).

Each goddess is invoked in conjunction with one of the directional sacred seats (pīṭhas/kṣetras, such as Prayāga, Vārāṇasī, Kolāpura, Aṭṭahāsa, and Jayantī) and corresponding sacred trees (udumbara, tāla, vaṭa, kadamba, nimba, karañja). Preserved in the Newar Buddhist tradition, the hymn concludes with a phalaśruti (vv. 61–67) promising protection from disease, conflicts, premature death, and hostile sorcery.

summary: A 15-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of praise (stotra) in anuṣṭubh metre addressed to Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (invoked as Lokanātha and Lokanāyaka). Verse 2 commemorates the Newar legend of the twelve-year drought in Nepal (dvādaśābdeṣu anāvṛṣṭiḥ) during the reign of Licchavi king Narendradeva (7th century CE), in which Avalokiteśvara (associated with Bungadyo / Karuṇāmaya) was established in Nepal to relieve famine and suffering. Most stanzas conclude with the prayerful refrain 'rakṣa māṃ lokanāyaka'.

attribution_note: Authorship is historically disputed across Buddhist traditions. The Tibetan tradition attributes the root verses to the Bodhisattva Maitreya and the prose commentary (vyākhyā) to Asaṅga. The Chinese tradition (beginning in Fazang's commentaries and subsequent catalogs) attributes the entire treatise (Jiujing yisheng baoxing lun, T 1611, translated by Ratnamati in 511 CE) to *Sāramati (Jianyi / Suoluomodi). Extant Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscripts discovered in Tibet carry no author colophon. While Johnston initially considered Sthiramati (later retracted), modern critical scholarship (Takasaki, Schmithausen, Kano) distinguishes earlier and later textual strata, placing the final compilation and commentary in the 5th century CE and largely corroborating the link to Sāramati.

summary: The Ratnagotravibhāga (also widely cited as the Mahāyānottaratantraśāstra or Uttaratantra) is the preeminent classical Indian treatise systematically articulating the doctrine of buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha). Structured around seven 'vajra points' (vajrapada)—Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, the element/lineage of awakening (dhātu/gotra), awakening itself (bodhi), enlightened qualities (guṇa), and buddha-activity (karman)—the text demonstrates that the primordial, luminous nature of mind is present within all sentient beings, concealed only by adventitious defilements (āgantukakleśa). It synthesizes and comments extensively upon key tathāgatagarbha sūtras, notably the Tathāgatagarbhasūtra, the Śrīmālādevīsiṃhanādasūtra, and the Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa.

summary: The Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī is a collection of ten philosophical monographs (nibandhas) composed in the 11th century CE by Ratnakīrti, a master at Vikramaśīla and pupil of Jñānaśrīmitra. The collection represents the final flourishing of classical Buddhist Pramāṇavāda and Sautrāntika-Yogācāra philosophy in northern India, formulating rigorous responses to Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā opponents. Major subjects addressed include the proof of the Buddha's omniscience (Sarvajñasiddhi), the refutation of God as creator (Īśvarasādhanadūṣaṇa), the apoha nominalist theory of word meaning (Apohasiddhi), positive and negative proofs of universal momentariness (Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi), the refutation of enduring entities (Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa), the logic of invariable concomitance and reduction of valid cognitions (Vyāptinirṇaya, Pramāṇāntarbhāvaprakaraṇa), and an ultimate idealist critique of external objects and other minds (Citrādvaitaprakāśavāda, Santānāntaradūṣaṇa).

summary: A 25-verse Sanskrit hymn of praise (stotra) dedicated to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (Lokeśvara), composed by the prominent 15th-century Indian master Vanaratna (1384–1468 CE). Drawing upon the cosmological motifs of the Kāraṇḍavyūha Sūtra, the hymn lauds Avalokiteśvara as the supreme protector from whose body major Hindu divinities (including Maheśvara, Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, Sarasvatī, Vāyu, and Varuṇa) emanate to guide diverse sentient beings. The poem concludes with praises of the bodhisattva's compassionate choice to remain in saṃsāra, his wonder-working powers, physical beauty, and manifestation through the three Buddha-bodies (kāyas).

summary: The Ratnāvalī ('Precious Garland') is a didactic and political epistle (rājaparikathā) in five chapters (500 verses) composed by Nāgārjuna and addressed to an Indian monarch (traditionally a Sātavāhana king). It integrates pragmatic ethical advice on statecraft, royal justice, and social welfare with central Madhyamaka philosophical teachings on emptiness (śūnyatā), the two truths, and the path of the bodhisattva. Whereas the work survives complete in Tibetan and Chinese translations, early modern Sanskrit editions, including this BST 10 text, preserve only chapters 1, 2.1–46, and 4 from a fragmentary Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript.

summary: The Rūpastava is a 24-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn praising the divine bodily appearance and auspicious marks of an enlightened being. Preserved within the Newar Buddhist liturgical corpus of the Kathmandu Valley, it offers an anatomical sequence of veneration, praising in turn the hair, face, crown, eyes, voice, body, garments, arms, hands, navel, and wheel-marked feet. Although designated in its colophon as a hymn to Avalokiteśvara, the refrains consistently praise the 'Daśabala' and the phalaśruti terms it a Sugatastava.

summary: The Saddharmalaṅkāvatārasūtra is an influential Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra that synthesizes Yogācāra consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā / cittamātra) doctrines with the tathāgatagarbha teaching. Framed as an exposition delivered by the Buddha on Mount Malaya in Laṅkā to the bodhisattva Mahāmati and king Rāvaṇa, it expounds the eight consciousnesses (especially ālayavijñāna), the five dharmas, the three intrinsic natures (trisvabhāva), the two kinds of selflessness (dharmanairātmya and pudgalanairātmya), and the doctrine of vegetarianism (māṃsabhakṣaṇaparivarta). The text exerted foundational influence across Mahāyāna philosophical schools, Tibetan scholasticism, and East Asian Chan/Zen traditions.

summary: The Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra ('The White Lotus of the True Dharma') is one of the most celebrated and influential Mahāyāna scriptures. It propounds the doctrine of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), declaring that the apparent three vehicles (śrāvakayāna, pratyekabuddhayāna, and bodhisattvayāna) are provisional pedagogical devices (upāyakauśalya) and that all beings are destined for unexcelled awakening. Renowned for its rich parables—such as the burning house, the prodigal son, the medicinal herbs, and the gem concealed in the garment—the sūtra also reveals the Buddha's lifespan to be immeasurable and his parinirvāṇa an expedient display. Composed in several developmental strata from roughly the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE, it became the doctrinal cornerstone of East Asian Buddhist traditions such as Tiantai, Tendai, and Nichiren.

summary: The Saddharmapārājikā is a late medieval Newar Buddhist ritual and expiation tract belonging to the distinctive Nepalese cluster of 'Pārājikā' texts (alongside the Vajrasattva-, Mañjuśrī-, Tārā-, and Lokeśvarapārājikā). Despite utilizing the monastic term pārājikā, the treatise does not govern monastic disciplinary codes, but rather adapts Dharmaśāstric notions of karmic ripening (karmavipāka) and atonement (prāyaścitta) to Newar Buddhist lay life. It specifies the penances and temporal periods required to purify grave sins (such as the slaughter of an arhat, a brahmin, or a cow), concluding with manual rites and mantras for purification with the five bovine products (pañcagavya) and kuśa water.

summary: The Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānasūtra is a massive Indian Buddhist canonical sūtra that combines early Abhidharma doctrine, cosmological description of realms of rebirth, and meditative praxis. Chapter 2 focuses on internal mindfulness of phenomena (dharmānupaśyanā / dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) undertaken by an ascetic practitioner (yogācāra), analyzing sensory experience, the eighteen errant movements of mind (aṣṭādaśa manovyabhicāraḥ), and karmic causation governing transmigration. Stuart's 2015 critical edition of this chapter is based on the single surviving Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscript preserved in the Tibet Autonomous Region.

summary: The Sahajadvibhujahevajrasādhana is a Tantric liturgical ritual work (sādhana) dedicated to the two-armed (dvibhuja) innate (sahaja) form of Hevajra. Authored by Alalavajra on the instruction of Nandipāda, the 74-verse text articulates the non-dual philosophy of sahaja mind, standard preparatory elements including the generation of bodhicitta and refuge, emptiness meditation, and the sequential visualization of two-armed Hevajra and his retinue.

summary: The Sambandhaparīkṣā ('Investigation of Relation') is one of Dharmakīrti's seven core pramāṇa works, dedicated to refuting real, mind-independent relations such as inherence (samavāya), contact (saṃyoga), and substantial causality. Dharmakīrti demonstrates that discrete entities are momentary particulars (svalakṣaṇa) existing solely in their own natures, and that relation is merely a conceptual construction (kalpanā) projected for verbal usage. This digital text transmits kārikās 1–22 along with the Sanskrit vyākhyā of the Digambara Jaina philosopher Prabhācandra, who extracted and critiqued them in his Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa.

summary: The Samyaksambuddhabhāṣitapratimālakṣaṇa (also known as the Pratimālakṣaṇa or Buddhapratimālakṣaṇa) is a primary manual of Buddhist iconometry (tālamāna). Framed as a discourse at Jetavana where the Buddha instructs Śāriputra on how devotees should fashion icons after the Teacher's parinirvāṇa, the text establishes canonical proportions (pramāṇa) for images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Across 54 verses, it details precise measurements in bodily units (aṅgula, mātrā, vyāma) for the uṣṇīṣa, cranial contours, facial features, torso, and limbs, as well as distinct facial types (such as oval and round) for various classes of divine, human, and semi-divine beings. Widely preserved in Nepalese manuscripts and incorporated into both the Tibetan Tengyur and the Chinese canon, the work served as a fundamental textual authority for religious sculpture and painting in northern Buddhism.

summary: The Samādhirājasūtra ('King of Samādhis Sūtra', often cited by Indian Madhyamaka commentators as Candrapradīpasūtra) is an influential Mahāyāna scripture in 40 chapters expounding the meditative absorption (samādhi) that reveals the fundamental equality and emptiness of all phenomena (sarvadharmasvabhāvasamatā). Delivered by the Buddha on Vulture Peak to the youth Candraprabha, the text combines exposition of non-arising and ultimate reality with teachings on ethical discipline, ascetic practices (dhūtaguṇa), dhāraṇī formulas, and past-life narratives (jātakas). It was widely quoted as a scriptural authority on emptiness by Candrakīrti, Śāntideva, and Prajñākaramati, and served as a foundational sūtra source for contemplative traditions in Tibet, particularly Sūtra Mahāmudrā.

summary: The Samājasādhanavyavastholi is a foundational ritual treatise on the generation stage (utpattikrama) of the Guhyasamājatantra according to the Ārya (Nāgārjuna) school. It structures the Guhyasamāja sādhana by establishing correspondences between Buddhist cosmogony—the periodic dissolution and reappearance of the physical receptacle (bhājanaloka) and sentient beings (sattvaloka)—and the yogic generation of the maṇḍala and its thirty-two deities. The text served as an essential authority for later commentarial traditions, prominently utilized by Tsongkhapa in his exposition of the generation stage.

summary: The Santānāntarasiddhi ('Proof of Other Mind-Streams') is a concise treatise by Dharmakīrti (c. 600–660 CE) traditionally numbered among his 'Seven Treatises' on logic and epistemology. Framed as a dialogue opening with a single verse and proceeding through 93 prose sections, it resolves the philosophical challenge of other minds from within the Vijñānavāda (Cittamātra) idealist system, directly rebutting the objection that idealism logically degenerates into solipsism. Dharmakīrti demonstrates that just as a realist infers intentional consciousness from observing physical movements and speech, an idealist can equally infer distinct intentional mental continua from coordinated sensory appearances without positing mind-independent external matter.

summary: The Santānāntarasiddhi ('Proof of Other Mental Continua') by Dharmakīrti (c. 6th–7th century) is a treatise in 93 verses demonstrating from an idealist (Vijñānavāda / Yogācāra) standpoint that the rejection of external physical reality does not entail solipsism, since purposive physical actions and speech permit a valid inference to the existence of other mental series. Vinītadeva's Santānāntarasiddhiṭīkā (c. 8th century) is the earliest surviving commentary on the text, providing word-by-word glosses and philosophical defense against external-world realist and solipsist objections. Because both works were largely lost in their original Sanskrit and survived intact only in Tibetan translation, this e-text comprises the modern Sanskrit back-translation reconstructed by J. S. Negi.

summary: The Saptajinastava ('Praise of the Seven Conquerors') is a short Buddhist hymn of praise composed in nine verses. The first seven stanzas venerate the lineage of the seven past Buddhas (Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni), followed by a stanza honoring the future Buddha Maitreya, and concluding with a dedication of merit (puṇyapariṇāmanā). The hymn is known from Sanskrit manuscripts in Nepal and Tibet as well as medieval Chinese and Tibetan translations.

summary: The Saptavidhānuttarastotra is an anonymous twelve-verse devotional hymn dedicated to Avalokiteśvara (invoked as Lokanātha). It adapts the classical Mahāyāna framework of the 'sevenfold supreme worship' (saptavidhā anuttarā pūjā)—salutation, veneration, refuge, confession, and merit-dedication—into a praise poem concluding with an aspiration for rebirth in Sukhāvatī. The hymn belongs to the liturgical corpus maintained in Nepalese Newar Buddhism.

summary: The Saptaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 700 Lines', also designated Mañjuśrīparivartāparaparyāyā or Puṇyakṣetranirdeśa) is an influential Mahāyāna scripture belonging to the Prajñāpāramitā corpus. Set in Śrāvastī's Jeta Grove, it consists of profound dialogues between the Buddha, Śāriputra, and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī emphasizing the unreality of dualistic categories, the unoriginated nature (anutpāda) of all dharmas, and the non-apprehending contemplation of the Tathāgata. The scripture is celebrated in East Asian Buddhist traditions for introducing the 'single-array absorption' (ekavyūhasamādhi, traditionally interpreted as the 'one-practice samādhi'), which links insight into the non-differentiated dharmadhātu to concentrated mindfulness of a Buddha.

summary: The Saptākṣarastotra is an anonymous eight-verse Buddhist hymn (ślokāṣṭaka) addressed to Āryāvalokiteśvara, reflecting the syncretic Newar Buddhist milieu of the Kathmandu Valley. The text explicitly invokes Avalokiteśvara as Lokanātha, Matsyendra (Matsyendranātha / Karuṇāmaya), and Viṣṇu, praises him alongside the four Buddhist consorts (Locanā, Māmakī, Tārā, and Pāṇḍarā), and describes him wearing Amitābha on his crown while offering protection against yakṣas, rākṣasas, vetālas, and nāgas.

summary: The Dohākoṣa of the siddha Saraha is a seminal collection of rhymed Apabhraṃśa couplets (dohās) teaching Sahajayāna and Mahāmudrā realisation. The poetry harshly critiques Vedic Brahmanism, Jain asceticism, and scholastic Buddhist classifications, pointing instead to the non-dual, spontaneously innate nature of the mind (sahaja). In this e-text, the dohās are preserved within the Sanskrit prose commentary (Dohākoṣapañjikā / Sahajāmnāyapañjikā) attributed to Advayavajra, which elucidates the tantric and philosophical meaning of each verse.

summary: The Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkārasūtra ('The Ornament of the Light of Wisdom that Enters the Domain of All Buddhas') is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra presented through dialogues between the Buddha and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta concerning the nature of awakening, the transcendent realm of the buddhas, and ultimate reality. The text emphasizes that all dharmas are unoriginated (anutpāda), non-dual, and that the fundamental nature of mind is luminous (prakṛtiprabhāsvara). Extensively cited in key Indian treatises including the Ratnagotravibhāga, the sūtra was known through three early Chinese versions and a Tibetan translation before a complete Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscript dating to the Pāla period was rediscovered in 1999 at the Potala Palace in Lhasa.

summary: The Sarvadurgatipariśodhanatantra ('Tantra of the Elimination of All Evil Destinies') is an influential Buddhist Yogatantra of the Vairocana cycle, dating roughly to the late 7th to 8th century CE. Set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the tantra opens with Śakra pleading with Śākyamuni to deliver the god Vimalamaṇiprabha, who has fallen into the lower realms upon his death. Centering on Sarvavid Vairocana and his maṇḍalas, the text provides elaborate ritual instructions—including initiations, sādhanas, apotropaic rites, and especially mortuary and post-mortem ceremonies—designed to purify negative karmic imprints and ensure liberation from adverse transmigrations.

summary: The Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṅgraha is the foundational root tantra of the Yogatantra class in Indian esoteric Buddhism, dating to the late 7th century CE. Centered on Mahāvairocana and the five Buddha families (kulas) within the Vajradhātu maṇḍala, it expounds the enlightenment of Sarvārthasiddhi via the five progressive realizations (pañcākārābhisambodhi) along with extensive rituals for initiation (abhiṣeka), mudrās, and mantras. It forms the primary doctrinal and ritual bedrock for East Asian esoteric Buddhism (Zhenyan and Shingon) and directly influenced subsequent Indo-Tibetan tantric traditions.

summary: A Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture set on Mount Potalaka, the realm of Avalokiteśvara, where the Buddha Śākyamuni enters a samādhi called *sarvasattvamahākaruṇājñānasthita*, radiating light throughout the cosmos to illuminate the Buddha-fields and alleviate the sufferings of all beings. Bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī, and Vajrapāṇi, along with an assembly of directional kings (lokapālas), yakṣiṇīs, and deities, offer and endorse protective dhāraṇī mantras for the benefit and safeguard of dharma-reciters in future ages. In South Asia the Sanskrit text is preserved among the 6th–7th-century Gilgit manuscripts, and it circulated in eastern and northern Buddhist traditions via Yijing's 701 CE Chinese rendering and an early 9th-century Tibetan translation.

summary: A short Mahāyāna devotional hymn of eleven verses in which the Buddha proclaims that propitiating and compassionately serving living beings (sattvārādhana) constitutes the true and highest adoration of the Tathāgata. The Buddha explains that his spiritual career, bodily sacrifices, and attainment of awakening were carried out entirely for the welfare of beings; therefore, harming beings injures the Buddha, while benefiting them brings supreme delight to him. The text was versified from or related to an episode in the canonical *Kṣāranadīsūtra.

summary: The Satyadvayāvatāra ('Entry into the Two Truths') is a concise 30-verse Madhyamaka treatise by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (982–1054 CE), composed during his stay in Suvarṇadvīpa at the request of the monk Devamati. It presents a Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka perspective on the two truths, classifying conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) into correct and incorrect, and arguing that ultimate reality (paramārthasatya) is beyond discursive and non-conceptual cognitions as well as formal pramāṇas. Because the original Sanskrit text does not survive, this e-text is a modern Sanskrit reconstruction (pratyuddhāra) based on the Tibetan canonical translation.

summary: The Satyasiddhiśāstra (also reconstructed as Tattvasiddhiśāstra; Chinese: Chengshi lun) is an extensive Buddhist scholastic treatise in 202 chapters by Harivarman (c. 3rd–4th century CE), reflecting Bahuśrutīya and Dārṣṭāntika/Sautrāntika doctrines. Organized around an introductory section and the Four Noble Truths, it defends a two-truth framework affirming the emptiness (śūnyatā) of both persons and dharmas, and expounds the progressive dismantling of provisional, phenomenal, and ultimate conceptual constructs. While lost in India, Kumārajīva's Chinese translation formed the foundational text of the Chinese Chengshi (Japanese Jōjitsu) school.

summary: The Saundarananda is an early classical Sanskrit mahākāvya in eighteen cantos composed by Aśvaghoṣa (c. 1st–2nd century CE). It recounts the conversion of the Buddha's handsome half-brother Nanda, depicting his infatuation with his wife Sundarī, his reluctant ordination, and his spiritual transformation guided by the Buddha. Employing ornate kāvya aesthetics, the work provides an elaborate exposition of Buddhist doctrine, sense-restraint, and meditation, culminating in Nanda's attainment of arhatship.

summary: The Sekoddeśa ('Summary of Initiation') consists of 174 verses traditionally considered an excerpt from the fifth chapter of the lost Kālacakra root tantra (Paramādibuddha). The text details subtle-body physiology, the visionary signs appearing in empty space (dhūmādi-nimitta), and the realization of imperishable bliss (akṣarasukha).

summary: The Sekoddeśapañjikā is an anonymous Indian Sanskrit commentary on the Sekoddeśa, a foundational scripture on initiations and yogic physiology belonging to the Kālacakra (Paramādibuddha) cycle. It provides verse-by-verse glosses explaining the stages of tantric consecration (abhiṣeka), the internal regulation of subtle winds and channels (nāḍī, prāṇāyāma), and the manifestation of divine forms (bimba) and mahāmudrā. The text is preserved incomplete in a unique Nepalese manuscript breaking off at verse 146, and was translated into Tibetan in the fourteenth century by Bu ston Rin chen grub.

summary: The Samāhitābhūmi ('Stage of Meditative Equipoise') constitutes the sixth chapter of the Maulī Bhūmi (Bahubhūmivastu) division of the Yogācārabhūmi. It offers an encyclopedic scholastic taxonomy of Buddhist concentration and meditation states, systematically treating the four dhyānas, eight liberations (vimokṣa), various samādhis, and meditative attainments (samāpatti), together with their accompanying mental factors (manaskāra) and meditative signs (nimitta). In modern Yogācāra scholarship, this section is widely recognized for preserving what Lambert Schmithausen identified as the earliest textual locus of the ālayavijñāna ('storehouse consciousness') concept, introduced to explain somatic survival and the continuity of mind during the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

summary: The Subodhālaṅkāra ('Lucid Ornamentation') is the foundational Theravāda manual of poetics and rhetoric in the Pāli language, composed in Sri Lanka in the late 12th or early 13th century by Saṅgharakkhita Mahāsāmi. Adapting classical Sanskrit kāvyaśāstra—primarily Daṇḍin's Kāvyādarśa—into Pāli, it systematically treats poetic faults (dosa), merits (guṇa), verbal and semantic figures of speech (alaṅkāra), and aesthetic sentiment (rasa), replacing Brahmanical illustrative verses with Buddhist devotions. In this e-text, all 371 Pāli stanzas are presented in full, alternating with an interlinear modern Sanskrit metrical rendering by Dr. Brahma Mitra Awasthi.

summary: The Suhṛllekha ('Letter to a Friend') is a celebrated Buddhist didactic poem of 123 stanzas traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna and addressed to a Śātavāhana monarch. Written in Āryāgīti metre, the text summarizes fundamental Mahāyāna and Buddhist lay ethics, including the six recollections, the ten virtuous actions, mindfulness, the hazards of sensory attachment, karma, the sufferings of cyclic existence (saṃsāra), and the bodhisattva path culminating in buddhahood. Because the original Sanskrit text has not survived in manuscript form and was preserved historically only in Tibetan and three Chinese translations, this electronic text reproduces a modern Sanskrit restoration (punaruddhāra) prepared by Dr. Padma Tendzin (CIHTS, 2002).

summary: The Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā), widely revered in East Asia as the Amitābha Sūtra, is a foundational scripture of Pure Land Buddhism. Set in Śrāvastī, Śākyamuni Buddha describes the western Buddha-field Sukhāvatī and its presiding Buddha Amitāyus (Amitābha) to his disciple Śāriputra, portraying in sensory detail its jeweled pavilions, radiant lotus ponds, music, and divine birds that ceaselessly proclaim the Dharma. The sūtra teaches that living beings who hear Amitāyus's name and hold it single-mindedly without distraction will be welcomed by Amitābha at the point of death and reborn in his realm, a promise affirmed by the Buddhas of the six directions.

summary: The Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha is a foundational Mahāyāna sūtra and the principal scriptural authority for Pure Land Buddhism. Set on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) in Rājagṛha, the Buddha Śākyamuni narrates to Ānanda how the monk Dharmākara, in the presence of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, generated the resolve for awakening and made forty-eight great vows to establish the western realm of Sukhāvatī and become the Buddha Amitābha (Amitāyus). The sūtra expounds the visual and spiritual splendors of this paradise, delineates the requirements for rebirth there through faith, recollection, and merits, and includes instructions addressed to the bodhisattva Ajita (Maitreya) on dispelling doubt.

summary: The Suprabhātastava ('Praise of the Auspicious Dawn') is a Buddhist hymn, mostly in mālinī, in which the poet contrasts the ever-awake Buddha with Hindu gods and sages (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Indra, Agni, Balarāma, Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, the ṛṣis), all shown as asleep in passion, under the refrain 'daśabala tava nityaṃ suprabhātaṃ prabhātam'. The colophon ascribes it to King Śrīharṣa. This e-text has the 25 stanzas of a Drepung manuscript, a longer recension than the usual 24.

summary: The Suprabhātastotra ('Auspicious Morning Hymn') is a 24-stanza devotional hymn in classical kāvya metres praising the Buddha (addressed throughout as Daśabala). Attributed to King Harṣadeva (Harṣavardhana of Kanauj, r. 606–647 CE), the composition contrasts the awakened state of the Buddha with celestial and Brahmanical gods (such as Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu, Indra, Balarāma, Gaṇapati, Kumāra), as well as celebrated Vedic sages and worldly ascetics, depicting them as languishing in sleep, attachment, and ignorance. Verses 2 through 18 culminate in the recurring daily refrain 'daśabala tava nityaṃ suprabhātaṃ prabhātam' ('O Ten-Powered One, may you always have an auspicious dawn').

summary: The Suvarṇaprabhāsasūtra ('Sūtra of the Golden Light') is an influential Mahāyāna canonical scripture that synthesizes doctrinal expositions of emptiness (śūnyatā) and the boundless lifespan of the Tathāgata with rituals of repentance and state protection. A pivotal episode centers on the bodhisattva Ruciraketu's vision of a golden drum radiating stanzas on confession and purification (deśanā). Protective deities including the Four Heavenly Kings (Caturmahārāja), Sarasvatī, Śrī, and Dṛḍhā pledge to guard righteous sovereigns and realms that uphold the sūtra, while subsequent chapters recount past-life narratives of the Buddha, notably the Vyāghrīparivarta (Mahāsattva jātaka) where the bodhisattva sacrifices his life to feed a starving tigress and her cubs.

summary: The Suvikrāntavikrāmiparipṛcchā (also known as the Sārdhadvisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, or Perfection of Wisdom in 2,500 Lines) is a canonical Mahāyāna sūtra in seven chapters. Set at the Veṇuvana in Rājagṛha, it features an extensive dialogue between the Buddha and the Bodhisattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin detailing the nature and cultivation of prajñāpāramitā. The sūtra expounds the core doctrine of the non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) and lack of intrinsic existence (asvabhāvatva) of all dharmas, maintaining that true bodhisattva practice avoids attachment to conceptual markers or spiritual attainments.

attribution_note: Anonymous; no author is named in the e-text or in the DSBC catalogue. The work is a short Sanskrit prose tract (with quoted verses) arguing FOR svabhāvavāda/ahetuvāda against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika causality (prāgabhāva, Īśvara) and against Śaṅkara's līlā explanation of creation (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya 2.1.33 is quoted as 'bhagavatpādāḥ'); the author speaks in the first person ('atra mayā ucyate'), cites Praśastapāda and the svabhāvavāda pūrvapakṣa verses that Śāntarakṣita reports in Tattvasaṅgraha ch. 4 (Svabhāvaparīkṣā, vv. 110ff.). Prose style (commas, polemics against Śaṅkara, compiled arguments) suggests a modern scholastic Sanskrit composition rather than a classical treatise, but this cannot be confirmed.

summary: A short anonymous Sanskrit prose tract defending svabhāvavāda (things arise from their own nature without causes) against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika causal theory (including prāgabhāva and Īśvara as creator) and against Śaṅkara's explanation of creation as līlā (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya 2.1.33). It closes by quoting the svabhāvavāda verses known from the pūrvapakṣa of Śāntarakṣita's Tattvasaṅgraha, ch. 4 (rājīvakesarādīnāṃ vaicitryaṃ kaḥ karoti..., kaṇṭakataikṣṇya). Despite its Madhyamaka classification in DSBC, it is not a Madhyamaka work.

summary: The Svastyayanagāthā is a 17-verse benedictory and apotropaic hymn preserved in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit within the Chatravastu narrative of the Mahāvastu (Vol. I, pp. 290–295). It represents the northern Buddhist Sanskrit parallel to the well-known Theravāda Ratana Sutta (Sn 2.1 / Khp 6), chanted by the Buddha upon arriving in epidemic-stricken Vaiśālī as an act of truth (satyakriyā) to expel malicious non-human spirits and restore welfare. Each stanza extols specific transcendent virtues of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, culminating in the protective refrain 'etena satyena susvasti bhotu manuṣyato vā amanuṣyato vā' ('by this truth may there be well-being, whether from humans or non-humans'). Transmitted also as an independent protective text (paritta/rakṣā), it is preserved in Tibetan translation in the Kangyur under the title bDe legs su 'gyur ba'i tshigs su bcad pa (Toh 818, Toh 1102).

summary: The Svayambhūpurāṇa is the foundational mythic chronicle and pilgrimage guide (sthala-māhātmya) of Newar Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley. It recounts the myth of the primordial lake (Nāgadaha) drained through the Chobhar gorge by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, followed by the appearance of the primordial lotus and the self-existent flame (svayambhūjyotis) of the Dharmadhātu enshrined within the Svayambhū Mahācaitya (Swayambhunath). The work incorporates visits of the previous Buddhas of antiquity, legends of local tīrthas, deities, and nāgas, and the transformation of the valley into a Buddhist kingdom. This 10-chapter recension represents the intermediate (madhyama) version of the text.

summary: The Svayaṃbhūstava is a seven-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of praise (stotra) addressed to Svayambhū, the primordial self-originated Buddha (Ādibuddha) manifest as flame or light (jyotīrūpa) at the Svayambhū Mahācaitya in Nepal. Reflecting medieval Nepalese syncretic devotion, the stotra identifies Svayambhū with the Three Jewels, the Bodhisattvas, the lokapālas, and major Hindu devas (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśa), as well as the source of cosmic creation via the five wisdoms (pañcajñāna). A concluding phalaśruti attributes the text to the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārāja) and promises sovereignty and liberation to those who recite it.

summary: The Sāmānyadūṣaṇa ('Refutation of Universals') by Aśoka (c. late 10th to early 11th c. CE) is a short polemical treatise defending Buddhist nominalism against the realist ontology of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā. Following Dignāga and Dharmakīrti, Aśoka argues that an eternal, unitary, and pervasive universal (sāmānya) cannot be established by either perception or inference, demonstrating that common verbal and mental designations are satisfactorily explained by causal capacities and differential exclusion (apoha). The text concludes with the celebrated five-fingers argument: one who claims to perceive a sixth common entity over and above the five distinct fingers might just as well perceive horns on their own head.

summary: A short instructional digest by Atiśa listing fifty "jewel-like" qualities and practices of a bodhisattva, each introduced by a simile: bodhicitta like the life-breath, emptiness and compassion like mother and father, the perfections like kinsfolk. summary: The Tarkabhāṣā ('Language of Logic') is a concise introductory manual of Buddhist epistemology and logic composed by Mokṣākaragupta, a monk-scholar of the Jagaddala Mahāvihāra in northern Bengal dating to the late 11th or 12th century CE. Structured in three chapters according to the Dignāga-Dharmakīrti epistemology—perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna)—it explains valid knowledge, definition and fallacies of the logical reason (hetu/liṅga), syllogistic debate, and core Mahāyāna philosophical doctrines. The treatise is particularly valuable as one of the latest surviving Sanskrit textbooks of late Indian Buddhist logic, integrating the philosophical developments of Prajñākaragupta, Jñānaśrīmitra, and Ratnakīrti on internal pervasion (antarvyāpti), universal momentariness (kṣaṇikatva), Sākāravāda, and nominal exclusion (apoha).

summary: The Tarkabhāṣāṭīkā (or Tarkabhāṣāvyākhyā) is a 20th-century Sanskrit commentary on the Tarkabhāṣā ('Language of Logic') of the late Buddhist logician Mokṣākaragupta (fl. late 11th–12th century, Jagaddala Mahāvihāra). Composed in 1942 by Pandit Embar Krishnamacharya for his editio princeps of the work in the Gaekwad's Oriental Series (No. 94), the commentary explicates the Buddhist manual across three chapters (direct perception, inference for oneself, and inference for others). The commentator draws extensively upon classical pramāṇa treatises—including Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya, Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇavārttika and Nyāyabindu, Dharmottara's ṭīkās, and Kamalaśīla's Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā—to explain Mokṣākaragupta's concise logic manual and clarify its debates with rival non-Buddhist traditions.

attribution_note: The treatise is traditionally attributed to Vasubandhu (Tianqin 天親) in the Chinese Buddhist canon (Taishō no. 1633, translated by Paramārtha in 550 CE) and early commentaries (such as those by Wengui and Kuiji). Modern scholars have debated this attribution: Giuseppe Tucci, Erich Frauwallner, and Hakuju Ui expressed skepticism, suggesting an earlier Buddhist author, whereas Boris Vassilieff and Motoi Ono (2017) have argued that it may represent an early logical treatise composed by Vasubandhu prior to his Vādavidhi. The Sanskrit original is lost; the present text is Giuseppe Tucci's 1929 Sanskrit retroversion from the Chinese.
