summary: The Tarkaśāstra (preserved in Chinese translation as the Rushi lun 如實論, Taishō 1633, translated by Paramārtha in 550 CE) is a major Buddhist treatise on debate and dialectics (vāda) representing the pre-Dignāga stage of Indian logic. It consists of three chapters: the first treats dialectical exchanges, valid proof, and the refutation of rival objections; the second provides a systematic classification and critique of sixteen futile rejoinders (jāti); and the third analyzes twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna). Because the Indic original is lost, the text survives in Sanskrit solely through Giuseppe Tucci's 1929 back-translation, which illustrates the historical evolution of the five-membered syllogism prior to Dignāga's reforms.

summary: The Tattvaratnāvaloka is a concise 20-verse tantric philosophical treatise by the early eleventh-century Vikramaśīla master Vāgīśvarakīrti. The work surveys and critiques diverse definitions of the spiritual goal (sādhya) and ultimate reality (tattva)—contrasting non-Buddhist views and standard Pāramitāyāna models with multiple Mantrayāna interpretations—and culminates in an exposition of the fourth initiation (caturthābhiṣeka). Vāgīśvarakīrti also composed an extensive prose autocommentary (Tattvaratnāvalokavivaraṇa), which served as an important point of reference in eleventh-century scholastic debates.

summary: The Tattvaratnāvalī ('Jeweled Garland of Reality') is an 11th-century doxographical treatise composed by the scholar-siddha Advayavajra (Maitrīpa). It classifies the Buddhist path into three vehicles (Śrāvakayāna, Pratyekabuddhayāna, and Mahāyāna) and four philosophical tenets (Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Madhyamaka), dividing the Mahāyāna into Pāramitānaya and Mantranaya. The treatise is famous for setting out early bipartite divisions within Yogācāra (Sākāra and Nirākāra) and Madhyamaka (Māyopamādvayavāda and Sarvadharmāpratiṣṭhānavāda), making it a key primary source for late Indian Buddhist doxographical literature (siddhānta).

summary: The Tattvasiddhi is a Buddhist tantric treatise in prosimetrum (89 stanzas and extensive prose commentary) attributed to Śāntarakṣita. summary: The Trisvabhāvanirdeśa ('Exposition of the Three Natures') is a concise verse work of 38 kārikās by Vasubandhu presenting the classical Yogācāra doctrine of the three natures: the imagined (parikalpita), dependent (paratantra), and consummate (pariniṣpanna). Using the simile of a magician conjuring an elephant from a piece of wood, Vasubandhu demonstrates how subject-object duality is an unreal mental construction upon causally dependent mental processes, and how liberation entails the cessation of this duality and the realization of non-dual reality (dharmadhātu).

The work defends core Buddhist philosophical doctrines—particularly momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga), the exclusion theory of meaning (apoha), and causal efficacy (arthakriyākāritva)—against the attacks of the 11th-century Nyāya master Udayana, especially those set forth in the Ātmatattvaviveka. Although published in 1984 under the title Udayananirākaraṇam and attributed to Ratnakīrti, philological research has shown the text to be anonymous and composed after Jñānaśrīmitra.

summary: The Upāyahṛdaya (preserved only in the 472 CE Chinese translation Fangbian xin lun 方便心論, T 1632, and represented in Sanskrit by Giuseppe Tucci's 1929 retroversion) is an early Buddhist handbook of disputation and dialectics dating to approximately the 3rd to 4th century CE. Composed in four chapters, the manual treats the justification and eight fundamental constituents of debate (including the four pramāṇas, examples, and fallacies), occasions of dialectical defeat (nigrahasthāna), exemplary orthodox debate exchanges, and twenty classes of counter-objections (jāti). It provides a valuable pre-Dignāga witness to the development of early Indian debate theory and epistemology parallel to the Carakasaṃhitā and the Nyāyasūtra.

summary: The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Diamond-Cutter Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra'), commonly known as the Diamond Sūtra or Triśatikā ('Three Hundred Lines'), is one of the most celebrated and influential scriptures in Mahāyāna Buddhism. Structured as a dialogue between the Buddha and the venerable Subhūti in the Jetavana grove at Śrāvastī, it systematically dismantles attachment to conceptual signs and ontological categories, teaching that bodhisattvas must practice generosity and cultivate supreme enlightenment without abiding in notions of self, living being, or dharma. The text is renowned for its characteristic dialectical formula asserting that a dharma is designated as such precisely because it is empty of intrinsic existence. First translated into Chinese by Kumārajīva in 401/402 CE, the sūtra became a cornerstone of East Asian Buddhist traditions—particularly Chan/Zen—and is celebrated for the 868 CE Dunhuang woodblock scroll, the world's earliest dated complete printed book.

summary: The Vajrapāṇināmāṣṭottaraśatastotra is a 21-verse Buddhist Sanskrit devotional hymn invoking the 108 epithets of the bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, identified here with Vajrasattva and primordial Bodhicitta. Verses 1–16 systematically invoke the deity under the attributes and virtues of the sixteen Vajrabodhisattvas of the Vajradhātu-maṇḍala (from Vajrasattva to Vajramuṣṭi), followed by verses 17–21 extolling his status as the origin of all Buddhas and declaring the spiritual fruit (phalaśruti) of reciting this litany. Derived from the culmination of the fundamental Yoga Tantra scripture Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, the work long enjoyed independent circulation in the devotional liturgy of Newar Buddhism.

summary: The Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra (also known as the Vajrasattvasādhana) is a foundational generation-stage (utpattikrama) meditation manual of the Ārya tradition of Guhyasamāja tantra exegesis, attributed to the tantric commentator Candrakīrti (c. 9th–10th century CE). It delineates the generation of the thirty-two deities of the Guhyasamāja maṇḍala centered on Vajrasattva in accordance with the process of human rebirth and embryonic development (bhavotpattikrama). Structured across three successive meditations—samādhirāja, maṇḍalarājāgrī, and karmarājāgrī—the practice systematically correlates ritual visualizations with canonical scriptural quotations cited across the seventeen chapters of the root Guhyasamājatantra.

summary: The Vajrasattvastotra is a short, eight-verse Newar Buddhist devotional hymn. It serves as a composite liturgical stotra in Newar Vajrayāna ritual manuals such as the Gurumaṇḍalārcana.

summary: The Vajrasattvapārājikā is an anonymous Newar Buddhist manual on expiation (prāyaścitta) and ritual purity, framed by homage to Vajrasattva and to the ācārya as Vajradhara. Despite the Vinaya term pārājikā in its title, it is addressed to Vajrācārya and lay communities, not to celibate monastics. It adapts Dharmaśāstra-style rules on liability and penance for homicide and cow-killing (govadha), birth and death impurity (sūtaka), purification (śaucācāra, including pañcagavya) and ancestral rites (śrāddha). The Sanskrit is irregular.

summary: The Vajrasūcī ('Diamond Needle') is a short Buddhist polemical tract against the brahmanical claim that brahminhood is determined by birth, arguing from brahmanical authorities (Veda, Manu, Mahābhārata) that brahminhood consists in virtue and self-restraint. This e-text gives only its verses: citations on ṛṣis of non-brahmin birth (Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra etc.), on the loss of brahmin status through conduct, and definitions of the true brahmin by truthfulness, austerity and compassion. summary: The Vajravilāsinīstotra is a 22-verse Sanskrit hymn of praise composed by the Bengali scholar-monk Mahāpaṇḍita Vibhūticandra (fl. late 12th – early 13th century CE) of Jagaddala Mahāvihāra. The hymn is dedicated to Vajravilāsinī, an amorous and playful form of the female buddha Vajrayoginī/Vajravārāhī in the Cakrasaṃvara cycle. Vibhūticandra weaves together vivid sensory descriptions of the goddess's physical beauty, ornaments, and union with Heruka with tantric esoteric physiology (nāḍīcakra) and realization of non-dual innate bliss (sahaja).

summary: The Vajravilāsinīsādhanāstava is a short seven-verse anonymous Tantric Buddhist hymn in praise of Vajravilāsinī, an aspect of Vajrayoginī/Vajravārāhī associated with Anuttarayogatantra cycles (notably Cakrasaṃvara). The verses depict esoteric internal yogic processes, the dissolution of duality symbolized by sun and moon, and the arising of innate bliss (sahaja). It concludes by emphasizing that definitive understanding of spiritual stages is obtained through direct oral instruction from a qualified master (gurumukha).

Preserved as part of the Guhyasamayasādhanamālā collection from Nepal, the hymn is traditionally attributed to the mahāsiddha Virūpa.

summary: An anonymous Tantric Buddhist hymn of adoration (praṇāma) in twenty-one verses (ekaviṃśikā) praising the goddess Vajrayoginī. Each verse concludes with the refrain 'namaste vajrayogini', addressing her esoteric yogic aspects: seated on the evaṃkāra, embodying innate bliss (sahajānanda), bearing skull-cup (kapāla), khaṭvāṅga, and chopper (kartrī), and residing in the eight cremation grounds. The hymn notably expresses an ecumenical and syncretic perspective (vv. 13–14), describing Vajrayoginī as manifesting as Śakti in Śaivism, Caṇḍī in sacred pilgrimage sites, Veda in the Vedic stream, and Kubjikā in the Kula tradition.

summary: The Vajrayoginyāḥ stutipraṇidhānam is an esoteric Vajrayāna hymn of praise and aspiration (stuti-praṇidhāna) dedicated to Trikāyavajrayoginī (the severed-headed form of Vajrayoginī, cognate with Chinnamuṇḍā / Chinnamastā). Attributed to the mahāsiddha Virūpa and associated with the Guhyasamayatantra cycle, the hymn details the visual and yogic iconography of the deity holding her severed head and drinking the nectar of blood along with her flanking yoginīs (Vajravarṇinī and Vajravairocanī), followed by a prayer for the purification of body, speech, and mind, destruction of obstacles, and the realization of mahāmudrā.

summary: The Vajrayānadarśanamīmāṃsā is a modern systematic treatise in Sanskrit composed by Bhikṣu Wangchuk Dorjee Negi examining the philosophy and hermeneutics of Vajrayāna Buddhism. Drawing upon major Tantras, classic Indian commentaries (including Candrakīrti's Pradīpodyotana and Ānandagarbha's works), and Tibetan scholastic sources, the author addresses the status of Tantra as buddhavacana, its relationship to the three turnings of the Dharma wheel, and the doctrine of the two stages (utpattikrama and niṣpannakrama). The treatise provides a thorough exposition of the integration of Madhyamaka emptiness, intrinsically luminous mind (prakṛtiprabhāsvara-citta), and tantric yogic praxis.

summary: A short four-verse Vajrayāna Buddhist hymn belonging to the Cakrasaṃvara/Heruka tradition. Verses 1 and 2 praise the male deity Heruka (addressed as Ubhayacittaheruka and Sahajātmaheruka) visualized within the internal centres (dhātumaṇḍala) and subtle channels (nāḍikā) of the body. The title refers to the esoteric 'spring drop' (vasantatilakā) central to subtle-body completion stage (niṣpannakrama) yoga.

summary: The Vasudhārādhāraṇī is a widely recited Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra centered on Vasudhārā, the goddess of wealth and grain. In the Kauśāmbī setting, the Buddha instructs the impoverished householder Sucandra on the protective incantation and ritual practices revealed by the ancient tathāgata Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa to overcome poverty and dispel harm. This e-text preserves a unique recension copied in 1638 CE (Vikrama Saṃvat 1695) in Gujarat, documenting the cross-sectarian adoption and ritual use of the Buddhist prosperity spell by Jaina communities.

summary: The Vasudhārānāmadhāraṇīstotra is an anonymous Buddhist devotional hymn praising the goddess Vasudhārā, the embodiment of wealth, prosperity, and spiritual abundance in Newar Mahāyāna-Vajrayāna tradition. Composed in 24 anuṣṭubh verses, the hymn lists 108 sacred names and epithets across the first 20 stanzas, invoking Vasudhārā simultaneously as a granter of worldly riches and as an embodiment of Mahāyāna perfections (Prajñāpāramitā, Dānapāramitā, Vīryapāramitā, Kṣāntipāramitā). The concluding stanzas (vv. 21–24) provide a phalaśruti describing the ritual efficacy of reciting the hymn thrice daily to eradicate grave karmic transgressions and attain rebirth in Sukhāvatī.

It then salutes the four goddesses (Locanā, Māmakī, Pāṇḍarā, Tārā) in the intermediate directions and Vajrasattva within the caitya; the colophon ascribes it to (the worship of) Buddhabhaṭṭāraka.

summary: The Vigrahavyāvartanī ('Dispeller of Disputes') is a core philosophical work by Nāgārjuna defending the Madhyamaka doctrine of universal emptiness (śūnyatā) against epistemological objections, particularly those framed by early Nyāya and realist Abhidharma thought. Consisting of 70 dialectical verses in the āryā metre and two concluding dedicatory stanzas, verses 1–20 present the opponent's objections (pūrvapakṣa), arguing that if words and means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) lack intrinsic reality (svabhāva), the Buddhist refutation of inherent existence is itself void and self-defeating. In verses 21–70 (uttarapakṣa), Nāgārjuna replies that empty words operate effectively like illusory creations acting upon illusions, famously declaring (kārikā 29) that he advances no independent ontological thesis (pratijñā) to suffer logical contradiction, before concluding in verses 71–72 with adoration of the Buddha.

summary: The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra set in Vaiśālī, centered on the lay bodhisattva Vimalakīrti, who feigns illness to receive visitors and instruct them. In a series of witty dialogues with major arhat disciples and bodhisattvas, Vimalakīrti dismantles dualistic attachments regarding renunciation, purity, and emptiness (śūnyatā), culminating in his famous silence to signify direct entry into non-duality (advayadharmamukha-praveśa). Long celebrated in East Asian Buddhism and Tibet via early translations, the complete Indic Sanskrit text was identified in 1999 in a 12th-century palm-leaf manuscript preserved at the Potala Palace in Lhasa.

summary: The Vimalaratnalekha ('Spotless Jewel Letter') is a Buddhist epistolary work (lekha) of 40 verses composed by the Indian master Atiśa Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna (982–1054 CE). Addressed to the Pāla ruler Nayapāla of Magadha, the letter provides moral, ethical, and spiritual instructions for a righteous Buddhist monarch. The work urges the cultivation of bodhicitta, constant mindfulness, restraint of the senses, avoidance of spiritual corruption and unwholesome associates (pāpamitra), and governance conducted in harmony with the Dharma.

summary: Guṇaprabha's Vinayasūtra is the definitive scholastic digest of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, condensing canonical narrative and disciplinary legal codes into concise aphorisms. This first chapter, the Pravrajyāvastu, sets forth monastic regulations and formal legal acts (karmavācanā) regarding novice reception (śrāmaṇeratvopanayana) and full ordination (upasaṃpad). Accompanied here by Guṇaprabha's auto-commentary (Vinayasūtravṛtti or Svavyākhyāna), it served as an authoritative reference work for Buddhist monastic jurisprudence in late Indian and Tibetan Buddhism.

summary: A Mahāyāna sūtra transmitted within the Ratnakūṭa collection that contrasts the monastic prātimokṣa rules of śrāvakas with the ethical conduct of bodhisattvas. The Buddha explains that while the śrāvaka discipline centers on strict detachment to avoid any rebirth in saṃsāra, bodhisattva discipline is guided by skillful means (upāyakauśalya) and intention, prioritizing the welfare and gathering of beings. Consequently, offenses rooted in aversion or hatred are considered severe for a bodhisattva because they cause abandonment of beings, whereas infractions rooted in desire can serve to gather beings and are deemed comparatively less obstructive. The sūtra concludes with an exposition by Mañjuśrī on the unconditioned, inherently pure nature of all dharmas.

summary: The Viśeṣastava ('Praise of the [Buddha's] Excellence') is a polemical hymn in anuṣṭubh by a convert from Brahmanism. Its author praises the Buddha by contrasting his freedom from passion and his wisdom with the deeds and teachings of Śiva, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, the ṛṣis and the non-Buddhist schools. In Tibet it was transmitted with Prajñāvarman's commentary and served as a major source on Indian mythology. The Sanskrit text became available only with the Drepung manuscript published in 2022.

summary: The Viśvaprakāśa ('Illumination of All [Words]') is a foundational 12th-century Sanskrit dictionary of homonyms (anekārthakośa) composed by the physician-poet Maheśvara in 1111/1112 CE. The lexicon classifies polysemous nouns alphabetically by final consonants (from ka through kṣa) and further subdivides them by syllable count, followed by a separate concluding chapter on indeclinables (anekārthāvyaya). Citing older authorities such as Kātyāyana, Vyāḍi, Bhāguri, and Śubhāṅga, it was widely utilized by classical commentators and served as the chief model for later homonym lexicons like Medinīkara's Medinīkośa.

summary: The Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi ('Proof of Mere Representation in Twenty Verses') is a foundational treatise of Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda philosophy composed by Vasubandhu in the 4th to 5th century CE. In twenty-two concise kārikās, Vasubandhu defends the thesis that external objects do not exist independently of cognition (vijñaptimātra), refuting realist objections regarding spatiotemporal determinacy, intersubjective consensus, and causal efficacy through comparisons with dreams and hell visions. The work also articulates a famous critique of atomism (paramāṇuvāda), arguing that indivisible partless atoms cannot coalesce into composite extended bodies without logical contradiction.

summary: The Viṃśatikākārikā ('Twenty Verses on Representation-Only') is a foundational Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda polemical treatise composed by Vasubandhu. The text refutes the reality of mind-independent external physical objects (bāhyārtha) through a rigorous critique of atomism (paramāṇuvāda), demonstrating that atomic partlessness and spatial extension are mutually incompatible. Vasubandhu defends the thesis that all experiential phenomena are appearances only (vijñaptimātra), answering realist objections by showing that spatial-temporal determination, intersubjective consistency, and practical efficacy can function without external objects, as seen in dreams, collective karmic hallucinations, and demonic mental projections.

summary: The Vādanyāya ('The Logic of Debate') is the last of Dharmakīrti's seven core treatises on epistemology and logic (pramāṇa), expounding his reform of dialectical and debate theory. Dharmakīrti mounts an extensive critique of the classical Nyāya system of twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna), arguing that genuine defeat in truthful philosophical inquiry (vāda) occurs under only two fundamental circumstances: the proponent's failure to state an essential component of a valid proof (asādhanāṅgavacana), and the respondent's failure to point out an actual fallacy (adoṣodbhāvana). Preserved in Sanskrit and heavily commented upon by thinkers such as Śāntarakṣita (in the Vipañcitārthā) and Vinītadeva, the text served as a foundational model for Buddhist disputation.

summary: The Vādanyāya ('Logic of Debate') is Dharmakīrti's final treatise on debate theory and the grounds of defeat (nigrahasthāna). Critiquing the classic Naiyāyika scheme of twenty-two defeat situations, Dharmakīrti reduces all points of defeat to two fundamental categories: failure to state an essential component of proof (asādhanāṅgavacana) by the proponent, and falsely alleging a defect where none exists (adoṣodbhāvana) by the opponent. Śāntarakṣita's 8th-century Vipañcitārthā is the sole surviving Sanskrit commentary on the text, providing extensive lexical explanations, contextual arguments, and refutations of rival non-Buddhist schools.

summary: The Vāgvāṇīstotra is a short devotional hymn of nine verses praising the goddess Sarasvatī under the designation Vāgvāṇī ('Speech/Voice'). Reflecting the syncretic devotional culture of the Kathmandu Valley, it invokes her simultaneously as 'jinapriyā' ('beloved of the Jina / Buddha') and 'keśavasya priyā' ('beloved of Viṣṇu'). In a brief narrative frame, the preceptor Bṛhaspati recites the hymn to obtain divine wisdom, and Sarasvatī promises eloquence, poetic inspiration (kavitva), and fame to all who recite it.

summary: The Vṛttamālāstuti is a specialized Buddhist devotional work and prosodical treatise composed by the Vikramaśīla philosopher Jñānaśrīmitra (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). Comprising 154 stanzas in praise of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, each verse defines and exemplifies a distinct Sanskrit metre while embedding its traditional metrical name. This e-text provides the complete root hymn accompanied by the learned prose commentary (vivṛti) of Śākyarakṣita (fl. late 11th–12th century CE), which discusses metrical caesurae, grammar, and literary nuances.

summary: A modern Sanskrit narrative poem (kāvya) depicting the life and devotion of Princess Yaśodharā, the wife of Prince Siddhārtha Gautama. Drawing upon classical Buddhist narrative lore and the Sinhala Yasodharāvata tradition, this opening instalment (verses 1–55) portrays Yaśodharā's grief and confusion upon discovering Siddhārtha's secret departure, her frantic search throughout the royal palace, discarding her ornaments, supplicating the deities, and reminiscing about their early marriage.

summary: The Yogaśataka is a short Āyurvedic compendium of about a hundred medical formulas (109 stanzas in this text), arranged by disease, beginning with fevers (jvaracikitsā), and attributed to Nāgārjuna. It circulated widely and was translated into Tibetan and Tocharian (Kuchean), which shows its early importance in Buddhist medicine.

summary: The Yogācārabhūmi is the fundamental encyclopedic compendium of the Yogācāra school of Indian Mahāyāna Buddhism. This digital text comprises the first five bhūmis of the seventeen stages in the basic section (Maulībhūmi): the stage connected with the five sensory consciousnesses (Pañcavijñānakāyasamprayuktā bhūmiḥ), the stage of mental consciousness (Manobhūmiḥ), and the three stages defined by the presence or absence of coarse discursive thinking and subtle investigation (Savitarkā savicārā, Avitarkā vicāramātrā, and Avitarkāvicārā bhūmayaḥ). These sections set out early Yogācāra psychology, sensory taxonomy, cognitive objects, caittas (mental concomitants), cosmology, the ālayavijñāna, karmic accumulation, and the degrees of spiritual realization (abhisamaya).

summary: The Yuktiṣaṣṭikārikā ('Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning') is an essential Madhyamaka treatise by Nāgārjuna, belonging to his collection of dialectical treatises (yuktikāya). In sixty verses following an opening homage to the Buddha, the work deconstructs substantialist assertions of existence (bhāva) and non-existence (abhāva), arguing that true understanding of dependent origination dissolves reified distinctions between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. The continuous Sanskrit original having been lost in India, the e-text represents Bimalendra Kumar's 1993 modern Sanskrit retroversion based on the Tibetan canonical translation.

summary: The Ādibuddhadvādaśakastotra is a short Sanskrit Buddhist devotional hymn of twelve anuṣṭubh verses, accompanied by a single phalaśruti verse, honoring the Primordial Buddha (Ādibuddha). The hymn identifies the Ādibuddha pantheistically and cosmically with the Three Jewels, the Five Buddhas, the cosmic elements, sensory powers, and the Brahmanical triad of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa. Attributed pseudepigraphically to Mañjuśrī, the text represents the late syncretic liturgical tradition of the Kathmandu Valley.

summary: The Ādikarmapradīpa ('Lamp for the Initial Practices') by Anupamavajra (ca. late 11th–early 12th century CE) is an influential ritual manual setting forth the daily liturgical, devotional, and meditative routine for novice Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna practitioners (ādikarmika). Starting with 15 opening verses that outline the sequence of daily observances, followed by an extensive prose commentary, the manual details morning purification, recitation of the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṅgīti and Praṇidhānas, water offerings to Jambhala and pretas, clay caitya molding (mṛccaitya), maṇḍala worship to the guru and tutelary deity, refuge and bodhisattva vows, and mealtime bali rituals. The work quotes extensively from canonical Mahāyāna sūtras and Vajrayāna tantras (notably preserving fragments of the lost Vidyādharapiṭaka) and remains a foundational prototype for Newar Buddhist daily rituals.

summary: The Ādikarmāvatāra is a Mahāyāna Buddhist ritual and daily practice manual intended for novice practitioners (ādikarmika), preserved in the Nepalese Sanskrit manuscript tradition. It delineates fundamental daily observances including taking refuge in the Three Jewels, moral confession (pāpadeśanā), generating bodhicitta, receiving the upāsaka precepts, cleaning and arranging the shrine, offering maṇḍalas and flowers, reciting dhāraṇīs, and honouring the spiritual teacher (guru). The work consists of instructional prose interspersed with 81 mnemonic verses and sūtra citations.

summary: A short supplement to Mañjukīrti's Ādikarmāvatāra, a manual for Buddhist beginners (ādikarmika). Opening with a salutation to Tārā, it explains how a spiritual friend should lead disciples of inferior, middling and superior capacity to refuge and bodhicitta. It cites instructions for the householder bodhisattva from the Ugraparipṛcchā and prescribes the refuge ritual, maṇḍala offerings and pūjā before an image of Śākyamuni. It closes with dedication verses, a prayer for the Teaching's long endurance and a meditation on benevolence (maitrīvihāra) with its dhāraṇī.

summary: The Ālambanaparīkṣā ('Investigation of the Percept') is a concise foundational treatise in eight verses by the Buddhist epistemologist Dignāga (c. 480–540 CE). Dignāga defines a perceptual cognitive object (ālambana) through two joint criteria: it must act as the causal condition (kāraṇa/pratyaya) producing the cognition, and the cognition must bear its subjective appearance or form (tadābhāsa/ākāra). Arguing against externalist atomism (specifically the Sarvāstivāda and Sautrāntika models), he demonstrates that neither individual atoms nor aggregated atomic composites meet both criteria, ultimately concluding that the object cognized is actually an internal mental aspect appearing as if external, establishing the Yogācāra idealist doctrine.

summary: The Ālambanaparīkṣā ('Investigation of the Perceptual Object') with its auto-commentary (vṛtti) by Dignāga (c. 480–540 CE) is a foundational treatise in eight verses expounding Yogācāra-vijñānavāda epistemology. Dignāga argues that external matter cannot serve as an object of cognition (ālambana), because neither indivisible atoms nor aggregated gross bodies fulfill the necessary twin criteria: being the cause that produces the cognition and presenting their likeness (ākāra) to consciousness. He concludes that the cognitive object is an internal mental appearance projected outward by beginningless cognitive latencies (vāsanā / śakti), establishing an epistemological basis for mind-only idealism.

summary: The Caturdharmanirdeśasūtra is a brief Mahāyāna scripture set in the Sudharmā council hall of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, in which the Buddha instructs the bodhisattva Maitreya on how to overcome and purify accumulated unwholesome actions. The discourse sets forth four factors, traditionally known as the four opponent powers (catuḥpratipakṣabala): remorse (vidūṣaṇāsamudācāra), antidotal virtuous deeds (pratipakṣasamudācāra), the resolve to refrain from repetition (pratyāpattibala), and reliance on refuge and bodhicitta (āśrayabala). Frequently cited by Indian masters, notably Śāntideva in the Śikṣāsamuccaya, it serves as the primary canonical foundation for Buddhist confession and purification rituals.

summary: The Dharmadhātugarbhavivaraṇa is a brief canonical prose commentary traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna that analyzes the famous Pratītyasamutpāda stanza ('ye dharmā hetuprabhavā hetuṃ teṣāṃ tathāgato hy avadat...'). Contrary to what the title suggests, the text does not discuss tathāgatagarbha doctrine, but instead provides an Abhidharmic classification of the twelve links into five causes (hetu: avidyā, saṃskāra, tṛṣṇā, upādāna, bhava) and seven results (phala: vijñāna, nāmarūpa, ṣaḍāyatana, sparśa, vedanā, jāti, jarāmaraṇa), concluding with an etymological gloss on the epithets 'Tathāgata' and 'Mahāśramaṇa' in terms of forward (anuloma) and reverse (pratiloma) dependent origination. Preserved in the Abhidharma section of the Tibetan Tengyur (Toh 4101), the digital text here represents a modern Sanskrit restoration from Tibetan by Gyaltsen Namdol (1997).

summary: The Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa is a massive composite Buddhist scripture and ritual manual (kalparāja) focused on the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, representing a key transition between Mahāyāna sūtra literature and Mantrayāna/Kriyātantra ritual systems. Dating in its various historical strata from roughly the 6th to 8th centuries CE, the work provides exhaustive instructions for mudrās, maṇḍalas, cloth-painting (paṭa), fire oblations (homa), mantras, astrology, and practices for attaining mundane powers as well as awakening. It is particularly renowned for chapter 53 (Rājavyākaraṇaparivarta), which contains a verse prophecy detailing north Indian dynastic history up to the rise of the Pāla Empire.

summary: The Āryamāyājālamahātantroddhṛtamaṇḍalagāthāṭippaṇī is an esoteric Buddhist annotation (ṭippaṇī) attributed to Nāgārjunapāda on two maṇḍala stanzas extracted from the Māyājālamahātantra. The work provides an internal, yogic, and perfection-oriented (ṣaṭpāramitā) reinterpretation of the materials and preparatory actions of maṇḍala ritual (such as smearing cow dung, sprinkling water, sweeping, and clearing insects) for practitioners of differing spiritual capacities (mṛdu, madhya, and adhimātra/nirālambana). Quoting repeatedly from the Hevajratantra, it interprets these ritual actions as internal cleansing of the mind, the rising of the inner caṇḍālī, and the cultivation of non-dual mahāmudrā.

summary: The Prajñāpāramitāvajracchedikāṭīkā is an extensive commentary by the 8th-century Indian master Kamalaśīla on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra ('Diamond Sūtra'). Following classical Indian scholastic structure—setting out the purpose (prayojana), concise overview (piṇḍārtha), word analysis (padārtha), internal connection (anusandhi), and answers to objections—Kamalaśīla expounds the sūtra from a Yogācāra-Mādhyamika perspective. He details the path of the bodhisattva across the three grounds (adhimukticaryābhūmi, śuddhādhyāśayabhūmi, and buddhabhūmi) and refutes substantialist views while demonstrating two-fold selflessness. Because the ancient Sanskrit manuscript is lost, this e-text represents a modern Sanskrit reconstruction (punaruddhāra) made from the Tibetan canonical version by Pema Tenzin.

summary: The Pratītyasamutpādamahāyānasūtra is a brief Mahāyāna scripture set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, where the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara petitions the Buddha to deliver a teaching yielding boundless merit for the assembly. In response, the Buddha recites the famed dependent arising verse (ye dharmā hetuprabhavā...) and equates dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) directly with the Dharma body (dharmakāya) of all Tathāgatas, stating that whoever perceives dependent arising sees the Tathāgata. He teaches that fashioning even miniature caityas, bodhi trees, and umbrellas and reciting or depositing this verse inside them yields vast, Brahma-like merit (brāhmaṃ puṇyam) leading to rebirth in the Brahmaloka and the Śuddhāvāsa heavens. The sūtra serves as a crucial canonical justification for the widespread medieval Asian Buddhist practice of depositing the ye dharmā creed into stūpas, plaques, and images as a dharmakāya relic (dharmadhātu).

summary: The Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā ('Questions of Rāṣṭrapāla') is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra included as assembly 18 in the Mahāratnakūṭa collection. Framed as a discourse at Gṛdhrakūṭa between the Buddha and the bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla, the text champions the ascetic ideal of forest dwelling (āraṇyaka) and dhūtaguṇa practice while mounting a severe critique against corrupt, comfortable urban monks of the decadent age (paścimakāla). The second half recounts fifty former-life tales (pūrvayoga) illustrating the Bodhisattva's extreme acts of self-sacrifice, culminating in the story of Prince Puṇyaraśmi.

summary: The Saṃghāṭasūtra is a prominent Mahāyāna scripture presented as a discourse delivered by the Buddha on Vulture Peak (Gṛddhrakūṭa) to the bodhisattva Sarvaśūra and a vast assembly. Operating as a devotional text and dharma-paryāya, it teaches the immense spiritual merit, purification of severe negative karma, and divine protection generated by hearing, copying, reciting, and revering the sūtra. Through extended parables, visionary accounts, and past-life narratives, the scripture underscores the inevitability of karmic consequences and the assurance of eventual awakening for all beings. It enjoyed extraordinary popularity across Northwest India and Central Asia from the 5th to the 8th centuries CE, attested by numerous Gilgit Sanskrit manuscripts as well as translations into Khotanese, Sogdian, Chinese, and Tibetan.

summary: The Āryasāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā (Toh 155 / T 599) is a concise Mahāyāna sūtra set in the underwater palace of the nāga king Sāgara. The Buddha explains that proclaiming and understanding the four aphorisms or summaries of the Dharma (caturdharmoddāna: all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all contaminated phenomena are suffering, all phenomena are without self, and nirvāṇa is peace) is tantamount to expounding all eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dharma (caturaśītidharmaskandhasahasra). As no ancient Sanskrit manuscript witness of this short recension survives, the Sanskrit text preserved here is a modern scholarly reconstruction from the Tibetan Kangyur version.

summary: The Triskandhasūtra ('Sūtra of the Three Heaps', commonly referred to in Tibetan practice as the Bodhisattvāpattideśanā or the Confession to the Thirty-Five Buddhas) is a Mahāyāna liturgical text used for purifying infractions of the bodhisattva vows and moral downfalls. Its title refers to three key ritual actions: confession of moral faults (pāpadeśanā), rejoicing in merits (anumodanā), and the dedication of merit toward supreme awakening (pariṇāmanā). While it circulates independently as a ritual text across Nepal and Tibet, the liturgy also constitutes the central confession pericope embedded within the Mahāyāna Vinayaviniścaya-Upāliparipṛcchāsūtra.

summary: The Āryatārānamaskāraikaviṃśatistotra ('Homage to Tārā in Twenty-One Verses') is one of the most prominent liturgies across Mahāyāna and Tibetan Buddhist traditions. Extracted from the root Tārā tantra cycle (Sarvatathāgatamātṛtārāviśvakarmabhavatantra), the hymn praises twenty-one distinct manifestations and iconographic aspects of the goddess Tārā, lauding her swift compassion, implements, colours, and protective efficacy against worldly hazards and inner defilements. The stotra concludes with a six-verse phalaśruti (vv. 22–27) that expounds the spiritual and mundane benefits conferred by daily morning and evening recitation.

summary: A ten-stanza Buddhist hymn (stotra) composed in ornate 21-syllable Sragdharā metre praising the goddess Tārā by the author Candradāsa. Following an introductory verse (v. 1), stanzas 2 through 9 systematically invoke Tārā's protection from the eight great perils (aṣṭamahābhaya)—wild beasts/lions, elephants, fire, poisonous snakes, bandits, bondage/imprisonment, shipwreck/drowning, and demons/disease—concluding with a tenth stanza on the worldly and spiritual rewards of remembering her name.

summary: The Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī is an influential Buddhist apotropaic and purificatory dhāraṇī scripture classified under Kriyātantra. In its narrative framework, the Buddha enters an adamantine absorption and inspires the yakṣa lord Vajrapāṇi to proclaim an unbreakable vajra incantation designed to dispel malignant spirits, afflictions, and karmic impediments. The text concludes with instructional verses detailing an ablution (snāna) ritual using a consecrated vase to purify pollutants, pacify planetary obstacles, and promote longevity.

summary: The Vimalakīrtinirdeśasūtra is a renowned Mahāyāna scripture set in Vaiśālī that centers on the enlightened householder bodhisattva Vimalakīrti, who feigns illness to create an occasion to teach visiting śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and celestial beings. Over twelve chapters, the text articulates core Mahāyāna themes including the purification of the Buddha realm (buddhakṣetrapariśuddhi), the exercise of skillful means (upāyakauśalya), the inconceivable liberation (acintyavimokṣa), and the realization of non-duality (advayadharmamukha), memorably epitomized by Vimalakīrti's eloquent silence. Notably, this particular e-text contains the modern Sanskrit reconstruction prepared from the Tibetan translation by L.M. Joshi and Bhikshu Pāsādika in 1981, prior to the 1999 recovery of the original Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscript in Lhasa.

summary: The Grahamātṛkādhāraṇī ('Mother of the planets') is a Buddhist dhāraṇī for pacifying the malign influence of the planets and lunar asterisms. Set in Aḍakavatī, it has the Buddha, at Vajrapāṇi's request, teach the worship, offerings and mantras of the nine grahas and the asterisms, with rules for recitation and its benefits. It is still recited in Newar Buddhism as part of the Saptavāra collection; this e-text reproduces a Nepalese print edited by Ratna Bahadur Vajracharya (NS 1080).

Devotional recitation of these names and spells is prescribed to dispel poverty, pacify obstacles, and confer prosperity and spiritual merit.

summary: A 70-verse metrical treatise summarizing the teachings of the Śālistambasūtra ('Rice Seedling Sūtra'). Using the botanical metaphor of a sprouting rice seed, it explains the Mahāyāna doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) by contrasting external (plant growth) and internal (psychophysical twelvefold) causal sequences, underscoring the absence of an agent (kartṛ), enduring self (ātman), or divine creator (īśvara). Because the original Sanskrit text is lost and survives only in Tibetan canonical translations (Toh 3985), this e-text represents the modern Sanskrit retroversion prepared by Sonam Rabten in 2004.

summary: The Śālistambakamahāyānasūtraṭīkā (also known as Śālistambakavistarākhyāṭīkā) is an extensive commentary on the Śālistambasūtra, elucidating the core Buddhist doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) through both outer (agricultural/sprout) and inner (twelvefold nidāna) causal frameworks. Canonical Tibetan tradition ascribes both the verse summary (Śālistambakakārikā) and this prose exposition to Nāgārjuna, but the inclusion of late concepts such as ālayavijñāna suggests a 6th- to 8th-century origin. As no original Sanskrit manuscript is extant, the present e-text consists of a modern Sanskrit retro-translation (punaruddhāra) prepared from the Tibetan Kangyur/Tengyur tradition by Dr. Sonam Rabten.

summary: The Maitreyavyākaraṇa ('Prophecy Concerning Maitreya') is a metrical Buddhist scripture in anuṣṭubh verse setting forth the future advent of the bodhisattva Maitreya as the next buddha of the current cosmic era. Framed as an exposition delivered by Śākyamuni Buddha to his disciple Śāriputra, the text describes the utopian state of Jambudvīpa and the capital Ketumatī ruled by the righteous universal monarch (cakravartin) Śaṅkha, Maitreya's birth into a brāhmaṇa family, his renunciation, enlightenment under the Nāga tree, and the three major preaching assemblies (saṃnipāta). It concludes by enjoining devotees to cultivate devotion toward the Three Jewels and practice Buddhist morality to ensure rebirth in Maitreya's presence.

summary: The Advayaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā is a condensed Mahāyāna scripture representing the Perfection of Wisdom in Fifty Lines (Ardhaśatikā or Pañcāśatikā Prajñāpāramitā). In late Newar scribal transmission, 'Ardhaśatikā' ('fifty units/lines') was corrupted via orthographic resemblance into 'Advayaśatikā' and incorporated into Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha collections, though the text contains neither mantras nor any doctrinal discussion of non-duality (advaya). Set at Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, the Buddha instructs Subhūti that all spiritual paths and dharmas—including the six perfections, the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the bodhipakṣa dharmas, and the distinctive Buddha-qualities—are encompassed within the perfection of wisdom, which is ungraspable, intrinsically pure, and comparable to empty space. The Chinese translation by Dānapāla (T 248) confirms its circulation by the late 10th century CE.

summary: The Amoghapāśahṛdayasūtra is a prominent Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture (classified as Kriyātantra in Tibetan tradition) focusing on Amoghapāśa Lokeśvara, an esoteric multi-armed form of Avalokiteśvara. Set on Mount Potalaka, the text recounts how Avalokiteśvara received this root heart-mantra (hṛdaya) in an earlier aeon from the Buddha Lokendrarāja, and details the extensive soteriological and mundane benefits of hearing, reciting, or writing it. It provides the central dhāraṇī formula alongside ritual procedures (vidhi/kalpa) for healing ailments, protection against danger, and purifying severe karmic offenses.

summary: The Āryānityatāsūtra is a short canonical discourse set at Jetavana in Śrāvastī, where the Buddha expounds that all conditioned phenomena (sarvasaṃskāra) are impermanent, unstable, and destined to perish. The sūtra systematically demonstrates that death is inevitable for all beings, from wealthy householders and universal monarchs to ascetics, gods of the three realms, and even arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas. It concludes with famous gāthās comparing life to earthen vessels made by a potter and ripe fruit destined to fall, culminating in the stanza: sarve kṣayāntā nicayāḥ patanāntāḥ samucchrayāḥ / saṃyogāśca viyogāntā maraṇāntaṃ hi jīvitam.

summary: The Ātreyatilaka (also titled Pratibimbalakṣaṇa) is a Sanskrit Buddhist manual of iconometry (śilpaśāstra) traditionally attributed to the sage Ātreya. Comprising 144 anuṣṭubh verses, it defines the tālamāna proportional canons and precise dimensional units (aṅgula, yava, kalā, etc.) for constructing sacred Buddhist images from crown to pedestal. The final section (vv. 141–144) details jīrṇoddhāra, prescribing religious rites for repairing, re-installing, or ritually decommissioning damaged, broken, or weathered earthen and metal icons.

summary: The Śabdabhedaprakāśa ('Illumination of Distinctions among Words') is a 12th-century Sanskrit orthographic lexicon composed by Maheśvara as a supplement to his homonym dictionary Viśvaprakāśa (1111 CE). In four sections (nirdeśas), it catalogues allowable variations in Sanskrit phonology and spelling: general vocalic/consonantal variants, the interchange of ba and va, alternations among the three sibilants (śa, ṣa, sa), and differences of gender (liṅgabheda). It served as a practical reference for poets and scholars to verify legitimate variants and support verbal figures of speech like anuprāsa, yamaka, and śleṣa.

summary: The Śaraṇagamanadeśanā is a short instructional work on the practice and significance of going for refuge (śaraṇagamana) to the Three Jewels, composed by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (ca. 982–1054 CE). The text structures the doctrine around fifteen headings: the foundation (adhiṣṭhāna), the twofold Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna states (sthiti), intentional disposition (āśaya), duration (avadhi), essence (svabhāva), standard measure (māna), method (naya), rules/precepts (śikṣā), etymological meaning (nirukti), functional role (kāritra), analogies (upamya), classification (bheda), faults of transgression (ādīnava), doctrinal meaning (artha), and twofold temporal benefits (anuśaṃsā). Preserved historically in the Tibetan Tanjur, this Sanskrit e-text represents a modern reconstruction published by Ramesh Chandra Negi in 1992.

summary: The Śatagāthā ('Hundred Verses', also known as the Gāthāśataka) is a Buddhist gnomic anthology (nītiśāstra) traditionally ascribed to Ācārya Vararuci. Preserved in the Tanjur (Toh 4332 / D 4332), where it was translated into Tibetan by Vinayacandra and Dharmaprajña (Chos kyi shes rab), the work gathers 107 didactic maxims on worldly wisdom, ethical conduct, true friendship, virtue, and impermanence. The Sanskrit text in this e-text is modern scholar Losang Norbu Shastri's reconstruction from the Tibetan text, collated against classical Sanskrit gnomic parallels.

summary: The Śayanāsanavastu ('Chapter on Bedding and Seats') is the 15th section of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu. summary: The Śikṣāsamuccaya ('Compendium of Training') is an 8th-century Mahāyāna manual composed by the Madhyamaka philosopher Śāntideva. Structured around 27 mnemonic root verses (kārikā) and Śāntideva's own detailed prose exposition, it organizes the bodhisattva training into the fourfold program of relinquishing, guarding, purifying, and increasing one's body (ātmabhāva), possessions (bhoga), and religious merit (puṇya). The work is celebrated as an essential sourcebook of Indian Mahāyāna literature, preserving extensive quotations from over a hundred sūtras that are otherwise lost in their Sanskrit originals.

summary: The Śikṣāsamuccayakārikā comprises twenty-seven mnemonic stanzas composed by Śāntideva (c. early 8th century CE), providing the architectural framework for his major anthology of Mahāyāna scriptures, the Śikṣāsamuccaya. Built upon a 4×3 matrix introduced in kārikā 4, the work coordinates four bodhisattva practices—renunciation (utsarga), protection (rakṣā), purification (śuddhi), and enhancement (vardhana)—across three domains: one's person (ātmabhāva), material goods (bhoga), and merit (śubha/puṇya). In Tibetan canonical collections, these 27 verses are preserved as an independent text (Toh 3939) intended for memorization.

summary: The Śrāvakabhūmi ('Stage of the Disciple') is the thirteenth section of the Maulī Bhūmi (basic section) of the Yogācārabhūmi corpus, constituting an extensive and systematic manual of Buddhist meditation and spiritual development. Structured into four yogasthānas (stages of spiritual practice), it treats the prerequisites for monastic life, spiritual disposition (gotra), initial entry into practice (avatāra), and the dual cultivation of calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) culminating in liberation. Although preserved as part of the Yogācāra canon, it systematically articulates classical Mainstream (Śrāvakayāna) praxis and doctrine.

summary: The Śrīguhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi (frequently cited as the Catuḥśatapañcāśikā) is an early classical ritual manual composed by Dīpaṃkarabhadra, one of the direct disciples of Buddhajñānapāda. summary: The Śrīguhyasamājatantra (also known as the Tathāgataguhyaka) is the foundational scripture of esoteric Mahāyāna Buddhism belonging to the Anuttarayoga / Mahāyoga class of tantras. In eighteen chapters (paṭalas 1–17 forming the root tantra and paṭala 18 serving as the Uttaratantra or explanatory continuation), it expounds the maṇḍala of the five Tathāgata families, deity yoga, consecration rituals, and subtle-body inner yogic practices. The scripture became the central root source for two major Indian commentarial lineages—the Ārya school associated with Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Candrakīrti, and the Jñānapāda school—profoundly shaping the development of Indo-Tibetan Vajrayāna scholasticism and meditative praxis.

summary: The Śrīhevajrabhaṭṭārakasya Cakraviṃśatikāstotra is a 20-verse tantric hymn of praise (stotra) composed by the siddha Saroruhavajra honoring the Anuttarayogatantra deity Hevajra and his retinue. The verses systematically praise the eight-faced, sixteen-armed form of Hevajra embracing Nairātmyā (vv. 1–8), followed by individual invocations of the eight yoginīs of his maṇḍala (Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī; vv. 9–16), their collective qualities (vv. 17–19), and a concluding philosophical praise of the nondual deity (v. 20).

summary: A Nepalese Buddhist ritual scripture presented as a dialogue on Mount Potalaka between the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (Lokeśvara) and the goddess Tārā. Despite the word 'parājikā' in its title, the work does not deal with classical monastic expulsions, but expounds portents and ominous signs (utpātalakṣaṇa) and their ritual pacification (utpātaśāntikakrama) through the recitation of the Mahāpañcarakṣā, homa oblations, bali rites, and donations to priests. The work reflects the protective and astrological practices characteristic of householder Newar Buddhism.

summary: The Śrīsahajasiddhi ('Accomplishment of the Innate') by the Mahāsiddha Ḍombīheruka (c. 8th century CE) is an early Vajrayāna treatise on completion-stage (utpannakrama) yoga in the Hevajra Tantra cycle. Across three concise chapters, it expounds the realization of sahaja through the four progressive blisses (caturānanda), internal subtle-body yoga (the arousal of the inner fire caṇḍālī at the navel cakra), the non-dual transformation of the passions (kleśa) into enlightened wisdom, and the observance of tantric commitments (samaya). Canonical Tibetan tradition classifies the work among the 'Seven Siddhi Texts' (Grub pa sde bdun).

summary: The Śākyasiṃhastotra (navagrahakṛtam) is a short Sanskrit Buddhist hymn of 10 stanzas composed in Toṭaka meter in praise of Śākyamuni Buddha (Śākyasiṃha). Verses 1–9 narrate key aspects of the Buddha's life and virtues: his golden appearance and destruction of Māra's army, his teaching of the ten pāramitās and four Noble Truths, his voluntary birth in the Śākya clan, his renunciation accompanied by Chandaka and Kaṇṭhaka, his forest austerities, his victory over Māra under the Bodhi tree, his reception of offerings from merchants, and his first turning of the wheel of the doctrine at the deer park in Vārāṇasī. The concluding phalaśruti stanza promises that whoever recites this hymn will be freed from disease and planetary afflictions (graharogabhaya) and will reach liberation.

summary: A nine-verse Buddhist devotional hymn composed in the Sragdharā metre addressed to Buddha Śākyamuni (Śākyasiṃha), dramatically framed as spoken by Surapati (Indra). summary: The Śākyasiṃhastotra (Viṣṇukṛta) is a short Sanskrit hymn of eleven verses in the Bhujaṅgaprayāta meter in praise of Gautama Buddha (Śākyasiṃha). summary: The Śālistambasūtra ('Rice Seedling Sūtra') is a foundational Mahāyāna sūtra on the doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). Prompted by the Buddha's concise statement that whoever sees dependent origination sees the Dharma and whoever sees the Dharma sees the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Maitreya expounds the teaching to Śāriputra using the analogy of a rice seedling sprouting and developing from a seed. The discourse distinguishes between external causality (the physical conditions governing plant growth) and internal causality (the twelvefold chain of psychic and karmic conditioning), demonstrating that all conditioned phenomena arise devoid of an independent agent, soul (ātman), or essence. Copiously cited by Madhyamaka authors such as Nāgārjuna, Candrakīrti, and Kamalaśīla, it served as one of the primary scriptural foundations for early Mahāyāna causal theory.

summary: An eight-verse devotional hymn (aṣṭaka) composed in Vasantatilakā meter praising Śāradā (Sarasvatī / Bhāratī) as the grantor of speech, wisdom, and freedom from mental dullness (jāḍyahantrī). Each stanza concludes with the refrain bowing before the blessed goddess (śrīśāradāṃ bhagavatīṃ satataṃ namāmi), describing her as swan-borne, radiantly white, and holding a vīṇā, crystal rosary, and manuscript. Transmitted in Newar Buddhist manuscript anthologies, the text exemplifies the integration of Sarasvatī veneration into Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna liturgical practice.

summary: The Śūnyatāsaptati ('Seventy Verses on Emptiness') is one of the foundational works of the Yukti (reasoning) corpus attributed to Nāgārjuna. In 73 verses (predominantly in anuṣṭubh meter), the text argues that all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas—including the twelve links of dependent origination, time, the agent and object of action, and nirvāṇa itself—are empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) because they are dependently co-arisen (pratītyasamutpanna). Rather than promoting nihilism, Nāgārjuna explains that establishing ultimate emptiness (śūnyatā / paramārtha) enables the valid and unhindered operation of conventional transactional reality (laukikavyavahāra).

summary: A Vajrayāna treatise belonging to the Yoginī/Ḍākinī tantra milieu associated with the Cakrasaṃvara and Abhidhānottara tantric cycles. It presents an exegesis of the four initiations (abhiṣeka), distinguishing transient physical pleasure (kṣarasukha) from the immutable bliss of gnosis (akṣarasukha / mahāsukha), and decodes the intentional twilight language (sandhyābhāṣā) of consort practices. The work quotes from texts including the Abhidhānottaratantra, the Vajrapañjara, and the Ratnacūḍāsūtra, concluding with verses emphasizing unwavering fidelity to the guru.

summary: A brief Mahāyāna praise hymn consisting of seven anuṣṭubh verses addressed to the Buddha (Śrī Mahābuddhabhaṭṭāraka). Despite the title invoking the 'six higher cognitions' (ṣaḍabhijñā), the six central stanzas address the Buddha by correlating the six sensory fields (ṣaḍviṣaya: rūpa, śabda, gandha, rasa, sparśa, dharma) with the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā: dāna, śīla, kṣānti, vīrya, dhyāna, prajñā/buddhi). The final verse serves as a phalaśruti, stating that reciting the hymn thrice daily frees one from the bonds of saṃsāra.

summary: The Ṣaḍgatistotra is a short six-verse Sanskrit Buddhist hymn dedicated to Avalokiteśvara. It venerates the Bodhisattva's physical iconography, auspicious ornaments, and boundless compassion in rescuing beings from cyclic existence across the six realms of rebirth (ṣaḍgati). The concluding verse offers a phalaśruti promising rebirth in the celestial realms of the gods for devoted recitation.

summary: The Ṣaṇmukhīdhāraṇī ('Dhāraṇī of the Six Gates') is a concise Mahāyāna dhāraṇī-sūtra set in the sky above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, where the Buddha addresses an assembly of bodhisattvas. The text articulates six core aspirations (mukha) designed to transform samsaric experiences, confess negative deeds, comprehend Māra's actions, and dedicate all root virtues and liberation to all sentient beings, followed by the protective dhāraṇī formula. Recitation three times by day and three times by night is taught to purify karmic obscurations and rapidly yield unexcelled awakening.

summary: The Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 150 Lines') is an influential Buddhist scripture bridging late Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā thought and esoteric Mantrayāna doctrine. It expounds the essential purity of all dharmas, declaring that worldly desires, passions, and sensory engagements are fundamentally pure (viśuddhi) when realized through non-dual transcendent wisdom. Known in East Asia as the Rishukyō (理趣經), primarily via Amoghavajra's 8th-century Chinese translation (T 243), the sūtra became one of the central liturgical recitations of the Japanese Shingon and Tendai traditions.

summary: The Atharvavedasaṃhitā in the Śaunaka recension is the fourth canonized Vedic saṃhitā, comprising twenty kāṇḍas of metrical hymns and prose mantras. Unlike the predominantly śrauta sacrificial orientation of the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, and Yajurveda, this collection largely focuses on domestic rites, healing, protection against curses and sorcery, royal rituals, and speculative cosmogonic hymns on cosmic principles such as Skambha, Prāṇa, and Rohita.

summary: The Maitrāyaṇīsaṃhitā is one of the surviving saṃhitās of the Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda, representing the liturgical tradition of the Maitrāyaṇīya school. It intermixes sacrificial mantras with archaic explanatory prose (brāhmaṇa-type discussions) on the origin and performance of śrauta rituals. Spanning four kāṇḍas, the work details rites such as the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa), the Agnihotra, the Soma rituals, and the Agnicayana, serving as a principal source for early Vedic language and ritual theology.

summary: The Samayaprakāśa ('Illumination of Ritual Times') is an extensive section of Mitramiśra's encyclopedic Dharmaśāstra digest, the Vīramitrodaya, composed in the early seventeenth century under King Vīrasiṃhadeva of Orchhā. It systematically analyzes the calendrical and temporal rules (kāla/samaya) governing Hindu ritual obligations, discussing lunar days (tithi), intercalary months (malamāsa), solar ingresses (saṅkrānti), festivals, and vows (vrata). Drawing heavily upon smṛti and purāṇic sources as well as medieval authorities, it became a standard authority for ritual timing within the Banaras school of Dharmaśāstra.

summary: The Śatapathabrāhmaṇa ('Brāhmaṇa of a Hundred Paths') is the monumental prose ritual commentary attached to the White (Śukla) Yajurveda and the most extensive surviving Brāhmaṇa text. It provides detailed liturgical instructions, theological rationales, cosmological speculations, and mythological narratives (including the flood legend of Manu and the story of Purūravas and Urvaśī) for the principal Vedic śrauta rituals, including the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Agnihotra, Cāturmāsya, Vājapeya, Rājasūya, Agnicayana (the construction of the bird-shaped brick fire-altar), Aśvamedha, and Pravargya. In the Mādhyandina recension, it is arranged in fourteen kāṇḍas reflecting two major liturgical traditions: Books 1–5 and 14 represent the tradition of Yājñavalkya, while Books 6–10 preserve the altar-building doctrine of Śāṇḍilya. Originating in northern India around 800–600 BCE, the work constitutes a crucial transitional monument between early Vedic ritualism and the nascent philosophical thought of the early Upaniṣads.

summary: The Āṅgirasasmṛti is a dharmaśāstra manual traditionally ascribed to the Vedic sage Aṅgiras, preserved as a medieval compilation. Arranged in two sections—Pūrvāṅgiras and Uttarāṅgiras (the latter in 12 adhyāyas)—the work provides detailed procedural guidance on domestic ritual ceremonies, śrāddha (ancestor offerings), and expiatory penances (prāyaścitta) for varied ritual lapses and purity violations. Numerous verses in this text correspond to citations attributed to Aṅgiras by medieval nibandha authors such as Viśvarūpa, Aparārka, and Hemādri.

summary: The Paramārthasāra ('Essence of Ultimate Truth'), traditionally attributed to Ādiśeṣa, is a concise philosophical poem of 85 āryā stanzas setting forth an early form of non-dualist Vedānta with strong Vaiṣṇava and Sāṅkhya-Yoga affinities. Identifying the ultimate reality (Brahman) with Viṣṇu, it elucidates the relationship between prakṛti and puruṣa, the nature of cosmic illusion (māyā/avidyā), and final release through knowledge. It is historically notable as the source text reworked by Abhinavagupta into his prominent Pratyabhijñā/Śaiva treatise of the same title.

summary: A 50-verse nondual Śaiva philosophical poem expounding supreme consciousness (Śiva/anuttara) as pure awareness (prakāśa) intrinsically united with reflective dynamism (vimarśa). It explains the manifestation and withdrawal of cosmic manifestation across the thirty-six principles (tattvas), establishing that objective reality is non-different from the supreme light, and describes spiritual liberation as the reabsorption of differentiated perception into universal spanda. Preserved primarily in Kashmirian manuscripts, it also enjoyed significant reception in South Indian Śākta Śaiva ritual traditions.

summary: The Ālambanaparīkṣā ('Investigation of the Perceptual Object') with its auto-commentary (vṛtti) by Dignāga (c. 480–540 CE) is a foundational treatise in eight verses expounding Yogācāra-vijñānavāda epistemology. Dignāga argues that external matter cannot serve as an object of cognition (ālambana), because neither indivisible atoms nor aggregated gross bodies fulfill the necessary twin criteria: being the cause that produces the cognition and presenting their likeness (ākāra) to consciousness. He concludes that the cognitive object is an internal mental appearance projected outward by beginningless cognitive latencies (vāsanā / śakti), establishing an epistemological basis for mind-only idealism.

summary: The Ālambanaparīkṣā ('Investigation of the Percept') is a concise foundational treatise in eight verses by the Buddhist epistemologist Dignāga (c. 480–540 CE). Dignāga defines a perceptual cognitive object (ālambana) through two joint criteria: it must act as the causal condition (kāraṇa/pratyaya) producing the cognition, and the cognition must bear its subjective appearance or form (tadābhāsa/ākāra). Arguing against externalist atomism (specifically the Sarvāstivāda and Sautrāntika models), he demonstrates that neither individual atoms nor aggregated atomic composites meet both criteria, ultimately concluding that the object cognized is actually an internal mental aspect appearing as if external, establishing the Yogācāra idealist doctrine.

summary: The Vallālacarita is a 16th-century Sanskrit biographical chronicle recounting the life, lineage, and reign of King Vallālasena (Ballāl Sen, r. c. 1158–1179 CE) of the Sena dynasty of Bengal. Completed around Śaka 1432 (1510 CE) at the behest of Buddhimanta Khān of Navadvīpa, the text blends historical memory with social legends. It is a central source for the study of medieval Bengali social history, particularly regarding the traditional origin of Kulīnism (kaulīnya-prathā) among Brahmins and Kāyasthas, the migration and gotras of Gauḍa Brahmins, and the royal reclassification and demotion of merchant (Suvarṇavaṇik) and yogic (Nāth) communities.

summary: The Ānandakanda is an encyclopedic medieval Tantric and alchemical treatise (Rasaśāstra), datable to approximately the 12th–13th century CE, structured in two major divisions: the Amṛtīkaraṇaviśrānti (26 chapters) and the Kriyākaraṇaviśrānti (10 chapters). It systematically synthesizes dhātuvāda (metallurgical operations and transmutation into precious metals) with dehavāda (iatrochemical rasāyana therapy aimed at rejuvenation and bodily immortality). The work is especially significant in the history of medicine and yoga for its detailed exposition of Haṭhayoga principles (Ṣaḍaṅgayoga, cakras, and prāṇāyāma) in ullāsa 1.20, as well as for preserving one of the earliest and most detailed accounts of the medicinal and ritual preparation of cannabis (bhaṅgā) in Sanskrit literature.

summary: The Dhvanyāloka ('Light on Suggestion') composed by Ānandavardhana in 9th-century Kashmir (reign of Avantivarman, c. 855–883 CE) is the foundational text of the dhvani school of Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra). Composed of mnemonic verses (kārikās) embedded within an extensive prose explanation (vṛtti) in four chapters (uddyotas), it argues that the essence or 'soul' of poetry is not found in literal meaning, figurative ornamentation, or stylistic qualities, but in suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha/dhvani). The work categorizes suggestion into three major varieties—vastu-dhvani (matter), alaṃkāra-dhvani (figures), and rasa-dhvani (aesthetic emotion)—permanently elevating aesthetic sentiment to the primary criterion of literary excellence in South Asian criticism.

summary: The Āpastambadharmasūtra constitutes the 28th and 29th praśnas of the Āpastamba Kalpasūtra belonging to the Taittirīya school of the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurveda, and is widely regarded as one of the oldest surviving Dharmasūtras (ca. 4th–3rd century BCE). Written in an archaic aphoristic style, it treats the duties of the four varṇas, student initiation (upanayana) and codes of conduct, rules of dietary purity, householder duties, ancestor rites (śrāddha), legal procedure, inheritance, and royal duties (rājadharma). It also contains the Adhyātmapaṭala (1.8.22–23), an important early philosophical discourse on the Ātman, and is a vital witness for pre-classical grammar and early Vedic orthopraxy.

summary: The Āpastambagṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual belonging to the Āpastamba branch of the Taittirīya school of the Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda, forming part of the larger Āpastamba Kalpasūtra corpus. Spanning 8 paṭalas (divided into 23 khaṇḍas), it sets forth the domestic rites and life-cycle ceremonies (saṃskāras), including marriage, conception, childhood sacraments, upanayana (initiation), daily and seasonal household oblations (pākayajñas), and ancestral offerings. The accompanying ritual mantras are drawn largely from the separate Āpastamba Mantrapāṭha (Ekāgnikāṇḍa). This e-text presents the complete sūtras accompanied in full by two classic commentaries: Haradatta's concise Anākulā (c. 12th century CE) and Sudarśanācārya's exhaustive Gṛhyatātparyadarśana (c. 14th–15th century CE).

summary: The Āpastambaśulbasūtra constitutes the 30th Praśna of the Āpastamba-Kalpasūtra within the Taittirīya tradition of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It contains classical Vedic geometry and measurement techniques for the layout and construction of sacrificial altars (vedis and citis), including methods for squaring the circle, transformation of areas, and the geometric property of the diagonal. This digital edition includes the root sūtras along with three South Indian commentaries: Kapardisvāmin's Kapardibhāṣya, Karavinda's Karavindīyā, and Sundararāja's Śulbapradīpa.

summary: The Āryānityatāsūtra is a short canonical discourse set at Jetavana in Śrāvastī, where the Buddha expounds that all conditioned phenomena (sarvasaṃskāra) are impermanent, unstable, and destined to perish. The sūtra systematically demonstrates that death is inevitable for all beings, from wealthy householders and universal monarchs to ascetics, gods of the three realms, and even arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas. It concludes with famous gāthās comparing life to earthen vessels made by a potter and ripe fruit destined to fall, culminating in the stanza: sarve kṣayāntā nicayāḥ patanāntāḥ samucchrayāḥ / saṃyogāśca viyogāntā maraṇāntaṃ hi jīvitam.

summary: The Āryabhaṭīya of Āryabhaṭa (composed 499 CE) is an early classic of Indian astronomy and mathematics divided into four chapters: Gītikāpāda (astronomical constants and alphabetical numeral notation), Gaṇitapāda (arithmetical, geometrical, and algebraic methods including the sine table and the kuṭṭaka algorithm for indeterminate linear equations), Kālakriyāpāda (reckoning of time, planetary velocities, and eccentric-epicyclic models), and Golapāda (celestial sphere and spherical astronomy). This volume features the 7th-century Āryabhaṭīyabhāṣya of Bhāskara I (written 629 CE at Valabhī), the oldest extant commentary on the text, noted for its extensive worked practical problems and defense of Āryabhaṭa's system. Because the manuscript tradition of Bhāskara's commentary breaks off after Golapāda 6, the missing final portion (Golapāda 7–50) is supplemented from the concise commentary of Someśvara (11th–12th century), which was composed directly as an abridgment of Bhāskara's bhāṣya.

summary: The Caryāmelāpakapradīpa ('Lamp that Integrates the Practices') by the tantric Āryadeva (c. 9th century) is a treatise of the Ārya tradition of the Guhyasamāja that sets out, in eleven chapters cast as answers to doubts (saṃśaya-pariccheda), the gradual path of the perfection stage: body, speech and mind isolation, illusory body, clear light and integration (yuganaddha). This e-text contains only the verses of the work, most of them citations from the Guhyasamāja and its explanatory tantras (Vajramālā, Saṃdhivyākaraṇa, etc.), together with the chapter colophons; the prose argument is not included.

summary: The Catuḥśatikā ('Four Hundred Verses') is the principal treatise of Āryadeva (c. 3rd century CE), the foremost disciple of Nāgārjuna, laying out the Madhyamaka philosophy across sixteen chapters. The first eight chapters focus on the bodhisattva's cultivation of merit by removing four fundamental delusions (regarding permanence, pleasure, purity, and selfhood), while chapters 9–16 refute non-Buddhist systems (such as Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika) and realists to establish universal emptiness (śūnyatā). This electronic text contains only 21 verses from chapters 1–5 preserved in secondary Sanskrit citations, as printed in the short appendix (pp. 159–160) of Bhagchandra Jain's 1971 edition.

summary: The Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa ('Treatise on the Purification of the Mind') is a Vajrayāna verse treatise in 134 kārikās expounding the principle that spiritual liberation depends entirely on internal mental purity rather than external ritual ablutions or rigid asceticism. It argues that emotional afflictions and transgressive practices, when transformed through discernment of emptiness and skilful means (upāya), serve as the very antidote to bondage, just as poison can cure poison or water remove water from the ear. Doctrinally aligned with the Guhyasamāja exegesis of the tantric Āryadeva (Āryadeva II), the text supports its tantric hermeneutic by citing classical Vinaya rules and Mahāyāna precedents to demonstrate that moral value resides strictly in intentionality (āśaya).

summary: Āryaśūra's Jātakamālā (c. 4th century CE) is a classic Buddhist campū-kāvya composition in ornate alternating verse and prose recounting previous lives of the Buddha to illustrate the perfections (pāramitā), such as generosity (dāna), morality (śīla), and patience (kṣānti). This e-text provides the critically edited Sanskrit text of stories 1 through 15 prepared by Albrecht Hanisch (2005), including the Vyāghrī-, Śibi-, Śaśa-, and Viśvantara-jātakas. Celebrated for its literary craftsmanship and moral elevation, the text exerted widespread influence across Buddhist Asia and served as a direct inspiration for narrative murals at Ajaṇṭā.

summary: The Jātakamālā ('Garland of Birth-Stories'), also entitled Bodhisattvāvadānamālā, is an ornate Buddhist campū composition (mixed verse and prose) by Āryaśūra, datable to approximately the 4th century CE. It retells thirty-four stories exemplifying the Bodhisattva's practice of the perfections (pāramitās), such as giving (dāna), moral discipline (śīla), and patience (kṣānti), in previous births as human, divine, or animal figures. Widely celebrated as a masterpiece of classical Sanskrit kāvya, strophes from this work are inscribed on the 5th-century murals at Ajanta.

summary: The Pāramitāsamāsa ("Compendium of the Perfections") is a kāvya-style verse treatise in six chapters on the six perfections of the bodhisattva: generosity, morality, patience, vigour, meditation and wisdom. summary: The Āyuḥparyantasūtra ('Discourse on the Limits of Lifespan') is a canonical Buddhist discourse delivered by the Buddha at Jetavana in Śrāvastī. It provides a comprehensive scholastic catalogue of the life expectancies of beings across the cosmological realms, progressing from the hells (naraka) and hungry ghosts (preta), through the four human continents (Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Avaragodānīya, and Uttarakuru), to the heavens of the desire, form, and formless realms up to the summit of cyclic existence (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). In addition to prose calculations correlating human and cosmological time spans, the sūtra incorporates verses explaining the karmic causes governing rebirth and longevity, closely paralleling early Abhidharma cosmological treatises such as the Lokaprajñapti.

summary: The Āśvalāyanaśrautasūtra is the primary ritual manual (kalpasūtra) of the Āśvalāyana recension of the Ṛgveda, codifying the sacrificial duties, recitations, and litanies of the hotṛ priest and his assistants. Structured into twelve adhyāyas (traditionally grouped into a pūrvārdha and an uttarārdha) and an appended Pravarādhyāya listing ancestral lineages, the text guides performances from the domestic Agnyādhāna, Agnihotra, and Darśapūrṇamāsa to complex Soma rituals, the Agnicayana, Sattras, and royal sacrifices such as the Aśvamedha. Closely affiliated with the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa, it serves as an indispensable primary source for the liturgy and practical execution of classical Vedic śrauta ritualism.

summary: The Rasendracintāmaṇi is an influential Sanskrit treatise on Rasaśāstra (iatrochemical alchemy and medicine) composed by the Nātha adept Ḍhuṇḍhukanātha, pupil of Kālanātha, generally dated between the 14th and 16th centuries CE. Written in verse interspersed with prose passages, the work describes the purification, processing, and calcination of mercury (pārada), metals, and minerals, as well as complex compound recipes for treating various illnesses and rejuvenating the body (rasāyana). The author strongly emphasizes firsthand laboratory experimentation and verification over uncritical textual transmission, and the work served as a primary source for subsequent treatises such as the Rasendrasārasaṃgraha.

summary: The Īśāvāsyopaniṣad (or Īśopaniṣad) forms the 40th and final chapter of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā of the Śukla Yajurveda, preserved here in its 18-mantra Kāṇva recension. It synthesizes the contemplation of the cosmos as pervaded by the Lord (īśa) with teachings on renunciation, the dual functions of action (avidyā/karman) and knowledge (vidyā), and final release. Śaṅkara's commentary (bhāṣya) interprets the work within classical Advaita Vedānta, arguing that ritual works pertain solely to worldly and heavenly ends while direct, non-dual knowledge of the self (ātman) alone eliminates ignorance and secures liberation.

summary: The Sāṃkhyakārikā (also known as Sāṃkhyasaptati), composed by Īśvarakṛṣṇa, is the foundational and earliest extant systematic treatise of the classical Sāṃkhya school of Indian philosophy. In 73 āryā verses, the text systematically expounds the dualistic metaphysics of pure conscious witness (puruṣa) and unmanifest primordial nature (prakṛti/pradhāna) along with its twenty-three evolutes. It details the three qualities (guṇas), the doctrine of pre-existent effect (satkāryavāda), epistemic means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), and the attainment of liberation (kaivalya) through discriminative knowledge (viveka).

summary: The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa (c. 4th–5th century CE) is the classical foundational text of the Sāṅkhya philosophical tradition, formulating its dualist metaphysics of conscious self (puruṣa) and primordial nature (prakṛti), the evolution of the twenty-five cosmic principles (tattvas), the three guṇas, and liberation through discriminative insight (vivekakhyāti). The Māṭharavṛtti is an essential early-to-medieval Sanskrit prose commentary that preserves traditional mythological background—such as the transmission lineage of Kapila and Āsuri—as well as detailed illustrative parables. Because it shares extensive verbatim and doctrinal parallels with the Gauḍapādabhāṣya and Paramārtha's 6th-century Chinese Suvarṇasaptati, it is an indispensable witness for tracing the evolution of classical Sāṅkhya exegesis.

summary: The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa (c. 4th–5th century CE) is the foundational surviving treatise of classical dualist Sāṃkhya philosophy, outlining the twenty-five tattvas, the satkāryavāda theory of causation, and liberation through the discriminative insight separating conscious spirit (puruṣa) from primordial matter (prakṛti). The Gauḍapādabhāṣya is an early, accessible prose commentary providing word glosses, mythological illustrative stories, and cosmological expositions. The commentary covers verses 1 through 69, concluding with a colophon verse declaring the exposition of the seventy stanzas complete, followed by the concluding historical transmission kārikās (70–72).

summary: The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa is the classical foundational treatise of Sāṃkhya philosophy, articulating its dualist ontology of insentient nature (prakṛti) and pure consciousness (puruṣa), the evolution of the twenty-five tattvas, three epistemic pramāṇas, and liberation through discriminative insight. The Jayamaṅgalā is an important early medieval running commentary (ṭīkā) that provides lucid grammatical and philosophical expositions for all 72 verses. It constitutes an essential witness for the early textual and doctrinal transmission of classical Sāṃkhya alongside the Gauḍapādabhāṣya, the Māṭharavṛtti, and the Yuktidīpikā.

summary: The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa (c. 4th–5th century CE) is the foundational and most authoritative classical treatise of the Sāṃkhya darśana. In approximately 72–73 āryā stanzas, it systematically expounds the dualistic metaphysics of unmanifest and manifest primordial nature (avyakta- and vyakta-prakṛti) alongside the multiplicity of pure conscious subjects (puruṣa). The text establishes the satkāryavāda theory of causation, analyzes the triad of guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas), charts the 25 evolutionary principles (tattvas) and psychological schema (buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas, indriyas, tanmātras, mahābhūtas), and teaches that discriminative insight (vivekakhyāti) dissolves the misidentification of consciousness with nature to achieve final isolation and liberation (kaivalya).

summary: The Sāṃkhyatattvavivecana is a post-classical commentary on the Tattvasamāsa, a concise 25-sūtra digest of Sāṃkhya philosophy. Composed by Kṣemānanda (Ṣimānanda), a Kānyakubja scholar resident in Iṣṭikāpura (Etawah), the text expounds fundamental ontological categories including the eight prakṛtis, sixteen vikāras, puruṣa, the three guṇas, evolution and dissolution, and liberation. Drawing upon late scholastic Sāṃkhya formulations, it dates to the early modern period (approx. 17th–18th century).

summary: The Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines') is the foundational and earliest extensive scripture in the Prajñāpāramitā corpus. Centered on dialogues between the Buddha and disciples including Subhūti, Śāriputra, and Ānanda at Vulture Peak, it expounds the core Mahāyāna doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā), the non-apprehension (anupalambha) of independent dharmas, and the altruistic path of the bodhisattva aiming at omniscience (sarvākārajñatā). Across 32 chapters, it promotes the veneration, recitation, and copying of Prajñāpāramitā manuscripts, culminating in the pilgrimage and self-sacrifice of Bodhisattva Sadāprarudita under the teacher Dharmodgata.
