attribution_note: Authorship is historically disputed. The unique Sanskrit manuscript does not record an author in its colophon, recording only the patron/scribe (paṇḍita-vaidya-śrī-Amaracandra). The Tibetan Tanjur (D 4053) attributes the Bhāṣya to Jinaputra (rgyal ba'i sras). In Chinese tradition, Kuiji states that an early commentary was composed by Buddhasiṃha, while Sthiramati compiled the composite Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā (T 1606). Tatia's editio princeps ascribed the Bhāṣya to Sthiramati following Pralhad Pradhan, but modern scholars (such as Noriaki Hakamaya and Robert Kritzer) distinguish the Bhāṣya from the Vyākhyā and accept Jinaputra as the traditional author.

summary: The Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya is an essential 6th-century Yogācāra prose commentary on Asaṅga's Abhidharmasamuccaya. It provides extensive analytical glosses on Asaṅga's concise definitions of mental factors, aggregates (skandha), sense bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and the path, harmonizing classical Abhidharma categories with foundational Yogācāra doctrines such as the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna). Preserved in a single palm-leaf manuscript discovered by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana in Tibet and in Tibetan translation, it is traditionally ascribed to Jinaputra.

summary: The Kādambarīkathāsāra is an eight-canto metrical epitome of Bāṇabhaṭṭa's celebrated 7th-century prose romance Kādambarī, composed in Kashmir in the late 9th century CE by Abhinanda, son of the Nyāya logician Jayanta Bhaṭṭa. It compresses Bāṇa's intricate, multilayered narrative of reborn lovers (Candrāpīḍa, Puṇḍarīka, Kādambarī, and Mahāśvetā) into accessible and elegant anuṣṭubh verse, omitting the extensive descriptive prose digressions of the original. The autobiographical prologue in canto 1 preserves valuable historical evidence for the author's family genealogy, recording their migration from Gauḍa to Dārvābhisāra and Kashmir, and noting that his ancestor Śaktisvāmin served as a minister under the Kārkoṭa ruler Lalitāditya Muktāpīḍa.

summary: The Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī (also known as the Laghuvimarśinī) is Abhinavagupta's running commentary on Utpaladeva's Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, the foundational work of the Pratyabhijñā school of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism. Spanning four thematic sections (adhikāras)—addressing cognitive awareness (jñāna), sovereign action (kriyā), scriptural authority (āgama), and metaphysical synthesis (tattvasaṅgraha)—it argues that liberation consists in recognizing one's essential identity with the supreme Lord (Paramaśiva). Abhinavagupta articulates a philosophy of consciousness founded on self-manifestation (prakāśa), reflective awareness (vimarśa), and divine autonomy (svātantrya), engaging in detailed refutations of Buddhist epistemological, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, and Sāṅkhya positions.

summary: The Anuttarāṣṭikā ('Eight Verses on the Supreme/Absolute') is a concise philosophical stotra in Śārdūlavikrīḍita metre composed by the Kashmir Śaiva master Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). It articulates the Trika doctrine of anupāya ('no-means'), demonstrating that because non-dual consciousness (cidadvaya) is already the intrinsic nature of all reality, outward spiritual transmission (saṃkrāma), formal meditation, and ascetic striving are superfluous. Rejection and acquisition are discarded in favor of resting peacefully in reality as it is (svastho yathāvasthitaḥ), recognizing the world as an effortless manifestation of one's own conscious nature.

summary: The Bhairavastava ('Hymn of Praise to Bhairava', also titled Bhairavastotra or Padyanavaka) is a short devotional hymn composed by the Kashmiri polymath Abhinavagupta. In the concluding tenth stanza, the author dates its completion to the tenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa in Laukika Samvat [40]68 (corresponding to December 992 or January 993 CE). The hymn integrates personal devotion (bhakti) with nondual Trika and Pratyabhijñā philosophy, celebrating the deity Bhairava as identical to the practitioner's innate, radiant consciousness (saṃvid) and describing the immediate removal of existential fear, karma, and death through direct realization of non-duality.

summary: The Bodhapañcadaśikā ('Fifteen Verses on Awakening') is a succinct didactic treatise composed by the Kashmiri polymath Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). As indicated in its concluding verse, it was written to introduce disciples of gentle intellect (sukumāramati) to the foundational non-dual metaphysics of Trika Śaivism. In fifteen kārikās, Abhinavagupta elucidates the single nature of consciousness (Bhairava/Parameśvara), the inseparability of the divine subject and creative power (śakti), the universe as an internal reflection (pratibimba) within the mirror of awareness, and the recognition that liberation (jīvanmukti) is the realization of unbroken wholeness.

summary: The Kramastotra (or Kramastava) is a 30-verse hymn composed by Abhinavagupta in December 990 CE (Laukika year 4066) celebrating the esoteric doctrine of the Krama (Kālīkula) lineage within Kashmir Śaivism. It delineates the twelve Kālīs (dvādaśakālī) and the cyclic unfolding of dynamic consciousness across the phases of creation (sṛṣṭi), preservation (sthiti), dissolution (saṃhāra), and the ineffable fourth state (anākhya/bhāsā). The hymn culminates in praise of Lord Manthānabhairava as the ultimate essence of the universe and closes with an explicit authorial colophon dating the text.

summary: The Mālinīvijayavārttika (also known as the Mālinīślokavārttika) is a major verse commentary composed by Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE) interpreting the opening sentence of the Mālinīvijayottaratantra, the foundational scriptural authority of the Trika Śaiva lineage. Arranged in two books (kāṇḍas), the text formulates a comprehensive theology of revelation (āgama), hermeneutics, and nondual metaphysics while mounting extensive polemics against Buddhist epistemologists, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā. Alongside the Tantrāloka and Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa, it represents one of Abhinavagupta's core scriptural syntheses.

summary: The Paramārthasāra ('Essence of Ultimate Reality') is an introductory compendium of 105 āryā stanzas by the Kashmiri master Abhinavagupta (c. late 10th – early 11th c. CE), articulating the metaphysical and soteriological core of nondual Trika Śaivism. Adapted from an earlier Vaiṣṇava work attributed to Ādiśeṣa, the treatise outlines the emanation of the thirty-six principles (tattvas) through the playful self-expression (krīḍā) and sovereign freedom (svātantrya) of Śiva-consciousness, the contracted state of worldly bondage (saṃsāra), and liberation through self-recognition (pratyabhijñā). Yogarāja's vivṛti commentary (late 11th c. CE) expands Abhinavagupta's compressed verses into a systematic philosophical treatise, refuting Advaita Vedānta and Buddhist positions while clarifying the nondual Śaiva doctrine of divine grace (śaktipāta / anugrahaśakti).

summary: The Paramārthasāra ('Essence of the Supreme Truth') is a concise philosophical compendium consisting of 105 verses composed in the late 10th or early 11th century CE by the polymath Abhinavagupta. It serves as an introductory summary of nondual Kashmir Śaivism (Trika and Pratyabhijñā), setting forth the emanation of cosmic reality across thirty-six tattvas structured into four spheres (aṇḍas), the soul's contraction through the impurities (malas) and limiting veils (kañcukas), and liberation through spontaneous recognition (pratyabhijñā) of one's identity with Paramaśiva. Abhinavagupta explicitly adapted this work from an earlier Advaita/Vaiṣṇava treatise attributed to Ādiśeṣa, rearticulating its teachings in accordance with the monistic Śaiva view.

summary: The Paryantapañcāśikā ('Fifty Verses on the Ultimate Limit') is a short philosophical treatise in 52 anuṣṭubh verses attributed to the non-dual Śaiva master Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). Synthesizing core teachings of the Trika and Krama traditions, the text delineates the non-dual reality of Bhairava, the manifestation and dissolution of the six cosmic paths (ṣaḍadhvan), and the four currents of energy (khecarī, gocarī, dikcarī, and bhūcarī) issuing from Vyomeśvarī into unitary consciousness. Known only from a single South Indian palm-leaf manuscript, the work was received and cited by later South Indian Śākta-Śaiva authors such as Maheśvarānanda and Madhurāja.

summary: The Tantrasāra ('Essence of Tantra') is Abhinavagupta's prose compendium summarizing the doctrinal and ritual core of his encyclopedic verse work, the Tantrāloka. Divided into twenty-two daily lessons (āhnikas), it expounds the non-dual metaphysics and soteriology of Trika Śaivism and Kaula ritual traditions, systematically covering the four means of liberation (anupāya, śāmbhava-, śākta-, and āṇavopāya) alongside detailed instructions for initiation (dīkṣā), mantras, and esoteric ritual practices.

summary: The Abhisamācārikadharma is a Vinaya treatise preserved by the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravāda school outlining everyday rules of proper conduct, deportment, and etiquette (abhisamācāra) for Buddhist monks, functioning as a vital complement to the formal offenses of the Prātimokṣasūtra. Preserved in a single 11th–12th century palm-leaf manuscript from Tibet, the text is arranged in seven sections (vargas) detailing duties regarding elders, lodging and furniture, the kaṭhina robe ceremony, wandering and resident monks, and daily bodily hygiene. Transmitted in an archaic layer of Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit, it provides uniquely detailed evidence for early to medieval Indian Buddhist monastic culture and daily praxis.

summary: The Abhisamayālaṅkāra ('Ornament for Clear Realization') is a foundational Mahāyāna verse treatise composed of 273 kārikās arranged across eight chapters (adhikāras). Attributed to Maitreya/Asaṅga (c. 4th century CE), it serves as a systematic hidden-meaning commentary on the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, organizing the progressive path to enlightenment into eight clear realizations (aṣṭāv abhisamayāḥ) and seventy distinct topics (arthasaptati). Regarded as one of the Five Treatises of Maitreya, it remains the principal pedagogical framework for Prajñāpāramitā scholasticism in Tibetan Buddhist monastic curricula and inspired major Indian commentaries by Vimuktisena, Haribhadra, and Ratnākaraśānti.

Prompted by Ānanda observing a magnificent eighty-gated multistoried hall (kūṭāgāra), the Buddha instructs that constructing even a miniature clay stūpa the size of an āmalaka fruit, with a parasol like a jujube leaf and a relic like a mustard seed, generates far greater merit than bestowing whole continents of jewels upon śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or the saṅgha, owing to the limitless nature of the Buddha's qualities. The sūtra survives in Sanskrit among the Gilgit manuscripts and the Potala collection, as well as in Tibetan (Toh 319) and Chinese versions (T 688, T 689, T 704).

summary: The Adhikaraṇavastu is the sixteenth chapter of the seventeen vastus comprising the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu. It systematically governs legal disputes within the monastic community, classifying conflicts into four types (vivādādhikaraṇa, anuvādādhikaraṇa, āpattādhikaraṇa, and kṛtyādhikaraṇa) and laying out the seven formal procedures (adhikaraṇa-śamatha) for resolving them. Preserved in a single 6th-century CE birch-bark manuscript from Gilgit as well as in the Tibetan Kanjur ('Dul ba, Toh 1-16), it is a vital primary document for the study of classical Buddhist jurisprudence.

summary: The Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 150 Lines'), also widely known as the Prajñāpāramitānaya or Rishukyō, is an esoteric scripture bridging late Prajñāpāramitā doctrine and Yoga Tantra ritualism. Expounded by Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas led by Mahāvairocana and Vajrapāṇi, the sūtra teaches seventeen aphorisms on the innate purity of passion, sensory experience, and phenomenal reality (viśuddhi-pada) through the lens of emptiness. The text occupies a central doctrinal and liturgical role in East Asian esoteric Buddhism (especially Japanese Shingon) and is also preserved across Tibetan canonical collections (Toh 17, Toh 489).

summary: The Advayaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā is a condensed Mahāyāna scripture representing the Perfection of Wisdom in Fifty Lines (Ardhaśatikā or Pañcāśatikā Prajñāpāramitā). In late Newar scribal transmission, 'Ardhaśatikā' ('fifty units/lines') was corrupted via orthographic resemblance into 'Advayaśatikā' and incorporated into Dhāraṇīsaṃgraha collections, though the text contains neither mantras nor any doctrinal discussion of non-duality (advaya). Set at Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, the Buddha instructs Subhūti that all spiritual paths and dharmas—including the six perfections, the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the bodhipakṣa dharmas, and the distinctive Buddha-qualities—are encompassed within the perfection of wisdom, which is ungraspable, intrinsically pure, and comparable to empty space. The Chinese translation by Dānapāla (T 248) confirms its circulation by the late 10th century CE.

summary: The Agnipurāṇa is one of the eighteen canonical Mahāpurāṇas, framed as a discourse imparted by the fire god Agni to the sage Vasiṣṭha. Renowned for its encyclopedic scope, it combines traditional Puranic cosmogony, genealogies, and avatāra narratives with extensive epitomes of classical and medieval technical disciplines. These include comprehensive manuals of temple architecture and iconography (vāstu- and śilpaśāstra), Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva tantric ritual and initiation (dīkṣā), statecraft and military science (rājanīti, dhanurveda), medicine (āyurveda), poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra), metrics (chandaḥ), and grammar. While preserving earlier epic-Puranic material, the compilation reached its extant encyclopedic form largely between the 9th and 11th centuries CE.

summary: The Ahorātravratacaityasevānuśaṃsāvadāna is a Buddhist narrative poem (avadāna) preserved in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts celebrating the spiritual merits and worldly rewards (anuśaṃsā) of the 'day-and-night vow' (ahorātravrata) performed during the worship and ritual service of caityas/stūpas. Framed as a dialogue between King Aśoka and the elder Upagupta, the text details the procedural rules of the vrata and illustrates its karmic efficacy through narratives of devotees whose stupa veneration purified negative karma and led to celestial rebirth and progress toward enlightenment. It constitutes a key textual witness for the devotional cult of the caitya and vow observances in Newar Buddhism.

summary: The prose recension of the Ahorātravratakathā is a late medieval Newar Buddhist narrative (vratakathā) explaining the ritual origin, liturgical observance, and spiritual benefits of the ahorātravrata ('day-and-night vow') associated with caitya and Dharmadhātu worship. Set in Kapilavastu as a dialogue between the Buddha Śākyamuni, Subhūti, and Vajradhara, the narrative recounts how the elder Śāriputra visited the city of Dharmapattana to instruct King Dharmadakṣa and Queen Suvratī in the vow, culminating in the king's attainment of liberation and seven maidens being reborn in Sukhāvatī. The text represents Newar Hybrid Sanskrit literature, combining avadāna-style storytelling with concrete ritual instructions for fasting, circumambulation, and caitya veneration.

summary: The Ahorātravratakathā is a Mahāyāna Buddhist narrative in verse composed in Newari Hybrid Sanskrit, belonging to the Nepalese vratakathā / vratāvadāna genre. It details the ritual procedures and religious merits of observing the ahorātravrata (a full 24-hour day-and-night observance) centered on the worship of the Dharmadhātucaitya and the deity Vāgīśvara (Mañjuśrī). Framed as a discourse of Śākyamuni Buddha to Subhūti at Jetavana, the narrative incorporates an embedded account in which the teacher Vasubandhu instructs King Indrapṛṣṭa of Gandhavatī, tracing the institution of the vow back to the primordial Buddha Vipaśyin.

summary: The Aitareyopaniṣad, embedded in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (II.4–6) of the Ṛgveda, is an early Vedic prose Upaniṣad that expounds the creation of the cosmos from the singular Ātman, the embodiment of cosmic faculties within man, the doctrine of the threefold births (trayo janmāḥ), and the foundational mahāvākya 'consciousness is Brahman' (prajñānaṃ brahma) [1.1.2111, 1.1.3212475]. This e-text contains the complete root text accompanied by Śaṅkara's classical Advaita Vedānta commentary (bhāṣya), which commences with an extensive Sambandhabhāṣya refuting the view that ritual works must be combined with knowledge (jñānakarmasamuccaya) to achieve liberation.

summary: The Ajitasenavyākaraṇa (or Ajitasenavyākaraṇanirdeśa) is a transitional Mahāyāna sūtra surviving in Sanskrit in the 6th–7th-century Gilgit cache and in Central Asian manuscript fragments, but absent from both the Tibetan and Chinese Buddhist canons. Structurally sharing traits with mainstream avadāna literature, it depicts the Buddha predicting future buddhahood (vyākaraṇa) for King Ajitasena of Rājagṛha. The text is celebrated in Buddhist studies for documenting an early developmental phase of the Mahāyāna, emphasizing devotion, the merit of hearing and pronouncing the Buddha's name, stūpa worship, and textual transmission prior to the full systematization of emptiness (dharmaśūnyatā) doctrine.

summary: The Ajitasenavyākaraṇa (or Ajitasenavyākaraṇanirdeśa) is an early Mahāyāna scripture preserved in Sanskrit in the Gilgit find and Central Asian fragments, with no known Tibetan or Chinese translations. Framed in the manner of an avadāna, it relates how the Buddha instructs King Ajitasena through the śrāvaka disciple Nandimitra, emphasizing the merit of generous giving (dāna) and the salvific power of reciting Buddha names. Because it articulates universal buddhahood and Mahāyāna devotion within a mainstream narrative setting without the doctrine of dharmaśūnyatā, it is frequently cited in modern scholarship examining the transitional formation of the early Mahāyāna.

summary: The Catuḥstavasamāsārtha ('Summary of the Meaning of the Four Hymns') by Paṇḍita Amṛtākara is an Indian Madhyamaka commentary clarifying the doctrinal and contemplative import of the Catuḥstava attributed to Nāgārjuna. Preserved uniquely in an incomplete palm-leaf manuscript found at Ngor Monastery in Tibet, the extant text comments upon portions of the Niraupamyastava and the entirety of the Acintyastava and Paramārthastava. It elucidates the hymns' praise of the Buddha through the lens of non-conceptual wisdom, dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), emptiness (śūnyatā), and the advanced stages of the bodhisattva path.

summary: The Amaruśataka is an anthology of approximately one hundred independent single-stanza verses (muktaka) in classical meters devoted to erotic love (śṛṅgāra). Each stanza presents a self-contained vignette illustrating psychological and emotional dynamics between lovers—including youthful modesty, lovers' quarrels and wounded pride (māna), separation (vipralambha), and reconciliation. Extensively cited by rhetoricians such as Ānandavardhana, Abhinavagupta, and Mammaṭa, the collection is regarded as an archetype of suggestive poetry (dhvani) and aesthetic flavor (rasa).

summary: The Amoghapāśahṛdayasūtra is a prominent Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture (classified as Kriyātantra in Tibetan tradition) focusing on Amoghapāśa Lokeśvara, an esoteric multi-armed form of Avalokiteśvara. Set on Mount Potalaka, the text recounts how Avalokiteśvara received this root heart-mantra (hṛdaya) in an earlier aeon from the Buddha Lokendrarāja, and details the extensive soteriological and mundane benefits of hearing, reciting, or writing it. It provides the central dhāraṇī formula alongside ritual procedures (vidhi/kalpa) for healing ailments, protection against danger, and purifying severe karmic offenses.

summary: The Anityatāsūtra is a short discourse delivered by the Buddha at the Jetavana in Śrāvastī explaining that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskārāḥ) are impermanent, unstable, and subject to change. The Buddha illustrates universal mortality across all classes of society, heavenly beings across the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness, and even enlightened beings (arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas). The sūtra concludes with four gnomic verses on mortality and destruction parallel to stanzas found in the Anityavarga of the Udānavarga.

summary: The Tarkasaṃgraha of Annambhaṭṭa (17th c.) is the definitive introductory primer of the syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika system, systematically outlining the seven ontological categories (padārtha) and four means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). This composite e-text contains the root text embedded with Annambhaṭṭa's auto-commentary (Tarkasaṃgrahadīpikā), Nīlakaṇṭha's widely taught 18th-century sub-commentary (Dīpikāprakāśikā or Nīlakaṇṭhī), and N.S. Rāmānuja Tātācārya's (1928–2017) modern sub-commentary (Bālapriyā). Together, these layered texts elucidate the terse mūla definitions and defend foundational Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika theses using the technical vocabulary and methodology of Navya-Nyāya dialectics.

summary: The Antarvyāptisamarthana ('Vindication of Internal Pervasion') by the 11th-century master Ratnākaraśānti is a pivotal text in late Buddhist epistemology. It champions the doctrine of 'internal pervasion' (antarvyāpti) in the proof of momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) from existence (sattva), arguing that invariable concomitance is grasped directly within the subject itself (pakṣa / sādhyadharmin) through conceptual entailment and an invalidating cognition (bādhakapramāṇa), thereby discarding external corroborating examples (dṛṣṭānta / bahirvyāpti) as superfluous.

summary: The Aparimitāyuḥsūtra is a Mahāyāna dhāraṇī-sūtra in which the Buddha Śākyamuni instructs Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta at Śrāvastī concerning the tathāgata Aparimitāyurjñānasuviniścitatejorāja, who presides over the zenith Buddha-field Aparimitaguṇasaṃcaya. The sūtra extols the recitation, writing, and veneration of this scripture and its central longevity dhāraṇī, assuring that these acts extend human lifespan to a full hundred years, absolve grave karmic faults, avert untimely death, and secure rebirth in Sukhāvatī. Widely diffused across Central Asia and Tibet, the text survives in thousands of Dunhuang manuscript copies as well as Sanskrit, Khotanese, Tibetan, and Chinese recensions.

summary: The Apohasiddhi is a concise philosophical treatise on semantics and epistemology by the 11th-century Buddhist logician Ratnakīrti of Vikramaśīla. Systematizing the arguments of his teacher Jñānaśrīmitra's Apohaprakaraṇa, Ratnakīrti rejects both exclusive affirmationism (vidhivāda) and pure negative exclusion (pratiṣedhavāda), arguing that words convey a positive entity intrinsically qualified by the exclusion of dissimilar things (anyāpohaviśiṣṭo vidhiḥ). The work forms an important milestone in late Buddhist nominalism, answering realist objections from the Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā systems.

summary: The Vairāgyaśataka ('Century of Verses on Renunciation') by the 16th-century polymath Appayadīkṣita is a didactic and devotional Sanskrit work consisting of 101 verses predominantly composed in the āryā metre. Following the classical gnomic tradition exemplified by Bhartṛhari, it reflects upon the vanity of worldly pursuits, the transient nature of wealth, youth, and bodily existence, and the pitfalls of sensual attachment. The poem culminates in praising the attainment of inner peace (śānti) and final spiritual liberation through devotion to Śiva at the holy sanctuary of Avimukta (Vārāṇasī).

summary: The Hetubinduṭīkā is a major 8th-century commentary by Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa on Dharmakīrti's Hetubindu ('Drop of Reason'), an independent tract dedicated to the logical reason (hetu) and Buddhist inferential theory. Arcaṭa offers comprehensive analyses of the three varieties of valid probans (svabhāva, kārya, and anupalabdhi), the formal criteria of the triple-character reason (trairūpya), perceptual judgments, and the inference of momentariness (kṣaṇikatvānumāna). It represents a crucial milestone in post-Dharmakīrti Pramāṇavāda and served as the primary basis for Durveka Miśra's sub-commentary Āloka.

summary: The Hetubinduṭīkā by Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa (c. 8th century CE) is an extensive commentary on Dharmakīrti's Hetubindu, an independent treatise examining the theory of logical reasons and inference. Arcaṭa discusses essential epistemological topics of Buddhist pramāṇavāda, including the preliminary statement of purpose (prayojana), the three conditions of a valid mark (trairūpya), the threefold classification of valid probantia, and the proof of momentariness (kṣaṇikatvānumāna). Preserved in Sanskrit and Tibetan, it served as a crucial intermediate authority between Dharmakīrti and later commentators such as Dharmottara and Durveka Miśra.

summary: The Arthaviniścayasūtra ('Sūtra on the Ascertainment of Meanings') is an early Buddhist doctrinal compendium that enumerates and defines twenty-seven core technical categories (dharmaparyāyas), including the five aggregates, eighteen dhātus, twelve āyatanas, twelvefold dependent origination, four noble truths, spiritual faculties, limbs of awakening, and the marks of a Buddha. Functioning as a concise catechism linking canonical discourse with emerging Abhidharma frameworks, the sūtra exhibits strong Sarvāstivāda and Sautrāntika doctrinal characteristics. Preserved in Sanskrit, Tibetan (Toh 317), and Chinese (T 762, T 763), it served as the basis for Vīryaśrīdatta's 8th-century Nālandā commentary, the Arthaviniścayasūtranibandhana.

summary: The Abhidharmasamuccaya is Asaṅga's definitive synthesis of Abhidharma doctrine from a Mahāyāna and Yogācāra perspective. The treatise is structured into two main parts: the Lakṣaṇasamuccaya, which categorizes dharmas across the skandhas, dhātus, āyatanas, and fifty-one mental factors (caittas), and the Viniścayasamuccaya, which analyzes the noble truths, doctrinal exposition, attainment of liberation, and rules of philosophical dialectic. Providing the scholastic foundation of Yogācāra dogmatics, it served as the standard textbook for Abhidharma study in Tibetan and East Asian Buddhism.

summary: The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra ('Ornament of the Mahāyāna Sūtras') is a foundational Yogācāra verse treatise of ca. 800 verses in 21 chapters; this e-text gives the verses alone, without Vasubandhu's bhāṣya. It defends the Mahāyāna as Buddha's word and treats refuge, gotra, bodhicitta, practice, reality (tattva), the perfections, the factors of awakening and the bodhisattva's qualities, ending with praises of the Buddha. It is one of the five treatises ascribed to Maitreya in the Tibetan tradition.

summary: The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra ('Ornament of the Mahāyāna Sūtras') is a foundational treatise of the Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda tradition, consisting of approximately 800 verse kārikās across 21 chapters accompanied by Vasubandhu's prose commentary (bhāṣya). It establishes the scriptural validity of the Mahāyāna and provides an extensive exposition of the bodhisattva path, synthesizing emptiness with classical Yogācāra tenets including the three natures (trisvabhāva), consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā), and the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparivṛtti). Topics range from lineage (gotra) and the generation of bodhicitta to the perfections (pāramitā), bodhisattva stages (bhūmi), and the resultant bodies of a Buddha (trikāya).

summary: The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra ('Ornament of the Mahāyāna Sūtras') is a foundational Yogācāra treatise of ca. 800 verses in 21 chapters, here transmitted together with its prose bhāṣya. It defends the authenticity of the Mahāyāna as Buddha's word and systematically treats refuge, spiritual lineage (gotra), the arising of bodhicitta, practice, reality (tattva), the perfections, the factors of awakening and the bodhisattva's qualities and stages, culminating in buddhahood. The bhāṣya explains each verse and supplies the structure of the argument; the work was translated into Chinese (T 1604) and Tibetan (D 4020, 4026) and commented upon by Asvabhāva and Sthiramati.

summary: The Triśatikāyāḥ prajñāpāramitāyāḥ kārikāsaptatiḥ ('Seventy Verses on the Perfection of Wisdom in Three Hundred Lines') is a verse treatise on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā composed by the Yogācāra master Asaṅga (c. 4th–5th century CE). Consisting of 77 mnemonic kārikās (despite the title's traditional designation as seventy), the work systematically analyzes the Diamond Sutra according to eighteen topics (sthāna), elucidating the bodhisattva path, the elimination of conceptual attachments, and the non-apprehension of dharmas from a Yogācāra perspective. It survives in Sanskrit in a single palm-leaf manuscript discovered at Ngor monastery and edited by Giuseppe Tucci.

summary: The Śarīrārthagāthā ('Verses on the Essential Meaning' or 'Collected-Meaning Verses') is a collection of 41 canonical and paracanonical verse groups embedded in the Cintāmayībhūmi ('Ground of Reflection'), part of the Maulī Bhūmiḥ of the Yogācārabhūmi. The stanzas derive from Āgama texts (particularly the Saṃyuktāgama) and the Udānavarga, treating fundamental Buddhist themes such as mindfulness, vigilance, and liberation from craving. In the Yogācārabhūmi, these received early verses are systematically gathered to provide the basis for an extensive philosophical and meditative commentary in accordance with Yogācāra doctrine.

summary: The Śrāvakabhūmi ('Stage of the Disciple') is the thirteenth section of the Maulī Bhūmi (basic section) of the Yogācārabhūmi corpus, constituting an extensive and systematic manual of Buddhist meditation and spiritual development. Structured into four yogasthānas (stages of spiritual practice), it treats the prerequisites for monastic life, spiritual disposition (gotra), initial entry into practice (avatāra), and the dual cultivation of calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) culminating in liberation. Although preserved as part of the Yogācāra canon, it systematically articulates classical Mainstream (Śrāvakayāna) praxis and doctrine.

Associated with both the Śaunaka and Paippalāda traditions and closely related to the Vaitānasūtra and Kauśikasūtra, it presents penances and restorative mantras primarily formulated for the brahman priest supervising the sacrifice.

summary: The Atharvavedapariśiṣṭa is a major collection of supplementary ancillary tracts belonging to the Śaunaka tradition of the Atharvaveda, traditionally organized into 72 numbered sections. Datable across several chronological strata between the late Vedic period and the middle of the first millennium CE, the corpus addresses rituals, ceremonies, and lore omitted or only briefly mentioned in the core Atharvan saṃhitā and kalpasūtras. It preserves extensive manuals on royal rituals and purohita duties (such as the puṣyābhiṣeka and rājadharma), divination and omen interpretation (adbhuta, śānti), astral science (nakṣatrakalpa), and early sectarian observances including the Pāśupata vrata.

summary: The Bodhipathapradīpa ('Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment') is a foundational Mahāyāna treatise composed c. 1042 CE at Tholing Monastery by Atiśa at the request of the Western Tibetan ruler Byang chub 'od. In 69 concise verses, it outlines the gradual course of spiritual development through the tripartite typology of spiritual capacities (adhama-, madhyama-, and uttamapuruṣa), harmonising sūtric bodhisattva practices with esoteric tantric initiations and monastic discipline. The original Sanskrit text being lost, this digital file contains Losang Norbu Shastri's 1984 Sanskrit back-translation from the Tibetan transmission, which historically gave rise to the entire Tibetan Lamrim ('Stages of the Path') genre.

summary: The Avadānaśataka ('A Century of Edifying Exploits') is one of the earliest and most structured Sanskrit anthologies of Buddhist narrative legends (avadāna), organized into ten thematic decades (vargas) containing ten stories each. Attributed to the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda school and datable to roughly the 2nd–3rd century CE, the work illustrates the inevitable workings of karma and retribution across rebirths, focusing on predictions of future buddhahood and pratyekabuddhahood, arhatship, past-life deeds of the Buddha (jātakas), the torments of pretas, and noble acts of charity (dāna). It preserves early canonical clichés and formulas, and survives in Sanskrit as well as canonical Tibetan (Toh 343) and Chinese (T 200) translations.

summary: The Bhagavadbhaktistotra is a non-dual Śaiva devotional hymn composed in ca. 65 stanzas by Avadhūtasiddha. Extolling Śiva as the supreme reality encompassing and transcending the perspectives of diverse philosophical traditions (including Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, Buddhism, and Vedānta), it was highly regarded in Kashmirian Śaiva circles and is quoted by Abhinavagupta in the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī and Yogarāja on the Paramārthasāra.

summary: The Aśokāvadāna is a major Sanskrit Buddhist narrative recounting the legendary life, conversion, and reign of the Mauryan emperor Aśoka, together with legends of the elder Upagupta and Aśoka's blinded son Kuṇāla. Formed within the (Mūla)sarvāstivāda tradition around the 2nd century CE, the narrative depicts Aśoka's dramatic transition from cruel despot ('Caṇḍāśoka') to righteous Buddhist monarch ('Dharmāśoka') who erects 84,000 stūpas throughout Jambudvīpa and gives away his royal treasury to the saṅgha. In Sanskrit the cycle is transmitted as chapters 26–29 of the Divyāvadāna anthology, while independent early versions survive in Chinese translation (T 2042 and T 2043).

summary: The Buddhacarita ('Acts of the Buddha') is an early Sanskrit court poem (mahākāvya) composed by the Buddhist author Aśvaghoṣa in the 1st–2nd century CE. Although the complete narrative comprised twenty-eight cantos narrating the life of Siddhārtha Gautama from his birth to his parinirvāṇa and the distribution of relics (fully preserved in Tibetan and Chinese translations), only the first fourteen cantos (concluding with the enlightenment) survive in the authentic Sanskrit manuscript tradition. Masterfully synthesizing sophisticated kāvya aesthetics with Buddhist philosophy, it is the earliest surviving complete court epic in Sanskrit literature.

summary: The Gurupañcāśikā ('Fifty Verses on the Guru') is a classic Vajrayāna manual prescribing the obligations, ritual protocols, and devotional posture of a disciple toward the spiritual master (vajrācārya). Drawing on doctrines found in major Anuttarayoga tantras such as the Guhyasamāja, it details the criteria for examining a guru and disciple, behavioral etiquette, samaya vows, and the karmic consequences of guru disparagement. Although traditionally attributed to the 1st–2nd-century CE poet Aśvaghoṣa, the work is a medieval tantric compilation (ca. 9th–10th century CE) that became an indispensable prerequisite curriculum text in Tibetan Buddhism.

summary: The Saundarananda is an early Buddhist Sanskrit mahākāvya in 18 cantos by Aśvaghoṣa relating the conversion of Nanda, the Buddha's handsome half-brother. Deeply attached to his beautiful wife Sundarī, Nanda is drawn into the monastic saṅgha against his inclination; the Buddha then uses a pedagogical device (upāya), first showing him celestial nymphs in Indra's heaven before having him guided toward the realization that even heavenly realms are ephemeral and fraught with suffering. The second half of the epic serves as an exposition of Buddhist mental training, psychological analysis, and meditative praxis (śamatha and vipaśyanā), culminating in Nanda's attainment of arhatship. In the final verses (18.63–64), Aśvaghoṣa explicitly declares his poetic purpose: he employed the sweet ornamentation of kāvya to make the bitter medicine of liberation (mokṣa) palatable to worldly audiences.

summary: The Saundarananda ('Handsome Nanda') by Aśvaghoṣa (c. 1st–2nd century CE) is one of the earliest extant Sanskrit mahākāvya court epics, preserved complete in eighteen cantos [1460, 1461]. It dramatizes the conversion of the Buddha's handsome half-brother Nanda, who is deeply attached to his sensual love for his consort Sundarī. Through skilful pedagogy, meditation instruction, and visions of heavenly nymphs juxtaposed with the perils of cyclic existence, the Buddha leads Nanda step by step to spiritual maturity and arhatship. In the closing stanzas (18.63–64), Aśvaghoṣa articulates a seminal defense of Buddhist kāvya, explaining that ornate poetry serves merely as a sweet coating to administer the bitter medicine of liberation (mokṣa).

summary: The Vajrasūcī ('Diamond Needle') is a short Buddhist polemical tract against the brahmanical claim that brahminhood is determined by birth, arguing from brahmanical authorities (Veda, Manu, Mahābhārata) that brahminhood consists in virtue and self-restraint. This e-text gives only its verses: citations on ṛṣis of non-brahmin birth (Vyāsa, Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra etc.), on the loss of brahmin status through conduct, and definitions of the true brahmin by truthfulness, austerity and compassion. The attribution to the poet Aśvaghoṣa is doubted by modern scholarship; the Chinese version (T 1642) names Dharmakīrti.

summary: The Harṣacarita ('The Deeds of Harṣa') is a 7th-century CE ornate Sanskrit prose biography (ākhyāyikā) by court poet Bāṇabhaṭṭa celebrating his patron King Harṣavardhana of Sthāṇvīśvara and Kanyākubja (reigned ca. 606–647 CE). The work opens with an autobiographical account of Bāṇa's Vātsyāyana lineage and his summons to court before turning to Harṣa's royal line, the demise of King Prabhākaravardhana, the murder of Harṣa's elder brother Rājyavardhana, Harṣa's accession to the throne, and the recovery of his widowed sister Rājyaśrī from the Vindhya forest. As the earliest surviving historical ākhyāyikā in Sanskrit literature, it is both an exemplar of high gadyakāvya style (noted for elaborate śleṣa and long compounds) and a primary witness to early medieval northern Indian political and religious life.

summary: The Brahmasūtra (also known as the Vedāntasūtra or Śārīrakasūtra), traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa, is the foundational systematizing text of the Vedānta school of Indian philosophy. Consisting of 555 terse aphorisms across four chapters (adhyāyas), it harmonizes Upaniṣadic statements regarding Brahman as the ultimate reality (samanvaya), defends Vedāntic doctrine against rival philosophical traditions such as Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhism, and Jainism (avirodha), outlines spiritual discipline and contemplative methods (sādhana), and delineates the nature and fruits of liberation (phala). This e-text preserves the full root text as isolated from Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya.

summary: The Bhāmatī by Vācaspatimiśra (fl. 9th–10th century CE) is an authoritative Advaita Vedānta sub-commentary (ṭīkā) on Śaṅkara's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya and the foundational text of the Bhāmatī school (contrasted with Prakāśātman's Vivaraṇa school). Synthesizing Śaṅkara's hermeneutics with insights from Maṇḍana Miśra's Brahmasiddhi, Vācaspati articulates classic doctrinal positions, notably that the individual self (jīva) is the locus (āśraya) of beginningless nescience (avidyā) while Brahman is its object (viṣaya), and that meditative contemplation (dhyāna/upāsanā) mediated by a purified internal organ (manas) serves as the proximate cause of liberating intuition. The text spans the entirety of the Brahmasūtras and generated an influential sub-commentarial lineage, prominent among which are Amalānanda's Kalpataru and Appayya Dīkṣita's Parimala.

summary: The Brahmasūtra (also known as Vedāntasūtra or Śārīrakasūtra), traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa, is the foundational aphoristic treatise of Vedānta philosophy and one of the three canonical pillars of the prasthānatrayī alongside the principal Upaniṣads and the Bhagavadgītā. In four chapters (adhyāyas)—devoted respectively to the concordance of scriptural texts (samanvaya), non-contradiction and refutation of rival systems (avirodha), spiritual practice and discipline (sādhana), and the fruit of liberation (phala)—it systematizes Upaniṣadic theology. This digital edition presents the complete root text according to the 545-sūtra recension followed by Rāmānuja in his Śrībhāṣya and preserved in the Viśiṣṭādvaita tradition, which differs in division and sūtra count from the 555-sūtra Advaita recension of Śaṅkara.

summary: The Bījanighaṇṭu (also termed Mantrakośa) is a tantric glossary in 87 verses containing cryptic names and esoteric designations for Sanskrit phonemes and mantric seed-syllables (bījas). Presented as a revelation spoken by Śiva and claiming derivation from the Bhūtaḍāmara and Yakṣaḍāmaratantra traditions, it supplies deity epithets and elemental associations for individual letters as well as composite syllables (such as śrīṃ, hrīṃ, krīṃ, and klīṃ). The work serves as a practical decoding key for reconstructing esoteric mantras (mantroddhāra) embedded in tantric ritual texts.

summary: The Baudhāyanadharmasūtra is one of the four surviving classical Vedic Dharmasūtras, forming part of the extensive Baudhāyana Kalpasūtra of the Taittirīya school (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda). Arranged across four praśnas, the treatise treats the authoritative sources of dharma, regional customs of northern and southern India, duties of the varṇas and āśramas, ritual purification, domestic law, inheritance, and expiations (prāyaścitta). Philological analysis indicates that praśnas 1 and 2 comprise the original sūtra core, whereas praśnas 3 and 4 represent later additions to the corpus.

summary: Chapters 29–33 of the tenth skandha of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa, known as the Rāsa-pañcādhyāyī ('five chapters on the rāsa dance'), narrate Kṛṣṇa's autumn-night circle dance (rāsalīlā) with the cowherd maidens (gopīs) of Vraja, his temporary disappearance to dispel their pride, their anguished laments and song of longing (Gopīgīta), and his reunion with them in ecstatic devotional union. This section is universally regarded as the aesthetic and devotional climax of the Purāṇa. The included commentary, the Bhāvārthadīpikā by Śrīdharasvāmin (c. 14th century), interprets the erotic-devotional līlā within an Advaita-theistic framework as the triumph over desire (kāmavijaya) and served as the authoritative baseline for all subsequent Vaiṣṇava hermeneutics.

summary: The Kāvyālaṃkāra of Bhāmaha (c. 7th century CE) is one of the earliest extant systematic treatises on classical Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra), establishing poetics as an autonomous discipline distinct from dramaturgy. In six chapters (paricchedas) comprising approximately 400 verses, the work treats poetic genres, thirty-nine figures of speech (alaṃkāra), poetic defects (doṣa), logical and epistemological argumentation (nyāya, including a famous refutation of the Buddhist apoha doctrine), and grammatical correctness (śabdaśuddhi). Bhāmaha famously defines kāvya as the unified harmony of word and meaning (śabdārthau sahitau kāvyam) and identifies vakrokti ('oblique/striking expression') as the indispensable hallmark of genuine poetic language.

summary: The Dūtavākya ('The Envoy's Message') is a one-act Sanskrit drama (vyāyoga) attributed to Bhāsa, based on Kṛṣṇa's peace embassy to the Kaurava court in Hastināpura from the Udyogaparvan of the Mahābhārata. In the drama, Duryodhana rejects Kṛṣṇa's peace proposal, ostentatiously insulting him by gazing at a painted scroll (citrapaṭa) depicting Draupadī's disrobing, and orders his attendants to bind the envoy. Kṛṣṇa assumes his cosmic form (viśvarūpa) and summons his personified celestial weapons (āyudhapuruṣas: Sudarśana, Kaumodakī, Śārṅga, Nandaka, and Pāñcajanya) to punish Duryodhana, until the blind king Dhṛtarāṣṭra rushes in to intercede and beg for divine forgiveness.

summary: The Svapnavāsavadatta ('The Dream of Vāsavadattā') is a six-act classical Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) dramatizing episodes from the Udayana legend cycle of the Bṛhatkathā. To facilitate King Udayana's political alliance with King Darśaka of Magadha and recapture his kingdom from the usurper Āruṇī, Minister Yaugandharāyaṇa arranges the staged death of Queen Vāsavadattā in a fire at Lāvāṇaka and conceals her under the identity of Lady Āvantikā in the care of Princess Padmāvatī. The dramatic and psychological climax occurs in Act 5 (the dream act / svapnāṅka), where the sleeping Udayana addresses Vāsavadattā in what he believes to be a dream while she secretly comforts him, leading to their eventual reunion and royal restoration in Act 6.

summary: The Gaṇakārikā is a concise, eight-verse doctrinal manual of the Lākulīśa-Pāśupata Śaiva tradition, organizing its theology, ascetic practice, and soteriological path into nine sets or 'groups' (gaṇa) encompassing forty technical categories. Bhāsarvajña's 10th-century commentary, the Ratnaṭīkā, provides an authoritative exposition of these terms, elucidating the duties of the religious preceptor (ācārya) and practitioner (sādhaka), yogic disciplines, and the ultimate attainment of duḥkhānta (the cessation of suffering). Alongside the Pāśupatasūtra and Kauṇḍinya's Pañcārthabhāṣya, it is one of the few surviving foundational primary texts of classical Pāśupata Śaivism.

summary: The Bhagavadāśayānusaraṇa (or Bhagavadgītābhāṣya) is Bhāskara's (c. early 9th century CE) commentary on the Bhagavadgītā, surviving only for chapters 1 through 9. From his Bhedābheda standpoint, Bhāskara argues that the individual self and the world are simultaneously different and non-different from Brahman, vigorously defends jñānakarmasamuccaya (the necessity of performing ritual action alongside knowledge for liberation), and sharply critiques Śaṅkara's radical doctrine of complete renunciation (sarvakarmasaṃnyāsa). The text is also an essential witness for the textual history of the Bhagavadgītā, reflecting an early recension close to the Kashmirian tradition.

summary: The Līlāvatī is the foundational arithmetic and geometry treatise composed around 1150 CE by Bhāskara II (Bhāskarācārya) as the opening part (pāṭīgaṇita) of his comprehensive astronomical work Siddhāntaśiromaṇi. Composed in verse and framed as poetic mathematical problems addressed to a maiden named Līlāvatī, it treats fundamental arithmetic operations, fractions, proportions (rule of three), progressions, commercial computation, plane and solid mensuration, shadow reckoning, linear indeterminate equations (kuṭṭaka), and combinatorics (aṅkapāśa). It became the standard pedagogical textbook of premodern Indian mathematics and exerted extensive influence across India and through Persian and modern European translations.

summary: The Mokṣopāyaṭīkā is an extensive Sanskrit commentary composed by the late seventeenth- to early eighteenth-century Kashmiri scholar Bhāskarakaṇṭha on the Mokṣopāya, the tenth-century Kashmiri philosophical narrative that represents the original recension of the Yogavāsiṣṭha. Bhāskarakaṇṭha comments on both the narrative and the non-dualist philosophy of the text from the perspective of Kashmir Śaiva and Vedāntic scholasticism. summary: The Tattvayāthārthyadīpana ('Illumination of the True Nature of the Principles') is a late 16th-century commentary by Bhāvāgaṇeśa Dīkṣita on the Tattvasamāsa, a concise 25-sūtra digest of Sāṃkhya philosophy. Following the theistic and Vedāntic harmonizing tendencies of his preceptor Vijñānabhikṣu, Bhāvāgaṇeśa synthesizes Sāṃkhya ontology with Vaiṣṇava theism and bhakti. The work systematically expounds the primary principles (tattva), cosmic evolution (saṃcara) and dissolution (pratisaṃcara), and the means of spiritual release.

Arranged into three divisions (Pūrvakhaṇḍa, Madhyakhaṇḍa, and Uttarakhaṇḍa), the work is renowned for its detailed Vargaprakaraṇa (materia medica / nighaṇṭu section), which integrates indigenous and imported substances, as well as for its early documentation of syphilis (phiraṅgaroga) and its treatment with China root (copacīnī). This e-text is an incomplete transcription containing only the first two drug groups (Harītakyādivarga and Karpūrādivarga) and an unfinished excerpt (vv. 1–54) of the third group (Guḍūcyādivarga).

summary: The Prakīrṇādhikāra is a foundational canonical manual belonging to the Vaikhānasa Vaiṣṇava Āgama tradition, attributed to the sage Bhṛgu as part of the Bhṛgusaṃhitā. Arranged in 37 chapters (comprising roughly 6,000 verses), the work focuses on temple ritual praxis (kriyāpāda), expounding architectural and ground testing (bhūparīkṣā), iconography, image installation (pratiṣṭhā) of Viṣṇu and attendant deities, ceremonial processions and festivals (utsavas), and extensive expiatory procedures (prāyaścitta/niṣkṛti) for ritual deviations. It forms one of the indispensable textual authorities for traditional temple worship in South Indian Vaikhānasa sanctuaries, such as Tirumala.

summary: The Svabodhasiddhi ('Attainment of Self-Awareness') is a concise Kashmirian Śaiva treatise in 33 verses attributed to Śrībhaṭṭa Bhūti, identified with Abhinavagupta's guru Bhūtirāja (10th century CE). The text teaches an immediate path to liberation through vigilant absorption in self-luminous awareness (svabodha, svasaṃvedana) and the dissolution of subject–object duality (grāhyagrāhakabhāva). Aside from doctrinal connections to the Krama system, it exhibits noteworthy doctrinal and terminological parallels with the Mokṣopāya.

summary: The Veṇīsaṃhāra ('The Binding of the Braid') is a six-act classical Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) by Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa (fl. c. 700 CE) based on the Mahābhārata war. The plot centres on the vow taken by Bhīmasena to avenge the public humiliation of Draupadī by slaying Duḥśāsana and Duryodhana, refusing to let her braid her hair until it has been washed and bound with their blood. Celebrated across classical Indian dramaturgy (notably in the Daśarūpaka and Sāhityadarpaṇa), the play is renowned as an archetype of the heroic (vīra) and furious (raudra) aesthetic sentiments and a model of classical plot construction (sandhis).

summary: The Bhagavadgītābhāṣya of Śaṅkara is the earliest surviving complete commentary on the Bhagavadgītā and forms a foundational pillar of the Advaita Vedānta scriptural triad (prasthānatrayī). Śaṅkara interprets the text as teaching that ultimate release (niḥśreyasa) is attained solely through knowledge of the non-dual Self (jñānaniṣṭhā) and the complete renunciation of action (sarvakarmasaṃnyāsa), rejecting the rival doctrine of combining knowledge with ritual obligation (jñānakarmasamuccaya). Desireless action (karmayoga) and devotional remembrance (bhakti) are treated as preparatory disciplines that purify the mind (cittaśuddhi) and prepare the seeker for discriminative knowledge. This e-text transmits chapters 1 through 17 of both the Bhagavadgītā root verses and Śaṅkara's commentary; chapter 18 is omitted.

summary: The Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharājasūtra is an influential Mahāyāna scripture devoted to Bhaiṣajyaguru, the Medicine Buddha, who presides over the eastern realm of Vaidūryanirbhāsā. The text relates the twelve vows made by the Buddha during his bodhisattva career to heal physical and mental infirmities, alleviate poverty and distress, and lead beings onto the Mahāyāna path. It prescribes devotional and ritual practices—including reciting his name and dhāraṇī, setting up forty-nine lamps and banners, and calling upon the twelve great yakṣa generals—to avert premature death and protect nations from calamity. Sanskrit manuscripts discovered at Gilgit date back to the 5th–7th centuries CE.

summary: The Bhaiṣajyavastu ('Chapter on Medicines') is the sixth section of the Vinayavastu in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya. While opening with monastic regulations concerning permissible medicines, dietary schedules, and the care of ill monks, the vast majority of the chapter is narrative, incorporating numerous avadānas, jātakas, legendary travels of the Buddha to northwest India, apotropaic formulas (including an early version of the Mahāmāyūrī spell), and prophecy accounts. The text survives in Sanskrit birch-bark manuscripts from Gilgit and the Schøyen Collection, alongside canonical translations into Tibetan and Chinese.

summary: Composed in 1900 in Bengali payyār verse by Kedāranātha Datta (Bhaktivinoda Ṭhākura), the Harināmacintāmaṇi is structured as an extended theological dialogue at Jagannātha Purī between Caitanya Mahāprabhu and Haridāsa Ṭhākura. Across fifteen chapters, it provides a comprehensive manual on the theology and contemplative practice of chanting the holy name of Kṛṣṇa (harināma). The treatise systematically details the ten offenses against the holy name (nāmāparādha), the intermediate stage of semblance chanting (nāmābhāsa), pure devotional chanting (śuddha-nāma), and an eightfold meditative progression (bhajana-praṇālī) culminating in pure love of Godhead (kṛṣṇa-prema).

summary: The Bhallaṭaśataka is a late 9th-century collection of allegorical epigrams (muktaka) in the anyokti (anyāpadeśa) mode composed by the Kashmiri court poet Bhallaṭa. Composed in a context of declining royal patronage under King Śaṅkaravarman of Kashmir (r. 883–902 CE), the collection uses descriptions of natural phenomena, animals, and plants to satirize corrupt rulers, uncultured patrons, and the humiliation of virtuous scholars. Noted for its mordant wit and double-edged phrasing (śleṣa), individual verses from the collection are extensively cited in later alaṃkāra treatises and subhāṣita anthologies.

summary: The Nāṭyaśāstra is the encyclopedic foundational treatise of classical Indian dramaturgy, performance, dance, and music, traditionally attributed to Bharata Muni. It provides detailed prescriptions on theatre architecture, preliminary rites (pūrvaraṅga), acting styles and bodily gestures (abhinaya), classifications of dramatic compositions (daśarūpaka), costuming, makeup, prosody, and musical scales and instruments. Its sixth and seventh chapters present the classical formulation of aesthetic relish (rasa) and emotional determinants and states (bhāva), establishing the bedrock of Indian aesthetic philosophy.

summary: The Vākyapadīya (also known as Trikāṇḍī) by Bhartṛhari (c. 5th century CE) is the foundational masterpiece of Classical Indian philosophy of grammar (vyākaraṇadarśana) and language. Structured into three books—the Brahmakāṇḍa (or Āgamakāṇḍa), Vākyakāṇḍa, and Padakāṇḍa (Prakīrṇakāṇḍa)—the text articulates the monistic doctrine of Śabdabrahman (the Word-Principle as absolute reality) and champions the holist theory of sentence meaning (sphoṭavāda and akhaṇḍavākyārtha). The work exercised a defining influence across Indian philosophical traditions, engaging deeply with Buddhist epistemology (notably Dignāga and Dharmakīrti), Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, and Kashmir Śaivism.

summary: The Vākyapadīya (also known as Trikāṇḍī) by Bhartṛhari (c. 5th century CE) is the foundational treatise of the philosophy of grammar (Vaiyākaraṇadarśana) in ancient India. In verse form (kārikā), the text develops the metaphysics of the Word-Principle (Śabdabrahman) as ultimate reality, the sphoṭa doctrine of indivisible semantic units, and syntactic theory centered on sentence meaning (akhaṇḍavākyavāda). summary: A collection of three 'centuries' (śataka) of gnomic and lyric epigrams traditionally attributed to Bhartṛhari: the Nītiśataka on worldly prudence, ethics, and civic conduct; the Śṛṅgāraśataka on the pleasures, moods, and pitfalls of erotic desire; and the Vairāgyaśataka on renunciation, transience, and ascetic withdrawal. The triad moves across the classic aims of life (dharma, artha, kāma) toward ultimate spiritual dispassion (vairāgya). Widely anthologized, memorized, and translated, it remains among the most influential works in the Sanskrit subhāṣita tradition.

summary: The Bhavasaṅkrāntisūtra is a short Mahāyāna sūtra set at the Veṇuvana near Rājagṛha, in which King Bimbisāra asks the Buddha how karmic actions that have long since ceased can reappear at the moment of death and produce rebirth if all conditioned entities (saṃskāra) are empty. The Buddha answers with the analogy of a man dreaming of a beautiful woman, demonstrating that although no permanent self or entity transmigrates from one world to another, rebirth occurs uninterruptedly through the causal stream of consciousness (cittasaṃtati). The text concludes with seven verses elucidating the relation between conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) and ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).

summary: A Sanskrit Vinaya formulary (karmavācanā) for the going-forth (pravrajyā) and full ordination (upasaṃpadā) of Buddhist nuns, belonging to the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition. It opens with the story of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī's request and the eight gurudharmas. It then gives the procedures and formulae for the candidate's preliminaries, the questioning about obstructive conditions (āntarāyikā dharmāḥ), and ordination before both saṅghas, and closes with admonitions to the newly ordained nun; the text breaks off in these admonitions. It survives in a single incomplete Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript in the Bodleian Library.

summary: The Bhikṣuṇīvinaya of the Ārya-Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school is the monastic disciplinary code and case-law collection for Buddhist nuns (bhikṣuṇīs). Transmitted in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit and preserved in a single medieval palm-leaf manuscript from Tibet, it comprises the full Bhikṣuṇīprātimokṣavibhaṅga (origin stories, precept formulations, word analyses, and non-offense clauses for the Prātimokṣa rules), followed by the Bhikṣuṇīprakīrṇaka (miscellaneous legal and institutional rules) and uddāna summaries of the Bhikṣuprakīrṇaka. As one of only two substantially preserved canonical nuns' Vibhaṅgas in an Indic language alongside the Pāli Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, it is a foundational source for the history of Buddhist monastic jurisprudence and early Buddhist women's orders.

summary: The Bhikṣukarmavākya is a Buddhist monastic ritual formulary (karmavācanā) belonging to the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya tradition. It sets forth the prescribed ecclesiastical formulas (jñapti and karmavācanā) and ceremonial procedures for admission into the order, covering going forth (pravrajyā), novice ordination (śrāmaṇera), and full higher ordination (upasaṃpadā). The text concludes with instructions regarding the basic training rules and the four root transgressions (pārājika) entailing defeat and expulsion.

summary: The Bodhisattvabhūmi constitutes the fifteenth and most influential section of the encyclopedic Yogācārabhūmi, composed in approximately the 4th century CE. It serves as an exhaustive manual of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path, systematically treating spiritual lineage (gotra), the generation of the aspiration for awakening (bodhicitta), the perfections (pāramitās), ethics (śīla), and the stages of spiritual maturation (vihāras and bhūmis). Its fourth chapter, the Tattvārthapaṭala, forms a cornerstone of early Yogācāra philosophy, presenting a foundational analysis of the inexpressible nature of reality (nirabhilāpyasvabhāva) underlying linguistic and conceptual designations (prajñapti).

summary: This is a short liturgical manual for conferring the threefold bodhisattva discipline: saṃvaraśīla, kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhakaśīla and sattvārthakriyāśīla. It covers the request to a qualified bodhisattva preceptor, confession, taking refuge, the threefold formal question and acceptance of the vows, and the sign that appears to the buddhas and bodhisattvas once the rite is complete. It ends with instructions for taking the vows by oneself before an image of the Tathāgata when no qualified preceptor is available. Much of the wording follows the vow ritual of the Śīlapaṭala of the Bodhisattvabhūmi.

summary: The Bower Manuscript is a famous birch-bark codex discovered in 1890 near Kucha along the Silk Road, datable to ca. the 4th to 6th centuries CE. It contains seven distinct Sanskrit texts, notably the Navanītaka (a foundational early Ayurvedic compendium of medical recipes, decoctions, and rasāyanas), two dice divination treatises (Pāśakakevalī), and portions of the Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī. It constitutes one of the earliest extant physical manuscripts from the Indian medical and Buddhist traditions.

summary: The Brahmabindūpaniṣad (frequently designated Amṛtabindūpaniṣad in Southern recensions and the Muktikā corpus) is a short 22-verse minor Upaniṣad belonging to the Yoga-Vedānta group. It famously opens by declaring the mind to be the root cause of both bondage and liberation (mana eva manuṣyāṇāṃ kāraṇaṃ bandhamokṣayoḥ). Combining yogic mental restraint with Advaitic metaphysics, it instructs the spiritual seeker to transcend scriptural verbalism and sound-based meditation on OM to realize the unconditioned, non-dual Brahman.

summary: The Brahmapurāṇa, conventionally listed first among the eighteen canonical Mahāpurāṇas and often designated the Ādipurāṇa, is framed as a cosmic discourse delivered by Sūta Lomaharṣaṇa to ṛṣis assembled in Naimiṣāraṇya. While retaining pañcalakṣaṇa subjects such as cosmogony, manvantaras, and royal genealogies (with extensive textual parallels to the Harivaṃśa and Viṣṇupurāṇa), the bulk of the extant text comprises regional pilgrimage guides (tīrthamāhātmya). Major components include the Puruṣottamakṣetramāhātmya, describing Vaiṣṇava worship at Jagannātha Purī and solar cults at Konark, and the Gautamīmāhātmya, dedicated to shrines along the Godāvarī river. The work is a composite redaction whose early core dates to the mid-first millennium CE, with pilgrimage layers continuing to expand between the 10th and 14th centuries CE.

summary: The fifth chapter of the Brahmasaṃhitā is a foundational scripture in the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition consisting of 62 verses spoken by Brahmā praising Kṛṣṇa (Govinda) as the Supreme Deity and primary cause of all causes. The text outlines the ontology and layout of Goloka Vṛndāvana, the mystery of the kāmagāyatrī mantra, cosmogenesis through the agency of Mahā-Viṣṇu, and the distinction between God, the jīvas, and material nature. Jīva Gosvāmin's commentary, the Digdarśanī, interprets the esoteric verses in accordance with Gauḍīya acintyabhedābheda theology, drawing extensively on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa.

summary: The Buddhabalādhānaprātihāryavikurvāṇanirdeśasūtra is a Mahāyāna sūtra set on the banks of the Nairañjanā river and in the Āmrapālī grove at Vārāṇasī, centering on the miraculous transformations (vikurvaṇa) and superhuman displays (prātihārya) brought forth through the Buddha's samādhi. Prompted by the Buddha, the bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi project radiant light across the ten directions to convert stubborn, immoral, and unfaithful beings, purifying their karmic defilements and gathering them before the Tathāgata. Through dialogues primarily involving Mañjuśrī, the sūtra sets forth a docetic Mahāyāna Buddhology, teaching that all conditioned phenomena, as well as the Buddha's earthly life and physical parinirvāṇa, are mere illusory displays (upāyakauśalya) like reflections in a clear mirror.

summary: The Padyacūḍāmaṇi ('Crest-jewel of verses') is a Sanskrit mahākāvya in ten cantos on the life of the Buddha, from his stay in the Tuṣita heaven through his birth as prince Siddhārtha, youth, marriage, the encounters that lead to renunciation, and austerities, to the defeat of Māra and Awakening under the Bodhi tree. summary: The Buddhist Yoga Manual (conventionally known as Yogalehrbuch) is an untitled Sanskrit meditation handbook surviving in fragmentary manuscript leaves in North Turkestan Brāhmī from the Kucha region along the northern Silk Road (dated palaeographically to c. 7th century CE). Rooted doctrinally in Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma while incorporating vivid internal visualizations and somatic manipulation of elements, it guides the practitioner (yogācāra) through stages of meditative contemplation such as ānāpānasmṛti, aśubhabhāvanā, and the four apramāṇas. The text constitutes a critical bridge between Indian meditation traditions and early medieval Chinese visualization texts (chanjing).

summary: The Rasasaṃketakalikā is a concise Rasaśāstra manual composed in 1474 CE (Vikrama Saṃvat 1531, indicated by the chronogram 'bhv-agni-tithi') in Yoginīpura (Delhi) by Cāmuṇḍa of the Kāyastha lineage (who also authored the Jvaratimirabhāskara in Mewār in 1489/1490 CE). Arranged across five chapters, the work details practical, streamlined methods for purifying (śodhana), binding (bandhana), and calcining (māraṇa) mercury and other metals, followed by diverse therapeutic formulations and treatments for mercury-induced toxicity. It reflects the late medieval trend towards accessible, therapeutically oriented iatrochemical handbooks.

summary: The Cīvaravastu ('Section on Robes') is the seventh section of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu. It prescribes the legal regulations governing monastic robes (cīvara), including permissible cloth materials, methods of cutting, sewing, and dyeing, distribution protocols, and the division and inheritance of the personal belongings of deceased monks (mṛtapariṣkāra). The legal rulings are embedded in extensive narrative material, notably the biography of the royal physician Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya, accounts of King Bimbisāra and the courtesan Āmrapālī, and narratives concerning the care and nursing of sick monks.

summary: The Bhāvopahārastotra is a 47-verse devotional hymn to Śiva composed by the Kashmirian master Cakrapāṇinātha, belonging to the non-dual Śaiva (Trika/Krama) tradition. The work interiorizes the liturgical implements and offerings of external ritual worship (pūjā), transforming each modality of perception and cognition into an oblation offered into supreme non-dual consciousness. The accompanying Vivaraṇa by Ramyadeva Bhaṭṭa provides a detailed philosophical commentary on the esoteric meaning of the hymn.

summary: The Śiṣyalekha ('Letter to a Disciple') is an ornate Buddhist didactic poem (dharmakāvya) in epistolary form (lekha), composed in sophisticated classical Sanskrit metres by Candragomin (c. 5th–7th century CE). Traditionally addressed to a disciple named Ratnakīrti who had abandoned monastic discipline due to romantic infatuation, the letter expounds the perils and sufferings of saṃsāra, the physical miseries of birth, aging, and death, the rarity of human life, and the compassionate ideal of the bodhisattva path dedicated to the liberation of all sentient beings.

summary: The Bodhisattvayogācāracatuḥśatakaṭīkā by Candrakīrti (c. 7th century CE) is an authoritative Prāsaṅgika-Mādhyamika subcommentary on Āryadeva's Catuḥśataka. The work expounds the cultivation of the bodhisattva path, dividing its sixteen chapters between conventional spiritual preparations (chapters 1–8: overcoming attachments to permanence, pleasure, purity, and selfhood) and philosophical refutations of intrinsic existence (svabhāva), external entities, time, and non-Buddhist systems (chapters 9–16). While fully preserved only in Tibetan translation (Toh 3865), this e-text contains the surviving Sanskrit palm-leaf fragments across all sixteen chapters, critically transcribed by Kōshin Suzuki.

summary: Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā ('Clear Words'), also titled Madhyamakaśāstravṛtti, is a 7th-century CE Sanskrit prose commentary on the 27 chapters of Nāgārjuna's fundamental Madhyamakaśāstra (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā). It is the only fully surviving Indian commentary on Nāgārjuna's root verses preserved in Sanskrit. Candrakīrti defines the Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka approach by defending Buddhapālita's method of reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) against Bhāvaviveka's use of autonomous inference (svatantra), making the work an essential foundation for the study of Indian and Tibetan Madhyamaka philosophy.

summary: The Candrasūtra is a short canonical Buddhist scripture belonging to the Saṃyuktāgama tradition (parallel to the Pāli Candimasutta, SN 2.9). It relates that when the moon deity is seized during an eclipse by the asura king Rāhu, the deity takes refuge in the Buddha. The Buddha then commands Rāhu to release the moon; terrified, Rāhu complies and explains to Bali Vairocana that disobedience to the Buddha's verse would cause his head to split into seven pieces.

summary: The Carmavastu is the fifth chapter of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, prescribing monastic rules governing the use of hides, leather mats, and footwear. It opens with the extensive narrative of the elder Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa, his perilous voyage, visit to the realm of pretas, and his subsequent ordination under Mahākātyāyana. Koṭīkarṇa's journey to visit the Buddha in Śrāvastī prompts the allowance of regional dispensations for monks residing in remote border territories (pratyantajanapada), such as wearing multiple-soled footwear, frequent bathing, and using leather sitting mats. The remainder of the vastu details monastic regulations regarding permissible and prohibited types of shoes and skins, as well as the authorized possession of leatherworking implements like awls, knives, and thongs.

summary: The Caturdharmanirdeśasūtra is a brief Mahāyāna scripture set in the Sudharmā council hall of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, in which the Buddha instructs the bodhisattva Maitreya on how to overcome and purify accumulated unwholesome actions. The discourse sets forth four factors, traditionally known as the four opponent powers (catuḥpratipakṣabala): remorse (vidūṣaṇāsamudācāra), antidotal virtuous deeds (pratipakṣasamudācāra), the resolve to refrain from repetition (pratyāpattibala), and reliance on refuge and bodhicitta (āśrayabala). Frequently cited by Indian masters, notably Śāntideva in the Śikṣāsamuccaya, it serves as the primary canonical foundation for Buddhist confession and purification rituals.

summary: The Chāndogyopaniṣad is one of the earliest and most important mukhya (principal) Upaniṣads, belonging to the Kauthuma/Rāṇāyanīya recension of the Sāmaveda. In eight adhyāyas, it progresses from esoteric meditations on the chanting of the Sāman and the sacred syllable Om (udgītha) to quintessential metaphysical doctrines of early Vedānta, including the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the dialogue of Satyakāma Jābāla, Uddālaka Āruṇi's instruction to Śvetaketu culminating in the mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' (6.8.7), and Prajāpati's teachings on the four states of the self. The accompanying commentary by Śaṅkarācārya interprets the text as an exposition of non-dual reality (advaita), demonstrating that ritual action produces transient heavenly realms, whereas direct knowledge of the non-dual Brahman-Ātman leads to absolute liberation (mokṣa).

summary: The Chandoviciti is a Sanskrit treatise on metrics. It is preserved only in fragments of a birch-bark manuscript from the Turfan finds (SHT 654), edited by Dieter Schlingloff in 1958. The surviving verses define metres in metrical form and name their basis as the sūtras of Yāska and Piṅgala, and verse II.1 names Mitradhara as the author. The fragments are early manuscript evidence for Sanskrit metrical theory outside the Piṅgala tradition proper. Ruixuan Chen (2013) improved their readings.

summary: The Kuṭṭanīmata ('The Bawd's Counsel', also known as Śambhalīmata) is a satirical and didactic verse novel comprising 1,059 stanzas mostly in the āryā metre, composed by Dāmodaragupta, prime minister to the Kārkoṭa king Jayāpīḍa of Kashmir (r. c. 779–813 CE). Framed as cynical instruction imparted in Vārāṇasī by the experienced madam Vikarālā to the young courtesan Mālatī on extracting wealth from suitors, the text incorporates several embedded narrative tales, including an invaluable eyewitness-like account of a dramatic staging of Harṣa's Ratnāvalī. It is a premier primary source for theatrical practice, erotology, and urbane courtly culture in early medieval northern India.

summary: The Caryāsaṅgrahapradīpa ('Lamp Compendium of Conduct') is a concise manual of daily Mahāyāna practice composed by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (982–1054 CE) during his journey through Nepal. Written for an elder monk who sought instruction focused on the Pāramitā path, the treatise lays out the daily routine of a bodhisattva: moral restraint, sensory control, division of the night for meditation and sleep, the sevenfold worship (saptāṅgapūjā), making stupas and images, and sharing food offerings with deities and beings. While acknowledging that Secret Mantra also attains awakening, it deliberately restricts its exposition to the exoteric Pāramitānaya.

summary: The Satyadvayāvatāra ('Entry into the Two Truths') is a concise 30-verse Madhyamaka treatise by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (982–1054 CE), composed during his stay in Suvarṇadvīpa at the request of the monk Devamati. It presents a Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka perspective on the two truths, classifying conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) into correct and incorrect, and arguing that ultimate reality (paramārthasatya) is beyond discursive and non-conceptual cognitions as well as formal pramāṇas. Because the original Sanskrit text does not survive, this e-text is a modern Sanskrit reconstruction (pratyuddhāra) based on the Tibetan canonical translation.

summary: A verse manual (c. 450 ślokas) by Dīpaṃkarabhadra, the successor of Buddhajñānapāda at Vikramaśīla, on the maṇḍala rite of the Guhyasamāja in the Jñānapāda tradition, centred on Mañjuvajra. It covers the qualifications of the officiant, preliminary worship and visualisation, preparation of the site, construction of the maṇḍala, the consecrations (abhiṣeka) of the disciple, and ancillary rites, including rites for the safety of the king. It was commented on by Ratnākaraśānti (Tōh. 1871) and drawn on by Abhayākaragupta in the Vajrāvalī (cf. Mori, "The Vajrāvalī and the Maṇḍalavidhi of 450 Verses").

summary: The Āpattideśanāvidhi is a concise liturgical manual attributed to Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (982–1054) formulating the ritual confession and disclosure (deśanā) of downfalls and ethical lapses (āpatti). The officiant/practitioner declares and repudiates ten unwholesome deeds, the five immediate retributions (ānantarya) and their parallels, and violations of prātimokṣa vows, bodhisattva trainings, and tantric pledges (samaya) before the gurus, buddhas, bodhisattvas, and sangha. The Sanskrit text transmitted here is a modern retroversion from the Tibetan Tanjur (Toh 3974) by Ramesh Chandra Negi.

summary: The Bodhisattvādikarmikamārgāvatāradeśanā is a practical liturgical and behavioral handbook by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (11th century) outlining the progressive spiritual discipline required of a beginner bodhisattva (ādikarmika). It provides step-by-step guidance on relying on a qualified spiritual teacher (kalyāṇamitra), taking refuge, generating bodhicitta, and performing the sevenfold supreme worship (saptavidhānuttarapūjā). It instructs the practitioner on cultivating calm abiding (śamatha) and special insight (vipaśyanā) according to the nine limbs set forth in Bodhibhadra's Samādhisambhāraparivarta, maintaining mindfulness of all phenomena as illusion-like (māyopama) in post-meditation, and promptly purifying ethical infractions.

summary: The Cittotpādasaṃvaravidhikrama is an 11th-century liturgical manual composed by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna setting forth the rite and sequence for arousing bodhicitta and formally receiving the bodhisattva discipline. Synthesizing the ritual traditions of Asaṅga's Bodhisattvabhūmi and Śāntideva's Śikṣāsamuccaya, it provides liturgies for taking refuge, petitioning a spiritual preceptor, taking the bodhisattva vows in the presence of an ācārya or directly before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas if no guru is present, and instructions on abandoning the four corrupting factors while cultivating the four counteracting wholesome factors. Although lost in its original Indic manuscript form, the work was preserved in the Tibetan Tengyur (Toh 3969) and reconstructed into Sanskrit in modern scholarship.

summary: The Daśakumāracarita ('Adventures of the Ten Princes') is a celebrated Sanskrit prose romance (gadyakāvya) by Daṇḍin (c. late 7th–early 8th century CE), recounting the interwoven picaresque adventures of Prince Rājavāhana and his nine companions across India as they seek romantic conquests, wealth, and political power. Distinctive for its vivid portrayal of secular, sub-courtly, and underworld life—featuring thieves, gamblers, courtesans, corrupt ministers, ascetics, and charlatans—the work is also famous for rhetorical tours de force, notably the seventh chapter composed entirely without labial phonemes (aniroṣṭhya). The surviving authentic composition covers eight central chapters, framed by later anonymous supplements (the Pūrvapīṭhikā and Uttarapīṭhikā) that supply the background and denouement of the cycle.

summary: The Daśakumāracarita ('The Tale of the Ten Princes') is a celebrated Sanskrit prose romance (gadyakāvya) composed by Daṇḍin (c. late 7th–8th century CE). Within a framing story of ten companion princes separated during an expedition and later reunited, each prince recounts his worldly adventures through the royal courts, forests, gambling dens, and underworlds of classical India. This e-text comprises three ucchvāsas from the core work: Ucchvāsa 3 (Upahāravarman's exploits regaining his ancestral realm of Mithilā through disguise, burglary, and court intrigue), Ucchvāsa 5 (Pramati's stratagems and winning of the princess Navamālikā in Ujjayinī), and Ucchvāsa 6 (Mitragupta's maritime adventures, capture by Yavanas, and four nested tales illustrating proper conduct).

summary: The Dantyoṣṭhavidhi is an Atharvavedic phonetic-orthographic treatise (lakṣaṇagrantha) comprising 23 ślokas in two adhyāyas. summary: A compilation of four canonical Āgama discourses reconstructed from Sanskrit manuscript fragments found in Central Asia (Turfan collection) expounding the ten powers (daśabala) of a Tathāgata. These powers—including perfect knowledge of what is possible and impossible (sthānāsthāna), the ripening of karma (karmavipāka), the states of meditative attainment (dhyānavimokṣasamādhisamāpatti), the spiritual faculties of sentient beings (indriyaparāparatā), and the eradication of contaminants (āsravakṣaya)—form the foundation of the Buddha's authority to proclaim the wheel of Dharma and utter his lion's roar (siṃhanāda). Belonging to the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda transmission, these discourses parallel texts in the Chinese Saṃyuktāgama (T 99, no. 684) and Pāli Dasabala suttas in the Saṃyutta and Aṅguttara Nikāyas.

summary: The Daśabhūmikasūtra ('Sūtra on the Ten Stages'), also preserved as a major chapter of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra, is one of the most influential texts in Mahāyāna Buddhist literature. Set in the realm of the Paranirmitavaśavartin deities, the text records an exposition by the bodhisattva Vajragarbha detailing the progressive ten stages (bhūmis) of spiritual ascent from Pramuditā to Dharmameghā. Each stage systematically outlines moral, meditative, and cognitive requirements, correlated directly with the perfections (pāramitās) and the realization of emptiness. Extensively cited by Indian master exegetes and commented on by Vasubandhu in his Daśabhūmikavyākhyāna, it became the foundational source of the Chinese Dilun (Daśabhūmika) school.

summary: The Devīgītā ('Song of the Goddess') comprises chapters 31 through 40 of the seventh skandha of the Devībhāgavata-Purāṇa (507 verses).
