summary: The Devīkālottarāgama (or Devīkālottara) is a concise 84-verse Śaiva scriptural text presented as a dialogue in which Śiva reveals the essence of liberating knowledge (jñāna) and conduct (ācāra) to the Goddess. Although presented in manuscript colophons as the 65th chapter of a putative 24,000-verse redaction of the Kālottara, it has circulated independently as a complete treatise. In marked contrast to ritual-oriented Śaiva Siddhānta scriptures, the work sets aside external worship, mantras, maṇḍalas, and prāṇāyāma in favor of meditation on non-dual, supportless awareness (nirālamba / niṣkala jñāna). Because of this contemplative orientation, it was commented upon by Nirañjanasiddha (drawing on a Kannaḍa commentary, likely from a Vīraśaiva context) and gained lasting reception in later South Indian Advaita-oriented Śaivism, including within the circle of Ramaṇa Maharṣi.

summary: Two short canonical sūtras copied one after the other in Gilgit manuscript no. 13. In the Devatāsūtra, a radiant deity visits the Buddha at the Jetavana in Śrāvastī and asks a series of riddle-like questions in verse. The Buddha's verse answers name speech, passion, hatred and ignorance as the worst dangers, patience and wisdom as armour and weapon, merit as the one possession fire, water and thieves cannot take, and the Buddha as the only physician. The Alpadevatāsūtra has the same setting: a deity asks which people go to heaven. Only the Buddha's first answers survive, praising restraint and abstention from killing.

summary: The Daśarūpaka ('Ten Forms of Dramatic Art') by Dhanañjaya is an influential late 10th-century treatise in four chapters (prakāśas or paricchedas) condensing and systematizing the dramaturgical teachings of the Nāṭyaśāstra. It offers an analytical framework for dramatic plot structure (vastu) and its stages of development (sandhis), classifications of dramatic heroes and heroines (netṛ), the ten major dramatic genres (rūpaka) and auxiliary mimetic forms (nṛtya), and aesthetic emotional response (rasa and bhāva). Composed under the patronage of the Paramāra king Muñja, it served for centuries as the standard textbook of Sanskrit dramaturgy.

summary: The Hetubindu ('Drop of Reason') is a core philosophical treatise by Dharmakīrti (c. 6th–7th century CE) expounding the theory of the logical reason or probans (hetu). Dharmakīrti defines the triple characteristic of valid evidence (trairūpya), classifies inferential evidence into effect (kārya), essential nature (svabhāva), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi), and refutes rival non-Buddhist views such as the sixfold characterization of the reason (ṣaḍlakṣaṇa). summary: The Hetubindu ('Drop of Reason') is an epistemological and logical treatise by the Buddhist master Dharmakīrti (c. 6th–7th century CE), counted among his seven fundamental pramāṇa works. The text focuses specifically on the theory of the logical reason or probans (hetu), elucidating its threefold character (trairūpya) and classifying valid reasons into identity (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi). It systematically investigates fallacies of reason (hetvābhāsa) and marks a pivotal development in Dharmakīrti's thought wherein explicit statement of the thesis (pakṣa) is treated as dispensable because it is already established by implication.

summary: The Nyāyabindu ('Drop of Logic') is Dharmakīrti's concise, quintessential manual of Buddhist logic and epistemology, distilling the core doctrines expounded at greater length in his Pramāṇavārttika and Pramāṇaviniścaya. In three aphoristic chapters, it presents perception (pratyakṣa) as non-conceptual and free from error, inference for oneself (svārthānumāna) grounded in the threefold mark (trairūpya) and ontological relation (svabhāvapratibandha), and inference for others (parārthānumāna) treating proof, examples, and logical fallacies. Due to its clarity and concision, it became the preeminent textbook of Buddhist pramāṇa across India and Tibet.

summary: The Nyāyabinduprakaraṇa ('A Drop of Logic') is Dharmakīrti's foundational introductory manual of Buddhist epistemology and logic, divided into three chapters: direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna). It defines valid cognition (pramāṇa), establishes the threefold mark of a sound logical reason (trairūpya), classifies inferential reasons into essential identity (svabhāva), causality (kārya), and non-perception (anupalabdhi), and details valid arguments and pseudo-reasons. This composite e-text presents Dharmakīrti's complete root treatise interleaved with the commentaries of Vinītadeva (Nyāyabinduvistaraṭīkā / Śiṣyahitā) and Dharmottara (Nyāyabinduṭīkā), together with an anonymous subcommentary (Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī) for the first chapter.

summary: The Nyāyabindu ('Drop of Logic') is Dharmakīrti's concise foundational primer on Buddhist epistemology and logic, articulating the core doctrines of the Dignāga–Dharmakīrti school. Written in terse prose aphorisms (sūtras), the work is structured into three chapters: direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna). It defines perception as non-conceptual (kalpanāpoḍha) and non-erroneous (abhrānta), formulates the threefold requirement of the logical reason (trairūpya), classifies valid reasons into essential nature (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi), and provides a taxonomy of logical fallacies. Due to its clarity and pedagogical conciseness, it became the primary introductory manual of Buddhist logic in India and Tibet.

summary: The Santānāntarasiddhi ('Proof of Other Mind-Streams') is a concise treatise by Dharmakīrti (c. 600–660 CE) traditionally numbered among his 'Seven Treatises' on logic and epistemology. Framed as a dialogue opening with a single verse and proceeding through 93 prose sections, it resolves the philosophical challenge of other minds from within the Vijñānavāda (Cittamātra) idealist system, directly rebutting the objection that idealism logically degenerates into solipsism. Dharmakīrti demonstrates that just as a realist infers intentional consciousness from observing physical movements and speech, an idealist can equally infer distinct intentional mental continua from coordinated sensory appearances without positing mind-independent external matter.

summary: The Sambandhaparīkṣā ('Investigation of Relations') is a concise treatise consisting of 25 verses in anuṣṭubh meter by the Buddhist epistemologist Dharmakīrti (c. 6th–7th century CE), traditionally counted as one of his 'seven treatises on valid cognition' (pramāṇa-prakaraṇa). In this work, Dharmakīrti develops an uncompromising nominalist critique of the ontological reality of relations, refuting real entities such as inherence (samavāya), contact (saṃyoga), and external causal connections between distinct momentary particulars (svalakṣaṇa). He concludes that all relations are conceptual constructions (kalpanā) superimposed on reality rather than mind-independent entities. Historically known in Sanskrit only through 22 verses cited by Jaina authors, the final three verses were recovered by Hideomi Yaita from the Tarkarahasya in 1989, and a complete Sanskrit manuscript of the text was subsequently identified at Drepung monastery.

summary: The Vādanyāya ('The Logic of Debate') is the last of Dharmakīrti's seven core treatises on epistemology and logic (pramāṇa), expounding his reform of dialectical and debate theory. Dharmakīrti mounts an extensive critique of the classical Nyāya system of twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna), arguing that genuine defeat in truthful philosophical inquiry (vāda) occurs under only two fundamental circumstances: the proponent's failure to state an essential component of a valid proof (asādhanāṅgavacana), and the respondent's failure to point out an actual fallacy (adoṣodbhāvana). Preserved in Sanskrit and heavily commented upon by thinkers such as Śāntarakṣita (in the Vipañcitārthā) and Vinītadeva, the text served as a foundational model for Buddhist disputation.

summary: The Vādanyāya ('Logic of Debate') is Dharmakīrti's final systematic treatise dedicated to dialectical methodology and the formal rules of philosophical debate. Dharmakīrti mounts a critical examination of the Naiyāyika theory of debate, rejecting the classical Nyāyasūtra taxonomy of twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna). He replaces them with two overarching criteria: the proponent's failure to present an essential member of a valid proof (asādhanāṅgavacana), and the opponent's alleging of a defect where none exists (adoṣodbhāvana).

In the eleventh century, the anthology was translated into Chinese by Richeng (Sūryayaśas) and others under the title Zhufajiyaojing (諸法集要經, Taishō 728).

summary: The Dharmaskandha ('Aggregation of Dharmas') is one of the seven canonical treatises of the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma Piṭaka (specifically counted among the 'six feet' or ṣaṭ-pādāḥ supporting the body of the Jñānaprasthāna) and is regarded alongside the Saṃgītiparyāya as representative of the earliest, sūtra-commentarial stratum of Abhidharma literature (c. 2nd–1st century BCE). The treatise compiles canonical doctrinal categories (mātṛkās)—such as the five precepts, stages of stream-entry, the limbs of awakening, dependent origination, and meditative absorptions—and glosses them with citations from early discourses. While preserved intact in Chinese translation (T 1537), the Indic text survives only in birch-bark manuscript leaves recovered from Gilgit and Central Asia.

summary: The Pavanadūta ('Wind Messenger') by Dhoyī is a 12th-century dūtakāvya composed in 104 mandākrāntā verses at the court of King Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal. Modeled closely on Kālidāsa's Meghadūta, the poem describes Kuvalayavatī, a Gandharva maiden on Mount Malaya in South India, who falls in love with Lakṣmaṇasena during his southern conquest (digvijaya) and sends the southern wind (pavana) to carry her message northward to his court at Gauḍa. In addition to being one of the earliest surviving full imitations of Kālidāsa's messenger model, the poem provides significant topographical, historical, and cultural data on late 12th-century Bengal and medieval India.

summary: The Gauragovindārcanasmaraṇapaddhati by Dhyānacandra Gosvāmī (late 16th to early 17th century CE) is an influential ritual and meditative guide (paddhati) in the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition. Elaborating upon the earlier manual of his teacher Gopāla Guru Gosvāmī, it provides systematic instructions for internal worship (arcana) and contemplative remembrance (smaraṇa) of Caitanya Mahāprabhu and the divine couple Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa through the eight periods of the day and night (aṣṭakālīya-līlā). It constitutes one of the earliest and most detailed textual sources for the practice of siddha-praṇālī and the meditation on eleven esoteric attributes (ekādaśa-bhāva) comprising the practitioner's spiritual identity (siddha-deha).

summary: The Rādhākṛṣṇāṣṭakālīyalīlāsmaraṇakramapaddhati is an authoritative 17th-century Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava manual for the practice of rāgānugā-sādhana (spontaneous devotional meditation). Expanding upon the template formulated by the author's preceptor Gopālaguru Gosvāmī, it provides an exact framework for the continuous remembrance (smaraṇa) and mental service (mānasī sevā) of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa throughout eight daily temporal divisions (aṣṭakālīya-līlā). The practitioner visualizes these pastimes in an internalized spiritual identity (siddha-deha) as an intimate female attendant (mañjarī-bhāva), accompanied by specific mantra recitations and time allotments.

summary: The Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārtha (also known as the Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārthasaṃgraha or Prajñāpāramitāsaṃgrahakārikā) is a 58-verse synopsis of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā composed by the Buddhist philosopher-epistemologist Dignāga (c. 480–540 CE). Dignāga organizes the sprawling scripture into thirty-two core thematic topics (dvātriṃśad arthāḥ), interpreting its insight through a Yogācāra doctrinal lens. The synthesis notably correlates the sūtra's teachings with sixteen aspects of emptiness, the counteracting of ten types of mental distraction (cittavikṣepa), and the three natures (trisvabhāva).

summary: The Divyāvadāna ('Divine Narratives') is an anthology of 38 Buddhist avadāna stories composed in Sanskrit, illustrating the workings of karma, past births, and moral causation through the lives of the Buddha, his disciples, householders, and monarchs. Compiled around the 2nd to 4th centuries CE, a major portion of the text draws directly from the Vinayavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition. Famous narrative components include the Aśokāvadāna cycle, Kuṇālāvadāna, Pūrṇāvadāna, and Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna.

summary: This e-text contains the oldest surviving specimens of Indian dramatic literature, discovered on palm-leaf fragments from Kizil near Turfan (Central Asia) and datable to the Kuṣāṇa period (c. 1st–2nd century CE). The principal identifiable play is Aśvaghoṣa's Śāriputraprakaraṇa (or Śāradvatīputraprakaraṇa), a nine-act play dramatizing the conversion of the Buddha's foremost disciples, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. Preserved alongside it are fragments of two anonymous Buddhist plays: an allegorical drama featuring personifications (Buddhi, Dhṛti, Kīrti) and a prakaraṇa or social comedy involving a courtesan (gaṇikā), a rogue (duṣṭa), and a jester (vidūṣaka). These fragments are of foundational importance for the history of classical Sanskrit theatre and the early history of Middle Indo-Aryan dialects (archaic forms of Māgadhī, Ardhamāgadhī, and Śaurasenī).

summary: The Dharmottarapradīpa ('Lamp on Dharmottara'), composed around the late 10th or early 11th century CE by Durveka Miśra, is an extensive Sanskrit sub-commentary (anuṭīkā) on Dharmottara's Nyāyabinduṭīkā, which comments on Dharmakīrti's foundational logical manual, the Nyāyabindu. Spanning three chapters—direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna)—the work defends and refines Buddhist pramāṇavāda against rival interpretations and Brahmanical critiques. It constitutes one of the most important late Indian sources for the internal development and terminology of the Dignāga-Dharmakīrti philosophical tradition.

summary: The Hetubinduṭīkāloka (also known as Arcaṭāloka) is an extensive Sanskrit sub-commentary (anuṭīkā) by the late Buddhist master Durvekamiśra (fl. c. late 10th to early 11th century CE) on Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa's Hetubinduṭīkā, which comments on Dharmakīrti's logical manual Hetubindu. Durvekamiśra, a disciple of Jitāri active in Eastern India, offers a detailed defense and critique of Arcaṭa's positions on the threefold character of logical evidence (trairūpya), the refutation of non-Buddhist theories (notably Naiyāyika and Mīmāṃsaka tenets), and disagreements with earlier commentators like Dharmottara. Preserved in a single palm-leaf manuscript from the Jaina bhaṇḍāras at Patan, it serves as an indispensable witness to late Indian Buddhist logico-epistemological philosophy (pramāṇavāda).

summary: The Dvāviṃśatyavadānakathā ('Narrative of Twenty-Two Avadānas') is a medieval Nepalese Buddhist narrative anthology organized around twenty-two core avadāna tales extolling the merits of donation (dāna), caitya and stūpa worship, and monastic veneration. Framed by an opening and closing dialogue between the Elder Upagupta and King Aśoka, it draws substantially on classical sources such as the Avadānaśataka and Divyāvadāna while also incorporating prose passages written in Newar Buddhist Sanskrit. The collection is arranged in 24 sections (kathās/sūtras), beginning with the exhortation to merit (puṇyaprotsāhana) and culminating in the Puṇyotsāhāvadānasūtra.

summary: The Ekādaśamukha (also known as Ekādaśamukhahṛdaya) is an early esoteric Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra in which the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara reveals his eleven-faced heart-spell (hṛdaya) before the Buddha in the Jetavana monastery at Śrāvastī. The text details ten mundane benefits (including freedom from illness, weapons, poison, fire, and untimely death) and four transcendental fruits (including beholding the Tathāgatas at death and rebirth in Sukhāvatī) promised to practitioners who recite the spell, followed by prescriptive ritual instructions for bali offerings, lustrations, and homa rites. Surviving in Sanskrit in a 5th- to 6th-century birch-bark manuscript unearthed at Gilgit, the scripture formed a foundational text for the cult of the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara throughout Central and East Asia.

summary: The Ekādaśamukhahṛdaya is an early esoteric Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra set in Śrāvastī. Avalokiteśvara expounds the eleven-faced heart-mantra to Śākyamuni, explaining ten worldly protections (such as defense against disease, poison, weapons, fire, and untimely death) and four transcendental blessings experienced at the time of death. The work details specific ritual actions, including oblations, homa rites, and the consecration of water, which served as the primary scriptural basis for the widespread cult and iconography of the Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara across Asia.

summary: The Ekottarāgama (or Ekottarikāgama, 'Increased by One Collection') is one of the four core Āgama collections in the early Buddhist canon, organizing discourses numerically according to groups of items (parallel to the Pāli Aṅguttara Nikāya). While the complete text survives only in an early Chinese translation (T 125), these Sanskrit fragments were identified among the Gilgit manuscripts in Jammu and Kashmir. The surviving portions include discourses on mental training, the senses, monastic offences (āpatti), and karmic retribution.

summary: The Tattvacintāmaṇi ('Thought-Jewel of Reality') by Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya (c. 14th century) is the foundational text of the Navya-Nyāya ('New Logic') school of Indian philosophy. Structured across four books corresponding to the four classical Nyāya pramāṇas (pratyakṣa, anumāna, upamāna, and śabda), the treatise introduced a formal technical language of relations, delimiters (avacchedaka), and qualifiers that transformed classical Sanskrit philosophical methodology. This e-text contains the first half of the fourth book (Śabdakhaṇḍa), which defends verbal testimony as an independent, irreducible source of valid knowledge against Vaiśeṣika and Buddhist reductionism, examines semantic preconditions for sentential comprehension (ākāṅkṣā, yogyatā, āsatti, tātparya), and investigates lexical signification up to the Jātiśaktivāda.

summary: The Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra is a major Mahāyāna scripture that circulated both independently and as the climactic final section of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra. It recounts the spiritual pilgrimage of the youth Sudhana, who is instructed by Mañjuśrī to seek out fifty-three spiritual mentors (kalyāṇamitra)—representing varied genders, occupations, and stations—to learn the practice of a bodhisattva. The narrative culminates in visions of Maitreya's kūṭāgāra and Samantabhadra, depicting the cosmos (dharmadhātu) as an interconnected web of mutual interpenetration and closing with the famous Samantabhadracaryāpraṇidhāna aspiration.

summary: The Gaṇapatihṛdayadhāraṇī (also known as the Gaṇapatihṛdaya) is a concise esoteric Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture framed as a discourse delivered by the Buddha to Ānanda on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) near Rājagṛha. It teaches the heart-mantras of Gaṇapati (invoked under names such as Mahāgaṇapati, Gaṇapati, Gaṇādhipati, and Gaṇeśvara) alongside ritual procedures and worldly benefits such as prosperity, protection from adversity, and retentive memory. In Nepalese Newar Buddhism, the text forms an established component of the liturgical Saptavāra ('Seven Days') cycle, traditionally recited on Tuesdays.

summary: The Garbhasaṅgraha ('Compendium of the Essence') is a concise 14-verse Mahāyāna work by Atiśa Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna (982–1054 CE). It sets forth the essential path of the Bodhisattva: recognizing suffering caused by dualistic grasping and afflictions, cultivating emptiness and compassion, generating bodhicitta, practicing the six perfections, progressing through the five paths, and removing the two obscurations to attain the three kāyas of awakening. No Indic manuscript survives; the text in this e-text is Ramesh Chandra Negi's 1992 modern Sanskrit retro-translation (punaruddhāra) made from the Tibetan Tengyur (Toh 3949 / Toh 4469).

summary: The Garbhopaniṣad is a minor Upaniṣad centered on embryology, human anatomy, and physiological contemplation integrated with Vedāntic and Sāṃkhya-Yoga soteriology. It details the month-by-month gestation of the embryo from conception to birth, the bodily components, humors, and tissues, and the fetus's awakening in the womb to memories of past lives and suffering, leading to a resolve to seek liberation through Maheśvara, Nārāyaṇa, or Yoga. The treatise concludes by homologizing the internal organs to the three Vedic fires and ritual instruments of the sacrificial arena and provides an enumeration of anatomical parts, identifying itself as a Paippalāda text on liberation.

summary: The Garuḍapurāṇa is one of the eighteen major canonical Mahāpurāṇas of the Vaiṣṇava tradition, framed as a dialogue between Viṣṇu and his vahana Garuḍa, recounted by Sūta to the sages of the Naimiṣāraṇya. The text is encyclopedic: the Pūrvakhaṇḍa treats cosmology, temple ritual, pilgrimage sites (Gayamāhātmya), astronomy, gemmology (ratnaparīkṣā), medicine and diagnosis (nidāna/cikitsā), governance, and grammar; the Pretakhaṇḍa functions as a principal Hindu manual of eschatology and mortuary ritual, detailing death, posthumous suffering, funerary rites (antyeṣṭi), and śrāddha; and the Brahmakāṇḍa presents a theological exposition of Vaiṣṇava metaphysics displaying close ties to Dvaita Vedānta. The composite work ranges in date from c. the 8th–10th century CE for the early encyclopedic core to the 14th–16th century CE for the late medieval Brahmakāṇḍa.

summary: The Gautamadharmasūtra is one of the foundational and earliest extant prose treatises of the Hindu legal and ritual tradition, affiliated with the Rāṇāyanīya branch of the Sāmaveda. Chapters 1–3 treat the primary sources of dharma (Veda, smṛti, and ācāra), rules governing initiation (upanayana) and student life (brahmacarya), purification rituals (śauca and ācamana), and a debate on the four stages of life (āśrama), culminating in the assertion of the superiority of the householder stage (gārhasthya). Maskarin's commentary (Maskaribhāṣya) provides one of the two primary classical commentaries on the text alongside Haradatta's Mitākṣarā.

summary: The Nyāyasūtra of Akṣapāda Gautama is the foundational text of the Nyāya school of classical Indian philosophy, systematically organizing epistemology, dialectics, debate methodology, and realist metaphysics across five books centered on sixteen topics (ṣoḍaśapadārtha). summary: The Nyāyasūtra, attributed to Akṣapāda Gautama, is the foundational treatise of the classical Nyāya school, defining sixteen epistemological and dialectical topics (ṣoḍaśa padārthāḥ), establishing four valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa: perception, inference, analogy, and testimony), and formulating the classical five-part inference schema alongside debate methodology. Vātsyāyana's Nyāyabhāṣya (c. 5th century CE) is the earliest extant commentary on the aphorisms, articulating a robust epistemological realism that defends the mind-independent reality of objects, the permanence of the self (ātman), and causal regularities against early Buddhist and skeptical challenges.

summary: The Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā is Vācaspatimiśra's foundational sub-commentary written to elucidate and defend Uddyotakara's Nyāyavārttika against the criticisms of Buddhist epistemologists, notably Dignāga and Dharmakīrti. The treatise provides an extensive exposition of Nyāya epistemology, realism, the pramāṇas, syllogistic inference, dialectical debate categories, and ontology. It forms the third tier of the classical four-work Nyāya exegesis known as the Nyāyacaturgranthikā.

summary: The Nyāyasūtra, attributed to Akṣapāda Gautama, is the foundational treatise of the Nyāya school of classical Indian epistemology and logic, redacted between approximately the 2nd century BCE and the 2nd century CE. In five books (adhyāyas) divided into ten daily reading units (āhnikas), it expounds sixteen dialectical and epistemological categories (padārthas), beginning with the four means of knowledge (pramāṇa: perception, inference, analogy, and testimony) and the twelve objects of knowledge (prameya). The treatise details procedures for philosophical debate, fallacy identification, and points of defeat (nigrahasthāna), subordinating rational inquiry to the attainment of liberation (apavarga) through correct knowledge of reality.

summary: The Ghaṭakarparakāvya is an early lyrical messenger poem (dūtakāvya) composed in virtuosic rhyming metres with elaborate paronomasia (yamaka). In it, a woman suffering separation (virahiṇī) at the onset of the monsoon season laments her solitude and appeals to rain clouds to convey a message to her absent husband. This e-text provides the text of the poem along with the Ghaṭakarparavivṛti (also styled Ghaṭakarparakulakavivṛti), a learned commentary by the Kashmiri aesthetician Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 1000 CE), who explicates its lexical and rhetorical intricacies and interprets the stanzas as an integrated poetic composition (kulaka).

summary: The Haribhaktivilāsa is the foundational ritual handbook and behavioural digest (smṛti / nibandha) of early modern Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism, composed in Vṛndāvana during the 1530s. Across its twenty vilāsas, the work systematizes normative devotional orthopraxy, citing thousands of verses from Purāṇic, Tantric, Pāñcarātra, and Vedic sources to ground devotional practices in canonical authority. This portion (vilāsas 1–11) treats initiation (dīkṣā), guru-disciple duties, morning rites, purification, sacred marks, offerings, and the elaborate procedures of daily temple and domestic worship (arcana).

summary: Gopadatta's Jātakamālā is an ornate Mahāyāna narrative work composed in campū style (alternating prose and verse), continuing the classical literary line of Āryaśūra and Haribhaṭṭa (c. 7th–8th century CE). This electronic text brings together 13 of these recovered legends, demonstrating Gopadatta's elaborate kāvya style and dramatic storytelling on Buddhist ethical themes.

summary: The Gopathabrāhmaṇa is the only surviving Brāhmaṇa text attached to the Atharvaveda tradition. Divided into two main sections, the Pūrvabhāga (five prapāṭhakas) presents cosmogonic narratives, mystical reflections on the syllable Om and the Gāyatrī, and an exaltation of the Atharvaveda and the supervising Brahman priest; the Uttarabhāga (six prapāṭhakas) treats Śrauta rituals in close structural alignment with the Vaitānasūtra. Recognized as one of the youngest extant Brāhmaṇas, it freely borrows and refashions passages from earlier Vedic texts, notably the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa and Kauṣītakibrāhmaṇa.

summary: The Gopathabrāhmaṇa is the sole surviving Brāhmaṇa associated with the Atharvaveda and is universally recognized as the latest text in the Vedic Brāhmaṇa genre. It comprises two principal sections: the Pūrvabhāga (5 prapāṭhakas) and the Uttarabhāga (6 prapāṭhakas). The Pūrvabhāga presents cosmogony, esoteric expositions of the sacred syllable Oṃ and vyāhṛtis, the origins of the Atharvan and Aṅgiras traditions, and the supremacy of the Atharvan Brahman priest, while the Uttarabhāga deals with solemn sacrificial rituals (such as the Agniṣṭoma), heavily adapting and reinterpreting material borrowed from earlier Brāhmaṇas of the Ṛgveda and Yajurveda.

summary: The Amaraughaśāsana ('Instruction on the Stream of Immortals') is an early Haṭhayoga manual preserved in Śāradā manuscripts from Kashmir and attributed to Gorakṣanātha. Comprising 80 prose aphorisms interspersed with explanatory kārikā verses, it details subtle anatomy (cakras, kandas, nāḍīs), breath control (kumbhaka), and bodily techniques aimed at arresting the flow of lunar nectar and overcoming death. Most distinctive are its descriptions of internal churnings and movements (sāraṇās) and the awakening of kuṇḍalinī through the squatting posture (utkaṭāsana), representing an important regional lineage of early Haṭhayoga practice.

summary: The Gorakṣaśataka ('Hundred Verses of Gorakṣa') is a seminal early manual of haṭhayoga traditionally attributed to Gorakṣanātha. The work expounds a six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) yoga system comprising posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), sense-withdrawal (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi). It provides fundamental descriptions of the body's esoteric anatomy—including the cakras, seventy-two thousand nāḍīs, and ten prāṇic winds—alongside mudrās and breath practices aimed at awakening kuṇḍalinī and attaining liberation (mukti).

summary: The Gorakṣaśataka ('Century of Verses of Gorakṣa') is a foundational Sanskrit manual of early Haṭhayoga attributed to the Nātha master Gorakṣanātha. This particular recension, recorded and translated by G. W. Briggs (1938), consists of 101 verses describing postures (specifically siddhāsana and padmāsana), the subtle channels and energy centers (nāḍīs and cakras), kuṇḍalinī, and breath regulation (prāṇāyāma and nāḍīśodhana). Text-historically, it represents the first half (pūrva-śataka) of the 200-verse work known as the Gorakṣapaddhati, differing substantially in structure and content from the recension critically edited by Kuvalayananda and Shukla.

summary: The Rasahṛdayatantra ('Heart of Mercury'), composed in 19 avabodhas (chapters) in āryā metre by Bhikṣu Govinda (Govindabhagavatpāda, c. 10th century CE), is the earliest surviving systematic treatise of the Sanskrit alchemical tradition (rasaśāstra). Written under the patronage of a Kirāta king named Madana, it details the eighteen operations (aṣṭādaśasaṃskārāḥ) on mercury, laboratory apparatuses (yantras), and formulas for transmuting base metals into gold (dhātuvedha) as well as creating elixirs for bodily immortality and rejuvenation (rasāyana). This e-text contains all 19 chapters of the root text accompanied by Caturbhujamiśra's Sanskrit commentary Mugdhāvabodhinī.

Arranged sequentially according to the verses of the Rājataraṅgiṇī, it systematically examines settlements, rivers, shrines, and sacred sites (tīrthas, nāgas), providing Sanskrit etymologies, textual citations (such as from the Nīlamatapurāṇa and Bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitā), and contemporary Kashmiri vernacular names and local traditions.

summary: The Grahamātṛkānāmadhāraṇī ('The Dhāraṇī of the Mother of Planets') is a short esoteric Buddhist astral-ritual text centered on Grahamātṛkā, the personified Buddhist Mother of Planets, and the propitiation of celestial bodies. Set in the city of Aḍakavatī where the Buddha instructs the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the text provides anthropomorphic iconographic descriptions, mandalas, offerings, and mantras for the nine planets (navagraha), the twenty-eight lunar asterisms (nakṣatra), and the twelve signs of the zodiac (rāśi) to avert astral and demonic afflictions. In Newar Buddhism, it forms the Saturday recitation within the widely recited Saptavāra ('Seven Days') dhāraṇī compendium.

summary: The Guṇakāraṇḍavyūhasūtra is an all-verse Mahāyāna sūtra composed in Nepal around the early 15th century as an extensive poetical reworking and expansion of the earlier prose Kāraṇḍavyūhasūtra. Framed as a dialogue between Jinaśrīrāja and Jayaśrī recounting the spiritual instructions given to King Aśoka by Upagupta, it glorifies the cosmic deeds and salvific emanations of Avalokiteśvara (Karuṇāmaya), promotes the six-syllable mantra (oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ), and details the merits of the poṣadha (aṣṭamīvrata) fasting ritual. Alongside the Svayaṃbhūpurāṇa, the work served as a foundational liturgical and doctrinal scripture for medieval and modern Newar Buddhism.

summary: The Nāgānanda ('Joy of the Serpents') is a five-act Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) attributed to King Harṣa of Kanauj (7th century CE), dramatizing the Buddhist legend of the Vidyādhara prince Jīmūtavāhana. The opening acts combine standard courtly kāvya romance with Jīmūtavāhana's courtship and marriage to Princess Malayavatī, while the fourth and fifth acts center on his Bodhisattva-like self-sacrifice: offering his own flesh on the slaughter stone to Garuḍa to rescue the young Nāga Śaṅkhacūḍa. Moved by Jīmūtavāhana's radical compassion and non-violence, Garuḍa renounces the slaughter of serpents and revives those previously consumed. Famous for invoking both the Buddha (munīndra / jina) and the Hindu goddess Gaurī, the work is an exceptional surviving exemplar of classical Buddhist dramatic literature.

summary: The Priyadarśikā is a classical four-act court drama (nāṭikā) attributed to King Harṣadeva (Harṣavardhana of Kanauj, r. c. 606–647 CE). Drawing upon the popular romantic cycle of King Udayana of Vatsa, it depicts Udayana's romance with Princess Priyadarśikā of Aṅga, who lives incognito as the handmaiden Āraṇyakā in Queen Vāsavadattā's harem. The play is particularly noted for containing one of the earliest extant examples of a play-within-a-play (garbhanāṭaka) in Sanskrit dramatic literature (Act 3), which brings about the discovery of the lovers and the heroine's eventual royal marriage.

summary: The Ratnāvalī is a four-act romantic court drama (nāṭikā) attributed to King Harṣa of Kanauj (Harṣavardhana, r. c. 606–647 CE). Based on the Udayana legendary cycle derived from Guṇāḍhya's Bṛhatkathā, it depicts King Udayana of Vatsa falling in love with Sāgarikā, an attendant to Chief Queen Vāsavadattā who is eventually revealed to be Princess Ratnāvalī of Siṃhala (Sri Lanka). Featuring motifs of mistaken identity, a pet starling (śārikā) repeating romantic secrets, and a faux palace fire staged by a court magician (aindrajālika), the play is treated by classical dramaturgs (such as Dhanañjaya in the Daśarūpaka) as the standard exemplar of the four-act nāṭikā genre.

summary: Haribhaṭṭa's Jātakamālā is an ornate collection of Buddhist birth stories composed in campū form (alternating classical Sanskrit prose and verse) around the 5th century CE. Written in deliberate emulation of Āryaśūra's famed Jātakamālā, Haribhaṭṭa's work illustrates the bodhisattva's cultivation of the perfections (pāramitā) while relying extensively on narrative traditions closer to the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda avadāna literature rather than the Pāli Jātakas. Long presumed lost except in Tibetan translation (Toh 4152), significant portions were rediscovered in Sanskrit manuscripts from Nepal and Tibet by Michael Hahn; this e-text compiles seventeen of those legends, concluding with the anonymous Śākyasiṃhajātaka.

summary: The Nyāyapraveśapravṛtti (also titled Śiṣyahitā or Nyāyapraveśakavṛtti) is an 8th-century commentary by the Śvetāmbara Jain master Haribhadrasūri on the Nyāyapraveśa, an introductory manual of Buddhist pramāṇa logic authored by Śaṅkarasvāmin (c. 6th century CE). Haribhadrasūri provides a concise, student-oriented word-by-word explanation of the treatise's definitions of valid proof (sādhana), refutation (dūṣaṇa), their corresponding fallacies (ābhāsa), direct perception (pratyakṣa), and inference (anumāna). The commentary is a major historical milestone illustrating the cross-sectarian study and integration of Dignāgean Buddhist epistemology into early medieval Jain intellectual culture.

summary: The Śāstravārtāsamuccaya ('Compendium of Philosophical Discourses') is a major 8th-century doxographical and polemical treatise in 701 anuṣṭubh verses across 11 chapters (stabakas) by the Śvetāmbara master Haribhadrasūri. The work presents a systematic survey and critique of non-Jain philosophical traditions, including Cārvāka materialism, theism (Īśvaravāda), Sāṃkhya dualism, Buddhist theories of momentariness (kṣaṇikavāda) and idealism (vijñānavāda/śūnyavāda), Advaita monism, and Mīmāṃsā rejections of omniscience. Haribhadra examines each perspective critically while adhering to the Jain framework of non-one-sided ontology (anekāntavāda) and concludes with an exposition of the nature of omniscience and spiritual liberation.

summary: The Harivaṃśa ('Genealogy of Hari') is the canonical supplement (khila) to the Mahābhārata, bridging late epic narrative with the early Purāṇas. summary: The Satyasiddhiśāstra (also reconstructed as Tattvasiddhiśāstra; Chinese: Chengshi lun) is an extensive Buddhist scholastic treatise in 202 chapters by Harivarman (c. 3rd–4th century CE), reflecting Bahuśrutīya and Dārṣṭāntika/Sautrāntika doctrines. Organized around an introductory section and the Four Noble Truths, it defends a two-truth framework affirming the emptiness (śūnyatā) of both persons and dharmas, and expounds the progressive dismantling of provisional, phenomenal, and ultimate conceptual constructs. While lost in India, Kumārajīva's Chinese translation formed the foundational text of the Chinese Chengshi (Japanese Jōjitsu) school.

summary: The Hastavālaprakaraṇa (comprising six root verses) and its autocommentary (vṛtti) analyze conventional reality using the classic Buddhist and Indian epistemological simile of a rope mistaken for a snake. While the original Indic Sanskrit manuscript is lost and the published Sanskrit text is a retro-translation from Tibetan and Chinese recensions, this e-text contains the complete set of six root verses along with the opening mangala and single introductory sentence of the vṛtti, omitting the prose commentary on the verses.

summary: The Rādhākṛṣṇārcanadīpikā ('Lamp Illuminating the Worship of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa') is a theological and ritual treatise in mixed prose and verse composed by Jīva Gosvāmin in the 16th century. It establishes the doctrinal justification for the paired worship of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa (specifically in the form of Rādhā-Dāmodara), drawing extensively on Purāṇic, Tantric, and Smṛti proof texts. Jīva argues that true worship of Bhagavān necessitates the worship of His devotees, establishes the gopīs as His foremost devotees, and demonstrates that Rādhā, as His supreme internal pleasure potency (hlādinī-śakti), must be worshipped alongside Him.

summary: The Saṅkalpakalpadruma is a late Sanskrit devotional-poetic work by Jīva Gosvāmin consisting of over 700 verses, composed in his old age as an address to his own mind (manaḥ-śikṣā). The work employs the allegory of a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) divided into four parts: root (janmādi-līlā, the manifest narrative pastimes of Kṛṣṇa), trunk (nitya-līlā, the eternal eightfold daily pastimes or aṣṭakālīya-līlā), branches (sarvartu-līlā, seasonal pastimes across the six seasons), and fruit (phala-niṣpatti, the ultimate attainment of loving service). It serves a contemplative function as a devotional distillation of the theology formulated in his magnum opus, the Gopālacampū, synthesizing manifest and unmanifest līlā for internal meditation.

summary: The Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkārasūtra ('The Ornament of the Light of Wisdom that Enters the Domain of All Buddhas') is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra presented through dialogues between the Buddha and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta concerning the nature of awakening, the transcendent realm of the buddhas, and ultimate reality. The text emphasizes that all dharmas are unoriginated (anutpāda), non-dual, and that the fundamental nature of mind is luminous (prakṛtiprabhāsvara). Extensively cited in key Indian treatises including the Ratnagotravibhāga, the sūtra was known through three early Chinese versions and a Tibetan translation before a complete Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscript dating to the Pāla period was rediscovered in 1999 at the Potala Palace in Lhasa.

summary: The Jñānāmṛtasārasaṃhitā (widely circulated under the title Nāradapañcarātra) is a late Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava saṃhitā in five major divisions (rātras) and sixty chapters, framed as a dialogue between Śiva and the celestial sage Nārada. Departing from the classical vyūha theology of early Pāñcarātra, the work places primary theological emphasis on the supreme cult of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa in Goloka, mantra devotion, and devotion to Kṛṣṇa (kṛṣṇa-bhakti). This digital file covers the first section (Prathamarātra, chapters 1–15), introducing the dialogue at Nārāyaṇāśrama and expounding the virtues of divine devotional service.

summary: The Jātakastava ('Praise of the Buddha\'s Former Births') by Jñānayaśas is a 20-stanza Mahāyāna devotional hymn (stotra) composed in the classical Śārdūlavikrīḍita metre. Framed by an opening confession of inadequate poetic capacity (verses 1–3) and a concluding dedication of merit for universal enlightenment (verses 19–20), stanzas 4–18 succinctly celebrate the Bodhisattva's extreme self-sacrificing deeds in previous lives—including feeding the tigress, giving away his wife and children, jumping into fire as the hare, giving up his tusks as Ṣaḍdanta, and slicing off his flesh as King Śibi. The Sanskrit text was preserved through Tibetan phonetic transliteration alongside a Tibetan translation in the Tengyur (Toh. 1178), representing the classical Sanskrit counterpart to the broader Asian tradition of jātaka encomia seen also in Khotanese.

summary: The Śivapūjāstava is a 47-verse liturgical hymn of the Śaiva Siddhānta tradition composed by Jñānaśambhu (fl. 12th century). It systematically traces the sequential procedures of daily Śiva worship (śivapūjā)—from morning contemplation, purificatory baths, and sandhyā rites to āsana visualization, nyāsa, external worship, homa, and final dismissals (visarga)—while interpreting each ritual gesture in terms of internal yogic meditation, discernment, and complete self-dedication (svātmanivedana).

summary: The Vṛttamālāstuti ('Garland of Metres Praise') is an 11th-century Buddhist devotional hymn and versified manual of Sanskrit metrics (chandaśśāstra) by the Vikramaśīla scholar-monk Jñānaśrīmitra. Comprising 154 stanzas praising the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (Mañjughoṣa), the work illustrates approximately 150 classical metres by weaving the metrical name directly into each stanza while exemplifying its metrical structure. Along with Ratnākaraśānti's Chandoratnākara, it was a fundamental textbook of prosody in late northern Buddhist monastic colleges and was translated into Tibetan by Pang Lotsāwa Lodrö Tenpa.

summary: The Sudhālaharī ('Wave of Nectar') is a devotional hymn (stotra) of 30 verses in Śārdūlavikrīḍita metre composed by the 17th-century poet-critic Jagannātha Paṇḍitarāja in praise of the Sun god (Sūrya). Part of Jagannātha's renowned group of five laharī poems, it vividly describes the rising sun, the dispersion of darkness, and the awakening of the cosmos, while praying for physical and spiritual illumination and purification.

summary: The Rasagaṅgādhara ('Bearer of the River of Aesthetic Emotion') by Jagannātha (mid-17th century) is widely regarded as the culminating philosophical masterpiece of classical Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra). Applying the analytical rigor and definitional apparatus of Navya-Nyāya logic, Jagannātha critically evaluates earlier poetic theorists, famously critiquing Mammaṭa, Viśvanātha, and Appayya Dīkṣita. This first chapter (ānana 1) defines poetry as language conveying a charming idea (ramaṇīyārthapratipādakaḥ śabdaḥ), classifies poetry into four levels of aesthetic merit, and provides an extensive analysis of the psychology and ontology of rasa, bhāva, and dhvani, illustrated throughout with original verses composed by the author.

summary: The Jaiminigṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual of the Jaiminīya (or Talavakāra) śākhā of the Sāmaveda. Structured in two praśnas comprising 24 and 9 khaṇḍas respectively, it begins with the standard model of the pārvaṇasthālīpāka offering and details domestic life-cycle rites (saṃskāras) such as upanayana, godāna, vivāha, and śrāddha, concluding with a navagrahaśānti. It constitutes an indispensable source for the domestic ritual liturgy of the Sāmaveda preserved primarily in South India (Tamil Nadu and Kerala).

summary: The foundational aphorisms of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā school attributed to Jaimini, accompanied by its earliest surviving commentary, the Śābarabhāṣya of Śabarasvāmin. Together they establish the epistemological foundations of Vedic exegesis, arguing for the intrinsic validity of cognition (svataḥprāmāṇya), the eternal authorlessness of the Veda (apauruṣeyatva), the inherent relation between word and referent, and the concept of unseen ritual efficacy (apūrva). This partial e-text encompasses adhyāyas 1 through 7, treating the sources of dharma, ritual classifications, subsidiary relations (śeṣatva), and the opening rules governing the transfer of ritual details (atideśa).

summary: The Mīmāṃsāsūtra (or Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra), traditionally attributed to Jaimini, is the foundational text of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā darśana. Arranged into twelve books (adhyāyas), hence known as the Dvādaśalakṣaṇī, the aphorisms formulate the rules of interpretation (nyāya) for the ritual injunctions (vidhi) of the Vedic corpus. The work provides systematic epistemological arguments for the intrinsicality of knowledge (svataḥprāmāṇya) and the eternality of language and the Veda, establishing hermeneutic canons that deeply influenced Dharmaśāstra, Vedānta, and Indian legal interpretation.

summary: The Kāśikāvṛtti is the earliest surviving complete running commentary (vṛtti) on the nearly 4,000 grammatical aphorisms of Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, jointly authored in the 7th century CE by Jayāditya (adhyāyas 1–5) and Vāmana (adhyāyas 6–8). It provides concise rule paraphrases, explicitly supplies ellipsed terms carried over by anuvṛtti, and presents an extensive corpus of illustrative examples and counterexamples drawn from classical usage and older treatises. By synthesizing Kātyāyana's vārttikas, Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya, and Candragomin's Cāndravyākaraṇa, the work served as the core pedagogical textbook of classical Pāṇinian grammar and inspired major sub-commentaries such as Jinendrabuddhi's Nyāsa and Haradatta's Padamañjarī.

summary: The Candrāloka is an elementary verse treatise on Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) composed by Jayadeva Pīyūṣavarṣa in ten chapters (mayūkhas) in straightforward anuṣṭubh meter. It methodically surveys poetic causes and definitions, word-powers (śaktivṛtti), poetic faults (doṣas), virtues (guṇas), figures of speech (alaṃkāras), and sentiment (rasa). The fifth mayūkha, treating figures of speech, is celebrated for its didactic technique wherein each definition serves simultaneously as an illustration of the figure defined; this chapter served as the direct basis for Appayya Dīkṣita's influential Kuvalayānanda.

summary: The Gītagovinda of Jayadeva (composed in late 12th-century Bengal) is a celebrated lyrical kāvya celebrating the passionate love, separation (viraha), and joyful reconciliation of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā. Comprising 12 cantos structured around 24 rhymed aṣṭapadīs (eight-couplet songs set to specific rāgas and tālas) framed by narrative and descriptive stanzas in classical metres, the work innovatively bridges classical Sanskrit kāvya traditions with vernacular song performance. Its synthesis of theological bhakti and refined erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) deeply influenced Gauḍīya and pan-Indian Vaiṣṇavism, inspiring enduring traditions of music, classical dance, and temple ritual across South Asia.

summary: The Tattvopaplavasiṃha ('The Lion that Devours all Principles/Categories') is a unique philosophical treatise of radical epistemological skepticism composed by Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa in the late 8th or early 9th century CE. Loosely affiliated with the Cārvāka/Lokāyata school, Jayarāśi turns dialectical reasoning against all accepted instruments of valid cognition (pramāṇas)—including perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony—arguing that because no pramāṇa can be established without begging the question, no metaphysical or empirical entities (tattvas) can be affirmed. The work is preserved in a single palm-leaf manuscript copied in 1292 CE at Dholkā, discovered in 1926 by Sukhlalji Sanghavi and Bechardas Doshi in the Saṅghavīnā Pāḍāno Bhaṇḍār at Pāṭan.

summary: The Sphuṭārthā Śrīghanācārasaṃgrahaṭīkā is a Buddhist Vinaya commentary by Jayarakṣita on the Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha, an otherwise lost metrical guide detailing the disciplinary code and daily conduct of novices (śrāmaṇeras). It covers novice training precepts (śikṣāpada), moral infractions, ritual procedures, and monastic etiquette. Known from a unique palm-leaf manuscript discovered in Tibet, the text is a vital Sanskrit source for Indian novice monasticism and has been linked by modern scholarship to the Mahāsāṃghika / Lokottaravādin lineage.

summary: The Hetutattvopadeśa ('Instruction on the True Nature of the Logical Reason') is an introductory compendium of Buddhist logic (hetuvidyā/pramāṇa) composed by Jitāri in the late 10th century. Following Dignāga's Nyāyapraveśa and Dharmakīrtian pramāṇa terminology, it systematically expounds proof (sādhana), refutation (dūṣaṇa), the threefold mark of the reason (trairūpya), and the various fallacies of the thesis (pakṣābhāsa), reason (hetvābhāsa), and example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa). This e-text preserves Durgacharan Chattopadhyaya's 1939 Sanskrit retro-translation made from the Tibetan translation prior to Tucci's recovery of the original palm-leaf manuscript.

summary: The Hetutattvopadeśa ('Instruction on the True Nature of the Logical Reason') is an introductory pedagogical primer on Buddhist logic (hetuvidyā) composed by the 10th-century scholar Jitāri. Closely following the model of the Nyāyapraveśa while incorporating Dharmakīrtian developments, the work outlines the three characteristics of a valid logical mark (trairūpya), the varieties of correct inferential reasons, and provides an exhaustive taxonomy of fallacies including defective theses (pakṣābhāsa), fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), and fallacious examples (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa).

summary: The Rājataraṅgiṇī of Jonarāja (commonly termed the Dvitīyā Rājataraṅgiṇī) is a 15th-century Sanskrit metrical chronicle of the rulers of Kashmir, composed at the court of Sulṭān Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn (r. 1420–1470 CE). Intended as a direct sequel to Kalhaṇa's 12th-century masterpiece, it traces the political history of Kashmir from the reign of Jayasiṃha (c. 1148/1149 CE) through the collapse of Hindu rule and the establishment of the Shah Mir dynasty until Jonarāja's death in 1459 CE. This e-text reflects Walter Slaje's critical edition, including both the genuine text and the interpolations/continuation known as Pseudo-Jonarāja.

summary: The Pañcasāyaka ('The Five Arrows', named for the flower arrows of Kāmadeva) is an influential medieval Sanskrit handbook of erotology (kāmaśāstra) in five chapters. Composed in the early 14th century by the Maithil scholar-courtier Jyotirīśvara Kaviśekhara, it draws upon earlier authorities including Vātsyāyana, Bābhravya, Nandikeśvara, and Kokkoka's Ratirahasya. The text outlines the typology of women (padminī, citriṇī, śaṅkhinī, hastinī) and men, lunar erogenous centers (candrakalā), copulatory postures (bandha), courtship, as well as cosmetic recipes, aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa), and erotic charms.

summary: The Ṛtusaṃhāra ('Gathering of the Seasons') is a descriptive lyric poem (khaṇḍakāvya) in six cantos, traditionally ascribed to Kālidāsa and widely regarded as his earliest surviving work. In rich sensory imagery, the poem depicts the six classical Indian seasons—summer, rains, autumn, early winter, winter, and spring—intertwining panoramic nature scenes with the erotic moods and romantic longings of lovers. Historically, it holds a seminal position in Indological history as the editio princeps of printed Sanskrit literature, published in Calcutta by Sir William Jones in 1792.

summary: The Kumārasambhava ('The Birth of Kumāra') is one of the celebrated mahākāvyas (court epics) composed by Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century CE). These eight cantos form the universally acknowledged genuine work of the poet, recounting the divine romance and union of Śiva and Pārvatī: from the magnificent description of the Himalayas and Pārvatī's birth, the destruction of Kāma by Śiva's third eye, Pārvatī's arduous penance and Śiva's testing of her devotion, through their celestial wedding and intimate divine honeymoon on Mount Gandhamādana in canto 8. The remaining cantos 9–17 found in extended vulgate manuscripts depict the actual birth of Kumāra (Kārttikeya) and the defeat of Tāraka, but are universally recognized as the composition of a later poet.

summary: The Meghadūta ('Cloud Messenger') of Kālidāsa is the foundational lyric poem of the sandeśakāvya genre in classical Sanskrit literature, composed entirely in the mandākrāntā meter. Exiled to Mount Rāmagiri for neglecting his duties, an attendant yakṣa begs a passing monsoon cloud to deliver a message of love and reassurance to his pining wife in the celestial city of Alakā. The poem comprises two sections: the Pūrvamegha, charting the cloud's scenic journey across the rivers, mountains, and cities of northern and central India, and the Uttaramegha, depicting the mythological splendors of Alakā and conveying the yakṣa's tender message. This e-text preserves the 111-stanza Kashmiri recension commented on by Vallabhadeva (c. 10th century).

summary: The Meghadūta ('The Cloud Messenger') is a classical lyric poem (khaṇḍakāvya / sandeśakāvya) composed in the seventeen-syllable mandākrāntā metre by Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century CE). Banished for a year to the remote hermitage of Rāmagiri by his master Kubera for neglect of duty, a grief-stricken yakṣa beseeches a passing monsoon cloud to convey a message of longing to his wife in the celestial Himalayan city of Alakā. The first part (Pūrvamegha) charts an evocative journey northward across central and northern India, depicting sacred shrines, rivers, and cities; the second part (Uttaramegha) describes Alakā, the melancholic condition of the yakṣa's beloved, and his intimate message of fidelity and prospective reunion. As the earliest surviving exemplar of its kind, the work established the widespread messenger-poem genre across South Asian and Inner Asian literatures.

summary: The Meghadūta ('Cloud Messenger') is a lyric poem composed in 111 mandākrāntā stanzas by Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century CE). An exiled yakṣa, separated from his beloved wife and pining on Mount Rāmagiri, enlists a passing monsoon cloud to carry a message of reassurance to his home in the mythical Himalayan city of Alakā. The poem is divided into two sections: the Pūrvamegha, charting the cloud's journey across the landscape of north-central India, and the Uttaramegha, describing the splendour of Alakā and the sorrow of the faithful wife. Recognized as Kālidāsa's lyric masterpiece, it established the dūtakāvya (messenger poem) genre throughout Indian literature and was translated into Tibetan, Sinhalese, and Mongolian.

summary: Kālidāsa's Raghuvaṃśa ('The Dynasty of Raghu') is a classic Sanskrit mahākāvya chronicling the legendary solar dynasty of Ayodhyā. Cantos 1–6 cover the reign and ascetic devotion of King Dilīpa and Queen Sudakṣiṇā to the sacred cow Nandinī, the birth and world-conquering digvijaya of King Raghu, Raghu's munificent gift-giving at the Viśvajit sacrifice, and the bridegroom-choice (svayaṃvara) assembly in which Princess Indumatī chooses Raghu's son Aja. This e-text transmits the root kāvya verses according to the Northern/Kashmirian textual transmission as preserved by the 10th-century Kashmirian commentator Vallabhadeva.

summary: A pivotal Mahāyāna sūtra dedicated to glorifying the salvific activities and cosmic compassion of Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara across various realms of saṃsāra, including Avīci hell and the preta realm. The text is historically famous as the earliest known source to teach the six-syllable mantra Oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ (the ṣaḍakṣarī mahāvidyā) and to detail its benefits and mandala ritual. Composed in northern India circa the 4th to 5th century CE, it demonstrates direct thematic engagements with contemporary Śaiva cosmologies—such as presenting Hindu deities like Maheśvara, Brahmā, and Nārāyaṇa as emanations from Avalokiteśvara's body—and provided the foundation for Avalokiteśvara worship and the Maṇi Kabum in Tibet.

summary: The Kāśyapaparivartasūtra is an early Mahāyāna scripture cast as a dialogue between the Buddha and Mahākāśyapa on Vulture Peak at Rājagṛha. It expounds the bodhisattva path, emphasizing moral purity and warning against spiritual hypocrisy, attachment to monastic privileges, and intellectual pride. The text famously articulates the Middle Way between the extremes of eternalism and annihilationism and contains the influential simile comparing the dogmatic reification of emptiness to a medicine that itself becomes a deadly disease.

summary: The Kāśyapaparivartasūtra (also known as the Kāśyapaparivarta or Ratnakūṭasūtra) is an archaic and foundational Mahāyāna scripture presented as a dialogue between Śākyamuni Buddha and Mahākāśyapa on Vulture Peak. It expounds core bodhisattva ethics, the Middle Way (madhyamā pratipad) avoiding eternalism and annihilationism, and the meditation on emptiness (śūnyatā), featuring the famous warning that reifying emptiness as a dogmatic view turns medicine into incurable poison. It also delivers severe critiques of counterfeit, self-serving monastics, providing essential scriptural authority frequently cited across Madhyamaka, Yogācāra, and Tibetan scholastic traditions.

summary: The Bhāvanāsārasaṃgraha is a major 19th-century Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava anthology compiled by Kṛṣṇadāsa Tātapāda of Govardhana as an aid to rāgānugā-bhakti meditation and interior mental service (mānasī-sevā). It synthesizes over three thousand verses drawn from foundational Gauḍīya kāvya, campū, and rasasūtra treatises (chiefly by Rūpa Gosvāmī, Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja, and Viśvanātha Cakravartin), systematically mapping them across the eight periods of the day and night (aṣṭakālīyalīlā) for Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa alongside Caitanya Mahāprabhu. This electronic text preserves the first two divisions, covering the dawn awakening (Niśāntalīlā) and morning activities (Prātarlīlā).

summary: The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhir anvayātmikā is a philosophical treatise by the eleventh-century Buddhist epistemologist Ratnakīrti (fl. c. 1000–1050 CE) of Vikramaśīla. It establishes the Buddhist doctrine of universal momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga) via positive pervasion (anvayavyāpti): whatever exists is causally efficient (arthakriyākārin), and causal efficiency can only occur instantaneously, not successively or simultaneously over time (kramākramābhyām). Defending the inference against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā realists, Ratnakīrti deploys reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) and contraposition (prasaṅgaviparyaya) to show that permanent entities cannot possess causal efficacy.

summary: The Bhairavānukaraṇastotra ('Hymn on the Assimilation to Bhairava') is a 48-verse non-dual Śaiva hymn composed by Kṣemarāja in āryā metre. Rather than offering purely devotional praises, the hymn systematically decodes the terrifying Agamic iconography of Svacchandabhairava—his many weapons, ornaments of skulls and elephant skin, charnel-ground setting, and retinue—interpreting them as symbolic expressions of the dynamic powers of supreme, unconditioned consciousness (cidbhairava). The stotra illustrates the Trika and Krama synthesis of ritual visualization, aesthetic sentiment, and non-dual recognition (pratyabhijñā).

summary: The Bodhavilāsa ('Play of Awakened Consciousness') is a concise Pratyabhijñā manual in 42 anuṣṭubh verses by the Kashmirian master Kṣemarāja (early 11th c. CE). Functioning as a versified epitome of the core doctrine set out in his Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya, the work expounds how autonomous universal consciousness (citi) contracts into individual minds (citta), continuously performs the five cosmic operations (pañcakṛtya), and recovers its innate liberation through steady contemplative discernment (vimarśa).

summary: The Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya ('Heart of Recognition') is an influential introductory manual of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism composed in the first half of the 11th century CE by Kṣemarāja, the principal pupil of Abhinavagupta. Composed specifically for practitioners and novices lacking training in formal logic (tarka), the treatise distills the core metaphysics and soteriology of Utpaladeva's Īśvarapratyabhijñā into twenty concise aphorisms accompanied by Kṣemarāja's own explanatory commentary. It outlines the cosmic dynamics of Citi (supreme consciousness), which freely manifests the universe, contracts itself into limited individual experients (paśu), and achieves liberation through the intuitive recognition of its inherent oneness with Śiva.

summary: The Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā ('Wish-Fulfilling Creeper of the Bodhisattva's Avadānas') is a monumental ornate Sanskrit kāvya collection composed in Kashmir around 1052 CE by the polymath Kṣemendra, recounting 108 edifying legends of previous lives and heroic deeds of the Buddha and bodhisattvas. The work attained celebrated status in Tibet, where it was translated in the 13th century and frequently depicted in narrative painting cycles. This e-text comprises the first volume of P.L. Vaidya's edition (Buddhist Sanskrit Texts 22) and preserves pallavas 1 through 48, from the Prabhāsāvadāna to the Hastakāvadāna.

summary: Pallava 93 of Kṣemendra's Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā comprises 111 classical Sanskrit verses retelling the legend of Sumāgadhā, daughter of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍada. Married into a non-Buddhist Jain (kṣapaṇaka) household in Puṇḍravardhana, Sumāgadhā is appalled by the behavior of the naked ascetics and miraculously invites the Buddha from Jetavana. The Buddha flies to Puṇḍravardhana with his retinue of arhats, converts her in-laws and the local populace through miracles and Dharma discourse, and reveals the karmic origins of her fortune from previous lifetimes.

summary: The Darpadalana ('Crushing of Pride') is a seven-chapter satirical and didactic poem (upadeśakāvya) composed in 11th-century Kashmir by Kṣemendra. Each chapter (vicāra) targets one of seven traditional causes of conceit (madahetavaḥ)—noble birth (kula), wealth (vitta), erudition (śruta), physical beauty (rūpa), valor (śaurya), munificence (dāna), and asceticism (tapas)—demonstrating through general moral reflections and illustrative narratives (dṛṣṭānta) how excessive vanity leads to downfall and ridicule. The text exemplifies Kṣemendra's characteristic witty satire, psychological insight, and sharp critique of contemporary Kashmiri manners.

summary: The Garbhāvakrāntyavadāna (designated Garbhāvakrāntinirdeśa in its colophon) forms the 10th pallava of Kṣemendra's 11th-century Buddhist narrative masterpiece, the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā. summary: Kalāvilāsa ('The Play of the Arts' or 'The Grace of Guile') is an eleventh-century satirical poem in ten cantos composed by the Kashmiri polymath Kṣemendra. Framed as instruction delivered by Mūladeva, the legendary prince of rogues, to Candragupta, the naive son of a wealthy merchant, the work catalogues and satirizes widespread forms of deceit, greed, and hypocrisy in medieval society—exposing corrupt bureaucrats and scribes (kāyasthas), merchants, quack physicians, astrologers, courtesans, and false ascetics—before concluding with an exposition of genuine, auspicious arts. Alongside Kṣemendra's Deśopadeśa and Narmamālā, it is a foremost specimen of social satire and didactic poetry (upadeśakāvya) in classical Sanskrit.

summary: The Narmamālā ('Garland of Mirth' or 'Garland of Satires') is a satirical poem in three chapters (parihāsas) composed in 11th-century Kashmir during the reign of King Ananta. It presents a caustic caricature and expose of corrupt scribe-officials (Kāyasthas and diviras), detailing their greed, oppression of the public, administrative malpractice, religious charlatanism, and domestic vices. Together with the Deśopadeśa, it is a key satirical source for socio-political life in medieval Kashmir.

summary: The Pratītyasamutpādāvadāna is the 75th pallava of Kṣemendra's Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā (completed c. 1051 CE). summary: The Sevyasevakopadeśa is a short didactic and satirical poem (upadeśakāvya) in 61 verses composed by the 11th-century CE Kashmiri writer Kṣemendra. It offers a piercing critique of courtly dependence, describing the degradation, anxiety, and humiliation endured by servants and dependents (sevaka) at the hands of arrogant patrons and masters (sevya). The work ultimately praises self-reliance, moral autonomy, and inner contentment (saṃtoṣa).

summary: The Sudhanakinnaryavadāna constitutes the 64th chapter (pallava) of Kṣemendra's 11th-century kāvya work, the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā. It narrates the romance of Prince Sudhana and the Kinnarī princess Manoharā, recounting their encounter, subsequent separation, Sudhana's perilous supernatural quest to find her in the Kinnara kingdom, and their eventual reunion. Framed in the context of the Buddha's past life, it explains karmic bonds relating to Yaśodharā.

summary: The Vaiśeṣikasūtra is the foundational treatise of the Vaiśeṣika school of classical Indian philosophy, traditionally attributed to Maharṣi Kaṇāda. Organised into ten adhyāyas of two āhnikas each, it elaborates an atomistic and pluralistic realist ontology structured around fundamental categories (padārtha): substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), motion/action (karman), generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya). The work investigates physical causation, the elementary constituents of matter, and perception and inference, maintaining that spiritual liberation (niḥśreyasa) arises from discriminative knowledge of reality induced by dharma.

summary: The Vaiśeṣikasūtra, attributed to the sage Kaṇāda (ca. 2nd c. BCE – 2nd c. CE), is the foundational aphoristic treatise of the Vaiśeṣika school of Indian philosophy. The text develops an analytical, realist ontology dividing reality into categories (padārthas)—substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), action (karman), universal (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya)—alongside early atomism and physical theories of causation. This digital version reproduces the older recension preserved in Candrānanda's Vṛtti (first edited by Muni Jambuvijaya in 1961), equipped with Masanobu Nozawa's textual apparatus detailing variants across the commentarial traditions of Śaṅkaramiśra and Bhaṭṭa Vādīndra.

summary: The Kaṭhināvadāna is a Buddhist narrative work belonging to the Sanskrit avadāna literature preserved in Nepalese manuscripts. It integrates Vinaya ritual prescriptions concerning the kaṭhina robe ceremony—detailing the cutting, sewing, ritual marking, and offering of monastic robes at the end of the rains retreat (varṣāvāsa)—with didactic avadāna stories illustrating the karmic merit of giving to the Saṅgha. summary: The Kaivalyopaniṣad is a celebrated text belonging to the Śaiva Upaniṣad corpus, preserved in recensions attached to both the Atharvaveda and the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Framed as a dialogue in which Brahmā instructs the Vedic seer Āśvalāyana on Brahmavidyā, it expounds the attainment of kaivalya (isolation / supreme liberation) through renunciation, faith, and inward meditation. It harmonizes non-dual Advaitic metaphysics with theistic contemplation of Rudra-Śiva (Umāsahāya), identifying the cosmic Absolute with the innermost transcendent witness (sākṣin, cinmātra) abiding in the cave of the heart.

Seven of the stanzas are opening maṅgala verses from Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī (1.2, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1, 5.1, 6.1, 8.1), while verse 17 is from Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa's 14th-century Stutikusumāñjali (15.37) and verse 18 is from Śrīvara's late 15th-century Rājataraṅgiṇī (1.1.2). summary: The Kalpadrumāvadānamālā ('Wish-Granting Tree Garland of Avadānas') is a medieval Nepalese Buddhist narrative collection composed in classical epic ślokas, framed as edifying instructions delivered by the arhat Upagupta to Emperor Aśoka. It metrically elaborates stories largely corresponding to tales in the Avadānaśataka and related narrative cycles. This tenth chapter, the Subhūtyavadāna, relates the former lives, renunciation, and moral cultivation of the elder Subhūti, extolling the practice of universal loving-kindness (maitrī) and dedication toward rebirth in Sukhāvatī.

summary: The Bhāvanākrama ('Stages of Meditation') by Kamalaśīla (c. 740–795 CE) is an influential triad of treatises formulating the graduated Mahāyāna path according to the Yogācāra-Madhyamaka synthesis. Composed in Tibet in connection with the Samyé (bSam yas) debate, it defends the classical Indian gradualist method of spiritual development against the sudden, non-conceptualizing quietism attributed to the Chinese Chan master Heshang Moheyan. Across the three works, Kamalaśīla systematizes the cultivation of compassion (karuṇā), the awakening mind (bodhicitta), and the balanced union (yuganaddha) of calm abiding (śamatha) and analytical discernment (vipaśyanā) leading to the non-conceptual realization of emptiness.

summary: The Madhyamakāloka ('Illumination of the Middle Way') is Kamalaśīla's (c. 740–795 CE) comprehensive independent treatise of Madhyamaka philosophy, traditionally counted among the 'Three Works of the Eastern Svātantrikas' (dbu ma shar ba gsum). Synthesizing Nāgārjunian emptiness with Dharmakīrtian epistemological logic (pramāṇa), the work systematically defends the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena (sarvadharmaniḥsvabhāvatā), expounds the doctrine of the two truths and the single vehicle (ekayāna), and refutes non-Buddhist as well as rival Buddhist positions. Although the original Sanskrit manuscript transmission is lost, the complete work survived in the Tibetan Tanjur (D 3887) and is represented here through Penpa Dorjee's 2001 Sanskrit reconstruction.

summary: The Prajñāpāramitāvajracchedikāṭīkā is an extensive commentary by the 8th-century Indian master Kamalaśīla on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra ('Diamond Sūtra'). Following classical Indian scholastic structure—setting out the purpose (prayojana), concise overview (piṇḍārtha), word analysis (padārtha), internal connection (anusandhi), and answers to objections—Kamalaśīla expounds the sūtra from a Yogācāra-Mādhyamika perspective. He details the path of the bodhisattva across the three grounds (adhimukticaryābhūmi, śuddhādhyāśayabhūmi, and buddhabhūmi) and refutes substantialist views while demonstrating two-fold selflessness. Because the ancient Sanskrit manuscript is lost, this e-text represents a modern Sanskrit reconstruction (punaruddhāra) made from the Tibetan canonical version by Pema Tenzin.

summary: The Navaślokī (also titled Āryāṣṭasāhasrikāyāḥ Prajñāpāramitāyāḥ Piṇḍārthaḥ) is a concise verse digest of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā attributed to Kambalapāda. The text consists of 14 ślokas: four introductory stanzas establishing that all perfections are unified in the Perfection of Wisdom, nine core stanzas that expound non-substantiality and emptiness using nine classical similes (including an optical reflection, a mirage, an echo, a dream, a mechanical puppet, and the moon in water), and a concluding dedication to supreme gnosis. The work represents an important synthesis of Prajñāpāramitā doctrine and Yogācāra-Madhyamaka philosophy and circulated widely in India, Tibet, and Song-dynasty China.

attribution_note: Both works are traditionally attributed to the primordial sage Kapila. The Tattvasamāsa is likewise a late medieval synopsis (c. 14th c. or slightly earlier) encapsulating core Sāṃkhya categories.

summary: The Sāṃkhyasūtra (or Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra) is an aphoristic treatise in six adhyāyas (527 sūtras) articulating Sāṃkhya metaphysics, traditionally attributed to Kapila but compiled in the late medieval period (c. 14th–15th century CE). The first three books expound core ontological doctrines (puruṣa, prakṛti, the evolutes, and the mechanics of bondage and liberation), the fourth provides illustrative parables and allegories, and the final two refute rival philosophical schools and recapitulate the system. Appended to the root text in this file is the Tattvasamāsa, a concise mnemonic compendium detailing the twenty-five tattvas and auxiliary categories of Sāṃkhya, arranged here in two sections: Tattvapāda and Prakīrṇapāda.

summary: The Karatoyāmāhātmya is an early medieval regional sthalamāhātmya in 85 verses extolling the sacred Karatoyā river and the holy precinct of Pauṇḍravardhana (modern Mahasthangarh, Bogra District, Bangladesh). Set as a dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī reported by Sūta to the sages, the text relates the mythic origin of the Karatoyā from the water poured onto Śiva's hands during his marriage to Pārvatī and surveys the holy bathing places, shrines, and lingas established by Paraśurāma in Pauṇḍrakṣetra. Verses from the text are cited in medieval dharmaśāstra and lexical commentaries as early as Sarvānanda's Ṭīkāsarvasva (1159 CE) and Devaṇabhaṭṭa's Smṛticandrikā, confirming its currency in the twelfth century.

summary: The Karmavastu is the tenth chapter of the Vinayavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, treating the validity and taxonomy of ecclesiastical legal acts (saṅghakarman). It categorizes monastic proceedings according to whether the monastic assembly is harmonious/complete (samagra) or fractured/incomplete (vyagra), and whether the execution adheres to the Dharma (dharmeṇa) or violates it (adharmeṇa). The chapter details procedures including motions (jñapti), single and fourfold proclamations (karmavācanā), and suspension (utkṣepaṇakarman) and rehabilitation (osāraṇakarman) of monks.

summary: The Karmavibhaṅgopadeśa is an anonymous Buddhist exegetical treatise (upadeśa) preserved in a single 15th-century Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript (dated Nepāla Saṃvat 531 / 1410 CE). Serving as an exposition and commentary to the Mahākarmavibhaṅga, it examines the mechanics of karma and karmic fruition (vipāka). The text defends and elucidates key doctrinal positions—such as why making offerings to a stūpa after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa remains profoundly meritorious despite the absence of an embodied recipient—by citing canonical Āgama/Nikāya, Abhidharma, and avadāna parallels.

summary: The Karuṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra ('The White Lotus of Compassion') is a prominent Mahāyāna scripture composed around the 3rd to 4th century CE. It contrasts the aspirations and vows of various buddhas and bodhisattvas: whereas buddhas such as Amitābha and Akṣobhya chose to preside over purified buddha-fields free of spiritual decline, Śākyamuni made vows in a past life as the priest Samudrareṇu to attain awakening and guide sentient beings in an impure world (the Sahā world) during the era of the five degenerations (pañcakaṣāya). The text celebrates Śākyamuni's supreme compassion, likening him to an exceptionally fragrant white lotus (puṇḍarīka) blooming amidst lesser flowers.

summary: The Kaṭhopaniṣad is a classical mukhya Upaniṣad of the Kaṭha school of the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurveda, framed as an initiatory dialogue between the boy Naciketas and Yama, the lord of death. When granted three boons, Naciketas bypasses earthly riches and longevity to demand knowledge of what transpires beyond death, prompting Yama to distinguish the path of spiritual good (śreyas) from the path of worldly pleasure (preyas) and reveal the immortal nature of the inner self (ātman). The text is renowned for its chariot allegory in Vallī 3—correlating the body with a chariot, the intellect with the charioteer, the mind with reins, and the senses with horses—and for providing one of the earliest textual formulations of proto-Sāṃkhya ontological gradations and the definition of yoga as steady sensorial restraint.

summary: The Arthaśāstra is ancient India's foundational treatise on statecraft, political economy, judicial administration, and diplomatic strategy. Divided into fifteen books (adhikaraṇas), it systematically covers the education and discipline of the king, ministerial appointments, internal civil and revenue administration, civil and criminal law (dharmasthīya and kaṇṭakaśodhana), espionage, interstate relations (the mandala theory and the sixfold foreign policy, ṣāḍguṇya), military logistics and warfare, and the methodological hermeneutics of treatises (tantrayukti). Treating artha (material welfare and power) as the foundation of royal and societal flourishing, it provides an exceptionally detailed blueprint for state institutions in classical India.

summary: The Kauthumagṛhyasūtra is a short domestic-ritual text (gṛhyasūtra) affiliated with the Kauthuma śākhā of the Sāmaveda, preserved in a single codex discovered in South India. In 21 brief khaṇḍas, it treats domestic ritual procedures, expiatory offerings (prāyaścitta), and specific rites such as the marriage to a Calotropis procera plant (arkakanyādāna) before a third marriage, while lacking standard household ceremonies like the regular vivāha. Because of its peculiar selection of rites and linguistic irregularities, scholars treat it as a late supplement or recast related to the Gobhilagṛhyasūtra tradition.

summary: A concise Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā sūtra spoken by the Buddha to Śakra (Kauśika) on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha. The text expounds the nondual nature of the perfection of wisdom through negative dialectical statements, eighteen modes of emptiness (aṣṭādaśaśūnyatā), and verses found in the Vajracchedikā and the opening maṅgalācaraṇa of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. It concludes with a series of protective mantras and dhāraṇīs honoring Prajñāpāramitā, bridging exoteric Prajñāpāramitā philosophy with esoteric protective practice.

summary: A concise independent manual (prakaraṇa) of the Sāṃkhya system by Kavirājayati, composed for students who find the study of extensive classical texts too laborious. The treatise outlines the threefold suffering (duḥkhatraya) and the means of its absolute elimination via discriminating knowledge (vivekakhyāti), the twenty-five principles (tattvas), causality (satkāryavāda), and the mechanism of cosmic evolution and individual liberation. It quotes Vācaspatimiśra's Tattvakaumudī and Vallabhācārya's Nyāyalīlāvatī.

summary: The Vṛttaratnākara by Kedārabhaṭṭa (c. 10th–11th century CE) is the most widespread and influential classical Indian manual of metrics (chandaḥśāstra). Across six chapters, it defines the metrical gaṇas and scanning rules, illustrating classical syllabic (varṇavṛtta) and moraic (mātrāvṛtta) meters via self-exemplifying verses (lakṣaṇa-lakṣya). This text is accompanied by the Sukavihṛdayānandinī, an extensive Sanskrit commentary completed by Sulhaṇa in 1189–1190 CE.

summary: The Vṛttaratnākara of Kedārabhaṭṭa (c. 10th–11th century CE) is the most widely disseminated and taught manual of classical Sanskrit prosody (chandaśśāstra) in South Asia. Structured in six concise chapters of 136 verses, it covers metrical definitions and the trika/gaṇa syllabic foot notation, mātrāvṛtta (moraic) metres, samavṛtta, ardhasamavṛtta, viṣamavṛtta, and the six metrical pratyayas (combinatorial algorithms such as prastāra, naṣṭa, and uddiṣṭa). Each metrical rule is cleverly composed in the very metre that it defines, serving simultaneously as definition and illustrative instance.
