summary: The Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra ('Heart Sūtra') is one of the most widely recited and influential texts of Mahāyāna Buddhism, condensing the vast Prajñāpāramitā literature into an essential doctrinal summary. This e-text presents the short recension (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā), which omits the traditional introductory frame (nidāna) and concludes directly with the mantra. Avalokiteśvara explains to Śāriputra that the five aggregates and all constituent phenomena of Buddhist abhidharma are empty of inherent existence ('form is emptiness, emptiness is form'), culminating in the celebrated mantra 'gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā'.

summary: The Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra ('Heart of the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra') is one of the most widely recited and commented-upon texts in Mahāyāna Buddhism. This e-text preserves the complete longer recension (vistaramātṛkā), which includes the full narrative setting (nidāna) on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha and concludes with the Buddha rising from samādhi to praise Avalokiteśvara's exposition. The bodhisattva expounds to Śāriputra the emptiness of intrinsic existence (svabhāvaśūnyatā) of all five aggregates, sense spheres, and Noble Truths, concluding with the famous mantra: gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.

summary: The Prakāśasaṃhitā (also referenced in manuscript catalogues as the Paramatattvanirṇayaprakāśasaṃhitā) is a Vaiṣṇava Āgamic text belonging to the Pāñcarātra canon, framed as a dialogue between Śrīhaṃsa (Viṣṇu) and Brahmā. Strikingly distinctive among Pāñcarātra saṃhitās, its doctrinal tenets closely mirror Dvaita Vedānta theology, including the innate threefold classification of individual souls (traividhya: muktiyogya, nityabaddha, and tamoyogya), the eightfold cosmic agency of Viṣṇu (sṛṣṭyādyaṣṭakartṛtva), cosmogony, and devotional ritual practices. Passages ascribed to a Prakāśasaṃhitā are cited as authoritative in the works of Madhvācārya and the later Dvaita tradition.

summary: The Pramāṇavārttika ('Commentary on Valid Cognition') is the foundational masterwork of Dharmakīrti (ca. 6th–7th century CE) and the definitive text of Buddhist epistemology, logic, and philosophy of language. Composed in verse as an extensive critical development of Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya, it establishes perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna) as the only two means of valid cognition, formulates the Buddhist theory of conceptual exclusion (apoha), and provides rational defenses of the Buddha's authority, rebirth, and the Four Noble Truths. This e-text contains the complete set of metrical root verses (kārikās) across four chapters arranged according to the commentarial tradition of Manorathanandin.

summary: The Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśasūtra is a canonical Buddhist discourse delivered by the Buddha at Jetavana in Śrāvastī. It is divided into two parts: the 'fundamental exposition' (ādi), which articulates the standard twelvefold formula of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) from ignorance (avidyā) to aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), and the 'detailed analysis' (vibhaṅga), which provides concise definitions of each link. The text represents an early stage of doctrinal systematization parallel to the Pāḷi Vibhaṅgasutta (SN 12.2), Sūtra 16 (Ādisūtra) of the Sanskrit Nidānasaṃyukta, Taishō 124 (translated by Xuanzang) in the Chinese Canon, and Toh 211 in the Tibetan Kangyur.

summary: The Pratītyasamutpādamahāyānasūtra is a brief Mahāyāna scripture set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, where the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara petitions the Buddha to deliver a teaching yielding boundless merit for the assembly. In response, the Buddha recites the famed dependent arising verse (ye dharmā hetuprabhavā...) and equates dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) directly with the Dharma body (dharmakāya) of all Tathāgatas, stating that whoever perceives dependent arising sees the Tathāgata. He teaches that fashioning even miniature caityas, bodhi trees, and umbrellas and reciting or depositing this verse inside them yields vast, Brahma-like merit (brāhmaṃ puṇyam) leading to rebirth in the Brahmaloka and the Śuddhāvāsa heavens. The sūtra serves as a crucial canonical justification for the widespread medieval Asian Buddhist practice of depositing the ye dharmā creed into stūpas, plaques, and images as a dharmakāya relic (dharmadhātu).

summary: The Pratisarākalpadhāraṇī is a short Buddhist apotropaic text consisting of a protective dhāraṇī and kalpa formulas centered on Mahāpratisarā, the chief goddess of the Pañcarakṣā pentad. Opening with an announcement of the Vidyādharakalpa and salutations to the Triratna and Śākyamuni Buddha, the text prescribes incantations and svāhā-formulas intended to ward off diseases, hostile spirits, poisons, and obstacles, while providing universal safety and purifying karmic obscurations. It represents an extracted or parallel ritual witness closely corresponding to sections found in the broader Mahāpratisarā-mahāvidyārājñī corpus.

summary: This text constitutes the second chapter (Svaparapratyakṣalakṣaṇanyāyanirṇaya) of the anonymous late Buddhist epistemological digest Tarkarahasya (ca. 11th–12th century CE). Following the Dignāga-Dharmakīrti tradition, it defines sensory perception (pratyakṣa) as non-conceptual (kalpanāpoḍha) and non-erroneous (abhrānta) cognition bearing a direct grasp of bare particulars (svalakṣaṇa). The chapter systematically critiques alternative theories and definitions of perception formulated by non-Buddhist traditions—including the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsakas, Śaivas, Vaiyākaraṇas, Naiyāyikas, Vaiśeṣikas, and Sāṃkhyas—as well as assessing earlier Buddhist definitions such as Vasubandhu's.

summary: The Pravāraṇāvastu is the third chapter (vastu) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, regulating the pravāraṇā ('invitation' / mutual admonition) rite held at the conclusion of the three-month rains-retreat (varṣā). In this ceremony, each monastic invites fellow members of the saṅgha to declare any transgression he may have committed—whether seen, heard, or suspected—enabling communal confession, amends, and reconciliation before the community departs. The text details the qualifications and appointment of the presiding pravāraka monk, the formal legal transactions (karmavācanā), provisions for sick monks participating by proxy, and regulations for postponing or staying the ceremony.

summary: The Pravrajyāvastu ('Chapter on Going Forth') is the opening section of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, detailing the monastic protocols, criteria, and disqualifications for entering the Buddhist Order (pravrajyā) and receiving full ordination (upasaṃpadā). Interspersed with the legal guidelines are extensive narrative episodes, including accounts of King Bimbisāra, early converts to the saṃgha, and the avadāna tales of Saṃgharakṣita and Nāgakumāra. The surviving Sanskrit text is preserved in fragmentary manuscript leaves from the 6th–7th-century Gilgit finds.

summary: The Padārthadharmasaṅgraha (also known as the Praśastapādabhāṣya), composed by Praśastapāda around the 6th century CE, is the defining classical exposition of the Vaiśeṣika philosophical school. Rather than commenting sequentially on Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣikasūtra, it presents an independent systematic categorization of reality into six fundamental ontological categories (padārthas: dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, and samavāya), establishing the conceptual foundation for all subsequent classical Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika philosophy.

summary: The Praśnopaniṣad is a classical Upaniṣad associated with the Pippalāda śākhā of the Atharvaveda, composed in mixed prose and verse. It is organized around six philosophical questions addressed by the sage Pippalāda to six seekers concerning the cosmic generation of creatures, the primacy and functions of prāṇa (vital breath), deep sleep, the meditation on the sacred praṇava Oṃ, and the sixteen-part person (ṣoḍaśakala puruṣa). The accompanying Praśnopaniṣadbhāṣya attributed to Śaṅkara expounds these teachings from an Advaita Vedāntic perspective, distinguishing lower knowledge (aparam brahma) from higher realization of the non-dual Self (param brahma).

summary: The Pudgalavastu is the twelfth section (vastu) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, setting forth ecclesiastical regulations for dealing with individuals (pudgala) guilty of saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses. Starting from the case of the monk Udāyī, the text classifies offending monks according to their degree of awareness, acknowledgment, and concealment of faults, prescribing corresponding sanctions such as probation (parivāsa), retroactive probation (mūlaparivāsa), demotion (mūlāpakarṣa), and the six-day penance (mānāpya). The Sanskrit text is preserved in the Gilgit manuscript discovery, and the chapter also survives in Tibetan translation, though it was not translated into Chinese by Yijing.

summary: The Kādambarasvīkaraṇasūtra with its accompanying prose commentary is a satirical, mock-śāstric text preserved in the Kāmaśāstra tradition. In 34 aphorisms and elaborate scholastic prose, it deploys the technical argumentation of Navya-Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā to argue that the consumption of liquor (kādambara / vāruṇī) before and during lovemaking is an indispensable causal prerequisite (paramakāraṇa) for sexual fulfillment. The author cites classical mahākāvyas (Raghuvaṃśa, Kirātārjunīya, Śiśupālavadha) as authorities and facetiously concludes that observant practitioners will attain pleasure, offspring, and the celestial abode of Urvaśī.

summary: The Ekākṣarakośa is a short monosyllabic dictionary (ekākṣarakośa) attributed to the 12th-century Buddhist grammarian and lexicographer Puruṣottamadeva. It catalogues individual vowels and consonant syllables together with their diverse divine, cosmological, and conventional lexical meanings. Originally composed to assist poets in metrical composition and verbal puzzles, it was later adopted by Tantric practitioners as a key manual for deciphering cryptic seed-syllables (bījamantras) and coded ritual formulae.

summary: The Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā ('Questions of Rāṣṭrapāla') is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra included as assembly 18 in the Mahāratnakūṭa collection. Framed as a discourse at Gṛdhrakūṭa between the Buddha and the bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla, the text champions the ascetic ideal of forest dwelling (āraṇyaka) and dhūtaguṇa practice while mounting a severe critique against corrupt, comfortable urban monks of the decadent age (paścimakāla). summary: The Sādhanādīpikā is a ten-chapter (kakṣā) ritual manual and theological treatise composed in the early seventeenth century by Rādhākṛṣṇadāsa Gosvāmī, head priest of the Śrī Govindadeva temple in Vrindavan. The work provides practical and esoteric instructions for vigraha-sevā, the sacred geography of Vraja-dhāma, the meaning of the eighteen-syllable Gopāla mantra, and the practice of rāgānugā-bhakti. Historically, it is a crucial doctrinal witness for the Gadādhara-parivāra, highlighting the worship of Gadādhara Paṇḍita as an incarnation of Rādhā.

summary: The Kāvyamīmāṃsā ('Inquiry into Poetry') by Rājaśekhara (fl. c. 880–920 CE) is a major classic of Sanskrit literary theory focused on the practical training and culture of a poet (kaviśikṣā). Although planned on an encyclopedic scale of eighteen books, only the first book, the Kavirahasya ('The Poet's Secret') in eighteen chapters, is extant. The work offers valuable documentation of early medieval Indian literary life, describing the allegorical personification of poetry (Kāvyapuruṣa), the nature of innate poetic talent (pratibhā), royal assemblies and salons (kavisabhā), the classification of borrowing and plagiarism (haraṇa), poetic conventions (kavisamaya), and Pan-Indian cultural geography (deśavibhāga).

summary: The Rāmodanta is an anonymous pedagogical Sanskrit poem summarizing the complete narrative of the Rāmāyaṇa in simple anuṣṭubh verse. Widely used across South India—particularly Kerala—as an introductory reader, it traditionally served as a student's first narrative text following the memorization of basic grammatical declensions and conjugations (such as the Siddharūpa). The original recension comprises 156 verses, encoded by the kaṭapayādi chronogram 'cinmayaḥ' (156) in the final verse, while popular later print editions expanded the text to 199 verses organized into seven kāṇḍas.

summary: The Haṃsadūta ('The Swan Messenger') is an early 16th-century Sanskrit messenger poem (dūtakāvya) in 142 śikhariṇī verses composed by Rūpa Gosvāmī. Modeled after Kālidāsa's Meghadūta, the poem describes Lalitā, a confidante of Rādhā, dispatching a swan from the banks of the Yamunā to Kṛṣṇa in Mathurā following his departure from Vraja. The bulk of the composition (verses 65–140) conveys Lalitā's message depicting Rādhā's distress in separation (vipralambha-śṛṅgāra) and reproaching Kṛṣṇa for abandoning the gopīs, synthesizing courtly lyric conventions with Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava devotional theology.

summary: The Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu ('Ocean of the Nectar of Devotional Rasa'), composed in 1541 CE by Rūpa Gosvāmin, is the foundational work of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava devotional theology and aesthetics. Adapting the classical rasa theory of Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and medieval alaṃkāraśāstra, Rūpa establishes devotion (bhakti) directed toward Kṛṣṇa not merely as a bhāva (transient emotional state), but as the supreme aesthetic and ontological sentiment (bhakti-rasa). Organised in four quadrants (pūrva, dakṣiṇa, paścima, and uttara vibhāgas), the text comprehensively systematises the categories of devotional practice (sādhana, bhāva, prema), the constituent components of aesthetic emotion (vibhāva, anubhāva, sāttvikabhāva, vyabhicāribhāva), the primary rasas (śānta, dāsya, sakhya, vātsalya, madhura), and the secondary devotional sentiments along with discordant mixtures (rasābhāsa).

summary: The Laghubhāgavatāmṛta is a foundational theological treatise composed by Rūpa Gosvāmī (mid-16th c. CE) summarizing and systematizing the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava ontology outlined in Sanātana Gosvāmī's Bṛhadbhāgavatāmṛta. The first part (Pūrvakhaṇḍa or Śrī-Kṛṣṇāmṛta) provides a rigorous scriptural classification of divine forms and avataric descents (svayaṃrūpa, tad-ekātma-rūpa, vilāsa, svāṃśa, āveśa, and prakāśa), demonstrating that Kṛṣṇa is the original supreme divinity (avatārī) rather than a subordinate incarnation of Viṣṇu. The shorter second part (Uttarakhaṇḍa or Śrī-Bhaktāmṛta) establishes a gradated hierarchy of devotees of Kṛṣṇa, culminating in the gopīs of Vraja and preeminently Śrī Rādhā.

summary: The Nāṭakacandrikā ('Moonlight of Drama') is a 16th-century dramaturgical treatise by Rūpa Gosvāmī, one of the Six Gosvāmins of Vṛndāvana. Synthesizing Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and especially Siṅgabhūpāla's Rasārṇavasudhākara—while consciously rejecting the formulation of the Sāhitya-darpaṇa—the work systematizes plot structure (sandhi, sandhyaṅga), hero types, and emotional states for dramatic poetry. It serves as both the dramaturgical theory behind Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava aesthetics and the technical companion to Rūpa's own devotional plays, Vidagdhamādhava and Lalitamādhava, establishing Kṛṣṇa as the ideal dramatic hero.

summary: The Padyāvalī is an important Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava anthology of devotional Sanskrit verses compiled by Rūpa Gosvāmī in the first half of the 16th century CE. It brings together 388 stanzas composed by over 120 authors, ranging from classical and medieval court poets (such as Jayadeva, Bilvamaṅgala, and Umāpatidhara) to Caitanya and his direct associates. Arranged thematically according to the nuances of bhakti-rasa, the efficacy of the divine name, and the pastimes of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa, the anthology served as a primary devotional and literary repository for later Gauḍīya tradition.

summary: The Ujjvalanīlamaṇi ('The Blazing Sapphire') is an influential 16th-century treatise on devotional aesthetics and theology by Rūpa Gosvāmin, one of the Six Gosvāmins of Vṛndāvana. Written as a specialized sequel to his Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, the work presents an exhaustive analysis of madhura-rasa (the erotic-devotional sentiment), which Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism regards as the supreme aesthetic manifestation of devotion to Kṛṣṇa. Rūpa adapts classical Sanskrit dramaturgical and kāvya taxonomies—including the classifications of hero and heroine (nāyaka- and nāyikā-bheda), supporting characters, excitant factors (vibhāva), involuntary physical responses (anubhāva), and permanent emotions (sthāyibhāva)—to explain the intimate loving relations between Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs of Vraja, culminating in the preeminence of Rādhā.

summary: The Muktācarita ('The Tale of the Pearl') is a campū-kāvya combining Sanskrit prose and verse, composed around the mid-16th century by Raghunāthadāsa Gosvāmī, one of the Six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana. Framed as a dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and his queen Satyabhāmā in Dvārakā, Kṛṣṇa recounts an incident from his youth in Vraja during the Dīpāvalī festival: when the gopīs refuse to give him pearls to ornament his beloved cows, Kṛṣṇa plants pearls in the earth and harvests bountiful pearl creepers, whereas the envious gopīs sow pearls with milk and butter but reap only thorny bushes. The work focuses on the witty banter, mock disputes, and commercial bargaining over the jewels between Kṛṣṇa, Subala, Madhumaṅgala, Rādhā, and Lalitā, illustrating the intimate erotic-devotional theology (mādhura-līlā) of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition.

The commentary opens with a salutation to the Arhats and explicitly names itself Kaṅkālādhyāyavārttika (v. 1). Manuscript colophons (e.g. Berlin Chambers 438, BORI 944) confirm that it was written in VS 1443 (1386 CE) at Pāṭan by Merutuṅgasūri of the Añcala Gaccha at the request of Rāvala Campaka (son of Bhaḍīga). summary: The Rasādhyāya (also known as Kaṅkālādhyāya or Kaṅkālayarasādhyāya) is a medieval Sanskrit alchemical (Rasaśāstra) manual attributed to a disciple of the Siddha Kaṅkālaya Yogin. In 21 chapters (adhikāras) and 481 verses, it details the purification and processing of mercury (the eighteen saṃskāras), methods of digestion (jāraṇa) and movement (sāraṇa), and the calcination and fixation (māraṇa) of metals and minerals for metallic transmutation (dhātuvāda) and longevity (dehasiddhi). This e-text preserves verses 1–302 along with the Kaṅkālādhyāyavārttika, a learned Sanskrit commentary composed in 1386 CE at Pāṭan by the Śvetāmbara Jain polymath Merutuṅgasūri.

summary: The Rasārṇava (ca. 12th century CE) is one of the principal classical treatises of Indian alchemy (Rasaśāstra), framed as a tantric dialogue between Bhairava and Devī. Across 18 chapters (paṭalas), it provides extensive descriptions of laboratory equipment (yantras), crucibles (mūṣās), furnaces, and mineralogical operations including the purification and fixation of mercury (rasabandha) and flame tests for metals. The physical transmutations are explicitly situated within a tantric soteriological framework aiming at bodily immortality (dehasiddhi) and living liberation (jīvanmukti).

summary: The Bhramaharanāma Hevajrasādhana ('Remover of Error') is a generation-stage (utpattikrama) liturgical and meditative manual for the sixteen-armed, eight-faced Hevajra in union with Nairātmyā and surrounded by the eight retinue goddesses. Composed in the early eleventh century by Ratnākaraśānti of Vikramaśīla, the work is notable for its explicit integration of Nirākāravāda Yogācāra philosophy into the initial contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatājñāna) that precedes deity visualization. It survives in Sanskrit manuscripts from Nepal and Tibet, as well as a Tibetan translation in the Tengyur (Toh 1245).

summary: The Sāratamā is an extensive Sanskrit commentary (pañjikā) by the Vikramaśīla master Ratnākaraśānti on the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, mapped onto the eight abhisamayas of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra. Ratnākaraśānti interprets the sūtra from an Alīkākāravāda Yogācāra perspective, systematically critiquing Haribhadra's four-kāya interpretation of Abhisamayālaṅkāra chapter 8 and defending a three-kāya buddhology.

attribution_note: Authorship is historically disputed across Buddhist traditions. The Tibetan tradition attributes the root verses to the Bodhisattva Maitreya and the prose commentary (vyākhyā) to Asaṅga. The Chinese tradition (beginning in Fazang's commentaries and subsequent catalogs) attributes the entire treatise (Jiujing yisheng baoxing lun, T 1611, translated by Ratnamati in 511 CE) to *Sāramati (Jianyi / Suoluomodi). Extant Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscripts discovered in Tibet carry no author colophon. While Johnston initially considered Sthiramati (later retracted), modern critical scholarship (Takasaki, Schmithausen, Kano) distinguishes earlier and later textual strata, placing the final compilation and commentary in the 5th century CE and largely corroborating the link to Sāramati.

summary: The Ratnagotravibhāga (also widely cited as the Mahāyānottaratantraśāstra or Uttaratantra) is the preeminent classical Indian treatise systematically articulating the doctrine of buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha). Structured around seven 'vajra points' (vajrapada)—Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, the element/lineage of awakening (dhātu/gotra), awakening itself (bodhi), enlightened qualities (guṇa), and buddha-activity (karman)—the text demonstrates that the primordial, luminous nature of mind is present within all sentient beings, concealed only by adventitious defilements (āgantukakleśa). It synthesizes and comments extensively upon key tathāgatagarbha sūtras, notably the Tathāgatagarbhasūtra, the Śrīmālādevīsiṃhanādasūtra, and the Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa.

summary: The Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā ('Verses on the Accumulation of Precious Qualities') is a metrical summary of early Prajñāpāramitā doctrine in 302 verses composed in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit. It expounds foundational Mahāyāna teachings, emphasizing the emptiness (śūnyatā) of the aggregates, the practice of non-abiding (asthānayoga), and the bodhisattva's dedication to awakening through compassion without grasping. While the root verses represent one of the earliest extant strata of Prajñāpāramitā literature (c. 100 BCE – 100 CE), this e-text preserves the 32-chapter Sanskrit recension revised and stabilized by the 8th-century scholar Haribhadra.

summary: The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi vyatirekātmikā is an epistemological treatise by the 11th-century Buddhist master Ratnakīrti demonstrating the universal momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) of all existents by way of negative pervasion (vyatirekavyāpti) or contraposition. Developing the earlier insights of his teacher Jñānaśrīmitra, Ratnakīrti argues that whatever lacks causal efficiency through succession or simultaneity (kramākrama) cannot exist, thereby proving that eternal entities are impossible and that only momentary particulars are real. The treatise is particularly famous for its thorough refutation of the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika objection of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi) when formulating inferences concerning uninstantiated or fictitious entities.

summary: The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Vyatirekātmikā ('Proof of Universal Momentariness by Negative Concomitance') is a short philosophical monograph by Ratnakīrti, condensing and defending the epistemological arguments of his master Jñānaśrīmitra. Complementing his Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Anvayātmikā (which argues via positive pervasion), this treatise argues from negative contraposition: non-momentary (enduring) entities cannot exercise causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya) either in succession (krama) or simultaneously (akrama), and therefore cannot exist. Ratnakīrti pays particular attention to defusing the Nyāya objection that an inference with a non-existent subject (the unproduced or eternal entity) incurs the fallacy of lack of substratum (āśrayāsiddhi).

summary: The Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī is a collection of ten philosophical monographs (nibandhas) composed in the 11th century CE by Ratnakīrti, a master at Vikramaśīla and pupil of Jñānaśrīmitra. The collection represents the final flourishing of classical Buddhist Pramāṇavāda and Sautrāntika-Yogācāra philosophy in northern India, formulating rigorous responses to Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā opponents. Major subjects addressed include the proof of the Buddha's omniscience (Sarvajñasiddhi), the refutation of God as creator (Īśvarasādhanadūṣaṇa), the apoha nominalist theory of word meaning (Apohasiddhi), positive and negative proofs of universal momentariness (Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi), the refutation of enduring entities (Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa), the logic of invariable concomitance and reduction of valid cognitions (Vyāptinirṇaya, Pramāṇāntarbhāvaprakaraṇa), and an ultimate idealist critique of external objects and other minds (Citrādvaitaprakāśavāda, Santānāntaradūṣaṇa).

summary: The Vādarahasya is a late Indian Buddhist epistemological treatise preserved in a single 42-folio manuscript in Proto-Bengali/Maithili script photographed by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana in Tibet (now preserved on film and glass negatives at the Bihar Research Society, Patna). The work defends core Buddhist philosophical doctrines—particularly momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga), the exclusion theory of meaning (apoha), and causal efficacy (arthakriyākāritva)—against the attacks of the 11th-century Nyāya master Udayana, especially those set forth in the Ātmatattvaviveka. Although published in 1984 under the title Udayananirākaraṇam and attributed to Ratnakīrti, philological research has shown the text to be anonymous and composed after Jñānaśrīmitra.

summary: The Ratnamālāvadāna ('Garland of Jewels of Edifying Deeds') is a late Sanskrit Buddhist metrical collection of thirty-eight avadāna tales framed as instruction given by the arhat Upagupta to Emperor Aśoka. It versifies and expands narratives familiar from older collections such as the Avadānaśataka, illustrating the inexorable results of karma, devotion to the Three Jewels, and the cultivation of the Mahāyāna pāramitās. Preserved in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts, it was critically edited in full by Kanga Takahata in 1954.

summary: The Rākṣasakāvya is a brief 20-verse poem in the vasantatilakā meter describing the arrival of the monsoon season. Notable for its dense wordplay, alliteration (yamaka), and obscure periphrastic expressions, the poem depicts a youthful traveler admiring rain clouds, peacocks, and flowering trees before returning home in a bullock cart with his wife. It is accompanied by the Sajjanānandadāyinī commentary, traditionally attributed to Ravideva and expanded by Kṛṣṇadhara Vyāḍi.

summary: The Revākhaṇḍa is a large purāṇic glorification (māhātmya) of the Narmadā (Revā) river in 232 chapters, narrated by Sūta to Śaunaka and the sages of the Naimiṣa forest. It recounts the origin of the river from Śiva, its imperishability through the cosmic dissolutions, and the legends and ritual merits of the many tīrthas along both banks from Amarakaṇṭaka to the sea near Bhṛgukaccha, with mantras for bathing, offerings and gifts. It is the main textual basis of the Narmadā circumambulation (parikramā); its attribution (Skanda- vs. Vāyupurāṇa) is discussed by J. Neuss.

summary: The Śṛṅgāratilaka ('Ornament of the Erotic') of Rudrabhaṭṭa is an influential treatise on Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) in three chapters (paricchedas). Composed around the 10th or 11th century CE, it represents an early milestone in transposing the aesthetic theory of rasa and emotional states (bhāvas) from dramaturgy (nāṭya) directly to poetic literature (kāvya). Focusing preeminently on the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) and the systematic typology of lovers and heroines (nāyaka- and nāyikā-bheda), Rudrabhaṭṭa illustrates theoretical definitions with original and anthologized kāvya stanzas.

summary: The Alaṅkārasarvasva of the 12th-century Kashmiri theorist Rājānaka Ruyyaka is one of the most influential classical treatises on Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra). Composed in sūtra style with an accompanying expository vṛtti, the work provides a rigorous and systematic taxonomy of poetic figures (śabdālaṅkāras and arthālaṅkāras), organizing them logically while synthesizing the Kashmiri dhvani doctrine. This e-text contains the opening theoretical exposition and sūtras 1 through 34 along with the Vimarśinī, the late 12th- to early 13th-century commentary by Jayaratha that defends Ruyyaka's definitions against contemporary critics like Śobhākaramitra.

attribution_note: The Alaṅkārasarvasva consists of concise aphorisms (sūtras) accompanied by an explanatory prose commentary (vṛtti) and illustrative citations. While the South Indian commentator Samudrabandha and the later commentator Vidyācakravartin attribute both sūtras and vṛtti to Ruyyaka (also named Rājānaka Rucaka), Jayaratha in his commentary Vimarśinī attributes the prose vṛtti to Ruyyaka's pupil Maṅkha (Maṅkhuka). Modern critical scholarship generally treats Ruyyaka as the principal author of the treatise, or at least of the foundational sūtras.

summary: The Alaṅkārasarvasva is an influential 12th-century Kashmiri treatise on Sanskrit poetics by Ruyyaka (c. 1135–1150 CE). Composed in concise sūtras accompanied by a prose vṛtti, the work provides an analytical and exhaustive classification of over eighty figures of sense and sound (alaṅkāra), integrating traditional rhetorical taxonomies with the dhvani framework established by Ānandavardhana and Mammaṭa. Its celebrated introductory Bhūmikā offers a critical historical review of earlier poetic theories (Bhāmaha, Udbhaṭa, Vāmana, Kuntaka, and Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka), demonstrating that ornamental figures are functionally subservient to suggested aesthetic emotion (rasa/vyaṅgyārtha).

summary: The Alaṅkārasarvasva ('The Essence of Poetic Figures') by the 12th-century Kashmiri theorist Ruyyaka is a standard manual of Sanskrit poetics that systematizes and analyzes more than eighty poetic figures (śabdālaṅkāras and arthālaṅkāras) within the dhvani-orientated framework of Ānandavardhana and Abhinavagupta. In this digital text, Ruyyaka's sūtras are provided alongside Vidyācakravartin's complete Sañjīvanī commentary.

summary: The Sahṛdayalīlā ('Play/Diversion of the Connoisseur') is a short aesthetic-erotic treatise in four chapters (ullekhas) by the 12th-century Kashmirian literary theorist Rājānaka Ruyyaka. Transferring analytical categories from poetics (guṇa, alaṅkāra, jīvita, and parikara) to female physical charm, Ruyyaka provides a taxonomy of ten innate qualities of feminine beauty (such as lāvaṇya, chāyā, and saubhāgya), personal ornamentation (gems, gold, garments, cosmetics), vital expressions of youth, and accompanying settings and retinues from the perspective of an urban aesthete (nāgaraka / sahṛdaya).

summary: The Vyaktivivekavyākhyā (also called Vyaktivivekavicāra) is a 12th-century commentary by the Kashmiri rhetorician Ruyyaka on Mahimabhaṭṭa's Vyaktiviveka. This text contains the second chapter (dvitīya vimarśa), which analyzes poetic defects (doṣas) and syntactic improprieties (śabdānaucitya), examining five major faults: vidheyāvimarśa (faulty predication/emphasis), prakramabheda (lack of syntactic parallelism), kramabheda (misplaced word order), paunaruktya (redundancy), and vācyāvacana / avācyavacana (omission or unwarranted inclusion of expressions). Although Mahimabhaṭṭa composed the root work as a polemic against Ānandavardhana's dhvani doctrine by seeking to subsume suggestion into logical inference (anumāna), Ruyyaka's commentary provides indispensable grammatical and rhetorical elucidations while critically scrutinizing Mahimabhaṭṭa's positions.

summary: The Sāṃkhyaparibhāṣā is a late, syncretistic definitional manual composed in mixed prose and verse. Although titled as a Sāṃkhya work, it integrates Sāṃkhya cosmological categories (the twenty-five tattvas) with Advaita Vedānta concepts—explicitly citing the classical Advaita guru lineage from Gauḍapāda to Śaṅkara and the fourfold spiritual prerequisites (sādhanacatuṣṭaya)—as well as elements of Yoga and Haṭhayoga praxis. The work survives in a single fragmentary manuscript witness edited by Vindhyeśvarīprasāda Dvivedin.

summary: The Sāṃkhyasūtravivaraṇa (also titled Kāpilasūtravṛtti in its closing colophon) is an anonymous post-classical commentary on the Tattvasamāsa, a concise 23-sūtra mnemonic compendium of orthodox Sāṃkhya topics traditionally ascribed to Kapila. The commentary glosses each sūtra in lucid prose, defining the eight creative causes (aṣṭau prakṛtayaḥ), sixteen modifications (ṣoḍaśa vikārāḥ), spirit (puruṣa), the three guṇas, cosmic emergence and dissolution (sañcara and pratisañcara), down to the three valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). It represents a concise late scholastic handbook expounding the classical Sāṃkhya dualist ontology and epistemology.

summary: The Sāmavedasaṃhitā is the liturgical verse collection (ārcika) providing the textual base (yoni) for the melodies (sāman) intoned by the Udgātṛ priest during Śrauta sacrificial rituals, particularly the Soma sacrifices. Preserved here in the standard Kauthuma recension, the collection comprises 1,875 mantras divided into the Pūrvārcika (single stanzas arranged by deity—principally Agni, Indra, and Soma Pavamāna—followed by the Āraṇyaka/Mahānāmnī section) and the Uttarārcika (strophes and triplets arranged according to ritual execution). With the exception of approximately 75 stanzas, all verses are drawn from the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā (predominantly Mandalas VIII and IX), frequently showing distinct dialectal and phonetic variations adapted to musical chant.

summary: The Sārdhatriśatikālottarāgama is an early Śaiva Siddhānta scripture composed of approximately 350 verses across 27 chapters (of which chapters 1–23 are preserved in this e-text), representing one of several recensions of the Kālottara textual family and traditionally viewed as an upāgama derived from the Vātulāgama. It provides a concise manual of Saiddhāntika ritual and doctrine, expounding mantroddhāra, mudrās, bhūtaśuddhi, internal and external worship, initiation (dīkṣā), prāṇāyāma and yoga, sonic cosmogenesis (nāda), expiatory rites, and the role of the spiritual guide. summary: The Sātvatatantra is a Vaiṣṇava scriptural text in nine paṭalas framed as a dialogue between Śiva and Nārada on Mount Kailāsa. Diverging from classical tantric ritual manuals, it centers on the philosophical cosmology of Viṣṇu-Kṛṣṇa, the emanation of the three cosmic puruṣa forms (Kāraṇodakaśāyī, Garbhodakaśāyī, and Kṣīrodakaśāyī Viṣṇu), and the supreme efficacy of bhakti and the divine name. It is entirely distinct from the ancient Pāñcarātra jewel-text Sātvatasaṃhitā and served as an important theological proof-text for Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava authors such as Rūpa, Sanātana, and Jīva Gosvāmin.

summary: The Sūryasiddhānta is the most prominent and authoritative classic of traditional Indian mathematical astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra). Composed in fourteen adhyāyas of Anuṣṭubh verses, it is framed as celestial instruction imparted by a solar deity to the asura Maya. The treatise expounds planetary mean and true motions, spherical astronomy, solar and lunar eclipses, planetary conjunctions, heliacal risings and settings, cosmography, astronomical instruments, and time measurement. The extant version reflects a medieval redaction that served as the primary foundation for calendar computation (pañcāṅga) across premodern India.

summary: The Saṃghāṭasūtra is a Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra set on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, consisting of dialogues between the Buddha and the bodhisattvas Sarvaśūra and Bhaiṣajyasena. It emphasizes the spiritual perils of cyclic existence, the visionary experiences of dying and intermediate states, karmic retribution and purification, and the boundless merit accrued from hearing, reciting, or copying the text. It was exceptionally widely copied in northwestern India and Central Asia, surviving in numerous Sanskrit manuscripts from Gilgit and Dunhuang, as well as Khotanese, Sogdian, Tibetan, and Chinese translations.

The text is celebrated as a classic witness to the Mahāyāna 'cult of the book', repeatedly emphasizing the limitless karmic merit, protection, and purification accrued through hearing, reciting, copying, and worshiping the sūtra itself. Multiple birch-bark copies were recovered from the Gilgit cache alongside covers that mark an early development in Indian book art; it also circulated widely in Central Asia, surviving in Khotanese fragments as well as early Chinese (T. 423 by Upaśūnya, 538 CE) and Tibetan translations.

Framed as a discourse given by Upagupta to King Aśoka, it narrates the tale of Sabhika, opening in Mathurā with the birth of a girl afflicted with the astrological status of a 'triyantrikā' (a child of three previous siblings of the opposite gender, regarded in Indian folklore as inauspicious), her upbringing by a wandering ascetic, and her subsequent Buddhist monastic ordination (pravrajyā) and spiritual realization. Tilak Raj Chopra critically edited the text as a philological supplement to his article investigating the Buddhist and New Indo-Aryan folk belief surrounding triyantara/teṃtara children.

summary: The Saddharmalaṅkāvatārasūtra is an influential Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra that synthesizes Yogācāra consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā / cittamātra) doctrines with the tathāgatagarbha teaching. Framed as an exposition delivered by the Buddha on Mount Malaya in Laṅkā to the bodhisattva Mahāmati and king Rāvaṇa, it expounds the eight consciousnesses (especially ālayavijñāna), the five dharmas, the three intrinsic natures (trisvabhāva), the two kinds of selflessness (dharmanairātmya and pudgalanairātmya), and the doctrine of vegetarianism (māṃsabhakṣaṇaparivarta). The text exerted foundational influence across Mahāyāna philosophical schools, Tibetan scholasticism, and East Asian Chan/Zen traditions.

summary: The Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra ('The White Lotus of the True Dharma') is one of the most celebrated and influential Mahāyāna scriptures. It propounds the doctrine of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), declaring that the apparent three vehicles (śrāvakayāna, pratyekabuddhayāna, and bodhisattvayāna) are provisional pedagogical devices (upāyakauśalya) and that all beings are destined for unexcelled awakening. Renowned for its rich parables—such as the burning house, the prodigal son, the medicinal herbs, and the gem concealed in the garment—the sūtra also reveals the Buddha's lifespan to be immeasurable and his parinirvāṇa an expedient display. Composed in several developmental strata from roughly the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE, it became the doctrinal cornerstone of East Asian Buddhist traditions such as Tiantai, Tendai, and Nichiren.

summary: The Samādhirājasūtra ('King of Samādhis Sūtra', often cited by Indian Madhyamaka commentators as Candrapradīpasūtra) is an influential Mahāyāna scripture in 40 chapters expounding the meditative absorption (samādhi) that reveals the fundamental equality and emptiness of all phenomena (sarvadharmasvabhāvasamatā). Delivered by the Buddha on Vulture Peak to the youth Candraprabha, the text combines exposition of non-arising and ultimate reality with teachings on ethical discipline, ascetic practices (dhūtaguṇa), dhāraṇī formulas, and past-life narratives (jātakas). It was widely quoted as a scriptural authority on emptiness by Candrakīrti, Śāntideva, and Prajñākaramati, and served as a foundational sūtra source for contemplative traditions in Tibet, particularly Sūtra Mahāmudrā.

summary: The Samādhirājasūtra (also known as the Candrapradīpasūtra) is a major Mahāyāna scripture centered on the meditative realization of the essential sameness of all phenomena (sarvadharmasvabhāvasamatā), through which all virtues of buddhahood and the bodhisattva path are perfected. It expounds the emptiness and non-substantiality of dharmas, the transcendent nature of the Tathāgata's dharmakāya, and the ideal ethical and ascetic conduct of bodhisattvas. The text is frequently cited by classical Indian Madhyamaka authors such as Candrakīrti and Śāntideva and plays a prominent role in Tibetan contemplative traditions.

summary: The Āptamīmāṃsā ('Critique of the Trustworthy Authority'), also known as the Devāgamastotra after its opening words, is a foundational 114-verse philosophical treatise by the Digambara master Ācārya Samantabhadra (ca. 5th–6th c. CE). Beginning as a theological inquiry into what qualifies an individual as a truly omniscient, authoritative teacher (āpta), it establishes that miracles and external divine manifestations cannot establish authority; rather, true authority belongs only to one who has eradicated internal passions and whose teachings cannot be invalidated by reason or experience. Samantabhadra applies the sevenfold conditional predication (syādvāda / saptabhaṅgī) and many-sided ontology (anekāntavāda) to refute one-sided (ekānta) philosophical positions across rival Indian traditions (Buddhist, Advaita Vedānta, Sāṅkhya, and Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika), creating the dialectical framework that shaped the subsequent Jain logical tradition.

summary: The Samyaksambuddhabhāṣitapratimālakṣaṇa (also known as the Pratimālakṣaṇa or Buddhapratimālakṣaṇa) is a primary manual of Buddhist iconometry (tālamāna). Framed as a discourse at Jetavana where the Buddha instructs Śāriputra on how devotees should fashion icons after the Teacher's parinirvāṇa, the text establishes canonical proportions (pramāṇa) for images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Across 54 verses, it details precise measurements in bodily units (aṅgula, mātrā, vyāma) for the uṣṇīṣa, cranial contours, facial features, torso, and limbs, as well as distinct facial types (such as oval and round) for various classes of divine, human, and semi-divine beings. Widely preserved in Nepalese manuscripts and incorporated into both the Tibetan Tengyur and the Chinese canon, the work served as a fundamental textual authority for religious sculpture and painting in northern Buddhism.

summary: The Saptaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 700 Lines', also designated Mañjuśrīparivartāparaparyāyā or Puṇyakṣetranirdeśa) is an influential Mahāyāna scripture belonging to the Prajñāpāramitā corpus. Set in Śrāvastī's Jeta Grove, it consists of profound dialogues between the Buddha, Śāriputra, and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī emphasizing the unreality of dualistic categories, the unoriginated nature (anutpāda) of all dharmas, and the non-apprehending contemplation of the Tathāgata. The scripture is celebrated in East Asian Buddhist traditions for introducing the 'single-array absorption' (ekavyūhasamādhi, traditionally interpreted as the 'one-practice samādhi'), which links insight into the non-differentiated dharmadhātu to concentrated mindfulness of a Buddha.

summary: The Sarvadurgatipariśodhanatantra ('Tantra of the Elimination of All Evil Destinies') is an influential Buddhist Yogatantra of the Vairocana cycle, dating roughly to the late 7th to 8th century CE. Set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the tantra opens with Śakra pleading with Śākyamuni to deliver the god Vimalamaṇiprabha, who has fallen into the lower realms upon his death. Centering on Sarvavid Vairocana and his maṇḍalas, the text provides elaborate ritual instructions—including initiations, sādhanas, apotropaic rites, and especially mortuary and post-mortem ceremonies—designed to purify negative karmic imprints and ensure liberation from adverse transmigrations.

summary: The Sarvajñatākāradhāraṇī is a Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture corresponding to Chapter 2 (Dhāraṇīmukhaparivarta) of the Karuṇāpuṇḍarīkasūtra ('White Lotus of Compassion'). It teaches the dhāraṇī formula for entering into the mode of omniscience (Sarvajñatākāradhāraṇīmukhapraveśa), functioning as a mnemonic and incantatory device granting bodhisattvas irreversible progress toward buddhahood and retention of the Dharma. Notably, the text contains an archaic incantation termed a 'Dravidian spell' (Dramiḍa-mantrapada) and circulated as an independent protective text in Nepalese manuscript traditions.

summary: The Sarvamatasaṃgraha is a concise Sanskrit doxography composed in Kerala from an Advaita Vedānta perspective. It opens with an epistemological overview (pramāṇanirūpaṇa) detailing eight means of valid cognition, followed by an exposition of heterodox (Cārvāka/Lokāyata, Jaina, and four Buddhist schools) and orthodox schools (Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā, and Uttara-Mīmāṃsā). The systems are presented in a hierarchical ascending order, concluding with non-dual Brahma-realization as the ultimate purport of philosophy.

summary: The Sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhānavyūhasūtra (also known by its longer title, Sarvatathāgatādhiṣṭhānasattvāvalokanabuddhakṣetrasaṃdarśanavyūha) is a Mahāyāna scripture set on Mount Potalaka, the abode of Avalokiteśvara. The Buddha enters a samādhi of great compassion that illuminates the cosmos, alleviating suffering and generating salvific transformations throughout the realms of existence. Expounding the protective power and spiritual empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna) of all buddhas, the text incorporates extensive dhāraṇī and protective incantations, featuring solemn pledges to protect the teaching by Vajrapāṇi, the Four Great Kings, and eighty yakṣiṇīs. Preserved in Sanskrit in the Gilgit manuscript cache (ca. 6th–7th century CE), it was translated into Chinese by Yijing in 701 CE (Taishō 1375) and into Tibetan (Toh 98 / Toh 507).

summary: The Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṅgraha is the foundational root tantra of the Yogatantra class in Indian esoteric Buddhism, dating to the late 7th century CE. Centered on Mahāvairocana and the five Buddha families (kulas) within the Vajradhātu maṇḍala, it expounds the enlightenment of Sarvārthasiddhi via the five progressive realizations (pañcākārābhisambodhi) along with extensive rituals for initiation (abhiṣeka), mudrās, and mantras. It forms the primary doctrinal and ritual bedrock for East Asian esoteric Buddhism (Zhenyan and Shingon) and directly influenced subsequent Indo-Tibetan tantric traditions.

summary: The Sarvopakāriṇī ('The All-Benefiting Gloss') is a concise, anonymous Sanskrit commentary on the Tattvasamāsa (also called Samāsasūtra or Kāpilasūtra), an ancient mnemonic outline of classical Sāṃkhya philosophy. It comments systematically on the 22 sūtras of this recension, expounding the 25 principles (tattvas), the forward and reverse evolutions of the guṇas (sañcāra and pratisañcara), the three kinds of suffering, the sources of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and the nature of liberation (mokṣa). Its opening lines preserve a notable scholastic tradition asserting that this 22-sūtra work represents the original seed of the system taught by Kapila as an avatāra of Nārāyaṇa, in contrast to the six-chapter Sāṃkhyasūtra composed by Kapila as an avatāra of Vaiśvānara.

summary: The Rasārṇavasudhākara ('Nectar-Moon to the Ocean of Rasa') is an encyclopedic 14th-century Sanskrit treatise on dramaturgy and aesthetics composed by King Siṃhabhūpāla II of the Recherla dynasty. Arranged into three comprehensive 'rays' (vilāsas)—Rañjakollāsa (dealing with dramatic personae, the typology of hero and heroine, and their aesthetic embellishments), Rasollāsa (treating the primary sentiments, transient emotions, excitant/ensuant factors, and the nature of aesthetic delight), and Nāṭakollāsa (treating plot structure, junctures/sandhis, and dramatic genres)—it synthesizes the traditions of Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra, Dhanañjaya's Daśarūpaka, and Bhoja's Śṛṅgāraprakāśa. The work is especially prized by later commentators (notably Mallinātha and the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theorists such as Rūpa Gosvāmin) for its rigorous definitions and rich repertoire of illustrative quotations drawn from classical poetry and drama.

attribution_note: The root work Nyāyāvatāra was traditionally ascribed to Siddhasena Divākara (author of the Sanmatitarka). Modern scholarship (notably Sukhlalji Sanghvi, M. A. The commentary Nyāyāvatāravivṛti was authored by the Śvetāmbara monk Siddharṣigaṇin (fl. early 10th c. CE, author of the Upamitibhavaprapañcākathā, c. 906 CE). summary: The Nyāyāvatāra is a concise 32-verse Jain treatise on epistemology and logic (pramāṇaśāstra) treating perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), verbal testimony, internal pervasion (antarvyāpti), and the doctrine of perspectives (naya) in the context of anekāntavāda. Historically ascribed to Siddhasena Divākara, the text is now dated to c. the 8th century CE and attributed to Siddhasena Mahāmati, who engaged systematically with the Buddhist logic of Dharmakīrti. Siddharṣigaṇin's 10th-century commentary, the Nyāyāvatāravivṛti, provides a comprehensive exposition of each verse, vigorously defending Jain epistemological positions against rival Buddhist, Nyāya, and Mīmāṃsā objections.

summary: The Sarvatathāgatoṣṇīṣasitātapatrānāmāparājitāpratyaṅgirāmahāvidyārājñī is an influential Mahāyāna/Vajrayāna apotropaic dhāraṇī scripture centered on the goddess Sitātapatrā ('The White Parasol'). Set in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the narrative recounts how Śākyamuni Buddha enters meditative absorption (samādhi), from whose crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa) emanates this protective incantation. The text provides extensive salutations to buddhas, bodhisattvas, and brahmanical deities, followed by powerful averting and binding formulas (pratyaṅgirā) designed to protect practitioners against evil spirits, demonic afflictions, curses, diseases, and untimely death.

summary: The Revākhaṇḍa is a sacred geographical and pilgrimage text (tīrthamāhātmya) celebrating the holy sites along the course of the Narmadā (Revā) River in Central India. Structured largely around dialogues between the sage Mārkaṇḍeya and Yudhiṣṭhira, the work delineates the ritual circumambulation (parikramā) of both the northern and southern banks, detailing origin legends, shrines, and devotional benefits (phala). As shown by Jürgen Neuss, this 116-chapter recension is the genuine Skandapurāṇa Revākhaṇḍa, distinct from the 232-chapter text of the Vāyupurāṇa tradition mistakenly printed as SkP 5.3 in the Veṅkaṭeśvara edition.

summary: The Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra (commonly designated the Smaller or Shorter Sukhāvatīvyūha, and known in East Asian tradition as the Amitābhasūtra / Amituo jing) is a foundational Mahāyāna scripture of Pure Land Buddhism. Set in the Jeta Grove at Śrāvastī, Śākyamuni Buddha describes to Śāriputra the wondrous adornments and spiritual delights of Sukhāvatī, the western realm presided over by the Buddha Amitāyus. The sūtra proclaims that those who hear Amitāyus's name and maintain focused mindfulness on it will be reborn in Sukhāvatī, a message attested by the buddhas of all directions.

summary: The Śāktavijñāna is a brief 30-verse manual of esoteric Śaiva-Śākta yoga attributed to Somānanda. It expounds thirteen stages or modes (trayodaśavidha) of kuṇḍalinī practice taught across the Trika scriptures: locus (sthāna), penetration (praveśa), form (rūpa), contemplative focus (lakṣa), diagnostic signs (lakṣaṇa), elevation (utthāpana), awakening (bodhana), rest in the centers (cakraviśrāma), ascent through the levels (bhūmikāgamana), penultimate state (antāvasthā), supreme rest in Śiva (viśrāma), radical transformation (pariṇāma), and subsequent return (āgamana).

summary: The Kathāsaritsāgara ('Ocean of the Streams of Story') is an encyclopedic 11th-century Sanskrit narrative poem composed in Kashmir by Somadeva for Queen Sūryavatī. Arranged into 18 lambakas and 124 taraṅgas, it preserves a major Kashmiri verse recension of Guṇāḍhya's lost Paiśācī epic, the Bṛhatkathā. The central frame tale follows Prince Naravāhanadatta's romantic adventures and quest to attain sovereignty over the Vidyādharas, embedding numerous cycles of folk tales, fables, and romances, including the Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā.

summary: The Rasendracūḍāmaṇi ('Crest-Jewel of the Lord of Essences [Mercury]') is an influential medieval alchemical and iatrochemical treatise in sixteen chapters composed by Somadeva, generally dated to the 12th century CE. It systematically describes the layout and staffing of the alchemical laboratory (rasaśālā), technical apparatus (yantras), crucibles (mūṣās), furnaces (koṣṭhīs), pits (puṭas), as well as the pharmaceutical processing, purification, incineration, and digestion (jāraṇa) of mercury, metals, and minerals. Its descriptions and classification of sādhāraṇa-rasas served as a direct foundational source for subsequent compendia such as the 13th-century Rasaratnasamuccaya.

summary: The Stūpalakṣaṇakārikā is an architectural and ritual verse treatise composed by Bhadravyūha of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school, setting forth the canonical dimensions, proportions, and structural units of Buddhist stūpas alongside a systematic doctrinal mapping of its components onto Buddhist dharmas (such as the 37 bodhipakṣikadharmas, the four noble truths, and the elements). It is accompanied by the anonymous Stūpalakṣaṇakārikāvivecana, a detailed prose commentary that interprets each stanza with reference to the Lokottaravādin Prakīrṇakavinaya and related monastic traditions. Preserved in a single early Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript, the work constitutes one of the rare surviving Sanskrit treatises on non-Tantric Buddhist stūpa architecture and architectural symbolism.

summary: The Vāsavadattā of Subandhu (composed c. late 6th to early 7th century CE) is an ornate classical Sanskrit prose romance (kathā). The narrative recounts how Prince Kandarpaketu and Princess Vāsavadattā experience dreams of each other, seek each other out, elope, undergo separation after Vāsavadattā is petrified into stone by an ascetic's curse, and are reunited once the touch of Kandarpaketu restores her to life. The work is famed for its extreme rhetorical display, notably pervasive paronomasia (śleṣa) across almost every syllable and sentence, which served as a major stylistic predecessor to Bāṇabhaṭṭa's prose romances.

summary: The Subhāṣitaratnakaraṇḍakathā ('Casket of Well-Spoken Jewels Discourse') is a late Buddhist homiletic poem of 191 verses arranged into 27 short thematic sections (kathās). It offers didactic exhortations on the rarity of human rebirth, dharma hearing, various ritual offerings to the Three Jewels, merit-making (puṇya), and the practice of the six perfections (pāramitās). Although traditionally attributed to Āryaśūra, the work quotes or parallels stanzas from Śāntideva's Bodhicaryāvatāra and is recognized by modern scholarship as a late medieval compilation (ca. 8th–9th century CE).

summary: The Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha is the primary canonical scripture of the Mahāyāna Pure Land tradition focusing on the Buddha Amitābha (Amitāyus) and his western realm, Sukhāvatī. Delivered by Śākyamuni Buddha on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, the sūtra relates the ancient past-life story of the monk Dharmākara, who under the guidance of Lokeśvararāja took forty-six (forty-eight in Chinese tradition) great bodhisattva vows (praṇidhāna) to establish a supreme realm. The text depicts the wondrous topography, jewel-trees, assemblies, and spiritual benefits of Sukhāvatī, while specifying the criteria for rebirth therein—chiefly generating the aspiration for awakening (bodhicittotpāda), sincere faith, ethical observance, and mindful recollection of Amitābha.

summary: The Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūhasūtra (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā), widely revered in East Asia as the Amitābha Sūtra, is a foundational scripture of Pure Land Buddhism. Set in Śrāvastī, Śākyamuni Buddha describes the western Buddha-field Sukhāvatī and its presiding Buddha Amitāyus (Amitābha) to his disciple Śāriputra, portraying in sensory detail its jeweled pavilions, radiant lotus ponds, music, and divine birds that ceaselessly proclaim the Dharma. The sūtra teaches that living beings who hear Amitāyus's name and hold it single-mindedly without distraction will be welcomed by Amitābha at the point of death and reborn in his realm, a promise affirmed by the Buddhas of the six directions.

summary: The Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha is a foundational Mahāyāna sūtra and the principal scriptural authority for Pure Land Buddhism. Set on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) in Rājagṛha, the Buddha Śākyamuni narrates to Ānanda how the monk Dharmākara, in the presence of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, generated the resolve for awakening and made forty-eight great vows to establish the western realm of Sukhāvatī and become the Buddha Amitābha (Amitāyus). The sūtra expounds the visual and spiritual splendors of this paradise, delineates the requirements for rebirth there through faith, recollection, and merits, and includes instructions addressed to the bodhisattva Ajita (Maitreya) on dispelling doubt.

summary: The Sumāgadhāvadāna is an independent Buddhist narrative work (avadāna) in mixed prose and verse relating the story of Sumāgadhā, daughter of the prominent merchant and patron Anāthapiṇḍada of Śrāvastī. Married into the household of Vṛṣabhadatta in Puṇḍravardhana (Bengal), whose family reveres the Nirgranthas (Jains), she is repelled by the naked ascetics and miraculously summons the Buddha and his disciples from her roof. The aerial arrival and marvelous transformations of the Buddha and the arhats convert her husband's family and the entire city to Buddhism. The text concludes with karmic explanations by the Buddha, including Sumāgadhā's past lives and the ten prophetic dreams of King Kṛkin.

summary: The Suvarṇaprabhāsasūtra ('Sūtra of the Golden Light') is an influential Mahāyāna canonical scripture that synthesizes doctrinal expositions of emptiness (śūnyatā) and the boundless lifespan of the Tathāgata with rituals of repentance and state protection. A pivotal episode centers on the bodhisattva Ruciraketu's vision of a golden drum radiating stanzas on confession and purification (deśanā). Protective deities including the Four Heavenly Kings (Caturmahārāja), Sarasvatī, Śrī, and Dṛḍhā pledge to guard righteous sovereigns and realms that uphold the sūtra, while subsequent chapters recount past-life narratives of the Buddha, notably the Vyāghrīparivarta (Mahāsattva jātaka) where the bodhisattva sacrifices his life to feed a starving tigress and her cubs.

After spurning the advances of the corrupt chief minister's wife, Suvarṇavarṇa is falsely accused and condemned to death, but is saved through the miraculous spiritual intervention of the Elder Ānanda and eventually renounces worldly life. The narrative illustrates karmic retribution, refuge in the Buddha and Saṅgha, and moral discipline; it is preserved in an 11th-century palm-leaf manuscript discovered in Tibet and was subsequently adapted in chapter 11 of the Nepalese Vratāvadānamālā.

summary: The Suvikrāntavikrāmiparipṛcchā (also known as the Sārdhadvisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, or Perfection of Wisdom in 2,500 Lines) is a canonical Mahāyāna sūtra in seven chapters. Set at the Veṇuvana in Rājagṛha, it features an extensive dialogue between the Buddha and the Bodhisattva Suvikrāntavikrāmin detailing the nature and cultivation of prajñāpāramitā. The sūtra expounds the core doctrine of the non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) and lack of intrinsic existence (asvabhāvatva) of all dharmas, maintaining that true bodhisattva practice avoids attachment to conceptual markers or spiritual attainments.

summary: The Svacchandatantra is a major scriptural authority of the Mantramārga belonging to the Bhairavāgama tradition (specifically the Dakṣiṇasrotas or southern current), datable to roughly the 7th–8th century CE or earlier. Arranged in fifteen paṭalas, it treats deity visualization, mantra installation, initiation (dīkṣā), cosmography and the six pathways (ṣaḍadhvan), subtle breath-yoga, and funerary and expiatory rites centered on the multi-armed Svacchandabhairava and his consort Aghoreśvarī. summary: The Svalpākṣarā prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in Few Syllables') is a short scripture belonging to the late, tantric phase of the Prajñāpāramitā literature. summary: The Svayambhūpurāṇa is the foundational mythic chronicle and pilgrimage guide (sthala-māhātmya) of Newar Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley. The work incorporates visits of the previous Buddhas of antiquity, legends of local tīrthas, deities, and nāgas, and the transformation of the valley into a Buddhist kingdom. summary: The Tārāsragdharāstotra is a prominent 37-verse Buddhist hymn composed entirely in the 21-syllable sragdharā metre by the 8th-century Kashmiri poet-monk Sarvajñamitra. Highly celebrated across South Asian and Tibetan Buddhism, the hymn was preserved with Jinarakṣita's Sanskrit commentary and multiple Tibetan translations.

summary: The Taittirīyopaniṣad is a principal Upaniṣad of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, comprising three chapters: Śikṣāvallī, Brahmavallī (or Brahmānandavallī), and Bhṛguvallī. summary: The Tarkabhāṣā ('Language of Logic') is a concise introductory manual of Buddhist epistemology and logic composed by Mokṣākaragupta, a monk-scholar of the Jagaddala Mahāvihāra in northern Bengal dating to the late 11th or 12th century CE. Structured in three chapters according to the Dignāga-Dharmakīrti epistemology—perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna)—it explains valid knowledge, definition and fallacies of the logical reason (hetu/liṅga), syllogistic debate, and core Mahāyāna philosophical doctrines. The treatise is particularly valuable as one of the latest surviving Sanskrit textbooks of late Indian Buddhist logic, integrating the philosophical developments of Prajñākaragupta, Jñānaśrīmitra, and Ratnakīrti on internal pervasion (antarvyāpti), universal momentariness (kṣaṇikatva), Sākāravāda, and nominal exclusion (apoha).

Chapter 5 begins 'anumānaṃ dvidhā — svārthaṃ, parārthaṃ ca' (Sh p. 75) and breaks off in the discussion of relation (sambandha, quoting Dharmakīrti's Sambandhaparīkṣā) with the editor's note '[itaḥ paraṃ mūlapustakaṃ nopalabhyate]'. summary: The Tarkarahasya ('Secret of Logic/Reasoning') is a late Indian Buddhist philosophical treatise and epistemological manual belonging to the Dignāga–Dharmakīrti school, preserved in a single Proto-Maithili/Proto-Bengali palm-leaf manuscript photographed by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana in Ngor monastery, Tibet. In five topical chapters, the text presents the definitions and number of valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), perception (pratyakṣa) and its subdivisions, epistemic objects, and inference and relations (examining Dharmakīrti's Sambandhaparīkṣā), while systematically refuting rival non-Buddhist views (Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Cārvāka). While its author remains unknown due to the lost manuscript conclusion and colophon, references to Dharmottara and Prajñākaragupta date the work to roughly the 10th or 11th century CE.

summary: The Tarkaśāstra (preserved in Chinese translation as the Rushi lun 如實論, Taishō 1633, translated by Paramārtha in 550 CE) is a major Buddhist treatise on debate and dialectics (vāda) representing the pre-Dignāga stage of Indian logic. It consists of three chapters: the first treats dialectical exchanges, valid proof, and the refutation of rival objections; the second provides a systematic classification and critique of sixteen futile rejoinders (jāti); and the third analyzes twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna). Because the Indic original is lost, the text survives in Sanskrit solely through Giuseppe Tucci's 1929 back-translation, which illustrates the historical evolution of the five-membered syllogism prior to Dignāga's reforms.

Structuring its inquiry around the classical framework of the Sāṃkhyakārikā, the work opens by establishing the necessity of philosophical inquiry due to the threefold misery (duḥkhatraya) and refuting both mundane and ritualistic Vedic remedies. It methodically expounds the twenty-five principles (tattvas) divided into primordial source (mūlaprakṛti), evolutes that produce further principles, mere modifications, and the transcendent conscious self (puruṣa), concluding with an exposition of the eight fundamental dispositions (bhāvas) and liberation through discriminative insight ('nāsmi na me nāham').

summary: The Tattvasamāsa ('Compendium of Principles') is a very brief mnemonic outline consisting of between 23 and 27 aphorisms (sūtras) that summarize the central ontological, cosmological, and psychological categories of classical Sāṃkhya philosophy. It lists the fundamental categories including the eight material causes (prakṛti), the sixteen evolutes (vikāra), the conscious subject (puruṣa), the three constituents (guṇa), cosmic evolution and dissolution, and the faculties and conditions governing bondage and release. Traditionally attributed to the mythic sage Kapila, the surviving text represents a medieval scholastic syllabus that served as the basis for several commentaries, such as those by Kṣemānanda, Bhāvāgaṇeśa, and the author of the Kramadīpikā.

summary: The Tattvasamāsasūtravṛtti (known from its closing verse as the Kramadīpikā) is an anonymous prose commentary on the Tattvasamāsa, a concise compendium of twenty-three sūtras setting forth the classical Sāṃkhya doctrinal topics. Framed as a dialogue in which the sage Kapila instructs a suffering brāhmaṇa, the commentary sequentially expounds the twenty-five principles (tattva), cosmic evolution and devolution, sources of action, types of bondage, and means of liberation. Composed in the postclassical period (conventionally dated to around the 14th century CE), it preserves archaic doctrinal rubrics and was one of the earliest Sāṃkhya texts introduced to modern European scholarship through the pioneering editions and translations of James R. Ballantyne and Max Müller.

summary: The Toḍalatantra is a concise Śākta scripture in ten chapters (paṭalas) preserved chiefly in eastern India. It expounds subtle yogic anatomy, microcosm-macrocosm homologies, and the pūjā, mantras, and iconography of Kālī, Tārā, and the Mahāvidyās along with their male Bhairava consorts. In its tenth chapter, it presents a well-known synthesis equating each of the ten Mahāvidyās with one of Viṣṇu's ten avatāras (such as Kālī with Kṛṣṇa and Tārā with the fish incarnation).

Its title refers to three key ritual actions: confession of moral faults (pāpadeśanā), rejoicing in merits (anumodanā), and the dedication of merit toward supreme awakening (pariṇāmanā). While it circulates independently as a ritual text across Nepal and Tibet, the liturgy also constitutes the central confession pericope embedded within the Mahāyāna Vinayaviniścaya-Upāliparipṛcchāsūtra.

summary: The Udānavarga is a canonical northern Buddhist anthology of aphoristic stanzas (udāna) arranged topically across 33 chapters (vargas), primarily preserved in the Sarvāstivāda and Mūlasarvāstivāda traditions. Functioning as the Sanskrit counterpart to the Pāli Dhammapada, the Pāli Udāna, and the Gāndhārī Dharmapada, it shares an ancient core of stanzas while expanding the collection to over a thousand verses. Preserved in Sanskrit manuscripts from Central Asian oasis sites along the Northern and Southern Silk Roads as well as in Tibetan and Chinese translations, it is a crucial witness to early Buddhist verse anthologies and sectarian transmission.

summary: The Pādatāḍitaka ('The Kick') by the late Gupta-era poet Śyāmilaka is the longest and most celebrated of the four satirical monologue plays preserved in the Caturbhāṇī. Spoken entirely by a viṭa (cosmopolitan man-about-town), the play recounts his journey through the streets of Sārvabhaumanagara (Ujjayinī) to convene a council of rogues to prescribe a comedic expiation (prāyaścitta) for a high-caste gentleman kicked on the head by a courtesan during a lovers' quarrel. Rich in social satire, vivid urban character sketches, and linguistic wit, it provides unparalleled insight into late classical Indian courtly and demi-monde life.

summary: The Nyāyavārttikatātparyapariśuddhi (also known as Nyāyanibandha) is Udayana's (c. 10th–11th century CE) sub-commentary on Vācaspati Miśra's Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, constituting the final tier of the classical fourfold commentarial corpus (Nyāyacaturgranthikā) on Gautama's Nyāyasūtra. This opening section (Adhyāya 1, Āhnika 1) examines the definition and nature of the sixteen Nyāya categories (padārtha), beginning with the instruments of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), the knowables (prameya), and the prerequisites of philosophical debate through final ascertainment (nirṇaya). Udayana vigorously defends Nyāya realism, epistemology, and natural theology against contemporary Buddhist epistemological and anti-realist objections.

summary: The Kāvyālaṃkārasārasaṃgraha ('Compendium of the Essence of Poetic Ornaments') by the Kashmiri rhetorician Udbhaṭa (fl. c. late 8th – early 9th century CE) is a major foundational treatise of Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra). In six chapters (vargas), it defines, illustrates, and classifies forty-one poetic figures of sound and sense, modifying Bhāmaha's schema and introducing new categories such as punaruktavadābhāsa, kāvyahetu, and kāvyadṛṣṭānta. The accompanying Laghuvṛtti by Pratīhārendurāja (fl. mid-10th century CE) is the earliest surviving commentary on the work, providing valuable syntactic analysis, philosophical contextualization (integrating Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya tenets), and critical discussion of the emerging dhvani doctrine.

summary: The Kokilasandeśa ('Message of the Cuckoo') is a 15th-century Sanskrit messenger poem (sandeśakāvya) composed by Uddaṇḍa Śāstrī in 162 Mandākrāntā verses, modelled upon Kālidāsa's Meghadūta. Separated from his beloved and magically transported to Kāñcīpuram, a hero entrusts a koel bird with delivering a message of love to his partner in Jayantamaṅgalam (Cennamaṅgalam) in Kerala. In charting the bird's flight path across southwestern India, the work provides rich topographical, religious, and socio-cultural depictions of medieval Kerala's towns, temples, and coastal society.

summary: The Upāyahṛdaya (preserved only in the 472 CE Chinese translation Fangbian xin lun 方便心論, T 1632, and represented in Sanskrit by Giuseppe Tucci's 1929 retroversion) is an early Buddhist handbook of disputation and dialectics dating to approximately the 3rd to 4th century CE. Composed in four chapters, the manual treats the justification and eight fundamental constituents of debate (including the four pramāṇas, examples, and fallacies), occasions of dialectical defeat (nigrahasthāna), exemplary orthodox debate exchanges, and twenty classes of counter-objections (jāti). It provides a valuable pre-Dignāga witness to the development of early Indian debate theory and epistemology parallel to the Carakasaṃhitā and the Nyāyasūtra.

summary: The Upasaṃpadājñapti is a liturgical legal formulary (karmavācanā) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya governing entry into the Buddhist monastic order. It sets out the motions (jñapti) and acts (karman) for the taking of lay vows (upāsakasaṃvara), the going forth from the household life (pravrajyā / novice ordination), and the higher monastic ordination (upasaṃpadā). The text details the formal examination of the candidate for disqualifying impediments (antarāyikā dharmāḥ), the request for preceptor and teachers, the unanimous declaration of the assembled saṅgha, and the subsequent instructions on fundamental monastic rules.

summary: The Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā along with its auto-commentary (vṛtti) by Utpaladeva constitutes the foundational philosophical treatise of the Pratyabhijñā ('Recognition') system of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism. Structured into four sections (adhikāras on knowledge, action, scriptural authority, and a summary of tattvas), the work argues dialectically against Buddhist epistemologists and other rivals to establish that all reality and individual consciousness are identical with the autonomous, self-luminous Lord (Maheśvara / Śiva), and that liberation consists in the explicit recognition of this identity.

summary: The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi ('Proof of a Conscious Knower') is one of three short treatises comprising Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayī, written in the first half of the 10th century to establish the foundational tenets of non-dual Pratyabhijñā philosophy. In 27 kārikās, Utpaladeva argues against Buddhist momentariness and static Vedāntic consciousness, maintaining that both cognition and practical causal efficacy (arthakriyā) require an active, self-reflective subject (vimarśa, ahaṃbhāva) rather than an insentient (jaḍa) continuum. In this edition, the lost original auto-commentary is replaced by a concise modern Sanskrit Vṛtti composed in 1919 CE by Kashmiri scholar Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī.

summary: The Śivastotrāvalī is a collection of twenty devotional hymns composed by the Kashmir Śaiva master and philosopher Utpaladeva (fl. c. 900–950 CE), pupil of Somānanda and formulator of the Pratyabhijñā school. Preserved and organized into twenty stotras by his disciples, the verses synthesize non-dual recognition philosophy with ecstatic bhakti and yearning for complete absorption in Śiva-consciousness. It remains one of the preeminent classics of Kashmiri Śaiva devotional literature.

summary: The Bhāmatī by Vācaspatimiśra (fl. 9th–10th century CE) is an authoritative Advaita Vedānta sub-commentary (ṭīkā) on Śaṅkara's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya and the foundational text of the Bhāmatī school (contrasted with Prakāśātman's Vivaraṇa school). Synthesizing Śaṅkara's hermeneutics with insights from Maṇḍana Miśra's Brahmasiddhi, Vācaspati articulates classic doctrinal positions, notably that the individual self (jīva) is the locus (āśraya) of beginningless nescience (avidyā) while Brahman is its object (viṣaya), and that meditative contemplation (dhyāna/upāsanā) mediated by a purified internal organ (manas) serves as the proximate cause of liberating intuition. The text spans the entirety of the Brahmasūtras and generated an influential sub-commentarial lineage, prominent among which are Amalānanda's Kalpataru and Appayya Dīkṣita's Parimala.

summary: The Mānamanohara of Vādivāgīśvara (ca. 11th–12th century CE) is an independent, dialectically sophisticated treatise of the Vaiśeṣika school. Setting out to vanquish rival disputants, the work systematically presents and defends Vaiśeṣika ontology and epistemology, featuring rigorous proofs for the existence of God (īśvarasiddhi), the composite whole (avayavisiddhi), indivisible atoms (paramāṇusiddhi), and the self (ātman), while defending the classic category doctrine against Buddhist, Mīmāṃsā, and Advaita Vedānta objections. The treatise was an influential reference point in late medieval philosophical debates and is cited by authors such as Citsukha, Śaśadhara, and Vedāntadeśika.

summary: The Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa ('Instruction on Cheating Death') by the late 10th- to early 11th-century Indian master Vāgīśvarakīrti is an influential Vajrayāna manual on diagnosing and averting untimely death. summary: The Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā is one of the three foundational classics of classical Ayurveda (the bṛhattrayī), composed in metrical verse by Vāgbhaṭa (ca. 7th century CE). summary: The Rasaratnasamuccaya is a seminal compendium of Indian alchemy (rasaśāstra) and iatrochemistry composed around the late 13th to early 14th century CE by Rasa-Vāgbhaṭa. Drawing extensively on earlier tantric and metallurgical authorities, it systematizes the purification (śodhana), incineration (māraṇa), and therapeutic compounding of mercury (pārada), mineral categories (mahārasa, uparasa, sādhāraṇarasa), gems, and metals, as well as describing laboratory design, apparatuses (yantra), crucibles (mūṣā), and fire pits (puṭa). This e-text contains chapters 1 through 18.29ab accompanied by the late modern Sanskrit commentary Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī and accompanying glosses.

summary: The Aṣṭāṅganighaṇṭu is an Ayurvedic medical lexicon (nighaṇṭu) in 408 verses attributed to Vāhaṭa. The first part glosses synonyms and therapeutic actions of the drug groups (gaṇas) taught in Vāgbhaṭa's classical treatises (primarily the Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha), while the second part (viprakīrṇa) inventories medicinal plants, foodstuffs, poisons, minerals, and general clinical terminology. It is historically notable as the earliest extant medical text to mention kumārī (Aloe vera), and it served as a recognized authority cited by medieval commentators including Indu, Aruṇadatta, and Hemādri.

summary: The Ayodhyākāṇḍa (Book 2) and Āraṇyakāṇḍa (Book 3) form the central narrative axis of the Rāmāyaṇa. In Book 2, Queen Kaikeyī's demands force King Daśaratha to abort Rāma's royal consecration and send him into fourteen-year exile with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa; Daśaratha dies of grief, and Bharata rejects the throne, governing from Nandigrāma with Rāma's wooden sandals on the seat of state. Book 3 recounts the trio's life in the Daṇḍaka forest, the mutilation of Śūrpaṇakhā and subsequent slaughter of the rākṣasa armies under Khara and Dūṣaṇa, the lure of the golden deer (Mārīca), the abduction of Sītā by Rāvaṇa, and Rāma's despairing trek toward Lake Pampā.

summary: The Ayodhyākāṇḍa forms the second book of Vālmīki's Rāmāyaṇa and depicts the succession crisis in Ayodhyā. Following Daśaratha's plan to crown Rāma as yuvarāja, Queen Kaikeyī, goaded by Mantharā, demands two boons: the exile of Rāma to the forest for fourteen years and the installation of Bharata as king. Rāma unhesitatingly departs with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, which precipitates Daśaratha's demise from grief; Bharata adamantly refuses the throne, follows Rāma to Citrakūṭa to plead for his return, and ultimately agrees to govern from Nandigrāma as regent for Rāma's wooden sandals (pādukā).

summary: The Janmamaraṇavicāra ('Investigation into Life and Death') is a short Kashmiri non-dual Śaiva philosophical treatise in mixed prose and verse by Bhaṭṭa Vāmadeva (fl. c. late 11th–early 12th century CE). Rooted in the Trika and Pratyabhijñā traditions, the work examines the cycle of transmigration, embryological development, and bodily death, interpreting empirical birth and dissolution as the contraction and expansion of autonomous supreme consciousness (Maheśvara). The treatise is notable for combining Kashmiri Śaiva metaphysics with Āyurvedic medical doctrine (such as the Suśrutasaṃhitā) and citations of lost Śaiva āgamas.

summary: The Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra is a foundational treatise of Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra) composed by the Kashmiri aesthetician Vāmana (fl. c. 800 CE). It is celebrated as the quintessential exposition of the Rīti school, formulating the influential doctrine that style/diction is the soul of poetry ('rītir ātmā kāvyasya'). Divided into five adhikaraṇas (Śārīra, Doṣadarśana, Guṇavivecana, Ālaṅkārika, and Prāyogika), it systematically details the definition and purpose of poetry, poetic defects (doṣas), the ten verbal and cognitive excellences (guṇas), rhetorical tropes (alaṅkāras), and rules for literary grammatical correctness. In this e-text, only the sūtrapāṭha (the aphoristic sūtras without the prose auto-commentary) is preserved.
