summary: The Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra along with its auto-commentary (Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti or Kavipriyā) by Vāmana (fl. late 8th to early 9th century CE, Kashmir) constitutes the defining work of the Rīti school of classical Sanskrit poetics [3-4]. Vāmana formulated the famous thesis that style (rīti) is the soul of poetry ('rītir ātmā kāvyasya', 1.2.6), distinguishing three primary styles (Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, and Pāñcālī) based on the presence of specific poetic qualities (guṇas) [63, 72]. Organised into five adhikaraṇas (Śārīra, Doṣadarśana, Guṇavivecana, Ālaṅkārika, and Prāyogika), the work presents a comprehensive taxonomy of poetic purpose, flaws (doṣas), aesthetic qualities (ten verbal and ten semantic guṇas), figures of speech (alaṅkāras), and rules for grammatical purity in poetry (śabdaśuddhi) [34, 295, 1080, 2265-2267].

summary: The Svabodhodayamañjarī ('Inflorescence of the Arising of Innate Awareness') is a short Kashmiri Śaiva contemplative tract of 45 verses composed by Vāmanadatta, son of Harṣadatta, around the mid-10th century. Closely resonant with the practical, anti-ritualist spirit of the Vijñānabhairavatantra, it presents methods for the effortless dissolution of conceptual thought (nirodha, vilaya) through ordinary perceptual and bodily experiences—such as eating, running, falling asleep, or attending to fading sounds and pleasant smells. Verses from the treatise are cited by Bhagavadutpala in the Spandapradīpikā and later Kashmiri commentators.

summary: The Vāmanapurāṇa is one of the eighteen traditional Mahāpurāṇas, nominally named after Viṣṇu's dwarf avatāra who subdues Bali. Despite its formal classification as a Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa, the majority of its narrative content is eclectic, with substantial sections devoted to Śaiva and Śākta mythology, including the myths of Satī and Pārvatī, Śiva's penance, the birth of Kārttikeya, and the goddess's battles with Mahiṣāsura and Andhaka. It also contains detailed sacred geography and pilgrim itineraries (māhātmya), focusing heavily on Kurukṣetra, Sthāṇutīrtha, and Prayāga. Modern scholars assign the compilation of the surviving recension to between the 9th and 11th centuries CE.

summary: The Saromāhātmya is a 27-chapter pilgrimage manual (tīrthamāhātmya) preserved as an insertion or appendix to the Vāmanapurāṇa (placed between chapters 23 and 24 in the All-India Kashiraj Trust critical edition). Framed as a discourse delivered by the bard Lomaharṣaṇa to the ṛṣis assembled in Kurujāṅgala, it provides an elaborate eulogy of Kurukṣetra and its sacred lakes, notably Brahmasaras (identified with Rāmahrada and Samantapañcaka) and Sannihita-saras, alongside sacred sites along the Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī rivers. The text blends pilgrimage itineraries with local mythology, celebrating Sthāṇutīrtha and recounting both Vaiṣṇava legends (the Vāmana avatāra) and Śaiva myths.

Across 17 khaṇḍas, it prescribes the full domestic ritual cycle, including the basic pākayajña setup, saṃskāras (such as upanayana, cūḍākaraṇa, and vivāha), śrāddha offerings, and domestic expiations (prāyaścittas). It shares close textual, liturgical, and terminological parallels with the Mānavagṛhyasūtra and Kāṭhakagṛhyasūtra of the broader Caraka-Yajurvedic ritual group.

summary: The Vāsiṣṭhadharmasūtra is one of the four surviving classical Dharmasūtras, composed in a mixture of aphoristic prose sūtras and metrical stanzas. It covers the sources of dharma, duties of the four classes (varṇa) and life stages (āśrama), marriage and women's status, impurity and purification, dietary laws, civil and criminal law, inheritance, penances (prāyaścitta), and royal governance. Considered historically to be relatively late among the canonical Dharmasūtras (c. 300–100 BCE), it quotes earlier authorities extensively and shares significant verse material with the Manusmṛti.

summary: The Kāmasūtra of Vātsyāyana (composed c. 3rd–4th century CE) is the foundational Sanskrit treatise on kāma (erotic desire, pleasure, and aesthetic enjoyment), one of the four traditional goals of human life (puruṣārtha). Divided into seven adhikaraṇas, the text surveys general principles of life, sexual union, courtship and marriage, the domestic conduct of wives, extramarital affairs, courtesans, and erotic/aphrodisiac recipes. Beyond physical intimacy, the work presents a detailed manual on urban sociology and the cultured lifestyle of the sophisticated citizen (nāgaraka), serving as the canonical source for all subsequent Indian erotic literature.

summary: The Kāmasūtra of Vātsyāyana (c. 3rd–4th century CE) is the foundational Sanskrit treatise on kāmaśāstra, systematically treating the pursuit of pleasure, courtship, love, and aesthetic refinement within the classical trivarga framework. Formally modeled on the scholastic prose structure of Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra, its seven books (adhikaraṇas) cover general principles of life, sexual technique, marriage, the duties of a wife, extramarital relations, the life and profession of courtesans, and esoteric erotic recipes. It provides an indispensable documentary view of urban culture (nāgaraka-vṛtta), gender relations, and material life in ancient and classical India.

summary: The Vīṇāśikhatantra is an early Śaiva tantra (c. 6th–8th century CE) and the sole surviving primary scripture of the Vāmasrotas ('Left Current') branch of the Mantramārga. It centers on the esoteric cult of Tumburu (a four-faced form of Śiva) and his four surrounding sister goddesses (Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā), detailing their maṇḍalas, mantra encodings (including early alphabet grids), initiation rituals (dīkṣā), and sādhanā procedures. The work is historically renowned as one of the four Vāma scriptures (along with the Śiraścheda, Sammohana, and Nayottara) cited in the 1052 CE Sdok Kak Thom inscription of Cambodia.

summary: The Vaikhānasadharmasūtra constitutes the dharmasūtra portion (Praśnas 8–10) of the Vaikhānasasmārtasūtra, belonging to the Taittirīya recension of the Black Yajurveda. Across three praśnas, the work details the duties and occupations of the four social classes (varṇas) and life-stages (āśramas), providing classical Sanskrit literature's most elaborate typology of hermits (vānaprasthas/vaikhānasas) and ascetics (bhikṣus). summary: The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Diamond-Cutter Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra'), commonly known as the Diamond Sūtra or Triśatikā ('Three Hundred Lines'), is one of the most celebrated and influential scriptures in Mahāyāna Buddhism. Structured as a dialogue between the Buddha and the venerable Subhūti in the Jetavana grove at Śrāvastī, it systematically dismantles attachment to conceptual signs and ontological categories, teaching that bodhisattvas must practice generosity and cultivate supreme enlightenment without abiding in notions of self, living being, or dharma. The text is renowned for its characteristic dialectical formula asserting that a dharma is designated as such precisely because it is empty of intrinsic existence. First translated into Chinese by Kumārajīva in 401/402 CE, the sūtra became a cornerstone of East Asian Buddhist traditions—particularly Chan/Zen—and is celebrated for the 868 CE Dunhuang woodblock scroll, the world's earliest dated complete printed book.

summary: The Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī is an influential Buddhist apotropaic and purificatory dhāraṇī scripture classified under Kriyātantra. In its narrative framework, the Buddha enters an adamantine absorption and inspires the yakṣa lord Vajrapāṇi to proclaim an unbreakable vajra incantation designed to dispel malignant spirits, afflictions, and karmic impediments. The text concludes with instructional verses detailing an ablution (snāna) ritual using a consecrated vase to purify pollutants, pacify planetary obstacles, and promote longevity.

summary: The Vajravidāraṇīdhāraṇī (also known as Vajravidāraṇādhāraṇī) is an apotropaic and purificatory dhāraṇī sūtra delivered by Vajrapāṇi through the spiritual power (anubhāva) of the Buddha. The scripture contains the root dhāraṇī along with heart (hṛdaya) and secondary heart (upahṛdaya) mantras intended to subdue harmful entities (grahas, bhūtas), neutralize sorcery, and clear karmic obscurations. It holds a major place in Indo-Tibetan Vajrayāna ritual as a primary text for ablution and purification (khrus chog) and is frequently included in Nepalese protective anthologies such as the Saptavāra.

summary: The Bṛhajjātaka (also known as Horāśāstra) by the 6th-century CE polymath Varāhamihira is the classical Sanskrit foundational treatise on natal astrology (horā / jātaka). Structured in 28 chapters in metrical verse, the text systematically synthesizes Greco-Babylonian planetary and zodiacal concepts with traditional Indian divination, covering planetary dignities, conception, congenital marks, planetary periods (daśā), and life-span calculations.

summary: The Bṛhatsaṃhitā ('Great Compendium') of Varāhamihira (ca. 6th century CE) is the fundamental classic of the saṃhitā (natural omen, divination, and mundane astrology) branch of Indian jyotiṣa. Arranged into 106 chapters and comprising nearly 4,000 stanzas, it serves as an encyclopaedia of classical Indian material and ritual life, treating topics such as planetary movements, eclipses, meteorology, ground water and rainfall, temple and residential architecture (vāstuvidyā), iconometry (pratimālakṣaṇa), gemmology (ratnaparīkṣā), perfumery (gandhayukti), agriculture, and physiognomy. It is an indispensable primary source for the history of science, material culture, and religious society in Gupta-era India.

summary: The Varṣāvastu ('Chapter on the Rains Retreat') is the fourth chapter of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, regulating the mandatory three-month monastic retreat (varṣā or varṣāvāsa) observed during the monsoon. It sets out the formal legal procedures (saṃghakarman) for entering the retreat, the election and duties of the assigner of dwelling places (śayanāsanagrāhaka), the distribution of rooms and seats by casting voting markers or tallies (śalākā), communal regulations during the retreat, and the precise conditions under which a monk may temporarily cross the monastic boundary (sīmā) for up to seven days. Preserved in Sanskrit in the Gilgit manuscripts as well as in Tibetan (Toh 1) and Chinese (T 1445) translations, it closely corresponds to the Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka of the Theravāda Pali Vinaya.

summary: The Laghusiddhāntakaumudī is an essential introductory primer of Pāṇinian Sanskrit grammar composed by Varadarāja in the seventeenth century. It condenses the comprehensive Siddhāntakaumudī of his teacher Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita into 1,279 select sūtras from Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, reorganized according to a topical, derivation-focused order (prakriyā) rather than the sequential order of the eight adhyāyas. Accompanied by Varadarāja's concise explanatory commentary (vṛtti) and standard grammatical derivations, the work has served for centuries as the primary pedagogical manual in traditional pāṭhaśālās and modern academic institutions.

summary: The Śatagāthā ('Hundred Verses', also known as the Gāthāśataka) is a Buddhist gnomic anthology (nītiśāstra) traditionally ascribed to Ācārya Vararuci. Preserved in the Tanjur (Toh 4332 / D 4332), where it was translated into Tibetan by Vinayacandra and Dharmaprajña (Chos kyi shes rab), the work gathers 107 didactic maxims on worldly wisdom, ethical conduct, true friendship, virtue, and impermanence. The Sanskrit text in this e-text is modern scholar Losang Norbu Shastri's reconstruction from the Tibetan text, collated against classical Sanskrit gnomic parallels.

summary: The Abhidharmakośakārikā consists of approximately six hundred verses in eight chapters composed by Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE), synthesizing the doctrinal system of the Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika school of Abhidharma. The text classifies all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena across eight subjects: ultimate constituents (dhātu), sensory and psychological faculties (indriya), cosmological realms (loka), intentional action (karma), underlying afflictions (anuśaya), noble spiritual paths and attainers (mārgapudgala), transcendent cognitions (jñāna), and meditative absorptions (samāpatti). Designed for memorization, it served as the baseline verse manual upon which Vasubandhu constructed his famous auto-commentary (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya) offering critical Sautrāntika critiques of Vaibhāṣika tenets, and it remains the fundamental Abhidharma textbook throughout East Asian and Tibetan Buddhism.

summary: The Abhidharmakośabhāṣya is Vasubandhu's (c. 4th–5th century CE) prose auto-commentary on his metrical Abhidharmakośakārikā, standing as the foundational masterwork of Buddhist Abhidharma scholasticism. Across eight chapters, the work details the constituents of reality (dhātu), sensory and spiritual faculties (indriya), cosmology and rebirth (loka), action and its fruits (karma), latent defilements (anuśaya), the path and spiritual attainments (mārga and pudgala), direct knowledges (jñāna), and meditative absorptions (samāpatti). Vasubandhu articulates the Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika system while frequently subjecting it to trenchant Sautrāntika critiques, concluding with an appended ninth chapter that refutes both the Buddhist Pudgalavādin thesis of an inexpressible person and Brahmanical theories of a permanent self (ātman).

summary: The Madhyāntavibhāga ('Distinguishing the Middle from the Extremes') is a short Yogācāra verse treatise in five chapters, here transmitted with Vasubandhu's prose bhāṣya. It treats the characteristics of unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) and emptiness, the three natures, the obscurations (āvaraṇa), reality (tattva), the cultivation of the antidotes with its stages and results, and the supremacy of the Great Vehicle, presented as a middle way between reification and denial. The Sanskrit text survives in a single manuscript discovered in Tibet; Sthiramati's ṭīkā comments on both kārikās and bhāṣya.

summary: The Pañcaskandhaprakaraṇa (or Pañcaskandhaka) is an introductory Abhidharma manual composed by Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE) that presents a systematic categorization of mental and physical phenomena according to the Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda framework. It defines the components of existence categorized under the five aggregates (skandhas), twelve sense fields (āyatanas), and eighteen elements (dhātus), famously incorporating the specifically Yogācāra doctrines of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and afflicted mentality (kliṣṭamanas) alongside the standard catalogue of fifty-one mental factors (caittas). This specific electronic text represents the 1955/1956 Sanskrit retro-translation from Tibetan executed by Shanti Bhikshu Shastri, which historically served as the primary Sanskrit surrogate for the work prior to the rediscovery and 2008 publication of the original Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscript from the Potala Palace.

summary: Vasubandhu's Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā ('Thirty Verses on Representation-Only') is a foundational work of Yogācāra/Vijñānavāda Buddhist philosophy outlining the three transformations of consciousness (ālayavijñāna, kliṣṭamanas, and pravṛttivijñāna), the three intrinsic natures (trisvabhāva), and the realization of cognition-only (vijñaptimātratā). Sthiramati's Triṃśikāvijñaptibhāṣya (c. 6th century CE) is the sole surviving Sanskrit commentary on the text preserved in the original language. It systematically expounds Yogācāra psychology, the nature of mental factors (caitta), the role of metaphorical designation (upacāra) in establishing consciousness-only without external objects, and the soteriological progression toward fundamental transformation (āśrayaparāvṛtti).

summary: The Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā (Thirty Verses on Representation-Only) by Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE) is a foundational treatise of Yogācāra Buddhism. In thirty concise kārikās, it expounds the threefold transformation of consciousness (vijñānapariṇāma)—the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the afflicted mentation (manas), and the six object-cognizing consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna)—alongside the doctrine of the three natures (trisvabhāva). The work outlines the path to realizing mere representation (vijñaptimātratā), culminating in the transformation of the psycho-physical base (āśrayaparāvṛtti) and liberation.

summary: The Trisvabhāvanirdeśa ('Exposition of the Three Natures') is a concise verse work of 38 kārikās by Vasubandhu presenting the classical Yogācāra doctrine of the three natures: the imagined (parikalpita), dependent (paratantra), and consummate (pariniṣpanna). Using the simile of a magician conjuring an elephant from a piece of wood, Vasubandhu demonstrates how subject-object duality is an unreal mental construction upon causally dependent mental processes, and how liberation entails the cessation of this duality and the realization of non-dual reality (dharmadhātu).

summary: The Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi with its autocommentary (Viṃśatikāvṛtti) is Vasubandhu's foundational defense of the Yogācāra doctrine that reality is cognition-only (vijñaptimātra) and devoid of external, mind-independent physical objects. The text systematically counters realist objections regarding spatiotemporal coordination, collective experience, and causal efficacy through analogies to dreams, collective torment in hell, and shared karmic fruition. It is especially famous for stanzas 11–15, which formulate a decisive refutation of atomism by demonstrating that physical atoms can neither possess parts nor be partless without rendering composite macroscopic extension conceptually impossible.

summary: The Vasudhārādhāraṇī is a widely recited Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra centered on Vasudhārā, the goddess of wealth and grain. In the Kauśāmbī setting, the Buddha instructs the impoverished householder Sucandra on the protective incantation and ritual practices revealed by the ancient tathāgata Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa to overcome poverty and dispel harm. This e-text preserves a unique recension copied in 1638 CE (Vikrama Saṃvat 1695) in Gujarat, documenting the cross-sectarian adoption and ritual use of the Buddhist prosperity spell by Jaina communities.

summary: The Vasudhārādhāraṇī is a Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture framed by a narrative setting in Kauśāmbī. The impoverished householder Sucandra approaches the Buddha to ask how one may obtain abundant wealth, grain, and prosperity in order to provide for a large family and sustain extensive charitable offerings. In reply, the Buddha imparts the Vasudhārā dhāraṇī received from the past Tathāgata Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa, detailing its ritual practice, protective benefits, and power to produce torrential rains of grain and precious treasures.

summary: The Vasudhārādhāraṇīsūtra is a canonical Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture set at Kauśāmbī, where the impoverished householder Sucandra asks Gautama Buddha how impoverished and ailing sentient beings may attain wealth, health, and relief from suffering. In response, the Buddha reveals the dhāraṇī, ritual procedures (kalpa), and recitation rules associated with the goddess of abundance, Vasudhārā, which he originally received in a previous aeon from the Buddha Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa. Emphasizing that material prosperity must be accompanied by ethical discipline and charitable giving (dāna), the scripture attained widespread popularity across South and Central Asia and continues to play a prominent role in Newar Buddhist ritual culture.

attribution_note: Authorship of the root verses (Spandakārikā) is traditionally debated: Kṣemarāja, Utpala Vaiṣṇava, and later Trika authors attribute them to Vasugupta (the receiver of the Śivasūtra), whereas earlier commentators such as Rāmakaṇṭha and Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara, as well as Abhinavagupta in certain contexts, attribute them to Vasugupta's pupil Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. The commentary Spandanirṇaya is securely attributed to Kṣemarāja (c. first half of the 11th century CE), pupil of Abhinavagupta.

summary: The Spandakārikā is a seminal verse treatise of the Spanda school of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, expounding spanda—the dynamic, unceasing pulsation of supreme consciousness (Śiva/Śakti) that underlies all cosmic manifestation, maintenance, and dissolution. Composed across four sections (niḥṣyandas), the verses present a contemplative methodology for yogic practitioners to recognize this vibrating consciousness within all sensory, cognitive, and affective states, leading to liberation in this life (jīvanmukti). This e-text provides the complete text of the kārikās together with the Spandanirṇaya, the influential eleventh-century commentary by Abhinavagupta's disciple Kṣemarāja, which systematically interprets the work through the synthetic theological framework of Trika and Pratyabhijñā.

attribution_note: Authorship has been disputed since the early medieval period. Kṣemarāja (in his Spandanirṇaya and Spandasaṃdoha) and Utpalavaiṣṇava (in his Spandapradīpikā) attribute the verses to Vasugupta, characterizing them as a concise versified exposition of the Śivasūtras revealed to him. In contrast, Utpaladeva (in his Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī), Abhinavagupta (in the Tantrāloka), and Rāmakaṇṭha (in his Spandavivṛti) explicitly attribute the Kārikās to Vasugupta's pupil Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. Modern scholars (e.g. Alexis Sanderson, Mark Dyczkowski) generally conclude that Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa was the author or formal systematizer of the verses based on Vasugupta's oral instruction.

summary: The Spandakārikā is the primary doctrinal and meditative manual of the Spanda branch of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, composed in the 9th century CE and attributed either to the sage Vasugupta or his disciple Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. Across approximately 53 verses, the text expounds the principle of spanda—the dynamic, unceasing pulse and creative vibration of absolute Consciousness (Śiva-Śakti) that constitutes the true nature of both macrocosmic manifestation and microcosmic cognitive awareness. Rather than prescribing the complete suppression of mental and sensory operations, the text teaches that by sustained introspective mindfulness of the subtle throb underlying emotions, sense-perceptions, and transitions between mental states, the practitioner attains direct recognition of their essential divine autonomy (svātantrya) and mastery over the psychic energies (cakreśvaratva).

summary: The Viṃśatikākārikā ('Twenty Verses on Representation-Only') is a foundational Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda polemical treatise composed by Vasubandhu. The text refutes the reality of mind-independent external physical objects (bāhyārtha) through a rigorous critique of atomism (paramāṇuvāda), demonstrating that atomic partlessness and spatial extension are mutually incompatible. Vasubandhu defends the thesis that all experiential phenomena are appearances only (vijñaptimātra), answering realist objections by showing that spatial-temporal determination, intersubjective consistency, and practical efficacy can function without external objects, as seen in dreams, collective karmic hallucinations, and demonic mental projections.

summary: The Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi ('Proof of Mere Representation in Twenty Verses') is a foundational treatise of Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda philosophy composed by Vasubandhu in the 4th to 5th century CE. In twenty-two concise kārikās, Vasubandhu defends the thesis that external objects do not exist independently of cognition (vijñaptimātra), refuting realist objections regarding spatiotemporal determinacy, intersubjective consensus, and causal efficacy through comparisons with dreams and hell visions. The work also articulates a famous critique of atomism (paramāṇuvāda), arguing that indivisible partless atoms cannot coalesce into composite extended bodies without logical contradiction.

summary: The Viṣṇudharma is an early Vaiṣṇava devotional and ritual handbook of approximately 4,200 verses in 105 chapters, generally dated to the 3rd–5th century CE. Framed as an exposition given by the sage Śaunaka to King Śatānīka, it instructs householders and lay devotees on the worship, liturgy, mental contemplation, vrata observances, and festivals dedicated to Viṣṇu. It represents one of the foundational texts of early non-sectarian Vaiṣṇavism, serving as a direct predecessor to the larger encyclopedic Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa and functioning alongside the roughly contemporary Śivadharmaśāstra as a crucial witness to early medieval devotional religion.

summary: The Viṣṇupurāṇa is one of the eighteen canonical Mahāpurāṇas and the classical exemplar of the traditional pañcalakṣaṇa structure (primary cosmogony, secondary creation, genealogies of gods and patriarchs, manvantara cycles, and dynastic histories). Comprising six books (aṃśas) arranged as a dialogue between Parāśara and Maitreya, it treats cosmology, geography, varṇāśramadharma, and devotes book five to an extensive early biography of Kṛṣṇa. Frequently dated in its core to the Gupta period (c. 4th–5th century CE), it is a foundational scripture for classical Vaiṣṇava theology and Vedāntic exegesis.

summary: The Pañcatantra is an ancient Indian prosimetric collection of didactic animal fables and apologues organized within an overarching narrative frame. Attributed to the sage Viṣṇuśarman, it is structured as a six-month pedagogical curriculum to instruct three unlettered princes in practical polity (nītiśāstra) and worldly conduct (artha). The collection consists of five books (tantras): Mitrabheda ('Separation of Friends'), Mitrasamprāpti ('Gaining of Friends'), Kākolūkīya ('Of Crows and Owls' / War and Peace), Labdhapraṇāśa ('Loss of Gains'), and Aparīkṣitakāraka ('Ill-Considered Action'). Transmitted across Eurasia through Borzūya's Middle Persian rendering and subsequent Arabic (Kalīla wa-Dimna), Syriac, Hebrew, and European versions, it is among the most influential and widely translated narrative cycles in world literature.

summary: The Viṣvaksenasaṃhitā is a canonical Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava Āgama comprising 39 chapters and around 2,800 verses, named after Viṣvaksena, the celestial marshal and gatekeeper of Viṣṇu. summary: The Subhāṣitaratnakoṣa ('Treasury of Well-Turned Verse') is an anthology of classical Sanskrit court poetry compiled by the Buddhist scholar Vidyākara around 1100 CE (with an expanded recension c. 1130 CE) in Bengal. Arranged into 50 thematic sections (vrajyās) encompassing 1,738 stanzas, it collects works from over two hundred poets, opening with Buddhist and Hindu devotional hymns and progressing through the seasons, love, social types, nature, gnomic sayings, and praise of poets. The work is a foundational witness to classical kāvya between 700 and 1050 CE, preserving extensive poetic material that would otherwise be entirely lost.

summary: The Tarkasopāna ('Staircase of Reasoning') is an introductory Sanskrit primer of Buddhist epistemological logic (pramāṇa) composed by Vidyākaraśānti (c. 11th–12th century CE). Structured into three chapters—perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna)—it provides a concise summary of the Dharmakīrtian system, heavily utilizing the work of Dharmottara. Together with Mokṣākaragupta's Tarkabhāṣā and Jitāri's Hetutattvopadeśa, it exemplifies the late medieval manual literature representing the culmination of Indian Buddhist logic.

summary: The Pratāparudrīya (or Pratāparudrayaśobhūṣaṇa) by Vidyānātha is a comprehensive early 14th-century manual of Sanskrit poetics and dramaturgy, composed at the court of the Kākatīya king Pratāparudra II of Warangal (r. c. 1295–1323 CE). Across nine chapters (prakaraṇas), it covers the hero (nāyaka), the nature of kāvya, dramaturgy (nāṭaka), rasa, poetic flaws (doṣa), poetic excellences (guṇa), and verbal and semantic ornaments (śabdālaṅkāra, arthālaṅkāra, miśrālaṅkāra). The treatise established a prominent South Indian tradition in which all illustrative examples exclusively praise the patron king, and its third chapter incorporates a complete five-act panegyrical play, the Pratāparudrakalyāṇa, designed as a model drama.

While mundane branches of learning emerge during the evolution of the world, they cannot eliminate suffering; only the Buddhas disclose the supreme science—the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to nirvāṇa.

summary: The Vijñānabhairava is an influential scripture of the Trika and Kaula non-dual Śaiva traditions of Kashmir, presented as an esoteric dialogue between Bhairava and the goddess Bhairavī. These techniques utilize breath movement, sensory and perceptual gateways, intervals between mental states, aesthetic absorption, and heightened affective experiences to induce spontaneous immersion (samāveśa) into the reality of Śiva.

summary: The Sāṅkhyasāra is an independent philosophical manual (prakaraṇa) of the Sāṅkhya system composed by the 16th-century synthesizer Vijñānabhikṣu. Structured into two parts—a Pūrvabhāga of four paricchedas and an Uttarabhāga of seven paricchedas—it sets out the nature of liberation (puruṣārtha), discriminative insight (vivekakhyāti), the material evolutes (prakṛti and tattvas), puruṣa, and the essential distinctions between self and non-self. The work encapsulates the core positions elaborated in his larger Sāṅkhyapravacanabhāṣya, harmonizing classic Sāṅkhya dualism with theistic elements and Pātañjala Yoga.

summary: The Mitākṣarā (properly Ṛjumitākṣarā) by the late 11th- to early 12th-century jurist Vijñāneśvara is the most authoritative and influential commentary on the Yājñavalkyasmṛti. Composed at Kalyāṇa under the Western Cālukya emperor Vikramāditya VI, the text encompasses the three major divisions of Dharmaśāstra: daily religious and social duties (ācāra), civil and criminal law and judicial procedure (vyavahāra), and penances and expiation (prāyaścitta). By applying Mīmāṃsā hermeneutical principles to reconcile divergent smṛti authorities, Vijñāneśvara established the legal foundation of the Mitākṣarā school of Hindu jurisprudence, which became the prevailing legal authority across most of the Indian subcontinent.

summary: The Vimalakīrtinirdeśa is an influential Mahāyāna sūtra set in Vaiśālī, centered on the lay bodhisattva Vimalakīrti, who feigns illness to receive visitors and instruct them. In a series of witty dialogues with major arhat disciples and bodhisattvas, Vimalakīrti dismantles dualistic attachments regarding renunciation, purity, and emptiness (śūnyatā), culminating in his famous silence to signify direct entry into non-duality (advayadharmamukha-praveśa). Long celebrated in East Asian Buddhism and Tibet via early translations, the complete Indic Sanskrit text was identified in 1999 in a 12th-century palm-leaf manuscript preserved at the Potala Palace in Lhasa.

summary: The Vimalakīrtinirdeśasūtra is a renowned Mahāyāna scripture set in Vaiśālī that centers on the enlightened householder bodhisattva Vimalakīrti, who feigns illness to create an occasion to teach visiting śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and celestial beings. Over twelve chapters, the text articulates core Mahāyāna themes including the purification of the Buddha realm (buddhakṣetrapariśuddhi), the exercise of skillful means (upāyakauśalya), the inconceivable liberation (acintyavimokṣa), and the realization of non-duality (advayadharmamukha), memorably epitomized by Vimalakīrti's eloquent silence. Notably, this particular e-text contains the modern Sanskrit reconstruction prepared from the Tibetan translation by L.M. Joshi and Bhikshu Pāsādika in 1981, prior to the 1999 recovery of the original Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscript in Lhasa.

summary: The Abhidharmadīpa is an orthodox Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika verse treatise dating to roughly the 5th–6th century CE. Composed in close structural and metrical imitation of Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośakārikā, it defends orthodox Vaibhāṣika ontology while polemicizing sharply against Vasubandhu's Sautrāntika positions and Mahāyāna doctrine. This e-text provides an incomplete transcription of the verses (kārikās 1–383, covering chapters 1–5) based on P. S. Jaini's 1959 edition of the unique Sanskrit manuscript recovered from Tibet.

summary: The Abhidharmadīpa along with its prose auto-commentary (Vibhāṣāprabhāvṛtti) is an important post-Vasubandhu Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika treatise composed around the 5th to 6th century CE. Written by an anonymous author conventionally designated as the Dīpakāra, it parallels the structure of Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya across eight chapters while defending orthodox Kāśmīra Vaibhāṣika positions. The work is noted for its rigorous defense of Vaibhāṣika realism and its polemical critiques directed against Sautrāntika doctrines and Vasubandhu (consistently called the 'Kośakāra').

summary: The Abhidharmadīpa is a late Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika philosophical treatise composed in metrical verse (kārikā) and arranged into eight chapters corresponding closely to the structure of Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośa. Written from an orthodox Kashmirian Vaibhāṣika perspective, it systematizes classical Vaibhāṣika Abhidharma doctrine while mounting explicit polemical counterattacks against Vasubandhu's Sautrāntika-leaning positions and Mahāyāna views. Known from an incomplete palm-leaf manuscript discovered in Tibet in 1937, the text preserves 597 verses out of an estimated original total of ca. 1,200.

summary: The Santānāntarasiddhi ('Proof of Other Mental Continua') by Dharmakīrti (c. 6th–7th century) is a treatise in 93 verses demonstrating from an idealist (Vijñānavāda / Yogācāra) standpoint that the rejection of external physical reality does not entail solipsism, since purposive physical actions and speech permit a valid inference to the existence of other mental series. Vinītadeva's Santānāntarasiddhiṭīkā (c. 8th century) is the earliest surviving commentary on the text, providing word-by-word glosses and philosophical defense against external-world realist and solipsist objections. Because both works were largely lost in their original Sanskrit and survived intact only in Tibetan translation, this e-text comprises the modern Sanskrit back-translation reconstructed by J. S. Negi.

summary: A Mahāyāna sūtra transmitted within the Ratnakūṭa collection that contrasts the monastic prātimokṣa rules of śrāvakas with the ethical conduct of bodhisattvas. The Buddha explains that while the śrāvaka discipline centers on strict detachment to avoid any rebirth in saṃsāra, bodhisattva discipline is guided by skillful means (upāyakauśalya) and intention, prioritizing the welfare and gathering of beings. Consequently, offenses rooted in aversion or hatred are considered severe for a bodhisattva because they cause abandonment of beings, whereas infractions rooted in desire can serve to gather beings and are deemed comparatively less obstructive. The sūtra concludes with an exposition by Mañjuśrī on the unconditioned, inherently pure nature of all dharmas.

summary: The Camatkāracandrikā is an eight-chapter (vilāsa) manual of Sanskrit poetics composed in the late 14th century CE by Viśveśvara Kavicandra at the court of King Siṅgabhūpāla II of Rācakoṇḍa. Modeling itself after earlier panegyrical alaṅkāra treatises such as Vidyānātha's Pratāparudrīya and Vidyādhara's Ekāvalī, the author crafts original illustrative verses that praise his royal patron. Conceptually, the work posits camatkāra (aesthetic wonder or delight) as the unifying essence of poetic beauty, systematizing its realization through seven distinct literary components: guṇa, rīti, rasa, vṛtti, pāka, śayyā, and alaṅkāra.

summary: The Catuḥślokī ('Four Stanzas') is a short Sanskrit devotional stotra composed by Yāmunācārya (c. 10th–11th century CE) in praise of the goddess Śrī (Lakṣmī). It celebrates her supreme majesty as the eternal consort of Puruṣottama (Viṣṇu) and formulates the theological concept of her role as mediatrix (puruṣakāra) through whose grace devotees gain access to the Lord and final liberation. The work forms one of the foundational scriptural authorities for Viśiṣṭādvaita theology regarding the ontological status and salvific function of Lakṣmī.

summary: The Saṃvitsiddhi is the third treatise of Yāmunācārya's (c. 10th–11th century CE) celebrated Siddhitraya ('Triad of Demonstrations'), a foundational work of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. Written primarily in verse with argumentative prose transitions, the work offers an extensive critique of Advaita Vedānta epistemology and ontology, refuting the concept of contentless, undifferentiated consciousness (nirviśeṣa-cinmātra), the unreality of difference, and the doctrine of anirvacanīyatva. Instead, Yāmuna demonstrates that consciousness (saṃvit) is inherently qualified, intentional, and the attribute of an enduring knowing self (jñātṛ). This text directly influenced Rāmānuja's Mahāsiddhānta in the Śrībhāṣya. The digital file presents the surviving portions of the Saṃvitsiddhi accompanied by the 20th-century Siddhāñjana commentary by P. B. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya.

summary: The Bṛhadyamasmṛti is an expanded metrical Dharmaśāstra text in five adhyāyas comprising 182 ślokas, traditionally attributed to Yama. The first four adhyāyas focus heavily on prāyaścitta (penance and atonement) for ritual, moral, and inter-caste transgressions, rules of purification (śuddhi), and ancestral rites (śrāddha). summary: The Yamasmṛti is a short metrical dharmaśāstra attributed to Yama, who is already cited by Yājñavalkya (1.4–5) as one of the twenty traditional authorities on dharma. This 78-verse recension focuses on expiations and atonements (prāyaścitta) for ritual and social offences—including surviving suicide attempts, consumption of prohibited food or intoxicating drink, and contacts with untouchables—as well as rules regarding menstrual taboos, the censure of failing to marry off daughters by age twelve, ceremonial impurity (āśauca, sūtaka), and sandhyā period prohibitions. The work is known in several distinct recensions across the manuscript tradition (including 78-, 99-, and 182-verse versions).

summary: The Laghuyamasmṛti is a short metrical dharmaśāstra in 99 anuṣṭubh verses belonging to the textual cycle attributed to Yama. It focuses predominantly on prāyaścitta (penance and ritual expiation) for offences such as improper contact with outcastes or impure persons, forbidden food consumption, and failed suicide attempts, alongside rules for personal bodily purity (śauca) and ancestral offerings (śrāddha and tarpaṇa). In modern scholarly taxonomy, this 99-verse recension is distinguished from the 78-verse Yamasmṛti and the 182-verse Bṛhadyamasmṛti.

summary: The Yamasmṛti is a metrical Dharmaśāstra code attributed to the sage and deity Yama. summary: The Rasaprakāśasudhākara is a major 13-chapter Sanskrit treatise on alchemy and iatrochemistry (rasaśāstra), composed by Yaśodhara Bhaṭṭa in Saurashtra (Gujarat). It describes the origins, grades, and eighteen purification and transmutational processes (aṣṭādaśa-saṃskāra) of mercury, followed by treatments of primary and secondary minerals (mahārasas and uparasas), metals, gemstones, and apparatus (yantras, crucibles). The text holds an important position in the history of Indian chemistry for offering one of the earliest explicit accounts of zinc (yaśada/rasaka-sattva) distillation extraction and for key iatrochemical formulations such as Somanāthī tāmrabhasma and calomel (karpūrarasa).

Arranged largely according to the classical eight branches (aṣṭāṅga) of Indian medicine, it provides practical remedies for fevers, gastrointestinal and urinary disorders, respiratory complaints, poisoning, pediatrics, and eye conditions, concluding with general principles of humoral pathology and regimen. summary: The Yuktidīpikā is the most comprehensive and philosophically intricate surviving classical commentary on Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhyakārikā, composed anonymously around the 7th–8th century CE. Arranged into eleven daily lessons (āhnikas) grouped into four topical sections (prakaraṇas), it defends classical Sāṃkhya metaphysics, satkāryavāda, and epistemology against sharp critiques from Buddhist (notably Dignāga), Nyāya, and Vaiśeṣika interlocutors. The commentary is exceptionally valuable for the history of Indian philosophy because it preserves detailed references to earlier, otherwise lost Sāṃkhya masters (such as Vindhyavāsin, Pañcaśikha, and Patañjali) and doctrinal structures from the ancient Ṣaṣṭitantra.

summary: The Śāṅkhāyanagṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual (gṛhyasūtra) of the Śāṅkhāyana branch of the Ṛgveda. summary: The Pramāṇavārttikaṭīkā by Śākyabuddhi (fl. c. 700 CE) is an early Buddhist epistemological sub-commentary on Dharmakīrti's Pramāṇavārttika and its autocommentary (Svavṛtti). summary: The Śālistambasūtra ('Rice Seedling Sūtra') is a foundational Mahāyāna sūtra on the doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). Prompted by the Buddha's concise statement that whoever sees dependent origination sees the Dharma and whoever sees the Dharma sees the Buddha, the Bodhisattva Maitreya expounds the teaching to Śāriputra using the analogy of a rice seedling sprouting and developing from a seed. The discourse distinguishes between external causality (the physical conditions governing plant growth) and internal causality (the twelvefold chain of psychic and karmic conditioning), demonstrating that all conditioned phenomena arise devoid of an independent agent, soul (ātman), or essence. Copiously cited by Madhyamaka authors such as Nāgārjuna, Candrakīrti, and Kamalaśīla, it served as one of the primary scriptural foundations for early Mahāyāna causal theory.

summary: The Bodhicaryāvatāra ('Entering the Way of Awakening') is an influential Mahāyāna verse manual and classic of Buddhist devotional-philosophical literature composed in ten chapters by Śāntideva. It outlines the spiritual cultivation of the bodhisattva, tracing the generation and stabilization of the awakening mind (bodhicitta), ritual confession, vigilance (apramāda), guard over awareness (saṃprajanya), and the perfections of patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), meditative absorption (dhyāna), and dedication of merit (pariṇāmanā). The ninth chapter develops a Madhyamaka dialectical critique of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), refuting rival Buddhist and non-Buddhist philosophical systems.

summary: The Bodhicaryāvatāra ('Entering the Bodhisattva Path') is an 8th-century Sanskrit didactic and philosophical poem by the Madhyamaka master Śāntideva. Arranged in ten chapters, it serves as a practical manual for generating and sustaining the awakening mind (bodhicitta) and cultivating the six bodhisattva perfections (pāramitās). The work is celebrated for its ethical power—notably the exchange of self and other (parātmaparivartana) in chapter 8—and its rigorous philosophical exposition in chapter 9 (Prajñāpariccheda), which defends Madhyamaka emptiness (śūnyatā) against rival Buddhist and non-Buddhist metaphysical positions.

summary: The Śikṣāsamuccaya ('Compendium of Training') is an 8th-century Mahāyāna manual composed by the Madhyamaka philosopher Śāntideva. Structured around 27 mnemonic root verses (kārikā) and Śāntideva's own detailed prose exposition, it organizes the bodhisattva training into the fourfold program of relinquishing, guarding, purifying, and increasing one's body (ātmabhāva), possessions (bhoga), and religious merit (puṇya). The work is celebrated as an essential sourcebook of Indian Mahāyāna literature, preserving extensive quotations from over a hundred sūtras that are otherwise lost in their Sanskrit originals.

summary: The Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna (Divyāvadāna Chapter 33) narrates how the low-caste Mātaṅga (Caṇḍāla) maiden Prakṛti falls in love with the Buddha's disciple Ānanda and attempts to entrap him with love sorcery, but is rescued by the Buddha, ordained as a bhikṣuṇī, and attains arhatship. In explaining this event, the Buddha recounts the past-life debate between Triśaṅku, the chieftain of the Caṇḍālas, and the learned Brahmin Puṣkarasārin, providing a vigorous critique of the Brahmanical hereditary caste hierarchy by arguing that the four varṇas are mere nominal conventions rather than innate biological categories. Within this dialogue, the text incorporates an encyclopedic treatise on pre-Hellenistic Indian divination, palmistry, and nakṣatra astronomy and astrology.

summary: The Śāṅkhāyanāraṇyaka (also known as the Kauṣītakyāraṇyaka) is the forest treatise of the Śāṅkhāyana/Kauṣītaki recension of the Ṛgveda, organized into 15 adhyāyas. Adhyāyas 1–2 expound the ritual recitation and symbolism of the Mahāvrata ceremony. Adhyāyas 3–6 form the major Kauṣītaki-Upaniṣad, addressing eschatology, breath (prāṇa) doctrine, and King Pratardana's dialogue with Indra, followed by the Saṃhitopaniṣad (adhyāyas 7–8) on mystic phonetic analysis, internal sacrificial rites, and an authenticating teacher lineage (adhyāya 15).

summary: The Kaṭhopaniṣad is a classical Vedic Upaniṣad framed as a dialogue between the young seeker Naciketas and Yama, the lord of death. Yama instructs Naciketas on the distinction between the pleasant (preyas) and the truly beneficial (śreyas), the famous chariot allegory illustrating the relationship between the self, intellect, mind, and senses, and the transcendent, immortal nature of the ātman. In his Kaṭhopaniṣadbhāṣya, Śaṅkara offers a rigorous Advaita Vedānta exposition, establishing that liberation (mokṣa) is achieved exclusively through the non-dual intuitive realization of the individual self's identity with Brahman rather than through ritual action or meditation.

summary: The Upadeśasāhasrī ('Thousand Teachings') is the principal non-commentarial treatise (prakaraṇagrantha) universally acknowledged as an authentic work of Ādi Śaṅkara (fl. c. 8th century CE). Consisting of a metrical section (Padyabandha, 19 chapters) and a prose section (Gadyabandha, 3 chapters), it presents a concise exposition of Advaita Vedānta focusing on the identity of the individual self (ātman) with absolute reality (Brahman). The text emphasizes the complete renunciation of ritual action (karma) in favor of knowledge (jñāna), explicates the Upaniṣadic mahāvākyas (especially 'tat tvam asi'), and demonstrates the pedagogical dialogue through which an enlightened teacher dismantles superimposition (adhyāsa) in a qualified pupil.

summary: The Vivekacūḍāmaṇi ('Crest-Jewel of Discrimination') is one of the most widely read verse manuals (prakaraṇa-grantha) of Advaita Vedānta, composed in 580 verses. Set as a pedagogical dialogue between a spiritual teacher and a qualified disciple, it outlines the fourfold qualifications of an aspirant (sādhana-catuṣṭaya), analyzes the three bodies and five sheaths (pañca-kośa), elucidates the nature of māyā and ignorance, and demonstrates the fundamental discrimination (viveka) between the eternal Self (ātman) and the non-Self (anātman). The work culminates in the direct realization of non-duality and the characteristics of the liberated sage (jīvanmukta).

It lays out the foundational epistemology of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā school: the investigation of dharma (dharmajijñāsā), Vedic injunction (codanā) as the sole epistemic means for suprasensory dharma, the definition of perception (pratyakṣa), and the innate, beginningless relationship between linguistic expressions and their meanings (autpattikaḥ śabdārthasaṃbandhaḥ). Under sūtra 1.1.5, Śabarasvāmin incorporates the famous Vṛttikāragrantha, which systematically defines the pramāṇas (including inference, analogy, presumption, and absence) and defends the permanent self (ātman) against Buddhist epistemological and idealist critiques.

In Tibetan canonical collections, these 27 verses are preserved as an independent text (Toh 3939) intended for memorization.

summary: The Atharvaśiropaniṣad ('Head of the Atharvaveda') is an early Śaiva and Pāśupata Upaniṣad traditionally attached to the Atharvaveda. It begins with the gods questioning Rudra about his identity, to which Rudra responds with a grandiose self-proclamation asserting that he is the sole eternal reality, transcendent and immanent in all deities, natural phenomena, and meters. The text expounds esoteric meditations on the sacred syllable Om (praṇava) and prescribes the observance of the Pāśupata vow (pāśupatavrata), including the application of sacred ashes (bhasmasnāna) for severance of worldly bondage (paśupāśa). Already cited in ancient Dharmasūtras (e.g. Gautama and Baudhāyana), it constitutes one of the foundational scriptural texts of early Śaivism.

summary: The Śivasūtra is the foundational revealed text of the non-dual Kashmiri Trika school, outlining the nature of supreme consciousness and the three successive means (upāyas)—śāmbhava, śākta, and āṇava—by which the bound soul realizes its inherent identity with Śiva. This e-text pairs the root sūtras with the Śivasūtravārttika of Varadarāja (alias Kṛṣṇadāsa), a verse exposition that versifies and condenses the classic prose interpretation provided in Kṣemarāja's 11th-century Śivasūtravimarśinī. Through accessible anuṣṭubh verses, Varadarāja systematically elucidates the metaphysical definitions of bondage, the dynamics of divine energy (spanda/mātṛkā), and yogic integration.

summary: The Śrāvakabhūmi ('Stage of the Disciple') is the thirteenth and second-largest treatise within the Maulī Bhūmi (Basic Section) of the Yogācārabhūmi corpus, serving as an encyclopedic meditation manual structured across four yogasthānas. This e-text contains Yogasthānas 1 and 2, which systematically treat the spiritual requisites of practice, the classification of disciples, qualified spiritual masters, ālambana (meditative objects), and initial tranquilization and insight. In addition, the file incorporates three other independent bhūmis from the Yogācārabhūmi edited as appendices in the 2007 Taisho publication: the Asamāhitā bhūmi (unconcentrated state), the Śrutamayī bhūmi (stage arisen from hearing), and the Cintāmayī bhūmi (stage arisen from reflection, concluding with the Ābhiprāyikārthagāthānirdeśa).

summary: The Śrīghanācārasaṃgraha ('Compendium of Conduct according to the Buddha') is a Buddhist Vinaya manual in verse outlining monastic discipline and deportment for novices (śrāmaṇera). Affiliated with the Mahāsāṃghika (or Lokottaravādin) disciplinary lineage, the work is organized into four adhyāyas treating the three refuges, the ten novice precepts (śikṣāpada), and supplementary rules of conduct. Because no separate manuscript of the root verses survives, the e-text presents the modern philological reconstruction by Sanghasen Singh extracted from the lemmata and glosses of Jayarakṣita's Sphuṭārthā commentary.

summary: The Ratnatrayaparīkṣā ('Examination of the Three Jewels') is an influential 10th–11th-century Sanskrit doctrinal treatise in 322 verses by the Kashmirian Śaiva Siddhānta scholar Śrīkaṇṭhasūri. Instead of examining the school's general ontological triad (pati, paśu, and pāśa), the work focuses specifically on the 'three jewels' defined as bindu (the material cause of pure sound, language, and the pure universe), śakti (the conscious power of the Lord), and śiva (the supreme agent and consciousness). Drawing heavily on earlier Kashmirian exegesis (especially Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha), it provides a detailed metaphysical exposition of the pure path (śuddhādhvan), phonematic cosmogony, and soteriological initiation.

The Buddha Śākyamuni expounds to the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara the virtues and future enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) of the goddess Śrī Mahādevī (the Brahmanical goddess Lakṣmī assimilated into the Mahāyāna pantheon), accompanied by a litany of her 108 auspicious names and dhāraṇī incantations. Devotional recitation of these names and spells is prescribed to dispel poverty, pacify obstacles, and confer prosperity and spiritual merit.

summary: The Śukasaptati ('Seventy Tales of the Parrot') is a popular Sanskrit frame-tale narrative (kathā). When the young merchant Madanavinoda embarks on a lengthy commercial journey abroad, his wife Prabhāvatī is tempted by dissolute companions to pursue illicit liaisons; her wise parrot keeps her at home each night by narrating an ingenious story of wit, trickery, or adulterous escape, cunningly breaking off the tale until dawn. Over the course of seventy consecutive nights, the parrot deters her from infidelity until the merchant returns. Renowned for its realistic depiction of rogue life and practical cleverness, the collection enjoyed immense popularity throughout Asia and formed the direct basis for the Persian Ṭūṭī-nāma.

summary: The Śvetāśvataropaniṣad is a classical metrical Upaniṣad belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda tradition, dating approximately to the late centuries BCE. Comprising six chapters, it synthesizes older Upaniṣadic non-dualism with an explicitly theistic framework, identifying the supreme transcendent Brahman with the personal deity Rudra-Śiva (also addressed as Hara, Īśa, and Maheśvara). The text incorporates concepts that later became central to classical Sāṃkhya and Yoga—such as pradhāna/prakṛti, puruṣa, the guṇas, and physical postures and breath control for meditation—and concludes with an influential early articulation of personal devotion (bhakti) toward God and the guru.

summary: The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad is a classical metrical Upaniṣad associated with the Black Yajurveda tradition, dating to approximately the late centuries BCE. It synthesizes Vedāntic non-dualism with early Sāṃkhya-Yoga categories, yogic contemplation and posture (adhyāya 2), and personal theism centered on Rudra-Śiva. The text outlines a threefold reality comprising the individual soul (bhoktṛ), the objective world (bhogya), and the supreme lord (preritṛ / īśa), and provides one of the earliest occurrences of the concept of bhakti in classical Sanskrit literature (6.23).

summary: The Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi is an anthology of 105 Tamil devotional verses by Kulacēkara Āḻvār forming part of the canonical Nālāyira Divya Prabandham. The collection comprises ten decades dedicated to Viṣṇu in various manifestations and shrines (such as Śrīraṅgam, Veṅkaṭam, and Tillai Cittirakūṭam), exploring diverse devotional stances (bhāvas) including bridal devotion, maternal tenderness as Kauśalyā and Yaśodā, and devotion to Rāma. summary: The Vajrāvalī (or Vajrāvalīnāmamaṇḍalopāyikā) by Abhayākaragupta (fl. late 11th–early 12th century, Vikramaśīla) is a comprehensive ritual compendium of late Indian tantric Buddhism. Structured around approximately fifty sequential rites (vidhi), it details the selection and purification of the ritual ground, maṇḍala construction and coloration, installation and consecration of images and monastic dwellings (pratiṣṭhā), the full progression of tantric initiations (abhiṣeka), post-initiatory observances (vrata), fire rituals (homa), and maṇḍala dissolution. Providing the liturgical framework for the maṇḍalas described iconographically in Abhayākaragupta's Niṣpannayogāvalī, the work became a foundational ritual authority in Nepalese and Tibetan Buddhist traditions.

summary: The Sārasvataprakriyā (or Sārasvatavyākaraṇa) by Anubhūtisvarūpācārya (c. 13th–14th century CE) is the standard introductory and procedural treatise of the non-Pāṇinian Sārasvata school of Sanskrit grammar. summary: The Bhelasaṃhitā is an early classical Āyurvedic treatise belonging to the Ātreya school of internal medicine (kāyacikitsā). Structured similarly to the Carakasaṃhitā across eight sthānas (Sūtra, Nidāna, Vimāna, Śārīra, Indriya, Cikitsā, Kalpa, and Siddhi), it expounds etiology, pathology, anatomy, embryology, and therapeutics. Preserved uniquely in a single fragmentary palm-leaf manuscript from Thanjavur, it constitutes a crucial early witness to classical Indian medical literature alongside Caraka and Suśruta.

Its stories are the deliverance of the sinner Ajāmila through the name of Nārāyaṇa, Dakṣa's progeny, Viśvarūpa and the Nārāyaṇakavaca, Indra's war with Vṛtra (a devotee-demon), King Citraketu, and the birth of the Maruts from Diti's puṃsavana vow. summary: Skandha 7 (15 adhyāyas) is narrated by Nārada to Yudhiṣṭhira. It tells how enmity, too, can lead to Viṣṇu (Śiśupāla, Jaya and Vijaya), and gives the story of Hiraṇyakaśipu and his devotee son Prahlāda, Prahlāda's teaching, and the Nṛsiṃha avatāra (adhyāyas 1–10). It ends with Nārada's exposition of varṇāśramadharma and the conduct of renunciants (adhyāyas 11–15). summary: The Candravṛtti is the primary commentary on the Candravyākaraṇa, an influential non-sectarian Sanskrit grammar composed by the Buddhist scholar Candragomin (c. 5th–6th century CE). Reorganizing and simplifying the Pāṇinian grammatical system, it omits Vedic accents and rules irrelevant to classical usage. This e-text provides the complete six adhyāyas of the root sūtras with the vṛtti and concludes with Candragomin's Varṇasūtra on phonetics.

summary: The Madhyamakāvatāra ('Entrance to the Middle Way') along with its autocommentary (Madhyamakāvatārabhāṣya) is Candrakīrti's 7th-century CE systematic introduction to Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. It integrates Madhyamaka philosophy into the Mahāyāna path structure of the ten bodhisattva stages (daśabhūmi) and perfections (pāramitā). This e-text preserves the newly recovered Sanskrit original of chapters 1 through 5, covering the bodhisattva stages of joy (Pramuditā), purity (Vimalā), luminosity (Prabhākarī), radiance (Arciṣmatī), and invincibility (Sudurjayā).

summary: The Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra (also known as the Ekallavīratantra) is an Anuttarayoga tantra centered on the wrathful deity Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa (Acala) and his consort Dveṣavajrī. Across 25 chapters, it covers maṇḍala construction, initiation rituals (abhiṣeka), the subtleties of the energetic channels and drops (nāḍī and bindu), the generation of the four joys (caturānanda) through yogic and erotic union, fierce magical and subjugation rites, and meditation upon non-duality.

summary: The Ācāryakriyāsamuccaya (commonly known as the Kriyāsamuccaya), composed by the late Indian tantric master Jagaddarpaṇa (Darpaṇācārya, c. 11th–12th century), is a comprehensive ritual manual synthesizing Vajrayāna liturgical practices across various tantric classes. This excerpt preserves the initiation section (abhiṣekapaṭala), treating essential preliminary purifications, the gurumaṇḍala rite, taking the vows (poṣadha), disciple admittance (śiṣyapraveśavidhi), and empowerment rites including the mālābhiṣeka. It is a fundamental ritual source preserved and actively used within the Newar Buddhist community.

coverage_note: Covers everything the 1954 edition contains: the introductory verses 1–27 (with gaps), the autobiographical prose frame, and the main narrative about the families of Rājahaṃsa and Mānasāra. This corresponds roughly to the Pūrvapīṭhikā part of the Daśakumāracarita story. Lacunae, marked '......', are frequent throughout. The text breaks off in mid-sentence in an embedded episode involving Mahāśvetā and Kādambarī, before the scribal colophon. The later portion of the work is lost; its contents are partly known from the verse summary Avantisundarīkathāsāra.
attribution_note: The opening rubric ('ācāryadaṇḍiviracitā avantisundarī') and the final colophon ('ityācāryadaṇḍinā kṛtā avantisundarī samāptā') ascribe the work to Daṇḍin, the author of the Kāvyādarśa, who is usually placed around the late 7th / early 8th century at the Pallava court of Kāñcī. Most scholars accept this ascription. The verse introduction praises earlier poets and gives an autobiographical account of the author's ancestry (Bhāravi/Dāmodara).

summary: The Avantisundarīkathā is a long ornate prose romance (kathā) ascribed to Daṇḍin. It opens with verses praising earlier poets (Vālmīki, Vyāsa, Subandhu, Śūdraka, Bhāsa, Sarvasena, Kālidāsa, Bāṇa, Mayūra and others), followed by an autobiographical account of the author's family and its connection with the Pallava court of Kāñcī. The main narrative tells, at much greater length, the story found in the Pūrvapīṭhikā of the Daśakumāracarita. The surviving text is lacunose and breaks off incomplete.

summary: The Krīḍākhaṇḍa ('Book of Divine Play') is the second and concluding part of the Gaṇeśapurāṇa, an Upapurāṇa central to the Gāṇapatya tradition. In 155 chapters, it narrates the cosmic deeds and avataras of Gaṇeśa across the four yugas: Mahotkaṭa in the Kṛtayuga, Mayūreśvara in the Tretāyuga, Gajānana in the Dvāparayuga, and Dhūmraketu in the Kaliyuga. Chapters 138–148 form the celebrated Gaṇeśagītā, wherein Gaṇeśa expounds yoga and non-dualist devotion to King Vareṇya, modeling its philosophy and verse forms directly on the Bhagavadgītā.

summary: The Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthāvyākhyā is an 8th-century commentary by Haribhadra on the verse summary of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā. The unique surviving Sanskrit manuscript discovered in Tibet is acephalous, preserving chapters 3 to 32.

summary: The Kāśikāvivaraṇapañjikā, commonly known as the Nyāsa, is an extensive sub-commentary composed by the Buddhist grammarian Jinendrabuddhi (ca. 8th century CE) on the Kāśikāvṛtti of Jayāditya and Vāmana. As the earliest surviving major commentary on the Kāśikāvṛtti, it elucidates the Pāṇinian sūtras, explains difficult nominal and verbal derivations, and incorporates important grammatical and philosophical debates. It served as the primary subject for subsequent grammatical works such as Maitreyarakṣita's Tantrapradīpa.

The composition details royal genealogy, mythical lineages, religious foundations, and royal decrees with exceptional grammatical and literary sophistication.

summary: The Rājataraṅgiṇī ('River of Kings'), composed by the Kashmiri poet Kalhaṇa between 1148 and 1150 CE, is the foremost work of historical narrative (itihāsa) in classical Sanskrit literature. Structured in eight books ('waves', taraṅgas) encompassing nearly 8,000 ślokas, it chronicles the dynastic history of Kashmir from mythological beginnings to the reign of Kalhaṇa's contemporary monarch Jayasiṃha. Written in the style of mahākāvya, the work explicitly takes śāntarasa (the aesthetic sentiment of peace and detachment) as its predominant mood while demonstrating critical use of earlier regional chronicles, inscriptions, and coins.

summary: The Acintyādvayakramopadeśa is an esoteric Buddhist tantric treatise of 124 verses attributed to the mahāsiddha Kuddālapāda, conveying an oral instruction lineage descending from Bhadrapāda. It presents the completion stage (utpannakrama) practice focused on realizing inconceivable nonduality (acintyādvaya), where insight (prajñā) and skillful means (upāya) are indivisibly experienced as Great Bliss (mahāsukha).

summary: The Meghadūta ('Cloud Messenger') is a celebrated Sanskrit lyric poem (khaṇḍakāvya / sandeśakāvya) in Mandākrāntā meter composed by Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century CE). It recounts the longing of an exiled Yakṣa who implores a passing monsoon cloud to carry a message of reassurance to his pining wife in the celestial city of Alakā. This digital edition presents the poem accompanied by four major Sanskrit commentaries: Vallabhadeva's Pañcikā, Dakṣiṇāvartanātha's Pradīpa, Mallinātha's Sañjīvinī, and Sumativijaya's Sugamānvayā Vṛtti (covering the Pūrvamegha).

summary: The Daśatattvasaṃgraha is a manual of the Jñānapāda school of Guhyasamāja exegesis setting out ten ritual 'fundamentals' (tattva) of the tantric master: the protective circle, the maṇḍala visualisation centred on Vajrasattva/Samantabhadra, mantra recitation, the secret and wisdom-knowledge consecrations, forceful practice (haṭha), bali offerings, two kinds of counter-magic (pratyaṅgirā) and the 'opening of the casket' (puṭodghāta). It combines verse with prose explanation and quotes tantras and Jñānapāda works such as Dīpaṃkarabhadra's Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi. It survives in a single incomplete manuscript.

summary: The Laghuśaṃvaratantra (also known as Cakrasaṃvaratantra or Śrīherukābhidhāna) is the foundational root scripture (mūlatantra) of the Cakrasaṃvara cycle, belonging to the Yoginītantra (Anuttarayogatantra) class of Indian Buddhist Tantra. Dating to roughly the late 8th or early 9th century, it is centered on the wrathful deity Heruka/Cakrasaṃvara embraced by Vajravārāhī, setting forth the 62-deity maṇḍala, cremation-ground rituals, internal and external sacred geography (the 24 pīṭhas), and esoteric mantras. A substantial portion of the text adapts and integrates verses and ritual structures directly from earlier Śaiva Vidyāpīṭha scriptures, including the Picumata/Brahmayāmala and the Jayadrathayāmala.

summary: The Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa is an influential 11th-century Digambara Jaina tantric manual dedicated to the goddess Padmāvatī, the yakṣiṇī and attendant deity (śāsanadevatā) of the 23rd Tīrthaṅkara Pārśvanātha. Composed across ten chapters (adhikāras), it expounds mantra lore, diagrammatic amulets (yantra), sakalīkaraṇa, nyāsa, the classical six esoteric magical operations (ṣaṭkarmāṇi, including stambhana, vaśīkaraṇa, and ākarṣaṇa), omenology (nimitta), and toxicology/anti-venom remedies (gāruḍatantra). The accompanying Sanskrit commentary (Vivaraṇa) by Bandhuṣeṇa provides word-by-word glosses and detailed ritual guidelines.

summary: The Guhyasiddhi ('Secret Accomplishment') is an influential late 8th- or 9th-century Vajrayāna treatise by Padmavajra, counted among the canonical Eight Accomplishment Texts (Aṣṭasiddhi). The work expounds the completion stage (utpannakrama) of esoteric yoga in alignment with early Guhyasamājatantra exegetical traditions. Across nine chapters, it treats non-dual realization, esoteric sacraments including consort practice (vidyāvrata) and antinomian conduct (unmattavrata), and devotion to the guru (paramārthācāryapūjā).

summary: The Paramasaṃhitā is an early canonical scripture of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, framed as a dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Devala reporting revelation received from Sanaka on Śvetadvīpa. In 31 chapters, it treats Vaiṣṇava cosmology, ritual worship, icon consecration, initiation (dīkṣā), and yoga, reconciling meditative visualization with temple and image devotion.

summary: The Śābdanirṇaya is an epistemological and linguistic treatise by the Advaita Vedāntin Prakāśātman (c. 10th–11th century CE). Consisting of 75 kārikās and an auto-commentary, it establishes verbal testimony (śabda) as an independent pramāṇa against Buddhist and Vaiśeṣika reductions to inference, critically examines Mīmāṃsā semantic theories (anvitābhidhāna and abhihitānvaya), and defends the capacity of Vedic language to impart immediate knowledge of non-dual Brahman.

summary: The Pādmasaṃhitā is one of the most influential Saṃhitās of the Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava tradition and one of the few that preserve the full four-part structure (catuṣpāda): Jñānapāda (cosmology and theology, framed as Kaṇva's report of Saṃvarta's teaching), Yogapāda, Kriyāpāda (temple building, iconography and installation), and Caryāpāda (daily and festival worship, mantroddhāra, expiations, domestic worship). It remains an authoritative ritual manual in South Indian Śrīvaiṣṇava temples. Its theology has been studied by S. Schwarz Linder (Vienna 2014).

summary: The Khasamaṭīkā (also entitled Khasamā) is an Anuttarayogatantra commentary by the Vikramaśīla scholar Ratnākaraśānti (fl. late 10th–early 11th century) on the Khasamatantra. Ratnākaraśānti explicates the root text's Sanskrit and Apabhraṃśa verses (dohās/dvipadikās) through the framework of Vijñānavāda/Alīkākāravāda, maintaining that the ultimate nature of mind and the dharmakāya is innately pure, luminous, and 'equal to space' (khasama). The work is complete across five chapters (paṭala).

summary: A 15-canto Sanskrit mahākāvya composed in the 13th century CE by Someśvaradeva, court priest to the Caulukya/Vāghelā rulers of Gujarat. Elaborating on the foundational framing story of the Devīmāhātmya from the Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa, the epic narrates the life of King Suratha: his loss of sovereignty, forest retreat, devotion and rigorous penance to the Goddess, her destruction of the demon army, and Suratha's restoration to power. The final canto (kavipraśasti) provides significant historical and genealogical information regarding Someśvara's family and his praise of the Jain minister Vastupāla.

summary: The Suśrutasaṃhitā is one of the three foundational classics of classical Āyurveda (the Bṛhat-trayī) and ancient India's premier authority on surgery (śalyatantra). Framed as instructions delivered by Divodāsa Dhanvantari, king of Kāśī, to his student Suśruta, it describes surgical instruments, practical anatomy through human cadaveric dissection, and operative procedures such as rhinoplasty, couching of cataracts, lithotomy, and abdominal suture. The treatise comprises 186 chapters divided across the five sthānas of the Pūrvatantra (Sūtra-, Nidāna-, Śārīra-, Cikitsā-, and Kalpasthāna) and the supplementary Uttaratantra, which treats ophthalmology and ENT (śālākya), pediatrics (kaumārabhṛtya), toxicology/psychiatry (bhūtavidyā), and general medicine (kāyacikitsā).

summary: The Sūktimuktāvalī is a large thematically arranged subhāṣita anthology compiled in the mid-13th century under Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa, a minister and commander of the Yādava king Kṛṣṇa of Devagiri. After a genealogical praśasti of the compiler's family, it collects verses by many named poets in more than a hundred paddhatis. The topics range from poets and poetry, good and bad men and animals and nature, through love and the seasons, to fate, generosity, forbearance, renunciation and praise of Śiva. It is an important source for verses and poet attributions that are otherwise lost, including the series of verses on poets ascribed to Rājaśekhara.

summary: The Sūktiratnakośa is a subhāṣita anthology of 659 verses compiled by Lakṣmaṇa Dīkṣita, whose family is described in the closing praśasti. It opens with verses in praise of the Jina (Ṛṣabha, Mahāvīra), Śiva and Viṣṇu, and on poets (Vālmīki, Kālidāsa). These are followed by thematic sections of gnomic, erotic and descriptive verses, many of which are also found in other anthologies and in poets such as Bhartṛhari. It survives in manuscripts from western Indian Jaina libraries.

summary: The Kumārasambhava ('The Birth of the War-God') is a celebrated mahākāvya composed by Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century CE), depicting the penance of Pārvatī, her marriage to Śiva, and their union. The commentary by the Kashmiri scholar Vallabhadeva (10th century) is the earliest surviving commentary on the epic, providing crucial textual evidence for the northern Śāradā recension across cantos 1 to 8.

summary: The Subhāṣitāvalī is a major classical Sanskrit anthology (kośa/saṅgraha) compiled by the Kashmiri scholar Vallabhadeva. Structured into 101 thematic sections (paddhatis) encompassing invocations, gnomic and didactic verses (nīti), seasonal and natural descriptions, erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), and detachment (vairāgya), it contains 3,527 stanzas that preserve selections from hundreds of classical poets, many of whom are known solely through this anthology.

summary: The Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī is an influential late 8th-century Sanskrit commentary by Vilāsavajra on the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti, interpreting the root text through the esoteric framework of the Māyājālatantra and the Vajradhātumaṇḍala of the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha. This critical edition covers chapters 1 through 5 (adhikāras 1–5), which detail the preliminary overview (śarīravyavasthāpana), the setting, the request of Vajrapāṇi, the response of Śākyamuni, and the exposition of the 86 name-mantras mapped onto the Vajradhātu mandala deities. It is the earliest surviving dated Sanskrit commentary on the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti.

The text reviews non-Buddhist views before systematizing four Buddhist views of the goal according to the Pāramitānaya and seven according to the Mantranaya, culminating in a detailed discussion of non-dual awareness, cognitive forms (ākāra), and the fourth consecration (caturthābhiṣeka) within the Guhyasamāja tantric lineage.

summary: The Īśvarasaṃhitā is a prominent canonical text of the Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava Āgama, traditionally treated as an elaboration of the foundational Sāttvatasaṃhitā. Spanning 25 chapters, it systematically sets forth temple rituals, daily worship (nityapūjā), the fivefold division of time (pañcakāla), temple layout, iconography, image consecration (pratiṣṭhā), initiation (dīkṣā), and expiation (prāyaścitta). It is historically significant in the South Indian Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition, notably informing ritual practice at Melkote (Yadugiri).

summary: The Kātantra (also known as Kalāpa or Kaumāra), attributed to Śarvavarman, is the foundational work of the earliest post-Pāṇinian Sanskrit grammatical school. Designed as an accessible alternative to Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī without employing the complex Śivasūtra pratyāhāra apparatus, it systematically treats phonology and sandhi, nominal morphology and compounds, verbal conjugation, and primary derivatives across four books. Durgasiṃha's Kātantravṛtti is the canonical commentary elucidating the sūtras, which established the school's doctrinal authority and ensured its widespread transmission throughout Kashmir, eastern India, Central Asia, and Tibet.

summary: The Abhisamayamañjarī is a detailed Sanskrit sādhana and visualization manual dedicated to the various forms of Vajrayoginī/Vajravārāhī within the Cakrasaṃvara tantric cycle. It expounds preparatory purifications, generation of the deity and maṇḍala, internal cakras, mantra recitations, and bali offerings. Composed by the late Indian master Śākyarakṣita (ca. 11th–12th c.), it represents a major witness to the esoteric goddess practices of late Indian Vajrayāna.

summary: The Anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā is a concise philosophical work in 51 anuṣṭubh verses belonging to the non-dual Śaiva (Trika/Spanda) tradition of Kashmir. It expounds the nature of ultimate reality (anuttara) as autonomous pure consciousness (cit, prakāśa) inherently endowed with dynamic self-awareness (vimarśa, svātantrya, spanda). The work systematically maps the manifestation and reabsorption of the thirty-six cosmic principles (ṣaṭtriṃśat-tattva) back into undivided supreme subjective awareness (aham).

summary: The Ānandatantra is a South Indian Kaula scripture in 20 chapters (paṭalas) framed as an esoteric dialogue between Śrīdevī and Kāmeśvara. Affiliating itself with the Bhagamālinīsaṃhitā of the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava corpus, the text details transgressive and non-dual Kaula ritual practices, emphasizing liṅgapūjā, yonipūjā, and internal subtle physiology, before concluding with expositions on philosophical systems, tantric sects, and social classifications.

summary: The Rāmārcanacandrikā is a five-chapter (paṭala) Vaiṣṇava ritual manual (paddhati) on the tantric worship of Rāma, composed by Ānandavana, a Daśanāmī ascetic and disciple of Mukundavana. Synthesizing Vaiṣṇava Āgama, Pāñcarātra, and Purāṇic authorities (including the Rāmatāpanīya Upaniṣad and Agastyasaṃhitā), the work details the qualifications and testing of guru and disciple, mantra purification (śodhana), initiation (dīkṣā), daily ritual worship, yantra construction, and vow observances such as Rāmanavamī.

summary: A comprehensive ritual manual (paddhati) and liturgical codex representing the Kashmirian Śākta-Śaiva tradition. It sets out elaborate procedural instructions for pūjā and fire oblations (homa/agnikārya) directed to Kashmirian regional goddesses and Śākta deities, including Śārikā, Śāradā, Mahārājñī, Kubjikā, and Tripurasundarī. The manuscript codex additionally incorporates several ancillary ritual tracts and hymns such as the Amṛteśvarapatrikā, the eighth mayūkha of the Arcāratna, and the Pañcamīstavarāja from the Rudrayāmalatantra.

summary: The Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa is an encyclopedic Buddhist ritual work belonging to the early Mantrayāna (traditionally classified in Tibetan canonical taxonomies as a Kriyātantra), framed as a Mahāyāna vaipulyasūtra delivered by Śākyamuni Buddha. This second volume (chapters 23–47) details ritual procedures including mantroddhāra (extraction of mantras), extensive mudrāvidhi (hand gestures and seals), maṇḍala construction, and karmavidhi rites associated with Mañjuśrī and retinue. It represents one of the earliest preserved Indian Buddhist tantric sourcebooks, integrating esoteric ritual technology with classic Mahāyāna doctrine.

summary: The Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa is an encyclopedic Buddhist ritual scripture centered on the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, classified in Tibetan tradition as a Kriyā-tantra. This concluding third volume (chapters 50–55) contains rituals for the wrathful deity Yamāntaka, alchemical practices (hemasādhana), and the celebrated fifty-first chapter (Rājavyākaraṇaparivarta), which records dynastic prophecies concerning ancient and early-medieval Indian monarchs.

summary: A transcription of a damaged South Indian palm-leaf bundle containing several Śaiva works. It opens with Appayya Dīkṣita's devotional hymn Ātmārpaṇastava (Ātmārpaṇastuti, 50 verses). Next comes his Śikhariṇīmālā with his own commentary Śivatattvaviveka, a polemical defence of Śiva's supremacy through Vedic, Purāṇic and Brahmasūtra exegesis, which breaks off near its end. Nigamajñānadeśika's Śivajñānabodhopanyāsa, an exposition of the twelve sūtras of the Śivajñānabodha, follows, and then a short Śrīcakranirmāṇavidhi and an unidentified prose fragment.

summary: The Mantrakoṣa of Āśāditya Tripāṭhin is a tantric ritual compendium (mantranibandha) organized into sixteen chapters (paricchedas). It outlines procedures and mantras for pūjā, dīkṣā, guru-śiṣya qualification, bhūtaśuddhi, mātṛkānyāsa, yantras, and mudrās, drawing upon authorities such as the Prapañcasāratantra. summary: The Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati is an encyclopedic manual of ritual, temple consecration, and mantra-śāstra composed by the Kerala Śaiva authority Īśānaśivagurudeva (c. 11th–12th century CE). This opening division, the Sāmānyapāda (paṭalas 1–14), provides the common preliminary framework for ritual activity, including the classifications and recitation of mantras, the nature of letters (mātṛkā), the dimensions and preparation of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) and diagrams (maṇḍala), morning ablutions, and the rites of the sacred fire (agnikalpa). Synthesizing Śaivasiddhānta tenets with regional Kerala tantric traditions, it serves as a key witness to medieval South Indian ritual literature.

summary: The Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati (also titled Siddhāntasāra) is an encyclopedic Śaivasiddhānta ritual compendium composed by the Kerala master Īśānaśivagurudeva around the late 11th to 12th century CE. It remains a foundational primary source for medieval South Indian and Kerala temple ritual traditions.

summary: The Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati (also known as Siddhāntasāra or Tantrapaddhati) is an encyclopedic Śaiva ritual digest composed around the 11th–12th century CE, combining Śaiva Siddhānta Āgamic prescriptions with medieval Kerala ritual practices. This fourth and final volume comprises the latter half of the Kriyāpāda (paṭalas 31 to 66), covering temple architecture (vāstu, adhiṣṭhāna, prāsāda), iconographic canons, installation ceremonies (pratiṣṭhā), and annual temple festivals, followed by the Yogapāda (3 paṭalas) presenting Ṣaḍaṅgayoga and esoteric Śaiva meditative practices leading to liberation.
