Preserved in GOML Madras MS R. 4353 (and copied as IFP transcript 762), it interprets the Pratyabhijñā system using Trika exegesis and the Parātriṃśikā tradition, prominently analyzing the root text through the esoteric heart-mantra (sauḥ). Portions of this commentary were famously consulted and published by K. A. Subramania Iyer and K. C. Pandey to supply a lacuna in Bhāskarakaṇṭha's Bhāskarī.

summary: The Ṣaṭtriṃśattattvasaṃdoha ('Compendium of the Thirty-Six Principles') consists of 21 āryā verses that systematically outline the ontology of Kashmir Shaivism (Trika and Pratyabhijñā). It describes the gradual unfoldment (sṛṣṭi) of the thirty-six tattvas from ultimate consciousness (śivatattva) to gross earth (dharaṇī) as the spontaneous playful vibration (svātantrya / spanda) of Paramaśiva. The work is studied alongside the concise Sanskrit commentary (Vivaraṇa) composed by the seventeenth-century scholar Rājānaka Ānanda.

summary: The Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī (often termed the Laghvīvimarśinī) is Abhinavagupta's shorter commentary on Utpaladeva's foundational treatise, the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, transmitted here with the eighteenth-century sub-commentary Bhāskarī by Bhāskarakaṇṭha. Structured across four adhikāras (Jñāna-, Kriyā-, Āgama-, and Tattvasaṃgraha-), the text systematically expounds the core doctrine of the Pratyabhijñā school: spiritual liberation is achieved through the recognition that the individual self is identical with the supreme conscious agent (Maheśvara/Śiva), who freely projects and absorbs the universe through his svātantrya. The commentary undertakes sustained philosophical critique against Buddhist epistemologists, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, and Advaita Vedānta, articulating a rigorous non-dual Śaiva philosophy of dynamic consciousness and self-awareness.

summary: This text comprises Volume 1 of Abhinavagupta's Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī (the Bṛhatī Vimarśinī), his extensive philosophical commentary on Utpaladeva's lost auto-commentary (Vivṛti/Ṭīkā) to the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā. It encompasses the first three chapters (āhnikas) of the Jñānādhikāra, establishing the purpose of the treatise (Upodghātāhnika), refuting the Buddhist argument regarding the non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) of the Self, and critiquing externalist and reductionist rival schools (paradarśana). The work serves as a foundational text for non-dual Kashmir Śaiva epistemology and remains the primary witness for reconstructing Utpaladeva's lost Vivṛti.

summary: The Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī (also known as the Bṛhatīvimarśinī) is Abhinavagupta's monumental philosophical commentary on Utpaladeva's Vivṛti to the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, completed c. 1015 CE. This volume contains the second half of the Jñānādhikāra (vimarśas 4–8), treating memory (smṛti), conceptual exclusion (apohana), manifestation (ābhāsa), and the unitary conscious knower (pramātṛ). It is a central masterpiece of non-dual Śaiva philosophy, featuring comprehensive critiques of rival epistemological systems, especially the Buddhist Sautrāntika and Yogācāra logicians.

summary: The Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī (also known as the Bṛhatī Vimarśinī) is Abhinavagupta's monumental philosophical commentary on Utpaladeva's auto-commentary (Vivṛti) to the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, completed around 1015 CE. This third volume covers the Kriyādhikāra (examining divine agency, temporal and spatial succession, causality, and relations), the Āgamādhikāra (integrating philosophical analysis with scriptural revelation and the 36 tattvas), and the concluding Tattvasaṅgrahādhikāra (summarizing the ontology and soteriology of recognizing oneself as Śiva). It represents one of the most sophisticated masterworks of classical non-dual Kashmir Śaivism.

summary: The Bhairavastava ('Hymn of Praise to Bhairava', also titled Bhairavastotra or Padyanavaka) is a short devotional hymn composed by the Kashmiri polymath Abhinavagupta. In the concluding tenth stanza, the author dates its completion to the tenth lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa in Laukika Samvat [40]68 (corresponding to December 992 or January 993 CE). The hymn integrates personal devotion (bhakti) with nondual Trika and Pratyabhijñā philosophy, celebrating the deity Bhairava as identical to the practitioner's innate, radiant consciousness (saṃvid) and describing the immediate removal of existential fear, karma, and death through direct realization of non-duality.

summary: The Bodhapañcadaśikā is a concise philosophical poem of fifteen stanzas (and one concluding stanza) composed by the Trika master Abhinavagupta as an accessible introduction for disciples unable to study his larger śāstric treatises. The work outlines core Pratyabhijñā and Trika tenets: the self-luminous and autonomous nature of supreme consciousness (Śiva), the non-difference of consciousness and its dynamic power (Śakti), the status of the universe as a reflection (pratibimba) within consciousness, and liberation as the immediate recognition of this non-duality. This e-text also provides the Sanskrit commentary (Vivaraṇa) composed in 1914/1915 CE by the Kashmiri pandit Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī.

summary: The Mālinīvijayavārttika (also known as the Mālinīślokavārttika) is a major verse commentary composed by Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE) interpreting the opening sentence of the Mālinīvijayottaratantra, the foundational scriptural authority of the Trika Śaiva lineage. Arranged in two books (kāṇḍas), the text formulates a comprehensive theology of revelation (āgama), hermeneutics, and nondual metaphysics while mounting extensive polemics against Buddhist epistemologists, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā. Alongside the Tantrāloka and Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa, it represents one of Abhinavagupta's core scriptural syntheses.

summary: The Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa is Abhinavagupta's (fl. c. 975–1025 CE) major and comprehensive commentary on the Parātrīśikā, a foundational Trika scripture traditionally regarded as part of the Rudrayāmala. Composed before the Tantrāloka, the work develops an exhaustive theological and philosophical exposition of non-dual Śaivism, the Unsurpassable reality (anuttara), phonematic emanation (mātṛkā and mālinī), and the mystery of the heart-mantra (SAUḤ). This edition (KSTS 18) presents the root verses with Abhinavagupta's full text accompanied by explanatory editorial glosses in brackets by Mahāmahopādhyāya Mukunda Rāma Śāstrī.

summary: The Paramārthasāra ('Essence of the Supreme Truth') is a concise manual of nondual Kashmir Śaivism in 105 āryā verses by Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE), adapting an earlier Vedāntic/Vaiṣṇava text attributed to Ādiśeṣa. It surveys the nondual nature of absolute consciousness (Śiva / Parasaṃvit), cosmic manifestation across the thirty-six categories (tattvas), the mechanisms of contraction and ignorance (māyā/avidyā), and liberation through intuitive recognition (pratyabhijñā). Yogarāja's eleventh-century Vivṛti, composed in Srinagar by a direct student of Kṣemarāja, offers an indispensable running prose commentary elucidating Abhinavagupta's verses in light of Trika and Pratyabhijñā doctrine.

summary: Āhnikas 15 through 37 form the extensive ritual, yogic, and canon-defining second half of Abhinavagupta's Tantrāloka, accompanied by Jayaratha's Viveka commentary. The text systematically expounds daily and occasional Trika worship, multiple grades and variations of initiation (dīkṣā), post-initiatory practice, construction of maṇḍalas, funerary and ancestral rites (antyeṣṭi, śrāddha), and esoteric Kaula ritual (āhnika 29). The work concludes in āhnika 37 with an evaluation of the Śaiva scriptural hierarchy, the transmission of the teaching, and Abhinavagupta's personal lineage.

summary: The Tantrāloka ('Light on the Tantras') is Abhinavagupta's monumental encyclopedic synthesis of nondual Kashmir Śaivism (Trika and Kaula), presenting a comprehensive exposition of Śaiva metaphysics, yoga, and ritual based primarily upon the Mālinīvijayottaratantra. Accompanied by Jayaratha's indispensable Viveka commentary, āhnikas 1–14 set forth the philosophical and soteriological core of the system. This includes the four means to liberation (anupāya, śāmbhavopāya, śāktopāya, and āṇavopāya), the cosmology of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), the doctrine of time (kāla), and the preliminary requirements for initiation (dīkṣā).

summary: The Tantrasāra ('Essence of Tantra') is an influential prose compendium composed by the 10th–11th-century Kashmiri polymath Abhinavagupta as an accessible digest of his monumental encyclopedic treatise, the Tantrāloka. Arranged into 22 āhnikas ('daily lessons'), the work systematically expounds the metaphysics, ritual, yoga, and soteriology of the non-dual Trika and Pratyabhijñā traditions. It is centrally structured around the hierarchy of means to spiritual liberation—anupāya, śāmbhavopāya, śāktopāya, and āṇavopāya—alongside an extensive treatment of the descent of divine grace (śaktipāta) and initiation rituals (dīkṣā).

summary: The Advayatārakopaniṣad is a short Yoga Upaniṣad reckoning as the 53rd text in the Muktikā canon and traditionally belonging to the Śuklayajurveda. It expounds Tārakayoga ('the deliverer yoga'), detailing the meditative absorption in internal and external light signs (antarlakṣya, bahirlakṣya, and madhyamalakṣya), the practice of the śāmbhavī mudrā, and the crossing over of saṃsāra into nondual Brahman. Upaniṣadbrahmayogin's Vivaraṇa interprets the yogic physiology and photic visions in terms of Advaita Vedānta metaphysics.

summary: The Agastyasaṃhitā is a foundational Vaiṣṇava ritual handbook framed as a dialogue between the sage Agastya and his disciple Sutīkṣṇa, incorporating teachings revealed by Śiva to Pārvatī. It expounds the mantras, dhyānas, yantras, dīkṣā procedures, temple rituals, and seasonal festivals centering on Rāma alongside Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, and Hanūmān. Dating between the 10th and 12th centuries CE, it is among the earliest extant saṃhitās documenting the institutionalized sectarian worship of Rāma.

summary: The Kriyākramadyotikā (frequently cited as Aghoraśivapaddhati) is the foremost ritual handbook of the South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta tradition, composed in 1157/1158 CE by Aghoraśivācārya. It codifies canonical Āgamic procedures for priestly daily and occasional liturgical rituals and remains the standard manual for hereditary śivācāryas. This e-text transmits the paddhati alongside Nirmalamaṇi's 16th-century commentary Prabhā (Asphuṭārthaprakāśikā) up through the Damanavidhi section, covering daily worship, dīkṣā, and annual pavitra- and damana-offering rites.

The Mahotsavavidhi provides exhaustive prescriptions for the temple's annual festival (mahotsava), including flag raising (dhvajārohaṇa), yāgaśālā ceremonies, processional rites, and sacred immersion. The Prāyaścittavidhi outlines expiatory rituals, homas, and rededications for ritual flaws, impurities, and structural disruptions in the Śiva temple.

summary: The Mahotsavavidhi is the section of Aghoraśiva's Kriyākramadyotikā (12th century; Davis dates its completion to 1157 CE) on the 'great festival' (mahotsava) of Śiva temples in the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta tradition. It prescribes the festival day by day: the preliminary rites for Vināyaka and the bull, flag-raising, the drum (bṛhattāla) rite and the sprouting of seeds, worship in the sacrificial pavilion and bali offerings, processions on vehicles and in the chariot, the final bath (tīrtha), flag-lowering and the rites for Caṇḍeśa and the devotees. It closes with shorter monthly, fortnightly, lunar-asterism and weekday festivals. Richard H. Davis translated it into English (2010).

summary: An anonymous Kashmiri ritual manual (paddhati) for the fire ritual (agnikārya/homa) in a Bhairava/Kaula-oriented Śaiva setting. It begins with worship of Pustakavāgīśvarī (Sarasvatī) and Gaṇapati, kalaśa worship, purification of the subtle body, and preparation and consecration of the kuṇḍa and fire. It then gives oblation and tarpaṇa sequences for many deities, including Durgā, the Lokeśas and the planets, and ends with an incomplete section on animal sacrifice. The Muktabodha description stresses its incidental information on Kashmiri cults, e.g. the goddess Siddhalakṣmī. The e-text is long (c. 224,000 characters), even though Muktabodha calls it 'short'.

summary: The Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā is an important theological and ritual text of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, presented as a revelatory discourse taught by Ahirbudhnya (Śiva) to Nārada. This first volume (adhyāyas 1–36) details the cosmogony and metaphysics of the school, emphasizing the six divine attributes (ṣaḍguṇa), the emanations of Viṣṇu (vyūhas), and the cosmogenetic activity of his śakti embodied in the Sudarśana cakra. It also includes comprehensive treatises on mantravidyā, yoga, royal apotropaic rituals, and military/weapon sorcery (astramantra).

summary: The Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā is a foundational scripture of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, presented as an exposition given by Ahirbudhnya (Śiva as an enlightened devotee and manifestation of Saṃkarṣaṇa) to the sage Nārada. This second volume covers chapters 37 through 60, focusing on the esoteric iconography and worship of the sixteen-armed Sudarśana, mantra diagrams (yantras), royal protection rituals, the philosophy and six limbs of self-surrender (nyāsa/prapatti), and a significant survey of classical philosophical systems (including the Ṣaṣṭitantra tradition of Sāṃkhya and Yoga). The volume concludes with an appendix containing the Śrīsudarśanasahasranāmastotra.

summary: The Matatrayaikyaprakāśikā ('Illumination of the Unity of the Three Systems', also titled Trimataikyaprakāśikā) is an 18th-century Vedāntic treatise by Aiyyaṇācārya, an adherent of Dvaita Vedānta and direct disciple of Vasudhendra Tīrtha (fl. 1750–1761 CE). In three chapters (paricchedas), the work undertakes an irenic harmonization of the three major Vedāntic traditions—Advaita (Śaṅkara), Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja), and Dvaita (Madhvācārya)—arguing that the primary tenets of Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita ultimately accord with the Dvaita siddhānta [37-38]. The text offers rare late-medieval testimony to inter-school Vedāntic reconciliation from an explicitly Dvaita perspective.

summary: The Amṛtabindūpaniṣad (also known as the Brahmabindūpaniṣad) is a concise Yoga Upaniṣad in 22 verses expounding the nature and control of the mind as the prime cause of bondage and liberation (mana eva manuṣyāṇāṃ kāraṇaṃ bandhamokṣayoḥ). It distinguishes the impure mind trapped in desires from the pure mind free of conceptualization, teaching the dissolution of thought into the soundless (aśabda) Brahman through meditation on the praṇava (Om). In this e-text, the root text is accompanied verse-by-verse by the complete Vivaraṇa commentary of Upaniṣadbrahmayogin (18th c.), who provides a non-dual Advaita Vedāntic interpretation and concludes by identifying the transcendental Brahman with Vāsudeva.

summary: The Amṛtanādopaniṣad is a classical Yoga Upaniṣad affiliated with the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda that outlines a sixfold yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga: pratyāhāra, dhyāna, prāṇāyāma, dhāraṇā, tarka, and samādhi). It uses the allegory of ascending the chariot of Oṃkāra to transcend worldly existence, details breath retention measured by specific mātrā counts, and describes the ascent of prāṇa through the crown of the head as the path to immortality. Upaniṣadbrahmayogin's commentary (Vivaraṇa) integrates these yogic techniques into an Advaita Vedāntic framework culminating in non-dual Self-realization.

summary: The Amṛteśatantra (commonly known as the Netratantra) is an influential Śaiva tantra dedicated to the worship of Amṛteśa / Mṛtyuñjaya and Amṛtalakṣmī. Across 24 chapters, it presents mantric procedures, yogic visualizations, initiation (dīkṣā), and extensive rites for pacification, healing, royal protection, and liberation. This e-text is a diplomatic transcription of an early dated palm-leaf manuscript from Nepal copied in Nepāla Saṃvat 320 (c. 1101 CE).

summary: The Amṛteśvaradīkṣāvidhi is a Śaiva ritual manual (paddhati/ṭippaṇaka) detailing the initiation procedures (dīkṣā) according to the Amṛteśvarabhairava (Netratantra) cult, composed by Viśveśvara. It opens with verses emphasizing the rarity and value of human birth and the impermanence of the body, before systematically setting forth the purification of tattvas, kalās, and cosmic realms (bhuvanas) necessary to liberate the disciple.

summary: The Anādivīraśaivasārasaṅgraha by Saṃpādanasiddhavīra is a Vīraśaiva theological compendium vindicating the antiquity (anāditva) of the Vīraśaiva tradition. It integrates scriptural citations from Vedic, Āgamic, and Purāṇic literature with expository prose, articulating doctrines of the aṣṭāvaraṇa and ṣaṭsthala. This first volume encompasses chapters 1 through 8, culminating in the Viśvotpattisthala.

summary: The Siddhāntasārāvalī of Trilocanaśivācārya (12th c.) is a verse compendium of Śaiva Siddhānta doctrine and ritual, arranged in the four pādas: jñāna, kriyā, yoga and caryā. Anantaśambhu's commentary explains it with extensive quotations from the Siddhāntāgamas and ritual manuals. Its topics include the categories pati, paśu and pāśa, the tattvas, daily and occasional worship, initiation (dīkṣā), yoga, and festivals and pratiṣṭhā (installation). This e-text transcribes a single incomplete and partly disordered IFP palm-leaf manuscript.

summary: The Aniruddhasaṃhitā is a Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava āgama in 34 chapters framed as a discourse given by the sage Bhṛgu on Mount Himavat. It covers the core ritual and temple curriculum of the tradition: initiation (dīkṣā), yantras and maṇḍalas, town and temple layout, iconometry and image consecration (pratiṣṭhā), daily and annual festival liturgies (mahotsava, pavitrārohaṇa, etc.), expiatory rites (prāyaścitta), and the installation of Viṣvaksena and the Āḻvārs/devotees (bhakta).

summary: A South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta funerary manual for initiates, transcribed from a single palm-leaf bundle. Its main part is the funeral 'with purification of the paths' (adhvaśuddhiyutāntyeṣṭi) for ācāryas, sādhakas and putrakas. It includes the post-mortem initiation (mṛtakadīkṣā) with the purification of the four kalās and their tattvas, bhuvanas, varṇas, padas and mantras, followed by cremation, and its colophon assigns it to Aghoraśiva's Kriyākramadyotikā. Further rites follow, each with its own colophon: Rudrabali, the setting up of the stone (pāṣāṇa), Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, and a short rite for a samayin.

summary: The Śivārcanacandrikā ('Moonlight on the Worship of Śiva') is a comprehensive ritual manual (paddhati) composed by the 16th-century South Indian polymath Appayadīkṣita for his patron Cinna Bomma Nāyaka of Vellore. Designed to instruct initiated householders and sovereigns in personal daily Śiva worship (ātmārthapūjā), the manual synthesizes prescriptions from Śaiva Siddhānta Āgamas and Smārta-Śaiva liturgies (relying heavily on Nīlakaṇṭhaśivācārya's Kriyāsāra). It covers all primary stages of worship, including preliminary purification (pañcaśuddhi), mental preparation, installation of the deity, linga worship, naivedya, and rules concerning ritual remnants (nirmālya).

summary: The Bṛhannīlatantra ('Great Nīla Tantra') is an important Kaula Śākta ritual work in 24 chapters (paṭalas) framed as an esoteric dialogue between Mahākālabhairava and the Goddess. Centered on the worship of the Mahāvidyās Tārā (specifically Nīlasarasvatī / Ugratārā) and Kālī, the text details mantras, yantras, dīkṣā procedures, puraścaryā, kavacas, and sahasranāmas. It also contains significant material on the Mahācīnācāra path, vīrasādhana, alchemical transmutation (rasaśāstra / dhātuvāda), and the worship of Annapūrṇā.

summary: Excerpts from the temple-festival (mahotsava) portion of the Kriyākramadyotikā of Aghoraśiva (12th c.), the most authoritative South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta paddhati, transcribed from a palm-leaf bundle. The excerpts cover the bṛhattāla rite (with its drum rhythms and invocations of the guardians of the directions), the navasandhi, monthly, full-moon and asterism festivals, a pacificatory fire rite (śāntihoma) and a long section on expiation (prāyaścitta) for ritual faults and pollution. It ends with an incomplete instruction on the fivefold seat worship (pañcāsana) and Āgama citations on Śivarātri.

It details the Brahmāstra mantra formulae, yantra diagrams, nyāsa rites, dhyāna visualizations, and praise-hymns primarily aimed at stambhana (immobilization/paralysis of enemies and obstacles), protection, and spiritual accomplishment.

It systematically catalogues the esoteric names, deities, bodily locations, and symbolic code-words associated with each syllable of the Sanskrit alphabet (mātṛkā)—from oṃkāra and a to kṣa—serving as a key for mantroddhāra (the deciphering and construction of secret mantras encoded in tantric treatises).

The text is preserved in a single unique manuscript witness held in Jammu.

summary: An anonymous Śākta tantra in 17 paṭalas, a dialogue between Śrīdevī and Īśvara. It treats the preliminaries of Tantric worship as a 'triad' (tattvatraya) of bhūtaśuddhi, nyāsa and prāṇāyāma, together with inner bathing and inner sandhyā, ajapā recitation, kuṇḍalinī and the six cakras, the dissolution of the 24 tattvas and inner worship. It ends with a praise of the book itself and a short prose summary of the bhūtaśuddhi procedure. Its date is uncertain; it belongs to the late, Bengal-centred layer of Śākta tantra literature.

The author, a Śrīvidyā initiate living in late seventeenth- or eighteenth-century Kashmir, provides an accessible prose elucidation (gadyamārgānusāriṇī) of Utpaladeva's verses. The unique surviving manuscript testifies to the pedagogical continuation and exegetical synthesis of the non-dual Pratyabhijñā system in pre-modern Kashmir.

summary: The Stavacintāmaṇi ('Wish-Fulfilling Gem of Hymns') is a 120-verse devotional hymn to Lord Śiva by Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa, synthesizing non-dual Kashmiri Śaiva metaphysics (Pratyabhijñā and Spanda) with ecstatic devotional surrender (bhakti). It extols Śiva and his Śakti as the pulsating supreme consciousness underlying the unfolding of speech (vāc) and the cosmos. Kṣemarāja's Vivṛti provides an extensive philosophical commentary elucidating the verses in terms of Trika and Spanda doctrines.

summary: The Vyomavyāpistava is a Śaiva Siddhānta hymn of 90 āryā stanzas expounding the theological and esoteric significance of the 81 distinct words (padas) that form the 368-syllable Vyomavyāpin mantra. Structured around liturgical worship on the nine-lotus mandala (navanābhamaṇḍala) documented in Āgamas such as the Mataṅga and Devīkālottara, the stanzas explain each pada as a manifestation of Paramaśiva. It is preserved here with the concise Laghuṭīkā of the 16th-century Cidambaram theologian Vedajñāna II, which provides word-by-word grammatical and ritual glosses.

summary: The Bhadrakālīpratiṣṭhāvidhi is a Tantric ritual manual (paddhati) for the consecration and installation (pratiṣṭhā/sthāpana) of the fierce goddess Bhadrakālī (identified in the opening verses as Cāmuṇḍā) in villages, towns, or sacred groves. It outlines the ritual calendar, construction and purification of the sacrificial pavilion (yāgaśālā) and fire-pits (kuṇḍa), gatekeeper invocations (toraṇapūjā), vase installations (kalaśasthāpana), nyāsa systems, mantras, and the culminating installation rites.

summary: The Sarvatobhadra is a 10th-century non-dualist commentary on the Bhagavadgītā by Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha, a prominent Kashmirian Pratyabhijñā scholar and disciple of Utpaladeva. Based on the distinct Kashmirian recension of the Gītā, Rāmakaṇṭha interprets Kṛṣṇa's instruction to Arjuna through an integrated philosophy of non-dual consciousness, synthesizing action (karma) and knowledge (jñāna) as inseparable dimensions of spiritual release. This digital text contains the root text and commentary for chapters 1 through 14.

summary: The Gītārthasaṃgraha is Abhinavagupta's philosophical commentary on the Bhagavadgītā written from the perspective of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism (Pratyabhijñā). It interprets Kṛṣṇa's instruction to Arjuna as a revelation of supreme non-dual consciousness (anuttara-saṃvid), synthesizing action (karma), knowledge (jñāna), and devotion (bhakti) as integrated expressions of divine sovereignty and self-awareness (svātantrya). The work reflects the Kashmirian recension of the Bhagavadgītā, containing distinct textual variants and additional verses.

summary: The Spandapradīpikā is an exegetical commentary on the Spandakārikā composed by Bhagavatutpala (Utpala Vaiṣṇava) of Kashmir, probably active around the tenth century. The commentary is notable for its syncretic perspective, interpreting non-dual Śaiva Spanda concepts through the lens of Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava theology and citing early canonical saṃhitās such as the Jayākhya, Sātvata, Pauṣkara, and Ahirbudhnya.

summary: The Varivasyārahasya ('Secret of Worship') is an influential 18th-century manual of Śrīvidyā theology, mantra-śāstra, and internal contemplative worship composed in 167 verses across two divisions (aṃśas) by the polymath Bhāskararāya Makhin, accompanied by his autocommentary, the Prakāśa. The text provides an exhaustive esoteric analysis of the fifteen-syllable Śrīvidyā mantra (pañcadaśākṣarī), demonstrating how each letter and component encodes cosmological principles, subtle yogic centers, deities, and philosophical correspondences across multiple hermeneutical registers (such as bhāvārtha, sampradāyārtha, nigarbhārtha, and mahātattvārtha). Synthesizing Śākta ritual theology with Advaita Vedānta, Bhāskararāya argues that the culmination of mantra worship is the non-dual realization of identity between the practitioner, the mantra, and the supreme Goddess (Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī) as pure consciousness.

summary: This compendium contains four esoteric Śākta/Kaula Upaniṣads—the Bhāvanopaniṣad, the Bahvṛcopaniṣad (here called Bahvṛcavedīyā Śrīlalitāmahātripurasundaryupaniṣad), the Devyatharvaśīrṣopaniṣad, and the Kaulopaniṣad—along with commentaries and liturgical instructions (prayogavidhi) by the 18th-century Śrīvidyā scholar Bhāskararāya. The texts formulate a nondual synthesis of Kaula ritual and Vedāntic metaphysics, equating the goddess Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī with absolute consciousness, the cosmos, the Śrīcakra, and the psychophysical body of the practitioner. Bhāskararāya's commentary internalizes esoteric Kaula worship as contemplative meditation (bhāvanā) on the identity between macrocosm and microcosm.

summary: The Sādhanamālā ('Garland of Sādhanas') is a prominent 11th–12th century anthology of Buddhist Vajrayāna ritual and meditation texts detailing the iconography, mantras, and visualization techniques for numerous tantric deities (such as Kurukullā, Vajravārāhī, Vajrayoginī, Mahāmāyā, Kṛṣṇayamāri, and Jambhala). Volume 2 contains sādhanas 171 through 312, many attributed to renowned Mahāsiddhas or extracted from Anuttarayoga tantric cycles. It serves as an indispensable reference work for the iconography, liturgy, and yogic practice of late Indian Buddhist Tantra.

summary: The Tattvaprakāśa ('Illumination of the Principles') is a canonical verse primer of Śaiva Siddhānta metaphysics traditionally attributed to King Bhojadeva of Dhārā (early 11th c.). The work systematically sets forth the dualist Siddhānta system structured by the three categories of Pati (Śiva), Paśu (individual souls), and Pāśa (bonds), mapping the unfolding of the 36 tattvas across the pure and impure realms. This digital text pairs the kārikās with two principal commentaries: Aghoraśivācārya's 12th-century Vṛtti, which rigorously defends classical dualist Siddhānta against monistic readings, and Śrīkumāra's Tātparyadīpikā, which seeks to harmonize Siddhānta philosophy with orthodox Vaidika and Mīmāṃsaka tenets.

summary: An early Śaiva Siddhānta ritual manual (paddhati) ascribed in its colophons to King Bhojadeva of Dhārā (11th c.). It is preserved here in an old Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript that has lost its opening leaves. It covers the daily rite (with the Sūrya worship that precedes Śiva worship), mudrās, expiation, the samaya- and nirvāṇa-initiations, the consecration of sādhaka and ācārya, the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan), the pavitraka festival, the installation of temple, liṅga, door, 'heart' and flagstaff, and the renovation of damaged images (jīrṇoddhāra). Sanderson has shown that the later Somaśambhupaddhati depends on it.

summary: The Tārārahasya ('Secret of Tārā') by the 16th-century Śākta master Brahmānandagiri is a fundamental ritual manual (nibandha) dedicated to the worship, mantras, and meditative forms (dhyāna) of the Mahāvidyā Tārā and her manifestations (such as Ugratārā, Nīlasarasvatī, and Ekajaṭā). Divided into four chapters (paṭalas), it incorporates both normative tantric ritual procedures and the esoteric Mahācīnakrama. Synthesizing citations from older authorities such as the Nīlatantra, Mahācīnatantra, and Rudrayāmala, it served as one of the primary handbooks of the Tārā cult across Bengal and Assam.

summary: The Tārārahasyavṛtti (or Tārārahasyavṛttikā) is a 15-chapter Śākta ritual manual focusing on the cult of Tārā and her related forms (Mahānīlasarasvatī, Ugratārā, Ekajaṭā). Authored by the Bengali tantric writer Śaṅkara, the text systematizes daily worship (nityapūjā), initiation (dīkṣā), preliminary recitation (puraścaraṇa), desire-oriented rites (kāmya), kumārī worship, stotras, oblations (homa), and esoteric contemplative meanings (vāsanā) drawn from scriptures like the Nīlatantra, Matsyasūkta, and Vīratantra.

summary: The Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī ('River of the Bliss of Śakti') is an influential 16th-century Śākta tantric digest (nibandha) composed by the Bengali master Brahmānandagiri in eighteen chapters (ullāsas). It provides a comprehensive manual of Tantric ritual and philosophy, synthesizing esoteric doctrine with practice and preserving extensive citations from earlier tantric texts that are otherwise lost. Topics covered across the eighteen ullāsas include subtle physiology and the subtle body, initiation (dīkṣā), yogic practice and Kuṇḍalinī, morning duties, āsana, internal and external worship (antaryāga and bahiryāga), rosaries and mantra-japa, protective sets (setu, mahāsetu, kullukā), puraścaraṇa, yantra and bali offerings, prāyaścitta, and homa rites.

summary: An anonymous Śaiva yoga text in which Śiva instructs Skanda. It covers the subtle body (the nine doors, nāḍīs such as piṅgalā and suṣumṇā, the vital winds), the 'joining to brahman' (brahmasandhāna) through the brahmadvāra, and yogic exit at death (utkrānti). It also treats the cosmogony from cicchakti, the composition of the human body, the nāda as brahman, and a purely mental worship (mānasayāga) with bathing at the inner Śivatīrtha. It closes with an internal fire worship (agnipūjā), in which the five breaths are offered into the fire in the heart.

summary: The Brahmavidyopaniṣad is a minor Yoga Upaniṣad of the Muktikā canon (canonically numbered 40), affiliated with the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It sets forth the esoteric meditation upon Brahman by means of the sacred syllable Om (praṇava) and the haṃsa mantra, analyzing the constituent acoustic elements (mātrās), bodily loci, internal resonance (nāda), and dissolution into non-dual consciousness. This e-text provides the complete 110 verses accompanied by the Advaita Vedānta commentary (Vivaraṇa) of Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: A South Indian ritual text for the temple cult of Bhadrakālī/Cāmuṇḍā and the Seven Mothers, styled a part of the 'Brahmayāmala in 100,000 verses'. It opens with the myth of the Mothers and Bhadrakālī killing the demon Dāruka. In 51 paṭalas it covers the festival of the Mothers, choice of site, iconography, temple building and installation, nyāsa, initiation, fire ritual, festivals, bali offerings, snapana, maṇḍalas, mudrās, renovation, caste rules for the temple (kṣetrācāra), the installation of tridents (śūla), expiation and funerary rules. Sanderson uses it as evidence for the civic role of Śaiva/Śākta officiants in settlement planning.

summary: The Candrāvalokana is a short Haṭhayogic tract framed as a dialogue between Maheśvara (Śiva) and Matsyendranātha. It is best known in yoga historiography as a key early source for the definition of śāmbhavīmudrā and the absorption (laya) of mind and breath, famously cited in chapter 4 of the Haṭhapradīpikā. It interprets esoteric yogic gazes through lunar allegories (amāvāsyā, pratipad, and paurṇamāsī).

summary: The Candrajñānāgama (or Candrajñāna) is a Śaiva revealed text framed as a teaching imparted on Mount Kailāsa by Śiva (Bhairava) to Candra. Distressed by the transient and illusory nature of worldly phenomena (māyā, indrajāla) and questioning the efficacy of conventional ritual and verbalized mantras, Candra receives esoteric instruction resolving these doubts into transcendent non-dual awareness. This digital text represents a diplomatic transcription of Banaras Hindu University MS C4243 (fols. 55a–67b).

summary: A compilation of chapters from the South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta scripture Candrajñāna, preserved in an IFP transcript. It covers the esoteric meaning of the five-syllable mantra (pañcākṣara) and temple festivals (utsava, mahotsava with flag-hoisting). It also gives the installation of Lakṣmī, the Ārdrā and Śivarātri observances, bali offerings, detailed impurity rules (āśauca) by caste and occupation, and a closing doctrinal chapter on knowledge (jñānadarśana) of the tattvas and liberation as union with Śiva (sāyujya).

summary: The Candrajñānāgama is the nineteenth of the canonical twenty-eight Śaiva Siddhāntāgamas and the ninth among the Rudrabhedas, transmitted in the Vīraśaiva tradition. Framed as an exposition delivered by Anantarudra to Bṛhaspati, this recension comprises the Kriyāpāda (twelve chapters) and Caryāpāda (eight chapters). The text outlines fundamental Śaiva metaphysics (Pati, Paśu, and Pāśa) and details distinctively Vīraśaiva observances, including the eight protective emblems (aṣṭāvaraṇa), the five codes of conduct (pañcācāra), daily rituals (āhnika), and death and funeral rites (śivamedha/aurdhvadehika).

summary: The Carcāstava is the second hymn of the prominent Kashmiri Śākta hymnological pentad, the Pañcastavī. Consisting of 31 stanzas addressed to Mahātripurasundarī, it synthesizes non-dual Kashmiri Śaiva/Śākta philosophy (Trika and Krama) with Śrīvidyā theology, celebrating the Goddess as supreme luminous and reflective awareness (parāvāc, vimarśa). This e-text provides the hymn together with the extensive Sanskrit commentary (ṭīkā/vivaraṇa) by the 20th-century Kashmiri pandit Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī.

summary: The Caturvedārthatātparyasaṃgraha (commonly known as the Śrutisūktimālā) is a 150-verse Śaiva philosophical and polemical work composed by Haradatta. Through an exegesis of Vedic passages, mantras, and Upaniṣadic texts, Haradatta demonstrates that Lord Śiva is the supreme Brahman and the ultimate purism (tātparya) of the four Vedas, defending Śaiva theism against rival school interpretations.

summary: The Vīraśaivotkarṣapradīpikā ('Illumination of the Excellence of Vīraśaivism') is a doctrinal polemical and theological treatise composed in mixed prose and verse by Sudhāpurastha Cannabasaveśvarasvāmin, affiliated with the Toṇṭada and Murughā Vīraśaiva lineages. Written in response to doctrinal questions raised by a scholar named Murughāya, it defends the Vedic status and spiritual supremacy of Vīraśaiva philosophy and practice, drawing upon Upaniṣadic, Purāṇic, and Śaivāgama authorities to elucidate key tenets such as the ṣaṭsthala, aṣṭāvaraṇa, pañcācāra, and atyāśrama. The e-text concludes with a brief excerpt from the thirteenth chapter of Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya's Kriyāsāra concerning qualifications for Śaiva consecration.

summary: The Svacchandapaddhati by Cidānandanātha (fl. c. 1375–1425) is an extensive Kaula Śrīvidyā ritual manual organized in nine chapters (spandas). Contrary to its title, which often leads to confusion with the Trika/Bhairava cult of the Svacchandatantra, the manual is dedicated to the esoteric daily worship (nityapūjā) of Goddess Mahātripurasundarī and the Śrīcakra. It provides systematic liturgical instructions covering morning rites, bodily and elemental purification (bhūtaśuddhi), complex nyāsa procedures (including the mahāṣoḍhānyāsa), vessel preparation (pātrāsādana), and the sequential worship of the nine enclosures (āvaraṇas) of the Śrīyantra.

summary: The Cinmayadīkṣāvidhāna is an anonymous Śaiva ritual manual (paddhati / vidhāna), closely aligned with the Vīraśaiva tradition, detailing the rite of consciousness-pervaded initiation (cinmayadīkṣā) and the accompanying worship and wearing of the liṅga (liṅgadhāraṇa). It lays down rules for constructing the ritual pavilion (maṇḍapa) and fire-altars (kuṇḍa), performing preliminary purifications and nyāsas, and administering the mantras aimed at effecting the identity of the soul with Śiva (śivajīvaikya).

summary: The Yantracintāmaṇi is a widely cited medieval Sanskrit tantric treatise on yantras composed by Dāmodara, son of Gaṅgādhara. Structured as a dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara upon Mount Kailāsa, the work provides detailed instructions for constructing, inscribing, and ritually activating yantras across eight principal sections corresponding to the ṣaṭkarman (vaśya, ākarṣaṇa, stambhana, vidveṣaṇa, māraṇa, uccāṭana) as well as rites for pacification (śānti), protection (rakṣā), and liberation from physical confinement (bandhamokṣa).

summary: A long Vaiṣṇava tantra that teaches the worship of Rāma, son of Daśaratha, as the supreme brahman. It is framed as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga's teaching to Śatānanda and other sages and styles itself a 'compendium of the meaning of the Veda' (Vedārthasaṃgraha). The first part (59 chapters) treats cosmology, dharma, mantra, initiation, puraścaraṇa and worship. The second part (45 chapters), with the sections Saubhāgyavidyodaya and Rājavidyāmāhātmya, adds strongly Śākta material, including Śrīcakra worship and the Rājarājeśvarī and Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa vidyās. The e-text is a transcription of a single Jammu manuscript.

summary: An anonymous Kashmiri manual for Śaiva (Bhairava-oriented) initiation, which Muktabodha describes as showing an intensely tantric local pantheon like Nepal's. The surviving part covers the preparatory days in detail: purification of the officiant, kalaśa installation, fire consecration, caru, and preparation of the disciple. It also maps the six paths (kalās, tattvas, bhuvanas) onto the disciple's body and gives the dream rite of the adhivāsa night. It then begins the third day (interpretation of dreams, drawing of the maṇḍala) before breaking off. Extensive marginal glosses in the manuscript are transcribed in round brackets.

summary: The Dīkṣottaraprakaraṇa constitutes the concluding nineteen-chapter section of the Niśvāsakārikā, an early metrical scripture of the Niśvāsa corpus of the Mantramārga. It systematically covers the rites and theology of tantric initiation (dīkṣā), the purification of the six cosmic pathways (ṣaḍadhvan), and interiorized yogic absorptions (lakṣya). The work represents an indispensable transitional witness for the development of classical Śaivasiddhānta ritual liturgy.

summary: The Darśanopaniṣad is one of the twenty minor Yoga Upaniṣads in the Muktikā canon, affiliated with the Sāmaveda. Framed as an instructional dialogue between Dattātreya and Sāṃkṛti, it details an eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga) integrated with Advaita Vedānta, covering the ten yamas and niyamas, āsanas, the subtle anatomy of fourteen principal nāḍīs and ten prāṇas, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi. This e-text presents the root Upaniṣad along with the Vivaraṇa of Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: The Dattātreyabodha is a Sanskrit yoga manual framed as a dialogue between the sage Dattātreya and his pupil Sāṅkṛti. Textual research by James Mallinson has shown that it represents a shortened South Indian recension of the early Haṭhayoga treatise Dattātreyayogaśāstra (ca. 13th century), focusing specifically on eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga) and rājayoga while omitting sections on mantrayoga, layayoga, and the haṭhayoga of Kapila. The work is celebrated for its egalitarian approach, teaching that anyone—regardless of age, disease, or religious affiliation—can attain yogic success through sustained practice rather than mere sectarian insignia or textual recitation.

summary: The Dattātreyatantra is a practical tantric handbook devoted to occult rituals and the sixfold magic acts (ṣaṭkarman). Structured as an inquiry by Dattātreya answered by Śiva on Mount Kailāsa, it details incantations, herbal preparations, and yantras for pacification, subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa), eradication (uccāṭana), and lethal destruction (māraṇa), concluding with formulas for warding off wild beasts, serpents, and poisons.

summary: A Kashmiri Śākta devotional booklet. It opens with a liturgy for the worship of the Goddess (Durgāpūjā) that invokes the Kashmiri goddesses Śārikā, Mahārājñī, Jvālāmukhī and others, with seat purification, nyāsa, invocation and offerings. A Sanskrit hymn to Mahārājñī (Khīr Bhavānī) by Paṇḍita Kṛṣṇa(kavi) follows. Then comes a collection of mystical sayings (vākyamañjarī) of the Kashmiri saint Rūpa Bhavānī (Alakṣyeśvarī), largely in Kashmiri and opening with a 'Nirvāṇadaśaka'. A ten-verse Sarasvatīstuti closes the booklet.

summary: The Devīrahasya is a Śākta tantric digest and ritual compilation framed as part of the Rudrayāmala, composed in Kashmir. It is structured into a Pūrvārdha of 25 paṭalas dealing with initiation, mantra vitalization and unlocking, puraścaraṇa, yantras, and ritual ingredients, followed by an Uttarārdha of 35 paṭalas providing pañcāṅgas (paṭala, kavaca, paddhati, sahasranāma, and stotra) for various deities. The appended text is the Uddhārakośa of Dakṣiṇāmūrtimuni, a 7-kalpa lexicon defining and deciphering tantric mantras.

summary: The Mantrakaumudī ('Moonlight of Mantras') is a 16th-century Maithila Tantric nibandha (ritual digest) by Mahāmahopādhyāya Devanātha Ṭhakkura Tarkapañcānana. Synthesizing citations from nearly one hundred earlier Tantric and Purāṇic works, it systematically covers guru-śiṣya qualifications, initiation (dīkṣā), the construction and use of rosaries (akṣamālā), ritual repetition (puraścaraṇa), nyāsa, and mantra-sādhana procedures. The work was influential in the Mithila Smārta-Tāntrika tradition for codifying mantra practice free of heterodox Vāmācāra rites.

summary: The Śāktapramoda ('Delight of the Śāktas') is a comprehensive late 19th-century liturgical digest (paddhati) compiled by Rājā Devanandanasiṃha Bahādur of Sheohar, Bihar, completed in 1889/1890 CE. It gathers sixteen distinct ritual manuals ('tantras'): ten dedicated to the Ten Mahāvidyās (Kālī, Tārā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Chinnamastā, Tripurabhairavī, Dhūmāvatī, Bagalāmukhī, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalā), one dedicated to maiden worship (Kumārītantra), and five to the Pañcāyatana deities (Śiva, Durgā, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, and Viṣṇu). For each deity, the manual provides iconographic meditation verses (dhyāna), mantra extraction procedures (mantroddhāra), yantra diagrams, nyāsa rites, daily worship sequences (saparyāpaddhati), kavacas, hṛdaya stotras, and litanies of names (śatanāma and sahasranāma) compiled from classical tantric scriptures.

summary: The Dhyānabindūpaniṣad is one of the classical Yoga Upaniṣads, focusing on the practice and philosophy of dhyāna (meditation) and nada-yoga. It expounds meditation on the sacred syllable Om (praṇava) along with its constituent mātrās, bindu, and nāda, the sixfold yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga), the nature of the jīva, and the awakening of Kuṇḍalinī to achieve non-dual liberation. The Vivaraṇa commentary by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin interprets the yogic terminology and practices from an Advaita Vedānta perspective of pure consciousness (brahmamātra).

summary: The Dhyānaratnāvalī ('Jewel-Garland of Meditative Visualizations') is a twelfth-century Śaiva Siddhānta digest attributed to Trilocanaśivācārya. It compiles iconographic visualization verses (dhyānaślokas) detailing the forms, attributes, weapons, postures, and retinues of Śiva, Devī, accompanying deities, cosmic principles (tattvas), kalās, and subtle somatic channels. The compendium functioned as an essential reference manual for Śaiva temple priests and practitioners during daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) worship.

summary: The Gautamatantra (also known as Gautamīyatantra) is a prominent Vaiṣṇava (Kṛṣṇaite) tantric text framed as a dialogue between Gautama and Nārada. It focuses upon the theology, mantra practice, and ritual worship of Kṛṣṇa, especially the ten-syllable Gopālamantra (gopījanavallabhāya svāhā). The text treats initiation (dīkṣā), nyāsa, dhyāna, yantras, and ritual attainment (siddhi), and was frequently cited by later Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava authorities including Sanātana Gosvāmin and Jīva Gosvāmin.

summary: The Gorakṣaśataka ('Century of Verses of Gorakṣa') is a foundational Sanskrit manual of early Haṭhayoga attributed to the Nātha master Gorakṣanātha. This particular recension, recorded and translated by G. W. Briggs (1938), consists of 101 verses describing postures (specifically siddhāsana and padmāsana), the subtle channels and energy centers (nāḍīs and cakras), kuṇḍalinī, and breath regulation (prāṇāyāma and nāḍīśodhana). Text-historically, it represents the first half (pūrva-śataka) of the 200-verse work known as the Gorakṣapaddhati, differing substantially in structure and content from the recension critically edited by Kuvalayananda and Shukla.

summary: The Gorakṣaguṭikā ('Pill/Amulet of Gorakṣa') is a late Nātha liturgical and mythological text framed as a Tantric Haragaurīsaṃvāda (dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī), claiming affiliation to the Kalpadrumavivekinī (or Kalpadrumasaṃhitā). Unlike standard Haṭha Yoga treatises, it centers on devotional ritual and Guru worship, recounting the miraculous birth and deeds of Gorakṣanātha in its opening chapter, followed by protective kavacas, mantras, and stotras (including his dvādaśanāma, aṣṭottaraśatanāma, and sahasranāma) across nine chapters (taraṅgas).

summary: The Gorakṣayogaśāstra (also called Mūlasāra) is a short Nātha yoga text of 65 verses framed in the style of a stotra/saṃvāda opened by Īśvara. summary: The Guhyasamājatantra is the foundational scripture of the Buddhist Mahāyoga / Anuttarayoga tantric class, centered on Akṣobhya and the fivefold Buddha family maṇḍala. Structured in eighteen chapters, it details deity visualization, mantras, ritual enactments, and subtle-body meditation forming the basis of generation (utpattikrama) and completion (niṣpannakrama) stage yogas. Celebrated for its paradoxical, antinomian imagery representing non-dual gnosis, it gave rise to two prominent Indian exegetical schools: the Jñānapāda school and the Ārya school.

summary: The Haṃsopaniṣad is a minor Yoga Upaniṣad associated with the Śukla Yajurveda (Muktikā #15), framed as an esoteric dialogue between Gautama and Sanatkumāra on haṃsavidyā as the prerequisite to Brahmavidyā. It elaborates on the ajapā-mantra ('haṃsa'/'so'ham') in relation to the rhythm of breath, the eight psychic attitudes conditioned by the petals of the heart lotus (anāhatacakra), and internal meditative absorption through the progressive manifestation of ten internal sounds (nāda). Upaniṣadbrahmayogin's 18th-century Vivaraṇa commentary interprets these subtle yogic and Haṭhayogic disciplines through the lens of strict Advaita Vedānta (sarvāpahnava), culminating in the realization of non-dual Brahman as the Paramahaṃsa.

This initial section (Ādikāṇḍa, paṭalas 1–14) covers the mythical descent of the text, site examination (bhūmisaṅgraha), soil purification, layout of the vāstumaṇḍala, laying of the foundation stone (iṣṭakānyāsa), and placement of primary sanctum deities.

summary: The Kaulāvalīnirṇaya is a major Kaula Śākta ritual compendium (tantranibandha) composed by Jñānānandaparamahaṃsa (also calling himself Jñānānandagiri). In 21 chapters (ullāsas), it synthesizes teachings and citations from numerous Tantric authorities on guru and disciple qualifications, initiation (dīkṣā), daily and esoteric worship, the ritual use of the five substances (pañcamakāra / kuladravya), cakra pūjā, Kuṇḍalinī yoga, and the status of an avadhūta.

summary: The Jñānārṇavatantra ('Ocean of Knowledge') is an authoritative scripture of the Śākta Tantric tradition and one of the principal scriptural sources for the Kādi division of Śrīvidyā. Cast in 26 paṭalas as a revelation by Īśvara to Devī, the work begins with esoteric expositions of the sacred alphabet (akṣamālā / mātṛkā), the phonematic matrix, and the threefold bindu. The remaining chapters detail the internal and ritual pūjā of Mahātripurasundarī and her attendants, yantra meditations, mantra recitation, and seasonal observances, culminating in the damanāropaṇa rite.

summary: A brief anonymous Śaiva Siddhānta tract on jñānadīkṣā, initiation through knowledge. It is not identical with the jñānadīkṣā chapters of the Acintyaviśvasādākhya or of Vedajñāna's Dīkṣādarśa, which open with a similar verse.

summary: The Pauṣkaravṛtti is an extensive 16th-century commentary by Jñānaprakāśācārya on the Jñānapāda (metaphysical section) of the Pauṣkarāgama, an authoritative Upāgama belonging to the Pārameśvara cycle of the Śaiva Siddhānta canon. The work expounds Siddhānta metaphysics and epistemology, offering systematic discussions on pati, paśu, pāśa, bindu, the subtle evolution of nāda, and the emergence of determinate cognition (savikalpakajñāna). Along with Umāpati Śivācārya's earlier Pauṣkarabhāṣya, it is one of the two foundational Sanskrit commentaries explaining the philosophical core of the Pauṣkara.

summary: The Prāsādacandrikā is a 16th-century Śaiva Siddhānta manual attributed to Jñānaprakāśa of Kamalālaya (Tiruvārūr). Based on Āgamic sources such as the Suprabhedāgama and Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṃgraha, it details the internal yogic pronunciation (uccāra) of the Prāsādamantra, the seven stages of unification (sāmarasya), internal junctures (viṣuva), and the ascent of consciousness through the cakras and subtle sound centers to Śiva.

summary: The Śivāgamādimāhātmyasaṃgraha is a 16th-century Śaiva Siddhānta doctrinal and apologetic compendium compiled by Jñānaprakāśa of Śālivāṭipura (Tirunelveli). Opening with a philosophical defense of the divine authorship and validity (prāmāṇya) of the Śaivāgamas against Mīmāṃsaka and smārta objections, the text establishes that both the Vedas and the Āgamas are authentic revelations produced by Paramaśiva. It systematically collates passages from the 28 Siddhānta Āgamas, the Upāgamas, the Purāṇas, and the Sūtasaṃhitā to vindicate Āgamic preeminence, the power of Śaiva initiation (śivadīkṣā), the status of devotees (bhaktas), and traditional sectarian observances such as the wearing of tripuṇḍra and rudrākṣa beads.

summary: The Śivāgamādimāhātmyasaṃgraha by Jñānaprakāśa of Śālīvāṭipura is a Saiddhāntika anthology and doctrinal treatise asserting the supreme scriptural authority of the Śaiva Āgamas over rival and non-Śaiva philosophical systems. Gathering testimonies from primary Āgamas (including Pauṣkara, Kāmika, Kiraṇa, and Aṃśumat) as well as Purāṇas, the text explains the emanation of scriptural wisdom as sound (nāda) from Sadāśiva and glorifies Śaiva initiation (dīkṣā), devotional duties, and observances.

summary: The Jñānasāra (also titled Nāthajñānasāra) is a brief anonymous Śaiva-Nātha dialogue between Śiva and Devī concerning the emergence of speech (vāk), mind (manas), and the vital breath (prāṇa). It expounds the nature, bodily loci, and guṇa-manifestations of the individual soul (jīva), contrasting external ritual/textual study with realization of the partless absolute (niṣkala brahma).

summary: The Jñānasaṅkalinītantra ('Tantra of the Collection of Gnosis') is a concise Śākta-Śaiva tantric treatise framed as a dialogue on Mount Kailāsa between Śiva and the Devī. It subordinates external ritualism, caste prescriptions, and scholastic learning to internal non-dual knowledge (brahmajñāna) and subtle yogic contemplation. The text expounds the esoteric anatomy of the body (piṇḍa) as identical to the cosmos (brahmāṇḍa), identifying the internal channels iḍā, piṅgalā, and suṣumnā with sacred rivers (Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī), and explains the symbolic significance of the Praṇava (Oṃ) alongside inner mudrās such as khecarī and śāmbhavī.

The full extent of the work is not known.

summary: A late South Indian Śaiva text calling itself an āgama, which Muktabodha describes as reading more like a tract on miscellaneous topics of Śaiva yoga. It grades sixteen "anta" viewpoints (Vedānta, Siddhānta, Nādānta, Yogānta, etc.), and treats Śiva, the bonds (pāśa), the five avasthās, the eight siddhis and cosmogony, and also names Śākta goddesses such as Kubjikā and Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī. Sanderson (The Śaiva Age, 2009) cites it among works that weave together Śaiva Siddhānta, Vedānta and a Śākta tradition of kuṇḍalinī-yoga and the cult of Tripurā, a combination he considers unlikely to predate the twelfth century.

summary: The Jñānaratnāvalī is a comprehensive 12th-century Śaiva Siddhānta ritual manual (paddhati) composed in Vārāṇasī by Jñānaśiva, a master in the Golakī-maṭha lineage. The work systematically expounds Saiddhāntika ritual praxis, including purificatory rites, daily worship (nityapūjā), the extensive sequence of initiation rituals (dīkṣā), installation (pratiṣṭhā), and seasonal ceremonies. Together with the Somaśambhupaddhati and Aghoraśiva's ritual works, it is one of the most critical textual witnesses for the reconstruction of medieval Śaiva liturgical traditions.

summary: The Stutikusumāñjali ('Flower-offering of Praise') is an acclaimed Śaiva devotional work by the 14th-century Kashmiri poet Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa, comprising 38 hymns (over 1,400 verses) dedicated to Śiva. Renowned for its integration of high classical kāvya aesthetics with devotional intensity, it displays elaborate śleṣa (wordplay), anuprāsa, and metrical dexterity. This e-text presents the complete work accompanied by prose word-order (anvaya) and the Sanskrit commentary Premamakaranda by the 20th-century pandit Premavallabha Tripāṭhī.

summary: The Jayākhyasaṃhitā is one of the oldest and most authoritative canonical scriptures of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, celebrated as one of the three foundational 'jewels' (ratnatraya) alongside the Sātvatasaṃhitā and Pauṣkarasaṃhitā. Spanning 33 paṭalas and roughly 4,500 anuṣṭubh verses, it expounds Vaiṣṇava theology, cosmology, the doctrine of divine emanations (vyūha), mantra systems, initiation (dīkṣā), daily and temple rituals, and yoga aimed at liberation (mukti). The text was widely cited by medieval Indian philosophers and theologians, including Utpaladeva, Abhinavagupta, and Rāmānuja.

summary: The Jayadrathayāmala (also known as the Tantrarājabhaṭṭāraka) is an extensive scriptural text of the Bhairavasrotas and a key authority for the Kālīkula and Krama traditions of Śāktism, organized into four ṣaṭkas. This fourth ṣaṭka, titled the Mudrāṣaṭka, focuses on esoteric ritual systems, ritual hand gestures (mudrās), yantras, and fierce forms of Kālī (notably Rāviṇī and Mahālakṣmī), providing crucial primary evidence for medieval non-dual Śākta-Śaiva ritual theology.

summary: The Mokṣasopāna ('Staircase to Liberation') is a Śākta-Śaiva treatise on esoteric yoga, cakra meditation, and internal worship affiliated with the Kubjikā tradition. It outlines the graded stages of spiritual ascent through the phonic and cosmological hierarchy (from praṇava and subtle sound vibrations up to unmanā) and meditation on the kuṇḍalinī and the goddess Kubjikā/Mahāmāyā. The e-text preserves the root text together with an anonymous prose commentary (Ṭīkā) transcribed directly from a Nepalese manuscript.

summary: The Kākacaṇḍeśvarīmata is an early Śākta-Śaiva alchemical (rasaśāstra) and iatrochemical tantra presented as a dialogue on Mount Kailāsa between Bhairava and the goddess Kākacaṇḍeśvarī (a form of Kālī/Cāmuṇḍā). The text details mercurial processing, calcination, mineral operations, and herbal recipes (kalpas) for rejuvenation (rasāyana) and therapeutic medicine. Preserved in Nepalese manuscripts, it represents an important early stratum in medieval Indian tantric alchemy.

summary: The Kālahastīśavilāsa is a Śaiva theological and polemical treatise written in mixed prose and verse to establish the supremacy (sarvotkarṣa) of Śiva as Kālahastīśa (the presiding deity of Śrīkālahasti). It debates sectarian opponents (chiefly Vaiṣṇavas) by interpreting Vedic, Upaniṣadic, and Purāṇic passages, citing authorities such as Haradatta to argue that terms like Brahman and Parameśvara refer exclusively to Śiva. This e-text contains the first chapter (vilāsa 1), transcribed from IFP/EFEO transcript T0378.

summary: The Kālikāpurāṇa is an influential Śākta Upapurāṇa composed in medieval Kāmarūpa (Assam), generally assigned to the 9th–11th centuries CE. It details the mythology of the Goddess in her manifestations as Kālī, Satī, Pārvatī, and Kāmākhyā, tracing the narrative of Satī's self-immolation and the dispersion of her limbs across sacred pīṭhas. The work serves as a foundational manual for Śākta ritual and worship in northeastern India, containing extensive sections on iconography, mantras, pilgrimage geography, and the famous Rudhirādhyāya on blood sacrifice.

summary: The Kālottaratantra (or Kālottara) is one of the earliest and most influential scriptural authorities of the Śaiva Siddhānta Mantramārga. Transmitted in multiple recensions of differing lengths, its texts provided the foundational mantric, ritual, and yogic framework for medieval Saiddhāntika liturgies and paddhatis. This digital text is a diplomatic transcription of a composite Nepalese paper manuscript preserving seven recensions: the Jñānapañcāśikā, Śatikakālottara (Kālajñāna), Sārdhaśatikakālottara, Dviśatikakālottara, Adhyuṣṭaśatikakālottara (Sārdhatriśatika), Saptaśatikakālottara, and Trayodaśaśatikakālottara.

summary: The Bṛhatkālottara ('Great Kālottara', also known as the Kālottaramahātantra) is the most extensive and encyclopedic redaction of the Kālottara corpus of the Śaiva Siddhānta. Set as a dialogue between Īśvara and Kārtikeya, the text provides exhaustive treatments of initiation (dīkṣā), temple architecture (prāsādalakṣaṇa), iconometry, linga installation (liṅgapratiṣṭhā), expiatory rituals (prāyaścitta), propitiatory ceremonies (śānti), and public festivals such as the damanotsava. Demonstrably later than early Kālottara recensions (such as the Sārdhatriśatikālottara) and dated by scholars to circa the tenth–eleventh century CE, it represents a crucial milestone in the development of public, temple-oriented Śaivism.

summary: A long South Indian recension of the Kālottara, a Śaiva Siddhānta scripture known in many recensions of very different length. In some seventy paṭalas this version treats mantra extraction, bathing, worship, mudrā and maṇḍala, dīkṣā and the six adhvans, yoga (nāḍīcakra, dhāraṇā, "vajrakavāṭa" meditations), vratas, prāyaścitta, gifts such as tulābhāra and hiraṇyagarbha, liṅga characteristics, installation (pratiṣṭhā), temple building and settlement planning. Its compilatory character suggests a relatively late redaction distinct from the short Sārdhatriśatikālottara commented on by Rāmakaṇṭha.

summary: The Kāmākhyātantra is a medieval Śākta-Kaula tantric text in nine chapters (paṭalas) structured as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and Devī. Centered on the goddess Kāmākhyā of Kāmarūpa (Assam) venerated as the cosmic Yoni and supreme Shakti, the work outlines mantra extraction, nyāsa, pañcatattva worship, yoni-pūjā, guru-śiṣya qualifications, pūrṇābhiṣeka, and rituals geared towards both siddhi and liberation.

summary: The Kāmadhenutantra is a late-medieval Śākta Tantra in twenty-four paṭalas structured as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī. It focuses primarily on phonematic mysticism (mātṛkā- and varṇa-vidyā), treating the fifty letters of the Sanskrit alphabet as vibrational sound-manifestations of Kālī and Vāc/Sarasvatī. The work details the esoteric esoteric values, bodily correlation (nyāsa), cakra centers, and meditative visualisations (dhyāna) for individual letters and key bījamantras.

summary: A manual of practical magic and medicine in sixteen upadeśas ascribed to Nityanātha, framed as a dialogue of Īśvara and the Goddess. It covers the six magical rites (vaśīkaraṇa, ākarṣaṇa, stambhana, mohana, uccāṭana, māraṇa), aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa), remedies against poison (viṣanivāraṇa), yakṣiṇī-sādhana, treasure-finding and other kautukas, and the purification of mercury and minerals (rasādiśodhana). The Kāmaratna was widely copied and printed in several recensions in North and East India.

summary: A large Tantric ritual compendium (nibandha) by Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa of Navadvīpa (16th–17th c.), compiled from quotations of numerous tantras (Jñānārṇava, Nigamakalpadruma, Kriyāsāra, Viśvasāra, Nīlatantra and others). In five paricchedas it covers the qualifications of guru and disciple, initiation, puraścaraṇa, general pūjā, and the mantras, worship, kavacas and stotras of many deities, especially the Mahāvidyās (Kālī, Tārā etc.), and finally the upacāras of worship. It became the standard handbook of Bengali Śākta ritual. This e-text adds an appendix of mantras and stotras for further deities.

summary: The Śrītattvanidhi ('Treasure of Realities') is an encyclopedic 19th-century Sanskrit compendium compiled under the auspices of Maharaja Kṛṣṇarāja Voḍeyar III of Mysore. Organized into nine thematic 'nidhis' (treasures), it compiles iconographic descriptions, dhyāna verses, astronomical lore, temple practices, and esoteric lore culled from Purāṇas, Āgamas, and Tantras. The final section (Kautukanidhi) contains celebrated descriptions of traditional games (including ganjifa) and 122 yoga postures (āsanas).

summary: The Parāprāveśikā is a short prose primer of nondual Kashmir Śaivism (Trika/Pratyabhijñā) composed by the 11th-century master Kṣemarāja. It expounds the nature of Parameśvara as pure light (prakāśa) and reflective awareness (vimarśa), details the thirty-six principles of cosmic manifestation (tattvas) from Śiva down to earth (pṛthivī), and introduces the supreme Śakti (Parā) and the esoteric significance of the mantra aham.

summary: The Kṣurikopaniṣad ('Razor Upaniṣad') is an early Yoga Upaniṣad affiliated with the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, counted as the 31st Upaniṣad in the Muktikā canon. It expounds yogic practice through the metaphor of a razor-sharp instrument of dhāraṇā and discriminative knowledge that cuts through karmic bonds, bodily attachment, and the knot of the heart (hṛdayagranthi). The text details steady posture, breath control coordinated with the twelve-mātrā praṇava, sense withdrawal, and subtle meditative ascension along the nāḍīs up to liberation. The e-text contains the entire mūla along with the vivaraṇa of Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: The Kaṅkālamālinītantra ('Tantra of the Goddess Garlanded with Skeletons') is a five-paṭala Śākta text of the Kālīkula tradition, internally attributed to the Southern transmission (Dakṣiṇāmnāya). summary: The Kaivalyasāra is a foundational Sanskrit Vīraśaiva theological and philosophical treatise composed by Maritoṃṭadārya (ca. 16th century CE). Structured around the system of 101 progressive spiritual stations (ekottaraśatasthala) divided across six major prakaraṇas, the treatise correlates Upaniṣadic śruti passages with Śaivāgamic doctrines to articulate the Śivādvaita philosophy. It systematically expounds the metaphysical non-dual union (aṅgaliṅgasāmarasya) between the individual practitioner (aṅga) and transcendent-immanent Śiva (liṅga).

summary: The Spandanirṇaya is Kṣemarāja's (fl. early 11th century CE) exhaustive prose commentary on the Spandakārikā, the foundational text of the Spanda school of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism. Having earlier commented on only the first stanza in his Spandasaṃdoha, Kṣemarāja composed this full exposition at the request of his pupil Śūra. Across fifty-two verses organized into four niḥṣyandas, the work establishes that reality and all experiential states are grounded in the dynamic, creative pulsation (spanda) of supreme consciousness (parasaṃvit), synthesizing the Spanda tradition with Pratyabhijñā and Trika philosophy.

summary: The Spandakārikā is a foundational philosophical and contemplative treatise of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, expounding the doctrine of spanda—the dynamic pulsation and vibration of pure consciousness through which Śiva creates, sustains, and withdraws the universe. This composite electronic text contains the root kārikās accompanied by two early commentaries: the Spandakārikāvṛtti by Vasugupta's direct disciple Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa (late 9th c. CE), which interprets the Spanda system through the conceptual lens of the Pratyabhijñā school.

summary: The Kamalā (also known as Kāmyakarmakamalā or Tripurasundarīpaddhati) is an extensive Śrīvidyā ritual manual composed in the 18th century by Prāṇamañjarī, the third wife of the Kumaoni tantric scholar Premanidhi Pant. Drawing primarily upon the Tantrarājatantra and related texts, it provides exhaustive instructions for the daily and optional/desire-oriented worship (kāmyakarman) of Tripurasundarī and the fifteen Nityā goddesses, detailing yantras, nyāsas, mantra-sādhanas, and homa rituals.

summary: The Kāmikāgama is the first and foremost of the twenty-eight canonical Mūlāgamas of the Śaiva Siddhānta tradition. Its Pūrvabhāga comprises seventy-five chapters (paṭalas) dealing comprehensively with the kriyāpāda (temple architecture, town planning, iconometry, and installation rites) and caryāpāda (daily obligatory and expiatory rituals). Specific topics include site examination (bhūparīkṣā), town and settlement planning, design of vimānas and prāsādas, and the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of Liṅgas and Śaiva icons.

summary: The Kāmikāgama is the first of the twenty-eight canonical root scriptures (mūlāgamas) of the Śaiva Siddhānta. Its Uttarabhāga comprises 98 chapters (paṭalas) providing detailed ritual injunctions for temple ritual, including public worship (parārthapūjā), image installation and temple consecration (pratiṣṭhā), expiatory rites (prāyaścitta), festival routines (utsava), and related domestic rites. Preserved in South Indian Grantha manuscripts and early liturgical prints, it serves as an indispensable practical authority for hereditary Tamil Śaiva temple priests (śivācāryas).

summary: The Kāraṇāgama is traditionally ranked fourth among the twenty-eight canonical Siddhāntāgamas; this e-text contains the ten-chapter Kriyāpāda section of its Uttarabhāga preserved in the Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyata) tradition. Structured as a divine discourse between Pārvatī and Śiva, the text establishes the supremacy of Vīraśaiva dharma, the observance of the śāmbhavavrata, and the transmission of the threefold initiation (vedhā-, mantra-, and kriyādīkṣā). It provides extensive ritual prescriptions for the worship, wearing, and maintenance of the personal liṅga (iṣṭaliṅga), culminating in expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) to be performed in the event of ritual errors or the loss of the liṅga (naṣṭaliṅga).

summary: The Karpūrādistotra (or Dakṣiṇakālikāsvarūpastotra) is an influential 22-verse Śākta hymn celebrating Dakṣiṇakālikā, traditionally attributed to Mahākāla. It systematically encodes the esoteric bījamantras (mantroddhāra), visualization (dhyāna), and Kaula ritual practices of Kālī. This e-text provides the root stotra together with the complete Sanskrit commentary Svarūpavyākhyā (also known as Vimalānandadāyinī) by Vimalānandasvāmī (Satīśacandra Rāya Caudhurī), which interprets the hymn's ritual and transgressive imagery in light of Kaula metaphysics and internal yogic sādhanā.

The work synthesizes Śākta devotionalism with the non-dual metaphysics of Kashmiri Pratyabhijñā philosophy in refined classical Sanskrit metre.

summary: This compendium contains four esoteric Śākta/Kaula Upaniṣads—the Bhāvanopaniṣad, the Bahvṛcopaniṣad (here called Bahvṛcavedīyā Śrīlalitāmahātripurasundaryupaniṣad), the Devyatharvaśīrṣopaniṣad, and the Kaulopaniṣad—along with commentaries and liturgical instructions (prayogavidhi) by the 18th-century Śrīvidyā scholar Bhāskararāya. The texts formulate a nondual synthesis of Kaula ritual and Vedāntic metaphysics, equating the goddess Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī with absolute consciousness, the cosmos, the Śrīcakra, and the psychophysical body of the practitioner. Bhāskararāya's commentary internalizes esoteric Kaula worship as contemplative meditation (bhāvanā) on the identity between macrocosm and microcosm.

summary: The Kriyāsāra ('Essence of Action') by Nīlakaṇṭha is a comprehensive thirty-two-chapter (upadeśa) theological and ritual digest of the Vīraśaiva tradition synthesizing Śaivāgama ritualism with Vedānta. This first volume encompasses Upadeśas 1 through 4, which set out an extensive metrical summary (kārikā) of the Brahmasūtras interpreted according to Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita / Śaiva Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine. It served as a major doctrinal authority in late medieval and early modern South India, significantly utilized by Appayya Dīkṣita in works such as the Śivārcanācandrikā.

summary: The Kubjikāguhyeśvarīpūjāpaddhati is a late 17th-century Nepalese Tantric ritual manual dedicated to Goddess Guhyeśvarī venerated in her Kubjikā aspect. Written in Sanskrit with extensive Newari liturgical directions and ritual glosses, it outlines standard liturgical procedures including bhūtaśuddhi, nyāsa, pātrapūjā, gurumaṇḍala worship, kramārcana, offerings (bali), and animal sacrifice (paśujāga). The surviving witness was written in 1689 CE (NS 809) by King Jitāmitramalla of Bhaktapur.

summary: The Kubjikātantra is a late medieval Śākta scripture of eastern Indian (Bengali or Maithili) origin in seventeen paṭalas. As noted by Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, despite sharing the deity name Kubjikā, it bears virtually no relation to the earlier Paścimāmnāya (Western Kaula) canonical corpus (such as the Kubjikāmata). Framed as a dialogue between Sadāśiva and Pārvatī, the text treats general eastern Śākta ritualism, including the Daśamahāvidyās (Kālī, Tārā, etc.), mantra-caitanya, yantra, nyāsa, and protective talismans, concluding in chapter 17 with the Mṛtavatsākavaca.

summary: A transcription of a Nepalese Kaula miscellany manuscript. It opens with the complete Kulānanda, a short dialogue between Bhairava and the Goddess ascribed to Matsyendranātha. The Kulānanda teaches yogic 'piercing' (vedha) of the bodily centres and the signs of possession (āveśa) and other immediate experiences (sadyapratyaya). Next comes a damaged passage on the marks of skull-bowls (kapāla), ascribed to the Picumata. The rest consists of fragmentary ritual texts: maṇḍala and gateway rites using Vedic mantras, homa, bali offerings, and samaya-vidyās of Kubjikā, Tārā and the Śrīvidyā goddesses.

summary: The Kulārṇavatantra ('Ocean of the Kula') is one of the foundational scriptural texts of the Kaula tradition within Śākta Tantrism, framed as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and the Goddess. Comprising seventeen ullāsas (chapters) and more than two thousand verses, the text presents the doctrine and ritual praxis of the Ūrdhvāmnāya (upper transmission). It systematically expounds the necessity of human embodiment for liberation, guru-śiṣya relations, dīkṣā, mantra-sādhana, and the sacramental integration of enjoyment (bhukti) with liberation (mukti) through the esoteric rites of the pañcamakāras.

Unusually structured as a nigama—wherein Śiva (Bhairava) serves as the questioner while the Goddess (Bhairavī/Kālī) reveals teachings—the text expounds the inner and outer rites of Kula worship, including mantra-sādhana, nyāsa, kulācāra practices, and philosophical discussions on Śiva and Śakti.

summary: A Nepalese manuscript labelled Kulasāra that actually contains chapters of three late Kaula works in the form of dialogues between Śiva and the Goddess. Chapters 24–26 of the Kulasārasaṃgraha, said to be part of the Somabhujāvalī, open with the myth of how the gods lost wine and discuss its purification and the vessels used for it. Chapters 1–5 of the Kulācāranirṇaya treat devotion to the guru and Kaula samaya conduct. A final 18th chapter (ullāsa) on Kaula funerary rites (antyeṣṭi) is followed by a note citing Subhagānandanātha. Muktabodha dates such texts after the 13th century.

summary: The Kulasāra is an early Kaula Śaiva scripture surviving in archaic Nepalese manuscripts and cited by non-dual Kashmiri Śaiva authors prior to the eleventh century. It expounds Kaula metaphysics—including the categories of piṇḍa, pada, rūpa, and rūpātīta, as well as Akula and Kula—combined with yogic practices for bodily internalization, mantra protection, visualization of Bhairava and yoginīs, non-dual ritual purity, and internal pilgrimage (caryā). This e-text preserves an unedited diplomatic transcript of chapters 4 (fragment) and 8–17 (incomplete).

summary: The Laghustava is the first of the five hymns comprising the Pañcastavī, an influential pentad of monistic Śākta hymns held in high esteem within the Trika and Śrīvidyā traditions of Kashmir. summary: The Lakṣmītantra is an influential Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava Āgama in 57 chapters, notable for elevating Lakṣmī, the dynamic Śakti of Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa, to the primary cosmological and soteriological agent. summary: The Lakṣmītantra is a major canonical Pāñcarātra scripture (saṃhitā), datable to c. 9th–12th century CE, notable for presenting the goddess Lakṣmī (Śrī) as the supreme creative and dynamic power (Śakti) of Nārāyaṇa. In 57 chapters, the text expounds Pāñcarātra cosmogony, the six divine gunas, the theory of vyūha emanations, mantraśāstra, ritual diagram construction (maṇḍala/yantra), and devotional surrender (nyāsa/prapatti). summary: The Śāradātilaka of Lakṣmaṇadeśikendra (c. 11th century) is one of the most widely influential compendia of mantraśāstra and Tantric ritual across medieval South Asia. Across 25 paṭalas, it integrates cosmology, phonic creation (śabdabrahman, nāda, bindu, kuṇḍalinī), dīkṣā, yantras, mudrās, and ritual procedures and dhyānas for Śākta, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and Saura deities. This e-text contains the complete root text together with the Padārthādarśa commentary completed by Rāghavabhaṭṭa in Vārāṇasī in 1493/1494 CE.

summary: The Lalitāsahasranāmastotra is the foremost devotional and liturgical hymn of the Śrīvidyā tradition, situated in the Lalitopākhyāna (Uttarabhāga) of the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa as a revelation delivered by Hayagrīva to the sage Agastya. Bhāskararāya's Saubhāgyabhāskara, completed in 1728 CE, is the definitive and encyclopedic commentary on the hymn, arranged across twelve sections termed kalās. The exegesis synthesizes Śākta Tantric theology, Śrīcakra and kuṇḍalinī metaphysics, Advaita Vedānta, and rigorous Mīmāṃsā and Vyākaraṇa hermeneutics to elucidate the esoteric multi-layered significance of each divine epithet.

summary: The Lalleśvarīvākyāni ('Sayings of Lalleśvarī') comprises 60 mystical Kashmiri quatrains (vākhs) by the 14th-century poet-saint Lallā (Lal Dĕd), accompanied verse-for-verse by Sanskrit metrical translations (arthacchāyāpadya) composed by the 18th-century Kashmiri Śaiva scholar Rājānaka Bhāskarakaṇṭha. Rooted in nondual Trika and Pratyabhijñā Śaivism, the verses convey internal yogic absorption, prāṇāyāma, mind control, critique of ritualism and external caste distinctions, and the nondual realization of the Self as Śiva. As the earliest attested literary compositions in the Kashmiri language, Lallā's verses hold foundational importance in Kashmiri literary and religious culture, while Bhāskarakaṇṭha's translation represents their earliest formal reception in classical Sanskrit scholarship.

summary: The Nityakarmavidhi is a daily ritual paddhati of the Kashmiri Smārta tradition following the Laugākṣi recension of the Kāṭhaka school. It details standard daily domestic rites, including ablution (snāna), morning and evening prayers (sandhyā), oblations to ancestors and gods (tarpaṇa), and eating regulations. The text concludes with a recitation of Abhinavagupta's 10-verse Śivastuti (Bhairavastotra).

summary: The Liṅgārcanatantra is a Śaiva-Śākta tantric scripture presented as a dialogue between Śiva and Devī (Harapārvatīsaṃvāda). It focuses on the ritual preparation, consecration, and worship of the liṅga—especially the pārthiva (clay/earth) liṅga—detailing required mantras, upacāras, and the esoteric merits of liṅgapūjā. The present transcription terminates abruptly during an exchange concerning the admissibility of ritual remnants (nirmālya) in paṭala 13.

summary: The Mālinīvijayottaratantra is the primary scriptural authority of the Trika school of non-dual Śaivism, regarded by Abhinavagupta as the foremost of the Śaiva tantras and providing the structural framework for his Tantrāloka. The text expounds Trika metaphysics, mantra phonology, ritual worship, and initiation (dīkṣā) centered on the three goddesses Parā, Parāparā, and Aparā. It is particularly renowned for its systematic presentation of Śaiva yoga, integrating varied contemplative paths into schemas of cognitive absorption (samāveśa) and stages of spiritual mastery.

summary: The Svātantryadīpikā is a 19th-century compendium of the core tenets of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism composed in four chapters (ullāsa) by Mānasarāma (Monga), a lineage forebear of Swami Lakshman Joo. Formulated as concise aphorisms accompanied by the author's own prose commentary, the treatise expounds the doctrine of divine absolute autonomy (svātantrya), the nature of consciousness (saṃvid), and the unfolding of the universal powers (śakti).

summary: The Mātṛkātantra is an unprinted Śākta-Śaiva tantric text framed as a dialogue on Mount Kailāsa between Caṇḍikā and Bhairava/Śaṅkara. It discusses alchemical procedures (dhātuvāda / rasaśāstra) with mercury (pārada) and herbal ingredients to create gold and silver for ritual worship during the Kaliyuga, outlines the recitation manual and benefits of the Caṇḍīpāṭha (Devīmāhātmya / Saptaśatī), and concludes with devotional hymns and protective armors including a Gurukavaca.

attribution_note: The Mṛgendrāgama (Mṛgendratantra) is an anonymous scriptural revelation of the Śaiva Siddhānta tradition, traditionally reckoned as an upāgama of the Kāmikāgama. The primary commentary (Mṛgendravṛtti) is by the Kashmiri exegete Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha (son of Vidyākaṇṭha I, 10th century CE). The sub-commentary (Dīpikā) on the Vidyāpāda is by the South Indian Siddhānta master Aghoraśivācārya (fl. 1157/1158 CE) of Chidambaram; Aghoraśiva's Dīpikā covers only the Vidyāpāda.

summary: The Mṛgendrāgama (or Mṛgendratantra) is an authoritative scripture of dualistic Śaiva Siddhānta, traditionally regarded as an upāgama of the Kāmikāgama. This e-text contains its philosophical Vidyāpāda and practical Yogapāda, which formulate core Siddhānta ontology across the categories of pati (the Lord), paśu (the bound individual), and pāśa (fetters/bonds), followed by an exposition of tantric yoga. The root text is accompanied by the influential 10th-century Kashmiri commentary (Mṛgendravṛtti) of Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha and the 12th-century South Indian sub-commentary (Dīpikā) of Aghoraśiva.
