summary: The Mṛgendrapaddhati is a South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta ritual handbook attributed to Aghoraśivācārya (12th century), structured according to the ritual prescriptions of the Mṛgendrāgama's kriyāpāda. It is accompanied by the Mṛgendrapaddhatiṭīkā of Vaktraśambhu (Naṭeśaguru), which clarifies the technical procedures of the manual. The combined work sets out daily worship (nityapūjā), purificatory and expiatory rites (prāyaścitta), basic initiation (samayadīkṣā), the sacred cord festival (pavitravidhi), and icon consecration (pratiṣṭhā).

summary: The Mṛtitattvānusmaraṇa is an eschatological and ritual text framed as a dialogue between Śrībhairava and Bhairavī, traditionally transmitted as a section of the Kashmiri Śaiva Bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitā. It provides a detailed account of the post-mortem journey of the soul, the geography and punishments of Yamaloka, the accounting of deeds by Citragupta, and the specific duties of relatives during dying, cremation (śāvasnāna, antyeṣṭi), the ten-day period (daśāha), and the performance of dīpaśrāddha to dispel the darkness of the pretamārga.

summary: The Mṛtyuñjayakalpa (as preserved in NGMCP MS 4-286, Reel A 172/6) is a comprehensive astrological (muhūrta, jyotiṣa) and ritual pacification (śānti) compendium from Nepal. It sets forth Sanskrit verses on auspicious timing for lifecycle rituals (saṃskāras such as puṃsavana, annaprāśana, cūḍākarma, and vidyārambha), planetary transits (grahacāra), astrological afflictions, prognostic diagrams (cakras), travel rules (yātrā), and various pacification rites to avert death and illness (mṛtyubhaya-śānti), accompanied by extensive Newari glosses.

summary: A Nepalese ritual manual (paddhati) setting forth the domestic and tantric liturgical procedures for the worship of Mṛtyuñjaya (Śiva). The text combines Sanskrit Vedic and tantric mantras with ritual instructions in Classical Newari, encompassing preliminary purification rites, Sūryapūjā, Viṣṇupūjā, the principal Mṛtyuñjayapūjā, and an appended rite for pacifying Saturn (Śanaiścarapāṭhavidhi).

summary: The Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇopaniṣad is a minor Yoga Upaniṣad affiliated with the Śukla Yajurveda, framed as a dialogue between the sage Yājñavalkya and the deity residing in the solar disc (ādityamaṇḍala, identified with Nārāyaṇa). In five brāhmaṇas, it synthesizes Haṭhayogic bodily techniques with Rājayoga and Advaita Vedāntic metaphysics, detailing a redefined eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga), contemplation of internal and external luminosity (tārakayoga), the five voids (vyomapañcaka), and the trans-mental absorption of amanaskayoga leading to manonāśa and jīvanmukti. In this file, the root text is accompanied by the complete Vivaraṇa commentary of the 18th-century Advaitin Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: A brief Tantric ritual manual on the procedure for mantra transmission (mantradāna), extracted from or attributed to the Mahākālasaṃhitā. It details the eightfold fragrant mixtures (gandhāṣṭaka) for Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, Gāṇapatya, and Śākta devotions, guidelines for placing ritual lamps, incense, and naivedya offerings, the rules for whispering mantras into the initiate's ear according to varna and gender, and concluding recitations exchanged between guru and disciple.

summary: An anonymous Nepalese ritual manual for the worship of Mahālakṣmī, in particular for undertaking her vrata (Mahālakṣmīvrata, with rites on the dark eighth day, kṛṣṇāṣṭamī). It is written in Newar-influenced ritual Sanskrit. It sets out the preliminary worship of guru and Gaṇapati, the sun offering, nyāsa, worship of the doorway, the maṇḍala deities and the lokapālas, the taking of the vrata, and a series of offerings, each with an accompanying verse. The manuscript breaks off during the offerings.

summary: The Mahānirvāṇatantra is an influential Śākta work structured as a discourse between Sadāśiva and the Goddess (Ādyā Śakti) on ritual and moral duty in the degraded Kali Yuga. It combines monotheistic Advaita Vedānta and the meditation on formless Brahman with devotional worship of Ādyā Kālī, while reforming traditional Kaula rituals such as the pañcatattva. Unusually among Tantras, it devotes extensive sections to social ethics, duties of the householder, sacramental ceremonies (saṃskāras), and civil law regarding marriage, property, and inheritance.

summary: The Svātantryadīpikā ('Lamp of Absolute Freedom') is a non-dual Kashmir Shaiva philosophical treatise in four chapters (ullāsas) attributed to Maheśvarācārya. summary: The Mahārthamañjarī ('Bouquet of the Great Meaning') accompanied by the Parimala ('Fragrance') auto-commentary is an important synthesis of non-dual Śaiva philosophy, integrating the esoteric goddess cycles of the Krama (Kālīkrama/Mahārtha) system with Pratyabhijñā and Spanda doctrines. Composed in South India at Cidambaram by Maheśvarānanda (Gorakṣa), the work expounds supreme non-dual consciousness unfolding through sensory cognition, the thirty-six tattvas, and internal ritual. The extensive Parimala commentary quotes numerous rare and lost Krama, Pratyabhijñā, and Kula texts (including Abhinavagupta's Kramakeli), demonstrating the transmission and vitality of Kashmiri tantric traditions in medieval Tamil South India.

summary: The Uttarabhāga of the Makuṭāgama (also designated Makuṭottara) is a canonical Śaiva scripture preserved in the Vīraśaiva tradition, cast as an esoteric dialogue between Paraśiva and Rudra. It comprises two sections: the Kriyāpāda (five paṭalas), detailing the theology of the Śāmbhavavrata (Śirovrata), daily observance (āhnika), and the rites and implements for personal liṅga worship; and the Caryāpāda (ten paṭalas), regulating initiation, post-mortem funerary rites (śivamedha / antyeṣṭi), commemorative ceremonies, and ritual purity (āśauca). The text provides a central scriptural justification for Vīraśaiva orthopraxy and continuous liṅga-wearing.

summary: The Gaurīkāñcalikātantra is a Śaiva-Śākta tantric medical-astrological treatise cast as a dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī. summary: The Akulavīratantra is an early Kaula / Yoginī Kaula scripture transmitted in the corpus attributed to Matsyendranātha. It teaches an uncompromising non-dual realization of ultimate reality as the Akulavīra ('Hero of the Transcendent'), attained as innate bliss (sahajānanda) beyond all conventional dharmas. The work critiques scholastic schools (Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist, Jaina, Mīmāṃsā, Somasiddhānta) and formal ritualism, emphasizing that spiritual freedom arises solely from dwelling in the unconditioned, all-pervading divine essence.

summary: The Jñānakārikā is a short Kaula verse text in three chapters (paṭalas) traditionally ascribed to Matsyendranātha. Preserved alongside the Kaulajñānanirṇaya, the treatise expounds non-dual gnosis (jñāna), liberation detached from mental supports and dualistic constructs (nirāśraya), and internalizes Kaula ascetic conduct (caryā), outward signs, and sacred sites.

summary: The Kaulajñānanirṇaya is a foundational Śaiva-Śākta scripture of the Yoginī Kaula (Matsyendramata) lineage, traditionally held to have been transmitted by the mahāsiddha Matsyendranātha in Candradvīpa. In 24 chapters (paṭalas), it expounds esoteric Kaula teachings, including the nonduality of Śiva and Śakti, the metaphysics of kula and akula, subtle yogic physiology (bindu, nāda, cakras), siddhi acquisition, and antinomian yoginī rituals. Surviving in a palm-leaf manuscript preserved in Nepal dating to the 11th century CE, it represents one of the earliest extant textual witnesses to Kaula tantrism.

summary: The Yogaviṣaya is a short Nātha yoga text of 33 verses ascribed to Matsyendranātha (Mīnanātha), who presents it as the teaching he received from Ādinātha. After verses on the guru lineage and the qualified disciple, it describes the six cakras from ādhāra to ājñā, the nāḍīs iḍā, piṅgalā and suṣumnā, the ten vital winds, the three granthis, the haṃsa (ajapā) mantra repeated 21,600 times a day, and the liṅgas and inner nectar in the head.

summary: The Merutantra is an encyclopedic Śaiva-Śākta tantric manual comprising 35 chapters (prakāśas), framed as a revelation given by Sadāśiva on Mount Meru to the gods after their distress under the demon Jalandhara. Functioning much like a nibandha (digest) of mantra-śāstra and ritual practice, it details initiation (dīkṣā), preliminary discipline (puraścaraṇa), nyāsa, and rituals for numerous deities, including Mahākāla, Devī, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, and Kārtavīryārjuna. Containing notable historical anachronisms, such as predictions naming London, Christianity, and the British (chapter 35), the text in its present form dates to the early modern period (ca. 16th–18th century CE).

summary: The Mohacūḍottara is an early Śaiva scriptural manual on installation (pratiṣṭhā-tantra) framed as a dialogue between Skanda and Śakra (Indra). It focuses on the ritual selection and testing of materials (stone, wood, metals), iconometry, the architecture of temples (prāsāda) and ritual halls (maṇḍapa), and the rites of consecration for liṅgas and deities. Preserved primarily in early Nepalese manuscripts, it forms an important witness to early medieval Śaiva architectural and ritual doctrine.

summary: The Muṇḍamālātantra is a late Śākta Kaula scripture in ten chapters (paṭalas). It is particularly prominent in tantric literature for establishing the explicit doctrinal and symbolic correspondences between the ten Mahāvidyās (Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, etc.) and the ten Avatāras of Viṣṇu. The work also details mantroddhāra, stotras, kavacas, and esoteric ritual practices including śavasādhanā.

summary: The Mudrāprakāśa is a Tantric digest by Rāmakiśora defining and explaining the formation, classification, and ritual application of hand gestures (mudrās) used in worship, nyāsa, and invocation. It systematically cites classical Tantric authorities, including the Mantradarpaṇa, Kṛṣṇānanda's Tantrasāra, the Kulārṇavatantra, Gautamīyatantra, and Jñānārṇavatantra.

summary: A 3,000-verse 'Sārasaṅgraha' recension of the Makuṭāgama (Makuṭatantra), one of the 28 Siddhāntāgamas of Śaiva Siddhānta, transmitted in an IFP transcript. summary: The Saubhāgyataraṅgiṇī is a Śrīvidyā liturgical manual (paddhati) dedicated to the worship of Mahātripurasundarī, composed by Mukunda. The text harmonizes Tantric ritual practice with orthodox Purāṇic and Vedic traditions, quoting extensively from Vedic texts, numerous Purāṇas (especially Kālikā and Kūrma), and Tantras including the Vāmakeśvara, Jñānārṇava, and Tantrarāja. Divided into chapters called 'waves' (laharī), the text sets forth daily ritual, mantra meditation, and yantra pūjā.

summary: The Nāṭyaśāstra is the foundational Sanskrit treatise on dramaturgy, performance, dance, music, and aesthetic theory, ascribed to the mythic sage Bharata Muni. This volume comprises chapters 1 through 7 accompanied by the Abhinavabhāratī commentary of Abhinavagupta (c. 10th–11th century CE). These chapters cover the mythological origins of drama, stagecraft and playhouse architecture (prekṣāgṛha), stage rituals (pūrvaraṅga), classical dance movements (karaṇas and aṅgahāras), and the foundational exposition of rasa (aesthetic relish) and bhāva (affective states).

summary: The Nādabindūpaniṣad is one of the twenty classical Yoga Upaniṣads belonging to the Muktikā canon and traditionally affiliated with the Ṛgveda. It opens by mapping the cosmic Praṇava (Oṃkāra) and its twelve constituent mātrās onto the sacred Haṃsa bird, delineating the respective planes attained through contemplation of each measure. It then expounds Nādānusandhāna (meditation on the inner mystic sound) seated in the Siddha posture, detailing the progression from coarse internal sounds to increasingly subtle vibrations, leading to dissolution of the mind (manolaya) into the supreme soundless Absolute. Upaniṣadbrahmayogin's Vivaraṇa interprets the entire yogic progression through the lens of non-dual Advaita Vedānta culminating in videhamukti.

summary: The Āścaryayogamālā ('Rosary of Wondrous Recipes/Applications'), also known as Yogaratnamālā or Yogaratnāvalī, is a medieval manual of magic and occult recipes (ṣaṭkarman) attributed to Nāgārjuna. Comprising approximately 140 verses, it details preparations and spells for subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa), dissension (vidveṣaṇa), immobilization (stambhana), invisibility, poison remedies, and other marvels. It is accompanied by the concise commentary (Laghuvṛtti) of the Śvetāmbara Jaina scholar Guṇākara.

summary: The Kriyāsāra ('Essence of Action') by Nīlakaṇṭha is a comprehensive thirty-two-chapter (upadeśa) theological and ritual digest of the Vīraśaiva tradition synthesizing Śaivāgama ritualism with Vedānta. summary: The Kriyāsāra ('Essence of Practice') by Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya (c. 14th–15th century CE) is a major Vīraśaiva metrical treatise harmonizing Śaiva ritual, ethical conduct, and devotional observance with the philosophical framework of the Brahmasūtras. Structured into thirty-one chapters (upadeśas), the text systematically expounds the doctrine of the 101 stages (ekottaraśatasthala) and daily religious duties. This portion comprises Upadeśas 5 through 14, focusing on regular and occasional duties (ācāra), the theological symbolism and rites of holy ash (bhasma) and rudrākṣa, ablutions, sandhyā, and the liturgical manual of Śiva worship (śivapūjā).

summary: The Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā is a major Vīraśaiva apologetic and theological treatise composed by Nandikeśvara. Applying Mīmāṃsā hermeneutical principles to Vedic, Upaniṣadic, Āgamic, and Smṛti citations, the work establishes the scriptural validity, necessity, and orthodoxy of constantly bearing the personal liṅga on the body (iṣṭaliṅgadhāraṇa) and examines associated Liṅgāyat funerary practices (nikṣepa/burial). The accompanying Sanskrit commentary, Śivā, written by Mahāmahopādhyāya Śivakumāra Śāstrī in 1903, provides exhaustive glosses and defends the dialectical arguments against rival philosophical schools.

summary: The Tārābhaktisudhārṇava ('Ocean of the Nectar of Devotion to Tārā') is an extensive 17th-century Śākta ritual digest (nibandha) dedicated to the worship of the Mahāvidyā Tārā in her various forms (including Ugratārā, Ekajaṭā, and Nīlasarasvatī). summary: The Netratantra ('Tantra of the Eye'), also known as Mṛtyuñjayabhaṭṭāraka or Amṛteśatantra, is an influential scripture of the Mantramārga Śaiva tradition in 22 chapters (adhikāras), composed in Kashmir between roughly 700 and 850 CE. Centering on the worship of Amṛteśvara and Amṛtalakṣmī through the conquering of death (mṛtyuñjaya) and the eye-mantra, it expounds esoteric yoga alongside comprehensive apotropaic rites, exorcism of malignant spirits, and pacification rituals essential to early medieval royal religion. The present e-text preserves the full root scripture accompanied by the master commentary Netroddyota by the 11th-century Kashmiri theologian Kṣemarāja, which integrates these dualistic Mantramārga rituals into nondualist Trika-Pratyabhijñā philosophy.

summary: The Nirvāṇaguhyakālīpūjā is a Tantric ritual handbook (paddhati) centered on the worship of Nirvāṇaguhyakālī, an esoteric form of Guhyakālī venerated in Nepalese Śākta traditions. summary: A short Śaiva yoga text of 90 anuṣṭubh verses structured as an instruction delivered by Bhagavān to Guha. It details internal breath retention (pūraka and kumbhaka), cessation of mental fluctuation (niścala citta), the contemplation of voidness (triśūnya, sāmarasya), five symbolic mudrās, and the synthesis of ascetic vows (vrata) with yoga practice leading to liberation (mokṣa).

summary: The Nirvāṇatantra is a late-medieval Śākta scripture framed as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and Caṇḍikā. In this 14-chapter recension, the text expounds cosmogony, identifying Kālī with supreme Brahman and prime source of the universe, along with the significance of the Gāyatrī mantra, spiritual lineage and devotion to the guru, and rituals of the five makāras. The concluding paṭalas delineate the duties of the four varṇas and āśramas, culminating in an exposition of the avadhūta ascetic path.

summary: The Niśvāsakārikā is an extensive metrical scripture belonging to the Niśvāsa corpus of the early Śaiva Mantramārga. Expanding upon the ritual, cosmological, and doctrinal frameworks set out in the earlier sūtra layers of the Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā, it details phonological cosmology (mātṛkā, praṇava, bindu, nāda), initiation rituals (dīkṣā), and yoga. This e-text transcribes the first transcript volume preserved at the French Institute of Pondicherry (IFP T0017A), comprising chapters 11 through 53.

summary: The Nityārcanapaṭala (also termed Vāsanārcanavidhi) from the Vātulatantra (Sahasrasaṃhitā recension) is an āgamic manual of daily Śaiva worship according to Śaivasiddhānta ritual doctrine. It details the classification of liṅgas (śailaja, ratnaja, lohaja, dāruja, mṛṇmaya, kṣaṇika), the distinction between ātmārtha (private) and parārtha (public) worship, the ritual roles of Ādiśaiva priests, preliminary purifications (pañcaśuddhi), āsanas, prāṇāyāma, and the full sequence of Śiva-pūjā.

summary: The Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava (the pūrvacatuḥśatī of the Vāmakeśvaratantra) and the Yoginīhṛdaya (its uttaracatuḥśatī) are foundational scriptures of Śākta Śrīvidyā. The first sets out the outer worship of Tripurasundarī and the sixteen Nityās: mantras, the Śrīcakra, mudrās and ritual applications. The second treats the inner meaning of cakra, mantra and pūjā. This e-text gives both with the Setubandha, the extensive commentary by the 18th-century scholar Bhāskararāya, which uses Mīmāṃsā methods to treat the two parts as one tantra in eight viśrāmas.

summary: The Nityādisaṅgraha is an extensive Kashmiri Śaiva ritual manual (paddhati) composed by Rājānaka Takṣakavarta. Synthesizing liturgical and mantric traditions from the Bhairavatantras and Śaiva Siddhānta (relying heavily on the Svacchandatantra), it details daily worship (nityapūjā), oblations, initiation obligations, ritual procedures for linga and sthaṇḍila worship, and occasion-specific rites such as the Śivarātri observance.

summary: The Pāśupatabrahmopaniṣad is a minor Yoga Upaniṣad associated with the Atharvaveda, structured around a dialogue between the creator Brahmā and his son Vaiśravaṇa (Vālakhilya). Across two sections (Pūrvakāṇḍa and Uttarakāṇḍa), the text internalizes Vedic sacrificial concepts, reinterpreting the sacrificial thread (yajñasūtra) and external ritual offerings as internal spiritual awareness, the Haṃsa mantra, and continuous contemplation of the Paramātman. It fuses Pāśupata Śaiva imagery with non-dual Vedāntic metaphysics. Upaniṣadbrahmayogin's commentary (Vivaraṇa) interprets the text from an Advaita Vedānta perspective, emphasizing the realization of unconditioned Brahman (niṣpratiyogika-brahman).

summary: The Śrītattvacintāmaṇi is a 26-chapter Śākta-tantric compendium composed in Sanskrit verse by the Bengali sādhaka Paramahaṃsa Pūrṇānanda in 1577 CE. summary: The Pañcaratnavyākhyācatuṣṭaya is a compilation of four Sanskrit Vīraśaiva exegetical works by Revaṇārādhya commenting on four five-verse hymns (Pañcaratnas) composed by his father, Sosale Vīraṇārādhya. The four commentaries—Tantrasāraprakāśikā, Tārakadīpikā, Śivatattvaprakāśikā, and Śrutyarthaprakāśikā—elucidate Śaiva ontology (pati, paśu, pāśa, and the ṣaḍadhvan) and synthesize Upanisadic and Śaivāgama teachings from a Vīraśaiva / Śivādvaita perspective.

summary: The Padyavāhinī is a Tantric ritual manual (paddhati) in verse composed by Śaṅkara, designed to synthesize the liturgical practices of the five currents (pañcasrotas) of the Śaiva-Śākta stream. Incorporating Śāmbhava, Trika, Śrīvidyā, and Krama elements, it details daily morning rites, guru-pūjā, mantra extraction (mantroddhāra), visualisations, and internal and external worship.

summary: The Pārānandasūtra (also called Pārānandamīmāṃsā) is an anonymous Śākta-Kaula ritual code written in sūtras, in two adhyāyas of seven āhnikas each, modelled on the Vedic and Mīmāṃsā sūtra style. It teaches one supreme Self, the Īśvaras and the countless souls. It describes the three paths of practice (dakṣiṇa, vāma and uttara), the qualifications of guru and disciple, initiation and order of precedence, daily and special worship, sacrificial sessions (satra) with offerings of wine and animals, expiations, and rules of conduct, and it often cites the differing opinions of named authorities.

summary: The Parātantra is a late medieval syncretic Śākta-Kaula scripture preserved in Nepal, framing its revelation within the Śiraścheda tradition. It systematically harmonizes the six transmissions (ṣaḍāmnāya) by assigning major Śākta lineages and deities—including Kubjikā (Western), Tripurasundarī (Southern), Guhyakālī and Siddhilakṣmī (Northern), and Vajrayoginī (Lower)—to six thrones, synthesizing them as manifestations of the singular supreme Goddess Parā. The text holds significant importance for the history of late medieval Newar esoteric liturgy and court ritual in the Kathmandu Valley.

summary: The Parātrīśikālaghuvṛtti (also known as Anuttaratattvavimarśinī) is a concise commentary on the Parātrīśikā (or Parātriṃśikā), a foundational 36-verse Trika Śaiva scripture held to be an excerpt from the Rudrayāmala. Traditionally attributed to Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE), the work elucidates the nature of the Supreme Reality (anuttara), phonematic emanation (mātṛkā and mālinī), and mantric realization. It serves as a brief, accessible digest alongside Abhinavagupta's elaborate masterwork on the same scripture, the Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa.

summary: The Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa (also entitled Tattvaviveka) is Abhinavagupta's exhaustive philosophical commentary on the Parātriṃśikā, a concise Śaiva scriptural revelation associated with the Rudrayāmala. Through thirty-seven root verses, Abhinavagupta elaborates non-dual Trika metaphysics, phonemic mysticism (mātṛkācakra), the nature of the ultimate reality (anuttara), and the dynamic of divine emission (visarga). Composed in Kashmir around 1000 CE, the work is considered one of the highest achievements of classical Indian tantric philosophy.

summary: The Parameśvarīmatatantra is a scripture of the Western Transmission (Paścimāmnāya) of Kaula Śaivism, intimately connected with the Kubjikā tradition (and explicitly identified as such in its final colophon: 'iti śrīkubjikāmate...'). Set as a dialogue between Mahābhairava and the Devī, its 56 chapters expound the cosmology and symbolism of Mount Meru, the sixfold lineage (ṣaḍvidha kulāmnāya), mantras, mudrās, yantras, and initiatory rites centered on the supreme goddess.

summary: The Paraśurāmakalpasūtra is a foundational manual of Śākta ritual worship in the Śrīvidyā (Kaula) tradition, composed in ten khaṇḍas of concise aphorisms. Traditionally attributed to Paraśurāma, it codifies ritual procedures, mantra transmission, dīkṣā, and Śrīcakra worship for Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī and affiliated deities such as Bālā, Mātaṅgī, and Vārāhī. This e-text presents the sūtras together with the comprehensive 19th-century commentary Saubhāgyodaya by Rāmeśvara.

summary: The Pauṣkarasaṃhitā is one of the principal canonical scriptures of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, revered alongside the Sāttvatasaṃhitā and Jayākhyasaṃhitā as one of the 'Three Gems' (ratnatraya). Across 43 chapters, it provides detailed instructions on ritual diagrams (maṇḍala), initiatory grades (samayī, putraka, sādhaka), installation (pratiṣṭhā), iconography, temple architecture, and caturvyūha theology. It is a major classical source for Śrīvaiṣṇava temple liturgy and ritual philosophy.

The main krama-worship runs from the gurupādukā invocation, nyāsas (aghora-, granthi-, dvādaśāṅga-, ṣaḍdūtī-, rudrakhaṇḍa-, mātṛkhaṇḍa-, trikhaṇḍā-nyāsa), kramadhyāna and vimalapañcaka through 'iti aṣṭāviṃśatikramma || 28 ||' to the colophon '[iti śrīpaścimajeṣṭhānjeṣṭhe āmnāya aṣṭāviṃśati krammārccaṇaṃ samāpta]' (segment 937 of 1476). After this come further rites: trikhaṇḍāpūjana, mūlasthāna devārcana, the catuḥṣaṣṭiyoginī-, mahā-, samaya- and śānti-bali, and gift/dakṣiṇā formulas with Newari rubrics ending '... upadohanārthaṃ || śubha ||'. The ilx_skt Muktabodha metadata (metadata/muktabodha.csv) marks the transcription as 'incomplete, lacking final colophon', with the colophon located 'in middle' (i.e. the samāpta colophon at seg. 937, followed by further rites). It could not be checked whether folios are missing, because the NGMCP description of the manuscript was not accessible.

summary: This is a Newar ritual manual (paddhati) of the Kubjikā cult (Paścimāmnāya, the 'Western Transmission'), mixing Sanskrit mantras with Newari ritual instructions. It sets out the worship of the goddess Kubjikā and her retinue in 28 sequences (aṣṭāviṃśatikrama): guru veneration, purification of the hands and of the vessels for water and arghya, bhūtaśuddhi, extensive nyāsas, meditation on the kramas, and worship of the lineages of Siddhas/Nāthas (navanātha, the 'ānanda' teachers). The manuscript then gives supplementary rites, chiefly bali offerings to Vaṭuka, the 64 yoginīs and other deities, and closing formulas for dakṣiṇā and gifts.

summary: An unpublished Nepalese Kaula ritual manual (paddhati) of the Western / elder transmission (Paścimajyeṣṭhāmnāya) focusing on the worship of the goddess Kubjikā and her retinue. It details sequences of nyāsa (kara-, vaktra-, aṅga-, and ṣaḍdūtīnyāsa), jar- and seat-installation, oblation (bali), the worship of the six transmissions (ṣaḍāmnāyapūjā), Yoginī groups, and concluding mantra transmission (upadeśa) regulations.

summary: The Phetkāriṇītantra is a medieval Śākta tantric scripture framed as a dialogue between Īśvara and the Devī, emphasizing mantra practice, yantras, and pragmatic sorcery (abhicāra and the ṣaṭkarman), especially kṛtyā-sādhana, māraṇa, and ceṭikā-sādhana. It is well known in Indological scholarship for preserving early, influential descriptions of fierce goddesses such as Dhūmāvatī and Ugratārā (Mahācīnakrama-Tārā), reflecting close interactions with Buddhist Vajrayāna sādhanas. The scripture served as a major source cited in later Nibandha compilations, including Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa's Tantrasāra and Brahmānanda Giri's Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī.

summary: The Piṅgalāmata (also titled Jayadrathādhikāra) is an early Śaiva pratiṣṭhātantra associated with the Vidyāpīṭha cycle (Brahmayāmala and Jayadrathayāmala). Uniquely among surviving early pratiṣṭhā literature—which is otherwise largely Śaivasiddhānta—it incorporates iconographic and ritual teachings of the Bhairavatantras, Yāmala, Vāma, and Trika traditions alongside classical procedures of image consecration, temple architecture, and urban planning. It survives in an important dated Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript transcribed in 1177 CE.

attribution_note: An anonymous Śaiva dialogue. Ṣaṇmukha (Skanda) asks Śiva (addressed as Śūlabhṛt) for the prāṇāgnihotra on behalf of 'alpavittā narāḥ' who cannot keep the Vedic agnihotra, and Śiva answers. Its question list ('śarīre'smin katy agnayaḥ, ko yajamānaḥ, kā patnī ...') and the answer 'puruṣo yajamānaḥ, prakṛtiḥ patnī ...' belong to the same tradition of the inner, bodily fire sacrifice as the Prāṇāgnihotra Upaniṣad. However, the frame and much of the wording differ, and the e-text is not a copy of that Upaniṣad. No source for the text was identified.

summary: A short anonymous Śaiva text in verse and prose on the 'agnihotra in the breath' (prāṇāgnihotra), taught by Śiva to Ṣaṇmukha for people who cannot afford the Vedic fire ritual. It maps the elements of the śrauta sacrifice (the fires, sacrificer, wife, priests, offerings, implements, altar and so on) onto the body, its faculties and the cosmos. It then describes the five vital breaths and their deities, and the eating of food as an inner fire offering. The surviving text breaks off in this last section.

summary: The Kamalā (also known as Kāmyakarmakamalā or Tripurasundarīpaddhati) is an extensive Śrīvidyā ritual manual composed in the 18th century by Prāṇamañjarī, the third wife of the Kumaoni tantric scholar Premanidhi Pant. Drawing primarily upon the Tantrarājatantra and related texts, it provides exhaustive instructions for the daily and optional/desire-oriented worship (kāmyakarman) of Tripurasundarī and the fifteen Nityā goddesses, detailing yantras, nyāsas, mantra-sādhanas, and homa rituals.

summary: An anonymous commentary (vyākhyā) on the Prāsādaṣaṭślokī, a Śaiva Siddhānta text consisting of six verses analyzing the Prāsādamantra (hauṃ). It explains the internal esoteric structure, kalās (specifically the twelve kalās), associated devatās, sonic micro-divisions (mātrā), and bodily locations from the mūlādhāra up to the brahmarandhra according to Śaivāgama teachings.

summary: The Prāsādaṣaṭślokī is a six-verse Śaiva esoteric text detailing the phonic, spatial, and yogic ascent of the Prāsādamantra (the bījamantra of Paramaśiva, hauṃ) from the mūlādhāra through bodily and cranial centers up to unmanā. The accompanying anonymous prose Vyākhyā explicates the twelvefold and sixteenfold divisions (kalā) of the mantra, its anatomical measurements (aṅgula), phonic stages, and internal absorption (laya). The transcript concludes with supplementary passages detailing the Kalāprāsāda and the yogic viṣuvats.

summary: The Prāyaścittasamuccaya of Hṛdayaśiva (10th century CE) is an early Śaiva Siddhānta digest on expiatory rites (prāyaścitta). In 46 sections, it compiles and systematizes scriptural prescriptions for correcting ritual infractions, handling damage or contamination to liṅgas and shrines, and atoning for violations of samaya vows, drawing extensively upon early Tantras such as the Niḥśvāsa, Kāmika, Picumata, and Vātula.

summary: The Prabhuliṅgalīlā is a Sanskrit Vīraśaiva hagiographical text presented as part of the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa, narrating the life, deeds, and teachings of the 12th-century saint Allama Prabhu. Closely related to Cāmarasa's 15th-century Kannada epic Prabhuliṅgalīle, it depicts Allama Prabhu's conquest of Māyā and his spiritual dialogues with prominent Vīraśaiva figures such as Gorakṣanātha, Muktāyakkā, and Basava, elucidating Vīraśaiva philosophical principles including the Ṣaṭsthala system.

summary: The Cinmantramālinī (subtitled Nityopāsanākrama) is a brief Śākta liturgical ritual manual (paddhati) expounding the daily worship sequence of the fifteen Nityā devīs of the Śrīvidyā tradition according to the Kādimata. It sets forth initial preparatory acts (snāna, prāṇāyāma, bhūtaśuddhi, guru-dhyāna, mātṛkā-nyāsa, and ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) followed by daily visualizations (dhyāna), bījamantras, mudrās, and recitation rules for each of the fifteen lunar days from Kāmeśvarī to Citrā.

summary: The Pratiṣṭhālakṣaṇasārasamuccaya ('Compendium of the Essence of Characteristics of Installation') is a 32-chapter Sanskrit handbook on Śaiva-dominated temple ritual, iconography, and image consecration (pratiṣṭhā), attributed to Vairocana (c. 11th–12th century). Compiled from various tantric āgamas and architectural treatises, it details temple building, iconometric proportions, ritual bathing, eye-opening ceremonies, installation of lingas and pantheon deities, and annual festivals such as pavitrārohaṇa. Transmitted chiefly in Nepal, the text is well known in art-historical literature, particularly for chapter 6, which served as a primary textual manual for Newar artists and manuscript illustrators.

summary: The Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya ('Heart of Recognition') is an introductory compendium of the Pratyabhijñā philosophy of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism composed in the early 11th century CE by Kṣemarāja. Formulated in twenty aphorisms (sūtras) accompanied by his auto-commentary, the work expounds how universal consciousness (Citi) contracts to manifest as the individual experiencer and how recognition of one's innate divine nature brings liberation. It serves as one of the most accessible and influential introductory treatises to the Pratyabhijñā and Trika traditions.

summary: The Kāmakalāvilāsa is a 55-verse Śrīvidyā treatise by Puṇyānanda expounding the non-dual cosmogonic and metaphysical doctrine of the Supreme Goddess Tripurasundarī. It details the emanation of the universe from the primordial union of illumination (prakāśa) and reflexive awareness (vimarśa) via the kāmakalā—the creative principle embodied in the three primal bindus. The text articulates the manifestation of sacred speech through the four levels of sound and maps this cosmogony onto the geometry and presiding deities of the Śrīcakra. The accompanying Cidvallī commentary by Naṭanānanda provides essential elucidation of the esoteric terminology and ritual correlations.

summary: The Kāmakalāvilāsa is a foundational doctrinal treatise of the Śrīvidyā tradition of Śākta Tantra, attributed to Puṇyānandanātha. In 55 verses, it sets forth the non-dual metaphysics of Kāmakalā—the creative pulsation and self-manifestation of pure consciousness (Prakāśa-Vimarśa / Śiva-Śakti)—and elaborates the esoteric emergence and symbolic structure of the Śrīcakra and the fifteen-syllabled mantra (Kādimata / Hādimata). The text is accompanied by the Cidvallī, the classic Sanskrit commentary by Naṭanānanda, which elucidates its dense philosophical vocabulary and meditative correspondences.

summary: The Puraścaryārṇava is a massive late 18th-century Śākta-Tāntrika ritual compendium (nibandha) compiled under the patronage of King Pratāpasiṃha Śāha of Nepal (r. 1775–1777). Organized into twelve taraṅgas ('waves'), it synthesizes scriptural injunctions from numerous Tantras and Purāṇas on the requirements and performance of puraścaryā (preparatory mantra realization) and ritual worship. This first volume encompasses taraṅgas 1 to 4, covering the transmission lines (ṣaḍāmnāya), diagrammatic testing of mantras (cakra-vicāra), pavillion and fire-altar (kuṇḍa) layout, qualifications of guru and śiṣya, and preliminary initiation (kriyāvatī dīkṣā).

summary: The Puraścaryārṇava ('Ocean of Preliminary Ritual Practice') is an encyclopedic Śākta-Tantric and Smārta ritual digest (nibandha) compiled in Nepal in the late eighteenth century under the royal patronage of King Pratāpasiṃha Śāha. This volume comprises taraṅgas 5 through 8, expounding tantric initiation procedures (dīkṣāprayoga), general rules and purificatory rituals for mantra practice (puraścaraṇa, rosary conventions, japa methods), sacrificial oblations and auxiliary rites (homa, tarpaṇa, mārjana, brāhmaṇabhojana), and individual puraścaraṇa routines for the mantras of Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, and Śiva. The digest is renowned for its vast collation and systematic synthesis of authoritative citations from tantras, purāṇas, and paddhatis.

summary: The Puraścaryārṇava ('Ocean of Preliminary Ritual Practice') is an encyclopedic Śākta and Tāntrika ritual digest (nibandha) compiled under the auspices of King Pratāpasiṃha Śāha of Nepal (r. 1775–1777). This third volume contains taraṅgas 9 through 12, completing the twelve-chapter digest. It covers the mantras and puraścaraṇa rituals of the Daśamahāvidyās (taraṅga 9), other deities including Sarasvatī alongside Vaidika mantras like the Gāyatrī (taraṅga 10), the worship of Durgā with an extensive manual for the autumnal Durgotsava / Navarātri (taraṅga 11), and the mantras, yantras, stotras, and kavacas of Brāhmī and various other deities (taraṅga 12). Citing scores of canonical tantras, Purāṇas, and earlier ritual paddhatis, it is an essential reference for northern Indian and Nepalese tantric liturgy.

summary: The Parātrīśikā (or Parātrīṃśikā) is an essential foundational scripture of Kashmir Śaivism's Trika lineage, traditionally received as an extract from the Rudrayāmalatantra. In 35 verses, Śiva (Bhairava) expounds to the Goddess the mystery of the supreme reality (anuttara), the Goddess Parā as non-dual awareness, and the esoteric phonemic emanations (mātṛkā) through which cosmos and mantra manifest. In this vivṛti, the late Kashmirian scholar Rājānaka Lakṣmīrāma provides a lucid, line-by-line exposition designed to make the dense tantric teachings accessible in light of Abhinavagupta's earlier exegetical work.

summary: The Nādakārikā (also known as Nādasiddhi) is a 26-verse treatise by the Kashmirian master Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha II establishing the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta metaphysics and epistemology of sound. Rāmakaṇṭha analyzes how momentary articulate speech sounds (dhvani, varṇa) convey meaning, critiquing both the Grammarians' sphoṭa doctrine and alternative models while positing nāda as a subtle, insentient material entity derived from bindu/kuṇḍalinī that serves as the substrate for speech manifestation. The text is accompanied by the vyākhyā of the 12th-century Tamil Śaiva theologian Aghoraśiva, which unpacks the polemical nuances and technical vocabulary.

summary: The Prāṇatoṣiṇī is a comprehensive nineteenth-century Śākta digest (nibandha) composed in Bengal in 1820–1821 CE, divided into seven thematic kāṇḍas. This third section, the Arthakāṇḍa, details daily ritual practices and conduct (ācāra, nityakarma), including veneration of the guru and strīguru, Kuṇḍalinī meditation, morning ablutions (snāna), the sanctity of the river Gaṅgā, twilight prayers (sandhyā), and the specifications of vessels and utensils for pūjā. It draws extensively on classical Tantras, Āgamas, and Purāṇas to codify Bengali ritual tradition.

summary: The Kāmyakāṇḍa forms the fourth book of the Prāṇatoṣiṇī, an influential 19th-century Śākta Tantric digest (nibandha) compiled in Bengal in 1821 CE by Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra under the auspices of Prāṇakṛṣṇa Viśvāsa. This section focuses on kāmya rituals (optional rites directed at specific worldly and spiritual fruits), detailing mantra practice, puraścaraṇa, rosary rites (mālāprakaraṇa), pilgrimage/pīṭha rules, prayogas for deities such as Kārtavīrya, Dhūmāvatī, and Ucchiṣṭacaṇḍālinī, as well as an exhaustive treatment of the autumn Durgotsava. It functions as an indispensable textual compendium preserving liturgical quotations from numerous otherwise obscure Tantras and Purāṇas.

This opening section, the Sargakāṇḍa (ten paricchedas), covers cosmogony, the manifestation of sound and language (śabdasṛṣṭi, sphoṭa, and varṇotpatti), bodily mysticism, embryology, and the classification of Tantric scriptures. The compendium is an indispensable source for Tantric textual history, preserving extensive extracts from numerous earlier tantras and digests that are otherwise rare or lost.

summary: The Nigamasāranirṇaya is a late Śākta/Kaula ritual digest (nibandha) composed by Ramāramaṇadeva. Drawing on and quoting numerous medieval and early modern tantric scriptures and manuals—including the Tantrakaumudī of Govinda Ṭhakkura (16th century), Tantracūḍāmaṇi, Gandharvatantra, Phetkāriṇītantra, and Jñānārṇava—it systematically establishes the mantras, cakras, nyāsa rituals, and worship procedures of Kaula goddesses, particularly Kālikā and various Vidyās, while addressing doctrinal consistency (ekavākyatā) across tantric sources.

summary: The Rudrayāmala is traditionally celebrated as one of the major early Śaiva-Śākta Yāmala tantras, although the ancient scripture cited by non-dual Kashmirian Śaiva authors survives only in fragmentary quotations. The extant Uttaratantra (presented here in its extensive 90-paṭala recension) is a later Kaula-Śākta compilation devoted to esoteric yoga, ritual, and mantra practice. It provides detailed expositions of Kuṇḍalinī yoga, subtle bodily physiology, the cakras along with their presiding Śaktis (Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Lākinī, Kākinī, Śākinī, and Hākinī), guru-sevā, and the worship of goddesses such as Kumārī, Tripurasundarī, and Mahākālī.

summary: The Kalpavṛkṣa (or Kalpavṛkṣabandha) is an unpublished non-dual Śaiva philosophical treatise by the 17th-century Kashmiri master Sāhiba Kaula. Written at the behest of Mahārāja Jayavantsiṃha of Maruvāṭa for the instruction of beginners (bālabodha), it synthesizes the viewpoints of Brahmādvaita, Śivādvaita, and Mahādvaita, articulating Pratyabhijñā and Spanda philosophy in accessible terms.

attribution_note: The root hymn is traditionally ascribed to Sāmba, son of Kṛṣṇa, whom Purāṇic accounts (e.g. Varāhapurāṇa, Sāmbapurāṇa) describe as worshipping the Sun god Sūrya to be cured of leprosy. Modern scholars view it as an early medieval (c. 8th-century) Kashmiri hymn blending Saura solar adoration with the esoteric yoga and metaphysics of Vāk (levels of speech). The commentary (Vivṛti or Ṭīkā) is by Rājānaka Kṣemarāja (early 11th century), disciple of Abhinavagupta, who signs his name in the closing stanza and interprets the stotra through the non-dual lens of Trika and Pratyabhijñā Śaivism.

summary: The Sāmbapañcāśikā is a 53-verse hymn celebrating Sūrya as Cidbhānu, the supreme luminary of pure consciousness. Traditionally attributed to Kṛṣṇa's son Sāmba, who is said to have worshipped the Sun to heal from leprosy, the hymn is an early medieval Kashmiri work that integrates solar devotion with Kundalinī yoga and the esoteric philosophy of Vāk (levels of cosmic speech). In his Vivṛti, the 11th-century polymath Rājānaka Kṣemarāja comments on the hymn from the perspective of non-dual Trika and Pratyabhijñā Śaivism, demonstrating that the solar deity is none other than the self-luminous awareness of Paraśiva.

A scribal colophon follows ("yādṛśaṃ pustakaṃ ... saṃvat phālguṇa saptamī ..."), so the copy in UPSS MS 5144 is complete as transmitted. The work's extent outside this manuscript is unknown. The language is mostly early modern Hindi with Sanskrit mantra and colophon material.

summary: The Sūkṣmāgama is a South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta scripture counted among the 28 Siddhāntāgamas. summary: The Prāsādamaṇḍana is a classical 15th-century Sanskrit manual on Hindu temple architecture (vāstuśāstra) composed by Maṇḍana, court architect to Mahārāṇā Kumbha of Mewar. summary: The Bhogakārikā ('Verses on Worldly Experience') by Sadyojyoti is a foundational philosophical treatise of the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta tradition and one of the eight canonical primers known collectively as the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa. In 146 verses, Sadyojyoti investigates the nature of bhoga (embodied experience of pleasure and pain), explaining how the bound individual soul (paśu)—whose innate powers of consciousness and action are obscured by beginningless primordial impurity (mala)—is endowed by Śiva with bodies, faculties, and worlds evolved out of māyā to experience karmic fruit and mature its impurity. Aghoraśiva's 12th-century vṛtti elucidates Sadyojyoti's concise verses line by line, rigorously defending the realist ontology of pati (Lord), paśu (soul), and pāśa (bond) against rival arguments from Sāṅkhya, Nyāya, and Buddhist philosophy.

summary: The Mokṣakārikā is an authoritative doctrinal treatise of classical dualist Śaiva Siddhānta composed by Sadyojyoti (c. late 7th–early 8th century CE), traditionally included as one of the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa. Across 157 verses, it expounds the nature of liberation (mokṣa), rejecting non-dualist and nihilistic theories to argue that liberation consists in the eradication of innate impurity (mala) and karma, whereby the liberated soul realizes innate omniscience and omnipotence equal to Śiva (śivasāmya). It is accompanied by the philosophically rigorous commentary (vṛtti) of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha II (fl. 10th century CE), who elaborates the epistemological and ontological arguments against rival Buddhist, Nyāya, and Vedāntic positions.

summary: The Paramokṣanirāsakārikā is an early Śaiva Siddhānta polemical and doxographical treatise by Sadyojyoti (c. late 7th to early 8th century CE), accompanied here by the comprehensive commentary (vṛtti) of Kashmirian theologian Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha II (fl. c. 950–1000 CE). Across 59 kārikās expounding a passage of the Rauravasūtra, the work systematically refutes twenty non-Śaiva and heterodox soteriological viewpoints—including Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Vedānta, Pāñcarātra, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist, Jaina, and non-Siddhānta Śaiva models—showing that liberation cannot consist in mere isolation, dissolution, cessation of consciousness, or acquisition of mundane qualities. In their place, Sadyojyoti and Rāmakaṇṭha defend the orthodox Siddhānta doctrine that liberation is the manifestation of the soul's innate, co-equal Śiva-nature (śivatvavyakti), consisting in unobstructed omniscience and omnipotence, actualized through initiation (dīkṣā).

summary: The Tattvatrayanirṇaya ('Determination of the Three Principles') by Sadyojyoti (c. late 7th to early 8th century CE) is a foundational philosophical treatise of dualist Śaiva Siddhānta, preserved as one of the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa. Across 32 kārikās condensing doctrines from the Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha, it establishes the three eternal realities: the Lord (Śiva / pati), bound souls (puruṣa / paśu), and the primordial material cause (māyā / pāśa), alongside the innate beginningless impurity (mala). Aghoraśiva's 12th-century vṛtti provides an authoritative word-by-word commentary that became central to the canonical South Indian exegetical tradition.

summary: The Nareśvaraparīkṣā ('Examination of the Soul and the Lord') by Sadyojyoti (c. late 7th–early 8th century CE) is an early systematic treatise of dualistic Śaiva Siddhānta. Comprising 183 verses across three kāṇḍas, it establishes the distinct ontologies of the individual soul (nara/paśu) and the supreme Lord (īśvara/pati), countering Buddhist, Sāṅkhya, and Advaitin models. The accompanying Prakāśa commentary by Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha (10th century CE) significantly elaborates the philosophical argumentation, mounting a sustained defense of the enduring, self-luminous self against Buddhist Sautrāntika and Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda critique.

summary: The Sarvollāsatantra is an important 15th-century Śākta-Kaula compendium (saṃgraha) attributed to the Bengali Tantric master Sarvānandanātha of Mehār. In 63 chapters (ullāsas), it compiles extensive citations from older tantras and āgamas on essential Kaula practices, including initiation (dīkṣā), guru veneration, the pañcatattvas, cakra-pūjā, and internal Kuṇḍalinī yoga. It is of notable historical importance for providing one of the earliest textual classifications of the ten Mahāvidyās.

attribution_note: The work is an anonymous metrical commentary on the Parātrīśikā. As demonstrated by Alexis Sanderson (2014, p. 28), invocatory verse 3 reveres Śiva dwelling in Kailāsa, Kashmir, Kāśī, and Vyāghrapurī (Chidambaram), indicating South Indian provenance. It belongs to the South Indian transmission based on the Parātrīśikālaghuvṛtti (traditionally ascribed to Abhinavagupta). The Muktabodha catalog erroneously applied the authorship of Somānanda (author of the Śāktavijñāna, the second text in KSTS 74) to this commentary.

summary: The Parātrīśikātātparyadīpikā is an anonymous medieval Śākta-Trika metrical commentary comprising 536 anuṣṭubh verses on the Parātrīśikā (the dialogue on supreme Goddess-consciousness from the Rudrayāmala). Composed in Chidambaram (Vyāghrapurī) in South India, it represents the South Indian transmission and adaptation of non-dual Śaivism based on the Parātrīśikālaghuvṛtti ascribed to Abhinavagupta. The work provides an esoteric exposition of phonemic cosmology (mātṛkā and mālinī), the manifestation of the thirty-six tattvas, and spiritual liberation through non-dual Śiva-Śakti realization.

summary: The Śivadṛṣṭi of Somānanda (early 10th c.) is the earliest treatise of the Pratyabhijñā school of Kashmirian non-dual Śaivism. In seven āhnikas of verse it argues that everything is Śiva, conscious and endowed with power, refutes rival positions (notably the grammarians' doctrine of Paśyantī, Śākta, Sāṃkhya, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist and other views), and ends with an account of the author's lineage. Utpaladeva's Vṛtti, which explains the text word by word, is preserved only up to 4.74.

No lacunae are marked in the transcription.

summary: The Ajñānadhvāntadīpikā is a tantric manual (mantrapaddhati) attributed to Somanātha, son of Maheśabhaṭṭa. It treats the qualifications of guru and śiṣya, astrologically auspicious timings for dīkṣā, mantra examination and purification (siddhādisādhana), nyāsa, and various practical rituals (prayogas) and yantras accompanied by vernacular Hindi commentary.

attribution_note: Commentary on Somaśambhu's Kriyākāṇḍakramāvalī (Somaśambhupaddhati, 11th c.). Section colophons attribute it to Trilocanaśivācārya; the final colophon calls him Tryambakaśambhu and the opening verse Netraśambhu, all variants of one name. He refers to his own earlier commentary on a work of Brahmaśambhu ('brahmaśambhuṭīkāyām'). The closing verses give a lineage running from the Āmardaka/Kolakī santāna through Somaśambhu and Jñānaśambhu.

It explains the procedures of daily worship, the occasional rites (pavitrārohaṇa, damanaka), expiation, initiation and consecration, quoting extensively from Siddhāntāgamas such as the Svāyambhuva, Mṛgendra, Mataṅga and Kiraṇa, and from exegetes such as Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha. summary: The Subodhamañjarī (also referred to in verse 44 as Svabodhodayamañjarī) is a short Sanskrit treatise in 44 verses by Vāmanadatta, son of the Mīmāṃsaka Harṣadatta. summary: The Suprabhedāgama is one of the twenty-eight canonical Mūlāgamas of dualist Śaiva Siddhānta, traditionally categorized among the five Śivabhedas emanating from the Vāmadeva face of Śiva. It is one of the relatively few Āgamas preserved across all four classical divisions (pādas): Kriyāpāda (temple layout, iconography, installation of liṅgas, and daily/occasional worship rituals), Caryāpāda (initiation, duties of devotees, royal rites, and expiation), Yogapāda (subtle anatomy, prāṇāyāma, and meditation), and Jñānapāda (cosmogony, thirty-six tattvas, and the adhvans). It has long served as a prominent ritual authority for South Indian temple architecture and liturgical performance.

summary: The Haṭhayogapradīpikā is the principal medieval manual of Haṭhayoga, composed around the 15th century CE by Svātmārāma. Synthesizing Nātha lineage teachings and earlier haṭha treatises, it details āsana, purification techniques (ṣaṭkarma), prāṇāyāma (kumbhaka), and mudrā/bandha as an essential physical progression culminating in Rājayoga (samādhi and nādānusandhāna). This e-text reproduces the root text alongside Brahmānanda's prominent ṭīkā, the Jyotsnā, which explicates the physiological and philosophical terminology.

summary: The Svacchandatantra is one of the principal surviving scriptures of the Bhairavatantra current of the Śaiva Mantramārga (datable approximately to the 6th–7th century CE). Presented as a dialogue between Svacchandabhairava and the Goddess, it details the construction of maṇḍalas, mantra dynamics, initiatory procedures (dīkṣā), post-initiatory vows, subtle yoga (uccāra and prāṇāyāma), esoteric cosmology, and secret initiation sign-language (chummakā). Kṣemarāja's extensive 11th-century commentary, the Uddyota, is a foundational monument of Kashmir Śaivism, systematically harmonizing the earlier dualist ritualist tantra with the monistic theology and ontology of the Trika and Pratyabhijñā schools.

summary: The Mātṛkācakraviveka is a medieval Śākta / Trika-Śrīvidyā treatise in four chapters (khaṇḍas) addressing the esoteric symbolism of the Sanskrit alphabet (mātṛkācakra). It explains how the phonemes represent the creative pulsation (vimarśaśakti) and body of Paraśiva, detailing the cosmology of sound, mantra, and Kuṇḍalinī yoga in relation to the Śrīcakra. The e-text includes the full Sanskrit commentary (vyākhyā) by Śivānanda Muni.

summary: The Tārārahasyavṛttikā by the Bengali author Śaṅkara is a Śākta manual of the worship of Tārā in her form as Mahānīlasarasvatī. Organised in 15 paṭalas, it compiles and explains passages from tantras such as the Nīlatantra, Gāndharvatantra and Matsyasūkta on daily worship, initiation, puraścaraṇa, occasional and optional rites, secret observances, worship of young girls (kumārī), the 'Chinese' mode of practice (mahācīnakrama), mantras, hymns, bhāvas, homa and inner yoga. This e-text has only the first eight paṭalas.

summary: A large commentary by Viśveśvara, son of Lakṣmīdhara, on the Tārāsahasranāma (the thousand names of Tārā, beginning "kailāsaśikharāsīnam"). In its colophons it is called Girijābhidhārthacintāmaṇi and it is divided into twelve mayūkhas. Each name is explained grammatically and etymologically, with citations from lexica, Purāṇas, tantras and śāstra works. The e-text is an unpublished diplomatic transcription of a Jammu manuscript dated saṃvat 1942 (1885/86 CE).

summary: The Tārātantra is a short Śākta scripture in six paṭalas formatted as a dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, devoted to the worship of the Mahāvidyā goddess Tārā (in forms such as Ugratārā and Ekajaṭā). It details her five-syllable root mantra, visualizations (dhyāna), daily liturgy (prātaḥkṛtya, guru-pūjā), and magical rites (ṣaṭkarman). The text is especially renowned for its integration of the Mahācīnakrama ('Chinese/Tibetan rite'), recounting how both the sage Vasiṣṭha and the Buddha attained spiritual perfection (siddhi) through this esoteric discipline.

summary: Tantrābhidhāna is an anthology of traditional Sanskrit Tantric lexica, seed-syllable glossaries (koṣa, nighaṇṭu), and gesture manuals compiled and published as Volume 1 of Arthur Avalon's Tantrik Texts series. The compilation provides technical keys for decoding secret seed-syllables (bīja), coded letter designations (saṅketa), and ritual gestures (mudrā) in Śākta and Tantric liturgical literature. summary: The Tantrarājatantra is one of the primary canonical scriptures of the Kādimata lineage within the Śākta Śrīvidyā tradition, structured in 36 chapters as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and the Devī. It presents comprehensive instruction on the worship of Lalitā Mahā-Tripurasundarī and the fifteen Nityā goddesses, detailing mantra formulas, yantra geometry, the nyāsa rites of the Śrīcakra, and non-dual Śākta metaphysics. In this edition, the scripture is accompanied by the running Manoramā commentary, written up through chapter 22 by the Kashmirian master Subhagānandanātha and finished for chapters 23–36 by his disciple Prakāśānandanātha.

It covers the veneration of the lineage of gurus, Gaṇapati, and Bhairava, the consecration of the water pot (kalaśapūjā), the invocation of solar, lunar, and fire energies into ritual vessels, and kuṇḍalinī meditation ascending from the mūlādhāra to the brahmarandhra. summary: The Tejobindūpaniṣad is one of the twenty Yoga Upaniṣads reckoned in the Muktikā canon. In six adhyāyas, it integrates yogic contemplation on the 'effulgent point' (tejobindu) with non-dual Advaita Vedānta philosophy, expounding a distinctive fifteen-limbed yoga (pañcadaśāṅgayoga) and teachings on jīvanmukti and videhamukti. Upaniṣadbrahmayogin's Vivaraṇa commentary provides a word-by-word exposition systematically interpreting all yogic disciplines and dialogues from the perspective of radical non-duality (advaita).

summary: The Troṭalātantra (or Troṭalamahātantra) is an early medieval Śaiva/Śākta tantric scripture framed as an exposition delivered by Śiva to Garuḍa (Tārkṣya). It centers on the goddess Troṭalā—identified with Tvaritā and linked with the Kubjikā tradition—so named because she shatters (troṭana) worldly bonds. The work covers her visual iconography, mantra formulas, internal yogic ascent through the centers to union with Bhairava, and rites for protection against poison and the subjugation of spirits.

summary: The Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra (also styled Uḍḍāmareśvaramahātantra or Mantracintāmaṇi) is a 15-chapter applied Tantric manual dedicated primarily to pragmatic magic and ritual pharmacology (ṣaṭkarman rites such as vaśīkaraṇa, uccāṭana, stambhana, and māraṇa). It details incantations, herbal and mineral recipes (auṣadhi), and counter-sorcery remedies for curing fevers, expelling demonic and planetary possession (bhūtas, grahas, brahmarākṣasas), counteracting poisons, and evoking yakṣiṇīs and related semi-divine entities for material acquisition. The work is structured as an instruction delivered by Śiva to Gaurī and belongs to the wider milieu of practical medieval grimoire literature closely allied with the Uḍḍīśa/Uḍḍāmara traditions.

summary: The Śataratnasaṃgraha is a classical Śaiva Siddhānta anthology compiled by Umāpatiśivācārya (c. 14th century), selecting approximately one hundred core verses from canonical Āgamas including the Svāyambhuva, Mataṅga, Kiraṇa, Niśvāsa, Mṛgendra, and Sarvajñānottara. The verses outline the central tenets of the tradition, specifically the threefold ontology of Pati (the Lord), Paśu (the individual soul), and Pāśa (the binding bonds), along with the efficacy of dīkṣā (initiation) and jñāna (gnosis) in achieving liberation. In this e-text, the verses are accompanied throughout by the Śataratnollekhanī, an extensive prose commentary that glosses and contextualizes each Āgamic quotation in accordance with classical dualistic Śaiva Siddhānta exegesis.

summary: The Mahānayaprakāśa ('Illumination of the Great Way') is an anonymous Sanskrit verse treatise belonging to the esoteric Krama (Mahānaya/Mahārtha) school of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism. Divided into nine ullāsas, it systematically presents the sequential and non-sequential cycles of divine manifestation and reabsorption, focusing on the wheels of deities (cakras), the pīṭhas, and the twelve forms of Kālī. It emphasizes the direct transmission of non-dual realization through the grace and penetrating glance of the guru (gurudṛkpāta) as superior to external ritual practices.

summary: The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi ('Proof of a Conscious Knower') is one of three short treatises comprising Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayī, written in the first half of the 10th century to establish the foundational tenets of non-dual Pratyabhijñā philosophy. In 27 kārikās, Utpaladeva argues against Buddhist momentariness and static Vedāntic consciousness, maintaining that both cognition and practical causal efficacy (arthakriyā) require an active, self-reflective subject (vimarśa, ahaṃbhāva) rather than an insentient (jaḍa) continuum. In this edition, the lost original auto-commentary is replaced by a concise modern Sanskrit Vṛtti composed in 1919 CE by Kashmiri scholar Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī.

summary: The Īśvarasiddhi ('Establishment of the Lord') is one of the three monographs comprising the Siddhitrayī by Utpaladeva (fl. c. 900–950 CE), the founding master of the Pratyabhijñā school of nondual Kashmir Shaivism. Consisting of 56 kārikās and the author's own prose vṛtti, the work defends the necessity of an intelligent conscious agent (Īśvara/Śiva) behind the cosmos. It critically examines rival models—particularly the Sāṅkhya theory of insentient material transformation (pariṇāmavāda) and the Nyāya inferential proof—before resolving divine agency into nondual recognition (pratyabhijñā).

summary: The Īśvarasiddhi ('Establishment of the Lord') is one of the three monographs comprising the Siddhitrayī by Utpaladeva (fl. c. 900–950 CE), the founding master of the Pratyabhijñā school of nondual Kashmir Shaivism. Consisting of 56 kārikās and the author's own prose vṛtti, the work defends the necessity of an intelligent conscious agent (Īśvara/Śiva) behind the cosmos. It critically examines rival models—particularly the Sāṅkhya theory of insentient material transformation (pariṇāmavāda) and the Nyāya inferential proof—before resolving divine agency into nondual recognition (pratyabhijñā).

summary: The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi ('Proof of a Conscious Knower') is one of three short treatises comprising Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayī, written in the first half of the 10th century to establish the foundational tenets of non-dual Pratyabhijñā philosophy. In 27 kārikās, Utpaladeva argues against Buddhist momentariness and static Vedāntic consciousness, maintaining that both cognition and practical causal efficacy (arthakriyā) require an active, self-reflective subject (vimarśa, ahaṃbhāva) rather than an insentient (jaḍa) continuum. In this edition, the lost original auto-commentary is replaced by a concise modern Sanskrit Vṛtti composed in 1919 CE by Kashmiri scholar Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī.

summary: The Sambandhasiddhi ('Establishment of Relation') is one of the three foundational polemical monographs constituting Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayī (fl. c. 925–975 CE). Composed in verse with an integral prose autocommentary (vṛtti), the text defends the ontological and linguistic reality of relations (sambandha) against Buddhist nominalist critiques, particularly Dharmakīrti's Sambandhaparīkṣā. Integrating Bhartṛhari's grammatical philosophy with non-dual Pratyabhijñā metaphysics, Utpaladeva argues that relation as identity-in-difference cannot subsist purely among insentient entities, but necessarily depends on the synthesizing, reflective awareness (vimarśa, anusaṃdhāna) of universal consciousness (Śiva).

summary: The Vāmakeśvarīmata (more commonly known as the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava) is a foundational scriptural tantra of the Kaula Śrīvidyā tradition dedicated to the goddess Tripurasundarī. It details the geometry and esoteric worship of the Śrīcakra, the mantras and iconography of the fifteen Nityā goddesses, ritual hand gestures (mudrās), and mantric practices. In this commentary (Vivaraṇa), the Kashmiri master Rājānaka Jayaratha interprets the Śākta liturgy through the non-dualistic philosophical lens of the Kashmir Śaiva Trika and Pratyabhijñā traditions.

summary: An extensive Śākta Kaula Tantra belonging to the Dakṣiṇāmnāya (Southern transmission) and associated in its opening verses with the Kāmarūpa pīṭha. Framed as a revelation by Caṇḍabhairava to Guhyakālikā, it centers on the worship of the goddess Vārāhī along with Sundarī and Kālikā, serving as a comprehensive manual of ritual procedures, mantras, yantras, nyāsa, and yogic practices. The text is cited in several major Tantric digests, providing a terminus ante quem prior to the late 18th-century Puraścaryārṇava.

summary: The Varāhopaniṣad is a minor Yoga Upaniṣad (reckoned as the 98th in the Muktikā canon) attached to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, framed as an instruction imparted by Viṣṇu in his boar form (Varāha) to the sage Ṛbhu. Across five adhyāyas, it enumerates the 24, 36, and 96 tattvas, details subtle yogic physiology (cakras, nāḍīs, and kuṇḍalinī), outlines prāṇāyāma and haṭhayogic disciplines, and elucidates the seven stages of spiritual knowledge (jñānabhūmikās) culminating in jīvanmukti. Upaniṣadbrahmayogin's commentary (Vivaraṇa) interprets the yogic practices in the light of Advaita Vedāntic non-dualism.

summary: The Vīrāgama (Vīratantra, 'Ṣaṭsahasrasaṃhitā') is one of the 28 Mūlāgamas of the Śaiva Siddhānta. The transcribed text, a Brahmā–Īśvara dialogue, covers mantroddhāra, ācārya qualifications, dīkṣā and abhiṣeka, the domestic saṃskāras from garbhādhāna to funerary rites, daily worship, mudrās, homa, festivals and expiations, and an extensive series of installation (pratiṣṭhā/sthāpana) and snapana rites for Śiva, Gaurī, Skanda, Jyeṣṭhā and other deities.

summary: A manuscript with two Śākta tantras. The Vīracūḍāmaṇi (11 paṭalas) gives the vīrācāra worship of Mahānīlasarasvatī/Tārā: morning rites, haṃsa-sādhana, offering japa to the deities of the cakras, dīkṣā, pūjā, mantroddhāra, homa and kāmya rites. It continues through arguments on aṣṭāvaraṇa, pañcācāra and ṣaṭsthala, and on iṣṭaliṅga versus sthiraliṅga worship. It breaks off mid-sentence ("tathā ca jaṅgamatattvasya sarvābhya..."). The author is therefore Vīracannabasava or a pupil recording his teaching. The attribution rests only on these verses.

summary: A late Vīraśaiva theological and polemical treatise composed in mixed verse and prose by Vīracannabasava of Sudhāpurī, writing within the lineage of the 15th–16th century saint Tōṭada Siddhēśvara and Murigā Śāntavīra. The work expounds classical Vīraśaiva doctrine, focusing on the eight protective shields (aṣṭāvaraṇa), five conducts (pañcācāra), six stages (ṣaṭsthala), and the superiority of personal liṅga worship (iṣṭaliṅga) over temple idols (sthiraliṅga). It supports its positions by citing extensive passages from Purāṇic and Tantric/Āgamic texts such as the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā, Pārameśvara, Kūrmapurāṇa, and Sūtasaṃhitā.

summary: The Vīraśaivācārapradīpikā is a 38-chapter ritual and doctrinal compendium of the Vīraśaiva tradition composed by Gurudeva. Tracing the author's lineage back to the renowned Ārādhyadīkṣā master Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya, the work synthesizes Vīraśaiva theology, ritual codes, liṅga worship, initiation, and devotional duties with extensive citations from Vedic, Upaniṣadic, Purāṇic, and Śaivāgama literature.

summary: An anonymous Vīraśaiva scripture cast as a dialogue between Devī and Śiva, whose colophons assign it to a 'Sahasrakoṭisaṃhitā'. It opens with a classification of Śaiva and other sectarian traditions and declares Vīraśaivism superior to them. Its chapters set out the stages (sthala) of Vīraśaiva devotion and the doctrine and worship of the prāṇaliṅga and its six petals (ṣaḍdala). The surviving part of the last chapter deals with the preparation and wearing of sacred ash (bhasma).

summary: The Vīraśaivasiddhāntottarakaumudī is a Vīraśaiva theological and ritual manual (paddhati) composed by Vīrabhadrārādhya. Drawing on Śaiva scriptures and āgamic traditions, it details the descent and role of the Gaṇendras, the path of bhakti, initiation (ṣaḍadhvadīkṣā), the bearing of the liṅga (liṅgadhāraṇa), and daily ritual observances (dinakarma) including sandhyopāsanā, bhasmasnāna, and agnikārya.

summary: The Vīraśaivasiddhāntottarakaumudī is a Vīraśaiva ritual and theological manual. This section, the Śivapūjāvidhi, details the liturgical sequence and inner significance of worshipping Śiva through the Guru, Liṅga, and Jaṅgama. It explains the reception and spiritual efficacy of pādodaka (sacred foot-wash) and prasāda, and expounds the performance of the ritual upacāras in association with the Pañcabrahma mantras.

summary: The first book (Vairāgyaprakaraṇa, 33 sargas) of the Yogavāsiṣṭha describes the profound disillusionment and existential grief of the young prince Rāma after his pilgrimage across the country. Confronting the transience of life, wealth, youth, and the physical body, Rāma articulates his despair before king Daśaratha and the royal assembly, creating the need for sage Vasiṣṭha's extensive exposition of non-dual liberation. Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī's accompanying commentary Tātparyaprakāśa provides word-by-word glosses and an orthodox Advaita Vedānta framing.

summary: The Mumukṣuvyavahāraprakaraṇa is the second book of the Yogavāsiṣṭha (or Mokṣopāya), consisting of twenty chapters. Addressing Rāma's spiritual disaffection introduced in the opening book (Vairāgyaprakaraṇa), this section analyzes the nature of human striving (pauruṣa) versus fate (daiva), details the narrative of Śuka's attainment of peace through King Janaka, and introduces the four 'gatekeepers of liberation' (dvārapālas: śama, vicāra, santoṣa, and sādhasaṅgama). The root text is accompanied throughout by the Advaita Vedāntic commentary Tātparyaprakāśa of Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī.

summary: The Utpattiprakaraṇa ('Section on Origin/Creation') is the third book of the Yogavāsiṣṭha (traditionally ascribed to Vālmīki), an extensive philosophical poem expounding non-dualism through dialogues between the sage Vasiṣṭha and Prince Rāma. This section demonstrates how the external universe arises as a mental illusion or conceptual vibration (saṃkalpa/cittaspanda) within unconditioned consciousness (cit/Brahman), using extended allegories such as the story of Queen Līlā and the story of Karkaṭī. The root verses are accompanied by Ānandabodhendrasarasvatī's classic Advaita Vedānta commentary, the Tātparyaprakāśa.

summary: The Sthitiprakaraṇa constitutes the fourth book of the Yogavāsiṣṭha (consisting of 62 sargas), elucidating the apparent preservation and sustenance (sthiti) of the manifest phenomenal cosmos from the perspective of radical non-dualism. Sage Vasiṣṭha instructs Prince Rāma through philosophical discourse and pedagogical narratives—such as the allegorical tales of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, and the story of the ascetic Dāśūra—demonstrating that the universe possesses no independent reality and is merely an ungrounded vibration of consciousness (cittaspanda) sustained by delusion. The accompanying commentary, the Tātparyaprakāśa by Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī, elucidates the text in terms of classical Advaita Vedānta epistemology and metaphysics.

summary: The Upaśamaprakaraṇa is the fifth prakaraṇa of the Yogavāsiṣṭha (or Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa), an encyclopedic philosophical text framed as instruction given by the sage Vasiṣṭha to Prince Rāma. It focuses on the calming or pacification (upaśama) of mental fabrications and the dissolution of worldly bondage through philosophical discourses and narrative parables (including the stories of Janaka, Bali, Prahlāda, and Uddālaka). The text is accompanied by the extensive commentary Tātparyaprakāśa of Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī.

summary: The Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa is the sixth and by far the longest book of the Yogavāsiṣṭha, divided into two halves (Pūrvārdha and Uttarārdha). It brings the philosophical instructions of sage Vasiṣṭha to Prince Rāma to their culmination, expounding the nature of ultimate liberation (nirvāṇa), the total dissolution of the conceptual mind and world-appearance into pure non-dual consciousness, and the state of the living-liberated sage (jīvanmukta). This volume preserves the text according to the vulgate tradition along with the Advaita commentary Tātparyaprakāśa by Ānandabodhendrasarasvatī.

summary: The Vāruṇapaddhati (or Ātmārthapūjāpaddhati) by Varuṇaśivācārya is a medieval Śaiva Siddhānta manual outlining personal daily worship (ātmārthapūjā), purificatory rites, and liturgical procedure based on the Siddhāntāgamas. This e-text provides the root text along with the detailed commentary (vyākhyā) by the 16th-century Cidambaram scholar Nigamajñānadeva II, whose introductory verses offer a valuable survey of earlier Saiddhāntika ritual authors.

summary: The foundational scripture of Kashmir Shaivism, the Śivasūtra, expounds non-dual Śaiva metaphysics and yogic realization across three sections corresponding to the divine (śāmbhava), cognitive (śākta), and individual (āṇava) means. The Śivasūtravārttika by Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara (c. 10th–11th century CE) is an early metrical commentary representing the direct lineage of Vasugupta and Kallaṭa. It provides an important alternative exegetical perspective to Kṣemarāja's later prose Śivasūtravimarśinī.

summary: The Śivasūtra is the foundational aphoristic scripture of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism (Trika), traditionally held to have been revealed by Śiva to Vasugupta (c. early 9th century) on Mount Mahādeva. Kṣemarāja's early 11th-century Śivasūtravimarśinī is the principal and most widely read commentary, structuring the three unmeṣas as expositions of the three progressively subtle means to liberation: śāmbhavopāya, śāktopāya, and āṇavopāya.

summary: The Vātūlanāthasūtra is a short Kashmiri Krama/Kaula text of thirteen aphorisms traditionally regarded as an oral revelation from the Yoginīs to the master Vātūlanātha. Accompanied by the commentary (vṛtti) of Anantaśaktipāda, the work articulates the Sāhasa ('sudden leap') transmission of nondual Śaivism, expounding the immediate entry (mahāsāhasa-vṛtti) into transcendent Śiva-consciousness that bypasses gradual contemplative disciplines. It constitutes an essential witness to the non-systematic, esoteric lineage of the Mahārtha school.

summary: The Vātulottara is a South Indian Śaiva scripture presenting itself as a supplement (uttara) to the Vātula(āgama), in the form of a Śiva–Pārvatī dialogue, with marked emphasis on Durgā/Caṇḍī worship ('durgābheda'). This transcript collects selected paṭalas on expiations and pacification of portents (earthquakes, eclipses, comets, damage to images and chariots, animals), Navarātri and tulābhāra rites, daily worship, temple features and homa, and ends with extracts ascribed to the Parameśvaratantra and the Candrajñāna.

summary: The Pāñcarātrarakṣā is an apologetic and liturgical treatise by the 14th-century Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya Vedānta Deśika (Veṅkaṭanātha). Extending the doctrinal arguments initiated in Yāmunācārya's Āgamaprāmāṇya, the text defends the canonical validity (prāmāṇya) and orthodox Vedic alignment of the Pāñcarātra Āgamas against critiques from Mīmāṃsakas and non-Vaiṣṇava traditions. Across three adhikāras, it validates the scriptural authority of the saṃhitās, delineates the eligibility and preparatory duties of initiated practitioners, and details the fivefold daily ritual timetable (pañcakālaprakriyā: abhigamana, upādāna, ijyā, svādhyāya, and yoga) incumbent upon a prapanna.

summary: The Vedāntasāravīraśaivacintāmaṇi is an influential late medieval/early modern scholastic compendium of Vīraśaiva doctrine, philosophy, and orthopraxy by Niṣṭhūra Nañjaṇa. Drawing on Upaniṣads, Śaivāgamas, Purāṇas, and earlier authorities like the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi, the Uttarakhaṇḍa expounds Vīraśaiva theological principles (liṅgāṅgasāmarasya, ṣaṭsthala), daily conduct, initiation, and funerary rituals (anteṣṭi).

summary: The Āśaucyadīpikā is a 16th-century Śaiva Siddhānta treatise on ritual impurity (āśauca / sūtaka) composed by Vedajñāna II of Vyāghrapura (Cidambaram). Citing both Siddhāntāgamas (such as the Pauṣkara, Kāmika, Makuṭa, and Vīra) and smṛti traditions, it determines the periods and procedures of purification resulting from birth and death, particularly in relation to an initiate's eligibility for Śiva worship (śivapūjā).

summary: The Dīkṣādarśa ('Mirror of Initiation') is a comprehensive 16th-century Śaiva Siddhānta ritual digest and manual (paddhati) composed by Vedajñāna II (son of Vāmadeva) of Cidambaram (Vyāghrapura). It systematically structures the rites of Śaiva initiation (dīkṣā) and associated temple and sacerdotal ceremonies, substantiating the procedures with extensive quotations from classical Siddhāntāgamas such as the Kāraṇa, Sarvajñānottara, Pauṣkara, and Parākhya tantras.

summary: The Śaivasiddhāntaparibhāṣāmañjarī (also referred to in the closing colophon as Paryāyamañjarī) by Vedajñāna II (Nigamajñānadeva, 16th century CE) is a versified terminological manual and digest of the Śaiva Siddhānta tradition. Arranged enumeratively in ten sections (vargas) covering groups of items from one to ten, it systematically outlines theological, ritual, and philosophical doctrines of Saiddhāntika dualism.

attribution_note: The Muktabodha catalogue (M00277) gives the author as Vidyākaṇṭha, which conflates this text with Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha II's Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi, a Saiddhāntika commentary on the Mayasaṃgraha that survives in a Jammu manuscript (Muktabodha M00575). Goodall, Kiraṇavṛtti vol. 1 (1998), introduction n. 10: 'There survive Nepalese manuscripts of a tantra called the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi whose ... discussion between Devī and Bhairava in which Bhairava is asking the questions, and it is not a tantra of the Śaiva Siddhānta.' The present text is such a Nepalese manuscript. It is quoted in later Śākta digests: the verse 'bhāvas tu trividho deva divyavīrapaśukramāt' (seg. 146) is cited as Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi by Bharati (The Tantric Tradition), and the Encyclopedia of Tantra cites Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi quotations via the Śyāmārahasya and Tantrasāra.

summary: This is a Śākta/Kaula text in the form of a dialogue in which Bhairava questions the Goddess. Its prose opening says that mantras do not succeed without the right inner disposition (bhāva). The surviving portion lists the divine, perfected and human lineages of gurus (divyaugha, siddhaugha, mānavaugha) for the cults of Kālikā, Tārā and other goddesses, then sets out the doctrine of the three dispositions of the practitioner (divya, vīra, paśu) and stresses that guru and kula are required for any entitlement to tantric practice. Verses from this Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi are quoted in later Śākta digests.

summary: The Vijñānabhairava is a celebrated nondual Śaiva tantric scripture of the Trika tradition, cast as a dialogue between Bhairava and the Goddess (Bhairavī). In response to questions on the ultimate nature of reality beyond ritual forms and dualistic concepts, Bhairava presents 112 dhāraṇās (meditative centering practices) utilizing the breath, void, sound, sensory perception, and direct nondual awareness to realize spontaneous identity with divine consciousness.

summary: The Vijñānabhairava is an authoritative non-dual Śaiva tantra presented as an esoteric dialogue between Bhairava and Bhairavī, setting forth 112 dhāraṇās (yogic and meditative contemplations) to attain union with the supreme Bhairava consciousness. summary: The Vijayottaratantra (also known as the Vijayottarasaṃhitā or Trisahasrasaṃhitā) is a Śaivasiddhānta Upāgama affiliated with the Vijayāgama, one of the 28 primary Śaiva Siddhānta Mūlāgamas. The scripture focuses predominantly on ritual procedure (kriyā) and priestly conduct (caryā), detailing daily Śiva worship (śivārcana), bodily and elemental purification (bhūtaśuddhi), fire ceremonies (agnikārya), and festival liturgies (including the bhaktotsava). It is a distinct Siddhānta ritual text and must not be confused with the Trika scripture Mālinīvijayottaratantra.

summary: The Vimalāvatītantra (also termed Vimalāvatī or Vimalāvatīpaddhati) is an extensive Śaiva Siddhānta ritual manual composed by Vimalaśiva, an ācārya who resided in Vārāṇasī. The work details worship procedures (pūjā), fire sacrifices (vahnikārya, homa), festive ritual observances such as pavitrarohaṇa and damanāropaṇa, subtle breath yoga, and various degrees of initiation (dīkṣā) alongside conduct codes for initiates.

summary: The Kālīkalpalatā (or Dakṣiṇakālīkalpalatā) by Vimarśānandanātha is a Śākta tantric liturgical manual (paddhati) detailing the worship of Dakṣiṇakālī and her consort Mahākāla. Comprising two sections designated as kusumas, the first treats preliminary purifications, ritual bathing, and tarpaṇa, while the second details the daily and elaborate pūjāvidhi, nyāsa rites, and offerings. Transcribed directly from an NGMCP manuscript dated VS 1754 (1697 CE), the text demonstrates established Dakṣiṇakālī ritualism in the Kathmandu Valley prior to the eighteenth century.

summary: The Virūpākṣapañcāśikā is a concise South Indian non-dual Śaiva treatise in 53 verses attributed to Virūpākṣanātha, deeply rooted in Pratyabhijñā and Trika philosophy. Arranged in four sections (skandhas), the work expounds that the objective universe constitutes the body of supreme consciousness (viśvaśarīratva), the ultimate unity of consciousness and manifest reality (prakāśaikātmya), reflexive awareness (pratyavamarśa), and mystical attainments (vibhūti/siddhi). This e-text features the root verses embedded within the authoritative Vivṛti commentary composed by Vidyācakravartin in the 14th century.

summary: A Vīraśaiva theological and ritual compendium expounding the origins, characteristics, and rites of the virakta (renunciant) and nirābhāri ascetics.
