summary: The Viśvasāratantra is an extensive medieval Śākta-Śaiva scripture in eight paṭalas, structured as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva (Mahākāla) and Pārvatī. Widely cited in later Nibandha and ritual literature such as Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa's Tantrasāra, the work expounds cosmology, mantra- and yantra-śāstra, initiation (dīkṣā), Kuṇḍalinī yoga, and the ritual cults of various goddesses, particularly Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā (Chinnamastā), Durgā, Guhyakālī, Tripurasundarī, and Sarasvatī. It is celebrated in Tantric literature as the source of the macrocosm-microcosm axiom 'yad ihāsti tad anyatra, yan nehāsti na tat kvacit' ('what is here is elsewhere; what is not here is nowhere').

summary: The Viśeṣārthaprakāśikā is a Vīraśaiva theological and ritual manual in verse composed by Māyideva (c. 14th–15th century). summary: The Āgamaprāmāṇya is a foundational philosophical and polemical treatise by the 10th-century Śrīvaiṣṇava master Yāmunācārya. The text defends the scriptural authority (prāmāṇya) and orthodox Vedic status of the Pāñcarātra Āgamas against charges of heterodoxy, invalidity, or non-Vedic origin raised primarily by Mīmāṃsakas and Advaitins. Yāmunācārya argues for the intrinsic validity and divine authorship of the Āgamas by Nārāyaṇa and defends the orthodox caste status and temple-worship rituals of the Bhāgavatas, laying the foundation for Rāmānuja's Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta.

summary: The Yogacūḍāmaṇyupaniṣad is a medieval Yoga Upaniṣad belonging to the Muktikā canon and traditionally affiliated with the Sāmaveda. It expounds a six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) integrating Haṭhayoga doctrines, including the subtle anatomy of the six cakras, sixteen ādhāras, the kanda and 72,000 nāḍīs, as well as prāṇāyāma, mudrās, bandhas, kuṇḍalinī, and meditation on Om. This e-text provides the complete 121 verses of the Upaniṣad along with the Advaita Vedānta commentary (Vivaraṇa) of Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: The Yogajāgama is traditionally enumerated as the second of the twenty-eight Mūlāgamas of the Śaivasiddhānta canon, categorized as one of the ten Śivabhedas. The text deals primarily with kriyā and caryā aspects of Śaiva temple ritual and architecture, including temple planning (prāsādalakṣaṇa), iconometry (pratimālakṣaṇa), the installation of attendant deities (parivārasthāpana), liṅga installation (liṅgasthāpana), fire rituals (agnikārya), and initiation rites (dīkṣā). This e-text is an unpublished diplomatic transcription of an incomplete palm-leaf manuscript preserved at the French Institute of Pondicherry (IFP MS 39691).

summary: The Yogakuṇḍalyupaniṣad is one of the twenty Yoga Upaniṣads belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. In three chapters, it presents haṭha- and laya-yogic practices directed toward awakening kuṇḍalinī, including breath restraint (prāṇāyāma), dietary discipline (mitāhāra), āsana, bandhas, and lambikā (khecarī) mudrā, integrated into a non-dual Advaita Vedānta soteriology. This e-text includes both the root Upaniṣad and the running Vivaraṇa commentary by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: The Yogapīṭhakramodaya (also titled Kramodaya) is an early Kaula Śākta text closely connected with the early Kubjikā tradition. Preserved in early palm-leaf manuscripts from Nepal (notably this witness dated Nepāla Saṃvat 307 / 1187 CE), the work describes the emanational sequence (krama/udaya) of the sacred seats (yogapīṭha), the lineage of Siddhas and Gurus (gurupaṅkti), mātṛkā phonematic deployment, cakra structures, and associated ritual and esoteric contemplative practices.

summary: The Yogasārasaṃgraha is an anonymous Śaiva-Śākta yoga compendium in sixteen chapters (adhyāyas). It integrates elements of Aṣṭāṅga, Haṭha, Kuṇḍalinī, and Rājayoga, quoting extensively from diverse texts such as the Yogaśaṅkara, Praṇavacintāmaṇi, Śvetāśvataropaniṣad, and Bhagavadgītā. It is completely distinct from Vijñānabhikṣu's well-known Pātañjala Yoga digest of the same title.

summary: The Yoginīhṛdaya ('Heart of the Yoginī') is a canonical scripture of the Śrīvidyā Kaula lineage, regarded as the Uttaracatuḥśatī (second part of 400 verses) of the Vāmakeśvaratantra. Across three chapters—Cakrasaṃketa, Mantrasaṃketa, and Pūjāsaṃketa—it presents the cosmogenetic and subtle-body symbolism of the Śrīcakra, the phonic emanation of Tripurasundarī's fifteen-syllable Vidyā, and esoteric internal ritual meditation. The accompanying Dīpikā by Amṛtānanda (ca. 12th–13th century CE) is the earliest extant commentary on the treatise, systematically interpreting its Śākta ritual liturgy through non-dual Pratyabhijñā and Trika philosophy.

summary: The Yoginītantra is a major late medieval Śākta tantric scripture composed in 16th-century Assam (ancient Kāmarūpa). Cast as a dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī, the text is arranged in two parts: the Pūrvakhaṇḍa (19 paṭalas), which details Kaula ritual liturgy, mantra lore, dīkṣā, and worship of Kālī; and the Uttarārdha / Kāmarūpādhikāra (up to 16 paṭalas), which serves as a sacred topography and sthalapurāṇa of Kāmarūpa, detailing sacred rivers, shrines, and the worship of the goddess Kāmākhyā. It is a critical document for the religious and political history of medieval Assam, containing valuable legends and references to the Koch dynasty.

summary: The Śāṇḍilyopaniṣad is a classical Yoga Upaniṣad framed as an instruction given by Atharvan to the sage Śāṇḍilya. Its first and longest chapter details an eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga) incorporating Haṭha-yogic practices, including ten yamas, ten niyamas, eight āsanas, detailed instructions on nāḍī-purification, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi. The second and third chapters expound the non-dual nature of Brahman in both saguṇa/sakala and nirguṇa/niṣkala aspects, integrating bodily yoga into Advaita Vedānta. In this edition, the text is accompanied by the complete Advaitic commentary (vivaraṇa) of Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: The Saundaryalaharī ('Wave of Beauty') is a celebrated Sanskrit devotional and tantric hymn of 100 verses composed in the śikhariṇī metre in honor of the Goddess Tripurasundarī. The first section (verses 1–41, often known as Ānandalaharī) expounds Śākta philosophy, Śrīcakra diagrammatics, mantra theory, and Kuṇḍalinī yoga, while the second section consists of an ornate head-to-foot (keśādipāda) stotra describing the Devi's form. This digital volume presents the edition published by the Oriental Research Institute, Mysore, featuring Lakṣmīdhara's authoritative 16th-century commentary aligning Śrīvidyā with orthodox Samayācāra, accompanied by the Bhāvanopaniṣad with Bhāskararāya's commentary and the Devīpañcastavī.

dharmanexus_title: Śabdārthacintāmaṇi (incomplete: breaks off in the closing verses)
coverage_note: The e-text runs from the maṅgala verses through all 25 paṭalas of the Śāradātilaka. Paṭala colophons in verse are preserved, e.g. 3rd (seg. 3156), 4th (seg. 4055) and 6th (seg. 4978). The commentary on the Śāradātilaka's final verses explains the 25 paṭalas as matching the 25 tattvas (seg. 13535–13540). It then breaks off mid-word in Premanidhi's own concluding verses (seg. 13563 'prodūṣaṇā thaṃ spṛ'). Muktabodha marks it 'incomplete'. Some of the 25 paṭala colophons are absent or garbled in the transcription. Only a few closing verses are probably missing.
attribution_note: The colophon verses give the author's family: 'yasyodyotamatī satī guṇavatī mātā pitomāpatir nāma premanidhīti panthakulabhūḥ kūrmācalo janmabhūḥ ... vārāṇasīvāsabhūḥ' (seg. 11468–11470). This makes him Premanidhi of the Pantha family, son of Umāpati, born in Kūrmācala (Kumaon) and resident in Vārāṇasī. He names himself again in seg. 7 ('premanidher dvijāt') and seg. 13561, and he worships Kārtavīryārjuna. He is the 18th-century tantric author whose wife Prāṇamañjarī commented on the Tantrarāja (N. N. Bhattacharyya, History of the Tantric Religion; Bharati, The Tantric Tradition).

summary: The Śabdārthacintāmaṇi is a large commentary by Premanidhi Pantha (18th c.) on Lakṣmaṇadeśika's Śāradātilaka, a major compendium of mantraśāstra in 25 paṭalas. It explains the verses at length with grammatical analysis, Nyāya-Mīmāṃsā argument and many citations from tantras. It also gives detailed procedures for ritual, maṇḍalas and fire-pits (kuṇḍa), yantras, nyāsa and the mantras of many deities.

summary: The Śaivabhūṣaṇa is a South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta ritual handbook (paddhati) consisting of 355 Sanskrit verses accompanied by an extensive bilingual Tamil prose commentary. It synthesizes prescriptions from the Kriyāpāda of the Śaivāgamas on topics including initiation (dīkṣā), the seven classes of Śaivas, qualifications of guru and disciple, daily rites (nityakarma), sūryapūjā, snapanavidhi, homa, temple festivals (utsava), and funerary rites (antyeṣṭi).

summary: The Śaivakālaviveka ('Discrimination of Auspicious Times for Śaiva Rites') is a 16th-century Śaivasiddhānta manual attributed to Nigamajñānamuni of Chidambaram. In 49 verses, it details the astrological considerations (muhūrta, tithi, nakṣatra, and lagna) required for temple construction and ritual performance, spanning from ground preparation (karṣaṇa) to deity installation (pratiṣṭhā). The text is accompanied by Gaṇapatibhaṭṭa's extensive prose commentary (vyākhyā), which cites canonical Siddhāntāgamas and standard jyotiṣa authorities.

summary: An anonymous South Indian ritual manual of the late Śaiva Siddhānta for worship of the Goddess in the sacrificial pavilion (śaktimaṇṭapa / śaktiyāga). It prescribes the preparation of the pavilion and vessels (vardhanī), the worship of the four doorways and their toraṇas (caturdvārapūjā), the altar (vedikārcana) and the āvaraṇa deities, and the invocation of Gaurī. Appended are several nyāsa procedures: Dūtikānyāsa, Devīśrīkaṇṭhanyāsa, Devīṣaḍadhvanyāsa, kalānyāsa and Śrīkaṇṭhamātṛkānyāsa.

summary: The Śaktisaṅgamatantra is a voluminous encyclopedic Śākta compendium divided into four khaṇḍas honoring Kālī, Tārā, Sundarī, and Chinnamastā, generally dated to the 16th–17th centuries CE. This first section, the Kālīkhaṇḍa (comprising 21 paṭalas), expounds the supreme theology, mantras, yantras, nyāsas, and Kaula ritual worship of Kālī. It sets forth tantric cosmology, distinguishes and systematizes the Kādi and Hādi ritual paths, and offers polemical defenses of tantric practice against non-tantric criticisms.

summary: The Sundarīkhaṇḍa is the third section of the extensive Śākta compendium Śaktisaṅgamatantra, framed as a dialogue between Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. In 21 chapters (paṭalas), it expounds rituals, mantras, and esoteric doctrines centering on the goddess Tripurasundarī (Lalitā) and the Śrīvidyā tradition, detailing initiation (dīkṣā), nyāsas, Śrīcakra worship, and related Mahāvidyās such as Dhūmāvatī. The section is also well known in South Asian historiography for its seventh paṭala (the Deśavyavasthāniyama / Ṣaṭpañcāśaddeśavibhāga), which provides a valuable late-medieval geographical gazetteer dividing the subcontinent into fifty-six regions.

Framed as a revelatory dialogue between Śiva (under names such as Ādinātha and Akṣobhya) and the Goddess (Mahogratārā), it delineates mantras, yantras, nyāsas, initiation rituals, and esoteric practices (including Cīnakrama and Pañcatattva) associated with the worship of Tārā and allied Śākta deities. This digital file is an incomplete transcription covering only chapters 1–47 (concluding at page 182 of Benoytosh Bhattacharyya's 1941 Baroda edition) out of the 71 chapters present in the printed volume.

summary: The Śambhunirṇaya (also known as the Śambhunirṇayatantra) is an influential Śāmbhava Kaula tantric ritual work divided into 26 avacchedas. It expounds initiation, maṇḍala layout, mantra pīṭhas, and the ritual framework of the Śāmbhava tradition, mentioning lineages and teachers such as Lakuleśin and Kroḍamuni. It circulated widely in South India, inspiring commentaries such as Śivānandamuni's Śambhunirṇayadīpikā.

summary: The Śambhunirṇayadīpikā is a Tantric commentary by Śivānandanātha on the Śambhunirṇaya (also known as the Sahasrārdhaśāsana or Mateśamata), an esoteric ritual work framed in 26 avacchedas. The surviving commentary covers maṇḍala construction, ritual procedures, the worship of naveśvaras and dūtīs, homa, therapeutic rituals, and contemplative yogic practices (dhyāna), breaking off incomplete during the discussion of śaktidhyāna in the eighth section.

summary: A commentary on the Śatarudriya (Rudrādhyāya, Taittirīyasaṃhitā 4.5) attributed to Abhinavaśaṅkara. The work interprets the Vedic mantras in accordance with Advaita Vedānta and Śaiva traditions, quoting from Upaniṣads, Purāṇas, and Śaiva literature, and provides the ritual context, dhyāna, and application for each mantra.

summary: The Mahānayaprakāśa ('Illumination of the Great Way') of Rājānaka Śitikaṇṭha is an important philosophical and ritual treatise belonging to the non-dual Śākta-Śaiva Krama tradition of medieval Kashmir. It comprises ninety-four vernacular verses (in Old Kashmiri / Apabhraṃśa / sarvabhāṣā) accompanied by the author's extensive Sanskrit prose auto-commentary (vivṛti), arranged across chapters designated as udayas. The work details the esoteric cosmology and internal esoteric liturgy of the Krama school centered on Kālī and the cycles of goddesses, presenting esoteric practices of trans-conceptual absorption (haṭhapāka, alaṃgrāsa) and internal pilgrimage where the practitioner's body serves as the sacred field (pīṭha).

attribution_note: Author: Śivānubhava Śivācārya, disciple of Cidghana Śivācārya, head of the Pūvvallī (Hooli) Pañcavarṇa Mahāmaṭha (final colophon, seg. 1322–1329; verse 16 'tatkarāmbhojajātena śivānubhavayoginā'). The opening verses give a lineage: Siddhacaitanya → Śivāditya, 'vaiśeṣikācārya' → Viśveśvara Śivācārya → Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya, author of the Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya → Cidghana. Gaurinath Sastri cites this guru list from the Śivādvaitadarpaṇa printed in 1928 to identify Śivāditya, author of the Saptapadārthī (Vyomavatī, part 1, introduction).

summary: The Śivādvaitadarpaṇa is a Vīraśaiva treatise in four paricchedas by Śivānubhava Śivācārya of the Pūvvallī (Hooli) maṭha. It defends the Śivādvaita or Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita reading of the Brahmasūtras in the line of Nīlakaṇṭha (Śrīkaṇṭha) Śivācārya's bhāṣya. Its chapters discuss the meaning of 'atha' in Brahmasūtra 1.1.1 and the Ānandamaya section, the nature of the soul (jīvatattvaviveka), Śivādvaita doctrine including dīkṣā and liṅgadhāraṇa (śivādvaitaviveka), and the meaning of the Upaniṣadic great sentences (mahāvākyārthaviveka). Its opening guru list has been used as evidence for the identity of Śivāditya, author of the Saptapadārthī.

summary: A composite e-text containing two Vīraśaiva/Śaiva philosophical treatises. The first, Svaprabhānanda's Śivādvaitamañjarī, defends Vīraśaiva Śivādvaita against Kevalādvaita Vedānta, opening with an examination and refutation of Śaṅkara's Adhyāsabhāṣya. The second, Śaṃbhudeva's Śaivasiddhāntadīpikā (also designated Pāśupatamataprakaraṇa), provides an exposition of Śaiva and Pāśupata doctrine, explaining the five bonds (pāśapañcaka), the attributes of released souls, and Śiva's fivefold cosmic activity (pañcakṛtya).

summary: The Kriyādīpikā of Śivāgrayogin (16th c.) is a Śaiva Siddhānta ritual manual for Śaivas of the fourth varṇa (sat-śūdras). The transcribed part covers daily conduct and saṃdhyā, pavitrāropaṇa and the cāturmāsya vow, initiation, the consecration of the ācārya (ācāryābhiṣeka) and funerary rites (antyeṣṭi). The manuscript transcribed here (IFP RE 15527) adds an anthology of other ritual texts. It includes extracts from Varuṇaśiva's Varuṇapaddhati and Aghoraśiva's Kriyākramadyotikā on pratiṣṭhā and antyeṣṭi, and Āgamic sections on jñānadīkṣā and rudrākṣa. It ends with Subrahmaṇya mantras, kavaca and stotras.

summary: The Śaivaparibhāṣā is a 16th-century Sanskrit manual of Śaiva Siddhānta philosophy composed by Śivāgrayogin, patterned after dialectical manuals such as the Vedāntaparibhāṣā. In five chapters, the work methodically details the epistemology (pramāṇa) and the three central ontological categories—the Lord (pati), the bound soul (paśu), and the fetters of bondage (pāśa)—before concluding with the path of initiation and liberation (mukti). Drawing heavily on the Saiddhāntika Āgamas (particularly the Pauṣkarāgama), it represents a major milestone in the late Sanskrit scholasticism of the school.

summary: The Kulapradīpa ('Lamp of the Kula') is a 17th-century or earlier Sanskrit Śākta-Kaula compendium (nibandha) in seven chapters (prakāśa) composed in verse by Śivānandācārya. Drawing heavily upon authoritative Āgamic sources such as the Kulārṇavatantra, Devīyāmala, and Pañcayāmala, it provides an exposition of the doctrines and ritual practices of the Kaula path, including the distinction between dakṣiṇa and vāma conduct, the purification and use of the five substances (pañcamakāra), dūtīyāga, and cakra worship. Manuscript evidence establishes a terminus ad quem for the work's composition of Saṃvat 1765 (1709 CE).

summary: The Yogacintāmaṇi by Śivānandasarasvatī (c. 16th–17th century) is a massive four-chapter compendium harmonizing classical Pātañjala Yoga, Advaita Vedānta, and Haṭhayoga traditions. It is famous for its encyclopedic compilation of quotations from the Yogasūtra, Purāṇas, Upaniṣads, and crucial medieval Haṭhayoga treatises including the Haṭhapradīpikā, Amṛtasiddhi, and Yogabīja.

summary: The Śivadharmaśāstra is the foundational text of the early medieval Śivadharma corpus, composed approximately between the 6th and 7th centuries CE. Addressed primarily to householders and lay devotees (upāsakas) rather than ascetic initiates, it articulates a comprehensive Śaiva religious way of life, including liṅga installation and worship, temple maintenance, the merit of devotional gifts (dāna), protective chants, expiations, and a Śaiva restructuring of the stages and duties of life (varṇāśramadharma). Framed as a discourse spoken by Nandikeśvara to Sanatkumāra, the work exercised vast influence on Śaiva devotionalism across South and Southeast Asia.

summary: The Śivadharmottara is an early medieval Śaiva religious treatise (c. 6th–8th century CE) forming the second foundational text of the Śivadharma corpus as a sequel to the Śivadharmaśāstra. Structured across twelve chapters as a discourse delivered by Nandikeśvara to Sanatkumāra on Mount Meru, it expounds lay and ascetic Śaiva religious practice (śivadharma), devotional liturgy, gifts (dāna), penances, and Śaiva yoga leading to liberation (mukti). It is celebrated especially for its second chapter on the gift of knowledge (vidyādāna), which contains one of premodern South Asia's most comprehensive early textual accounts of book production, manuscript copying, scribal decorum, and the ritual veneration of texts.

summary: The Śivasūtra is the foundational scriptural text of non-dual Kashmir Shaivism (Trika/Pratyabhijñā), traditionally revealed to Vasugupta on Mount Mahādeva. summary: The Śivasaṃhitā is one of the classic Sanskrit manuals on Haṭha and Rāja Yoga, probably composed between the fourteenth and early sixteenth centuries CE in or near Varanasi. Structured as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī, it synthesizes Advaita Vedānta philosophy with Śākta-Śaiva subtle anatomy (nāḍīs, cakras, kuṇḍalinī), prāṇāyāma, mudrās, and meditation. It is especially noted for its inclusive soteriological stance, affirming that householders (gṛhastha) as well as renunciants can attain liberation through yoga.

summary: The Śivasahasranāmastotra from the Ādityapurāṇa (also termed Mṛtyuñjayasahasranāmastotra) is a stotra of one thousand epithets addressed to Śiva. It is framed by a dialogue narrating how Viṣṇu, seeking to defeat the Daityas, installed a liṅga on Mount Himavat and propitiated Śiva with one thousand names and one thousand lotus blossoms to receive the Sudarśanacakra. This e-text is an unpublished diplomatic transcription of IFP manuscript 32407 prepared for the Muktabodha Indological Research Institute.

summary: The Śivasiddhāntacandrikā is a Vīraśaiva (Śivādvaita) verse treatise by Siddhanañjeśa Śivācārya of the Pūvallī (Hooli) maṭha. It has an introductory chapter and four paricchedas. It is framed as a dialogue in which the guru Cidghana, disciple of Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya, instructs King Satyendra Cola after initiating him. The teaching covers Śivādvaita doctrine with the Vīraśaiva aṣṭāvaraṇa, pañcācāra, ṣaṭsthala, liṅgadhāraṇa and liṅgāṅgaikya, and ends with the liberation in life (jīvanmukti) of the king.

summary: The Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi is the foundational systematic Sanskrit doctrinal treatise of the Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyata) tradition, providing the canonical exposition of Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita philosophy. Arranged in 21 paricchedas in the form of an instruction delivered by Ācārya Reṇuka to Sage Agastya, it elaborates the system of the 101 stages of spiritual ascent (ekottaraśatasthala) structured across the six primary stations (ṣaṭsthala). Maritoṇḍadārya's commentary, the Tattvapradīpikā, substantiates the philosophical and theological positions of the root kārikās with extensive citations from Vedic, Upaniṣadic, and Śaivāgama literature.

summary: A composite South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta manuscript on temple festivals (utsava) and seasonal observances. It contains short tracts on the Dhanurmāsa worship, the Kṛttikā lamp festival, Dīpāvali and Navarātri, as well as rakṣoghnahoma, mudrās, the sixteen upacāras and dravyāhuti homa. Its core is a series of festival chapters from the Cintya (Pratiṣṭhātantra), covering sprouting, flag-hoisting, drum-beating, bali processions, vehicle and chariot processions, tīrtha and cūrṇotsava, with the corresponding expiations (prāyaścitta). It also has utsava chapters of the Sūkṣma, Makuṭa and Kāraṇa Āgamas.

summary: An anonymous Śrīvaiṣṇava manual of domestic (gṛhya) rites in Sanskrit with Tamil rubrics, preserved in IFP manuscript 31231. Its main subject is the annual śrāddha for the father (pratyābdikaśrāddha), performed both by the pārvaṇa procedure with homa and in the shortened saṅkalpa form, with Mahāviṣṇu as protector of the rite. It also gives procedures for rekindling the domestic fire (agnisandhāna), aupāsana, the student's aupāsana and pañcagavya. It ends with a cosmographic saṅkalpa formula and fragmentary Tamil–Maṇipravāḷa notes.

attribution_note: The ascription to Bādarāyaṇa/Vyāsa is pseudepigraphic. Colophons present the work as a 'svarūpagrantha' and 'paramarahasya' in the form of a dialogue between Skanda (Kumāra) and Agastya. It is a Sanskrit Vīraśaiva work and should not be confused with the Telugu Basavapurāṇamu of Pālkuriki Somanātha (13th c.) or the Kannada Basavapurāṇa of Bhīma Kavi (1369). summary: The Sanskrit Basavapurāṇa (Basaveśvarapurāṇa) is a Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyat) purāṇa in 43 adhyāyas, framed as a dialogue in which Skanda answers Agastya's questions. It narrates the birth of Basava (Basaveśvara) as a partial incarnation of Nandin, his marriage, his service at the court of Bijjala and his miracles. It also tells the legends of many Śaiva and Vīraśaiva devotees (e.g. Kannappa, Dīpada Kaliya, Moligemāra, Śivanāgadeva) and argues for Vīraśaiva doctrine and practice against Vedic ritualism and rival sects. It closes with a scene in which Viśvakarman weighs the work against Vyāsa's other compositions and finds it the best of all purāṇas.

summary: An unpublished Śrīvidyā ritual manual (paddhati) detailing the worship of Mahātripurasundarī through the Śrīcakra. The text opens with preliminary rites including Dīpapūjākalpa, sets out the nyāsas and dhyāna for the Ṣoḍaśākṣarī and Pañcadaśākṣarī mantras, details guru-pūjā, and systematically covers the worship of the deities presiding over the nine enclosures (navāvaraṇa) of the Śrīcakra from Trailokyamohana to Sarvānandamaya, concluding with Vedic recitations including Pavamānasūkta and Puruṣasūkta.

summary: The Ratnatrayaparīkṣā ('Examination of the Three Jewels') is one of the eight classical treatises (Aṣṭaprakaraṇa) of the dualist Sanskrit Śaiva Siddhānta tradition. Unlike the tripartite categorization of souls, bonds, and the Lord (paśu, pāśa, pati), the 'three jewels' investigated here are Śiva (the conscious efficient cause), Śakti (Śiva's innate conscious energy), and Bindu (the pure material cause / mahāmāyā). The accompanying commentary, the Ratnatrayollekhinī by Aghoraśivācārya (12th c. CE), offers comprehensive ontological and exegetical analysis according to the dualist Śiddhānta school.

summary: The Śrīkarabhāṣya is the primary Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyat) bhāṣya on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtras, expounding the doctrine designated as Viśeṣādvaita or Bhedābhedātmaka-Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita. Śrīpati establishes Paraśiva as the supreme non-dual Brahman, arguing for a relation of natural difference during bondage and non-difference upon liberation (bhedābheda) between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman. The text also integrates and validates distinctive Vīraśaiva socio-religious practices such as liṅgadhāraṇa, bhasma, and rudrākṣa on Vedic and Upaniṣadic authorities.

summary: The Kramadīpikā ('Lamp of Ritual Sequence') is an influential 15th-century Vaiṣṇava ritual and mantric manual in eight chapters (paṭalas) composed by Keśava Bhaṭṭa (Kāśmīrika Keśavabhaṭṭa) of the Nimbārka tradition. It provides detailed procedures for the tantric and Pāñcarātra worship of Kṛṣṇa-Gopāla and Rādhā, focusing heavily on the eighteen-syllable Gopālamantra (as well as ten-syllable variants), yantras, nyāsas, mudrās, daily pūjā, initiation, and homa. The treatise was widely regarded as an authoritative handbook across medieval Vaiṣṇava traditions and is quoted extensively in Gauḍīya ritual literature, notably Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmin's Haribhaktivilāsa.

summary: The Cidgaganacandrikā ('Moonlight in the Sky of Consciousness') is an influential 12th-century philosophical and liturgical poem of the Krama (Mahānaya / Kālīkrama) tradition of Kashmir Śaivism, composed by Śrīvatsa. Structured in four reflections (vimarśas) comprising 312 verses, the work functions as an elaborate poetic commentary (pañcikā) on Siddhanātha's Kramastuti. It eulogizes Goddess Kālī as supreme Parāśakti, synthesizing non-dual Śākta-Śaiva metaphysics with esoteric ritual doctrines through the exposition of cyclical emanations, the circle of the thirteen Kālīs, and the Śākta path (śāktopāya) leading to liberation.

summary: The Śukavākya is a didactic dialogue in Purāṇic verse recounting an exchange between the sage Vyāsa and his son Śuka. summary: The Advaitamakaranda is a celebrated short Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa in 28 anuṣṭubh verses by Lakṣmīdhara Kavi. summary: The Advaitasiddhi is a monumental 16th-century polemical treatise of Advaita Vedānta by Madhusūdanasarasvatī, composed primarily in response to Vyāsatīrtha's Dvaita masterwork Nyāyāmṛta. Formulated using the rigorous technical terminology of Navya-Nyāya, the work systematically refutes Dvaita critiques across four paricchedas. It is celebrated for its intricate dialectical defense of the five classical definitions of the world's falsity (mithyātva), non-dual scriptural hermeneutics, and the Advaitic conception of mokṣa.

summary: Advaitānubhūti is a short Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa in 84 anuṣṭubh verses expounding non-dualism. summary: The Anātmaśrīvigarhaṇaprakaraṇa is an 18-verse Advaita Vedānta didactic poem traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarācārya. Through the recurring question and refrain 'tataḥ kiṃ ... yena svātmā naiva sākṣātkṛto 'bhūt' ('what then of it, if one has not directly realized one's own Self?'), the text systematically dismisses secular learning, wealth, physical pleasures, social honors, austerities, yogic powers, and celestial realms as worthless in the absence of direct Self-realization (ātmasākṣātkāra).

summary: The Bhagavadbhaktirasāyana is a prominent 16th-century treatise by the Advaita master Madhusūdana Sarasvatī synthesizing Advaita Vedānta philosophy with devotional aesthetics (rasaśāstra). Over three ullāsas, the work formulates bhakti (devotion to Kṛṣṇa) as an autonomous aesthetic rasa and the ultimate puruṣārtha, adapting classical Nāṭyaśāstra categories (vibhāva, anubhāva, vyabhicāribhāva, sthāyibhāva) into a theological framework. An extensive autocommentary (ṭīkāmatallikā) accompanies the first ullāsa.

summary: The Bhedojjīvana ('Reviving Difference') is a short polemical treatise by the Dvaita scholar Vyāsatīrtha (c. 1460–1539). It defends the reality of the five kinds of difference (pañcabheda), especially between God and souls and between souls, with perception, inference and scripture, against Advaita. In this e-text each passage of the root text is followed by six later Mādhva commentaries and glosses, by Bhagavantarāya, Ānandatīrtha (son of Mudgalārya), Kumbhārī Vāsudevācārya, Hulagī Śrīnātha, Kāśī Timmaṇṇācārya and Śarkarā Śrīnivāsa. Much of this commentary is navya-nyāya analysis of the inferences used.

summary: The Bhāṭṭarahasya (also called Bhāṭṭatantrarahasya) is a 17th-century treatise by Khaṇḍadeva on the semantics of verbal cognition (śābdabodha) according to the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā school. Formulated in the precise terminology of Navya-Nyāya, it examines the definitions of dharma and adharma, the semantic import of injunctive endings (vidhi) and productive agency (bhāvanā), verbal roots (dhātu), verbal suffixes (ākhyāta), and case terminations (vibhakti). This incomplete e-text ends with the discussion of the nominative case.

summary: The Catuḥśatikā ('Four Hundred Verses') is the principal treatise of Āryadeva (c. 3rd century CE), the foremost disciple of Nāgārjuna, laying out the Madhyamaka philosophy across sixteen chapters. The first eight chapters focus on the bodhisattva's cultivation of merit by removing four fundamental delusions (regarding permanence, pleasure, purity, and selfhood), while chapters 9–16 refute non-Buddhist systems (such as Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika) and realists to establish universal emptiness (śūnyatā). This electronic text contains only 21 verses from chapters 1–5 preserved in secondary Sanskrit citations, as printed in the short appendix (pp. 159–160) of Bhagchandra Jain's 1971 edition.

summary: The Cidgaganacandrikā is an esoteric hymn and foundational philosophical work belonging to the Krama lineage of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism and Śāktism. Arranged in four vimarśas, it synthesizes Kaula and Krama doctrines regarding the twelve Kālīs, the divine void of pure consciousness (cidgagana), and the cyclical phases of manifestation and dissolution. This e-text provides the first two vimarśas accompanied by Karrā Agnihotra Śāstrin's 20th-century Sanskrit commentary Divyacakorikā.

summary: The Daśaślokīstuti is a ten-verse devotional hymn (stotra) dedicated to Śiva accompanied by Ambā (Sāmba), traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. Verse 1 invokes Sāmba across all eight grammatical cases (vibhakti-stuti), while the subsequent verses praise his cosmic supremacy and purāṇic exploits—such as the burning of Tripura, the drinking of the Hālāhala poison, and his superiority over Brahmā and Viṣṇu—each concluding with the refrain 'tasmin me hṛdayaṃ sukhena ramatāṃ sāmbe parabrahmaṇi'.

summary: The Dvaitadyumaṇipariśiṣṭa is a Dvaita Vedānta polemical treatise functioning as a supplement (pariśiṣṭa) to the Dvaitadyumaṇi. It critiques Advaita Vedānta epistemology and ontology, focusing on the reality of difference (bheda) between jīva and Brahman even in liberation (mukti), the analysis of the supreme human end (parameṣṭa / puruṣārtha), and theories of error and non-existence (such as anirvacanīyakhyāti, asatkhyāti, and shell-silver illusion).

summary: The Dvādaśastotra is a collection of twelve devotional hymns composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha, 13th c.), the founder of Dvaita Vedānta. Addressed to Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa, the hymns combine personal devotion and iconographic meditation with Dvaita theological doctrines, emphasizing the absolute sovereignty and independence of Viṣṇu. Appended to the text is the Kandukastuti, a short praise poem describing Kṛṣṇa playing with a ball.

summary: The Dṛgdṛśyaviveka (also known as Vākyasudhā) is a concise 46-verse Advaita Vedānta introductory treatise (prakaraṇagrantha) analyzing the fundamental distinction between the unchanging subject/seer (dṛś, sākṣin) and the changing objective realm/seen (dṛśya). It outlines the two powers of māyā (vikṣepa and āvaraṇa), the threefold definition of the individual soul (jīva: pāramārthika, vyāvahārika, and prātibhāsika), and describes six kinds of samādhi (savikalpa and nirvikalpa, internal and external) as practical means for realizing non-dual Brahman.

summary: The Gītātātparyanirṇaya is one of two treatises on the Bhagavadgītā composed by Madhvācārya (the other being the Gītābhāṣya). summary: The Jinendraguṇasaṃstuti is a Jain philosophical stotra of 50 verses celebrating the qualities of the Jina. summary: The Karmanirṇaya ('Determination of Ritual Action') is one of the ten philosophical treatises (Daśaprakaraṇa) composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha), the founder of Dvaita Vedānta. In this work, Madhva interprets the Mahānāmnī verses and Vedic ritual injunctions of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka, arguing against Advaitin views of ritual non-efficacy and an unqualified (nirguṇa) Brahman. summary: The Kenopaniṣadbhāṣya (specifically the Padabhāṣya) is Śaṅkara's definitive word-by-word commentary on the Kenopaniṣad (belonging to the Jaiminīya/Talavakāra school of the Sāmaveda). He argues against the necessity of ritual actions (karma) for ultimate liberation, showing that final freedom (amṛtatva) arises exclusively from unmediated Self-knowledge.

summary: The Laghuvākyavṛtti is a concise Advaita Vedānta tract in 18 anuṣṭubh verses traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarācārya. It presents a contemplative method for discriminating between pure witness-consciousness (śuddhabodha) and changing mental modifications (vṛtti) or the reflected ego (cidābhāsa). By recognizing the pure consciousness persisting in the silent interval between mental thoughts, the seeker is led to verify the non-dual import of the mahāvākya 'ahaṃ brahma'.

summary: The Muṇḍakopaniṣadbhāṣya is Śaṅkara's classic Advaita Vedānta commentary on the Muṇḍakopaniṣad of the Atharvaveda. In his commentary, Śaṅkara elucidates the fundamental distinction between lower knowledge (aparā vidyā), comprising ritual works and external learning, and higher knowledge (parā vidyā), which leads directly to the imperishable Brahman (akṣara). He emphasizes renunciation (saṃnyāsa) as a prerequisite for liberating knowledge and interprets key allegories, including the archery metaphor of Om and the famous image of the two birds perched on the same tree.

summary: The Mīmāṃsāparibhāṣā of Kṛṣṇayajvan (ca. 17th century) is a widely read elementary manual (prakaraṇa) of the Bhāṭṭa school of Pūrvamīmāṃsā. Composed in clear introductory prose for students (bālānām), it systematizes the essential categories of ritual hermeneutics, including the definition of dharma, the classification of Vedic injunctions (vidhi, arthavāda, mantra, nāmadheya, niṣedha), the six means of subsidiary application (viniyogapramāṇas), and the six principles governing ritual sequence (krama). Along with the Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa of Āpadeva and the Arthasaṃgraha of Laugākṣi Bhāskara, it serves as a standard textbook for classical Indian ritual and exegetical theory.

summary: The Naiṣkarmyasiddhi ('Establishment of Actionlessness') is an independent prakaraṇa work in four adhyāyas composed in mixed verse and prose by Sureśvara, a direct disciple of Śaṅkarācārya. The text provides a systematic philosophical defense of Advaita Vedānta soteriology, arguing that liberation (mokṣa) is achieved solely through knowledge (jñāna) of the non-dual Self and rejecting the necessity of ritual action (karma) or the combination of knowledge and action (jñānakarmasamuccaya). It examines nescience (avidyā), the method of superimposition and rescission (adhyāropāpavāda), and the direct liberating knowledge generated by Upaniṣadic mahāvākyas.

summary: The Kārikāvalī (also known as Bhāṣāpariccheda) together with its auto-commentary, the Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī, is a standard 17th-century manual of the syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika system composed by Viśvanātha Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya. Spanning 168 metric kārikās and accompanying prose, the work systematically explains the seven ontological categories (dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, samavāya, and abhāva) alongside the four Nyāya means of valid cognition (pratyakṣa, anumāna, upamāna, and śabda). Due to its precision and accessible pedagogical organization, it became one of the standard foundational textbooks of Navya-Nyāya philosophy across traditional pandit schools.

summary: The Pañcadaśī ('Fifteen Chapters') is an influential 14th-century manual of Advaita Vedānta traditionally attributed to Vidyāraṇya (and in part to Bhāratītīrtha). It is divided into three pentads corresponding to the tripartite nature of Brahman: Viveka-pañcaka (discrimination of existence, sat), Dīpa-pañcaka (illumination of consciousness, cit), and Ānanda-pañcaka (nature of bliss, ānanda). Through pedagogical metaphors—such as the picture-canvas (citradīpa) and the stage lamp (nāṭakadīpa)—the work systematically expounds non-dual ontology, epistemology, and liberation (jīvanmukti).

Presenting epistemology in accordance with the Brahmatarka, Madhva defines valid knowledge (yathārthaṃ pramāṇam) and divides pramāṇa into kevalapramāṇa (veridical cognition) and anupramāṇa (means of knowledge: perception, inference, and scriptural testimony). The treatise systematically analyzes definitions, scopes, and fallacies, defending Dvaita realism against Advaita and other rivals.

summary: The Pramāṇapaddhati is an influential primer of Dvaita epistemology and logic composed by Jayatīrtha (14th century CE). Systematizing the epistemological doctrine set forth in Madhvācārya's Pramāṇalakṣaṇa, the treatise is divided into three sections corresponding to the three valid means of knowledge accepted in Dvaita: perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), and verbal testimony (āgama). It provides clear definitions of pramāṇa, discusses truth and error, expounds syllogistic reasoning and fallacies (hetvābhāsas), and defends the authoritativeness and intrinsic validity (svataḥprāmāṇya) of Vedic scripture.

summary: The foundational text of classical Yoga philosophy (Pātañjala Yoga), comprising the root aphorisms and their earliest authoritative commentary across four chapters (Samādhipāda, Sādhanapāda, Vibhūtipāda, and Kaivalyapāda). Developing a dualist ontology closely allied with classical Sāṅkhya, the work provides a detailed analysis of mental modifications (cittavṛtti), afflictions (kleśa), meditative stages and extraordinary powers (vibhūti/siddhi), and the ultimate liberation of puruṣa in isolation (kaivalya). Composed between c. 325 and 425 CE, it defined the philosophical vocabulary and meditative path of classical yoga across the Indian tradition.

summary: The Ratnamālāvadāna ('Garland of Jewels of Edifying Deeds') is a late Sanskrit Buddhist metrical collection of thirty-eight avadāna tales framed as instruction given by the arhat Upagupta to Emperor Aśoka. It versifies and expands narratives familiar from older collections such as the Avadānaśataka, illustrating the inexorable results of karma, devotion to the Three Jewels, and the cultivation of the Mahāyāna pāramitās. Preserved in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts, it was critically edited in full by Kanga Takahata in 1954.

summary: The Sarvavedāntasiddhāntasārasaṃgraha is a comprehensive verse manual (prakaraṇa) of 1006 kārikās presenting an accessible overview of classical Advaita Vedānta philosophy. Structured largely as an instructional dialogue between guru and disciple, it systematically treats the four qualifications for study (anubandhacatuṣṭaya), discrimination of real and unreal (nityānityavastuviveka), renunciation, the nature of avidyā and superimposition (adhyāropa/apavāda), the interpretation of the Upaniṣadic mahāvākyas, and the attainment of jīvanmukti.

summary: The Siddhāntaleśasaṅgraha is an influential 16th-century doxographical compendium of Advaita Vedānta by Appayyadīkṣita. Organized into four paricchedas, the work systematically presents and reconciles the divergent doctrines, sub-schools, and interpretations developed by post-Śaṅkara Advaitins (including the Bhāmatī and Vivaraṇa traditions). It analyzes key topics such as the nature and locus of avidyā, the ontological status of jīva and īśvara, the theory of error (adhyāsa), and the direct means of release.

summary: The Smṛtimuktāvalī of Kṛṣṇācārya, a pupil of Rāghavendra Tīrtha, is a dharmaśāstra digest (nibandha) written for the Mādhva (Dvaita) community. It argues that Mādhva practice rests on smṛti, that ritual duties are to be done without desire for results as worship of Hari, and that smṛti and purāṇa are authoritative. It then sets out calendrical rules (seasons, months, intercalary and 'empty' months, Cāturmāsya, fortnights). The e-text breaks off in the section on the time for the single daily meal (ekabhukta).

summary: The Svayambhūpurāṇa is the foundational mythic chronicle and pilgrimage guide (sthala-māhātmya) of Newar Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley. It recounts the myth of the primordial lake (Nāgadaha) drained through the Chobhar gorge by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, followed by the appearance of the primordial lotus and the self-existent flame (svayambhūjyotis) of the Dharmadhātu enshrined within the Svayambhū Mahācaitya (Swayambhunath). The work incorporates visits of the previous Buddhas of antiquity, legends of local tīrthas, deities, and nāgas, and the transformation of the valley into a Buddhist kingdom. This 10-chapter recension represents the intermediate (madhyama) version of the text.

summary: The Sāṃkhyakośa is a 20th-century Sanskrit terminological lexicon of classical Sāṃkhya philosophy composed by Ācārya Kedāranātha Tripāṭhī in 1974 CE (VS 2030). Arranged in alphabetical order, it defines and explains core technical concepts, epistemological categories, ontological principles, and stock illustrations (dṛṣṭāntas) of the system, substantiating explanations with citations from the Sāṃkhyakārikā, Sāṃkhyasūtra, Gauḍapāda, and Vijñānabhikṣu.

coverage_note: Contains all 72 kārikās of the Sāṃkhyakārikā alongside the full Jayamaṅgalā commentary, beginning with its initial maṅgala verse ('adhigatatattvālokaṃ...') and concluding with the terminal colophon following kārikā 72.
attribution_note: The root verses are composed by Īśvarakṛṣṇa (c. 4th–5th century CE). The commentary's manuscript colophon credits 'Śrīmatparamahaṃsaparivrājakācāryaśrīgovindabhagavatpūjyapādaśiṣya Śrīśaṅkarabhagavat' (traditionally identified with Ādi Śaṅkarācārya). However, modern scholarship (beginning with Gopinath Kaviraj and Haradatta Sharma) rejects this attribution to the Advaita Vedāntin and assigns the text to a distinct Sāṃkhya commentator conventionally designated as Śaṅkara-ārya or Śaṅkarārya (c. 8th century CE).

summary: The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa is the classical foundational treatise of Sāṃkhya philosophy, articulating its dualist ontology of insentient nature (prakṛti) and pure consciousness (puruṣa), the evolution of the twenty-five tattvas, three epistemic pramāṇas, and liberation through discriminative insight. The Jayamaṅgalā is an important early medieval running commentary (ṭīkā) that provides lucid grammatical and philosophical expositions for all 72 verses. It constitutes an essential witness for the early textual and doctrinal transmission of classical Sāṃkhya alongside the Gauḍapādabhāṣya, the Māṭharavṛtti, and the Yuktidīpikā.

summary: The Sūtradīpikā (also known as Brahmasūtradīpikā) is a concise commentary on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra from the perspective of Dvaita (Mādhva) Vedānta, composed by Jagannāthayati, a disciple of Raghunāthatīrtha. The work presents the sūtras organized by adhikaraṇa, glossing individual terms to demonstrate that Vedic revelation consistently proclaims Lord Viṣṇu as the supreme, unconditioned Brahman possessing infinite auspicious attributes.

summary: An anonymous Mādhva (Dvaita) commentary on the whole Brahmasūtra. For each adhikaraṇa it states the topic, gives the opponent's view (often an inference in navya-nyāya style), quotes the sūtra with a short word-gloss ('asyārthaḥ') and then argues the Dvaita conclusion. Throughout, Brahman is identified with Viṣṇu, and Viṣṇu, the souls and the world are held to be really different.

summary: The Tantrasārasaṅgraha is a practical liturgical and ritual treatise in four chapters by the Dvaita Vedānta teacher Madhva (13th century). Drawing upon Pāñcarātra and tantric ritual traditions, it outlines mantroddhāra (with particular focus on the Praṇava, Nārāyaṇāṣṭākṣara, and Dvādaśākṣara mantras), the construction of altars and sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa-maṇḍala), temple building, image installation (pratiṣṭhā), and daily icon worship grounded in Vedic hymns.

summary: The Taptacakrāṅkanavidhvaṃsana is an Advaita polemical treatise composed by Garuḍācalayajvan of the Veṅkaṭagiri court. It rejects the Pāñcarātra and Śrīvaiṣṇava practice of bodily branding with hot iron emblems of Viṣṇu's disc and conch (taptacakrāṅkana), demonstrating through Mīmāṃsā exegetical rules and Dharmaśāstra citations that Vedic passages like 'pavitraṃ te vitatam' pertain to Śrauta rituals (such as the droṇakalaśa filter in Somayāga) rather than corporal branding.

summary: The Tarkabhāṣā ('Language of Logic') is a concise introductory manual of Buddhist epistemology and logic composed by Mokṣākaragupta, a monk-scholar of the Jagaddala Mahāvihāra in northern Bengal dating to the late 11th or 12th century CE. Structured in three chapters according to the Dignāga-Dharmakīrti epistemology—perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna)—it explains valid knowledge, definition and fallacies of the logical reason (hetu/liṅga), syllogistic debate, and core Mahāyāna philosophical doctrines. The treatise is particularly valuable as one of the latest surviving Sanskrit textbooks of late Indian Buddhist logic, integrating the philosophical developments of Prajñākaragupta, Jñānaśrīmitra, and Ratnakīrti on internal pervasion (antarvyāpti), universal momentariness (kṣaṇikatva), Sākāravāda, and nominal exclusion (apoha).

summary: The Tattvabodha is a concise introductory catechism (prakaraṇa) of Advaita Vedānta traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. Written primarily in simple didactic prose, it defines fundamental concepts and technical terms, including the fourfold preliminary qualifications (sādhanacatuṣṭaya), the three bodies (śarīratraya), the five sheaths (pañcakośa), the three states of experience (avasthātraya), and the manifestation of the twenty-four cosmic principles. It culminates in an exposition of the non-difference between the individual soul and the supreme reality (jīveśvaraikya) and describes the nature and state of the liberated being (jīvanmukta).

summary: The Tattvavaiśāradī (also known as Pātañjalabhāṣyavyākhyā) is the fundamental classical sub-commentary on the Pātañjalayogaśāstrabhāṣya (Vyāsabhāṣya), composed by the tenth-century polymath Vācaspatimiśra. This text presents the four pādas of the Yogasūtra together with Vācaspati's extensive explanation of the Bhāṣya, clarifying technical Yoga psychology and metaphysics while defending the dualist system against Buddhist and other philosophical interlocutors. It remains one of the primary authorities in the classical Yoga tradition.

summary: The Tattvopadeśa is an Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa text of 87 verses traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. Structured as pedagogical instructions from a preceptor to a disciple, the treatise analyzes the Upaniṣadic mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' ('Thou art that'). It systematically isolates the conscious witness (ātman) from bodily, sensory, and mental superimpositions, elucidates the role of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) in understanding non-difference, and emphasizes steady devotion and non-duality toward the guru.

summary: The Tattvopaplavasiṃha ('The Lion that Devours all Principles/Categories') is a unique philosophical treatise of radical epistemological skepticism composed by Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa in the late 8th or early 9th century CE. Loosely affiliated with the Cārvāka/Lokāyata school, Jayarāśi turns dialectical reasoning against all accepted instruments of valid cognition (pramāṇas)—including perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony—arguing that because no pramāṇa can be established without begging the question, no metaphysical or empirical entities (tattvas) can be affirmed. The work is preserved in a single palm-leaf manuscript copied in 1292 CE at Dholkā, discovered in 1926 by Sukhlalji Sanghavi and Bechardas Doshi in the Saṅghavīnā Pāḍāno Bhaṇḍār at Pāṭan.

summary: The Tithinirṇaya is a short astronomical and calendrical treatise of 29 verses composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha) as part of his Sarvamūlagrantha corpus. It sets forth mathematical procedures, sine tables (jyāvākya), and correctional calculations (saṃskāra) for establishing the exact duration of lunar days (tithi). The text is intended to settle the proper timing for ritual fasts (upoṣaṇa), particularly Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī, in accordance with Dvaita tradition.

summary: The Vaiśeṣikasūtra attributed to Kaṇāda is the foundational text of the Vaiśeṣika school, establishing its realist ontological ontology around six ontological categories (padārthas): dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, and samavāya (with non-existence, abhāva, treated subsequently). The Upaskāra ('Supplement' / 'Exposition') by the 15th-century Mithilā philosopher Śaṅkaramiśra served historically as the primary transmitted commentary on the sūtras, elucidating the aphorisms through a lens influenced by classical and early Navya-Nyāya debate.

summary: The Vedāntaparibhāṣā is a classic 17th-century manual of Advaita Vedānta epistemology and ontology by Dharmarājādhvarīndra. Formulating Advaita concepts in the precise technical style of Navya-Nyāya, the work defines and defends the six pramāṇas (pratyakṣa, anumāna, upamāna, āgama, arthāpatti, and anupalabdhi) according to the Vivaraṇa tradition. Its final chapters delineate the central subject matter (viṣaya) as the identity of jīva and Brahman, and the ultimate aim (prayojana) as liberation (mokṣa).

summary: The Vivaraṇaprameyasaṃgraha is an influential 14th-century Advaita Vedānta compendium attributed to Vidyāraṇya (or Bhāratītīrtha), providing a systematic summary of Prakāśātman's Pañcapādikāvivaraṇa across nine varṇakas. It examines key tenets of the Vivaraṇa tradition including the locus and nature of avidyā, theories of error (khyātivāda), the nature of the witness consciousness (sākṣin), and the interpretation of the Mahāvākyas, while systematically refuting rival Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, and Buddhist doctrines. This e-text is an incomplete transcription containing only the early sections of the first varṇaka.

summary: The Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya is the longest and doctrinally central treatise among the ten philosophical monographs (Daśaprakaraṇa) of Madhva (13th c. CE), the founder of Dvaita Vedānta. In three chapters (paricchedas), it establishes the intrinsic validity of knowledge (svataḥprāmāṇya), the authorlessness (apauruṣeyatva) and primary authority of the Vedas, and the ontological reality of difference (bheda) against Advaita non-dualism and the doctrine of māyā. The second and third chapters demonstrate that the supreme deity Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa) is entirely free from imperfections (nirdoṣa) and possessed of infinite auspicious attributes (aśeṣasadguṇapūrṇa).

summary: The Vyomavatī by the Śaiva-Vaiśeṣika master Vyomaśiva (10th century CE) is the earliest surviving commentary on Praśastapāda's Padārthadharmasaṅgraha, pre-dating the commentaries of Śrīdhara (Nyāyakandalī) and Udayana (Kiraṇāvalī). It provides an extensive defense and elaboration of the classical Vaiśeṣika categories (substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, and inherence), addressing epistemology, ontology, and the Vaiśeṣika doctrine of liberation. The work is noted for its rigorous polemical engagements with Buddhist (especially Dharmakīrtian), Jaina, and Mīmāṃsaka positions, as well as its integration of Śaiva theological perspectives.

summary: The Vākyavṛtti is an Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa text in 53 verses framed as a dialogue between a preceptor and a spiritual aspirant. It offers an exposition of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' ('That thou art'). Through an analysis of the indirect meanings (lakṣaṇā) of 'tvam' (the inner conscious witness) and 'tat' (pure Brahman), it demonstrates the identity of the individual self and the absolute.

summary: The Yatīndramatadīpikā ('Lamp on the doctrine of the king of ascetics', i.e. Rāmānuja), also called the Śārīrakaparibhāṣā, is a short introductory manual of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta by Śrīnivāsadāsa, a disciple of Mahācārya (17th c.). Its ten chapters (avatāras) first treat the three means of knowledge (perception, inference, verbal testimony) and then the categories of the knowable: prakṛti, time, the eternal realm (nityavibhūti), attributive knowledge (dharmabhūtajñāna, with the means of liberation), the individual self, God, and the non-substances (adravya). It is widely used as a primer of Rāmānuja's system.

summary: The Yogatārāvalī is a short Sanskrit treatise in 29 verses bridging Haṭhayoga physical practices with Rājayoga meditation. It describes the practice of the three bandhas (mūla, uḍḍīyana, jālandhara), kevalakumbhaka, and absorption in inner sound (nādānusandhāna) as the means to dissolve mental fluctuations into amanaska (the transcendent mindless state) and yoganidrā. While traditionally ascribed to Ādi Śaṅkara, it is characteristic of the late medieval syncretism between Haṭhayogic methods and non-dual Advaita metaphysics.

summary: The Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā along with its auto-commentary (vṛtti) by Utpaladeva constitutes the foundational philosophical treatise of the Pratyabhijñā ('Recognition') system of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism. summary: The Īśāvāsyopaniṣad (or Īśopaniṣad) forms the 40th and final chapter of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā of the Śukla Yajurveda, preserved here in its 18-mantra Kāṇva recension. It synthesizes the contemplation of the cosmos as pervaded by the Lord (īśa) with teachings on renunciation, the dual functions of action (avidyā/karman) and knowledge (vidyā), and final release. Śaṅkara's commentary (bhāṣya) interprets the work within classical Advaita Vedānta, arguing that ritual works pertain solely to worldly and heavenly ends while direct, non-dual knowledge of the self (ātman) alone eliminates ignorance and secures liberation.

summary: The Śarīravāda is a short Viśiṣṭādvaita polemical treatise (vāda) by Anantārya of Yādavādri (Melkote) on the defining property (pravṛttinimitta) of the word 'body' (śarīra). It argues that 'bodyhood' is not a jāti and examines the Śrībhāṣya definition: a substance that a conscious being can wholly control and support for its own purposes, and that is entirely subsidiary (śeṣa) to it. It does so with reference to the Śrutaprakāśikā and the Nyāyasiddhāñjana, in Navya-Nyāya style. It also discusses related questions such as the inner self's entering (anupraveśa) and the soul's departure and movement.

summary: The Śataślokī is an Advaita Vedānta verse compendium composed in sragdharā metre and traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarācārya. Across 101 verses, it systematically expounds key Advaitic teachings, including the role of the guru, the illusion of the empirical world, self-realization through discrimination between ātman and anātman, the interpretation of Upaniṣadic Mahāvākyas, and the nature of jīvanmukti. While firmly integrated into the Advaita curriculum, modern philology regards the work as an unauthentic composition of the later Śaṅkara tradition.

summary: The Śaṅkarapādabhūṣaṇa is a 19th-century Advaita polemical work by Raghunātha Śāstrī Parvate. summary: The Śrībhāṣya is Rāmānuja's (c. 11th–12th century CE) magisterial commentary on the Brahmasūtra of Bādarāyaṇa, serving as the foundational philosophical text of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. In it, Rāmānuja systematically refutes Advaita non-dualism and Bhedābheda, establishing that the Supreme Brahman is identical with Nārāyaṇa, endowed with infinite auspicious qualities. He elaborates the doctrine of the world and souls as forming the 'body' (śarīra) of the Lord, who is their innermost ruler (antaryāmin).

summary: The Śāntikamalākara (also known as Śāntiratna) is a comprehensive Dharmaśāstra digest (nibandha) on expiatory, pacification, and averting rites (śānti) compiled by Kamalākarabhaṭṭa in the early 17th century. It synthesizes Vedic, Purāṇic, and smṛti authorities to establish liturgies for countering portents, astrological afflictions (ariṣṭa, grahaśānti), inauspicious birth constellations, and natural calamities. This digital text represents a South Indian liturgical edition complete with introductory svastivācana and purificatory rituals.

summary: The Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya ('Compendium of the Six Philosophical Systems') of the Jain polymath Haribhadrasūri (c. 8th century CE) is an early and influential doxography summarizing six major Indian philosophical traditions: Bauddha, Naiyāyika, Sāṃkhya, Jaina, Vaiśeṣika, and Jaiminīya (Mīmāṃsā), followed by a brief examination of the materialist Cārvāka/Lokāyata school. Composed in 87 concise anuṣṭubh stanzas, it is celebrated for its irenic and objective presentation of rival schools. summary: The Amarakoṣa (formally Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana) of Amarasiṃha (c. 6th century CE) is the foundational synonymic and homonymic verse lexicon of Classical Sanskrit. Structured into three kāṇḍas (svarga-, bhūmi-, and sāmānya-kāṇḍa), it arranges nouns conceptually by taxonomy, cosmology, society, and grammatical categories. The Amaraviveka of Maheśvara is an influential commentary elucidating word origins, alternative grammatical readings, and referencing classical lexicographical and grammatical sources.

Texts of this genre served as reference tools for poets (especially for citrakāvya), scribes, and practitioners interpreting tantric bījamantras.

summary: The Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra is an encyclopedic 11th-century Sanskrit treatise on classical Indian architecture (vāstuśāstra), urban planning, civil engineering, painting (citraśāstra), and iconography, composed by King Bhoja of Dhārā (r. c. 1010–1055 CE). Comprising 83 chapters, the work covers town and palace planning, residential layout, temple typologies (including detailed treatments of Nāgara and Bhūmija styles), mechanical apparatuses and automata (yantras, ch. 31), painting methods, and dance-based sculptural postures and hand gestures.

summary: The Saṅgītaratnākara ('Ocean of Music'), authored in the early 13th century by Śārṅgadeva at the court of King Siṅghaṇa II of Devagiri, is the foundational medieval treatise on Indian music and performing arts. Arranged into seven chapters (saptādhyāyī), it provides an exhaustive analysis of notes and intervals (svara), melodic modes (rāga), miscellaneous musicological concepts (prakīrṇa), song and meter forms (prabandha), rhythm and metrics (tāla), musical instruments (vādya), and dance (nartana). The treatise forms an essential transition between ancient dramatic musical theory (gāndharva/mārga) and the regional performance traditions (deśī) that developed into modern Hindustani and Carnatic classical music.

summary: The Bhaviṣyapurāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, in the vulgate divided into Brāhma-, Madhyama-, Pratisarga- and Uttaraparvan. The Brāhmaparvan is known for its material on sun worship and the Maga (Bhojaka) priests. The Pratisargaparvan contains genealogies and 'prophecies' that run up to the Mughal and British periods and are evidently very late additions. The Uttaraparvan (also transmitted separately as Bhaviṣyottarapurāṇa) is largely a compendium of vratas, dānas and festivals, told as a dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.

summary: The Kapilapurāṇa is a short Upapurāṇa in 21 chapters, in which the sage Kapila answers King Śalyajit about the holy places of Utkala (Odisha). summary: The Kālikāpurāṇa is an influential Śākta Upapurāṇa composed in medieval Kāmarūpa (Assam), generally assigned to the 9th–11th centuries CE. It details the mythology of the Goddess in her manifestations as Kālī, Satī, Pārvatī, and Kāmākhyā, tracing the narrative of Satī's self-immolation and the dispersion of her limbs across sacred pīṭhas. The work serves as a foundational manual for Śākta ritual and worship in northeastern India, containing extensive sections on iconography, mantras, pilgrimage geography, and the famous Rudhirādhyāya on blood sacrifice.

summary: The Vāyupurāṇa is widely regarded by Indologists as one of the oldest surviving Mahāpurāṇas, closely related in content and wording to the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa. Framed as a discourse recited by the wind god Vāyu to the sages in Naimiṣāraṇya, it preserves an archaic core adhering faithfully to the classical pañcalakṣaṇa topics: cosmogony, recreation, genealogies of gods and kings, manvantaras, and dynastic history. summary: The Māheśvarakhaṇḍa is the opening book of the medieval 81,000-verse vulgate recension of the Skandapurāṇa. It consists of three distinct sub-sections: the Kedārakhaṇḍa, recounting major Śaiva myths (such as Dakṣa's sacrifice, the churning of the ocean, and the marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī) alongside the sacred topography of Kedāranātha and Himalayan tīrthas; the Kaumārikākhaṇḍa, centering on Skanda's birth and the slaying of Tārakāsura, the pilgrimage site of Stambhatīrtha (Khambhāt, Gujarat), and the narrative of Barbarīka; and the Aruṇācalamāhātmya (Pūrvārdha and Uttarārdha), extolling the primordial linga of fire at Mount Aruṇācala (Tiruvannamalai, Tamil Nadu) and the merits of its circumambulation.

summary: The Vaiṣṇavakhaṇḍa is the second major book of the vulgate seven-part recension of the Skandapurāṇa, comprising nine distinct māhātmyas devoted to Vaiṣṇava sacred geography, liturgical calendars, and theology. It contains extensive sthala-māhātmyas sanctifying major pan-Indian pilgrimage destinations, including Veṅkaṭācala (Tirupati), Puruṣottamakṣetra (Puri Jagannātha), Badarikāśrama, and Ayodhyā, alongside liturgical manuals detailing the religious merit of vows and ablutions performed during the holy months of Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Vaiśākha. It also includes the Bhāgavatamāhātmya and the Vāsudevamāhātmya, the latter integrating late Pāñcarātra theology with devotional cults of Kṛṣṇa-Vāsudeva. Composed and compiled incrementally between roughly the 10th and 16th centuries CE, the collection forms an invaluable textual witness to medieval Indian pilgrimage networks and temple institutions.

Arranged into four distinct sections—Prabhāsakṣetramāhātmya, Vastrāpathakṣetramāhātmya, Arbudakhaṇḍa, and Dvārakāmāhātmya—it forms a massive compendium of sacred geography and pilgrimage lore (tīrthamāhātmya) centered on western India, notably the Somanātha jyotirliṅga, Mount Girnar, Mount Abu, and Dwarka. summary: The Pulastyasmṛti is a concise Dharmaśāstra text in 28 anuṣṭubh verses framed as instruction given by the sage Pulastya to ṛṣis gathered at Kurukṣetra. It defines five categories of dharma (varṇadharma, āśramadharma, varṇāśramadharma, guṇadharma, and naimittikadharma) and surveys the duties belonging to the four social classes and four life stages. The text concludes with summary principles on the sources and resolution of legal authority (śruti, smṛti, nyāya) and a concluding rule on purification.

summary: The Advaitaśataka ('Centuria on Non-Duality') is a 100-verse didactic Vedantic tract (prakaraṇa) summarizing fundamental teachings of Advaita ('sarvavedāntasaṃgraha'). It expounds the nature of the four bodies (sthūla, sūkṣma, kāraṇa, and the transcendent sāmānya/turīya deha), the jīva's bondage through ignorance (ajñāna) and identification with the bodily apparatus, the operation of prārabdha karma, and final emancipation through recognition of one's intrinsic identity with Śiva as unconditioned consciousness (jñaptimātra).

summary: The Alaṅkārasaṅgraha is a 14th-century treatise on Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra) and dramaturgy (nāṭyaśāstra) composed in 11 paricchedas by Amṛtānandayogin under the patronage of King Manma. It integrates poetic theory with theatrical rules, discussing auspicious syllabic patterns (varṇagaṇa), word and meaning (śabdārtha), aesthetic sentiment (rasa), heroes and heroines (netṛbheda), figures of speech (alaṅkāra), poetic faults and virtues (doṣa and guṇa), dramatic junctures and plots (sandhyaṅga), major dramatic genres (rūpaka), theatrical embellishments (nāṭyālaṅkāra), and court panegyric compositions (cāṭuprabandha).

summary: The Ardhanārīnaṭeśvarastotra (or Ardhanārīnaṭeśvarāṣṭaka) is an eight-verse hymn dedicated to the androgynous composite form of Śiva and Pārvatī (Ardhanārīśvara). In each stanza, the poet pairs and contrasts the feminine half (Pārvatī) and the masculine half (Śiva) in appearance, ornaments, and cosmic roles (such as creation through lāsya and cosmic dissolution through tāṇḍava), closing each verse with the dual refrain 'namaḥ śivāyai ca namaḥ śivāya'. Traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkarācārya, the poem concludes with a phalaśruti verse promising auspiciousness and longevity.

summary: The Aucityavicāracarcā is an 11th-century treatise on poetic theory by the Kashmiri polymath Kṣemendra. Formulating the Aucitya doctrine of alaṅkāraśāstra, Kṣemendra establishes appropriateness or propriety (aucitya) as the vital essence (jīvita) of poetic art, arguing that poetic ornaments (alaṅkāra) and qualities (guṇa) fail without it. The treatise defines and analyzes twenty-seven distinct loci of propriety (including word, case, verbal syntax, gender, meter, time, place, and rasa), examining each through classical quotations illustrative of poetic excellence or flaw.

summary: The Avadhūtagītā is a classical text of radical non-dualism (Advaita) traditionally ascribed to the sage Dattātreya. Across eight chapters, it expounds the true nature of the Self (ātman) as all-pervasive, immutable consciousness entirely free from superimposition, ritual action, bondage, and release. The closing chapter gives an esoteric acrostic etymology defining the characteristics of an avadhūta through the four syllables a, va, dhū, and ta.

summary: Avimāraka is a six-act Sanskrit drama traditionally attributed to Bhāsa, dramatizing a romantic tale likely drawn from the Bṛhatkathā cycle. The narrative follows Prince Viṣṇusena, who lives incognito in the outcast community under the name Avimāraka due to a sage's curse, and falls in love with Princess Kuraṅgī after rescuing her from an elephant attack. summary: The Bhajagovindastotra (also known as Mohamudgara) is an extremely popular didactic hymn in rhyming moric metre, traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara and his disciples. summary: The Bhāvaprakāśa of Bhāvamiśra (16th century CE) is one of the three authoritative treatises constituting the Laghutrayī ('Lesser Triad') of classical Indian medicine. Structured into three parts (Pūrvakhaṇḍa, Madhyakhaṇḍa, and Uttarakhaṇḍa), it provides an encyclopedic synthesis of Āyurvedic theory, nosology, dravyaguṇa (materia medica), therapeutics, and rejuvenation (rasāyana). summary: The Campūrāmāyaṇa (also known as Bhojacampū) is a celebrated Sanskrit mahācampū combining prose and verse to retell the Rāmāyaṇa narrative. summary: The Citramīmāṃsā is an influential treatise on Sanskrit alaṅkāraśāstra (rhetoric/poetics) by Appayya Dīkṣita (late 16th century). Intended as an exhaustive study of figures of sense (arthālaṅkāra), the work breaks off unfinished during the treatment of atiśayokti (hyperbole). Its critical definitions and illustrative verses became a central reference point in late classical poetics, prompting Paṇḍitarāja Jagannātha's polemical critique, the Citramīmāṃsākhaṇḍana.

summary: Cārudatta (also known as Daridracārudatta) is a classical Sanskrit-Prakrit play in four acts attributed to Bhāsa. It relates the romance between Cārudatta, an impoverished and noble merchant of Ujjayinī, and the wealthy courtesan Vasantasenā, intertwined with scenes involving the thief Sajjalaka (Śarvilaka) and the thief's burglary of Cārudatta's house. The surviving text breaks off at the end of the fourth act without a formal conclusion or bharatavākya, paralleling the first four acts of Śūdraka's ten-act Mṛcchakaṭikā.

summary: The Dhūrtasamāgama ('The Gathering of Rogues') is a satirical farce (prahasana) composed in the early 14th century by the Maithili court poet and scholar Jyotirīśvara Kaviśekhara. Written under the Karṇāṭa ruler Narasiṃhadeva of Mithila, the play mocks the moral hypocrisy and greed of religious ascetics and legal figures. Its plot depicts a wandering ascetic (Viśvanagara) and his disciple (Durācāra) quarreling over the favors of a courtesan (Anaṅgasenā), who then submit their dispute to a corrupt and lascivious Brahmin arbitrator (Asajjātimiśra).

summary: The Siṃhāsanadvātriṃśikā ('Thirty-Two Tales of the Throne'), also known as Vikramacarita or Dvātriṃśatputtalikā, is an acclaimed Sanskrit frame-story cycle celebrating the generosity, courage, and moral rectitude of the legendary King Vikramāditya. Whenever King Bhoja of Dhārā attempts to ascend the unearthed magical throne of Vikrama, each of the thirty-two statuettes (puttalikā) restraining him narrates an episode from Vikramāditya's life, challenging Bhoja to match such magnanimity. This e-text provides the complete Northern vulgate recension, including the opening Bhartṛhari legends, all thirty-two tales, and the liberation of the statues from their curse.

summary: The Gaṇeśabhujaṃgastotra is a nine-verse devotional hymn addressed to Gaṇeśa, composed in the rhythmic bhujaṅgaprayāta metre. The hymn concludes with a phalaśruti verse extolling the spiritual and worldly merits attained through daily morning recitation.

summary: The Gorakṣaśataka ('Hundred Verses of Gorakṣa') is a seminal early manual of haṭhayoga traditionally attributed to Gorakṣanātha. The work expounds a six-limbed (ṣaḍaṅga) yoga system comprising posture (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), sense-withdrawal (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi). It provides fundamental descriptions of the body's esoteric anatomy—including the cakras, seventy-two thousand nāḍīs, and ten prāṇic winds—alongside mudrās and breath practices aimed at awakening kuṇḍalinī and attaining liberation (mukti).

summary: The Gurugītā ('Song of the Guru') is a devotional and liturgical dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī, traditionally presented as part of the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the Skandapurāṇa. The text establishes the essential identity of the guru with supreme Brahman and Śiva, delineating the merits of guru devotion, contemplation, and esoteric mantric practice. It is widely recited across diverse devotional and tantric traditions, notably in the Dattātreya, Nātha, and modern Advaita and Siddha Yoga lineages.

The work combines classical court-poetic conventions with historical and regional bardic narratives.

summary: The Haribhaktivilāsa is the foundational ritual handbook and behavioural digest (smṛti / nibandha) of early modern Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism, composed in Vṛndāvana during the 1530s. Across its twenty vilāsas, the work systematizes normative devotional orthopraxy, citing thousands of verses from Purāṇic, Tantric, Pāñcarātra, and Vedic sources to ground devotional practices in canonical authority. This portion (vilāsas 1–11) treats initiation (dīkṣā), guru-disciple duties, morning rites, purification, sacred marks, offerings, and the elaborate procedures of daily temple and domestic worship (arcana).

summary: The Kramadīpikā is an authoritative eight-chapter Vaiṣṇava ritual and mantra manual (paddhati/tantranibandha) focused on the worship of Kṛṣṇa Gopāla, composed by the Nimbārka master Keśava Kāśmīrī (c. 14th–15th century CE). It systematically expounds initiation (dīkṣā), mantras (especially the ten-syllable and eighteen-syllable Gopāla mantras), daily worship, nyāsas, yantras, mudrās, and homa rites. Widely adopted across Vaiṣṇava denominations, it is extensively cited as a primary authority by Sanātana Gosvāmin in the Gauḍīya ritual compendium Haribhaktivilāsa and is accompanied in this e-text by Govindabhaṭṭācārya's commentary, the Vivaraṇa.

summary: The Madhyamavyāyoga ('The Middle One') is a one-act Sanskrit drama belonging to the vyāyoga genre, traditionally attributed to Bhāsa. Drawing on characters from the Mahābhārata, the play depicts Ghaṭotkaca demanding the sacrifice of the middle son of a wandering Brahmin family as food for his mother Hiḍimbā. Bhīma, the middle Pāṇḍava, intervenes by offering himself as the substitute victim, leading to a trial of strength and the joyful reunion of Bhīma with his demon-born son and wife.

summary: The Mānasollāsa is an influential metrical exposition (vārttika) in ten chapters (ullāsas) expounding Śaṅkara's celebrated ten-verse hymn, the Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotra. Traditionally ascribed to Sureśvara, the text systematically develops the hymn's pithy Advaita Vedānta doctrines, treating themes such as the illusory nature of phenomenal diversity (māyā/vivarta), the mirror-like reflection of the world in pure consciousness, the critiques of rival philosophical views (including Buddhist Śūnyavāda and Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika), and the ultimate identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Parameśvara (Śiva-Dakṣiṇāmūrti).

summary: The Naiṣadhīyacarita (or Naiṣadha) by the philosopher-poet Śrīharṣa (12th century CE) is one of the five celebrated mahākāvyas ('great court epics') of classical Sanskrit literature. Across 22 cantos, it narrates the story of King Nala and Princess Damayantī up to their wedding and honeymoon, elaborating on the Nalopākhyāna from the Mahābhārata. Famed for its intricate linguistic craftsmanship, double entendres (śleṣa), and profound philosophical references, the work is traditionally regarded as the ultimate test of scholarship ('naiṣadhaṃ vidvad-auṣadham').

summary: The Nāradabhaktisūtra is a classic Sanskrit treatise of 84 sūtras outlining the philosophy and practice of devotion (bhakti). summary: The Nītiprakāśikā is a Sanskrit treatise on statecraft (nītiśāstra) and the science of warfare (dhanurveda), framed as a dialogue between the sage Vaiśampāyana and King Janamejaya. It provides detailed classifications and descriptions of traditional weapons (mukta, amukta, muktāmukta, yantramukta), battle formations (vyūha), military tactics, and the ethical and administrative duties of kings (rājavyāpāra).

summary: The Nṛsiṃhasarasvatyaṣṭaka is an eight-verse devotional stotra dedicated to Nṛsiṃha Sarasvatī (c. 1378–1459 CE), an influential master in the Dattātreya tradition of western India. It praises the guru's spiritual attributes, ascetic discipline, and holy presence at the confluence of the Kṛṣṇā and Pañcagaṅgā rivers.

summary: The Padminīpariṇaya is a ten-act Sanskrit drama (styled a prakaraṇa in its opening) by Elattūr Sundararāja Bhaṭṭācārya, a nineteenth-century South Indian Vaiṣṇava poet. Under the story of prince Bhāskara (the sun) winning princess Padminī (the lotus), with a sub-plot of Kumudākara and Kaumudī and the guidance of the yogin Śāradānanda, it allegorically retells the Rāmāyaṇa (Bhāskara = Rāma, Padminī = Sītā/Lakṣmī, Jīmūta = Rāvaṇa), as Varadarāja's prefatory Kathāsaṅgraha explains.

summary: The Pañcarātra ('Five Nights') is a three-act Sanskrit play (dramatic type: samavakāra) attributed to Bhāsa, dramatizing an altered episode from the Virāṭaparvan of the Mahābhārata. summary: The Prakāśasaṃhitā (also referenced in manuscript catalogues as the Paramatattvanirṇayaprakāśasaṃhitā) is a Vaiṣṇava Āgamic text belonging to the Pāñcarātra canon, framed as a dialogue between Śrīhaṃsa (Viṣṇu) and Brahmā. Strikingly distinctive among Pāñcarātra saṃhitās, its doctrinal tenets closely mirror Dvaita Vedānta theology, including the innate threefold classification of individual souls (traividhya: muktiyogya, nityabaddha, and tamoyogya), the eightfold cosmic agency of Viṣṇu (sṛṣṭyādyaṣṭakartṛtva), cosmogony, and devotional ritual practices. Passages ascribed to a Prakāśasaṃhitā are cited as authoritative in the works of Madhvācārya and the later Dvaita tradition.

summary: The Prameyaratnāvalī is an 18th-century philosophical and theological manual composed by the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava thinker Baladevavidyābhūṣaṇa. Structured around nine core philosophical propositions (prameyas) derived from the Mādhva tradition—including the supreme reality of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa, the ontological reality of the created world, the real distinction between souls and God, and the three means of valid knowledge (pratyakṣa, anumāna, and śabda)—the work validates Gauḍīya theology through extensive śruti, smṛti, and Purāṇic citations.

summary: A four-act political drama (nāṭikā or prakaraṇa) attributed to the early playwright Bhāsa, depicting the prelude to the Svapnavāsavadatta. It focuses on Yaugandharāyaṇa, the devoted prime minister of King Udayana of Vatsa, who takes a solemn vow (pratijñā) to liberate his monarch after Udayana is captured through a ruse by King Mahāsena (Pradyota) of Ujjayinī. summary: The Pratimānāṭaka ('The Statue Play') is a seven-act drama attributed to Bhāsa, dramatizing the Rāmāyaṇa story from the aborted consecration of Rāma to his return to Ayodhyā. The central dramatic invention occurs in Act 3 in the ancestral gallery (pratimāgṛha), where Bharata deduces King Daśaratha's death upon seeing his portrait statue installed alongside those of deceased ancestors. The play portrays Kaikeyī's demands in a sympathetic light, explaining them through an inescapable ancestral curse rather than malice.

summary: The Suvarṇamālāstuti is an alphabetical devotional hymn (mātṛkā- or akṣaramālāstuti) addressed to Śiva as Sāmba Sadāśiva, traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara. The text blends Vedāntic philosophical references (such as śruti citations and upādhi terminology) with Śaiva devotional praise.

summary: The Uddhavagītā is a major philosophical and devotional dialogue contained within the eleventh book (Skandha 11) of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa. Prior to his departure from the earthly realm, Kṛṣṇa imparts his final instructions to his close companion and devotee Uddhava, synthesizing Advaitic metaphysics, Sāṅkhya-Yoga cosmology, and devotional theism (bhakti-yoga). Notable sub-episodes within the instruction include the dialogue of the Avadhūta (Dattātreya) recounting his twenty-four spiritual teachers drawn from nature, the Haṃsagītā, and the Bhikṣugītā.
