summary: The Ujjvalanīlamaṇi ('The Blazing Sapphire') is an influential 16th-century treatise on devotional aesthetics and theology by Rūpa Gosvāmin, one of the Six Gosvāmins of Vṛndāvana. Written as a specialized sequel to his Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, the work presents an exhaustive analysis of madhura-rasa (the erotic-devotional sentiment), which Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism regards as the supreme aesthetic manifestation of devotion to Kṛṣṇa. Rūpa adapts classical Sanskrit dramaturgical and kāvya taxonomies—including the classifications of hero and heroine (nāyaka- and nāyikā-bheda), supporting characters, excitant factors (vibhāva), involuntary physical responses (anubhāva), and permanent emotions (sthāyibhāva)—to explain the intimate loving relations between Kṛṣṇa and the gopīs of Vraja, culminating in the preeminence of Rādhā.

summary: The Uttararāmacarita ('The Later Deeds of Rāma') is a celebrated Sanskrit nāṭaka in seven acts composed by Bhavabhūti (early 8th century CE). dramatizing the later life of Rāma after his return to Ayodhyā, particularly the abandonment of Sītā due to civic suspicion, Rāma's sorrow in the Daṇḍaka forest, and their reunion. Celebrated as the paramount dramatic expression of the pathetic sentiment (karuṇarasa), especially in the third act ('Chāyā'), the play reimagines the tragic conclusion of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa into a poignant dramatic reconciliation.

summary: The Vyaktiviveka is an 11th-century treatise on Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra) by Rājānaka Mahimabhaṭṭa of Kashmir. It was written to refute the theory of suggestion (dhvani/vyañjanā) formulated by Ānandavardhana, arguing that all implied aesthetic meanings are fully explainable by logical inference (anumāna). This first chapter (vimarśa 1) mounts an epistemological critique of Ānandavardhana's definition and main divisions of dhvani.

summary: The Stotraratna ('Jewel of Hymns'), traditionally also known as the Āḻavandārstotra, is a landmark devotional poem composed by Yāmunācārya (c. 10th–early 11th century CE) in praise of Viṣṇu/Nārāyaṇa. Comprising 65 verses (verses 1–64 preserved in this e-text), the hymn opens with reverential homage to ancestral teachers including Nāthamuni and Parāśara, before formulating the theological principles of absolute surrender (śaraṇāgati / prapatti), spiritual unworthiness (ākiñcanya), and complete reliance upon divine grace. Synthesizing the devotional fervor of the Tamil Āḻvārs with formal Pāñcarātra and early Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta doctrine, the hymn profoundly shaped Rāmānuja's religious thought and remains a central liturgical text in the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition.

summary: The Śaraṇāgatigadya is a seminal devotional prose work (gadya) in the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta tradition attributed to Rāmānuja, forming the first component of his Gadyatraya. It takes the form of an imaginary dialogic prayer wherein the aspirant first surrenders to Śrī (Lakṣmī) as mediatrix (puruṣakāra) at Śrīraṅgam, and then through her intercession performs total self-surrender (prapatti / śaraṇāgati) to Nārāyaṇa (Śrīraṅganātha), seeking eternal service (kaiṅkarya).

summary: The Śivabhujaṅga is a devotional hymn to Śiva in 40 verses in the bhujaṅgaprayāta metre, traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara. summary: A hymn of 29 sragdharā verses ascribed to Śaṅkara, describing Śiva's body from head to foot (keśādipādānta). It moves from the matted locks, the tripuṇḍra mark and the third eye through the face, the five faces (Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, Īśāna), the throat, the arms and the torso, down to the toenails and the dust of his feet. Each part is invoked to bless or protect the listeners, and the hymn closes with a verse on Śiva's supreme, attributeless splendour.

summary: The Śivanavaratnastava ('Nine-Gem Praise of Śiva') is a short devotional hymn extracted from the Sūtasaṃhitā of the Skandapurāṇa. Consisting of nine verses in praise of Śiva spoken by Bṛhaspati followed by three verses of phalaśruti narrated by Sūta, it extols Śiva through metaphysical and yogic epithets (including references to the mūlādhāra and nābhikanda) as the supreme Brahman and granter of liberation.

summary: A short hymn to Śiva ascribed to Śaṅkara. summary: The Śivapratipādanastotra is a short devotional hymn of 21 verses praising Śiva, extracted from the Skandapurāṇa in the context of a dialogue between Nandīśvara and Viṣṇu. summary: The Śivasahasranāmastotra ('Hymn of the Thousand Names of Śiva') is a major Śaiva devotional hymn extracted from the Anuśāsanaparvan of the Mahābhārata (adhyāya 17). Narrated by Upamanyu to Kṛṣṇa, who in turn recounts it to Yudhiṣṭhira, the hymn contains the one thousand epithets of Śiva originally revealed to the sage Taṇḍi. It synthesizes Vedic, cosmogonic, and philosophical aspects of Śiva and forms one of the standard liturgical sahasranāmas of the Hindu tradition.

summary: The Śivatāṇḍavastotra is a hymn ascribed to Rāvaṇa, in the pañcacāmara metre except for the last verse. With heavy alliteration and onomatopoeia ('dhagad-dhagad-dhagaj-jvalal-…', 'dhimid-dhimid-dhimi-dhvanan-mṛdaṅga …'), it celebrates Śiva's fierce tāṇḍava dance, the Gaṅgā in his matted locks, his serpent ornaments and the fire of his forehead eye. The poet longs for equanimity and for devotion to Śiva. The last two verses give a phalaśruti for daily recitation and for recitation after pūjā on pradoṣa.

summary: The Śivānandalaharī ('Wave of the bliss of Śiva') is a hymn of 100 verses to Śiva in various metres, traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara. summary: The Śivāparādhakṣamāpaṇastotra ('Hymn Seeking Forgiveness for Transgressions from Śiva') is a 14-verse devotional stotra traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. The speaker reviews the phases of life—the womb, childhood, youth, and aging—confessing sins of commission, ritual omissions, and sensory distraction, before beseeching Śiva for forgiveness and spiritual liberation. The concluding verse ('karacaraṇakṛtaṃ vākkāyajaṃ...') is widely recited across Hindu tradition as a general prayer of absolution.

summary: The Gurvaṣṭaka is an eight-verse devotional hymn (with one benedictory phalaśruti stanza) emphasizing devotion to the spiritual preceptor (guru). summary: The Śrīkṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta (or Kṛṣṇakarṇāmṛta) is an influential Sanskrit devotional lyric celebrating the beauty, sweetness (mādhurya), and sports of Kṛṣṇa in Vraja. In the southern recension, the work consists of three cantos (āśvāsas) of approximately one hundred verses each; the eastern (Bengal) tradition preserves primarily the first canto, famously brought to Bengal by Caitanya Mahāprabhu, where it became a cornerstone of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava aesthetics and devotion.

summary: The Rāmagītā is an Advaita Vedānta philosophical dialogue forming the fifth chapter of the Uttarakāṇḍa of the Adhyātmarāmāyaṇa. In response to questions posed by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma teaches that release from saṃsāra is attained not by ritual works (karma) or a combination of knowledge and action (jñānakarmasamuccaya), but solely through direct knowledge (jñāna) of the non-dual Self (ātman). The work systematically synthesizes classical Upaniṣadic Advaita epistemology with devotion to Rāma.

summary: The Rāmahṛdaya ('Heart of Rāma') is a nine-verse Advaita teaching from the first sarga of the Bālakāṇḍa of the Adhyātmarāmāyaṇa, which circulates on its own as a stotra. Narrated by Śiva, it gives Rāma's instruction to Hanumān on the self, the non-self and the supreme self. It uses the analogy of threefold space (total space, space enclosed in a pond, and space reflected in its water) for brahman, consciousness delimited by the intellect, and its reflection (ābhāsa). Liberation comes through knowing identity by the mahāvākyas, combined with devotion to Rāma.

summary: The Śrīveṅkaṭeśaprapatti is a 16-verse Śrīvaiṣṇava stotra of ritual self-surrender (śaraṇāgati/prapatti) addressed to Lord Veṅkaṭeśvara of Tirumala. The opening verse invokes Śrī (Lakṣmī) as the divine mediator (puruṣakāra), followed by fourteen verses praising the Lord's lotus feet, and a closing declaration of service (kaiṅkarya).

summary: The Śṛṅgāraprakāśa is an encyclopedic masterwork of Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra) and dramaturgy (nāṭyaśāstra) in 36 chapters (prakāśas) composed by King Bhoja of Dhārā (11th century). Chapters 1 to 12 form the foundational half of the work, treating grammatical and semantic theory (śabdārtha, padārtha, vākyārtha, vṛtti), literary flaws (doṣa), excellences (guṇa), ornamentation (alaṅkāra), and dramatic and poetic genres (prabandha). The remainder of the work (chapters 13–36, omitted here) develops Bhoja's famous aesthetic theory that śṛṅgāra (identified with ego/self-awareness, ahaṃkāra/abhimāna) is the single supreme and all-encompassing rasa.

summary: The Ūrubhaṅga ('The Shattering of the Thighs') is a one-act Sanskrit drama (often classified as an utsṛṣṭikāṅka) attributed to Bhāsa, based on the final mace duel between Duryodhana and Bhīma in the Mahābhārata. Uniquely in classical Sanskrit drama, which traditionally avoids tragic conclusions, the play focuses on the dying Duryodhana, portraying him as a heroic, remorseful, and dignified figure who accepts his fate and counsels peace. It culminates in his vision of heaven and death on stage, followed by Aśvatthāman's vow of nocturnal vengeance.

summary: The Akṣamālikopaniṣad is a minor Śaiva Upaniṣad affiliated with the Ṛgveda. Formatted as an instructional dialogue between Prajāpati and Guha (Kārttikeya), it describes the proper materials, construction, stringing, and ritual consecration of a japa rosary (akṣamālā). Each of the fifty beads is consecrated with one of the Sanskrit phonemes (mātṛkā) from 'a' to 'kṣa' alongside specific divine energies, concluding with the efficacy and spiritual fruits of reciting mantras with it.

summary: The Atharvaśikhopaniṣad is a minor Śaiva text associated with the Atharvaveda, listed among the fourteen Śaiva Upaniṣads in the Muktikā canon. Framed as a discourse delivered by the sage Atharvan to Pippalāda, Aṅgiras, and Sanatkumāra, it expounds meditation upon the sacred syllable Om (Praṇava). The text identifies the constituent mātrās of Om with Vedic fires, deities, worlds, and states of consciousness, establishing the fourth transcendental quarter (turīya) as Śiva (Īśāna, Śaṃbhu), who is the ultimate reality and sole cause to be meditated upon.

summary: The Avyaktopaniṣad is a minor Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad traditionally affiliated with the Sāmaveda. It presents a cosmogonic narrative in which Prajāpati (Brahmā) emerges from the primordial golden egg and seeks the unmanifest source of creation (Avyakta), revealed to him as Nṛsiṃha (Narasimha). Through the contemplation and ritual-philosophical repetition of the Nṛsiṃhānuṣṭubha-mantra ('ugraṃ vīraṃ mahāviṣṇum...'), Prajāpati gains the knowledge and capacity required to create the world.

summary: The Bhasmajābālopaniṣad is a sectarian Śaiva Upaniṣad affiliated with the Atharvaveda. Cast as an exposition imparted on Mount Kailāsa by Mahādeva (Śiva) to Bhusuṇḍa Jābāla, it establishes the ritual gathering, purification, and preparation of cow-dung sacred ash (bhasma) and prescribes the precise Vedic mantras for marking the body with the tripuṇḍra. The second chapter focuses on the sacred geography and liberative power of Kāśī (Varanasi) as an embodiment of the liṅga, detailing the strict behavioral observances demanded of residents therein.

summary: The Dakṣiṇāmūrtyupaniṣad is a minor Śaiva Upaniṣad framed as an inquiry by Śaunaka and other ṛṣis to the sage Mārkaṇḍeya at the Mahābhāṇḍīra fig tree in Brahmāvarta regarding the secret of immortality. Mārkaṇḍeya reveals the knowledge of Śiva in the form of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, providing multiple mantra formulas (including 24-, 9-, 18-, and 12-syllable mantras and the anuṣṭubh mantrarāja) along with their corresponding dhyāna verses, mudrās, and nyāsa rituals. The work synthesizes ritual tantric upāsanā with Advaita Vedānta by identifying Dakṣiṇāmūrti with ultimate non-dual consciousness (śemuṣī).

summary: The Dattātreyopaniṣad is a sectarian Upaniṣad belonging to the Vaiṣṇava group and traditionally affiliated with the Atharvaveda. Structured as an instruction given by Nārāyaṇa to Brahmā on the supreme liberating principle (tāraka), the text details the meditation and sacred mantras of Dattātreya. It teaches the one-syllable (dāṃ), six-syllable, eight-syllable, twelve-syllable, sixteen-syllable, and anuṣṭubh mantras, providing their corresponding ṛṣi, meter, devatā, bīja, śakti, kīlaka, nyāsa applications, and the spiritual fruits of recitation.

Consisting of thirteen verses and a concluding prose formula, it praises the supreme non-dual principle (identified with the single syllable Oṃ / Brahman) as both the transcendent origin and the immanent cosmic creator manifesting as Rudra, Viṣṇu, Hiraṇyagarbha, and all living forms. The work is split into two halves: the Gopālapūrvatāpinī expounds the eighteen-syllable Gopāla mantra, the yantra, and the meditational identification of Gopāla Kṛṣṇa with the supreme non-dual Brahman; the Gopālottaratāpinī presents a dialogue between the gopīs led by Gāndharvī (Rādhā) and the sage Durvāsas, resolving the paradox of Kṛṣṇa as an eternal, non-attached ascetic despite his romantic sports in Vṛndāvana.

summary: The Kṛṣṇopaniṣad is a minor Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad in two sections (khaṇḍas) that presents an allegorical and metaphysical interpretation of the Kṛṣṇa avatāra. It begins with the forest ascetics encountering Rāma and wishing to embrace him; Rāma instructs them to become gopīs in his future incarnation as Kṛṣṇa. The subsequent text allegorizes the actors, weapons, and adversaries of the Kṛṣṇa mythos, equating Kṛṣṇa with the supreme non-dual Brahman, his associates with divine and scriptural principles, and his foes with negative mental states.

summary: The Maithilīmahopaniṣad is a short Rāmaite Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣadic text framed in its colophon as part of the fifth adhyāya of the Vālmīkisaṃhitā. In the dialogue, seven sage-inquirers (Lāṭyāyana, Kauñjāyana, Khāḍāyana, Bhalandana, Vilva, Ailākya, and Tālukṣya) approach the enthroned goddess Maithilī (Sītā) seeking instruction on what ought to be recited, attained, meditated upon, and known for liberation. Sītā teaches the supreme efficacy of Rāma's name and the six-syllable mantra, concluding with a lineage of transmission passing from Rāma to herself, Hanumān, Brahmā, Vasiṣṭha, Parāśara, Vyāsa, and Śuka.

summary: The Maitrāyaṇyupaniṣad (or Maitrī Upaniṣad) is a late classical Vedic Upaniṣad traditionally attached to the Maitrāyaṇīya śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Framed as an exposition by the ascetic sage Śākāyanya to King Bṛhadratha, it integrates early Vedānta with concepts from early Sāṃkhya and Yoga, notably presenting one of the earliest systematic descriptions of a sixfold yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga). The text addresses existential suffering, the distinction between the elemental self (bhūtātman) and the transcendent immortal self, and meditation on Om, the sun, and prāṇa.

summary: The Muktikopaniṣad is a late Vedāntic text framed as a dialogue between Śrī Rāma and Hanūmān in Ayodhyā. It is famous for formulating the canonical catalog of 108 Upaniṣads mapped to the four Vedic Saṃhitās and describing four graduated forms of liberation (sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya) leading to kaivalya. The second adhyāya draws heavily on philosophical formulations related to the Mokṣopāya/Yogavāsiṣṭha tradition, focusing on the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanākṣaya), the dissolution of the mind (manonāśa), and the attainment of jīvanmukti and videhamukti.

summary: The Muṇḍakopaniṣad is a classical verse Upaniṣad affiliated with the Atharvaveda tradition. Divided into three muṇḍakas, each comprising two khaṇḍas, it structures its philosophical instruction as a dialogue between the sage Aṅgiras and the householder Śaunaka. The text is renowned for distinguishing lower ritual and empirical knowledge (aparā vidyā) from higher liberating knowledge of the imperishable Brahman (parā vidyā), and it contains foundational Upaniṣadic allegories including the two birds on the same tree, the bow and arrow aimed at Brahman, and the national motto of India ('satyam eva jayate').

summary: The Nirālambopaniṣad ('Upaniṣad of the Supportless') is a minor Upaniṣad of the Sāmānya Vedānta group, classified under the Śukla Yajurveda. Arranged as an Advaita catechism, it poses and systematically defines over thirty core ontological, cosmological, and soteriological terms—including Brahman, Īśvara, Jīva, Prakṛti, Karma, Jñāna, Ajñāna, Bandha, Mokṣa, and Saṃnyāsa. It concludes that ultimate reality is non-dual consciousness devoid of worldly support (nirālamba), accessible through experiential realization of the mahāvākyas.

summary: The Nṛsiṃhottaratāpanīyopaniṣad is a Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad belonging to the Atharvaveda tradition, forming the second part of the composite Nṛsiṃhatāpanīyopaniṣad. In nine khaṇḍas, it develops an Advaitic metaphysical synthesis of the Oṃkāra and the four quarters/states of the Ātman (jāgrat, svapna, suṣupta, turīya) closely adapted from the Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad, identifying the supreme non-dual Brahman with Lord Nṛsiṃha.

summary: The Paiṅgalopaniṣad is a late classical Sāmānya Vedānta Upaniṣad affiliated with the Śukla Yajurveda, framed as an esoteric dialogue between the sage Paiṅgala and his teacher Yājñavalkya. Across four adhyāyas, it expounds an Advaita Vedāntic synthesis covering cosmology and quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), the three bodies (śarīratraya) and states of consciousness, an exegesis of the Mahāvākyas (especially 'tat tvam asi'), and the path to jīvanmukti and final release.

summary: The Prāṇāgnihotropaniṣad is a minor Upaniṣad belonging to the Sāmānya Vedānta group, traditionally connected with the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda or Atharvaveda. It internalizes the Vedic Agnihotra sacrifice as the 'Śārīrayajña' (bodily sacrifice), identifying daily food consumption and the movement of the vital breaths (prāṇas) with the ritual oblations into the internal fires. By establishing the body as the sacred sacrificial ground, it teaches liberation (mokṣa) through knowledge without the necessity of external rites.

summary: The Rudrahṛdayopaniṣad is a minor Śaiva Upaniṣad traditionally belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Framed as an exchange between Śuka and Vyāsa on the ultimate identity of the gods, it propounds non-difference between Rudra and Viṣṇu, asserting that worship or enmity toward one is directed at the other. It analyzes divine reality across male and female dualities and culminates in an Advaitic exposition of Brahman as transcendent consciousness (saccidānanda) accessible via higher knowledge (parā vidyā).

summary: The Rāmarahasyopaniṣad is a late medieval Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad affiliated with the Atharvaveda and numbered 54 in the Muktikā anthology. summary: The Rāmatāpinyupaniṣad (also known as Rāmatāpanīyopaniṣad) is a Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad associated with the Atharvaveda tradition, divided into the Pūrvatāpinī and Uttarātāpinī sections. The Pūrvatāpinī (five sections) expounds the theological identity of Rāma as the supreme non-dual Brahman, establishing the iconography, the six-syllable Rāma mantra, and yantric ritual worship. The Uttarātāpinī (five khaṇḍas) identifies Rāma with the saving Tāraka mantra imparted at Vārāṇasī and correlates his forms with the states of consciousness and the praṇava (Om).

summary: The Sarasvatīrahasyopaniṣad ('The Secret Teaching of Sarasvatī') is a Śākta Upaniṣad associated with the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda and listed as number 106 in the Muktikā canon. Structured as a dialogue between the sage Āśvalāyana and inquiring ṛṣis, the text presents the worship of goddess Sarasvatī as supreme non-dual consciousness (cit-śakti). It incorporates classical Ṛgvedic verses to Sarasvatī embedded within tantric bījamantras and nyāsa rituals, concluding with an Advaita Vedānta exposition of the mahāvākyas and samādhi.

summary: The Sarvasāropaniṣad is a short Sāmānya-Vedānta Upaniṣad structured as a catechistic glossary of Advaita metaphysics. In twenty-one prose passages and concluding verses, it poses and answers questions defining fundamental concepts: bondage (bandha), liberation (mokṣa), avidyā, vidyā, the four states of consciousness (jāgrat, svapna, suṣupti, turīya), the five sheaths (pañcakośa), the soul and witness consciousness (kartṛ, jīva, kṣetrajña, sākṣin, kūṭastha, antaryāmin), concluding with the identification of the innermost self (pratyagātman) with unconditioned Brahman.

summary: The Skandopaniṣad is a minor Upanishad associated with the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda (No. 51 in the Muktikā canon). Opening with a speaker's declaration to Mahādeva of his identity with Acyuta and Śiva (attributed to Skanda), the text teaches radical non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Śiva, as well as the ultimate identity of Śiva and Viṣṇu ('śivāya viṣṇurūpāya śivarūpāya viṣṇave'). It synthesizes Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava devotional motifs into Advaita Vedānta, concluding with the Vedic refrain 'tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam'.

summary: The Subālopaniṣad is a classical Sāmānya Vedānta Upaniṣad associated with the Śukla Yajurveda, framed as a dialogue between the sage Subāla and the creator Prajāpati/Brahman. It details cosmogony from primal darkness (tamas) through the cosmic egg and the cosmic Puruṣa, followed by dissolution (pralaya) of elements back into the supreme deity Nārāyaṇa. It also elaborates subtle heart anatomy, the nature of the inner ruler (antaryāmin), and conditions for liberation, serving as a foundational proof-text in Rāmānuja's Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta for the doctrine of the world as the body of Brahman (śarīra-śarīrī-bhāva).

summary: The Sāmarahasyopaniṣad is a late sectarian Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad presenting esoteric Braj devotional theology framed as an inquiry by Brahmā's sons (Sanaka and others) into the eternal līlā of Vaikuṇṭha and Vraja, followed by a dialogue between Nārāyaṇa and Lakṣmī. The text exalts Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa (Puruṣottama, Rasikānanda) as the supreme transcendent non-dual reality beyond the kṣara and akṣara realms. It details the nature of jīvas, the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), and the transformation of worldly passions into sādhanā through the esoteric path of aesthetic devotion (rasamārga / snehamārga).

summary: The Sāvitryupaniṣad is a minor Upaniṣad affiliated with the Sāmaveda and grouped among the Sāmānya Vedānta Upaniṣads. It elaborates nine cosmic and microcosmic generative pairs (mithuna) representing Savitṛ and Sāvitrī—such as fire and earth, wind and ether, mind and speech, and man and woman. It connects this duality to the three pādas of the Gāyatrī mantra and concludes with the Balā and Atibalā vidyā formulas.

summary: The Sītopaniṣad is a Vaiṣṇava-Śākta minor Upaniṣad affiliated with the Atharvaveda. In a dialogue between Prajāpati and the gods, Sītā is identified as Mūlaprakṛti and the praṇava, acting as the dynamic cosmic power of Rāma. summary: The Tejobindūpaniṣad is one of the twenty Yoga Upaniṣads reckoned in the Muktikā canon. In six adhyāyas, it integrates yogic contemplation on the 'effulgent point' (tejobindu) with non-dual Advaita Vedānta philosophy, expounding a distinctive fifteen-limbed yoga (pañcadaśāṅgayoga) and teachings on jīvanmukti and videhamukti. summary: The Tripurātāpinyupaniṣad is a Śākta Upaniṣad belonging to the Śrīvidyā tradition and traditionally affiliated with the Atharvaveda. summary: The Tārasāropaniṣad is a Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad of the Muktikā canon (associated with the Śukla Yajurveda). Formulated as dialogues between Bṛhaspati, Bharadvāja, and Yājñavalkya, it identifies the ultimate liberating mantra (tāraka) imparted at Avimukta (Vārāṇasī) as the eight-syllabled Nārāyaṇa mantra (oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya) and Praṇava (oṃ). The text correlates the component morphemes and phonemes of the mantra with deities and figures of the Rāmāyaṇa—equating them with Jāmbavān, Hari/Sugrīva, Hanumān, Śatrughna, Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, and Rāma as the supreme Puruṣottama.

summary: The Vajrasūcyupaniṣad ('Diamond Needle Upaniṣad') is a short prose treatise traditionally linked to the Sāmaveda that critically examines the defining criteria of a Brāhmaṇa. Through sequential refutations, it denies that brāhmaṇahood consists in the individual self (jīva), the physical body (deha), caste or lineage by birth (jāti), scriptural learning (jñāna), ritual action (karma), or religious merit (dhārmika). It concludes that a true Brāhmaṇa is defined exclusively by direct experiential realization of the non-dual, attribute-free Brahman (sat-cit-ānanda) coupled with self-mastery and absence of egotism.

summary: The Viśvaṃbharopaniṣad is a sectarian Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad styled as an Atharvavedic dialogue between sage Śāṇḍilya and Mahāśambhu (Śiva). It glorifies Śrī Rāma as the ultimate reality beyond saguṇa and nirguṇa, from whom all avatāras (including Kṛṣṇa and Nārāyaṇa) manifest. The text instructs the practitioner in principal Rāma mantras (ṣaḍakṣara, aṣṭākṣara, and dvayamantra), diagrammatic yantra preparation, nyāsa rituals, and daily pūjā offerings.

summary: The Vāsudevopaniṣad is a minor sectarian Vaiṣṇava Upaniṣad, listed as the 56th text in the Muktikā canon and traditionally attached to the Sāmaveda. Structured as a dialogue between Bhagavān Vāsudeva and the sage Nārada, it outlines the ritual requirements and sacred mantras for applying the vertical sectarian forehead mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) using sacred clay (gopīcandana). It interprets the puṇḍra mystically through the syllables of Oṃ (A-U-M) and the manifestations of Viṣṇu, concluding with the spiritual rewards of unswerving devotion to Vāsudeva.

summary: The Yogakuṇḍalyupaniṣad is one of the twenty Yoga Upaniṣads belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. In three chapters, it presents haṭha- and laya-yogic practices directed toward awakening kuṇḍalinī, including breath restraint (prāṇāyāma), dietary discipline (mitāhāra), āsana, bandhas, and lambikā (khecarī) mudrā, integrated into a non-dual Advaita Vedānta soteriology. This e-text includes both the root Upaniṣad and the running Vivaraṇa commentary by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: The Ārṣeyopaniṣad is an archaic prose Upaniṣad written in Vedic Brāhmaṇa-like style. It records a theological dispute (brahmodya) among five ancient sages—Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Gautama, and Vasiṣṭha—who successively critique each other's conceptions of Brahman (intermediate space, the cosmic egg/water, the solar light, and the golden person) as perishable (ārta), culminating in Vasiṣṭha's exposition of Brahman as the all-encompassing, imperishable inner Ātman approached through neti neti.

summary: The Ātmabodhopaniṣad (also referred to at its conclusion as the Ātmaprabodhopaniṣad) is a minor Sāmānya Vedānta Upaniṣad affiliated with the Ṛgveda and designated as the 42nd text in the Muktikā anthology. Adhyāya 1 delineates meditation on Nārāyaṇa via the aṣṭākṣaramantra, the inner luminosity of Brahman in the heart lotus, and liberation. Adhyāya 2 forms an extended monistic hymn of Self-knowledge, declaring the transcendent Self to be unattached, beyond the three bodies (sthūla, liṅga, kāraṇa), and identical with pure, non-dual consciousness.

summary: The Śarabhopaniṣad is a minor sectarian Śaiva Upaniṣad affiliated with the Atharvaveda and numbered 50th in the Muktikā canon. Formulated as a dialogue where Brahmā instructs the sage Paippalāda on the supremacy of Śiva among the Trimūrti, it recounts how Śiva assumed the eight-legged form of the Śarabha beast to pacify and overpower Narasiṃha (Viṣṇu). Weaving mythological feats with classical Upaniṣadic phrases, it extols Śiva/Rudra as the supreme non-dual Brahman.

summary: The Śukarahasyopaniṣad (also known as the Rahasyopaniṣad) is a minor Sāmānya Vedānta Upaniṣad counted as number 35 in the Muktikā canon of 108 Upaniṣads. Framed as an initiation given by Śiva to Vyāsa's son Śuka during his upanayana, it details the ritual and esoteric exposition of the four Vedic Mahāvākyas together with their nyāsa, dhyāna, and viniyoga. Upon receiving this instruction, Śuka attains jīvanmukti and renounces the worldly life.

summary: The Śārīrakopaniṣad is a minor Sāmānya Vedānta Upaniṣad affiliated with the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda (no. 62 in the Muktikā canon). It provides an anatomical and psychological exposition of the human embodiment (śarīra) integrating Sāṅkhya cosmology and Vedāntic metaphysics. It details the five gross elements (mahābhūtas) and their bodily constituents, the sensory and motor faculties (indriyas), the fourfold internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the three guṇas, and the four states of consciousness (jāgrat, svapna, suṣupti, turīya), concluding with the identification of the seventeenfold subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) and the supreme Self transcending the embodied soul (jīva/kṣetrajña).

summary: The Śāṇḍilyopaniṣad is a classical Yoga Upaniṣad framed as an instruction given by Atharvan to the sage Śāṇḍilya. Its first and longest chapter details an eight-limbed yoga (aṣṭāṅga-yoga) incorporating Haṭha-yogic practices, including ten yamas, ten niyamas, eight āsanas, detailed instructions on nāḍī-purification, prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi. The second and third chapters expound the non-dual nature of Brahman in both saguṇa/sakala and nirguṇa/niṣkala aspects, integrating bodily yoga into Advaita Vedānta. In this edition, the text is accompanied by the complete Advaitic commentary (vivaraṇa) of Upaniṣadbrahmayogin.

summary: The Bhelasaṃhitā is an early classical Āyurvedic treatise belonging to the Ātreya school of internal medicine (kāyacikitsā). Structured similarly to the Carakasaṃhitā across eight sthānas (Sūtra, Nidāna, Vimāna, Śārīra, Indriya, Cikitsā, Kalpa, and Siddhi), it expounds etiology, pathology, anatomy, embryology, and therapeutics. Preserved uniquely in a single fragmentary palm-leaf manuscript from Thanjavur, it constitutes a crucial early witness to classical Indian medical literature alongside Caraka and Suśruta.

summary: The Bhāṣikasūtra (or Bhāṣikapariśiṣṭasūtra), traditionally attributed to Kātyāyana, is a short phonetic treatise (pariśiṣṭa) of the Śukla Yajurveda setting forth the rules of accentuation (bhāṣikasvara) in Brāhmaṇa prose, particularly the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa. It formulates the two-accent system (udātta and anudātta) of the Brāhmaṇa in contrast to the tripartite mantra accentuation, describes verbal accent shift, and correlates recitation tones with musical pitches.

summary: The Chāndogyabrāhmaṇa (widely known as the Mantrabrāhmaṇa) is a Vedic ritual text of the Kauthuma śākhā of the Sāmaveda comprising two prapāṭhakas of eight khaṇḍas each. It compiles liturgical verses and formulas for domestic (gṛhya) ceremonies, including marriage, garbhādhāna, upanayana, and funeral rites, functioning as the mantra collection corresponding to the Gobhilagṛhyasūtra. In the larger ten-chapter Chāndogya corpus, these two chapters immediately precede the eight chapters constituting the Chāndogyopaniṣad.

summary: The Ekāgnikāṇḍa (also known as the Mantrapāṭha or Mantraprapāṭhaka) is a liturgical collection of Vedic mantras belonging to the Taittirīya recension of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, arranged specifically for the domestic rituals (saṃskāras) of the Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra. Divided into two prapāṭhakas, it provides the mantras recited during marriage, conception, childhood rites, upanayana, samāvartana, and household domestic rites. summary: The Hārītasaṃhitā is a Sanskrit Āyurvedic treatise presented as an instructional dialogue between the sage Ātreya and his pupil Hārīta. Divided into six divisions (sthānas)—including Prathama- (Prakīrṇa- / Sūtra-), Dvitīya- (Doṣadhātu-), Tṛtīya- (Cikitsā-), Kalpa-, and Śārīrasthāna, followed by a pariśiṣṭa—it treats nosology, clinical therapy, pharmacology, and dietetics. The surviving recension is a later medieval synthesis rather than the ancient lost treatise cited by early commentators.

summary: The Jaiminīyopaniṣadbrāhmaṇa is a Vedic prose text of the Jaiminīya (Talavakāra) school of the Sāmaveda, functioning as its Āraṇyaka. In four adhyāyas it gives esoteric interpretations of the sāman chant (especially the gāyatra-sāman and the udgītha), the syllable om, prāṇa and the correspondences between ritual, cosmos and person. The fourth adhyāya contains the Kena Upaniṣad (4.18–21), and the text ends with an exposition of the Sāvitrī verse (4.27–28).

summary: The Kaṭhāraṇyaka is the Āraṇyaka of the Kaṭha (Caraka-Kaṭha) śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It survives in fragmentary form, chiefly in a Śāradā birch-bark manuscript from Kashmir kept at Tübingen. It is a brāhmaṇa-style exposition of the Pravargya (the hot-milk offering in the Mahāvīra pot) and its prāyaścittas, and ends with the Gharmājaṭhara and Śukriya brāhmaṇas.

summary: The Kāśyapasaṃhitā (Vṛddhajīvakīyatantra) is an early Āyurvedic compendium centred on kaumārabhṛtya (care of children, together with pregnancy and the postnatal period). It is framed as Kaśyapa's teaching to Vṛddhajīvaka and was redacted by Vātsya. It covers infant feeding and electuaries (lehana), dentition, children's diseases, demonic seizers (grahas) including the Revatīkalpa, and treatments for mothers and wet-nurses. It survives only in one incomplete Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript, first published by Hemarāja Śarmā in 1938.

summary: The Nāḍīparīkṣā ('Examination of the Pulse') is an Āyurvedic manual of pulse diagnosis traditionally attributed to Maharṣi Kaṇāda. summary: The Rasendracintāmaṇi is an influential Sanskrit treatise on Rasaśāstra (iatrochemical alchemy and medicine) composed by the Nātha adept Ḍhuṇḍhukanātha, pupil of Kālanātha, generally dated between the 14th and 16th centuries CE. Written in verse interspersed with prose passages, the work describes the purification, processing, and calcination of mercury (pārada), metals, and minerals, as well as complex compound recipes for treating various illnesses and rejuvenating the body (rasāyana). The author strongly emphasizes firsthand laboratory experimentation and verification over uncritical textual transmission, and the work served as a primary source for subsequent treatises such as the Rasendrasārasaṃgraha.

summary: The Suśrutasaṃhitā is one of the three foundational classics of classical Āyurveda (the Bṛhat-trayī) and ancient India's premier authority on surgery (śalyatantra). Framed as instructions delivered by Divodāsa Dhanvantari, king of Kāśī, to his student Suśruta, it describes surgical instruments, practical anatomy through human cadaveric dissection, and operative procedures such as rhinoplasty, couching of cataracts, lithotomy, and abdominal suture. The treatise comprises 186 chapters divided across the five sthānas of the Pūrvatantra (Sūtra-, Nidāna-, Śārīra-, Cikitsā-, and Kalpasthāna) and the supplementary Uttaratantra, which treats ophthalmology and ENT (śālākya), pediatrics (kaumārabhṛtya), toxicology/psychiatry (bhūtavidyā), and general medicine (kāyacikitsā).

summary: The Taittirīyabrāhmaṇa is the principal Brāhmaṇa prose text of the Taittirīya recension of the Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda. Structured into three kāṇḍas, it expounds the theological rationale, liturgical formulas, and rituals of major śrauta rites including the Agnyādhāna, Gavāmayana, Vājapeya, Soma sacrifices, Nakṣatreṣṭis, Sautrāmaṇī, Aśvamedha, and Agnicayana. summary: The Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā is one of the three foundational classics of classical Ayurveda (the bṛhattrayī), composed in metrical verse by Vāgbhaṭa (ca. 7th century CE). Renowned for its poetic lucidity and practical therapeutic orientation, it became the preeminent medical handbook across South Asia, Central Asia, and Tibet.

summary: The Vājasaneyisaṃhitā (Mādhyandina recension) is the foundational mantra collection of the White (Śukla) Yajurveda, preserving the formulas and verses recited by the adhvaryu priest during śrauta sacrificial rites. Unlike the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurvedic saṃhitās, which intermingle liturgical formulas with brāhmaṇa prose exposition, the White Yajurveda separates the liturgical mantras into this collection, relegating exegesis to the Śatapatha-Brāhmaṇa. In 40 adhyāyas, it covers ceremonies including the New and Full Moon sacrifices (Darśapūrṇamāsa), the Soma ritual (Agniṣṭoma), the piling of the fire altar (Agnicayana), and major royal offerings (Vājapeya, Rājasūya, Aśvamedha, Puruṣamedha), concluding in its final chapter with the Īśāvāsyopaniṣad.

summary: The Ṛgvedaprātiśākhya is the oldest surviving phonological and metric treatise (prātiśākhya) of the Vedic literature, affiliated with the Śākala recension of the Ṛgveda and traditionally attributed to Śaunaka. Organized into three adhyāyas comprising eighteen paṭalas, it systematically describes Vedic phonetics, sandhi rules, accentuation (svara), syllable length, meter (chandas), and the phonetic modifications required to derive the continuous saṃhitāpāṭha from the word-by-word padapāṭha. It forms an indispensable source for the history of Vedic phonology and early Indian grammatical thought.

summary: The Amoghānandinīśikṣā is a 130-verse phonetic manual (śikṣā) of the Mādhyandina (Vājasaneyi) school of the Śukla Yajurveda. It lists Saṃhitā words to be pronounced with labial b (oṣṭhya) versus dental/labio-dental v (dantya), distinguishes heavy, light and lighter (laghūtara) v, and treats nāda, nasalisation (anunāsika, raṅga), pluti and the syllable-counts of recitation units, closing with verses on the value of lakṣaṇa and correct recitation. The e-text adds the opening and closing verses of a 57-verse 'second part' attributed to the same tradition.

summary: The Dhātupāṭha is the canonical verbal inventory of the Pāṇinian grammatical tradition (Vyākaraṇa), serving as the foundational auxiliary text to the Aṣṭādhyāyī. It arranges approximately two thousand verbal roots into ten conjugation classes (gaṇas), starting from bhvādi and ending with curādi. Each entry provides the root's base form with diacritical markers (anubandhas) denoting accent, voice (parasmaipada, ātmanepada, or ubhayapada), and morphophonological traits, alongside traditional semantic glosses.

summary: The Aṣṭādhyāyī of Pāṇini (c. 4th century BCE) is the foundational masterpiece of Sanskrit linguistics and the primary Vedāṅga text for grammar (Vyākaraṇa), formulating nearly 4,000 highly condensed aphoristic rules across eight chapters. summary: The Baudhāyanagṛhyasūtra is a principal domestic ritual manual of the Baudhāyana school of the Black Yajurveda (Kṛṣṇayajurveda, Taittirīya śākhā). Structured in four praśnas, it covers the seven standard pākayajña archetypes and life-cycle rites (saṃskāras) from marriage (vivāha) through pregnancy, birth, childhood ceremonies, Vedic initiation (upanayana), study vows, ancestral offerings, house construction, and domestic prāyaścittas. It constitutes the gṛhya component of the comprehensive Baudhāyana Kalpasūtra.

summary: The Baudhāyanaśrautasūtra, of the Taittirīya school of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, is generally regarded as the oldest extant Śrautasūtra. It prescribes, largely from the Adhvaryu's standpoint, the solemn rites from the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Agnyādheya, Agnihotra, Paśubandha and Cāturmāsya through the Agniṣṭoma, Agnicayana, Vājapeya, Rājasūya, Aśvamedha and sattras. Distinctive are its discursive Dvaidha sections recording differing opinions of Baudhāyana, Śālīki, Aupamanyava and other teachers, followed by Karmānta and Prāyaścitta sections.

summary: The Baudhāyanaśulbasūtra is the oldest known Indian mathematical treatise, belonging to the Kalpasūtra of the Taittirīya school of the Black Yajurveda (circa 800–500 BCE). It contains detailed geometric rules and measurement techniques for the construction of Vedic sacrificial altars (vedi and agnicayana), including the geometric statement of the Pythagorean theorem, methods for squaring the circle and circling the square, and precise fractional approximations of the square root of two.

summary: The Bhāradvājaśikṣā is a Vedāṅga phonetic treatise belonging to the Taittirīya recension of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, traditionally ascribed to the sage Bharadvāja. summary: The Baudhāyanadharmasūtra is an ancient prose legal manual (dharmasūtra) belonging to the Baudhāyana carana of the Taittirīya recension of the Black Yajurveda. Arranged in four books (praśnas), it outlines sources of dharma, regional customs, student life, marriage, inheritance, penances (prāyaścitta), dietary rules, and ascetic codes. Modern scholarship dates the foundational core (praśnas 1–2) to roughly the 3rd–2nd century BCE, with praśnas 3–4 reflecting later accretions.

summary: The Bṛhaddevatā ('Great [Index of] Deities') is an extensive metrical treatise in eight adhyāyas belonging to the Vedāṅga and Anukramaṇī literature of the Ṛgveda, traditionally attributed to Śaunaka. Composed predominantly in anuṣṭubh verses, it systematically catalogs the deities presiding over every hymn, verse, hemistich, and quarter-verse of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā in sequential order. In addition to ritual classification and etymological remarks reflecting Nirukta traditions, the work is especially renowned for preserving early narrative legends (ākhyānas) explaining the mythical contexts of the hymns.

summary: The Golādhyāya is the last division of Bhāskara II's Siddhāntaśiromaṇi (1150 CE). It covers spherical astronomy and cosmology: the shape and support of the earth, the bhuvanakośa, the rationale (vāsanā) of mean and true planetary motion, sines, and the construction of the armillary sphere. This e-text gives the first half of the Golādhyāya with Bhāskara's own Vāsanābhāṣya and the long 17th-century Marīci commentary by Munīśvara, which quotes earlier authorities at length. The text is preceded by the editor's Sanskrit introduction.

summary: The Hiraṇyakeśiśrautasūtra (also designated Satyāṣāḍhaśrautasūtra) is an extensive manual of Vedic ritual belonging to the Taittirīya recension of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, sharing substantial textual and ritual parallels with the Āpastambaśrautasūtra. Spanning 29 praśnas and concluding with a pariśiṣṭa, it presents exhaustive prescriptions for the Śrauta sacrifices—from the basic Darśapūrṇamāsa and Agnyādhāna to complex Soma rituals, the Agnicayana, Sattras, and Pitṛmedha. This digital text represents an OCR reproduction of the 10-volume Ānandāśrama edition containing both the root sūtras and two standard traditional commentaries, the Vaijayantī and Jyotsnā.

summary: The Jaṭāmaṇivyākhyāna (or Jaṭāmaṇitātparya) is an ancillary Vedic phonetic-recitational treatise (vikṛti-lakṣaṇa) explaining the rules and sandhi adjustments required for reciting the Taittirīya Saṃhitā in the jaṭāpāṭha ('braided') modification. Referring to the Taittirīya Prātiśākhya and related grammatical rules, it treats standard two-word combinations as well as complex three-word sequences (trikrama), illustrating the permutations (anuloma and viloma) through sacrificial mantra citations.

summary: The Jñāpakasaṃgrahapariśiṣṭa supplements Nāgeśabhaṭṭa's Jñāpakasaṃgraha. It collects further rules that the Mahābhāṣya derives by jñāpaka (inference from the wording of Pāṇini's sūtras) and that Nāgeśa did not include. summary: The Jñāpakasaṃgraha is a Vyākaraṇa treatise attributed to Nāgeśabhaṭṭa (17th–18th century). It systematically compiles principles and implicit rules (jñāpaka) deduced from Pāṇini's formulation of the sūtras as discussed in Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya, specifically focusing on those not covered by traditional collections of paribhāṣās. This e-text covers all eight adhyāyas of the root text alongside the detailed modern commentary 'Vivṛti' by the traditional South Indian scholar Navalpakkam Rāmānujācārya.

summary: The Karaṇapaddhati is an astronomical and mathematical manual (karaṇa) composed around 1730 CE by Putumana Somayājin of the Kerala school. Across ten adhyāyas, the treatise presents practical algorithms for planetary longitudes, eclipses, gnomon shadow reckoning, and spherical astronomy. In Chapter 6, it notably formulates infinite series expansions for π, sine, and cosine functions derived from the lineage of Mādhava of Saṅgamagrāma.

This e-text contains solely the initial Saṃjñāprakaraṇa, covering definitions and technical meta-language.

summary: The Manaḥsvāraśikṣā is a short Vedāṅga treatise on the phonetic and accentual recitation (svara and avasāna) of the Śuklayajurveda (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā Mādhyandina school). In 64 thematic sections, it groups Vedic mantra incipits (pratīkas) according to accent patterns (udātta, anudātta, kampa, jātya) and metrical pause distribution (tripadā, niravasāna, caturavasāna). Traditionally attributed to Yājñavalkya, it serves as a mnemonic and phonological manual for Vedic chanters.

summary: The Mānavaśrautasūtra is the śrauta ritual manual of the Mānava school of the Maitrāyaṇīya branch of the Black Yajurveda, written mainly from the Adhvaryu's perspective. It covers the new- and full-moon sacrifices and the other prakṛti rites, the Agniṣṭoma, expiations, the Pravargya, the iṣṭis, the Agnicayana, the Vājapeya and Rājasūya. This e-text also contains the Mānava Śulbasūtra and a series of appendices (pratigraha, Rudrajapa, pravara lists, śrāddha rules).

summary: The Māṇḍūkīśikṣā is the metrical śikṣā of the Atharvaveda, ascribed to Maṇḍūka. In 181 verses it treats the three speeds of recitation (druta, madhyama, vilambita), the seven musical notes and how they relate to the Vedic accents, the hand movements that accompany accented recitation and their faults, defects of pronunciation, and rules on sandhi, consonant doubling and other points of phonetics.

summary: The Nighaṇṭu is the oldest surviving Vedic word-list. It has three parts: synonym lists (naighaṇṭuka-kāṇḍa, adhyāyas 1–3), difficult and homonymous words (naigama, 4) and names of deities (daivata, 5). Yāska's Nirukta is the Vedāṅga treatise on etymology and Vedic exegesis and is built as a commentary on the Nighaṇṭu. It sets out the four word classes (nāman, ākhyāta, upasarga, nipāta), defends the derivation of nouns from verbal roots, and explains the Vedic words and deities with citations of the mantras. The e-text adds the later Pariśiṣṭa (adhyāyas 13–14).

summary: A short Vedic lakṣaṇa (śikṣā) tract from the Taittirīya tradition. It explains the Nāradabaiṭ, a mnemonic syllable code ascribed to Nārada that encodes the counts of anuvākas and vākyas in the Taittirīyasaṃhitā. Seven paribhāṣā verses set out the rules (which vowels count, how conjunct consonants count in kaṭapayādi fashion, and the bindu-marked syllables ma, da, ga, ta, sa standing for tens). The author's prose commentary, Bhāvaprakāśikā, follows, and then the code strings for all seven kāṇḍas.

summary: The Nāradasaṃhitā is a Sanskrit astrological treatise belonging to the saṃhitā branch of jyotiṣa, traditionally ascribed to the mythical sage Nārada. Across 55 chapters, it treats planetary motions, calendar cycles, muhūrta for domestic rituals (saṃskāras) and everyday activities, portents (utpāta), weather signs, and śrāddha timings. This e-text includes the root verses alongside the Hindi commentary Saralā by Vasatirāma Śarman.

summary: The Padacandrikā is a metrical Vedāṅga grammatical and phonological handbook belonging to the Śukla Yajurveda (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā) tradition of Yājñavalkya. It explains Vedic accentuation (svara, including the eight svarita types), euphonic combination (sandhi), augment rules, vowel lengthening, and phonological features critical to the recitation and analysis of the Vedic Pada text.

summary: The Paramalaghumañjūṣā is Nāgeśabhaṭṭa's briefest handbook summarizing the linguistic and semantic theories developed in his Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā. This partial text covers the nature of linguistic power (śakti, lakṣaṇā, vyañjanā), the sphoṭa doctrine, and the four traditional requisites for sentential comprehension: mutual expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), semantic fitness (yogyatā), contiguity (āsatti), and speaker intention (tātparya).

summary: The Pariṣkāradarpaṇa ('Mirror of Refinements') by the modern traditional scholar Veṇīmādhava Śukla is a pedagogical manual of Navya-Nyāya and Navya-Vyākaraṇa analytical techniques (pariṣkāra), written specifically for students of grammar (śābdika). The text provides precise definitions and dialectical distinctions for technical scholastic concepts including viṣayatā, pratiyogitā, anuyogitā, avacchedakatā, paryāpti, kāraṇatā, and the semantic analysis of sentence meaning (śābdabodha).

summary: The Phiṭsūtra is an auxiliary treatise (paribhāṣā/svara supplement) of the Pāṇinian grammatical tradition attributed to Śāntanava. Spanning 87 sūtras divided across four pādas, the work formulates accentual rules (svara) directly governing nominal stems (phiṭ / prātipadika) without presupposing derivational morphemic analysis. summary: The Chandaḥsūtra of Piṅgala is the foundational classical treatise on Sanskrit metrics (chandas), traditionally classified as the primary surviving manual of the Chandas Vedāṅga. summary: The Siddhāntatattvaviveka is an influential Sanskrit astronomical treatise completed in Varanasi in 1658 CE by Kamalākara, belonging to the prominent Golagrāma family of astronomers. Written partly in opposition to Munīśvara's Siddhāntasārvabhauma, the treatise defends the traditional Sūryasiddhānta framework while integrating Greco-Arabic and Persian astronomical concepts, such as Ulugh Beg's tables, optics, and advanced spherical trigonometry. The included Śeṣavāsanā is the author's own supplementary exposition clarifying subtle mathematical demonstrations and geometrical rationales.

summary: The Svaraśikṣā is a short Vedic phonetic treatise (śikṣā) in 35 verses dedicated to accentuation (svara). It defines the primary accents—udātta, anudātta, svarita, and pracaya—along with their physiological correlates, deity associations, hand-gesture markers (hastasvara), and the classical varieties of the svarita accent (jātya, kṣaipra, abhinihita, praśliṣṭa, etc.). It emphasizes the grave consequences of faulty recitation and the ritual merit of accurate accentuation.

summary: The Puṣpasūtra (also known as the Sāmaprātiśākhya or Phullasūtra) is the phonological and melodic manual (prātiśākhya) of the Kauthuma and Rāṇāyanīya śākhās of the Sāmaveda. In ten prapāṭhakas, it details how Ṛgvedic verses (arcas) are transformed into musical chants (sāmans), codifying vocal lengthening, elisions, tone accents, stobhas (melodic vocables), and stotriya structural divisions.

summary: The Sāmavedasaptalakṣaṇa ('Saptalakṣaṇa') is a metrical collection of seven lakṣaṇa treatises auxiliary to the Sāmaveda padapāṭha, cataloguing words subject to particular sandhi phenomena: visarga elision (Śamāna, with notes on visarga retention and the nasal raṅga), e/ai-final words (Viliṅghya), n-final words before n- (Napara), t-final words (Tapara), shortened vowels (Hrasvasaṃgrahaṇa), word-initial a-vowels (Avarṇi) and words without avagraha (Anavagrahalakṣaṇa). Each rule is illustrated by mnemonic lists of Sāmaveda word forms with counts of the sūtras covered.

It cites the Mahābhāṣya, Bhartṛhari, Durga and the lexicographers.

summary: The Taittirīyaprātiśākhya is the phonological and phonetic treatise belonging to the Taittirīya recension of the Black Yajurveda (Kṛṣṇayajurveda). In 24 adhyāyas, it provides detailed rules on phonetic inventory, euphonic combination (sandhi), accentuation (svara), moric quantity, and pronunciation necessary to transition between the continuous saṃhitāpāṭha and the uncombined padapāṭha. It cites numerous early phoneticians, including Ātreya, Pauṣkarasādi, Plākṣi, and Vālmīki.

summary: The Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra is an influential 17th-century treatise on semantic theory and linguistic philosophy in the Pāṇinian school by Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa. It serves as an abridgement of his larger Bṛhadvaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa, commenting on the 74 kārikās of the Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakārikā composed by his uncle Bhaṭṭojīdīkṣita. The work systematically articulates and defends the grammarians' semantic doctrines regarding the meaning of verbal roots (dhātvartha), suffixes (tiṅartha, kṛdartha), nominal cases (subartha), compounds (samāsa), and sphoṭa against the opposing positions of the Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā traditions.

summary: The Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra is Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa's (17th century) condensation of his larger commentary, the Bṛhadvaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa, expounding the 74 grammatical-philosophical kārikās (Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakārikā) of his uncle Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita. It constitutes a foundational treatise of the Navya-Vyākaraṇa school of linguistic philosophy, systematically articulating semantic theories regarding verbal roots, affixes, case endings, compounds, and the doctrine of sphoṭa in vigorous polemic with Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā. This digital edition presents Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa's treatise accompanied throughout by Harivallabha's Darpaṇa commentary.

summary: The Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā (commonly referred to as Bṛhanmañjūṣā to distinguish it from the Laghu- and Paramalaghu-mañjūṣā) is Nāgeśabhaṭṭa's masterwork on the philosophy of language and semantic theory in the Pāṇinian tradition. It systematically investigates word meaning, communicative functions (śakti, lakṣaṇā, vyañjanā), verbal roots, morphemes, case relations, and sentential comprehension, critically engaging the positions of Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā. The treatise concludes with a rigorous exposition of the sphoṭa doctrine as the ontological core of meaningful language.

summary: The Vedaparibhāṣākārikāśikṣā is a brief 11-verse manual belonging to the Mādhyandina branch of the Śukla Yajurveda. summary: The Vyāsaśikṣā is a prominent phonetic manual (śikṣā) belonging to the Taittirīya śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Arranged in 28 sections (prakaraṇas) comprising 525 verses, it details rules of accentuation (svara), sandhi, consonant gemination (dvitva), and recitation modes (pada, krama, and jaṭā) characteristic of the Taittirīya textual tradition. It shares a deep structural relationship with the Taittirīya Prātiśākhya.

summary: The Vākyapadīya (c. 5th century CE) by Bhartṛhari is the foundational treatise of the philosophy of grammar (Vyākaraṇadarśana) and classical Indian semantic theory. Comprising three books—Brahmakāṇḍa (on Śabdabrahman and the metaphysics of language), Vākyakāṇḍa (on sentence-meaning wholism and the sphoṭa doctrine), and Padakāṇḍa or Prakīrṇaka (fourteen specialized treatises exploring universals, particulars, relations, time, action, and case-roles)—it articulates a non-dualist linguistic philosophy that shaped subsequent debates across Buddhist, Mīmāṃsā, and Nyāya traditions. This e-text contains the complete kārikās across all three books together with their principal classical Sanskrit commentaries.

summary: The Saptalakṣaṇa is a set of seven mnemonic treatises for the Taittirīya Saṃhitā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. They list the words that need special treatment when the padapāṭha is converted into saṃhitā, and the reverse. The parts cover the elision of visarjanīya after ā (śamāna), words that resist the usual sandhi (vilaṅghya), words followed by n- or t- (napara, tapara), groups of words with a- and ā- (avarṇi, āvarṇi), and words that are not divided by avagraha in the padapāṭha (aniṅgya). summary: The Yājñavalkyaśikṣā is an authoritative Vedāṅga phonetic treatise affiliated with the Śukla Yajurveda (Vājasaneyi) tradition. Traditionally attributed to Yājñavalkya, it systematizes Vedic accentuation (traisvarya: udātta, anudātta, and svarita), duration (mātrā), recitation faults (pāṭhadoṣa), manual mudrās accompanying recitation, and specific euphonic sandhi rules.

summary: The Āgniveśyagṛhyasūtra is a domestic ritual manual belonging to the Agniveśya school of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, closely affiliated with the Vādhūla ritual tradition. Structured across three praśnas, it details the domestic sacraments (saṃskāras) such as upanayana and vivāha, domestic offerings, śrāddha and antyeṣṭi (funerary) ceremonies, and extensive prāyaścitta (expiatory) rituals.

summary: The Āpastambaśrautasūtra constitutes the Śrauta manual (Praśnas 1–24) of the larger Āpastamba Kalpasūtra belonging to the Taittirīya recension of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. summary: The Āpiśalaśikṣā is an ancient Sanskrit phonetic treatise (śikṣā) traditionally attributed to the pre-Pāṇinian grammarian Āpiśali. Composed predominantly in brief prose sūtras framed by introductory and concluding anuṣṭubh verses, it provides a rigorous physiological analysis of Sanskrit sound production across sthāna (articulatory place), karaṇa (active articulator), antaḥprayatna (internal effort), bāhyaprayatna (external effort), articulatory pressure (sthānapīḍa), and phonation/accentuation processes (prakrama). It is regarded as one of the earliest and most systematically organized phonetic manuals in the Vedāṅga tradition.

It is not a recension of the calendrical Vedāṅgajyotiṣa of the Ṛg- and Yajurveda. It deals with electional astrology: which activities suit each of the fifteen muhūrtas, the eleven karaṇas, the tithis and their five classes, the seven weekdays, and the nine groups of nakṣatras counted from one's birth star.

summary: The Śabdakaustubha is an extensive commentary on Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī composed in the 17th century by Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita. In contrast to his thematic Siddhāntakaumudī, this treatise comments on the sūtras in their sequential order, providing deep grammatical, hermeneutical, and philosophical analyses drawing heavily on Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa's Pradīpa. The author left the commentary unfinished, terminating at the conclusion of the first pāda of adhyāya 3 (sūtra 3.1.150).

summary: The Śaiśirīyaśikṣā is a phonetic manual (śikṣā) belonging to the Ṛgvedic tradition, associated with the Śaiśira branch of the Śākala recension. Written in anuṣṭubh verse with illustrative examples (nidarśanas), it describes the inventory of 63 or 64 speech sounds, the articulatory organs (sthāna and karaṇa), mora timing (mātrā), accents (udātta, anudātta, svarita, pracaya), and phonetic sandhi modifications occurring during Ṛgvedic chant recitation.

summary: The Śamānaśikṣā is a short Vedāṅga phonetic manual intended for reciters of the Ṛgveda (Bahvṛcas). summary: The Śaunakaśikṣā is a Vedāṅga phonetic treatise (śikṣā) in 67 verses associated with the tradition of Śaunaka, focusing on orthoepic rules for the recitation of the Ṛgveda. summary: The Śaunakīyā Caturādhyāyikā (commonly called the Atharvavedaprātiśākhya) is the prātiśākhya belonging to the Śaunakīya recension of the Atharvaveda. In four chapters (adhyāyas), it presents the phonological and grammatical rules governing the relationship between the Atharvavedic Padapāṭha and Saṃhitāpāṭha, treating sound inventory, accentuation (svara), sandhi modifications, and krama-recitation. It is a foundational early text of ancient Indian phonetics, first edited and analyzed in the West by William Dwight Whitney in 1862.

summary: The Śābdikābharaṇa (also designated in colophons as Dhātupratyayapañcikā) is a Pāṇinian grammatical work on verbal morphology composed by Hariyogin (Prollanācārya). The treatise begins with an epistemological and philosophical preface (bhūmikā) evaluating the eternity (nityatva) versus non-eternity (anityatva) of phonemes (varṇa) and recognitive cognition (pratyabhijñā), before providing a systematic grammatical commentary on the roots of the ten verbal classes (daśagaṇa), the kaṇḍvādayaḥ, and sautradhātus according to Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī.

summary: The Ṣaṭkāraka with its commentary Saṃbandhodyota is a concise Buddhist Sanskrit grammatical treatise on kāraka syntax and case relations by Rabhasanandin. Opening with homage to the Buddha, the treatise analyzes the six kārakas, syntactic relations (saṃbandha), and case inflection through the framework of whether an argument is expressed (ukta) or unexpressed (anukta) by verbal, kṛt, or taddhita affixes. The commentary illustrates syntactic principles with distinctively Buddhist examples alongside standard grammatical patterns.

summary: The Ṣoḍaśaślokīśikṣā is a concise Vedāṅga phonetic treatise in sixteen verses attributed to Rāmakṛṣṇa. It describes the traditional 63-sound inventory, classification and accents of vowels (svara), consonants, pratyāhāras, and places of articulation (sthāna). It concludes with guidelines for proper articulation, citing the classic simile of a tigress carrying her cubs without biting or dropping them.

summary: The Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā is an important theological and ritual text of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, presented as a revelatory discourse taught by Ahirbudhnya (Śiva) to Nārada. This first volume (adhyāyas 1–36) details the cosmogony and metaphysics of the school, emphasizing the six divine attributes (ṣaḍguṇa), the emanations of Viṣṇu (vyūhas), and the cosmogenetic activity of his śakti embodied in the Sudarśana cakra. It also includes comprehensive treatises on mantravidyā, yoga, royal apotropaic rituals, and military/weapon sorcery (astramantra).

summary: The Akulavīratantra is an early Kaula / Yoginī Kaula scripture transmitted in the corpus attributed to Matsyendranātha. It teaches an uncompromising non-dual realization of ultimate reality as the Akulavīra ('Hero of the Transcendent'), attained as innate bliss (sahajānanda) beyond all conventional dharmas. The work critiques scholastic schools (Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist, Jaina, Mīmāṃsā, Somasiddhānta) and formal ritualism, emphasizing that spiritual freedom arises solely from dwelling in the unconditioned, all-pervading divine essence.

summary: The Aṃśumatkāśyapāgama (closely related to and often cited as the Kāśyapaśilpa or Kāśyapaśilpaśāstra) is an authoritative Śaiva Siddhānta Āgamic treatise centered on temple architecture (vāstu), sacred iconography (mūrtilakṣaṇa / citra), and ritual consecration. Framed as an exposition delivered by Śiva to the sage Kāśyapa summarizing the ancient Aṃśumān tantra, it details temple layout, ground examination, foundation deposits, and structural elements of vimānas, maṇḍapas, and prākāras, followed by extensive rules on iconometric proportions (tālamāna) and iconographic forms of Śiva, Devī, and associated divinities.

summary: The Jayākhyasaṃhitā is one of the oldest and most authoritative canonical scriptures of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, celebrated as one of the three foundational 'jewels' (ratnatraya) alongside the Sātvatasaṃhitā and Pauṣkarasaṃhitā. Spanning 33 paṭalas and roughly 4,500 anuṣṭubh verses, it expounds Vaiṣṇava theology, cosmology, the doctrine of divine emanations (vyūha), mantra systems, initiation (dīkṣā), daily and temple rituals, and yoga aimed at liberation (mukti). The text was widely cited by medieval Indian philosophers and theologians, including Utpaladeva, Abhinavagupta, and Rāmānuja.

summary: The Kriyādhikāra is an authoritative canonical text of the Vaikhānasa Vaiṣṇava tradition, attributed to the sage Bhṛgu and forming part of the Bhṛgusaṃhitā. It provides comprehensive technical instructions on temple architecture, image manufacture and consecration (pratiṣṭhā), daily and festival rituals, and prāyaścitta expiations. Throughout the text, Vaikhānasa temple ritual is framed as vaidikārcā adhering to the Vaikhānasasūtra, distinguished from tāntrika forms such as Pāñcarātra.

summary: The Kriyākairavacandrikā is a Pāñcarātra ritual handbook (prayoga) composed by Varāhaguru. Arranged in 37 chapters (paricchedas), it provides practical guidelines for Vaiṣṇava temple rites, including site selection (bhūparīkṣā), plowing (karṣaṇa), layout, temple architecture, installation (pratiṣṭhā) of icons and ancillary shrines, daily worship (nityotsava), and annual purification rites such as pavitrāropaṇa.

summary: The Kriyākramadyotikā (frequently cited as Aghoraśivapaddhati) is the foremost ritual handbook of the South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta tradition, composed in 1157/1158 CE by Aghoraśivācārya. It codifies canonical Āgamic procedures for priestly daily and occasional liturgical rituals and remains the standard manual for hereditary śivācāryas. This e-text transmits the paddhati alongside Nirmalamaṇi's 16th-century commentary Prabhā (Asphuṭārthaprakāśikā) up through the Damanavidhi section, covering daily worship, dīkṣā, and annual pavitra- and damana-offering rites.

summary: The Lakṣmītantra is a major canonical Pāñcarātra scripture (saṃhitā), datable to c. 9th–12th century CE, notable for presenting the goddess Lakṣmī (Śrī) as the supreme creative and dynamic power (Śakti) of Nārāyaṇa. In 57 chapters, the text expounds Pāñcarātra cosmogony, the six divine gunas, the theory of vyūha emanations, mantraśāstra, ritual diagram construction (maṇḍala/yantra), and devotional surrender (nyāsa/prapatti). In this e-text, the root verses are accompanied throughout by the modern Sanskrit commentary (Tattvaprakāśanī) by Pandit V. Krishnamacharya.

summary: The Paramapuruṣasaṃhitā is a Vaiṣṇava Āgama text belonging to the Pāñcarātra corpus, presented as an exposition given by Nārada to sages on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī. summary: The Pārameśvarasaṃhitā is a Pāñcarātra saṃhitā traditionally regarded as derived from the Pauṣkarasaṃhitā (one of the 'three jewels') and closely associated with the liturgy of the Raṅganātha temple at Śrīraṅgam. Framed as Śāṇḍilya's teaching to the sage Sanaka on Mount Totādri, its 26 chapters treat theology, temple construction, image installation (pratiṣṭhā), daily worship, festivals (mahotsava), expiations (prāyaścitta, including tulābhāra and hiraṇyagarbha), and the worship of the Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha mahāyantra, whose description draws on the Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā.

summary: The Prayogamañjarī is an influential 10th/11th-century Śaiva ritual manual (paddhati) composed in Kerala by Ravi, son of Aṣṭamūrti. Rooted in the Śaiddhāntika tradition and central to the medieval temple ritual literature of Kerala, it served as a primary source for Īśānaśiva's Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati. This digital entry is an unfinished stub preserving only the opening four and a half verses of chapter 1.

Across 33 chapters, it treats temple architectural planning, iconography, consecration (pratiṣṭhā), daily and festival liturgies (utsava), expiation (prāyaścitta), initiation (dīkṣā), and ritual hand gestures (mudrā).

Spanning 25 paricchedas, it details the metaphysics of the cāturvyūha, meditative visualization of divine forms, mantra installation, initiation (dīkṣā), and temple consecration rituals. This e-text provides the complete root saṃhitā together with the extensive bhāṣya of the Melkote ritualist-scholar Alaśiṅgabhaṭṭa.

summary: The Viśvāmitrasaṃhitā is a canonical Pāñcarātra Āgama text structured as a dialogue between the sage Viśvāmitra and Kāśyapa. Across 27 chapters, it covers the core ritual and theological topics of the Pāñcarātra tradition, including initiation (dīkṣā), mantras, mudrās, daily worship (pañcakālapūjā), temple iconography, consecration rites (pratiṣṭhā), utsava ceremonies, and expiatory procedures (prāyaścitta).

summary: The Viṣṇusaṃhitā is a canonical scriptural work of the Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava tradition in 30 paṭalas. Structured as an exchange between the sage Aupamanyava and the Siddha Sumati on Mount Śrīśaila, it treats temple architecture, iconographic types (pratimālakṣaṇa), installation rites (pratiṣṭhā), daily and festival rituals, expiations (prāyaścitta), mudrās, and a distinctive six-limbed yoga system (ṣaḍaṅgayoga).

summary: The Yajñādhikāra is a canonical ritual manual (saṃhitā) belonging to the Vaikhānasa Vaiṣṇava Āgama corpus, traditionally attributed to the sage Bhṛgu. It expounds temple architecture, vāstumaṇḍala preparations, installation of icons (pratiṣṭhā), daily and seasonal oblations, and expiatory rites (niṣkṛti) to counteract procedural blemishes. Alongside the Kriyādhikāra, Khilādhikāra, and Prakīrṇādhikāra, it constitutes one of the four major Ādhikāra treatises of the Bhṛgu division.

summary: The Āgamaprāmāṇya is a foundational philosophical and polemical treatise by the 10th-century Śrīvaiṣṇava master Yāmunācārya. The text defends the scriptural authority (prāmāṇya) and orthodox Vedic status of the Pāñcarātra Āgamas against charges of heterodoxy, invalidity, or non-Vedic origin raised primarily by Mīmāṃsakas and Advaitins. Yāmunācārya argues for the intrinsic validity and divine authorship of the Āgamas by Nārāyaṇa and defends the orthodox caste status and temple-worship rituals of the Bhāgavatas, laying the foundation for Rāmānuja's Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta.
